Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

The Minor Collection

Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Nettippakaraṇa

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Mahākāruṇikaṃ [V 0.0133][M 0.0001] nāthaṃ, ñeyyasāgarapāraguṃ;

Vande nipuṇagambhīra-vicitranayadesanaṃ.

I pay homage to the Lord, the Great Compassionate One, who has reached the far shore of the ocean of knowable things, whose teaching has subtle, profound, and wonderful methods.

Vijjācaraṇasampannā, yena niyyanti lokato;

Vande tamuttamaṃ dhammaṃ, sammāsambuddhapūjitaṃ.

By which Dhamma, being endowed with knowledge and conduct, they escape from the world; I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Sīlādiguṇasampanno, ṭhito maggaphalesu yo;

Vande ariyasaṅghaṃ taṃ, puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ.

Endowed with virtues beginning with morality, standing firm in the paths and fruits, I venerate that noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.

Vandanājanitaṃ puññaṃ, iti yaṃ ratanattaye;

Hatantarāyo sabbattha, hutvāhaṃ tassa tejasā.

By the power of that merit thus generated by paying homage to the Three Jewels, I, having become one whose obstacles are destroyed everywhere,

Ṭhitiṃ [V 0.0134] ākaṅkhamānena, ciraṃ saddhammanettiyā;

Dhammarakkhitanāmena, therena abhiyācito.

Having been respectfully requested by the elder named Dhammarakkhita, who desires the long stability of the Netti of the good Dhamma,

Padumuttaranāthassa, pādamūle pavattitaṃ;

Passatā abhinīhāraṃ, sampattaṃ yassa matthakaṃ.

Whose aspiration, made at the feet of the Lord Padumuttara and having reached its culmination, was seen [by our Buddha],

Saṃkhittaṃ vibhajantānaṃ, eso aggoti tādinā;

Ṭhapito etadaggasmiṃ, yo mahāsāvakuttamo.

Who, as the supreme great disciple, was placed in the position of pre-eminence by the Such-a-one (the Buddha) with the words, 'Among those who analyze the concise, this one is the chief.'

Chaḷabhiñño vasippatto, pabhinnapaṭisambhido;

Mahākaccāyano thero, sambuddhena pasaṃsito.

Endowed with the six higher knowledges, attained to mastery, possessed of analytical knowledge that has broken through, the elder Mahākaccāyana, praised by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Tena [M 0.0002] yā bhāsitā netti, satthārā anumoditā;

Sāsanassa sadāyattā, navaṅgassatthavaṇṇanā.

By him was spoken the Netti, approved by the Teacher, ever connected to the nine-fold Dispensation, an explanation of its meaning.

Tassā gambhīrañāṇehi, ogāhetabbabhāvato;

Kiñcāpi dukkarā kātuṃ, atthasaṃvaṇṇanā mayā.

Although, because of its nature of having to be penetrated by profound knowledges, an explanation of the meaning of that Netti is difficult for me to compose,

Saha saṃvaṇṇanaṃ yasmā, dharate satthusāsanaṃ;

Pubbācariyasīhānaṃ, tiṭṭhateva vinicchayo.

Since the Teacher’s Dispensation endures together with its commentary, the decision of the former teacher-lions indeed stands firm.

Tasmā tamupanissāya, ogāhetvāna pañcapi;

Nikāye peṭakenāpi, saṃsanditvā yathābalaṃ.

Therefore, relying on that, having plunged into the five Nikāyas and also having compared them with the Peṭaka,

Suvisuddhamasaṃkiṇṇaṃ, nipuṇatthavinicchayaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, samayaṃ avilomayaṃ.

Not contradicting the tradition of the dwellers in the Great Monastery, which is very pure, unmixed, and has subtle decisions on the meaning,

Pamādalekhaṃ vajjetvā, pāḷiṃ sammā niyojayaṃ;

Upadesaṃ vibhāvento, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Having avoided scribal errors due to negligence, correctly applying the Pāḷi, and explaining the method, I shall compose the explanation of the meaning according to my ability.

Iti [V 0.0135] atthaṃ asaṅkiṇṇaṃ, nettippakaraṇassa me;

Vibhajantassa sakkaccaṃ, nisāmayatha sādhavoti.

Therefore, O good people, listen respectfully to me as I analyze the unmixed meaning of the Nettippakaraṇa.

Tattha kenaṭṭhena netti? Saddhammanayanaṭṭhena netti. Yathā hi taṇhā satte kāmādibhavaṃ nayatīti “bhavanettī”ti vuccati, evamayampi veneyyasatte ariyadhammaṃ nayatīti saddhammanayanaṭṭhena “nettī”ti vuccati. Atha vā nayanti tāyāti netti. Nettippakaraṇena hi karaṇabhūtena dhammakathikā veneyyasatte dassanamaggaṃ nayanti sampāpentīti, nīyanti vā ettha etasmiṃ pakaraṇe adhiṭṭhānabhūte patiṭṭhāpetvā veneyyā nibbānaṃ sampāpiyantīti netti. Na hi nettiupadesasannissayena vinā aviparītasuttatthāvabodho sambhavati. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “tasmā nibbāyitukāmenā”tiādi. Sabbāpi hi suttassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanā nettiupadesāyattā, netti ca suttappabhavā, suttaṃ sammāsambuddhappabhavanti.

In this context, for what reason is it called 'Netti'? It is 'Netti' in the sense of leading to the good Dhamma. For just as craving leads beings to states of existence such as the sensual realm and is thus called 'bhavanettī' (the guide to existence), so too this treatise leads trainable beings to the noble Dhamma, and is thus called 'Netti' in the sense of leading to the good Dhamma. Or alternatively, 'they lead by means of it,' thus it is 'Netti.' For by means of the Nettippakaraṇa, which is an instrument, Dhamma-preachers lead trainable beings to the path of vision, causing them to attain it. Or, trainable beings are led, brought to Nibbāna, having been established in this treatise which is a foundation; thus, it is 'Netti.' Indeed, without reliance on the method of the Netti, a non-perverse understanding of the meaning of the suttas is not possible. For thus it is said: 'Therefore, by one who wishes to be extinguished...' and so on. For every explanation of the meaning of a sutta is dependent on the method of the Netti; the Netti has the suttas as its source, and the suttas have the Perfectly Enlightened One as their source.

Sā panāyaṃ netti pakaraṇaparicchedato tippabhedā hāranayapaṭṭhānānaṃ vasena. Paṭhamañhi hāravicāro, tato nayavicāro, pacchā paṭṭhānavicāroti. Pāḷivavatthānato pana saṅgahavāravibhāgavāravasena duvidhā. Sabbāpi hi netti saṅgahavāro vibhāgavāroti vāradvayameva hoti.

This Netti, however, is threefold according to the divisions of the treatise, by way of the Hāras, Nayas, and Paṭṭhānas. For first comes the examination of the Hāras, then the examination of the Nayas, and afterward the examination of the Paṭṭhānas. But from the standpoint of the Pāḷi arrangement, it is twofold, by way of the Comprehensive Section (Saṅgahavāra) and the Analytical Section (Vibhāgavāra). For the entire Netti consists solely of these two sections: the Comprehensive Section and the Analytical Section.

Tattha [M 0.0003] saṅgahavāro ādito pañcahi gāthāhi paricchinno. Sabbo hi pakaraṇattho “yaṃ loko pūjayate”tiādīhi pañcahi gāthāhi apariggahito nāma natthi. Nanu cettha paṭṭhānaṃ asaṅgahitanti? Nayidamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, mūlapadaggahaṇena paṭṭhānassa saṅgahitattā. Tathā hi vakkhati – “aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā kuhiṃ daṭṭhabbā sāsanapaṭṭhāne”ti. Mūlapadapaṭṭhānāni hi atthanayasaṅkhārattikā viya aññamaññaṃ saṅgahitāni.

Here, the Comprehensive Section (Saṅgahavāra) is initially defined by five verses. Indeed, there is no entire meaning of the treatise that is unencompassed by these five verses beginning with “That which the world reveres.” Now, might one say that the Paṭṭhāna is not included here? This should not be seen as such, for the Paṭṭhāna is included by the taking up of the root terms. For thus it will be said: “Where are the eighteen root terms to be seen? In the establishment of the teaching (sāsanapaṭṭhāna).” Indeed, the root terms and the establishments, like the threefold sets of meaning-method, and formations, are mutually included.

Vibhāgavāro pana uddesaniddesapaṭiniddesavasena tividho. Tesu “tattha katame soḷasa hārā”ti ārabhitvā yāva “bhavanti aṭṭhārasa padānī”ti ayaṃ uddesavāro. “Assādādīnavatā”ti ārabhitvā yāva “tettiṃsā ettikā nettī”ti ayaṃ niddesavāro. Paṭiniddesavāro pana hāravibhaṅgavāro hārasampātavāro nayasamuṭṭhānavāro sāsanapaṭṭhānavāroti catubbidho. Tesu “tattha katamo desanāhāro”ti ārabhitvā yāva “ayaṃ pahānena samāropanā”ti ayaṃ hāravibhaṅgavāro. Tattha “katamo desanāhārasampāto”ti ārabhitvā yāva “anupādisesā ca nibbānadhātū”ti ayaṃ hārasampātavāro. Etthāha – hāravibhaṅgahārasampātavārānaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Vuccate – yattha anekehipi udāharaṇasuttehi eko [V 0.0136] hāro niddisīyati, ayaṃ hāravibhaṅgavāro. Yattha pana ekasmiṃ sutte aneke hārā sampatanti, ayaṃ hārasampātavāro. Vuttañhetaṃ peṭake –

The Analytical Section (Vibhāgavāra), however, is threefold: by way of Summary (Uddesa), Exposition (Niddesa), and Detailed Explanation (Paṭiniddesa). Among these, starting from “Here, what are the sixteen hāras?” up to “there are eighteen terms,” this is the Summary Section (Uddesavāra). Starting from “With gratification and danger” up to “thirty-three are such nettis,” this is the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra). The Detailed Explanation Section (Paṭiniddesavāra), however, is fourfold: the Analysis of Hāras (Hāravibhaṅgavāra), the Combination of Hāras (Hārasampātavāra), the Arising of Nayas (Nayasamuṭṭhānavāra), and the Establishment of the Teaching (Sāsanapaṭṭhānavāra). Among these, starting from “Here, what is the hāra of instruction?” up to “this is inclusion by abandonment,” this is the Analysis of Hāras Section (Hāravibhaṅgavāra). Here, starting from “What is the combination of the hāra of instruction?” up to “and the Nibbāna-element without remainder,” this is the Combination of Hāras Section (Hārasampātavāra). Here one asks: What is the differentiation between the Analysis of Hāras Section and the Combination of Hāras Section? It is said: Where a single hāra is explained through many illustrative discourses, this is the Analysis of Hāras Section. But where many hāras converge in a single discourse, this is the Combination of Hāras Section. For this was stated in the Peṭaka:

“Yattha ca sabbe hārā, sampatamānā nayanti suttatthaṃ;

Byañjanavidhiputhuttā, sā bhūmī hārasampāto”ti.

And where all the hāras, converging, lead to the meaning of the sutta, because of the multiplicity in the method of phrasing, that ground is the Hārasampāta (combination of hāras).

Nayasamuṭṭhānasāsanapaṭṭhānavāravibhāgo pākaṭo eva. Sāsanapaṭṭhānavāro pana saṅgahavāre viya uddesaniddesavāresupi na sarūpato uddhaṭoti. Etthāha – “idaṃ nettippakaraṇaṃ mahāsāvakabhāsitaṃ, bhagavatā anumodita”nti ca kathametaṃ viññāyatīti? Pāḷito eva. Na hi pāḷito aññaṃ pamāṇataraṃ atthi. Yā hi catūhi mahāpadesehi aviruddhā pāḷi, sā pamāṇaṃ. Tathā hi agarahitāya ācariyaparamparāya peṭakopadeso viya idaṃ nettippakaraṇaṃ ābhataṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmāssa nidānaṃ na vuttaṃ. Sāvakabhāsitānampi hi subhasutta- (dī. ni. 1.444 ādayo) anaṅgaṇasutta- (ma. ni. 1.57 ādayo) kaccāyanasaṃyuttādīnaṃ [M 0.0004] nidānaṃ bhāsitanti? Nayidaṃ ekantikaṃ. Sāvakabhāsitānaṃ buddhabhāsitānampi hi ekaccānaṃ paṭisambhidāmagganiddesādīnaṃ dhammapadabuddhavaṃsādīnañca nidānaṃ na bhāsitaṃ, na ca tāvatā tāni appamāṇaṃ, evamidhāpi daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The division of the section on the arising of methods and the section on the foundations of the teaching is indeed evident. But the section on the foundations of the teaching, like in the Comprehensive Section, is not extracted in its own form in the Summary and Exposition Sections either. Here, a questioner asks: “This Nettipakaraṇa was spoken by a great disciple and was approved by the Blessed One—how is this to be known?” From the Pāḷi itself. For indeed, there is no authority more excellent than the Pāḷi. For whichever Pāḷi is not in conflict with the four Great References, that Pāḷi is the authority. For so it is that, like the Peṭakopadesa, this Nettipakaraṇa has been handed down by an irreproachable lineage of teachers. If this is so, why was its introduction not stated? For indeed, the introduction is stated for discourses spoken by disciples, such as the Subhasutta, the Anaṅgaṇasutta, the Kaccāyanasaṃyutta, and so on. This is not an invariable rule. For of some discourses spoken by disciples, such as the Paṭisambhidāmagga, Niddesa, etc., and of some spoken by the Buddha, such as the Dhammapada, Buddhavaṃsa, etc., the introduction was not stated. Yet merely by that, they are not without authority. Thus it should be seen here also.

Nidānañca nāma suttavinayānaṃ dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaupālittherādīhi mahāsāvakeheva bhāsitaṃ, idañca mahāsāvakabhāsitaṃ, theraṃ muñcitvā anaññavisayattā imissā vicāraṇāyāti kimetena nidānagavesanena, atthoyevettha gavesitabbo, yo pāḷiyā aviruddhoti. Atha vā pāḷiyā atthasaṃvaṇṇanābhāvato na imassa pakaraṇassa visuṃ nidānavacanakiccaṃ atthi, paṭisambhidāmagganiddesādīnaṃ viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And the introduction, so-called, of the Suttas and Vinaya was spoken only by the great disciples, such as the treasurer of the Dhamma, the Elder Upāli, and others. This treatise, too, was spoken by a great disciple, for, except for the Elder, this composition is not the domain of another. Therefore, what is the use of this search for an introduction? Here, only that meaning should be sought which is not in conflict with the Pāḷi. Alternatively, because it is a commentary on the meaning of the Pāḷi, this treatise has no separate task of stating an introduction, just as in the case of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, Niddesa, and so on. Thus it should be understood.

Idāni etasmiṃ pakaraṇe nānappakārakosallatthaṃ ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo – sabbameva cetaṃ pakaraṇaṃ sāsanapariyeṭṭhibhāvato ekavidhaṃ, tathā ariyamaggasampādanato vimuttirasato ca. Byañjanatthavicārabhāvato duvidhaṃ, tathā saṅgahavibhāgabhāvato dhammavinayatthasaṃvaṇṇanato lokiyalokuttaratthasaṅgahaṇato rūpārūpadhammapariggāhakato lakkhaṇalakkhiyabhāvato pavattinivattivacanato sabhāgavisabhāganiddesato sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇadhammavibhāgato ca.

Now, in this treatise, for the purpose of skill in various ways, this division should be understood. And this entire treatise is of one kind because it is an investigation of the teaching's meaning; likewise, it is of one kind because it accomplishes the noble path and because it has the taste of liberation. It is of two kinds because it is an examination of the letter and the meaning; likewise, because it consists of the Comprehensive Section and the Division Section; because it explains the meaning of the Dhamma and Vinaya; because it comprehends worldly and supramundane meanings; because it grasps material and immaterial phenomena; because it consists of the characteristic and the characterized; because it speaks of occurrence and cessation; because it points out similar and dissimilar phenomena; and because it divides common and uncommon phenomena.

Tividhaṃ puggalattayaniddesato tividhakalyāṇavibhāgato pariññattayakathanato pahānattayūpadesato [V 0.0137] sikkhattayasaṅgahaṇato tividhasaṃkilesavisodhanato mūlagītianugītisaṅgītibhedato piṭakattayatthasaṃvaṇṇanato hāranayapaṭṭhānappabhedato ca.

It is of three kinds: because it points out the triad of individuals; because it divides the threefold good; because it speaks of the triad of full understanding; because it instructs on the triad of abandoning; because it comprehends the triad of trainings; because it purifies the threefold defilements; because of the distinction of Mūlagīti, Anugīti, and Saṅgīti; because it is a commentary on the meaning of the three Piṭakas; and because of the distinction of the Hāras, Nayas, and Paṭṭhānas.

Catubbidhaṃ catuppaṭisambhidāvisayato catunayadesanato dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīrabhāvato ca. Pañcavidhaṃ abhiññeyyādidhammavibhāgato pañcakkhandhaniddesato pañcagatiparicchedato pañcanikāyatthavivaraṇato ca. Chabbidhaṃ chaḷārammaṇavibhāgato chaajjhattikabāhirāyatanavibhāgato ca. Sattavidhaṃ sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitiparicchedato. Navavidhaṃ suttādinavaṅganiddesato. Cuddasavidhaṃ suttādhiṭṭhānavibhāgato. Soḷasavidhaṃ aṭṭhavīsatividhañca sāsanapaṭṭhānappabhedato. Caturāsītisahassavidhaṃ caturāsītisahassadhammakkhandhavicārabhāvatotiādinā nayena pakaraṇavibhāgo veditabbo.

It is of four kinds: because it is the domain of the four analytical knowledges; because it teaches the four methods; and because of the profundity of the Dhamma, of meaning, of teaching, and of penetration. It is of five kinds: because it divides phenomena such as that which is to be directly known; because it points out the five aggregates; because it defines the five destinations; and because it opens up the meaning of the five Nikāyas. It is of six kinds: because it divides the six sense-objects; and because it divides the six internal and external sense bases. It is of seven kinds: because it defines the seven stations of consciousness. It is of nine kinds: because it points out the nine limbs of the teaching beginning with Sutta. It is of fourteen kinds: because it divides the foundations of the Suttas. It is of sixteen kinds and twenty-eight kinds: because of the divisions of the foundations of the teaching. It is of eighty-four thousand kinds: because it examines the eighty-four thousand units of the Dhamma. By this method and so on, the division of the treatise should be known.

Tattha sāsanapariyeṭṭhibhāvatoti sakalaṃ nettippakaraṇaṃ sikkhattayasaṅgahassa navaṅgassa satthusāsanassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanābhāvato. Ariyamaggasampādanatoti [M 0.0005] dassanabhūmibhāvanābhūmisampādanato. Vimuttirasatoti sāsanassa amatapariyosānattā vuttaṃ. Byañjanatthavicārabhāvatoti hārabyañjanapadakammanayānaṃ byañjanavicārattā atthapadaatthanayānaṃ atthavicārattā vuttaṃ. Saṅgahavibhāgabhāvo parato āvi bhavissati. Dhammavinayatthasaṃvaṇṇanatoti sakalassāpi pariyattisāsanassa dhammavinayabhāvato vuttaṃ. Lakkhaṇalakkhiyabhāvatoti nettivacanassa lakkhaṇattā udāharaṇasuttānañca lakkhiyattā vuttaṃ. Sabhāgavisabhāganiddesatoti samānajātiyā dhammā sabhāgā, paṭipakkhā visabhāgā, taṃvicārabhāvatoti attho. Sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇadhammavibhāgatoti pahānekaṭṭhasahajekaṭṭhatādisāmaññena ye dhammā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ nāmavatthādinā sādhāraṇā tabbidhuratāya asādhāraṇā ca, taṃvibhāgato duvidhanti attho.

Therein, as to 'because it is an investigation of the teaching's meaning': this is because the entire Nettipakaraṇa is an explanation of the meaning of the Teacher's nine-limbed teaching, which is comprised of the three trainings. As to 'because it accomplishes the noble path': this is because it accomplishes the plane of vision and the plane of development. As to 'because it has the taste of liberation': this is stated because the teaching has the Deathless as its culmination. As to 'because it is an examination of the letter and the meaning': this is stated because of the examination of the letter in the Hāras, Byañjanapadas, and Kammanayas, and the examination of the meaning in the Atthapadas and Atthanayas. The nature of the Comprehensive and Division sections will become clear later. As to 'because it explains the meaning of the Dhamma and Vinaya': this is stated because the entire scriptural teaching consists of Dhamma and Vinaya. As to 'because it consists of the characteristic and the characterized': this is stated because the statements of the Netti are the characteristic and the example suttas are the characterized. As to 'because it points out similar and dissimilar phenomena': phenomena of a similar nature are 'similar'; opposing phenomena are 'dissimilar'. 'Because it examines them'—this is the meaning. As to 'because it divides common and uncommon phenomena': those phenomena that are common to other phenomena by way of name, basis, etc., due to a commonality such as being abandoned by the same thing or co-arising in the same thing, and those that are uncommon due to the absence of that commonality; 'of two kinds because it divides them'—this is the meaning.

Puggalattayaniddesatoti ugghaṭitaññuādi puggalattayaniddesato. Tividhakalyāṇavibhāgatoti ādikalyāṇādivibhāgato. Mūlagītianugītisaṅgītibhedatoti paṭhamaṃ vacanaṃ mūlagīti, vuttasseva atthassa saṅgahagāthā anugīti, taṃtaṃsuttatthayojanavasena vippakiṇṇassa pakaraṇassa saṅgāyanaṃ saṅgīti, sā therassa parato pavattitāti veditabbā, etāsaṃ tissannaṃ bhedato tividhanti attho. Pañcakkhandhaniddesatoti rūpādipañcakkhandhasīlādipañcadhammakkhandhaniddesato pañcavidhanti attho. Suttādhiṭṭhānavibhāgatoti lobhadosamohānaṃ alobhādosāmohānaṃ kāyavacīmanokammānaṃ saddhādipañcindriyānañca vasena cuddasavidhassa suttādhiṭṭhānassa vibhāgavacanato cuddasavidhanti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyanti na papañcitaṃ.

‘By the exposition of the triad of individuals’ means by the exposition of the triad of individuals such as the ugghaṭitaññu. ‘By the division of the threefold good’ means by the division of the good in the beginning and so forth. ‘By the distinction of the root-recitation, subsequent-recitation, and collective-recitation’: the first utterance is the root-recitation; the summary verse of the meaning already stated is the subsequent-recitation; the collective recitation of the scattered treatise by means of connecting the meaning of the various suttas is the collective-recitation. It should be known that this collective-recitation was set forth after the Elder. By the distinction of these three, it is threefold—this is the meaning. ‘By the exposition of the five aggregates’ means by the exposition of the five aggregates such as form and the five groups of Dhamma-factors such as virtue, it is fivefold—this is the meaning. ‘By the division of the foundations of the discourses’ means by the statement classifying the fourteenfold foundations of the discourses by way of greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, bodily, verbal, and mental actions, and the five faculties such as faith, it is fourteenfold—this is the meaning. The remainder is easily understood, thus it is not elaborated upon.

1. Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Chapter on Inclusion

Evaṃ [V 0.0138] anekabhedavibhatte nettippakaraṇe yadidaṃ vuttaṃ “saṅgahavibhāgavāravasena duvidha”nti, tattha saṅgahavāro ādi. Tassāpi “yaṃ loko pūjayate”ti ayaṃ gāthā ādi. Tattha yanti aniyamato upayoganiddeso, tassa “tassā”ti iminā niyamanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Lokoti kattuniddeso. Pūjayateti kiriyāniddeso. Salokapāloti kattuvisesanaṃ. Sadāti kālaniddeso. Namassati cāti upacayena kiriyāniddeso[M 0.0006]. Tassāti sāminiddeso. Etanti paccattaniddeso. Sāsanavaranti paccattaniddesena niddiṭṭhadhammanidassanaṃ. Vidūhīti karaṇavacanena kattuniddeso. Ñeyyanti kammavācakakiriyāniddeso. Naravarassāti “tassā”ti niyametvā dassitassa sarūpato dassanaṃ.

In the Nettipakaraṇa, thus divided into many sections, it was said: ‘It is twofold by way of the chapter on inclusion and the chapter on division.’ Therein, the chapter on inclusion is the beginning. Of that too, this verse, ‘That which the world reveres,’ is the beginning. Therein, 'yaṃ' is an indicator of the objective case in an unrestricted sense; its restriction should be known by this word 'tassā'. 'Loko' is an indicator of the agent. 'Pūjayate' is an indicator of the action. 'Salokapālo' is a qualifier of the agent. 'Sadā' is an indicator of time. 'Namassati ca' is an indicator of the action with augmentation. 'Tassā' is an indicator of the possessor. 'Etaṃ' is an indicator of the subject. 'Sāsanavaraṃ' is a showing of the Dhamma indicated by the indicator of the subject. 'Vidūhi' is an indicator of the agent by means of the instrumental word. 'Ñeyyaṃ' is an indicator of the action in the passive voice. 'Naravarassa' is a showing, in its own form, of that which was shown by being restricted with 'tassā'.

Tattha lokiyanti ettha puññāpuññāni tabbipāko cāti loko, pajā, sattanikāyoti attho. Loka-saddo hi jātisaddatāya sāmaññavasena niravasesato satte saṅgaṇhāti. Kiñcāpi hi lokasaddo saṅkhārabhājanesupi diṭṭhappayogo, pūjanakiriyāyogyabhūtatāvasena pana sattalokavacano eva idha gahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pūjayateti mānayati, apacāyatīti attho.

Therein, because merit and demerit and their result exist (lokiyanti) herein, it is 'loka'. The meaning is progeny, the host of beings. For the word 'loka', being a generic term, generally encompasses all beings without remainder. And although the word 'loka' is seen to be used for the world of formations and the container world, nevertheless, here it should be understood that it is taken only as a word for the world of beings, by virtue of their being suitable for the act of veneration. 'Pūjayate' means 'reveres', 'honors'—this is the meaning.

Lokaṃ pālentīti lokapālā, cattāro mahārājāno. Lokiyā pana indayamavaruṇakuverā lokapālāti vadanti. Saha lokapālehīti salokapālo, “loko”ti iminā tulyādhikaraṇaṃ. Atha vā issariyādhipaccena taṃtaṃsattalokassa pālanato rakkhaṇato khattiyacatumahārājasakkasuyāmasantusitasunimmitaparanimmitavasavattimahābrahmādayo lokapālā. Tehi saha taṃtaṃsattanikāyo salokapālo lokoti vutto. Atha vā “dveme, bhikkhave, sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālentī”ti (a. ni. 2.9; itivu. 42) vacanato hirottappadhammā lokapālā. Tehi samannāgato loko salokapālo. Hirottappasampannā hi pāpagarahino sappurisā dhammacchandavantatāya bhagavati pūjānamakkāraparā hontīti.

They protect the world (lokaṃ pālenti), thus they are world-protectors (lokapālā): the four great kings. Worldly people, however, say that Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kuvera are the world-protectors. 'With the world-protectors' (saha lokapālehi), thus 'with its world-protectors' (salokapālo); it is in apposition with this word 'loko'. Alternatively, because they protect and guard the various worlds of beings through sovereignty and lordship, kings, the four great kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Paranimmitavasavattī, Mahābrahmā, and others are world-protectors. The various hosts of beings together with them are called 'the world with its world-protectors' (salokapālo loko). Alternatively, from the saying, ‘Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world,’ the qualities of moral shame and moral dread are the world-protectors. The world endowed with them is 'with its world-protectors' (salokapālo). For good people endowed with moral shame and moral dread, who censure evil, due to their desire for the Dhamma, are devoted to the veneration of and homage to the Blessed One.

Sadāti [V 0.0139] sabbakālaṃ rattiñceva divā ca, sadāti vā bhagavato dharamānakāle tato parañca. Atha vā sadāti abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva sāsanantaradhānā, tato parampi vā. Mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya hi mahābodhisattā bodhiyā niyatatāya buddhaṅkurabhūtā sadevakassa lokassa pūjanīyā ceva vandanīyā ca honti. Yathāha bhagavā sumedhabhūto –

‘Sadā’ means always, both night and day; or ‘sadā’ means during the time the Blessed One was present and thereafter. Alternatively, ‘sadā’ means from the time of the aspiration up until the disappearance of the Dispensation, and even after that. For from the time of the great aspiration, the great Bodhisattas, being destined for enlightenment and having become Buddha-sprouts, are worthy of veneration and homage by the world with its devas. As the Blessed One said when he was Sumedha:

“Dīpaṅkaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mama kammaṃ pakittetvā, dakkhiṇaṃ pādamuddhari.

“Dīpaṅkara, the world-knower, the worthy recipient of offerings, having praised my deed, raised his right foot.

“Ye [M 0.0007] tatthāsuṃ jinaputtā, padakkhiṇamakaṃsu maṃ;

Devā manussā asurā ca, abhivādetvāna pakkamu”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.75-76);

“Those sons of the Conqueror who were there, circumambulated me to the right; devas, humans, and asuras, having paid homage, departed.” (Bv 2.75–76)

Namassati cāti keci kesañci pūjāsakkārādīni karontāpi tesaṃ apākaṭaguṇatāya namakkāraṃ na karonti, na evaṃ bhagavato, yathābhūtaabbhuggatakittisaddatāya pana bhagavantaṃ sadevako loko pūjayati ceva namassati cāti attho. “Sadā naramanusso”ti keci paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Tassāti yaṃ sadevako loko pūjayati ceva namassati ca, tassa. Etanti idāni vattabbaṃ buddhiyaṃ viparivattamānaṃ sāmaññena dasseti. Sāsanavaranti taṃ sarūpato dasseti. Tattha diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ satte sāsati vineti etenāti sāsanaṃ, tadeva ekantaniyyānaṭṭhena anaññasādhāraṇaguṇatāya ca uttamaṭṭhena taṃtaṃabhipatthitasamiddhihetutāya paṇḍitehi varitabbato vā varaṃ, sāsanameva varanti sāsanavaraṃ. Vidūhīti yathāsabhāvato kammakammaphalāni kusalādibhede ca dhamme vidantīti vidū, paṇḍitamanussā, tehi. Ñātabbaṃ, ñāṇamarahatīti vā ñeyyaṃ. Naravarassāti purisavarassa, aggapuggalassāti attho.

Regarding 'namassati ca': some, while making offerings and giving honor to certain individuals, do not pay homage because their virtues are not manifest. It is not so with the Blessed One; rather, because his fame has arisen in accordance with truth, the world with its devas both venerates and pays homage to the Blessed One—this is the meaning. Some recite 'sadā naramanusso', but that is not good. 'Tassā' refers to him whom the world with its devas both venerates and pays homage. 'Etaṃ' generally shows that which is now to be said, which is presently occurring in the intellect. 'Sāsanavaraṃ' shows that in its own form. Therein, it instructs (sāsati) and disciplines (vineti) beings appropriately with this regarding the ultimate benefits of the present life and the future life, thus it is the Teaching (sāsana). That same Teaching is excellent (vara) because of its supreme nature, in that it leads exclusively to release and possesses unique qualities; or because it is to be chosen (varitabbato) by the wise as it is the cause for the accomplishment of various aspirations. The Teaching itself is excellent, thus it is the 'excellent Teaching' (sāsanavaraṃ). 'Vidūhi': they know (vidanti) action and the fruit of action, and dhammas with distinctions such as wholesome, etc., according to their true nature, thus they are the wise (vidū); it means 'by the wise'. 'Ñeyyaṃ' means it is to be known (ñātabbaṃ), or it is worthy of (arahati) knowledge (ñāṇaṃ). 'Naravarassa' means of the excellent person, of the foremost individual—this is the meaning.

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo anaññasādhāraṇamahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiguṇavisesayogena sadevakena lokena pūjanīyo namassanīyo ca bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, tassa loke uttamapuggalassa etaṃ idāni amhehi vibhajitabbahāranayapaṭṭhānavicāraṇavisayabhūtaṃ sāsanaṃ ādikalyāṇatādiguṇasampattiyā varaṃ aggaṃ uttamaṃ nipuṇañāṇagocaratāya paṇḍitavedanīyamevāti. Bhagavato hi vacanaṃ ekagāthāmattampi saccapaṭiccasamuppādakhandhāyatanadhātindriyasatipaṭṭhānādisabhāvadhammaniddhāraṇakkhamatāya [V 0.0140] soḷasahārapañcanayasoḷasaaṭṭhavīsatividhapaṭṭhānavicārayogyabhāvena ca paramagambhīraṃ atthato agādhapāraṃ saṇhasukhumañāṇavisayamevāti. Tenevāha – “paññavantassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo duppaññassā”ti (dī. ni. 3.358; a. ni. 8.30). Atha vā bhagavato sāsanaṃ pariññākkamena lakkhaṇāvabodhappaṭipattiyā suññatamukhādīhi ogāhitabbattā aviññūnaṃ supinantenapi na visayo hotīti āha – “vidūhi ñeyya”nti. Tathā ca vuttaṃ – “etu viññū puriso”tiādi.

This is the meaning: That Blessed One—the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is worthy of offerings and veneration by the world with its devas due to his possession of special qualities not shared with others, such as great compassion and the knowledge of omniscience—is the supreme person in the world. His Dispensation, which has now become the subject of our investigation of the hāras, nayas, and paṭṭhānas to be analyzed, is excellent, foremost, and supreme due to its possession of qualities such as being good in the beginning; and because it is the domain of subtle knowledge, it is to be known only by the wise. Indeed, the word of the Blessed One, even a single verse, is exceedingly profound, has a shore that cannot be fathomed in meaning, and is the domain only of subtle and refined knowledge, because of its capacity to determine the intrinsic nature of things such as the Truths, Dependent Origination, the aggregates, the sense bases, the elements, the faculties, and the foundations of mindfulness, and because of its suitability for investigation through the sixteen hāras, the five nayas, and the sixteen or twenty-eight kinds of paṭṭhānas. Therefore, he said: “This Dhamma is for one with wisdom; this Dhamma is not for one without wisdom.” Alternatively, because the Dispensation of the Blessed One must be penetrated by the practice of understanding the characteristics through the sequence of full understanding, by means of the entrances such as emptiness, it is not an object even in a dream for the unwise. Thus, he said: “To be known by the wise.” And so it is said: “Let a wise person come,” and so forth.

Apare [M 0.0008] pana “taṃ tassa sāsanavara”nti paṭhanti, tesaṃ matena yaṃ-saddo sāsana-saddena samānādhikaraṇoti daṭṭhabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti yaṃ sāsanavaraṃ salokapālo loko pūjayati namassati ca, taṃ sāsanavaraṃ vidūhi ñātabbanti. Imasmiñca naye lokapāla-saddena bhagavāpi vuccati. Bhagavā hi lokaggatāyakattā nippariyāyena lokapālo, tasmā “tassā”ti lokapālassa satthunoti attho. Salokapāloti cettha lokapāla-saddo guṇībhūtopi satthuvisayattā sāsana-saddāpekkhatāya sāmibhāvena sambandhīvisesabhūto padhānabhūto viya paṭiniddesaṃ arahatīti.

Other teachers, however, recite it as ‘taṃ tassa sāsanavaraṃ’. According to their view, the word ‘yaṃ’ should be understood as having the same locus as the word ‘sāsana’. This is the meaning: That excellent Dispensation, which the world with its world-guardian offers to and venerates, that excellent Dispensation should be known by the wise. And in this method, the Blessed One is also spoken of by the word ‘lokapāla’ (world-guardian). Indeed, the Blessed One, because of being the supreme leader of the world, is unequivocally the world-guardian. Therefore, ‘tassa’ means ‘of the Teacher, the world-guardian’. And here in the phrase ‘salokapālo’, although the word ‘lokapāla’ has become subordinate, because it refers to the Teacher, has dependence on the word ‘sāsana’, and is a specific relation by way of ownership, it is worthy of being referred back to as if it were primary.

Kathaṃ pana sayaṃ dhammassāmī bhagavā dhammaṃ pūjayatīti? Nāyaṃ virodho. Dhammagaruno hi buddhā bhagavanto, te sabbakālaṃ dhammaṃ apacāyamānāva viharantīti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ yvāyaṃ dhammo mayā abhisambuddho, tameva dhammaṃ sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.173; a. ni. 4.21).

But how then does the Blessed One, himself the master of the Dhamma, worship the Dhamma? This is not a contradiction. Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, hold the Dhamma in reverence; they dwell at all times paying homage to the Dhamma. And this has been said: “What if I were to dwell honoring, respecting, and depending on this very Dhamma that has been fully awakened to by me?”

Api ca bhagavato dhammapūjanā sattasattāhappaṭipattiādīhi dīpetabbā. Dhammassāmīti ca dhammena sadevakassa lokassa sāmīti attho, na dhammassa sāmīti. Evampi namassatīti vacanaṃ na yujjati. Na hi bhagavā kañci namassatīti, esopi niddoso. Na hi namassatīti padassa namakkāraṃ karotīti ayameva attho, atha kho garukaraṇena tanninno tappoṇo tappabbhāroti ayampi attho labbhati. Bhagavā ca dhammagarutāya sabbakālaṃ dhammaninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena viharatīti. Ayañca attho “yena sudaṃ svāhaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.387) evamādīhi suttapadehi dīpetabbo. “Vidūhi neyya”ntipi [V 0.0141] pāṭho, tassa paṇḍitehi saparasantānesu netabbaṃ pāpetabbanti attho. Tattha attasantāne pāpanaṃ bujjhanaṃ, parasantāne bodhananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the Blessed One's worship of the Dhamma should be shown by means of practices such as that during the seven weeks. And 'Dhammassāmī' (Master of the Dhamma) means master of the world with its devas through the Dhamma, not master of the Dhamma. Even so, the statement 'he venerates' is not suitable, for the Blessed One does not venerate anyone. This too is without fault. For the word 'namassati' (he venerates) does not only have the meaning 'he performs an act of veneration'; but rather, this meaning is also obtained: 'through respect, he is inclined towards it, slopes towards it, and tends towards it'. And the Blessed One, due to his reverence for the Dhamma, dwells at all times with an attitude of being inclined, sloping, and tending towards the Dhamma. This meaning should be shown by Sutta passages such as: “by which I indeed dwell perpetually…” There is also the reading ‘vidūhi neyyaṃ’ (to be led by the wise); its meaning is that it should be led and brought by the wise into their own and others' mental continuities. Therein, bringing it into one's own continuity is understanding, and into others' continuities is causing to understand, that is, teaching; this should be understood.

Evaṃ bhagavato sadevakassa lokassa pūjanīyavandanīyabhāvo aggapuggalabhāvo ca vuccamāno guṇavisiṭṭhataṃ dīpeti, sā ca guṇavisiṭṭhatā mahābodhiyā veditabbā. Āsavakkhayañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānañca āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ “mahābodhī”ti vuccati. Sā aviparītadhammadesanato tathāgate suppatiṭṭhitāti viññāyati[M 0.0009]. Na hi savāsananiravasesakilesappahānaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇañca vinā tādisī dhammadesanā sambhavati. Iccassa catuvesārajjayogo. Tena dasabalachaasādhāraṇañāṇaaṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhammādisakalasabbaññuguṇapāripūrī pakāsitā hoti. Etādisī ca guṇavibhūti mahākaruṇāpubbaṅgamaṃ abhinīhārasampattiṃ purassaraṃ katvā sampāditaṃ samattiṃsapāramisaṅkhātaṃ puññañāṇasambhāramantarena na upalabbhatīti hetusampadāpi atthato vibhāvitā hotīti evaṃ bhagavato tīsupi avatthāsu sabbasattānaṃ ekantahitappaṭilābhahetubhūtā ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā niravasesā buddhaguṇā imāya gāthāya pakāsitāti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, the Blessed One's state of being worthy of offerings and veneration by the world with its devas, and his state of being the foremost person, being spoken of, illuminates his distinction in virtue. And that distinction in virtue should be understood through the Great Enlightenment. Indeed, the knowledge of omniscience which has the knowledge of the destruction of the taints as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause, is called 'Great Enlightenment'. It is known to be well-established in the Tathāgata because of his teaching of the Dhamma without distortion. For such a teaching of the Dhamma is not possible without the complete abandonment of defilements together with their latent tendencies and without unobstructed knowledge. Thus, his possession of the four kinds of confidence. Through this, the complete fulfillment of all the qualities of an omniscient one—such as the ten powers, the six uncommon knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—is declared. And such a splendor of virtues is not obtained without the accumulation of merit and knowledge, known as the thirty perfections, which was accomplished by making the perfection of the aspiration, preceded by great compassion, the forerunner. Thus, the perfection of the cause is also explained in meaning. In this way, it should be understood that the Buddha-qualities of the Blessed One—which are the cause for the attainment of the sole welfare for all beings in all three states of existence, are good in the beginning, the middle, and the end, and are without remainder—are declared by this verse.

Dutiyanaye pana yasmā sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ saphalaṃ ariyamaggasāsanaṃ tassa ārammaṇabhūtañca amatadhātuṃ tadadhigamūpāyañca pubbabhāgapaṭipattisāsanaṃ tadatthaparidīpanañca pariyattisāsanaṃ yathārahaṃ saccābhisamayavasena abhisamento svākkhātatādiguṇavisesayuttataṃ manasikaronto sakkaccaṃ savanadhāraṇaparipucchādīhi paricayaṃ karonto ca sadevako loko pūjayati nāma. Lokanātho ca sammāsambodhippattiyā veneyyānaṃ sakkaccaṃ dhammadesanena “ariyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhiṃ desessāmi” (ma. ni. 3.136; saṃ. ni. 5.28; peṭako. 24), “maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko seṭṭho” (dha. pa. 273; kathā. 872; netti. 125; peṭako. 30), “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati” (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34), “khayaṃ virāgaṃ amataṃ paṇītaṃ” (khu. pā. 6.4; su. ni. 227), “ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā” (dī. ni. 2.373; ma. ni. 1.106; saṃ. ni. 5.367), “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇa”ntiādīhi (ma. ni. 3.420; netti. 5) vacanehi thomanena ca pūjayati nāma. Tasmā sāsanavarassa pūjanīyabhāvo idha vuccamāno anavasesato dhammaguṇe dīpetīti ye ariyabhāvādayo niyyānādayo khayavirāgādayo madanimmadanādayo asaṅkhatādayo svākkhātatādayo [V 0.0142] ādikalyāṇatādayo ca anekehi suttapadehi paveditā aneke dhammaguṇā, te niravasesato imāya gāthāya pakāsitāti veditabbā.

In the second method, however, because the world with its devas is said to honor the teaching of the noble path—which comprises the threefold training and is with its fruit—, the deathless element which is its object, the teaching of the preliminary-part practice which is the means for its attainment, and the teaching of the scriptures which explains its meaning, by appropriately realizing them through the realization of the truths, by attending to their state of being endowed with special qualities such as being well-proclaimed, and by respectfully becoming familiar with them through listening, bearing in mind, questioning, and so on. And the Lord of the World, by having attained perfect self-enlightenment, is said to honor the teaching by respectfully teaching the Dhamma to those who are to be trained and by praising it with words such as: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the noble right concentration,” “Of paths, the eightfold is best,” “Bhikkhus, whatsoever things there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the chief of them,” “The destruction, dispassion, the deathless, the sublime,” “Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings,” “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning,” and so on. Therefore, the worthiness of honor of the excellent teaching, being spoken of here, reveals the qualities of the Dhamma without remainder. Thus, it should be understood that the many qualities of the Dhamma—such as the state of being noble, leading forth, destruction and dispassion, the dispelling of intoxication, the unconditioned, being well-proclaimed, being good in the beginning, and so on—proclaimed in numerous sutta passages, are revealed without remainder by this verse.

Yasmā [M 0.0010] pana ariyasaccappaṭivedhena samugghāṭitasammohāyeva paramatthato paṇḍitā bālyādisamatikkamanato, tasmā bhāvitalokuttaramaggā sacchikatasāmaññaphalā ca ariyapuggalā visesato vidūti vuccanti. Te hi yathāvuttasāsanavaraṃ aviparītato ñātuṃ netuñca saparasantāne sakkuṇantīti aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūhassa paramatthasaṅghassāpi idha gahitattā ye suppaṭipannatādayo anekehi suttapadehi saṃvaṇṇitā ariyasaṅghaguṇā, tepi niravasesato idha pakāsitāti veditabbā.

Because, however, it is only those whose delusion has been completely cut off through the penetration of the noble truths who are, in the ultimate sense, wise—due to having overcome foolishness and so on—therefore, the noble individuals who have developed the supramundane path and have realized the fruits of recluseship are especially called 'the discerning.' For indeed, they are able to know the excellent teaching as stated without distortion and to establish it in their own and others' continuities. Therefore, because the ultimate Saṅgha, the community of the eight noble individuals, is also included here, it should be understood that those qualities of the noble Saṅgha—such as being of good conduct, and so on—praised in numerous sutta passages, are also revealed without remainder here.

Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya sātisayaṃ ratanattayaguṇaparidīpanaṃ katvā idāni –

Thus, having made a surpassing explanation of the qualities of the Triple Gem by means of the first verse, now—

“Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā;

Sacittapariyodapanaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti. (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183; netti. 30, 50, 116, 124) –

“The non-doing of all evil, the undertaking of the wholesome, the purification of one’s own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”

Vacanato saṅkhepato sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanaṃ, taṃ pana sikkhattayaṃ ñāṇavisesavisayabhāvabhedato avatthābhedato ca tividhaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Sutamayañāṇagocaro ca yo “pariyattisaddhammo”ti vuccati. Cintāmayañāṇagocaro ca yo ākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantīhi gahetabbākāro vimuttāyatanaviseso “paṭipattisaddhammo”ti vuccati. Vipassanāñāṇādisahagato bhāvanāmayañāṇagocaro ca yo “paṭivedhasaddhammo”ti vuccati. Evaṃ tividhampi sāsanaṃ sāsanavaranti padena saṅgaṇhitvā tattha yaṃ paṭhamaṃ, taṃ itaresaṃ adhigamūpāyoti sabbasāsanamūlabhūtaṃ attano pakaraṇassa ca visayabhūtaṃ pariyattisāsanameva tāva saṅkhepato vibhajanto “dvādasa padānī”ti gāthamāha.

Because of this statement, the teaching, in brief, comprises the threefold training. That threefold training, however, is of three kinds by the distinction of its being the domain of special knowledge and by the distinction of its stage. How? There is that which is the domain of knowledge based on learning, which is called the 'true Dhamma of the scriptures.' There is that which is the domain of knowledge based on reflection, which is a special basis for liberation whose nature is to be grasped through considering its aspects, deliberation, and approval through scrutiny of views, and is called the 'true Dhamma of practice.' And there is that which is the domain of knowledge based on development, accompanied by insight knowledge and so on, which is called the 'true Dhamma of penetration.' Thus, having included all three kinds of teaching with the term 'excellent teaching,' among them, the first is the means for attaining the others. Therefore, being the root of the entire teaching and the subject of his own treatise, first briefly analyzing only the teaching of the scriptures, he speaks the verse beginning, “twelve terms.”

Tattha dvādasāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Padānīti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Tesu byañjanapadāni pajjati attho etehīti padāni. Atthapadāni pana pajjanti ñāyantīti padāni. Ubhayampi vā ubhayathā yojetabbaṃ byañjanapadānampi aviparītaṃ paṭipajjitabbattā, atthapadānaṃ uttarivisesādhigamassa [V 0.0143] kāraṇabhāvato, tāni padāni parato pāḷiyaññeva āvi bhavissantīti tattheva vaṇṇayissāma. Atthasūcanādiatthato suttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ saṅgahesu –

Therein, 'twelve' is the delimitation by number. 'Terms' is the indication of the delimited things. Among them, 'expression-terms' are 'terms' because meaning is reached by them. 'Meaning-terms,' however, are 'terms' because they are reached or known. Or, both should be applied in both ways, because expression-terms are also to be practiced without distortion, and because meaning-terms are a cause for the attainment of further distinction. Those terms will become clear later in the Pāḷi itself, so we will explain them there. It is a 'sutta' because of the meaning of indicating the meaning, and so on. For this has been said in the commentaries—

“Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato;

Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca, ‘sutta’nti akkhāta”nti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā; dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā);

“Because it indicates meanings, is well-spoken, brings increase, and flows forth; because it protects well, and because it is analogous to a thread, it is called ‘Sutta’.”

Tadetaṃ [M 0.0011] tattha suttapiṭakavasena āgataṃ, idha pana piṭakattayavasena yojetabbaṃ. “Dvādasa padāni sutta”nti vuttaṃ, yaṃ pariyattisāsananti attho. Taṃ sabbanti taṃ “sutta”nti vuttaṃ sakalaṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Byañjanañca attho cāti byañjanañceva tadattho ca. Yato “dvādasa padāni sutta”nti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – atthasūcanādito suttaṃ pariyattidhammo, tañca sabbaṃ atthato dvādasa padāni cha byañjanapadāni ceva cha atthapadāni cāti. Atha vā yadetaṃ “sāsanavara”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ suttaṃ, pariyattisāsanassa adhippetattā. Atthato pana dvādasa padāni, byañjanatthapadasamudāyabhāvato. Yathāha – “byañjanañca attho cā”ti. Taṃ viññeyyaṃ ubhayanti yasmiṃ byañjane atthe ca vacanavacanīyabhāvena sambandhe suttavohāro, tadubhayaṃ sarūpato viññātabbaṃ tattha katamaṃ byañjanaṃ katamo atthoti? Tenevāha – “ko attho byañjanaṃ katama”nti.

That has come there by way of the Sutta Piṭaka, but here it should be connected by way of the three Piṭakas. When it is said, “The Sutta has twelve terms,” the meaning is the scriptural Dispensation. ‘All of that’ means that the entire word of the Buddha is called ‘Sutta.’ ‘Both phrasing and meaning’ refers to the phrasing and its meaning. Since it is said, “The Sutta has twelve terms,” this is what is meant: the scriptural Dhamma is the Sutta because it indicates the meaning and so forth, and all of that, in terms of its substance, consists of twelve terms: six phrasing-terms and six meaning-terms. Alternatively, that which is called “the excellent Dispensation” is all the Sutta, because the scriptural Dispensation is intended. In terms of meaning, however, there are twelve terms, because of its nature as a collection of phrasing-terms and meaning-terms. As it is said: “Both the phrasing and the meaning.” That twofold should be known: wherein the designation ‘Sutta’ applies to the phrasing and the meaning connected by the relationship of expression and expressed, that twofold should be known in its own nature. Therein, what is the phrasing, and what is the meaning? Therefore, it is said: “What is the meaning? What is the phrasing?”

Evaṃ “sāsanavara”nti vuttassa suttassa pariyattibhāvaṃ tassa ca atthabyañjanapadabhāvena veditabbataṃ dassetvā idāni tassa pavicayupāyaṃ nettippakaraṇaṃ padatthavibhāgena dassetuṃ “soḷasahārā”ti gāthamāha.

Thus, having shown that the Sutta called “the excellent Dispensation” has the nature of scripture, and that it is to be known through its state as meaning-terms and phrasing-terms, now, in order to show the Nettippakaraṇa treatise—which is the means for its analysis—by way of a division of the terms’ meanings, he stated the verse beginning, “soḷasahārā.”

Tattha soḷasa hārā etissāti soḷasahārā. Pañcanayā aṭṭhārasamūlapadāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Atha vā soḷasa hārā soḷasahārā. Evaṃ itaratthāpi. Hāranayamūlapadāni eva hi saṅkhepato vitthārato ca bhāsitāni nettīti. Sāsanassa pariyeṭṭhīti sāsanassa atthapariyesanā, pariyattisāsanassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanāti attho, sakalasseva vā sāsanassa atthavicāraṇāti attho. Paṭipattipaṭivedhepi hi nettinayānusārena adhigacchantīti. Mahakaccānenāti kaccoti purātano isi, tassa vaṃsālaṅkārabhūtoyaṃ mahāthero “kaccāno”ti vuccati. Mahakaccānoti pana [V 0.0144] pūjāvacanaṃ, yathā mahāmoggallānoti, “kaccāyanagottaniddiṭṭhā”tipi pāṭho. Ayañca gāthā nettiṃ saṅgāyantehi pakaraṇatthasaṅgaṇhanavasena ṭhapitāti daṭṭhabbā. Yathā cāyaṃ, evaṃ hāravibhaṅgavāre taṃtaṃhāraniddesanigamane “tenāha āyasmā”tiādivacanaṃ, hārādisamudāyabhūtāyaṃ nettiyaṃ byañjanatthasamudāye ca sutte kiṃ kena viciyatīti vicāraṇāyaṃ āha – “hārā byañjanavicayo”tiādi.

Therein, ‘soḷasahārā’ means ‘that in which there are sixteen hāras.’ For ‘pañcanayā’ and ‘aṭṭhārasamūlapadā’ as well, this same method should be understood. Alternatively, ‘soḷasahārā’ means ‘sixteen hāras.’ So too in the other cases. For indeed, the hāras, nayas, and mūlapadas, spoken of in brief and in detail, are the Netti. ‘Sāsanassa pariyeṭṭhi’ (The Quest for the Dispensation) means the search for the meaning of the Dispensation, that is, the explanation of the meaning of the scriptural Dispensation; or, it means the investigation of the meaning of the entire Dispensation. For, they also understand the Dispensation of practice and penetration by following the Netti method. ‘By Mahākaccāna’: ‘Kacca’ is an ancient sage, and this great elder, being an ornament to his lineage, is called ‘Kaccāna.’ ‘Mahākaccāna,’ however, is a term of reverence, just like ‘Mahāmoggallāna.’ There is also the reading, ‘indicated by the Kaccāyana clan.’ And this verse should be understood as having been placed by the compilers of the Netti for the purpose of summarizing the meaning of the treatise. Just as with this verse, so too in the section on the analysis of the hāras, at the conclusion of the exposition of each hāra, the statement beginning, “Therefore, the venerable one said…” should be noted. Regarding the inquiry, “In the Netti, which is a collection of hāras and so forth, and in the Sutta, which is a collection of phrasing and meaning, what is analyzed by what?” he said, “hārā byañjanavicayo” (The hāras are the analysis of the phrasing), and so forth.

Tattha [M 0.0012] soḷasapi hārā mūlapadaniddhāraṇamantarena byañjanamukheneva suttassa saṃvaṇṇanā honti, na nayā viya mūlapadasaṅkhātasabhāvadhammaniddhāraṇamukhenāti te “byañjanavicayo suttassā”ti vuttā. Atthanayā pana yathāvuttaatthamukheneva suttassa atthasampaṭipattiyā hontīti āha – “nayā tayo ca suttattho”ti. Ayañca vicāraṇā paratopi āgamissati. Keci “nayo cā”ti paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Ubhayaṃ pariggahītanti hārā nayā cāti etaṃ ubhayaṃ suttassa atthaniddhāraṇavasena parisamantato gahitaṃ sabbathā sutte yojitaṃ. Vuccati suttaṃ vadati saṃvaṇṇeti. Kathaṃ? Yathāsuttaṃ suttānurūpaṃ, yaṃ suttaṃ yathā saṃvaṇṇetabbaṃ, tathā saṃvaṇṇetīti attho. Yaṃ yaṃ suttanti vā yathāsuttaṃ, sabbaṃ suttanti attho. Nettinayena hi saṃvaṇṇetuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ nāma suttaṃ natthīti.

Therein, all sixteen hāras are expositions of the Sutta by means of the phrasing alone, without determining the root terms; they are not, like the nayas, expositions by means of determining the intrinsic natures designated as root terms. Therefore, they are called “the analysis of the Sutta’s phrasing.” The meaning-nayas, however, are for the purpose of understanding the Sutta’s meaning precisely by means of the meaning as stated; hence, he said, “The three nayas are the Sutta’s meaning.” This analysis will also come up later. Some read “nayo cā” (and the naya), but that is not good. ‘Both are included’ means that this twofold—the hāras and the nayas—is completely grasped for the purpose of determining the Sutta’s meaning and is applied to the Sutta in every way. It is said of the Sutta, it speaks of it, it explains it. How? ‘Yathāsuttaṃ’ means ‘in accordance with the Sutta,’ that is, it explains a Sutta in the way that it should be explained. Alternatively, ‘yathāsuttaṃ’ means ‘whatever Sutta,’ the meaning being ‘every Sutta.’ For indeed, there is no Sutta whatsoever that cannot be explained by the Netti method.

Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ – “sāsanavaraṃ vidūhi ñeyya”nti, tattha nettisaṃvaṇṇanāya visayabhūtaṃ pariyattidhammameva pakārantarena niyametvā dassetuṃ “yā cevā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, regarding what was said—“The excellent Dispensation is to be known by the wise”—in order to define and show, in another way, that the scriptural Dhamma itself is the domain of the Netti’s exposition, that which begins “yā ceva” was stated.

Tattha atthesu kataparicchedo byañjanappabandho desanā, yo pāṭhoti vuccati. Tadattho desitaṃ tāya desanāya pabodhitattā. Tadubhayañca vimuttāyatanasīsena paricayaṃ karontānaṃ anupādāparinibbānapariyosānānaṃ sampattīnaṃ hetubhāvato ekantena viññeyyaṃ, tadubhayavinimuttassa vā ñeyyassa abhāvato tadeva dvayaṃ viññeyyanti imamatthaṃ dasseti yā ceva…pe… viññeyyanti. Tatrāti tasmiṃ vijānane sādhetabbe, nipphādetabbe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Ayamānupubbīti ayaṃ vakkhamānā anupubbi hāranayānaṃ anukkamo, anukkamena vakkhamānā hāranayāti attho. Navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhīti suttādivasena navaṅgassa sāsanassa pariyesanā, atthavicāraṇāti attho. Sāmiatthe vā etaṃ paccattaṃ navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhiyā anupubbīti. Atha vā anupubbīti karaṇatthe paccattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathāvuttavijānane sādhetabbe vakkhamānāya hāranayānupubbiyā ayaṃ navavidhasuttantassa atthapariyesanāti.

Therein, the discourse (desanā) is the composition of phrasing with its divisions made in regard to the meanings; it is what is called the text (pāṭha). Its meaning is the discoursed (desitaṃ), because it is made known by that discourse. And that twofold should certainly be known, because for those who practice with the basis of liberation as the main point, it is the cause of attainments that culminate in final Nibbāna without clinging. Or, because there is nothing to be known apart from that twofold, only that pair is to be known—this meaning is shown by “yā ceva… viññeyyaṃ.” ‘Tatra’ (therein) is a locative referring to that knowing which is to be accomplished and perfected. ‘Ayamānupubbī’ (this sequence) means this is the sequence, the order of the hāras and nayas that will be explained; the meaning is the hāras and nayas that will be explained in order. ‘Navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhi’ (the quest through the ninefold Suttanta) is the search for the nine-limbed Dispensation by way of the Suttas and so forth; the meaning is the investigation of the meaning. Alternatively, this nominative is in the genitive sense: the sequence of the quest through the ninefold Suttanta. Or, in ‘anupubbī,’ the nominative is in the instrumental sense. This is what is meant: in the knowing to be accomplished as stated, this is the search for the meaning of the ninefold Suttanta by means of the sequence of hāras and nayas that will be explained.

Etthāha [V 0.0145] – kathaṃ panettha geyyaṅgādīnaṃ suttabhāvo, suttabhāve ca tesaṃ kathaṃ sāsanassa navaṅgabhāvo. Yañca saṅgahesu vuccati “sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇa”nti, tathā ca sati suttaṅgameva na [M 0.0013] siyā. Athāpi visuṃ suttaṅgaṃ siyā, maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ (khu. pā. 5.1 ādayo; su. ni. 261 ādayo) suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā, gāthābhāvato dhammapadādīnaṃ viya, geyyaṅgasaṅgaho vā siyā, sagāthakattā sagāthāvaggassa viya, tathā ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānanti. Vuccate –

Herein, an objector states: How, in this matter, could there be the nature of Sutta for the Geyya component and others? And if they have the nature of Sutta, how could the Dispensation have the nature of being nine-membered? And as for what is stated in the commentaries—"a Sutta with verses is Geyya; a Sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa"—if that is so, there would not be a Sutta component at all. And if there were a separate Sutta component, the Maṅgala Sutta and others would not be included in the Sutta component, just as the Dhammapada and others are not, due to their being verses. Or, they might be included in the Geyya component because they have verses, like the Sagāthāvagga. Similarly, in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others, the sections with verses would be included in the Geyya component. The refutation is stated:

Suttanti sāmaññavidhi, visesavidhayo pare;

Sanimittā niruḷhattā, sahatāññena nāññato.

Sutta is the general rule; the others are specific rules, which are with characteristics, are well-established, are conjoined with another, and are not from another.

Sabbassāpi hi buddhavacanassa suttanti ayaṃ sāmaññavidhi. Tathā hi “ettakaṃ tassa bhagavato suttāgataṃ suttapariyāpannaṃ (pāci. 1242), sāvatthiyā suttavibhaṅge, sakavāde pañca suttasatānī”tiādivacanato vinayābhidhammapariyattivisesepi suttavohāro dissati. Tadekadesesu pana geyyādayo visesavidhayo tena tena nimittena patiṭṭhitā. Tathā hi geyyassa sagāthakattaṃ tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Lokepi hi sasilokaṃ sagāthakaṃ cuṇṇiyaganthaṃ geyya”nti vadanti. Gāthāvirahe pana sati pucchitvā vissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa. Pucchāvissajjanañhi “byākaraṇa”nti vuccati. Byākaraṇameva veyyākaraṇanti. Evaṃ sante sagāthakādīnampi pañhāvissajjanavasena pavattānaṃ veyyākaraṇabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, geyyādisaññānaṃ anokāsabhāvato “gāthāvirahe satī”ti visesitattā ca. Tathā hi dhammapadādīsu kevalaṃ gāthābandhesu sagāthakattepi somanassañāṇamayikagāthāyuttesu “vuttañheta”ntiādivacanasambandhesu abbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttesu ca suttavisesesu yathākkamaṃ gāthāudānaitivuttakaabbhutadhammasaññā patiṭṭhitā, tathā satipi gāthābandhabhāve bhagavato atītāsu jātīsu cariyānubhāvappakāsakesu jātakasaññā. Satipi pañhāvissajjanabhāve sagāthakatte ca kesuci suttantesu vedassa labhāpanato vedallasaññā patiṭṭhitāti evaṃ tena tena sagāthakattādinā nimittena tesu tesu suttavisesesu geyyaṅgādisaññā patiṭṭhitāti visesavidhayo suttaṅgato pare geyyādayo.

Indeed, for all of the Buddha's Word, 'Sutta' is a general rule. For thus it is: from statements such as 'So much of the Blessed One's teaching has come down as Sutta, is included in the Sutta,' 'in the Suttavibhaṅga at Sāvatthī,' and 'five hundred suttas in his own discourse,' the term 'Sutta' is seen even in the specific scriptural collections of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma. However, in some portions thereof, Geyya and the others are established as specific rules by this or that characteristic. For instance, for Geyya, having verses is the characteristic for its being so. For even in the world, a prose work with stanzas or with verses is called 'Geyya.' But when there is an absence of verses, the state of answering after being asked is the characteristic of Veyyākaraṇa. For a question-and-answer is called 'byākaraṇa,' and byākaraṇa itself is Veyyākaraṇa. If this is so, would those with verses and so on that proceed by way of question-and-answer also attain the state of Veyyākaraṇa? They would not. Why? Because the designations Geyya and so on leave no opportunity, and because it was specified 'when there is an absence of verses.' For thus it is: in the Dhammapada and others, which are solely compositions of verses; and also in specific suttas that, despite having verses, are connected with verses of joyful knowledge, are connected with statements such as 'This was said by the Blessed One,' or are connected with marvelous phenomena, the designations Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and Abbhutadhamma are established respectively. Similarly, despite being a composition of verses, in those suttas that proclaim the power of the Blessed One's conduct in past births, the designation Jātaka is established. And in certain suttas, despite the presence of question-and-answer and of verses, the designation Vedalla is established because they cause one to obtain knowledge (veda). Thus, by this or that characteristic, such as having verses, the designations Geyya component and so on are established in these or those specific suttas. Therefore, Geyya and the others, which are apart from the Sutta component, are specific rules.

Yaṃ panettha geyyaṅgādinimittarahitaṃ suttaṃ, taṃ suttaṅgaṃ visesasaññāparihārena sāmaññasaññāya pavattanatoti. Nanu ca sagāthakaṃ [M 0.0014] suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇanti suttaṅgaṃ na sambhavatīti codanā tadavatthā evāti? Na tadavatthā, sodhitattā. Sodhitañhi [V 0.0146] pubbe gāthāvirahe sati pucchāvissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimittanti. Yañca vuttaṃ – “gāthābhāvato maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā”ti, tampi na, niruḷhattā. Niruḷho hi maṅgalasuttādīsu suttabhāvo, na hi tāni dhammapadabuddhavaṃsādayo viya gāthābhāvena paññātāni, kintu suttabhāveneva. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “suttanāmaka”nti nāmaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

Herein, whatever sutta is devoid of the characteristics of the Geyya component and so forth, that is the Sutta component, because it proceeds by the general designation, having abandoned the specific designations. But is it not so that the objection—'A sutta with verses is Geyya, a sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa, therefore a Sutta component is not possible'—still stands? It does not still stand, because it has been clarified. For it was clarified before that when there is an absence of verses, the state of question-and-answer is the characteristic for its being Veyyākaraṇa. And as for what was said, 'Due to being verses, the Maṅgala Sutta and others would not be included in the Sutta component,' that too is not correct, because it is well-established. For in the Maṅgala Sutta and others, the nature of Sutta is well-established. They are not known by their nature as verses, like the Dhammapada, Buddhavaṃsa, and others, but rather by their nature as Sutta. For that very reason, in the commentary, the term 'named' was used in the phrase 'named a Sutta.'

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “sagāthakattā geyyaṅgasaṅgaho vā siyā”ti, tadapi natthi, yasmā sahatāññena. Saha gāthāhīti hi sagāthakaṃ. Sahabhāvo ca nāma atthato aññena hoti, na ca maṅgalasuttādīsu gāthāvinimutto koci suttappadeso atthi. Yo saha gāthāhīti vucceyya, na ca samudāyo nāma koci atthi. Yadapi vuttaṃ – “ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānaṃ geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti, tadapi na aññato. Aññā eva hi tā gāthā, jātakādipariyāpannattā. Ato na tāhi ubhatovibhaṅgādīnaṃ geyyaṅgabhāvoti evaṃ suttādīnaṃ aṅgānaṃ aññamaññasaṅkarābhāvo veditabbo. Yasmā pana sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ yathāvuttanayena atthānaṃ sūcanādiatthena suttantveva vuccati, tasmā vuttaṃ – “navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhī”ti.

But as for what was said, 'Or, because it has verses, it might be included in the Geyya component,' that too is not the case, because it is defined by being together with another. For `sagāthakaṃ` means 'together with verses.' And the state of being together, in reality, is with something else. But in the Maṅgala Sutta and others, there is no portion of the sutta that is separate from the verses, of which it could be said that it is 'together with verses.' Nor is there any such composite entity. And as for what was said, 'In the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others, the sections with verses would be included in the Geyya component,' that too is not correct, because they are from another source. For those verses are indeed other verses, because they are included in the Jātakas and so on. Therefore, because of those verses, the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others do not have the nature of the Geyya component. Thus, the non-intermingling of the components, Sutta and so on, with one another should be understood. Moreover, because all the Buddha's Word, in the manner described, is called 'Sutta' due to its meaning of indicating benefits and so on, therefore it was said by the Teacher: 'the investigation of the ninefold Suttanta.'

Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on Compilation is concluded.

2. Uddesavāravaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Summary Section

1. Evaṃ [V 0.0147] saṅgahavārena saṅkhepato dassite hārādayo idāni vibhāgena dassetuṃ “tattha katame soḷasa hārā”tiādidesanā āraddhā. Tattha tatthāti yaṃ vuttaṃ – “soḷasahārā nettī”ti, tasmiṃ vacane, tissaṃ vā gāthāyaṃ, yāni hāranayamūlapadāni uddhaṭāni, tesūti attho. Katameti pucchāvacanaṃ. Pucchā ca nāmesā pañcavidhā adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā vimaticchedanāpucchā anumatipucchā kathetukamyatāpucchāti. Tāsu ayaṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā. Soḷasāti gaṇanavasena paricchedo. Tena nesaṃ na tato uddhaṃ adho cāti etaparamataṃ [M 0.0015] dasseti. Sā cetaparamatā parato āvi bhavissati. Hārāti gaṇanavasena paricchinnānaṃ sāmaññato dassanaṃ. Desanā vicayotiādi sarūpadassanaṃ.

2. Thus, the hāras and so forth, having been shown briefly in the Section on Compilation, now, in order to show them in detail, the teaching beginning with “Therein, what are the sixteen hāras?” has been commenced. Therein, the word ‘therein’ refers to what was said—“the sixteen hāras are the Netti”—in that statement, or in that verse, among those hāras, methods, and root-terms which have been extracted; this is the meaning. ‘What are’ is an interrogative expression. Now, a question is of five kinds: the question for illuminating the unseen, the question for confirming the seen, the question for dispelling doubt, the question for consent, and the question from a desire to speak. Among these, this is the question from a desire to speak. ‘Sixteen’ is a delimitation by way of number. By this, it shows that for them there is nothing more or less than that number, thus indicating their limit. And that limit will become clear later. ‘Hāras’ is a general designation for what has been delimited by way of number. The words beginning with ‘Desanā, Vicaya’ show their individual nature.

Tattha kenaṭṭhena hārā? Harīyanti etehi, ettha vā suttageyyādivisayā aññāṇasaṃsayavipallāsāti hārā, haranti vā sayaṃ tāni, haraṇamattameva vāti hārā phalūpacārena. Atha vā harīyanti voharīyanti dhammasaṃvaṇṇakadhammapaṭiggāhakehi dhammassa dānaggahaṇavasenāti hārā. Atha vā hārā viyāti hārā. Yathā hi anekaratanāvalisamūho hārasaṅkhāto attano avayavabhūtaratanasamphassehi samuppajjanīyamānahilādasukho hutvā tadupabhogījanasarīrasantāpaṃ nidāghapariḷāhupajanitaṃ vūpasameti, evametepi nānāvidhaparamattharatanappabandhā saṃvaṇṇanāvisesā attano avayavabhūtaparamattharatanādhigamena samuppādiyamānanibbutisukhā dhammapaṭiggāhakajanahadayaparitāpaṃ kāmarāgādikilesahetukaṃ vūpasamentīti. Atha vā hārayanti aññāṇādīnaṃ hāraṃ apagamaṃ karonti ācikkhantīti vā hārā. Atha vā sotujanacittassa haraṇato ramaṇato ca hārā niruttinayena, yathā – “bhavesu vantagamano bhagavā”ti (visuddhi. 1.144; pārā. aṭṭha. 1.1 verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā). Ayaṃ tāva hārānaṃ sādhāraṇato attho.

Therein, in what sense are they called ‘hāras’? They are called ‘hāras’ because by them, or in them, ignorance, doubt, and perversion concerning subjects such as suttas and geyyas are dispelled (harīyanti); or because they themselves dispel them; or because it is simply the act of dispelling (haraṇamatta)—thus they are called ‘hāras’ by metaphorical application to the result. Alternatively, they are called ‘hāras’ because they are used or spoken of (harīyanti, voharīyanti) by those who expound the Dhamma and those who receive the Dhamma, by way of giving and receiving the Dhamma. Or, they are called ‘hāras’ because they are like a necklace (hāra). For just as a collection of many gems, called a necklace, having delightful pleasure produced by the touch of the gems that are its parts, allays the bodily torment of those who wear it, a torment generated by the heat of summer; so too these special expositions, which are compositions of various ultimate truths as gems, having the bliss of Nibbāna produced by the attainment of the ultimate truths as gems that are their parts, allay the torment in the heart of those who receive the Dhamma, a torment caused by defilements such as sensual passion. Alternatively, they are called ‘hāras’ because they bring about the removal (hāraṃ), the departure (apagamaṃ), of ignorance and so forth, or because they declare it. Alternatively, they are called ‘hāras’ by way of etymology (niruttinayena) from their capturing (haraṇa) and delighting (ramaṇa) the minds of the listeners, just as it is said: ‘The Bhagavā is so called because his going (gamana) in states of existence (bhavesu) has been vomited forth (vanta)’. This, for now, is the general meaning of ‘hāras’.

Asādhāraṇato pana desīyati saṃvaṇṇīyati etāya suttatthoti desanā, desanāsahacaraṇato vā [V 0.0148] desanā. Nanu ca aññepi hārā desanāsaṅkhātassa suttassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanato desanāsahacārinovāti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana hāro yebhuyyena yathārutavaseneva viññāyamāno desanāya saha caratīti vattabbataṃ arahati, na tathā pare. Na hi assādādīnavanissaraṇādisandassanarahitā suttadesanā atthi. Assādādisandassanavibhāvanalakkhaṇo cāyaṃ hāroti.

However, in a specific sense, it is called ‘Desanā’ (Teaching) because the meaning of the sutta is taught (desīyati) and expounded (saṃvaṇṇīyati) by it; or it is called ‘Desanā’ because it accompanies the teaching. But is it not the case that other hāras also accompany the teaching, since they expound the meaning of the sutta, which is designated as ‘teaching’? This is true. However, this hāra, being for the most part understood directly as it is heard, deserves to be called ‘accompanying the teaching’; not so the others. For there is no teaching of a sutta that is devoid of showing gratification, danger, and escape. And this hāra has the characteristic of clarifying the showing of gratification and so forth.

Viciyanti etena, ettha vā padapañhādayo, viciti eva vā tesanti vicayo. Pāḷiyaṃ pana vicinatīti vicayoti ayamattho dassito.

It is called ‘Vicaya’ (Investigation) because by it, or in it, terms, questions, and so forth are investigated (viciyanti); or it is simply the investigation (viciti) of these. In the Pāḷi, however, the meaning is shown thus: ‘because one investigates (vicinati), it is Vicaya’.

Yuttīti upapattisādhanayutti, idha pana yuttivicāraṇā yutti uttarapadalopena “rūpabhavo rūpa”nti yathā, yuttisahacaraṇato vā. Idhāpi desanāhāre vuttanayena attho vitthāretabbo.

‘Yutti’ (Reasoning) is reasoning that establishes appropriateness. Here, however, ‘yuttivicāraṇā’ (investigation of reasoning) becomes ‘yutti’ through the elision of the final word, just as ‘rūpabhava’ (form-existence) becomes ‘rūpa’; or it is called ‘yutti’ because it accompanies reasoning. Here too, the meaning should be elaborated according to the method stated for the Desanā hāra.

Padaṭṭhānanti [M 0.0016] āsannakāraṇaṃ, idhāpi padaṭṭhānavicāraṇātiādi vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

‘Padaṭṭhāna’ (Proximate Cause) is the immediate cause. Here too, the explanation that ‘the investigation of the proximate cause’ is called ‘proximate cause’, and so forth, should be understood in the way already stated.

Lakkhīyanti etena, ettha vā ekalakkhaṇā dhammā avuttāpi ekavacanenāti lakkhaṇaṃ.

It is called ‘Lakkhaṇa’ (Characteristic) because by it, or in it, even unstated dhammas that share a single characteristic are characterized (lakkhīyanti) through the mention of one.

Viyūhīyanti vibhāgena piṇḍīyanti etena, ettha vāti byūho. Nibbacanādīnaṃ sutte dassiyamānānaṃ catunnaṃ byūhoti catubyūho, catunnaṃ vā byūho etthāti catubyūho.

It is called ‘Byūha’ (Arrangement) because by it, or in it, things are analyzed (viyūhīyanti) and grouped (piṇḍīyanti). ‘Catubyūha’ (Fourfold Arrangement) is the arrangement of the four things shown in the sutta, beginning with derivation; or it is called ‘Catubyūha’ because in it there is an arrangement of four.

Āvaṭṭīyanti etena, ettha vā sabhāgā visabhāgā ca dhammā, tesaṃ vā āvaṭṭananti āvaṭṭo.

It is called ‘Āvaṭṭa’ (Revolving) because by it, or in it, similar and dissimilar dhammas are made to revolve (āvaṭṭīyanti); or it is the revolving (āvaṭṭanaṃ) of those dhammas.

Vibhajīyanti etena, ettha vā sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇānaṃ saṃkilesavodānadhammānaṃ bhūmiyoti vibhatti, vibhajanaṃ vā etesaṃ bhūmiyāti vibhatti.

It is called ‘Vibhatti’ (Division) because by it, or in it, the grounds of common and uncommon dhammas of defilement and cleansing are divided (vibhajīyanti); or it is the division (vibhajanaṃ) of their grounds.

Paṭipakkhavasena parivattīyanti iminā, ettha vā sutte vuttadhammā, parivattanaṃ vā tesanti parivattano.

It is called ‘Parivattana’ (Reversal) because by this, or in this, the dhammas stated in the sutta are reversed (parivattīyanti) by way of opposition; or it is the reversal (parivattanaṃ) of those.

Vividhaṃ [V 0.0149] vacanaṃ ekassevatthassa vācakametthāti vivacanaṃ, vivacanameva vevacanaṃ, vividhaṃ vuccati etena atthoti vā vivacanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

It is called ‘Vevacana’ (Synonym) because herein there are various words (vividhaṃ vacanaṃ) expressing a single meaning. ‘Vivacana’ itself is ‘Vevacana’. Or, it is called ‘Vivacana’ because by it the meaning is expressed in various ways (vividhaṃ). The rest is as previously explained.

Pakārehi pabhedato vā ñāpīyanti iminā, ettha vā atthāti paññatti.

It is called ‘Paññatti’ (Designation) because by this, or in this, meanings (atthā) are made known (ñāpīyanti) through modes (pakārehi) or distinctions (pabhedato).

Otārīyanti anuppavesīyanti etena, ettha vā suttāgatā dhammā paṭiccasamuppādādīsūti otaraṇo.

It is called ‘Otaraṇa’ (Application) because by it, or in it, the dhammas found in the suttas are made to enter into (otārīyanti) and are applied to (anuppavesīyanti) frameworks such as Dependent Origination.

Sodhīyanti samādhīyanti etena, ettha vā sutte padapadatthapañhārambhāti sodhano.

It is called ‘Sodhana’ (Clarification) because by it, or in it, the words, the meanings of words, and the initial points of questions in a sutta are purified (sodhīyanti) and resolved (samādhīyanti).

Adhiṭṭhīyanti anupavattīyanti etena, ettha vā sāmaññavisesabhūtā dhammā vinā vikappenāti adhiṭṭhāno.

It is called ‘Adhiṭṭhāna’ (Determination) because by it, or in it, general and specific dhammas are determined (adhiṭṭhīyanti) and accepted as they are presented (anupavattīyanti), without further interpretation (vinā vikappena).

Parikaroti abhisaṅkharoti phalanti parikkhāro, hetu paccayo ca, parikkhāraṃ ācikkhatīti parikkhāro, hāro, parikkhāravisayattā parikkhārasahacaraṇato vā parikkhāro.

That which prepares (parikaroti) and conditions (abhisaṅkharoti) the result (phalaṃ) is a ‘parikkhāra’ (requisite); it is a cause and a condition. The hāra that explains this requisite is called ‘Parikkhāra’. Or, it is called ‘Parikkhāra’ because its subject is the requisite, or because it accompanies the requisite.

Samāropīyanti etena, ettha vā padaṭṭhānādimukhena dhammāti samāropano. Sabbattha ca bhāvasādhanavasenāpi attho sambhavatīti tassāpi vasena yojetabbaṃ.

It is called ‘Samāropana’ (Ascription) because by it, or in it, dhammas are ascribed (samāropīyanti) by means of the proximate cause and so forth. And in all cases, a meaning is also possible by way of derivation in an abstract sense (bhāvasādhana); therefore, the connection should also be made in that way.

Tassāti [M 0.0017] yathāvuttassa hāruddesassa. Anugītīti vuttassevatthassa sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ anupacchā gāyanagāthā, tāsu osānagāthāya atthato asaṃkiṇṇāti padatthena saṅkararahitā, tena yadipi keci hārā aññamaññaṃ avisiṭṭhā viya dissanti, tathāpi tesaṃ atthato saṅkaro natthīti dasseti. So ca nesaṃ asaṅkaro lakkhaṇaniddese supākaṭo hoti. Etesañcevāti etesaṃ soḷasannaṃ hārānaṃ. Yathā asaṅkaro, tathā ceva bhavati. Kiṃ bhavati? Vitthāratayā vitthārena. Nayavibhatti nayena upāyena ñāyena vibhāgo. Etena taṃ eva asaṅkiṇṇataṃ vibhāveti. Keci “vitthāranayā”ti paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ, ayañca gāthā kesuci potthakesu natthi.

Tassa means of the aforementioned summary of the hāras. Anugīti means verses sung afterward for the easy comprehension of the meaning that has been stated. Among those verses, in the concluding verse, “unmixed in meaning” means free from mixture by way of the meaning of the words. By this, it shows that although some hāras may appear as if undifferentiated from one another, nevertheless, there is no mixture in their meaning. And that non-mixture of theirs becomes very clear in the explanation of the characteristics. “And of these” means of these sixteen hāras. Just as there is non-mixture, so indeed it is. What is it? By way of detail, in detail. Nayavibhatti means division by method, by means, by knowledge. By this, it clarifies that very non-mixture. Some read “vitthāranayā”, but that is not good. And this verse is not found in some books.

2. Evaṃ hāre uddisitvā idāni naye uddisituṃ “tattha katame”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nayanti saṃkilese vodānāni ca vibhāgato ñāpentīti nayā, nīyanti vā tāni etehi[V 0.0150], ettha vāti nayā, nayanamattameva vāti nayā, nīyanti vā sayaṃ dhammakathikehi upanīyanti suttassa atthapavicayatthanti nayā. Atha vā nayā viyāti nayā. Yathā hi ekattādayo nayā sammā paṭivijjhiyamānā paccayapaccayuppannadhammānaṃ yathākkamaṃ sambandhavibhāgabyāpāravirahānurūpaphalabhāvadassanena asaṅkarato sammutisaccaparamatthasaccānaṃ sabhāvaṃ pavedayantā paramatthasaccappaṭivedhāya saṃvattanti, evametepi kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgadhammavibhāgadassanena aviparītasuttatthāvabodhāya abhisambhuṇantā veneyyānaṃ catusaccappaṭivedhāya saṃvattanti. Atha vā pariyattiatthassa nayanato saṃkilesato yamanato ca nayā niruttinayena.

2. Thus, having summarized the hāras, now, to summarize the nayas, the passage beginning with “Tattha katame” is stated. Therein, they are called nayā because they make known (nayanti) the defilements and the purifications by way of distinction. Or, they are called nayā because those [defilements and purifications] are known (nīyanti) by means of these or within these. Or, they are called nayā because they are merely the act of making known (nayana). Or, they are called nayā because they themselves are known (nīyanti) or brought forward by Dhamma-preachers for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the Sutta. Alternatively, they are called nayā because they are like methods (nayā viya).
