For just as the methods of unity and so forth, when rightly penetrated, make known the nature of conventional truth and ultimate truth without confusion—by showing, in order, the connection, distinction, absence of activity, and the state of the fruit being in accordance with the cause for causes and the phenomena arisen from them—they conduce to the penetration of the ultimate truth. Similarly, these [special expositions], by showing the distinction of phenomena into dark and bright counterparts and accomplishing an unerring understanding of the Sutta's meaning, conduce to the penetration of the Four Truths for those to be trained. Alternatively, by way of etymology, they are called nayā because of making known (nayanato) the meaning of the scriptures and because of restraining (yamanato) from defilements.

Nandiyāvaṭṭotiādīsu nandiyāvaṭṭassa viya āvaṭṭo etassāti nandiyāvaṭṭo, yathā hi nandiyāvaṭṭo antoṭhitena padhānāvayavena bahiddhā āvaṭṭati, evamayampi nayoti attho. Atha vā nandiyā taṇhāya pamodassa vā āvaṭṭo etthāti nandiyāvaṭṭo. Tīhi avayavehi lobhādīhi saṃkilesapakkhe alobhādīhi ca vodānapakkhe pukkhalo sobhanoti tipukkhalo. Asantāsanajavaparakkamādivisesayogena sīho bhagavā, tassa vikkīḷitaṃ desanāvacīkammabhūto vihāroti katvā vipallāsatappaṭipakkhaparidīpanato sīhassa vikkīḷitaṃ etthāti sīhavikkīḷito, [M 0.0018] nayo. Balavisesayogadīpanato vā sīhavikkīḷitasadisattā nayo sīhavikkīḷito. Balaviseso cettha saddhādibalaṃ, dasabalāni eva vā. Atthanayattayadisābhāvena kusalādidhammānaṃ ālocanaṃ disālocanaṃ. Tathā ālocitānaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ atthanayattayayojane samānayanato aṅkuso viya aṅkuso. Gāthāsu lañjeti pakāseti suttatthanti lañjako, nayo ca so lañjako cāti nayalañjako. Gatāti ñātā, matāti attho. So eva vā pāṭho. Sesaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

Regarding Nandiyāvaṭṭo and so on: it is called Nandiyāvaṭṭo because its whirling is like that of a nandiyāvaṭṭa flower. For just as a nandiyāvaṭṭa flower revolves outward with its principal part situated inside, so too does this naya revolve; this is the meaning. Alternatively, it is Nandiyāvaṭṭo because herein is the whirling of delight (nandi), that is, of craving (taṇhā) or joy (pamoda). It is Tipukkhalo because it is excellent with three components: with greed and so forth on the side of defilement, and with non-greed and so forth on the side of purification. The Blessed One is a lion (sīho) due to possessing special qualities such as fearlessness, swiftness, and exertion. His sport (vikkīḷitaṃ) is the abiding which is the verbal action of teaching. Thus, because it reveals the perversions and their opposites, it is Sīhavikkīḷito, the naya, for the lion's sport is herein. Or, because it shows the possession of special strength, the naya is Sīhavikkīḷito due to its similarity to a lion's sport. And here, special strength is the power of faith and so forth, or it is indeed the ten powers. The examination (ālocanaṃ) of wholesome phenomena and so on, by way of being the group of three methods of meaning, is Disālocanaṃ. Because it brings together (samānayanato) those phenomena thus examined in the application of the group of three methods of meaning, it is like a goad (aṅkuso viya), hence Aṅkuso. In the verses, it is lañjako because it marks (lañjeti) or clarifies (pakāseti) the meaning of the Sutta. It is both a naya and a lañjako, hence Nayalañjako. Gatā means known (ñātā), that is, understood (matā). Or that (matā) is the reading itself. The rest should be understood by the method already stated.

3. Evaṃ nayepi uddisitvā idāni mūlapadāni uddisituṃ “tattha katamānī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha mūlāni ca tāni nayānaṃ paṭṭhānabhāgānañca patiṭṭhābhāvato padāni ca adhigamūpāyabhāvato koṭṭhāsabhāvato cāti mūlapadāni. Kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena, kucchitānaṃ vā pāpadhammānaṃ salanato viddhaṃsanato, kusānaṃ vā rāgādīnaṃ lavanato, kusā viya vā lavanato, kusena vā ñāṇena lātabbato pavattetabbato kusalāni, tappaṭipakkhato akusalānīti padattho veditabbo.

3. Thus, having also summarized the nayas, now, to summarize the root terms, the passage beginning with “Tattha katamāni” is initiated. Therein, they are mūlapadāni (root terms) because they are both roots (mūlāni), being the foundation for the nayas and the divisions of the foundation (paṭṭhānabhāga), and they are terms (padāni), being the means of attainment and the sections. They are kusalāni (wholesome) because of the meaning of being produced from skill; or because of shaking or destroying contemptible, evil states; or because of cutting the kusas (contemptible things), i.e., lust, etc.; or because of cutting like kusa grass; or because they are to be obtained or brought about by kusa, i.e., by wisdom. They are akusalāni (unwholesome) because they are the opposite of that. The meaning of the term should be understood thus.

Evaṃ gaṇanaparicchedato jātibhedato ca mūlapadāni dassetvā idāni sarūpato dassento saṃkilesapakkhaṃyeva [V 0.0151] paṭhamaṃ uddisati “taṇhā”tiādinā. Tattha tasati paritasatīti taṇhā. Avindiyaṃ vindati, vindiyaṃ na vindatīti avijjā, vijjāpaṭipakkhāti vā avijjā. Lubbhanti tena, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva vā soti lobho. Dosamohesupi eseva nayo. Asubhe “subha”nti pavattā saññā subhasaññā. Sukhasaññādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Saṅgahanti gaṇanaṃ. Samosaraṇanti samoropanaṃ.

Thus, having shown the root terms by way of numerical limitation and by distinction of kind, now, showing them according to their intrinsic nature, the Teacher first summarizes only the side of defilement with the words beginning “taṇhā”. Therein, it is taṇhā (craving) because it thirsts (tasati) or is parched (paritasati). It is avijjā (ignorance) because it finds what is not to be found and does not find what is to be found; or, it is avijjā because it is the opposite of knowledge. It is lobho (greed) because they are greedy on account of it, or it is greedy itself, or it is merely the act of being greedy. This same method should be seen also for dosa (hatred) and moha (delusion). The perception that occurs as “beautiful” in what is not beautiful is subhasaññā (perception of beauty). The meaning of sukhasaññā (perception of pleasure) and so on should also be understood by this same method. Saṅgahaṃ means counting. Samosaraṇaṃ means inclusion.

Paccanīkadhamme sametīti samatho. Aniccādīhi vividhehi ākārehi passatīti vipassanā. Alobhādayo lobhādipaṭipakkhato veditabbā. Asubhe “asubha”nti pavattā saññā asubhasaññā, kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Saññāsīsena hi desanā. Dukkhasaññādīsupi eseva nayo.

It is samatho (calm) because it pacifies opposing states. It is vipassanā (insight) because it sees in various ways, such as impermanence, etc. Non-greed and so on should be understood as the opposite of greed and so on. The perception that occurs as “not beautiful” in what is not beautiful is asubhasaññā (perception of non-beauty), which is the foundation of mindfulness that is the contemplation of the body. For the teaching is given with perception as the head. This same method should be seen also for dukkhasaññā (perception of suffering) and so on.

Idaṃ uddānanti idaṃ vuttasseva atthassa vippakiṇṇabhāvena nassituṃ adatvā uddhaṃ dānaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ uddānaṃ, saṅgahavacananti attho. “Cattāro vipallāsā”tipi [M 0.0019] pāṭho. Kilesabhūmīti saṃkilesabhūmi sabbesaṃ akusaladhammānaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānattā. Kusalānaṃ yāni tīṇi mūlāni. “Kusalānī”tipi paṭhanti. Satipaṭṭhānāti asubhasaññādayo sandhāyāha. Indriyabhūmīti saddhādīnaṃ vimuttiparipācanindriyānaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānattā vuttaṃ. Yujjantīti yojīyanti. Khoti padapūraṇe, avadhāraṇatthe vā nipāto. Tena ete evāti dasseti. Aṭṭhārasevāti vā. Mūlapadāti mūlapadāni, liṅgavipallāso vā.

Idaṃ uddānaṃ (this summary): this statement is a 'protection above' (uddhaṃ dānaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ), not allowing the meaning that has already been stated to be destroyed by being scattered. It is a statement of summary (saṅgahavacanaṃ); this is the meaning. There is also the reading, “Cattāro vipallāsā.” Kilesabhūmi (the plane of defilements) is the plane of defilement (saṃkilesabhūmi) because it is the place of assembly for all unwholesome states. The phrase is Kusalānaṃ yāni tīṇi mūlāni (Of the wholesome, the three roots). Some also read it as Kusalāni. The statement satipaṭṭhāna is said in reference to the perception of foulness and so on. The statement indriyabhūmi (the plane of the faculties) is said because it is the place of assembly for the faculties that ripen into liberation, such as faith and so on. Yujjanti means they are joined. Kho is a particle used for filling out a verse, or a particle used in the sense of emphasis. By that, it shows, “Precisely these are the root terms,” or, “Precisely eighteen terms are the root terms.” Mūlapadā means mūlapadāni (root terms), or it is a gender inversion.

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Section on Exposition (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā) is completed.

3. Niddesavāravaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Section on Detailed Exposition (Niddesavāravaṇṇanā)

4. Evaṃ [V 0.0152] uddiṭṭhe hārādayo niddisituṃ “tattha saṅkhepato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ uddesapāṭhe. Saṅkhepato netti kittitāti samāsato nettippakaraṇaṃ kathitaṃ. Hāranayamūlapadānañhi sarūpadassanaṃ uddesapāṭhena katanti. Ettha ca hāranayānaṃ –

4. Thus, in order to expound in detail the hāras and so on, which have been pointed out in brief, the passage beginning with “Tattha saṅkhepato” was commenced. Therein, tatthā means “in that exposition text.” “Saṅkhepato netti kittitā” means the Netti treatise is spoken of concisely. Indeed, the showing of the intrinsic nature of the hāras, nayas, and root terms was done by the exposition text. And here, of the hāras and nayas—

Sāmaññato visesena, padattho lakkhaṇaṃ kamo;

Ettāvatā ca hetvādī, veditabbā hi viññunā.

Generally and specifically, the meaning of the term, the characteristic, the order, the extent, and the cause and so on, should indeed be known by the wise person.

Tesu avisesato visesato ca hāranayānaṃ attho dassito. Lakkhaṇādīsu pana avisesato sabbepi hārā nayā ca yathākkamaṃ byañjanatthamukhena navaṅgassa sāsanassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanalakkhaṇā. Visesato pana tassa tassa hārassa nayassa ca lakkhaṇaṃ niddese eva kathayissāma. Kamādīni ca yasmā nesaṃ lakkhaṇesu ñātesu viññeyyāni honti, tasmā tānipi niddesato parato pakāsayissāma.

Among these, the meaning of the hāras and methods has been shown both generally and specifically. But regarding the characteristics and so on, generally, all hāras and methods, in due order, have the characteristic of elucidating the meaning of the nine-limbed Teaching, with the meaning of the expression being primary. Specifically, however, we will state the characteristic of each respective hāra and method only in the detailed exposition. And since the order and so on are easily known when their characteristics are known, we will therefore clarify them also after the detailed exposition.

Hārasaṅkhepo

Summary of the Hāras

1. Yā pana assādādīnavatātiādikā niddesagāthā, tāsu assādādīnavatāti assādo ādīnavatāti padavibhāgo. Ādīnavatāti ca ādīnavo eva. Keci “assādādīnavato”ti paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Tattha assādīyatīti assādo, sukhaṃ somanassañca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu [M 0.0020] assādo”ti (ma. ni. 1.166; saṃ. ni. 3.26). Yathā cetaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, evaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇampi. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “so tadassādeti taṃ nikāmetī”ti “rūpaṃ assādeti abhinandati, taṃ ārabbha rāgo uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.424), “saṃyojanīyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.53) ca[V 0.0153]. Assādeti etāyāti vā assādo, taṇhā. Taṇhāya hi kāraṇabhūtāya puggalo sukhampi sukhārammaṇampi assādeti. Yathā ca taṇhā, evaṃ vipallāsāpi. Vipallāsavasena hi sattā aniṭṭhampi ārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhākārena assādenti, evaṃ vedanāya sabbesaṃ tebhūmakasaṅkhārānaṃ taṇhāya vipallāsānañca assādavicāro veditabbo.

1. As for the exposition verses beginning with 'assādādīnavatā', in them the word-division of 'assādādīnavatā' is 'assādo ādīnavatā'. And 'ādīnavatā' is simply 'ādīnavo'. Some read it as 'assādādīnavato', but that is not good. Therein, 'it is relished', therefore it is gratification; this is pleasure and mental joy. For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, whatever pleasure and mental joy arise dependent on the five aggregates of clinging, this is the gratification in the five aggregates of clinging.” And just as this pleasure and mental joy are gratification, so too is a desirable object. This too has been said: “He relishes it, he desires it”; “He relishes form, delights in it, and in relation to it, lust arises”; and “For one who constantly sees gratification in things that are fettering.” Or, 'one relishes by means of this', therefore it is gratification; this is craving. For with craving as the cause, a person relishes both pleasure and a pleasurable object. And just as craving is gratification, so too are the perversions. For by the power of perversions, beings relish even an undesirable object in the manner of a desirable one. Thus, the investigation of gratification should be understood in relation to feeling, all formations of the three realms, craving, and the perversions.

Kathaṃ pana dukkhādukkhamasukhavedanānaṃ assādanīyatāti? Vipallāsato sukhapariyāyasabbhāvato ca. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “sukhā kho, āvuso visākha, vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā. Dukkhā vedanā ṭhitidukkhā vipariṇāmasukhā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā ñāṇasukhā aññāṇadukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.465). Tattha vedanāya aṭṭhasatapariyāyavasena, tebhūmakasaṅkhārānaṃ nikkhepakaṇḍarūpakaṇḍavasena, taṇhāya saṃkilesavatthuvibhaṅge nikkhepakaṇḍe ca taṇhāniddesavasena, vipallāsānaṃ sukhasaññādivasena dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatavasena ca vibhāgo veditabbo.

But how is there relishability in painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings? Due to perversion and to the existence of a designation as pleasure. For thus it has been said: “Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is pleasant while it lasts and painful when it changes. Painful feeling is painful while it lasts and pleasant when it changes. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant with knowledge and painful without knowledge.” Therein, the division of feeling should be known by way of the one hundred and eight aspects; the division of the formations of the three realms by way of the Nikkhepakaṇḍa and the Rūpakaṇḍa; the division of craving by way of the exposition of craving in the Saṃkilesavatthuvibhaṅga and the Nikkhepakaṇḍa; and the division of the perversions by way of the perception of pleasure and so on, and by way of the sixty-two kinds of wrong views.

Ādīnavo dukkhā vedanā tissopi vā dukkhatā. Atha vā sabbepi tebhūmakā saṅkhārā ādīnavo. Ādīnaṃ ativiya kapaṇaṃ vāti pavattatīti hi ādīnavo, kapaṇamanusso, evaṃsabhāvā ca tebhūmakā dhammā aniccatādiyogena. Yato tattha ādīnavānupassanā āraddhavipassakānaṃ yathābhūtanayoti vuccati. Tathā ca vuttaṃ – “yaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṃ pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ādīnavo”ti. Tasmā ādīnavo dukkhasaccaniddesabhūtānaṃ jātiyādīnaṃ aniccatādīnaṃ dvācattālīsāya ākārānañca vasena vibhajitvā niddisitabbo.

Danger is painful feeling, or the three kinds of suffering. Or, all formations of the three realms are danger. For, because it proceeds as extremely wretched and miserable, it is called danger, like a wretched person; and the phenomena of the three realms have such a nature due to their connection with impermanence and so on. For this reason, for those who have undertaken insight meditation, the contemplation of danger therein is called the method of seeing things as they truly are. And thus it has been said: “Bhikkhus, that the five aggregates of clinging are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the five aggregates of clinging.” Therefore, danger should be expounded by analyzing it by way of birth and so on, which are the exposition of the truth of suffering, and by way of the forty-two aspects such as impermanence.

Nissarati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ, ariyamaggo. Nissaratīti vā nissaraṇaṃ nibbānaṃ. Ubhayampi sāmaññaniddesena ekasesena vā “nissaraṇa”nti [M 0.0021] vuttaṃ. Pi-saddo purimānaṃ pacchimānañca sampiṇḍanattho. Tattha ariyamaggapakkhe satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ sattattiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ kāyānupassanādīnañca tadantogadhabhedānaṃ vasena nissaraṇaṃ vibhajitvā niddisitabbaṃ.

'One escapes by means of this', therefore it is escape; this is the Noble Path. Or, 'one escapes', therefore it is escape; this is Nibbāna. Both are called 'escape' by way of a general designation or by way of an elliptical compound. The particle 'pi' has the meaning of combining what precedes and what follows. Therein, on the side of the Noble Path, escape should be analyzed and expounded by way of the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness, and by way of the contemplation of the body and so on, with their divisions included therein.

Nibbānapakkhe pana kiñcāpi asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā nippariyāyena vibhāgo natthi. Pariyāyena pana sopādisesanirupādisesabhedena. Yato vā taṃ nissaṭaṃ, tesaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.3) dassitappabhedānaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ channaṃ dvārānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ channaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ taṃtaṃdvārappavattānaṃ [V 0.0154] channaṃ channaṃ viññāṇaphassavedanāsaññācetanātaṇhāvitakkavicārānaṃ pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ channaṃ dhātūnaṃ dasannaṃ kasiṇāyatanānaṃ asubhānaṃ kesādīnaṃ dvattiṃsāya ākārānaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ lokiyānaṃ indriyānaṃ kāmadhātuādīnaṃ tissannaṃ dhātūnaṃ kāmabhavādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ appamaññānaṃ āruppānaṃ dvādasannaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṅgānañcāti evamādīnaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ nissaraṇabhāvena ca vibhajitvā niddisitabbaṃ.

On the side of Nibbāna, however, although there is no distinction of the unconditioned element in an absolute sense, it should be expounded by distinguishing it conventionally, by way of the division into that with residue remaining and that without residue remaining. Or, because it is the escape from them, it should be expounded by distinguishing it as the escape from all these conditioned phenomena: the six sense-bases such as the eye, whose distinctions are shown in the Paṭisambhidāmagga; the six sense-objects such as forms; the six each of consciousnesses, contacts, feelings, perceptions, volitions, cravings, initial thoughts, and sustained thoughts occurring at each respective door; the six elements such as the earth element; the ten kasiṇa absorptions; the thirty-two parts of the body beginning with hair of the head; the five aggregates; the twelve sense-spheres; the eighteen elements; the mundane faculties; the three realms such as the sensuality-sphere; the three sets of three kinds of existence such as sensual existence; the four jhānas; the immeasurables; the formless attainments; and the twelve factors of dependent origination, and so on.

Phalanti desanāphalaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Yaṃ desanāya nipphādīyati. Nanu ca nibbānādhigamo bhagavato desanāya nipphādīyati. Nibbānañca “nissaraṇa”nti iminā vuttamevāti? Saccametaṃ, tañca kho paramparāya. Idha pana paccakkhato desanāphalaṃ adhippetaṃ. Taṃ pana sutamayañāṇaṃ. Atthadhammavedādiariyamaggassa pubbabhāgappaṭipattibhūtā chabbisuddhiyo. Yañca tasmiṃ khaṇe maggaṃ anabhisambhuṇantassa kālantare tadadhigamakāraṇabhūtaṃ sampattibhavahetu ca siyā. Tathā hi vakkhati – “attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca, evaṃ maccutaro siyāti (su. ni. 1125; kathā. 226; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchā 144, mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88; netti. 5; peṭako. 22) idaṃ phala”nti, “dhammo have rakkhati dhammacārinti idaṃ phala”nti (jā. 1.10.102-103; 1.15.385) ca. Etena nayena devesu ca mānusesu ca āyuvaṇṇabalasukhayasaparivāraādhipateyyasampattiyo upadhisampattiyo cakkavattisirī devarajjasirī cattāri sampatticakkāni sīlasampadā samādhisampadā tisso vijjā cha abhiññā catasso paṭisambhidā sāvakabodhi paccekabodhi sammāsambodhīti sabbāpi sampattiyo puññasambhārahetukā bhagavato desanāya sādhetabbatāya phalanti veditabbā.

'Fruit' means the fruit of the teaching. But what is that? That which is accomplished through the teaching. Indeed, is not the attainment of Nibbāna accomplished through the Blessed One’s teaching? And is not Nibbāna already spoken of by this term 'escape'? This is true, but that is so by way of succession. Here, however, the direct fruit of the teaching is intended. That is the knowledge born of hearing, and the six purifications, which are the preliminary practice for the Noble Path that begins with understanding the meaning and the Dhamma. And for one who does not accomplish the path at that moment, it may in another time become the cause for its attainment and the basis for a fortunate existence. Thus he will say: “Having dispelled self-view, thus one may cross over death—this is the fruit,” and, “Indeed, the Dhamma protects one who lives by the Dhamma—this is the fruit.” In this way, among devas and humans, the accomplishments of long life, beauty, strength, happiness, fame, retinue, and sovereignty; the accomplishments of personal existence; the glory of a wheel-turning monarch; the glory of a divine king; the four wheels of accomplishment; perfection in virtue; perfection in concentration; the three knowledges; the six direct knowledges; the four analytical knowledges; the enlightenment of a disciple; the enlightenment of a private buddha; and supreme full enlightenment—all such accomplishments, having the accumulation of merit as their cause, should be known as 'fruit' because they are to be achieved through the Blessed One’s teaching.

Upāyoti [M 0.0022] ariyamaggapadaṭṭhānabhūtā pubbabhāgappaṭipadā. Sā hi purimā purimā pacchimāya pacchimāya adhigamūpāyabhāvato paramparāya magganibbānādhigamassa ca hetubhāvato upāyo. Yā ca pubbe vuttaphalādhigamassa upāyapaṭipatti. Keci pana “saha vipassanāya maggo upāyo”ti vadanti, tesaṃ matena nissaraṇanti nibbānameva vuttaṃ siyā. Phalaṃ viya upāyopi pubbabhāgoti vuttaṃ siyā, yaṃ pana vakkhati “sabbe dhammā…pe… visuddhiyāti (dha. pa. 279; theragā. 678) ayaṃ upāyo”ti. Etthāpi pubbabhāgappaṭipadā eva udāhaṭāti sakkā viññātuṃ. Yasmā pana “te pahāya tare oghanti idaṃ nissaraṇa”nti ariyamaggassa nissaraṇabhāvaṃ vakkhati. Ariyamaggo hi oghataraṇanti.

'Means' is the preliminary practice that is the proximate cause of the noble path, and it is also the practice that is the means for attaining the previously mentioned fruit. For that practice is the 'means' because each preceding stage is the means for attaining each subsequent stage, and because it is the cause for successively attaining the path and Nibbāna. Some, however, say, 'The path together with insight is the means.' According to their view, by 'escape' only Nibbāna would be meant. Just as 'fruit' was spoken of as the preliminary part, 'means' too would have to be spoken of as the preliminary part. But what he will state is, 'All phenomena... for purification—this is the means.' Here too, it can be understood that only the preliminary practice is pointed out. Moreover, since he will state that the noble path is the escape by saying, 'Having abandoned them, one crosses the flood—this is the escape,' it follows that by the term 'escape' not only Nibbāna is meant, but the path is also meant. For the noble path is indeed the crossing of the flood.

Āṇattīti [V 0.0155] āṇārahassa bhagavato veneyyajanassa hitasiddhiyā “evaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti vidhānaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu, mogharājāti (su. ni. 1125; kathā. 226; netti. 5; peṭako. 22; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchā 144, mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88) āṇattī”ti.

'Command' is the injunction of the Blessed One, who is worthy of giving commands, for the accomplishment of the welfare of those to be trained: 'You should practice thus.' Indeed, he will say, 'Look upon the world as empty, Mogharāja—this is the command.'

Yogīnanti catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāya yuttappayuttānaṃ veneyyānaṃ, atthāyāti vacanaseso. Desanāhāroti etesaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ assādādīnaṃ vibhajanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso desanāhāro nāmāti attho. Etthāha – kiṃ panetesaṃ assādādīnaṃ anavasesānaṃ vacanaṃ desanāhāro, udāhu ekaccānanti? Niravasesānaṃyeva. Yasmiñhi sutte assādādīnavanissaraṇāni sarūpato āgatāni, tattha vattabbameva natthi. Yattha pana ekadesena āgatāni, na vā sarūpena. Tattha anāgataṃ atthavasena niddhāretvā hāro yojetabbo. Ayañca attho desanāhāravibhaṅge āgamissatīti idha na papañcito.

Regarding 'for yogis': the remainder of the phrase to be supplied is 'for the welfare of' the receptive individuals who are diligently engaged in the cultivation of the meditation subject of the four truths. 'Hāra of the teaching' means: a special exposition characterized by the analysis of these aforementioned things such as gratification is called the 'hāra of the teaching'. Here it is asked: Is the 'hāra of the teaching' the statement of all these things such as gratification without remainder, or of only some? Of all without remainder, indeed. For in a sutta where gratification, danger, and escape are present in their own form, there is nothing further to be said. But where they are present only partially, or not in their own form, the hāra should be applied by determining what is not present by way of its meaning. And this meaning will be forthcoming in the analysis of the hāra of the teaching, so it is not elaborated upon here.

2. Yaṃ pucchitanti yā pucchā, viciyamānāti vacanaseso. Vissajjitaṃ anugītīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tattha vissajjitanti vissajjanā, sā ekaṃsabyākaraṇādivasena catubbidhaṃ byākaraṇaṃ. Ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, tena gāthāyaṃ avuttaṃ padādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tā pana pucchāvissajjanā kassāti āha “suttassā”ti. Etena sutte āgataṃ pucchāvissajjanaṃ vicetabbanti dasseti. Yā ca anugītiti vuttasseva atthassa yā anu pacchā gīti anugīti, saṅgahagāthā, pucchāya vā anurūpā gīti. Etena pubbāparaṃ [M 0.0023] gahitaṃ. Byākaraṇassa hi pucchānurūpatā idha pubbāparaṃ adhippetaṃ. Yā “pucchānusandhī”ti vuccati. Purimaṃ “suttassā”ti padaṃ pubbāpekkhanti puna “suttassā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena suttassa nissayabhūte assādādike pariggaṇhāti. Ettāvatā vicayahārassa visayo niravasesena dassito hoti. Tathā ca vakkhati vicayahāravibhaṅge “padaṃ vicinati…pe… anugītiṃ vicinatī”ti.

2. Regarding `yaṃ pucchitaṃ` (what was asked), it means `yā pucchā` (the question); `viciyamānā` (being investigated) is the remainder of the statement that should be supplied. In the phrase `vissajjitaṃ anugīti` (the answer and the recitation in response) as well, this same method is to be applied. Therein, `vissajjitaṃ` means the answer, and that answer is fourfold by way of categorical explanation and so on. The particle `ca` has the meaning of grouping together; by it, one includes unstated words and so on in the verse. To whom, then, do these questions and answers belong? To this, it is said: 'of the discourse' (`suttassa`). By this, it is shown that the questions and answers that have come in the discourse are to be investigated. And `yā anugīti` (the recitation in response) is the recitation that comes after the meaning already stated—an `anugīti` is a summary verse, or a recitation suitable to the question. By this, what precedes and what follows is grasped. For the suitability of the answer to the question is here intended as 'what precedes and what follows,' which is called `pucchānusandhi` (the sequence of the question). The former word `suttassa` is dependent on what precedes it, and so `suttassa` is stated again. By that latter term, it comprehends gratification and so on, which are the basis of the discourse. By this much, the scope of the Guideline of Investigation is shown without remainder. And so it will be said in the Analysis of the Guideline of Investigation: 'One investigates the word... one investigates the recitation in response.'

Tattha sutte sabbesaṃ padānaṃ anupubbena atthaso byañjanaso ca vicayo padavicayo. “Ayaṃ pucchā adiṭṭhajotanā diṭṭhasaṃsandanā vimaticchedanā anumatipucchā kathetukamyatāpucchā sattādhiṭṭhānā dhammādhiṭṭhānā ekādhiṭṭhānā anekādhiṭṭhānā sammutivisayā paramatthavisayā atītavisayā anāgatavisayā paccuppannavisayā”tiādinā pucchāvicayo veditabbo. “Idaṃ vissajjanaṃ [V 0.0156] ekaṃsabyākaraṇaṃ vibhajjabyākaraṇaṃ paṭipucchābyākaraṇaṃ ṭhapanaṃ sāvasesaṃ niravasesaṃ sauttaraṃ anuttaraṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttara”ntiādinā vissajjanavicayo.

Therein, the investigation of all words in a discourse, sequentially, both in terms of meaning and expression, is the Investigation of Words. The Investigation of Questions should be understood by way of: 'This question is one that illuminates the unseen, one that corroborates the seen, one that severs uncertainty, a question for confirmation, a question born of a desire to speak, one founded on beings, one founded on dhammas, one founded on a single thing, one founded on multiple things, one whose domain is convention, one whose domain is the ultimate reality, one whose domain is the past, one whose domain is the future, one whose domain is the present,' and so on. The Investigation of Answers should be understood by way of: 'This answer is a categorical explanation, an analytical explanation, an explanation by counter-question, a setting aside, one with a remainder, one without a remainder, one with something superior, one with nothing superior, worldly, supramundane,' and so on.

“Ayaṃ pucchā iminā sameti, etena na sametī”ti pucchitatthaṃ ānetvā vicayo pubbenāparaṃ saṃsanditvā ca vicayo pubbāparavicayo. “Ayaṃ anugīti vuttatthasaṅgahā avuttatthasaṅgahā tadubhayatthasaṅgahā kusalatthasaṅgahā akusalatthasaṅgahā”tiādinā anugītivicayo. Assādādīsu sukhavedanāya “iṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, taṇhāya “ārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, vipallāsānaṃ “viparītaggahaṇalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, avasiṭṭhānaṃ tebhūmakadhammānaṃ “yathāsakalakkhaṇā”tiādinā sabbesañca dvāvīsatiyā tikesu dvācattālīsādhike ca dukasate labbhamānapadavasena taṃtaṃassādatthavisesaniddhāraṇaṃ assādavicayo.

The investigation by bringing forth the meaning of what was asked, thus: ‘This question agrees with this answer, but does not agree with that one,’ and the investigation by connecting what precedes with what follows, is the Investigation of What Precedes and Follows. The Investigation of the Recitation in Response is by way of: ‘This recitation in response summarizes the stated meaning, summarizes the unstated meaning, summarizes the meaning of both, summarizes the wholesome meaning, summarizes the unwholesome meaning,’ and so on. Among allure and so on, the investigation of pleasant feeling is by way of ‘it has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object,’ and so on; of craving, by way of ‘it has the characteristic of grasping an object,’ and so on; of the perversions, by way of ‘they have the characteristic of grasping pervertedly,’ and so on; of the remaining phenomena of the three planes, by way of ‘they have their own respective characteristics,’ and so on. And for all of them, in the twenty-two triads and in the one hundred and forty-two dyads, by way of the terms that are found, the determination of the specific meaning of each respective allure is the Investigation of Allure.

Dukkhavedanāya “aniṭṭhānubhavanalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, dukkhasaccānaṃ “paṭisandhilakkhaṇā”tiādinā, aniccatādīnaṃ ādiantavantatāya aniccantikatāya ca “aniccā”tiādinā sabbesañca lokiyadhammānaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyahānabhāgiyatādivasena ādīnavavuttiyā okāraniddhāraṇena ādīnavavicayo. Nissaraṇapade ariyamaggassa āgamanato [M 0.0024] kāyānupassanādipubbabhāgappaṭipadāvibhāgavisesaniddhāraṇavasena nibbānassa yathāvuttapariyāyavibhāgavisesaniddhāraṇavasenāti evaṃ nissaraṇavicayo. Phalādīnaṃ taṃtaṃsuttadesanāya sādhetabbaphalassa tadupāyassa tattha tattha suttavidhivacanassa ca vibhāganiddhāraṇavasena vicayo veditabbo. Evaṃ padapucchāvissajjanapubbāparānugītīnaṃ assādādīnañca visesaniddhāraṇavaseneva vicayalakkhaṇo “vicayo hāro”ti veditabbo.

The investigation of painful feeling is by way of ‘it has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object,’ and so on; of the truths of suffering, by way of ‘they have the characteristic of rebirth-linking,’ and so on; of impermanence and so on, because of having a beginning and an end and because of having an impermanent nature, by way of ‘they are impermanent,’ and so on. And for all worldly phenomena, by way of being on the side of defilement, on the side of decline, and so on, the Investigation of Danger is through the determination of the inferiority of the occurrence of danger. In the section on escape, regarding the noble path, because of its arising, by way of determining the specific analysis of the preliminary practice such as contemplation of the body; and regarding Nibbāna, by way of determining the specific analysis of the method as stated—thus is the Investigation of Escape. The investigation of fruit and so on is to be understood by way of determining the analysis of the fruit to be accomplished, its means, and the statement of the sutta method in each respective discourse. Thus, that which has the characteristic of investigation by way of determining the specifics of words, questions, answers, what precedes and follows, recitations in response, and of allure and so on, should be known as the ‘Guideline of Investigation.’

3. Sabbesanti soḷasannaṃ. Bhūmīti byañjanaṃ sandhāyāha. Byañjanañhi mūlapadāni viya nayānaṃ hārānaṃ bhūmi pavattiṭṭhānaṃ, tesaṃ byañjanavicārabhāvato. Vuttañhi – “hārā byañjanavicayo”ti, peṭakepi hi vuttaṃ – “yattha ca sabbe hārā, sampatamānā nayanti suttatthaṃ. Byañjanavidhiputhuttā”ti. Gocaroti suttattho. Suttassa hi padatthuddhāraṇamukhena hārayojanā. Tesaṃ byañjanatthānaṃ. Yuttāyuttaparikkhāti yuttassa ca ayuttassa ca upaparikkhā. “Yuttāyuttiparikkhā”tipi pāṭho, yuttiayuttīnaṃ vicāraṇāti attho. Kathaṃ pana tesaṃ yuttāyuttajānanā? Catūhi mahāpadesehi avirujjhanena. Tattha byañjanassa tāva sabhāvaniruttibhāvo adhippetatthavācakabhāvo ca yuttabhāvo. Atthassa pana suttavinayadhammatāhi avilomanaṃ[V 0.0157]. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana parato āvi bhavissati. Hāro yuttīti niddiṭṭhoti evaṃ sutte byañjanatthānaṃ yuttāyuttabhāvavibhāvanalakkhaṇo yuttihāroti veditabbo.

3. As for ‘sabbesaṃ’ (of all), it means of the sixteen. The word ‘bhūmi’ (ground) is said in reference to ‘byañjanaṃ’ (the expression). For the expression is the ground, the place of occurrence, for the guidelines, just as the root words are for the methods, because they (the guidelines) investigate the expression. For it is said: ‘The guidelines are the investigation of the expression.’ And in the Peṭaka it is also said: ‘Where all the guidelines, converging, lead to the meaning of the discourse through the diversity of the method of expression.’ ‘Gocaro’ (the domain) is the meaning of the discourse. For the application of the guidelines occurs by means of extracting the word-meanings of the discourse. Of those expressions and meanings, ‘yuttāyuttaparikkhā’ is the examination of the suitable and the unsuitable. There is also the reading ‘yuttāyuttiparikkhā,’ which means the investigation of suitability and unsuitability. But how is the knowledge of their suitability and unsuitability obtained? Through non-contradiction with the four great references. Therein, for the expression, its suitability is its being a natural expression and its being a conveyor of the intended meaning. As for the meaning, its suitability is its non-opposition to the Sutta, the Vinaya, and the nature of things. This is the summary here; the detail will become clear later. As for ‘The guideline is pointed out as suitability,’ it means that which has the characteristic of demonstrating the state of suitability and unsuitability of the expressions and meanings in a discourse should be known as the Guideline of Suitability.

4. Dhammanti yaṃ kiñci suttāgataṃ kusalādidhammamāha. Tassa dhammassāti tassa yathāvuttassa kusalādidhammassa. Yaṃ padaṭṭhānanti yaṃ kāraṇaṃ, yonisomanasikārādi sutte āgataṃ vā anāgataṃ vā sambhavato niddhāretvā kathetabbanti adhippāyo. Itīti evaṃ, vuttanayenāti attho. Yāva sabbadhammāti yattakā tasmiṃ sutte āgatā dhammā, tesaṃ sabbesampi yathānurūpaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ niddhāretvā kathetabbanti adhippāyo. Atha vā yāva sabbadhammāti suttāgatassa dhammassa yaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, tassapi yaṃ padaṭṭhānanti sambhavato yāva sabbadhammā padaṭṭhānavicāraṇā kātabbāti attho. Eso hāro padaṭṭhānoti evaṃ sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānabhūtā dhammā tesañca padaṭṭhānabhūtāti sambhavato padaṭṭhānabhūtadhammaniddhāraṇalakkhaṇo padaṭṭhāno nāma hāroti attho.

4. By ‘dhamma’ is meant whatever wholesome dhamma, etc., has come in the sutta. ‘Of that dhamma’ means of that wholesome dhamma, etc., as has been said. ‘Which is the proximate cause’ means which cause—such as wise attention, etc.—whether it has come in the sutta or has not come, should be determined and stated according to what is possible; this is the intention. ‘Iti’ means ‘thus, by the method that has been stated.’ ‘Up to all dhammas’ means that for however many dhammas have come in that sutta, the proximate cause of all of them should be determined and stated appropriately; this is the intention. Alternatively, regarding ‘up to all dhammas’: whatever is the proximate cause of a dhamma that has come in the sutta, and whatever is the proximate cause of that proximate cause as well—thus, the investigation of proximate causes should be carried out up to all dhammas, according to what is possible; this is the meaning. Regarding ‘this is the guideline Padaṭṭhāna’: thus, there are dhammas that are the proximate causes of the dhammas that have come in the sutta, and there are further proximate causes of those proximate causes—thus, the guideline named ‘Padaṭṭhāna’ has the characteristic of determining dhammas that are proximate causes, according to what is possible; this is the meaning.

5. Vuttamhi [M 0.0025] ekadhammeti kusalādīsu khandhādīsu vā yasmiṃ kismiñci ekadhamme, sutte sarūpato niddhāraṇavasena vā kathite. Ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā kecīti ye keci dhammā kusalādibhāvena rūpakkhandhādibhāvena vā tena dhammena samānalakkhaṇā. Vuttā bhavanti sabbeti te sabbepi kusalādisabhāvā, khandhādisabhāvā vā dhammā sutte avuttāpi tāya samānalakkhaṇatāya vuttā bhavanti ānetvā saṃvaṇṇanāvasenāti adhippāyo. Ettha ca ekalakkhaṇāti samānalakkhaṇā vuttā. Tena sahacāritā samānakiccatā samānahetutā samānaphalatā samānārammaṇatāti evamādīhi avuttānampi vuttānaṃ viya niddhāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. So hāro lakkhaṇo nāmāti evaṃ sutte anāgatepi dhamme vuttappakārena āgate viya niddhāretvā yā saṃvaṇṇanā, so lakkhaṇo nāma hāroti attho.

5. ‘When one dhamma is stated’ means: when any one dhamma among wholesome dhammas, etc., or among the aggregates, etc., is taught in the sutta, either in its own nature or by way of determination. ‘Whatever dhammas have a single characteristic’ means: whatever dhammas, by being wholesome, etc., or by being the aggregate of form, etc., have a characteristic in common with that dhamma. ‘All are said to be stated’ means: all those dhammas, whether having a wholesome nature, etc., or having the nature of an aggregate, etc., even if unstated in the sutta, are, because of that common characteristic, brought in by way of explanation and are considered stated; this is the intention. And here, by ‘of a single characteristic,’ dhammas of a common characteristic are stated. Therefore, by means of co-arising, common function, common cause, common result, common object, and so on, the determination of even the unstated should be known as being like that of the stated. ‘That guideline is named Lakkhaṇa’ means: thus, the explanation that arises by determining even a dhamma that has not come in the sutta as if it had come, in the manner stated—that is the guideline named ‘Lakkhaṇa’; this is the meaning.

6. Neruttanti niruttaṃ, padanibbacananti attho. Adhippāyoti buddhānaṃ sāvakānaṃ vā tassa suttassa desakānaṃ adhippāyo. Byañjananti byañjanena, karaṇe hi etaṃ paccattaṃ. Kāmañca sabbe hārā byañjanavicayā, ayaṃ pana visesato byañjanadvāreneva atthapariyesanāti katvā “byañjana”nti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati – “byañjanena suttassa neruttañca adhippāyo ca nidānañca pubbāparānusandhi ca gavesitabbā”ti. Athāti padapūraṇamattaṃ. Desanānidānanti nidadāti phalanti nidānaṃ, kāraṇaṃ, yena kāraṇena desanā pavattā, taṃ desanāya pavattinimittanti attho. Pubbāparānusandhīti pubbena ca aparena ca anusandhi. “Pubbāparena sandhī”tipi [V 0.0158] pāṭho, suttassa pubbabhāgena aparabhāgaṃ saṃsanditvā kathananti attho. Saṅgītivasena vā pubbāparabhūtehi suttantarehi saṃvaṇṇiyamānassa suttassa saṃsandanaṃ pubbāparānusandhi. Yañca pubbapadena parapadassa sambandhanaṃ, ayampi pubbāparānusandhi. Eso hāro catubyūhoti evaṃ nibbacanādhippāyādīnaṃ catunnaṃ vibhāvanalakkhaṇo catubyūho hāro nāmāti attho.

6. 'Nerutta' is nirutta (etymology); the meaning is 'explanation of the word'. 'Adhippāya' is the intention of the teachers of that sutta, whether Buddhas or their disciples. 'Byañjana' means 'by the letter/expression', for this nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. And while it is true that all hāras are investigations of the letter/expression, this one, however, is especially a search for the meaning only through the door of the letter/expression; having considered this, it is called 'byañjana'. For thus it will be said: "Through the letter/expression, the etymology of the sutta, the intention, the cause, and the connection of the preceding and succeeding should be investigated." 'Atha' is merely a particle that fills out the phrase. 'Desanānidāna' (cause of the teaching) means: it gives a result, therefore it is 'nidāna' (cause); the cause by which the teaching occurred, that is, the reason for the teaching's occurrence; this is the meaning. 'Pubbāparānusandhi' is the connection with the preceding and with the succeeding. There is also the reading 'pubbāparena sandhi'; the meaning is the stating of the meaning by connecting the latter part of the sutta with the former part. Or, by way of the recitation, the connection of the sutta being explained with other suttas that are preceding and succeeding is 'pubbāparānusandhi'. And whatever connection there is of a later word with a preceding word, this too is 'pubbāparānusandhi'. 'This hāra is Catubyūha' means: thus, the special explanation characterized by the clarification of the four—etymology, intention, etc.—is the hāra named 'Catubyūha'; this is the meaning.

7. Ekamhi padaṭṭhāneti ekasmiṃ ārambhadhātuādike parakkamadhātuādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānabhūte dhamme desanāruḷhe sati. Pariyesati sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānanti tassa visabhāgatāya aggahaṇena vā sesakaṃ pamādādīnaṃ āsannakāraṇattā padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ kosajjādikaṃ dhammantaraṃ pariyesati paññāya gavesati, pariyesitvā ca saṃvaṇṇanāya yojento desanaṃ [M 0.0026] āvaṭṭati paṭipakkheti vīriyārambhādimukhena āraddhasuttaṃ vuttanayena pamādādivasena niddisanto desanaṃ paṭipakkhato āvaṭṭeti nāma. Āvaṭṭo nāma so hāroti desanāya gahitadhammānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammavasena āvaṭṭanalakkhaṇo āvaṭṭo hāro nāmāti attho.

7. Regarding 'in one proximate cause': this refers to when a dhamma, such as the element of initiating energy, etc., which is the proximate cause of the element of exertion, etc., has been taken up in the teaching. Regarding 'one seeks the remaining proximate cause': this means one seeks, one searches with wisdom for another dhamma, the remaining one—such as laziness, etc., which is the proximate cause because it is the near cause of negligence, etc.—either because of its dissimilarity or because it was not mentioned in the sutta. And having sought, applying it in the explanation, one revolves the teaching, one counters it. By indicating the sutta that was begun by way of initiating effort, etc., in the manner stated, by way of negligence, etc., one is said to revolve the teaching from the opposite side. Regarding 'that hāra is named Āvaṭṭa': the meaning is that the special explanation characterized by revolving by way of similar and dissimilar dhammas of the dhammas taken up in the teaching is the hāra named 'Āvaṭṭa'.

8. Dhammanti sabhāvadhammaṃ, taṃ kusalādivasena anekavidhaṃ. Padaṭṭhānanti yasmiṃ patiṭṭhite uttari guṇavisese adhigacchati, taṃ visesādhigamanakāraṇaṃ. Bhūminti puthujjanabhūmi dassanabhūmīti evamādikaṃ bhūmiṃ. Vibhajjateti vibhāgena katheti. Sādhāraṇeti dassanapahātabbādināmavasena vā puthujjanasotāpannādivatthuvasena vā sādhāraṇe avisiṭṭhe samāneti attho. Vuttavipariyāyena asādhāraṇā veditabbā. Neyyo vibhattīti yathāvuttadhammādīnaṃ vibhajano ayaṃ hāro vibhattīti ñātabboti attho. Tasmā saṃkilesadhamme vodānadhamme ca sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇato padaṭṭhānato bhūmito ca vibhajanalakkhaṇo “vibhattihāro”ti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

8. 'Dhamma' means intrinsic nature; it is of many kinds by way of wholesome, etc. 'Proximate cause' means that cause, being established in which, one attains further special qualities; it is the cause for the attainment of distinction. 'Level' means a level such as the level of an ordinary person, the level of vision, and so on. 'One analyzes' means one speaks with division. 'Common' means common, undifferentiated, same—either by way of the name 'to be abandoned by vision', etc., or by way of the basis of an ordinary person, a stream-enterer, etc.; this is the meaning. By way of the opposite of what was said, 'uncommon' should be known. Regarding `Neyyo vibhatti` ('Vibhatti is to be understood'): the meaning is that this hāra, which is the analyzer of the dhammas and so on as stated, is to be known as 'Vibhatti'. Therefore, the special explanation characterized by analyzing defiled dhammas and purified dhammas by way of common and uncommon, by way of proximate cause, and by way of level, should be seen as the 'Vibhatti-hāra'.

9. Niddiṭṭheti kathite sutte āgate, saṃvaṇṇite vā. Bhāviteti yathā uppannasadisā uppannāti vuccanti, evaṃ bhāvitasadise bhāvetabbeti attho. Pahīneti etthāpi eseva nayo. Parivattati paṭipakkheti vuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ ye paṭipakkhā, tesaṃ vasena parivattetīti attho. Evaṃ niddiṭṭhānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭipakkhato parivattanalakkhaṇo “parivattano hāro”ti veditabbo.

9. Regarding 'indicated': this means stated, having come in the sutta, or explained. Regarding 'developed': just as things similar to what has arisen are called 'arisen', so too, that which is to be developed is called 'developed' when it is similar to what has been developed; this is the meaning. Regarding 'abandoned', here too this same method applies. Regarding 'one reverses, one counters': this means one reverses by way of whatever are the opposites of the stated dhammas; this is the meaning. Thus, the special explanation characterized by reversing from the opposite of the indicated dhammas should be known as the 'Parivattana-hāra'.

10. Vividhāni ekasmiṃyeva atthe vacanāni vivacanāni, vivacanāni eva vevacanāni, pariyāyasaddāti attho. Tāni vevacanāni. Bahūnīti anekāni. Tu-saddo avadhāraṇe. Tena bahū eva pariyāyasaddā vevacanahārayojanāyaṃ kathetabbā, na katipayāti dasseti[V 0.0159]. Sutte vuttānīti navavidhasuttantasaṅkhāte tepiṭake buddhavacane bhāsitāni. Etthāpi tu-saddassa attho ānetvā yojetabbo, tena pāḷiyaṃ āgatāniyeva vevacanāni gahetabbānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekadhammassāti ekassa padatthassa. Yo jānāti suttavidūti yathā “sappissa jānāhī”ti vutte “sappinā vicārehi, sappiṃ dehi, dethā”ti vā āṇāpetīti attho, evaṃ yo suttakovido dhammakathiko ekassa [M 0.0027] atthassa bahūpi pariyāyasadde vicāreti vibhāveti yojetīti attho. Vevacano nāma so hāroti tassa atthassa vuttappakārapariyāyasaddayojanālakkhaṇo vevacanahāro nāma. Tasmā ekasmiṃ atthe anekapariyāyasaddayojanālakkhaṇo “vevacanahāro”ti veditabbaṃ.

10. Various words for a single meaning are `vivacanāni`. `Vivacanāni` themselves are `vevacanāni`; the meaning is synonymous terms. Those are the `vevacanāni`. `Bahūni` means numerous. The particle `tu` is for emphasis. By that, it shows that many synonymous terms should be stated in the application of the `vevacanahāra`, not just a few. `Sutte vuttāni` (spoken in the Suttas) means spoken in the Buddha's word, the Tipiṭaka, which is designated as the ninefold Suttanta. Here too, the meaning of the particle `tu` should be brought in and applied; thus it is said that only the `vevacanāni` that have come in the Pāḷi canon should be taken. `Ekadhammassāti` means of the meaning of a single term. Regarding `Yo jānāti suttavidū` (one who knows is an expert in the Suttas): the meaning is that just as when it is said, 'Know of the ghee,' one commands, 'Manage with ghee,' 'Give ghee,' or 'Give (plural) ghee'; so too, a Dhamma-speaker who is skilled in the Suttas examines, clarifies, and applies even many synonymous terms for a single meaning. Regarding 'that `hāra` is named `vevacana`': the `vevacanahāra` is that which has the characteristic of applying synonymous terms for that meaning in the manner described. Therefore, that which has the characteristic of applying numerous synonymous terms for a single meaning is to be known as the `vevacanahāra`.

11. Dhammanti khandhādidhammaṃ. Paññattīhīti paññāpanehi pakārehi ñāpanehi, asaṅkarato vā ṭhapanehi. Vividhāhīti nikkhepappabhavādivasena anekavidhāhi. So ākāroti yo ekassevatthassa nikkhepappabhavapaññattiādivasena anekāhi paññattīhi paññāpanākāro. Ñeyyo paññatti nāma hāroti paññattihāro nāmāti ñātabbo. Tasmā ekekassa dhammassa anekāhi paññattīhi paññāpetabbākāravibhāvanalakkhaṇo “paññattihāro”ti veditabbaṃ.

11. `Dhammanti` means phenomena such as the aggregates, etc. `Paññattīhīti` means by ways of making known, by modes, by ways of informing, or by ways of establishing without confusion. `Vividhāhīti` means of many kinds, by way of classification, origin, etc. Regarding `So ākāro` ('that mode'): it is whatever mode there is of making known a single meaning by means of many designations, such as those of classification, origin, and so on. Regarding `Ñeyyo paññatti nāma hāro` ('The `hāra` named Paññatti is to be understood'): this means it is to be known as the `paññattihāra`. Therefore, that which has the characteristic of clarifying the mode to be made known for each and every phenomenon by means of many designations is to be known as the `paññattihāra`.

12. Paṭiccuppādoti paṭiccasamuppādo. Indriyakhandhāti indriyāni ca khandhā ca. Dhātuāyatanāti dhātuyo ca āyatanāni ca. Etehīti yo dvādasapadiko paccayākāro yāni ca dvāvīsatindriyāni ye ca pañcakkhandhā yā ca aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo yāni ca dvādasāyatanāni, etehi sutte āgatapadatthamukhena niddhāriyamānehi. Otarati yoti yo saṃvaṇṇanānayo ogāhati, paṭiccasamuppādādike anupavisatīti attho. Otaraṇo nāma so hāroti yo yathāvutto saṃvaṇṇanāviseso, so otaraṇahāro nāma. Ca-saddena cettha suññatamukhādīnaṃ gāthāyaṃ avuttānampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ paṭiccasamuppādādimukhehi suttatthassa otaraṇalakkhaṇo otaraṇo hāro nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

12. “Paṭiccuppādo” is paṭiccasamuppādo. “Indriyakhandhā” means faculties and aggregates. “Dhātuāyatanā” means elements and bases. “Etehi” means: by these—the twelve-factored mode of conditionality, the twenty-two faculties, the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the twelve bases—which are determined by means of the meaning of the terms that have come in the Sutta. “Otarati yo” means: whatever method of commentary descends into, or enters fittingly into, dependent origination and so on; this is the meaning. That hāra called “otaraṇa” is the specific method of commentary as described; that is called the otaraṇahāra. And here, by the particle “ca,” the inclusion should be seen even of things not mentioned in the verse, such as the approach of emptiness and so on. Thus, it should be known as the otaraṇo hāro which has the characteristic of descending into the meaning of the Sutta through approaches such as dependent origination and so on.

13. Vissajjitamhīti buddhādīhi byākate. Pañheti ñātuṃ icchite atthe. Gāthāyanti gāthāruḷhe. Idañca pucchantā yebhuyyena gāthābandhavasena pucchantīti katvā vuttaṃ. Yamārabbhāti sā pana gāthā yaṃ atthaṃ ārabbha adhikicca pucchitā, tassa atthassa. Suddhāsuddhaparikkhāti padaṃ sodhitaṃ, ārambho na sodhito, padañca sodhitaṃ ārambho ca sodhitoti evaṃ padādīnaṃ sodhitāsodhitabhāvavicāro[V 0.0160]. Hāro so sodhano nāmāti yathāvuttavicāro sodhano hāro nāma. Evaṃ sutte padapadatthapañhārambhānaṃ sodhanalakkhaṇo “sodhano hāro”ti veditabbaṃ.

13. “Vissajjitamhi” means when explained by the Buddha and others. “Pañhe” means regarding a meaning one wishes to know. “Gāthāyaṃ” means when it is put into a verse. And this is said because those who ask, for the most part, ask by way of verse composition. “Yamārabbha” means: concerning whatever meaning that verse was asked, having taken it as the subject and based it thereon; of that meaning. “Suddhāsuddhaparikkhā” is the investigation of the state of being purified or unpurified of the term and so on, thus: 'the term is purified, the undertaking is not purified'; or 'both the term and the undertaking are purified.' That hāra called “sodhana” is: the aforementioned investigation is the sodhanahāra. Thus, it should be known as the sodhano hāro which has the characteristic of purifying the term, the meaning of the term, the question, and the undertaking that have come in the Sutta.

14. Ekattatāyāti [M 0.0028] ekassa bhāvo ekattaṃ, ekattameva ekattatā, tāya ekattatāya. Eka-saddo cettha samānasaddapariyāyo, tasmā sāmaññenāti attho. Visiṭṭhā mattā vimattā, vimattāva vemattaṃ, tassa bhāvo vemattatā, tāya vemattatāya, visesenāti attho. Te na vikappayitabbāti ye dhammā “dukkhaṃ samudayo”tiādinā sāmaññena, “jāti jarā kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā”tiādinā visesena ca sutte desitā, te “kimettha sāmaññaṃ, ko vā viseso”ti evaṃ sāmaññavisesavikappanavasena na vikappayitabbā. Kasmā? Sāmaññavisesakappanāya vohārabhāvena anavaṭṭhānato kāladisāvisesādīnaṃ viya apekkhāsiddhito ca. Yathā hi “ajja hiyyo sve”ti vuccamānā kālavisesā anavaṭṭhitasabhāvā “purimā disā pacchimā disā”ti vuccamānā disāvisesā ca, evaṃ sāmaññavisesāpi. Tathā hi “idaṃ dukkha”nti vuccamānaṃ jātiādiapekkhāya sāmaññampi samānaṃ saccāpekkhāya viseso hoti. Esa nayo samudayādīsupi. Eso hāro adhiṭṭhānoti evaṃ suttāgatānaṃ dhammānaṃ avikappanavasena sāmaññavisesaniddhāraṇalakkhaṇo adhiṭṭhāno hāro nāmāti attho.

14. “Ekattatāya” means: the state of being one is ekattaṃ; ekattaṃ itself is ekattatā; by that ekattatāya. And here, the word “eka” is a synonym for the word “samāna.” Therefore, the meaning is 'by generality.' A distinct measure is vimattā; vimattā itself is vemattaṃ; the state of that is vemattatā; by that vemattatāya. The meaning is 'by particularity.' “Te na vikappayitabbā” means: those phenomena taught in the Sutta both generally, such as 'suffering, origin,' and so on, and particularly, such as 'birth, aging, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence,' and so on—those phenomena should not be differentiated by way of conceptualizing generality and particularity, thinking, 'What here is generality, and what is particularity?' Why? Because they are unfixed, like the particulars of time, direction, and so on, due to the conceptualization of generality and particularity being a matter of convention, and because they are established relatively. For, just as the particulars of time spoken of as 'today, yesterday, tomorrow' and the particulars of direction spoken of as 'eastern direction, western direction' are of an unfixed nature, so too are generality and particularity. For that which is spoken of as 'this is suffering,' while being a generality in relation to birth and so on, becomes a particularity in relation to the truths. This same method applies to the origin and so on as well. “Eso hāro adhiṭṭhāno” means: thus, the adhiṭṭhāno hāro is that which has the characteristic of determining generality and particularity by way of not conceptualizing the phenomena that have come in the Sutta; this is the meaning.

15. Ye dhammāti ye avijjādikā paccayadhammā. Yaṃ dhammanti yaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ paccayuppannadhammaṃ. Janayantīti nibbattenti. Paccayāti sahajātapaccayabhāvena. Paramparatoti paramparapaccayabhāvena, anurūpasantānaghaṭanavasena paccayo hutvāti attho. Upanissayakoṭi hi idhādhippetā. Purimasmiṃ avasiṭṭho paccayabhāvo. Hetumavakaḍḍhayitvāti taṃ yathāvuttapaccayasaṅkhātaṃ janakādibhedabhinnaṃ hetuṃ ākaḍḍhitvā suttato niddhāretvā yo saṃvaṇṇanāsaṅkhāto, eso hāro parikkhāroti evaṃ sutte āgatadhammānaṃ parikkhārasaṅkhāte hetupaccaye niddhāretvā saṃvaṇṇanalakkhaṇo parikkhāro hāroti attho.

15. “Ye dhammā” means those causal phenomena beginning with ignorance. “Yaṃ dhammaṃ” means that conditionally arisen phenomenon beginning with formations. “Janayanti” means they produce. “Paccayā” means in the manner of a co-nascent condition. “Paramparato” means in the manner of a sequential condition; the meaning is: having become a condition by way of connecting a suitable continuity. For here, the category of decisive support condition is intended. In the former, the remaining state of being a condition is intended. “Hetumavakaḍḍhayitvā” means: having drawn out and determined from the Sutta that cause—which is designated as the aforementioned condition and is differentiated by kinds such as generative—whatever is designated as the explanation, that hāra is parikkhāra. Thus, the parikkhāro hāro has the characteristic of explaining by determining the cause-and-condition, designated as requisites, for the phenomena that have come in the Sutta; this is the meaning.

16. Ye dhammāti ye sīlādidhammā. Yaṃmūlāti yesaṃ samādhiādīnaṃ mūlabhūtā, te tesaṃ samādhiādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvena samāropayitabbāti sambandho. Ye cekatthā pakāsitā munināti ye ca rāgavirāgācetovimuttisekkhaphalakāmadhātusamatikkamanādisaddā anāgāmiphalatthatāya ekatthā buddhamuninā paridīpitā, te aññamaññavevacanabhāvena samāropayitabbāti sambandho. Samāropanañcettha sutte yathārutavasena [M 0.0029] niddhāraṇavasena vā gayhamānassa sikkhattayasaṅkhātassa [V 0.0161] sīlādikkhandhattayassa pariyāyantaravibhāvanamukhena bhāvanāpāripūrikathanaṃ, bhāvanāpāripūrī ca pahātabbassa pahānenāti pahānasamāropanāpi atthato dassitā eva hoti. Esa samāropano hāroti esa sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānavevacanabhāvanāpahānasamāropanavicāraṇalakkhaṇo samāropano nāma hāroti attho.

16. “Ye dhammā” means: which phenomena such as virtue and so on. “Yaṃmūlā” means: which are the root-cause of concentration and so on; the connection is that those phenomena should be applied to that concentration and so on as their proximate cause. “Ye cekatthā pakāsitā muninā” means: and which terms such as rāgavirāga, cetovimutti, sekkhaphala, kāmadhātusamatikkamana, and so on, having the same meaning in the sense of the fruit of non-returning, were illuminated by the Buddha-sage; the connection is that they should be applied as synonyms for one another. And herein, attribution is the stating of the fulfillment of development by means of revealing alternative terms for the three aggregates beginning with virtue, known as the threefold training, which is taken from the Sutta either by way of the literal text or by way of determination. And since the fulfillment of development occurs through the abandoning of what is to be abandoned, the attribution by way of abandoning is also shown in meaning. “Esa samāropano hāro” means: this hāra which has the characteristic of investigating the attribution of phenomena that have come in the Sutta by way of proximate cause, synonym, development, and abandoning, is the hāra named samāropano; this is the meaning.

Nayasaṅkhepo

Summary of the Methods

17. Evaṃ gāthābandhavasena soḷasapi hāre niddisitvā idāni naye niddisituṃ “taṇhañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha taṇhañca avijjampi cāti sutte āgataṃ atthato niddhāraṇavasena vā gahitaṃ taṇhaṃ avijjañca yo netīti sambandho. Yo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso taṃ neti saṃkilesapakkhaṃ pāpeti saṃkilesavasena suttatthaṃ yojetīti adhippāyo. Samathenāti samādhinā. Vipassanāyāti paññāya, yo neti vodānapakkhaṃ pāpeti, tathā suttatthaṃ yojetīti adhippāyo. Saccehi yojayitvāti nayanto ca taṇhā ca avijjā ca bhavamūlakattā samudayasaccaṃ, avasesā tebhūmakadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, samathavipassanā maggasaccaṃ, tena pattabbā asaṅkhatadhātu nirodhasaccanti evaṃ imehi catūhi saccehi yojetvā. Ayaṃ nayo nandiyāvaṭṭoti yo taṇhāvijjāhi saṃkilesapakkhassa suttatthassa samathavipassanāhi vodānapakkhassa catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso, ayaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭo nayo nāmāti attho. Ettha ca nayassa bhūmi gāthāyaṃ “nayo”ti vuttā, tasmā saṃvaṇṇanāvisesoti vuttaṃ. Na hi atthanayo saṃvaṇṇanā, catusaccapaṭivedhassa anurūpo pubbabhāge anugāhaṇanayo atthanayo. Tassa pana yā ugghaṭitaññuādīnaṃ vasena taṇhādimukhena nayabhūmiracanā, tattha nayavohāro.

17. Thus, having expounded all sixteen hāras by means of the verse composition, now, in order to expound the methods, that which begins with 'taṇhañca' is stated. Therein, regarding 'taṇhañca avijjampi ca', the connection is with 'yo neti' ('which leads'), governing craving and ignorance, which have come in the Sutta or are taken by way of determining the meaning. The intended meaning is: that special exposition which leads it, causes it to arrive at the side of defilement, and connects the meaning of the Sutta by way of defilement. 'Samathena' means by concentration. 'Vipassanāya' means by wisdom; the intended meaning is: that which leads, causes it to arrive at the side of purification, and similarly connects the meaning of the Sutta. Regarding 'saccehi yojayitvā': and while leading, one connects with these four truths thus: craving and ignorance, because they are the root of becoming, are the truth of origin; the remaining phenomena of the three realms are the truth of suffering; serenity and insight are the truth of the path; the unconditioned element to be attained by that is the truth of cessation. 'Ayaṃ nayo nandiyāvaṭṭo' means: that special exposition which has the characteristic of leading the meaning of the Sutta on the side of defilement by means of craving and ignorance, and on the side of purification by means of serenity and insight, through the connection with the four truths—this is named the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method; this is the meaning. And herein, the ground of the method is stated as 'nayo' in the verse; therefore, it is stated by us as 'special exposition'. For the method of meaning is not the exposition; the method of meaning is the method of investigation in the preliminary stage, which is suitable for the penetration of the four truths. But for that method of meaning, there is the construction of the ground of the method by means of craving, etc., according to those of quick understanding, etc.; therein occurs the designation 'method'.

18. Akusaleti dvādasacittuppādasaṅgahite sabbepi akusale dhamme. Samūlehīti attano mūlehi, lobhadosamohehīti attho. Kusaleti sabbepi catubhūmake kusale dhamme. Kusalamūlehīti kusalehi alobhādimūlehi yo neti. Nayanto ca kusalākusalaṃ māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtaṃ na hotīti bhūtaṃ. Paṭaghaṭādayo [M 0.0030] viya na sammutisaccamattanti tathaṃ. Akusalassa iṭṭhavipākatābhāvato kusalassa ca aniṭṭhavipākatābhāvato vipāke sati avisaṃvādakattā avitathaṃ neti. Evametesaṃ tiṇṇampi padānaṃ kusalākusalavisesanatā daṭṭhabbā. Atha vā akusalamūlehi akusalāni kusalamūlehi ca kusalāni nayanto ayaṃ nayo bhūtaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ neti, cattāri saccāni niddhāretvā yojetīti attho. Dukkhādīni hi bādhakādibhāvato [V 0.0162] aññathābhāvābhāvena bhūtāni, saccasabhāvattā tathāni, avisaṃvādanato avitathāni. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāni avitathāni anaññathānī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090). Tipukkhalaṃ taṃ nayaṃ āhūti yo akusalamūlehi saṃkilesapakkhassa kusalamūlehi vodānapakkhassa suttatthassa catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso, taṃ tipukkhalaṃ nayanti vadantīti attho.

18. "Akusale" refers to all unwholesome states included in the twelve consciousness-arisings. "Samūlehi" means: with their own roots, that is, with greed, hatred, and delusion; this is the meaning. "Kusale" refers to all wholesome states in the four planes. "Kusalamūlehi" means: which leads by wholesome roots such as non-greed, etc. And while leading the wholesome and unwholesome, it is existent, since it is not non-existent like a magical illusion, a mirage, etc. It is true, since it is not mere conventional truth like pots, cloth, etc. It leads what is non-erroneous, since it is non-deviating when there is a result, owing to the absence of desirable results for the unwholesome and the absence of undesirable results for the wholesome. Thus, the quality of being a qualifier for the wholesome and unwholesome of all these three terms should be seen. Alternatively, while leading the unwholesome by unwholesome roots and the wholesome by wholesome roots, this method leads what is existent, true, and non-erroneous; it determines and connects the four truths; this is the meaning. Indeed, suffering, etc., are existent because of their nature of oppressing, etc., and because of the absence of another nature. They are true because of their true nature. They are non-erroneous because they are non-deviating. For this was stated by the Blessed One: "These four, monks, are true, non-erroneous, not otherwise." "Tipukkhalaṃ taṃ nayaṃ āhu" means: that special exposition which has the characteristic of leading the meaning of the Sutta on the side of defilement by unwholesome roots and on the side of purification by wholesome roots, through the connection with the four truths—that they call the Tipukkhala method; this is the meaning.

19. Vipallāsehīti asubhe subhantiādinayappavattehi catūhi vipallāsehi. Kileseti kilissanti vibādhiyantīti kilesā, saṃkiliṭṭhadhammā, saṃkilesapakkhanti attho. Keci “saṃkilese”tipi paṭhanti, kilesasahiteti attho. Indriyehīti saddhādīhi indriyehi. Saddhammeti paṭipattipaṭivedhasaddhamme, vodānapakkhanti attho. Etaṃ nayanti yo subhasaññādīhi vipallāsehi sakalassa saṃkilesapakkhassa saddhindriyādīhi vodānapakkhassa catusaccayojanavasena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso, etaṃ nayaṃ nayavidū saddhammanayakovidā, atthanayakusalā eva vā sīhavikkīḷitaṃ nayanti vadantīti attho.

19. "Vipallāsehi" means: by the four distortions that proceed in the manner of 'in the foul, it is fair', etc. "Kilese" refers to defilements; they are so called because they are defiled and oppressed. This means defiled states, that is, the side of defilement; this is the meaning. Some also read "saṃkilese"; the meaning is: accompanied by defilements. "Indriyehi" means: by the faculties such as faith, etc. "Saddhamme" means: the good doctrine of practice and penetration; the meaning is: the side of purification. Regarding "etaṃ nayanti": that special exposition which has the characteristic of leading the meaning of the Sutta of the entire side of defilement by means of distortions such as the perception of the fair, etc., and the meaning of the Sutta of the side of purification by means of the spiritual faculties such as faith, etc., by way of connection with the four truths—that special exposition, those who know the methods, who are skilled in the method of the good doctrine, or indeed those skilled in the method of meaning, call the Sīhavikkīḷita method; this is the meaning.

20. Veyyākaraṇesūti tassa tassa atthanayassa yojanatthaṃ katesu suttassa atthavissajjanesūti attho. Tenevāha “tahiṃ tahi”nti. Kusalākusalāti vodāniyā saṃkilesikā ca tassa tassa nayassa disābhūtadhammā. Vuttāti suttato niddhāretvā kathitā. Manasā volokayateti te yathāvuttadhamme citteneva “ayaṃ paṭhamā disā ayaṃ dutiyā disā”tiādinā tassa tassa nayassa disābhāvena upaparikkhati, vicāretīti attho. “Olokayate te abahī”tipi [M 0.0031] pāṭho. Tattha teti te yathāvuttadhamme. Abahīti abbhantaraṃ, citte evāti attho. Taṃ khu disālocanaṃ āhūti olokayateti ettha yadetaṃ olokanaṃ, taṃ disālocanaṃ nāma nayaṃ vadanti. Khu-ti ca nipāto avadhāraṇe. Tena olokanameva ayaṃ nayo, na koci atthavisesoti dasseti.

20. The meaning of `Veyyākaraṇesu` is: in the explanations of the meaning of the Sutta, made for the purpose of applying that particular method of meaning. For that very reason, the Teacher said, “here and there.” `Kusalākusalā` refers to the purifying and the defiling, which are the dhammas that have become the directions of each particular method. `Vuttā` means: spoken after having been extracted from the Sutta. Regarding `Manasā volokayati`, the meaning is: one examines and investigates with the mind itself those aforementioned dhammas by way of their being the directions of each particular method, as in “this is the first direction, this is the second direction,” and so on. There is also the reading, `Olokayate te abahī`. Therein, `te` refers to those aforementioned dhammas. `Abahī` means internally, that is, within the mind itself. As for `Taṃ khu disālocanaṃ āhū`, it means: in the word `olokayati`, whatever this looking is, they call that looking the method named ‘direction-looking’ (`disālocana`). The particle `khu` is used for emphasis. By this, it is shown that this method is the looking itself, and there is no special meaning.

21. Oloketvāti paṭhamādidisābhāvena upaparikkhitvā. Disālocanenāti disālocananayena karaṇabhūtena. Yena hi vidhinā tassa tassa atthanayassa yojanāya disā olokīyanti, so vidhi disālocananti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ukkhipiyāti uddharitvā, disābhūtadhamme suttato niddhāretvāti attho. “Ukkhipiya yo samānetī”tipi paṭhanti, tassattho – “yo tesaṃ disābhūtadhammānaṃ samānayanaṃ karotī”ti. Yanti vā kiriyāparāmasanaṃ[V 0.0163]. Samānetīti samaṃ, sammā vā āneti tassa tassa nayassa yojanāvasena. Ke pana āneti? Sabbe kusalākusale taṃtaṃnayadisābhūte. Ayaṃ nayoti samānetīti ettha yadetaṃ taṃtaṃnayadisābhūtadhammānaṃ samānayanaṃ, ayaṃ aṅkuso nāma nayoti attho. Etañca dvayaṃ “vohāranayo, kammanayo”ti ca vuccati.

21. `Oloketvā` means: having examined by way of being the first direction, and so on. `Disālocanena` means: by the `disālocana` method, which is the instrument. Indeed, the procedure by which the directions are examined for the application of that particular method of meaning is called `disālocana`; or, the meaning here should be understood thus. `Ukkhipiya` means: having lifted up, that is, having extracted the dhammas that have become the directions from the Sutta. They also read, `Ukkhipiya yo samānetī`, and its meaning should be understood thus: “the method which brings about the proper collation of those dhammas that have become the directions.” Or, the word `yaṃ` refers to the action. `Samānetī` means: it brings evenly, or rightly, by means of the application of that particular method. But what does it bring? It brings all the wholesome and unwholesome dhammas that have become the directions of that particular method. Regarding the phrase `Ayaṃ nayo` (this is the method), in the context of the reading `samānetī`, the meaning is: whatever this proper collation of the dhammas that have become the directions of that particular method may be, this is the method named `aṅkusa` (the goad). And this pair is also called the ‘conventional method’ (`vohāranaya`) and the ‘action method’ (`kammanaya`).

22. Evaṃ hāre naye ca niddisitvā idāni nesaṃ yojanakkamaṃ dassento “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”ntiādimāha. Tattha paṭhamaṃ soḷasa hārā “yojetabbā”ti vacanaseso. Hārasaṃvaṇṇanā paṭhamaṃ kātabbā byañjanapariyeṭṭhibhāvatoti adhippāyo. Disalocanatoti disālocanena, ayameva vā pāṭho. Aṅkusena hīti hi-saddo nipātamattaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

22. Having thus explained the `hāras` and the methods, now, showing the sequence of their application, the author said, “first, the sixteen `hāras`,” and so on. Therein, for “first, the sixteen `hāras`,” the remainder of the phrase, “are to be applied,” should be supplied. The intention is that the explanation of the `hāras` should be done first, because it is an investigation of the expression. `Disālocanato` means `disālocanena` (by `disālocana`), or this itself is the reading. In `Aṅkusena hi`, the word `hi` is merely a particle. The rest is self-evident.

Dvādasapadaṃ

The Twelve Terms

23. Idāni yesaṃ byañjanapadānaṃ atthapadānañca vasena dvādasa padāni suttanti vuttaṃ, tāni padāni niddisituṃ “akkharaṃ pada”ntiādimāha. Tattha apariyosite pade vaṇṇo akkharaṃ pariyāyavasena akkharaṇato asañcaraṇato. Na hi vaṇṇassa pariyāyo vijjati, atha vaṇṇoti kenaṭṭhena vaṇṇo? Atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṭṭhena. Vaṇṇo eva hi ittarakhaṇatāya aparāparabhāvena pavatto padādibhāvena gayhamāno yathāsambandhaṃ taṃ taṃ atthaṃ vadati[M 0.0032]. Ekakkharaṃ vā padaṃ akkharaṃ, keci pana “manasā desanāvācāya akkharaṇato akkhara”nti vadanti.

23. Now, to point out those terms—by means of which expression-terms and meaning-terms it was said that a sutta has twelve terms—the author said, “a letter, a word,” and so on. Therein, in an incomplete word, a `vaṇṇa` (sound) is an `akkhara` (letter) in a figurative sense, because it does not perish (`akkharaṇato`) and does not move (`asañcaraṇato`). Indeed, a synonym for `vaṇṇa` does not exist. Then for what reason is a `vaṇṇa` called a `vaṇṇa`? Because it explains the meaning (`atthasaṃvaṇṇana`). Indeed, it is the `vaṇṇa` itself which, due to its momentary nature and occurring successively, when grasped as a word and so on, expresses that particular meaning according to the connection. Or, a single-letter word is an `akkhara`. Some, however, say: “A teaching by mind, or by speech, is an `akkhara` because it does not perish (`akkharaṇato`).”

Padanti pajjati attho etenāti padaṃ, taṃ nāmapadaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ upasaggapadaṃ nipātapadanti catubbidhaṃ. Tattha “phasso vedanā citta”nti evamādikaṃ satvappadhānaṃ nāmapadaṃ. “Phusati vedayati vijānātī”ti evamādikaṃ kiriyāpadhānaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ. Kiriyāvisesaggahaṇanimittaṃ “pa” iti evamādikaṃ upasaggapadaṃ. Kiriyāya satvassa ca sarūpavisesappakāsanahetubhūtaṃ “eva”nti evamādikaṃ nipātapadaṃ.

As for `pada` (word): the meaning is known (`pajjati`) by means of it, therefore it is a `pada`. It is fourfold: a noun-word (`nāmapada`), a verb-word (`ākhyātapada`), a prefix-word (`upasaggapada`), and a particle-word (`nipātapada`). Therein, that which is substance-predominant, such as “contact, feeling, consciousness,” is a noun-word. That which is action-predominant, such as “one touches, one feels, one knows,” is a verb-word. That which is the cause for grasping a specific action, such as `pa`, is a prefix-word. That which is the cause for making manifest the specific nature of both an action and a substance, such as `eva`, is a particle-word.

Byañjananti saṅkhepato vuttaṃ padābhihitaṃ atthaṃ byañjayatīti byañjanaṃ, vākyaṃ. Taṃ pana atthato padasamudāyoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Padamattasavanepi hi adhikārādivasena labbhamānehi padantarehi anusandhānaṃ katvāva atthasampaṭipatti hotīti vākyameva atthaṃ byañjayati. Niruttīti ākārābhihitaṃ nibbacanaṃ nirutti.

As for `byañjana` (expression): it makes manifest (`byañjayati`) the meaning expressed by words spoken in brief, therefore it is a `byañjana`; it is a sentence (`vākya`). But that sentence, in terms of meaning, should be understood as a collection of words. Indeed, even when only a single word is heard, the understanding of the meaning occurs only after making a connection with other words obtained by means of the topic of discussion, and so on. Therefore, it is the sentence itself that makes the meaning manifest. As for `nirutti` (etymology): the derivation (`nibbacana`) spoken of in the `ākāra` (analysis of a sentence) is `nirutti`.

Niddesoti [V 0.0164] nibbacanavitthāro niravasesadesanattā niddeso. Padehi vākyassa vibhāgo ākāro. Yadi evaṃ padato ākārassa ko visesoti? Apariyosite vākye avibhajjamāne vā tadavayavo padaṃ. Uccāraṇavasena pariyosite vākye vibhajjamāne vā tadavayavo ākāroti ayametesaṃ viseso. Chaṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ chaṭṭhavacanaṃ. Ākāro chaṭṭhavacanaṃ etassāti ākārachaṭṭhavacanaṃ, byañjanapadaṃ. Ettha ca byañjananti imassa padassa anantaraṃ vattabbaṃ ākārapadaṃ niddesapadānantaraṃ vadantena “ākārachaṭṭhavacana”nti vuttaṃ, padānupubbikaṃ pana icchantehi taṃ byañjanapadānantarameva kātabbaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “aparimāṇā byañjanā aparimāṇā ākārāti, byañjanehi vivarati ākārehi vibhajatī”ti ca. Keci pana “ākārapadabyañjananiruttiyo ca niddeso”ti paṭhanti. Ettāva byañjanaṃ sabbanti yānimāni akkharādīni niddiṭṭhāni, ettakameva sabbaṃ byañjanaṃ, etehi asaṅgahitaṃ byañjanaṃ nāma natthīti attho.

As for `niddesa` (exposition): it is the detailed explanation of the derivation (`nibbacana-vitthāro`) and is called `niddesa` because it is a teaching without remainder. The division of a sentence by means of words is `ākāra` (analysis). If so, what is the difference between a `pada` and an `ākāra`? In an uncompleted or undivided sentence, its component is a `pada`. In a sentence that is completed by pronunciation or is being divided, its component is an `ākāra`. This is the difference between them. The sixth term is `chaṭṭhavacana`. The `ākāra` is the sixth term of this `byañjanapada` (expression-term), hence it is `ākārachaṭṭhavacana`. And here, the `ākāra`-term, which should be stated immediately after the term `byañjana`, was called `ākārachaṭṭhavacana` by the author who stated it after the `niddesa`-term. However, those who desire the proper sequence of terms should place it immediately after the `byañjana`-term. For thus it will be said: “The expressions are immeasurable, the analyses are immeasurable,” and “One reveals with expressions, one divides with analyses.” Some, however, read: `ākārapadabyañjananiruttiyo ca niddeso`. As for `ettāva byañjanaṃ sabbaṃ` (this much is all the expression): whatever these letters and so on that have been pointed out, this much alone is all the `byañjana`. There is no so-called `byañjana` that is not included in these; this is the meaning.

24. Saṅkāsanāti saṃkhittena kāsanā. Pakāsanāti paṭhamaṃ kāsanā, kāsīyati dīpīyatīti attho. Iminā hi atthapadadvayena akkharapadehi vibhāviyamāno atthākāro gahito. Yasmā akkharehi suyyamānehi suṇantānaṃ visesavidhānassa katattā padapariyosāne [M 0.0033] padatthasampaṭipatti hoti. Tathā hi vakkhati “tattha bhagavā akkharehi saṅkāseti padehi pakāsetīti, akkharehi padehi ca ugghāṭetī”ti ca.

24. `Saṅkāsanā` is showing in brief. `Pakāsanā` is showing firstly; the meaning is 'it is shown, it is illuminated.' By these two meaning-terms, the aspect of the meaning, being made known by letters and words, is grasped. Because, for those who hear the letters being heard, due to a special arrangement having been made, comprehension of the word's meaning occurs at the end of the word. Thus indeed, it will be said: 'Therein, the Blessed One indicates with letters and makes plain with words,' and 'by letters and words he opens up.'

Vivaraṇāti vitthāraṇā. Vibhajanā ca uttānīkammañca paññatti ca vibhajanuttānīkammapaññatti. Tattha vibhajanāti vibhāgakaraṇaṃ, ubhayenāpi niddisanamāha. Idha purimanayeneva byañjanākārehi niddisiyamāno atthākāro dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uttānīkammaṃ pākaṭakaraṇaṃ. Pakārehi ñāpanaṃ paññatti. Dvayenāpi paṭiniddisanaṃ katheti. Etthāpi niruttiniddesasaṅkhātehi byañjanapadehi niddisiyamāno atthākāro vutto, yo paṭiniddisīyatīti vuccati. Etehīti etehi eva saṅkāsanādivinimuttassa desanātthassa abhāvato. Atthoti suttattho. Kammanti ugghaṭanādikammaṃ. Suttatthena hi desanāya pavattiyamānena ugghaṭitaññuādiveneyyānaṃ cittasantānassa pabodhanakiriyānibbatti. So ca suttattho saṅkāsanādiākāroti. Tena vuttaṃ – “attho kammañca niddiṭṭha”nti.

'Vivaraṇā' is detailed explanation. And 'vibhajanā' (analysis), 'uttānīkamma' (making manifest), and 'paññatti' (designation) are 'vibhajanuttānīkammapaññatti'. Therein, 'vibhajanā' is the act of making a division; by both, it states the detailed indication. Here, it should be understood that, by the same method as before, the aspect of the meaning, being indicated in detail by the modes of expression, is shown. 'Uttānīkamma' is making manifest. 'Paññatti' is making known by way of modes. By both, it speaks of further detailed indication. Here too, the aspect of the meaning, being indicated in detail by the expression-terms called 'etymological explanation', is stated, which is said to be 'further indicated in detail'.
