'Etehi' means by these very things, because there is no meaning of the teaching apart from 'saṅkāsanā' and so on. 'Attho' is the meaning of the sutta. 'Kamma' is the action of disclosing and so on. For, by the meaning of the sutta being set forth by the teaching, the accomplishment of the action of awakening occurs in the mental continuum of disciples such as the 'ugghaṭitaññu'. And that meaning of the sutta has the aspect of 'saṅkāsanā' and so on. Therefore it is said: 'The meaning and the action have been indicated.'

25. Tīṇīti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ, tayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Navahi padehīti navahi koṭṭhāsehi[V 0.0165]. Attho samāyuttoti attho sammā yutto na vinā vattati. Sabbassa hi buddhavacanassa catusaccappakāsanato atthanayānañca catusaccayojanavasena pavattanato sabbo pāḷiattho atthanayattayasaṅgahito saṅkāsanādiākāravisesavutti cāti.

25. The word 'tīṇi' is stated with a change of gender; it is meant to be 'tayo'. 'By nine terms' means by nine portions. 'The meaning is connected' means the meaning is rightly connected; it does not occur without. Indeed, because all the Buddha's speech explains the Four Truths, and because the meaning-methods proceed by way of connection with the Four Truths, all the meaning of the Pāḷi is both included in the three meaning-methods and has its occurrence with the specific aspects of 'saṅkāsanā' and so on.

26. Idāni yathāniddiṭṭhe desanāhārādike nettippakaraṇassa padatthe sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ gaṇanavasena paricchinditvā dassento “atthassā”tiādimāha. Tattha catubbīsāti soḷasa hārā cha byañjanapadāni dve kammanayāti evaṃ catubbīsa. Ubhayanti cha atthapadāni tayo atthanayāti idaṃ navavidhaṃ yathāvuttaṃ catubbīsavidhañcāti etaṃ ubhayaṃ. Saṅkalayitvāti sampiṇḍetvā. “Saṅkhepayato”tipi pāṭho, ekato karontassāti attho. Ettikāti etappamāṇā, ito vinimutto koci nettipadatthā natthīti attho.

26. Now, for the sake of easy grasping of the meanings of the terms of the Nettippakaraṇa, such as the Desanāhāra, which have been indicated in detail, showing them by defining them by way of number, he states 'atthassa' and so on. Therein, 'twenty-four' is: sixteen Hāras, six expression-terms, and two Kamma-nayas; thus twenty-four. 'Both' is: the six meaning-terms and the three meaning-methods, thus this ninefold division, and the twenty-fourfold division as stated; thus these two. 'Having combined' means having condensed. There is also the reading 'saṅkhepayato', the meaning of which is 'for one who makes them one'. 'Ettikā' means of this measure; the meaning is that there is no meaning of a Netti term apart from this.

Evaṃ tettiṃsapadatthāya nettiyā suttassa atthapariyesanāya yo “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”nti nayehi paṭhamaṃ hārā saṃvaṇṇetabbāti hāranayānaṃ saṃvaṇṇanākkamo dassito, svāyaṃ hāranayānaṃ desanākkameneva [M 0.0034] siddho. Evaṃ siddhe sati ayaṃ ārambho imamatthaṃ dīpeti – sabbepime hārā nayā ca iminā dassitakkameneva suttesu saṃvaṇṇanāvasena yojetabbā, na uppaṭipāṭiyāti.

Thus, for the investigation of the meaning of a sutta by means of the Netti with its thirty-three term-meanings, the sequence of explanation for the Hāras and Nayas has been shown by the Pāḷi 'the sixteen Hāras first,' meaning that the Hāras should be explained first, before the Nayas. This very sequence for the Hāras and Nayas is established by the sequence of the teaching itself. This being established, this undertaking clarifies this meaning: all these Hāras and Nayas should be applied in the suttas by way of explanation according to this very sequence that has been shown, not out of sequence.

Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ, yadete hārā nayā ca imināva kamena desitāti? Yadipi nāyamanuyogo katthaci anukkame nivisati, api ca dhammadesanāya nissayaphalatadupāyasarīrabhūtānaṃ assādādīnaṃ vibhāvanasabhāvattā pakatiyā sabbasuttānurūpāti suviññeyyabhāvato paresañca saṃvaṇṇanāvisesānaṃ vicayahārādīnaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvato paṭhamaṃ desanāhāro dassito.

What is the reason here that these Hāras and Nayas are taught in this very sequence? Although this inquiry does not apply to just any sequence, nevertheless, because the Desanāhāra has the nature of clarifying gratification and so on—which are the support, fruit, means to that fruit, and body of the Dhamma teaching—it is by nature suitable for all suttas. And because it is easy to understand, and because it serves as the foundation for the special explanations of others, such as the Vicayahāra, the Desanāhāra is shown first.

Padapucchāvissajjanapubbāparānugītīhi saddhiṃ desanāhārapadatthānaṃ pavicayasabhāvatāya tassa anantaraṃ vicayo. Tathā hi vakkhati “padaṃ vicinati…pe… āṇattiṃ vicinati anugītiṃ vicinatī”ti.

Because of its nature of investigating the term-meanings of the Desanāhāra, together with the questioning and answering of terms and the preceding and subsequent recitation, the Vicayahāra is shown immediately after it. Thus indeed, it will be said: 'He investigates the term... he investigates the instruction, he investigates the recitation.'

Vicayena hārena pavicitānaṃ atthānaṃ yuttāyuttivicāraṇā yuttāti yuttivicāraṇabhāvato vicayānantaraṃ yuttihāro vutto. Tathā hi vakkhati – “vicayena hārena vicinitvā yuttihārena yojetabba”nti.

Because the consideration of the appropriateness or inappropriateness of the meanings investigated by the Vicayahāra is suitable, and because of its nature of considering appropriateness, the Yuttihāra is stated after the Vicayahāra. Thus indeed, it will be said: 'Having investigated with the Vicayahāra, one should apply the Yuttihāra.'

Yuttāyuttānaṃyeva [V 0.0166] atthānaṃ upapattianurūpaṃ kāraṇaparamparāya niddhāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ padaṭṭhānacintanaṃ kattabbanti yuttihārānantaraṃ padaṭṭhānahāro dassito. Tathā hi vakkhati – “yo koci upanissayo yo koci paccayo ca, sabbo so padaṭṭhāna”nti.

Because the reflection on the 'padaṭṭhāna'—which has the characteristic of determining, by a succession of causes and in accordance with the grounds, the very meanings that are appropriate and inappropriate—should be done, the Padaṭṭhānahāra is shown after the Yuttihāra. Thus indeed, it will be said: 'Whatever supporting condition, whatever condition, all that is 'padaṭṭhāna'.'

Yuttāyuttānaṃ kāraṇaparamparāya pariggahitasabhāvānaṃyeva ca dhammānaṃ avuttānampi ekalakkhaṇatāya gahaṇaṃ kātabbanti dassanatthaṃ padaṭṭhānānantaraṃ lakkhaṇo hāro vutto. Tathā hi lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅge “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā paṭiccasamuppādaṃ dassetvā “evaṃ ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

For the purpose of showing that the grasping of even those dhammas not stated—which have the very nature of being comprehended by a succession of causes, both appropriate and inappropriate—should be done because of their having a single characteristic, the Lakkhaṇahāra is stated after the Padaṭṭhānahāra. Thus indeed, in the analysis of the Lakkhaṇahāra, having shown dependent origination beginning with 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise,' it is said: 'Thus, those dhammas that are of a single characteristic...'

Atthato niddhāritānampi dhammānaṃ nibbacanādīni vattabbāni, na sutte sarūpato āgatānamevāti dassanatthaṃ lakkhaṇānantaraṃ catubyūho vutto. Evañhi niravasesato atthāvabodho hoti, evañca katvā “yadā hi bhikkhu atthassa ca nāmaṃ jānāti dhammassa ca nāmaṃ jānāti tathā tathā naṃ abhiniropetī”ti anavasesapariyādānaṃ vakkhati. Tathā “punappunaṃ gabbhamupetī”ti ettha “ye jarāmaraṇena aṭṭiyitukāmā bhavissanti[M 0.0035], te bhavissanti bhojane mattaññuno indriyesu guttadvārā”tiādinā sammāpaṭipattiṃ adhippāyabhāvena vakkhati.

For the purpose of showing that derivations and so forth are to be stated even for phenomena that have been determined by way of meaning, and not only for those that have come in their own form in the sutta, the Catubyūha is stated after the Lakkhaṇahāra. For in this way, there is an understanding of the meaning without remainder. And having done so, he will state the exhaustive comprehension without remainder [with the words]: “When indeed a bhikkhu knows the name of the meaning and the name of the Dhamma, he applies it to him in such and such a way.” Likewise, in this Pāḷi text, “Again and again he goes to the womb,” he will state the right practice by way of the speaker’s intention, beginning with: “Those who will be vexed by aging and death will be moderate in eating, with guarded doors in the sense faculties.”

Nibbacanādhippāyanidānavacanehi saddhiṃ sutte padatthānaṃ suttantarasaṃsandanasaṅkhāte pubbāparavicāre dassite tesaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammantarāvaṭṭanaṃ sukhena sakkā dassetunti catubyūhānantaraṃ āvaṭṭo vutto. Teneva hi “ārambhatha nikkamathā”ti gāthāyaṃ ārambhanikkamanabuddhasāsanayogadhunanehi vīriyasamādhipaññindriyāni niddhāretvā tadanuyogassa mūlaṃ “pamādo”ti suttantare dassito pamādo āvaṭṭito.

When, together with the statements of derivation, the speaker's intention, and the cause, the examination of before and after—which is known as correlation with other suttas—of the meanings of the terms in the sutta has been shown, it is possible to easily show their revolving among similar and dissimilar phenomena. Therefore, immediately after the fourfold arrangement, the method of revolving is stated. For by that very reason, in the verse “Strive, go forth,” having determined the faculties of energy, concentration, and wisdom by means of striving, going forth, application in the Buddha’s Dispensation, and shaking off, negligence—which is shown in another sutta as the root of non-application to that—is made to revolve.

Sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭane niyojite sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇavasena saṃkilesavodānadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānato bhūmito ca vibhāgo sakkā sukhena yojitunti āvaṭṭānantaraṃ vibhattihāro vutto. Yato vibhattihāravibhaṅge “katame dhammā sādhāraṇā? Dve dhammā sādhāraṇā, nāmasādhāraṇā vatthusādhāraṇā cā”ti ārabhitvā “micchattaniyatānaṃ sattānaṃ aniyatānañca sattānaṃ dassanappahātabbā kilesā sādhāraṇā, puthujjanassa sotāpannassa ca kāmarāgabyāpādā sādhāraṇā”tiādinā sabhāgavisabhāgapariyāyavanteyeva dhamme vibhajissati.

When the revolving of similar and dissimilar phenomena has been applied, the analysis of defiled and purified phenomena by way of common and uncommon, and by way of proximate cause and plane, can be easily applied. Therefore, immediately after the method of revolving, the method of analysis is stated. Because in the analysis of the method of analysis, beginning with “Which phenomena are common? Two phenomena are common: common in name and common in basis,” he will analyze only those phenomena that have the characteristic of being similar and dissimilar, beginning with: “The defilements to be abandoned by seeing are common to beings fixed in wrongness and to beings not fixed; sensual lust and ill will are common to the worldling and the stream-enterer.”

Sāvajjānavajjadhammānaṃ [V 0.0167] sappaṭibhāgābhāvato tesaṃ vibhāge kate suttāgate dhamme akasirena paṭipakkhato parivattetuṃ sakkāti vibhattianantaraṃ parivattanahāro vutto. Tathā hi “sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassa micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā bhavatī”ti paṭivibhattasabhāve eva dhamme parivattanahāravibhaṅge udāharissati.

Because blameworthy and blameless phenomena have counterparts, when their analysis has been made, it is possible to convert the phenomena that have come in the sutta to their opposite without difficulty. Therefore, immediately after the method of analysis, the method of conversion is stated. For that very reason, in the analysis of the method of conversion, he will give as an example only those phenomena whose nature has been analyzed as having an opposite portion, as in: “For a person with right view, wrong view is overcome.”

Paṭipakkhato parivattitāpi dhammā pariyāyavacanehi bodhetabbā, na sutte āgatāyevāti dassanatthaṃ parivattanānantaraṃ vevacanahāro vutto.

For the purpose of showing that even phenomena that have been converted to their opposite are to be made known by synonymous terms, and not only those that have come in the sutta, the method of synonyms is stated immediately after the method of conversion.

Evaṃ te dhammā pariyāyasaddatopi vibhāvitā hontīti pariyāyato pakāsitānaṃ dhammānaṃ pabhedato paññattivasena vibhajanaṃ sukhena sakkā ñātunti vevacanahārānantaraṃ paññattihāro vutto. Tathā hi sutte āgatadhammānaṃ pariyāyapaññattivibhāgaṃ subodhanañca paññattihāravibhaṅge vakkhati.

In this way, those phenomena are also clarified by synonymous terms. Since the analysis of phenomena explained by way of synonyms—by means of designation according to their distinction—can be easily known, the method of designation is stated immediately after the method of synonyms. For that very reason, in the analysis of the method of designation, he will state the analysis of the phenomena that have come in the sutta by way of synonymous designation, and their good understanding.

Pabhāvapariññādipaññattivibhāgamukhena [M 0.0036] paṭiccasamuppādasaccādidhammavibhāge kate sutte āgatadhammānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādādimukhena avadhāraṇaṃ sakkā dassetunti paññattianantaraṃ otaraṇo hāro vutto. Tathā hi “uddhaṃ adho”ti gāthaṃ uddisitvā “vippamutto”ti padena asekkhaṃ vijjaṃ niddhāretvā “vijjuppādā avijjānirodho”tiādinā paṭiccasamuppādaṃ udāharissati.

When the analysis of phenomena such as dependent origination and the truths has been made by means of the analysis of designations such as the designation of origin and the designation of full understanding, it is possible to show the determination of the phenomena that have come in the sutta by means of dependent origination and so forth. Therefore, immediately after the method of designation, the method of descent is stated. For that very reason, having pointed out the verse “Above, below,” and having determined the knowledge of the non-learner with the term “fully liberated,” he will give dependent origination as an example, beginning with: “From the arising of knowledge, there is the cessation of ignorance.”

Dhātāyatanādīsu otāritānaṃ sutte padatthānaṃ pucchārambhavisodhanaṃ sakkā sukhena sampādetunti otaraṇānantaraṃ sodhano hāro vutto. Tathā hi vakkhati – “yattha evaṃ suddho ārambho, so pañho vissajjito bhavatī”tiādi.

For the meanings of the terms in the sutta that have been made to descend into the elements, sense bases, and so forth, the purification of the question and the beginning can be easily accomplished. Therefore, immediately after the method of descent, the method of purification is stated. For that very reason, he will state, beginning with: “Where there is thus a purified beginning, that question is answered.”

Visodhitesu sutte padapadatthesu tattha labbhamānasāmaññavisesabhāvo sukaro hotīti dassetuṃ sodhanānantaraṃ adhiṭṭhāno hāro dassito. Sodhano hi adhiṭṭhānassa bahūpakāro, tato eva hi “yathā yathā vā pana pucchitaṃ, tathā tathā vissajjayitabba”nti vakkhati.

To show that when the meanings of the terms and their meanings in the sutta have been purified, the state of being general and specific which is obtainable therein becomes easy to do, the method of determination is shown immediately after the method of purification. Indeed, the method of purification is of great help to the method of determination. For it is for that very reason that he will state: “In whatever way one is asked, in that way it should be answered.”

Sāmaññavisesabhūtesu sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇesu dhammesu paveditesu parikkhārasaṅkhātassa sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇarūpassa paccayaheturāsissa pabhedo suviññeyyoti adhiṭṭhānānantaraṃ parikkhāro vutto[V 0.0168]. Tathā hi vakkhati “asādhāraṇalakkhaṇo hetu, sādhāraṇalakkhaṇo paccayo. Yathā kiṃ bhave, yathā aṅkurassa nibbattiyā bījaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ, pathavī āpo ca sādhāraṇā”tiādi.

When phenomena that are general and specific, common and uncommon, have been made known, the distinction of the aggregate of conditions and causes—which is called requisites and has the nature of being common and uncommon—is easy to understand. Therefore, immediately after the method of determination, the method of requisites is stated. For that very reason, he will state, beginning with: “The cause has an uncommon characteristic, the condition has a common characteristic. How might this be? Just as for the production of a sprout, the seed is uncommon, while earth and water are common.”

Asādhāraṇe sādhāraṇe ca kāraṇe dassite tassa attano phalesu kāraṇākāro tesaṃ hetuphalānaṃ pabhedato desanākāro bhāvetabbapahātabbadhammānaṃ bhāvanāpahānāni ca niddhāretvā vuccamānāni sammā suttassa atthaṃ tathattāvabodhāya saṃvattantīti parikkhārānantaraṃ samāropano hāro dassitoti. Idaṃ hārānaṃ anukkamakāraṇaṃ.

When uncommon and common causes are shown, the mode of being a cause in its own fruits, the mode of teaching by way of the distinction of those causes and fruits, and the development and abandonment of phenomena to be developed and abandoned, when determined and stated, conduce to the correct understanding of the meaning of the sutta for the sake of understanding its true nature. Therefore, immediately after the method of requisites, the method of inclusion is shown. This is the reason for the sequence of the methods.

Nayānaṃ pana veneyyattayappayojitattā atthanayattayūpadesassa tadanukkameneva nandiyāvaṭṭādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ atthanayānaṃ kamo veditabbo. Ugghaṭitaññuādayo hi tayo veneyyā nandiyāvaṭṭādayo payojenti. Tasmā te uddesaniddesapaṭiniddesā viya yathākkamaṃ tesaṃ upakārāya [M 0.0037] savaṃttantīti. Tathā hi nesaṃ cattāro cha aṭṭha ca mūlapadā niddiṭṭhā. Itarassa pana nayadvayassa atthanayattayassa bhūmiyā ālocanaṃ tassa tattha samānayanañcāti iminā kāraṇena uddesakkamo veditabbo. Na hi sakkā anoloketvā samānetunti.

As for the methods, because the instruction on the three modes of meaning is applied by the three types of trainees, the order of the three modes of meaning, such as Nandiyāvaṭṭa and so forth, should be known only by the sequence of those trainees. Indeed, the three trainees, such as the ugghaṭitaññū, apply the modes of meaning such as Nandiyāvaṭṭa. Therefore, those modes of meaning, like the summary statement, detailed explanation, and re-explanation, exist in sequence for their benefit. For that very reason, for them, four, six, and eight root terms are indicated. As for the other two methods, their stated sequence should be known for this reason: there is the scrutiny of the domain of the three modes of meaning and its proper harmonization in each respective domain. For it is not possible to harmonize without scrutinizing.

Etaparamatā ca hārānaṃ ettakehi pakāravisesehi atthanayattayasahitehi suttassa attho niddhāriyamāno veneyyānaṃ alamanuttarāya paṭhamāya bhūmiyā samadhigamāyāti veditabbo. Dassanabhūmisamanuppattiatthā hi nettippakaraṇadesanāti. Atha vā etadantogadhattā sabbesaṃ suttassa saṃvaṇṇanāvisesānaṃ ettāvatā hārānaṃ daṭṭhabbā. Yattakā hi suttassa saṃvaṇṇanāvisesā, sabbe te nettiupadesāyattāti vuttovāyamattho.

The extent of the Hāras should be known to be this much: because the meaning of the sutta, being determined by these many special distinctions together with the three modes of meaning, is suitable for the trainees to realize the unsurpassed first ground. For the teaching of the Nettipakaraṇa has the purpose of attaining the ground of vision. Alternatively, the extent of the Hāras should be understood as this much, because all the special expositions of the sutta are included within them. Indeed, whatever special expositions of the sutta exist, all of them are dependent on the instruction of the Netti. Thus, this meaning has already been stated.

Tathā hi ye keci suttassa saṃvaṇṇanāpakārā niddisīyanti. Seyyathidaṃ – suttassa samuṭṭhānaṃ vattabbaṃ, adhippāyo vibhāvetabbo, anekadhā padattho saṃvaṇṇetabbo, vidhi anuvādo ca veditabbo, virodho samādhātabbo, anusandhiyā anurūpaṃ nigametabbanti. Tathā suttassa payojanaṃ piṇḍattho padattho anusandhi codanā parihāro ca atthaṃ vadantena vattabbāti. Tathā upogghāṭapadaviggahapadatthacālanāpaccupaṭṭhānāni vattabbānīti.

For that very reason, whatever kinds of exposition of a sutta are indicated—namely: the origin of the sutta should be stated, the intention should be clarified, the meaning of the term should be expounded in various ways, the rule and the supplementary statement should be known, the contradiction should be resolved, and it should be concluded in accordance with the connection. Furthermore, the purpose of the sutta, the summary meaning, the meaning of the term, the connection, the objection, and the refutation should be stated by one explaining the meaning. Furthermore, the introduction, the analysis of the term, the meaning of the term, the objection, and the refutation should be stated.

Tathā tisso kathā ekanāḷikā caturassā nisinnavattikā. Tattha pāḷiṃ vatvā ekekapadassa atthakathanaṃ ekanāḷikā nāma.

Similarly, there are three kinds of discourse: Ekanāḷikā, Caturassā, and Nisinnavattikā. Among them, reciting the Pāli and then explaining the meaning of each and every term is called Ekanāḷikā.

Paṭipakkhaṃ [V 0.0169] dassetvā paṭipakkhassa upamaṃ dassetvā sapakkhaṃ dassetvā sapakkhassa upamaṃ dassetvā kathanaṃ caturassā nāma.

A discourse that shows the opposing side, shows an analogy for the opposing side, shows one's own side, and shows an analogy for one's own side, is called Caturassā.

Visabhāgadhammavaseneva pariyosānaṃ gantvā puna sabhāgadhammavaseneva pariyosānagamanaṃ nisinnavattikā nāma.

Reaching a conclusion solely by way of dissimilar phenomena, and then again reaching a conclusion solely by way of similar phenomena, is called Nisinnavattikā.

Bhedakathāya tatvakathāya pariyāyavacanehi ca suttaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbanti ca evamādayo. Tesampi ettheva avarodho, yasmā te idha katipayahārasaṅgahitāti.

And [the view that] the sutta should be expounded by way of analytical discourse, by way of discourse on the true meaning, and by synonymous words, and so forth. These too are included right here, because they are encompassed here by a few Hāras.

Nayānaṃ pana yasmā ugghaṭitaññuādayo tayo eva veneyyā saccābhisamayabhāgino tadatthāya ca atthanayadesanā, tasmā satipi saṃkilesavodānadhammānaṃ [M 0.0038] yathāvuttamūlapadabhedato vaḍḍhetvā vibhajitabbappakāre tathā mūlapadāni avaḍḍhetvā veneyyattayavaseneva etaparamatā vuttā. Navasu navasu eva hi mūlapadesu sabbesaṃ saṃkilesavodānadhammānaṃ antogadhabhāvato na tāni vaḍḍhetabbāni veneyyattayādhikārato na hāpetabbānīti nayānaṃ etaparamatā daṭṭhabbā.

As for the methods, because only the three types of trainees, such as the ugghaṭitaññū, are partakers in the realization of the truths, and the teaching of the modes of meaning is for that purpose, therefore, even though there is a way of dividing the phenomena of defilement and purification by expanding them from the aforesaid distinctions of the root terms, this extent is stated only by way of the three types of trainees, without expanding the root terms in that way. For, because all phenomena of defilement and purification are included within just nine root terms each, they should not be expanded; and as it is the domain of the three types of trainees, they should not be reduced. Thus, the extent of the methods should be understood as this much.

Kammanayānaṃ pana ālocanasamānayanato aññassa pakārantarassa asambhavato etaparamatā. Hetvādīti ettha ādisaddena phalabhūmiupanisāsabhāgavisabhāgalakkhaṇanayādayo pariggahitā. Tesu hetūti kāraṇaṃ, yo dhammotipi vuccati, so pana paccayabhāvena ekavidho. Kārako sampāpakoti duvidho. Puna kārako ñāpako sampāpakoti tividho. Hetuhetu paccayahetu uttamahetu sādhāraṇahetūti catubbidho. Paccayadhammo kusalo akusalo saddo ariyamaggoti pañcavidho. Tathā sabhāgahetu asabhāgahetu ajjhattikahetu bāhirahetu janakahetu pariggāhakahetu sādhāraṇahetu asādhāraṇahetu samanantarahetu paramparahetu sahajātahetu asahajātahetu sāsavahetu anāsavahetūtiādinā anekavidho cāti veditabbo.

As for the Kamma methods, this is their extent, because of the impossibility of another kind of distinction apart from scrutiny and harmonization. Here, in 'cause, etc.', by the word 'etc.' are included: result, plane, support-condition, similar phenomena, dissimilar phenomena, characteristic, method, and so forth. Among these, 'cause' means reason, which is also called 'dhamma'. That cause is onefold by way of being a condition. It is twofold as agent-cause and producer-cause. Again, it is threefold as agent, indicator, and producer. It is fourfold as root-cause, condition-cause, supreme cause, and common cause. It is fivefold as condition-phenomenon, wholesome, unwholesome, sound, and the noble path. Furthermore, it should be known that it is manifold in ways such as: similar cause, dissimilar cause, internal cause, external cause, generative cause, supportive cause, common cause, uncommon cause, contiguity-cause, succession-cause, conascence-cause, non-conascence-cause, cause with taints, and cause without taints.

Phalampi paccayuppannabhāvena ekavidhaṃ. Adhigantabbatopi sampāpakahetuvasena phalapariyāyo labbhatīti nibbattetabbaadhigantabbabhāvato duvidhaṃ. Ñāpetabbanibbattetabbapattabbato tividhaṃ. Paccayuppannavipākakiriyāvacanatthanibbānavasena pañcavidhaṃ. Sabhāgahetunibbattaṃ asabhāgahetunibbattanti evamādivasena anekavidhañcāti veditabbaṃ. Tathā lokiyaṃ lokuttaranti. Tattha lokuttaraṃ cattāri sāmaññaphalāni. Lokiyaphalaṃ duvidhaṃ kāyikaṃ mānasañca[V 0.0170]. Tattha kāyikaṃ pañcadvārikaṃ, avasiṭṭhaṃ mānasaṃ. Yañca tāya tāya suttadesanāya sādhetabbaṃ, tadapi phalanti.

The result, too, is onefold by way of being condition-arisen. It is twofold by way of being what is to be produced and what is to be attained, because the term 'result' is obtained by way of the producer-cause and also because it is what is to be attained. It is threefold by way of being what is to be known, what is to be produced, and what is to be attained. It is fivefold by way of being condition-arisen, resultant, functional, a verbal meaning, and Nibbāna. And it should be known that it is manifold by way of being produced by a similar cause, produced by a dissimilar cause, and so forth. Similarly, it is mundane and supramundane. Among them, the supramundane is the four fruits of recluseship. The mundane result is twofold: bodily and mental. Among them, the bodily is that which occurs at the five doors; the remainder is mental. And whatever is to be accomplished by means of this or that sutta teaching, that too is a result.

Bhūmīti sāsavabhūmi anāsavabhūmi saṅkhatabhūmi asaṅkhatabhūmi dassanabhūmi bhāvanābhūmi puthujjanabhūmi sekkhabhūmi asekkhabhūmi sāvakabhūmi paccekabuddhabhūmi sammāsambuddhabhūmi jhānabhūmi asamāhitabhūmi paṭipajjamānabhūmi paṭipannabhūmi paṭhamābhūmi yāva catutthībhūmi kāmāvacarabhūmi yāva lokuttarabhūmīti bahuvidhā. Tattha sāsavabhūmi parittamahaggatā dhammā. Anāsavabhūmi appamāṇā dhammā. Saṅkhatabhūmi nibbānavajjā sabbe sabhāvadhammā. Asaṅkhatabhūmi appaccayā [M 0.0039] dhammā. Dassanabhūmi paṭhamamaggaphaladhammā. Bhāvanābhūmi avasiṭṭhamaggaphaladhammā. Puthujjanabhūmi hīnamajjhimā dhammā. Sekkhabhūmi cattāro ariyamaggadhammā heṭṭhimā ca tayo phaladhammā. Asekkhabhūmi aggaphaladhammā. Sāvakapaccekabuddhabuddhadhammā sāvakādibhūmiyo. Jhānabhūmi jhānadhammā. Asamāhitabhūmi jhānavajjitā dhammā. Paṭipajjamānabhūmi maggadhammā. Paṭipannabhūmi phaladhammā. Paṭhamādibhūmiyo saha phalena cattāro maggā apariyāpannā dhammā “paṭhamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā”tiādivacanato. Kāmāvacarādibhūmiyo kāmāvacarādidhammā. Ye ca dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ hāranayānaṃ patiṭṭhānabhāvena suttesu niddhārīyanti, tepi bhūmiyoti viññātabbā.

The plane (bhūmi) is of many kinds: the plane with taints, the plane without taints, the conditioned plane, the unconditioned plane, the plane of vision, the plane of development, the plane of ordinary people, the plane of trainees, the plane of those beyond training, the plane of disciples, the plane of Paccekabuddhas, the plane of Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, the plane of jhāna, the plane of the unconcentrated, the plane of those practicing, the plane of those who have practiced, the first plane up to the fourth plane, the plane of the sense-sphere up to the supramundane plane. Therein, the plane with taints consists of limited and exalted phenomena. The plane without taints consists of immeasurable phenomena. The conditioned plane consists of all phenomena of intrinsic nature, excluding Nibbāna. The unconditioned plane consists of phenomena without conditions. The plane of vision consists of the phenomena of the first path and fruit. The plane of development consists of the phenomena of the remaining paths and fruits. The plane of ordinary people consists of inferior and middling phenomena. The plane of trainees consists of the four noble path phenomena and the three lower fruit phenomena. The plane of those beyond training consists of the highest fruit phenomena. The phenomena pertaining to disciples, Paccekabuddhas, and Buddhas are the planes of disciples and so forth. The plane of jhāna consists of jhāna phenomena. The plane of the unconcentrated consists of phenomena excluding jhāna. The plane of those practicing consists of path phenomena. The plane of those who have practiced consists of fruit phenomena. The four paths, together with the fruit, which are unincluded phenomena, are the first planes and so forth, due to the saying 'attaining the first plane,' and so forth. The phenomena pertaining to the sense-sphere and so forth are the planes of the sense-sphere and so forth. And those phenomena which are determined in the Suttas as the basis for those various methods of conveyance—those phenomena too should be understood as planes.

Upanisāti balavakāraṇaṃ, yo upanissayapaccayoti vuccati. Yañca sandhāya sutte “dukkhūpanisā saddhā saddhūpanisaṃ ‘sīla’nti yāva vimuttūpanisaṃ vimuttiñāṇadassana”nti vuttaṃ. Api ca upanisāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye siddhante hadayabhūtaṃ abbhantaraṃ vuccati. Idhāpi nettihadayaṃ, yaṃ sammā pariggaṇhantā dhammakathikā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sutte āgatadhammamukhena sabbahāranayayojanāya samatthā honti. Kiṃ panetaṃ nettihadayaṃ? Yadidaṃ etasseva tettiṃsavidhassa pakaraṇapadatthasoḷasassa aṭṭhavīsatividhapaṭṭhānavibhaṅgasahitassa visayo saha nimittavibhāgena asaṅkarato vavatthito.

Upanisā is a strong condition, which is called the decisive-support condition (upanissayapaccaya). And with reference to this, it is said in the Sutta: 'Faith has suffering as its strong condition, virtue has faith as its strong condition,' up to 'the knowledge and vision of liberation has liberation as its strong condition.' Moreover, upanisā is called the innermost, the heart-essence, in this or that established doctrine. Here too, the heart of the Netti is called upanisā; by properly grasping which, Dhamma-preachers are able to apply all the methods of conveyance through the entry point of the Dhamma that has come down in each Sutta. And what is this heart of the Netti? It is this domain of this very thirty-threefold treatise—which has sixteen kinds of textual terms and is accompanied by the analysis of the twenty-eight kinds of foundations of the teaching—that is established without confusion, together with the analysis of the sign.

Seyyathidaṃ – desanāhārassa assādādayo visayo, tassa assādādivibhāvanalakkhaṇattā. Tassa assādo sukhaṃ somanassanti evamādivibhāgo, tassa nimittaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇādi, ayañca attho desanāhāravicayahāraniddesavaṇṇanāyaṃ vitthārato pakāsito eva. Sutte āgatadhammassa sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavisayo āvaṭṭahāro, tadubhayaāvaṭṭanalakkhaṇattā. Sutte āgatadhammānaṃ paccanīkadhammavisayo [V 0.0171] parivattanahāro, paṭipakkhadhammaparivattanalakkhaṇattā. Padaṭṭhānaparikkhāresu āsannakāraṇaṃ upanissayakāraṇañca padaṭṭhānaṃ, hetu parikkhāroti ayametesaṃ viseso.

That is to say: the domain of the method of exposition is gratification and so forth, because it is characterized by the analysis of gratification and so forth. Its analysis is: gratification, happiness, joy, and so forth; its sign is a pleasing object and so forth. And this meaning has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the exposition of the method of exposition and the method of investigation. The method of revolving has as its domain the revolving of similar and dissimilar phenomena with respect to the Dhamma that has come down in the Suttas, because it is characterized by the revolving of both of these. The method of transformation has as its domain opposing phenomena with respect to the Dhamma that has come down in the Suttas, because it is characterized by the transformation of opposing phenomena. Among proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna) and requisites (parikkhāra): the immediate cause and the decisive-support condition are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna); the root cause (hetu) is the requisite (parikkhāra). This is their distinction.

Sabhāgavisabhāgadhammā ca tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ anukūlapaṭikūladhammā yathākkamaṃ veditabbā. Yathā – sammādiṭṭhiyā sammāsaṅkappo sabhāgo, micchāsaṅkappo visabhāgoti iminā nayena sabbaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgato veditabbaṃ.

Similar and dissimilar phenomena should be understood respectively as the favorable and unfavorable phenomena of those respective phenomena. For example: with respect to right view, right intention is similar, and wrong intention is dissimilar. In this way, everything should be understood in terms of similarity and dissimilarity.

Lakkhaṇanti [M 0.0040] sabhāvo. So hāranayānaṃ niddese vibhāvito eva.

Characteristic (lakkhaṇa) is intrinsic nature (sabhāva). That has already been explained in the exposition of the methods of conveyance.

Yaṃ panetaṃ hetuādivisesavinimuttaṃ hāranayānaṃ yojanānibandhanaṃ, so nayo. Yathāha – lakkhaṇahāre “evaṃ ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā kiccato ca lakkhaṇato ca sāmaññato cā”tiādi. Tathā vicayena hārena vicinitvā yuttihārena yojetabbāti. Tathā sodhanahārādīsu suddho ārambho hoti, so pañho vissajjito bhavatīti evamādi. Ekattādayopi nayā idha nayoti gahetabbā.

Now, that which is free from distinctions such as cause and so forth, and is the binding principle for the application of the methods of conveyance—that is a method (naya). As it is said in the method of characteristics: 'Thus, those phenomena that share a single characteristic, whether in function, characteristic, or generality,' and so on. Similarly: 'Having investigated with the method of investigation, it should be connected with the method of reason.' Likewise, in the method of purification and so forth: 'The beginning becomes purified, that question is answered,' and so on. The methods of unity and so forth should also be taken as 'method' here.

Evaṃ hetuphalādīni upadhāretvā nesaṃ vasena tattha tattha sutte labbhamānapadatthaniddhāraṇamukhena yathālakkhaṇaṃ ete hārā nayā ca yojetabbā. Visesato pana padaṭṭhānaparikkhārā hetuvasena. Desanāvicayacatubyūhasamāropanā hetuphalavasena. Tathā vevacanapaññattiotaraṇasodhanā phalavasenevāti keci. Vibhatti hetubhūmivasena. Parivatto visabhāgavasena. Āvaṭṭo sabhāgavisabhāgavasena. Lakkhaṇayuttiadhiṭṭhānā nayavasena yojetabbāti. Ettāvatā ca yaṃ vuttaṃ –

Thus, having considered causes, results, and so forth, by means of them, these methods of conveyance (hāra) and methods (naya) should be applied according to their characteristics, through the entry point of determining the meaning of terms found in the various Suttas. Specifically, the methods of proximate cause and requisites should be applied by way of cause. The methods of exposition, investigation, fourfold arrangement, and superimposition should be applied by way of cause and result. Likewise, some say that the methods of synonymy, concept, descent, and purification should be applied solely by way of result. The method of grammatical case should be applied by way of cause and plane. The method of transformation should be applied by way of dissimilarity. The method of revolving should be applied by way of similarity and dissimilarity. The methods of characteristic, reason, and determination should be applied by way of method (naya). And by this much, what was said is:

“Sāmaññato visesena, padattho lakkhaṇaṃ kamo;

Ettāvatā ca hetvādī, veditabbā hi viññunā”ti.

“In general and in particular, the meaning of the terms, the characteristic, and the order; by this much, causes and so forth should indeed be understood by the wise.”

Ayaṃ gāthā vuttatthā hoti.

This verse has the meaning that has been stated.

Niddesavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section of the exposition is completed.

4. Paṭiniddesavāravaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Section of Detailed Exposition

1. Desanāhāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Analysis of the Method of Exposition

5. Evaṃ [V 0.0172] hārādayo sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ gāthābandhavasena sarūpato niddisitvā idāni tesu hāre tāva paṭiniddesavasena vibhajituṃ “tattha katamo desanāhāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha katamoti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Desanāhāroti pucchitabbadhammanidassanaṃ. Kiñcāpi desanāhāro niddesavāre sarūpato dassito, paṭiniddesassa pana visayaṃ [M 0.0041] dassento “assādādīnavatā”ti gāthaṃ ekadesena paccāmasati. Ayaṃ desanāhāro pubbāparāpekkho. Tattha pubbāpekkhatte “katamo desanāhāro”ti pucchitvā “assādādīnavatā”ti sarūpato dassitassa nigamanaṃ hoti. Parāpekkhatte pana “ayaṃ desanāhāro kiṃ desayatī”ti desanākiriyāya kattuniddeso hoti. Tena desanāhārassa anvatthasaññataṃ dasseti. Desayatīti saṃvaṇṇeti, vitthāretīti attho.

5. Thus, having expounded the modes and so forth in their own nature by means of composing in verse for the purpose of easy comprehension, now, among them, in order to analyze the modes firstly by way of detailed exposition, the passage beginning, 'Therein, what is the mode of teaching?' is commenced. Therein, 'what is it?' is a question asked out of a desire to explain. 'The mode of teaching' is an indication of the phenomenon to be inquired about. Although the mode of teaching has been shown in its own nature in the section on exposition, nevertheless, while showing the scope of the detailed exposition, it reviews in part the verse beginning 'assādādīnavatā.' This 'mode of teaching' is relative to what precedes and what follows. Therein, in the case of being relative to what precedes, having asked, 'What is the mode of teaching?', it is the conclusion of that which was shown in its own nature as 'assādādīnavatā.' In the case of being relative to what follows, however, 'What does this mode of teaching teach?' is the designation of the agent of the action of teaching. Thereby, it shows that 'desanāhāra' is a designation corresponding to its meaning. 'Teaches' means 'explains, elaborates'—such is the meaning.

Idāni anena desetabbadhamme sarūpato dassento “assāda”ntiādimāha, taṃ pubbe vuttanayattā uttānameva. Tasmā ito parampi avuttameva vaṇṇayissāma. “Kattha pana āgate assādādike ayaṃ hāro saṃvaṇṇetī”ti anuyogaṃ manasikatvā desanāhārena saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammaṃ dassento “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādikaṃ sabbapariyattidhammasaṅgāhakaṃ bhagavato chachakkadesanaṃ ekadesena dasseti.

Now, showing by this mode the phenomena to be taught in their own nature, he states that which begins with 'gratification.' Since that is of a method already stated previously, it is indeed evident. Therefore, from here onward, we will explain only what has not been stated. Having borne in mind the inquiry, 'Wherein does this mode explain gratification and so forth that have occurred?', and showing the phenomenon to be explained by the mode of teaching, he indicates in part the Blessed One's Chachakka discourse, which encompasses all the scriptural teaching, beginning with, 'I will teach you the Dhamma, O monks.'

Tattha dhammanti ayaṃ dhamma-saddo pariyattisaccasamādhipaññāpakatipuññāpattiñeyyādīsu bahūsu atthesu diṭṭhappayogo. Tathā hi “idha, bhikkhu, dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇātī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.73) pariyattidhamme dissati. “Diṭṭhadhammo pattadhammo”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.299; mahāva. 18) sacce. “Evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto ahesu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.13, 145) samādhimhi. “Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo”ti evamādīsu (jā. 1.1.57; 1.2.147-148) paññāyaṃ. “Jātidhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattāna”nti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 2.398; ma. ni. 1.131) pakatiyaṃ[V 0.0173]. “Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.10.102; 1.15.385) puññe. “Cattāro pārājikā dhammā”ti evamādīsu (pārā. 233) āpattiyaṃ. “Kusalā dhammā akusalādhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. tikamātikā 1) ñeyye. Idha pana pariyattiyaṃ daṭṭhabboti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.mūlapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā; dha. sa. aṭṭha. cittuppādakaṇḍa 1; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 1.1).

Therein, regarding 'dhammaṃ,' this word 'dhamma' is seen to be used in many meanings, such as scriptural teaching, truth, concentration, wisdom, nature, merit, offense, the knowable, and so forth. For instance, in passages such as, 'Here, a monk learns the Dhamma,' it is seen in the sense of scriptural teaching. In passages such as, 'one who has seen the truth, attained the truth,' it is seen in the sense of truth. In passages such as, 'Those Blessed Ones were of such qualities,' it is seen in the sense of concentration. In passages such as, 'Truth, wisdom, perseverance, and generosity,' it is seen in the sense of wisdom. In passages such as, 'of beings, O monks, who have the nature of birth,' it is seen in the sense of nature. In passages such as, 'The Dhamma surely protects one who practices the Dhamma,' it is seen in the sense of merit. In passages such as, 'the four pārājika offenses,' it is seen in the sense of offense. In passages such as, 'wholesome states, unwholesome states,' it is seen in the sense of the knowable. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of scriptural teaching.

Voti pana ayaṃ vo-saddo “handa dāni, bhikkhave, pavāremi vo”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.215) ettha upayogatthe āgato. “Sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīya”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.273) karaṇatthe. “Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyakammantā”tiādīsu padapūraṇe. “Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.72) sampadānatthe. Idhāpi sampadānatthe evāti daṭṭhabbo.

Furthermore, regarding 'vo,' this word 'vo' occurs in the accusative sense, as in, 'Come now, monks, I invite you (vo).' In passages such as, 'For you (vo), monks, who have gathered, two things are to be done,' it occurs in the agentive sense. In passages such as, 'Those of you (vo) who are noble, with perfectly pure bodily conduct,' it occurs as an expletive. In passages such as, 'I announce to you (vo), monks,' it occurs in the dative sense. Here too, it should be understood as being in the dative sense.

Bhikkhanasīlatādiguṇayogena [M 0.0042] bhikkhū, bhinnakilesatādiguṇayogena vā. Atha vā saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhantīti bhikkhū. Bhikkhaveti tesaṃ ālapanaṃ. Tena te dhammassavane niyojento attano mukhābhimukhaṃ karoti. Desessāmīti kathessāmi. Tena nāhaṃ dhammissaratāya tumhe aññaṃ kiñci kāreyyāmi, anāvaraṇañāṇena sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ paccakkhakāritāya pana dhammaṃ desessāmīti idāni pavattiyamānaṃ dhammadesanaṃ paṭijānāti. Ādikalyāṇantiādīsu ādimhi kalyāṇaṃ ādikalyāṇaṃ, ādikalyāṇametassāti vā ādikalyāṇaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Tattha sīlena ādikalyāṇaṃ. Samādhinā majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Paññāya pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Buddhasubuddhatāya vā ādikalyāṇaṃ. Dhammasudhammatāya majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Saṅghasuppaṭipattiyā pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Atha vā ugghaṭitaññuvinayanena ādikalyāṇaṃ. Vipañcitaññuvinayanena majjhekalyāṇaṃ neyyapuggalavinayanena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Ayamevattho idhādhippeto.

They are 'bhikkhus' (monks) due to their connection with qualities such as the characteristic of begging, or due to their connection with qualities such as having destroyed the defilements. Or, they are 'bhikkhus' because they see (ikkhanti) danger (bhayaṃ) in saṃsāra. 'Bhikkhave' (O monks) is the vocative address to them. By that, wishing to urge them to listen to the Dhamma, he makes them face him. 'I will teach' means 'I will speak.' By this, he undertakes to give the Dhamma teaching that is now to be delivered, as if saying: 'I, by my mastery over the Dhamma, will not make you do anything else; but because I have directly realized all knowable phenomena with my unobstructed knowledge, I will teach the Dhamma.' In the phrases beginning 'good in the beginning,' 'good in the beginning' (ādikalyāṇaṃ) means good at the beginning, or it is that which has good at its beginning. This same method applies to the remaining two phrases. Therein, it is good in the beginning through morality, good in the middle through concentration, and good in the end through wisdom. Or, it is good in the beginning through the Buddha's perfect Buddhahood, good in the middle through the Dhamma's excellent nature as Dhamma, and good in the end through the Sangha's excellent practice. Or again, it is good in the beginning through the disciplining of the person of quick understanding, good in the middle through the disciplining of the person of developed understanding, and good in the end through the disciplining of the person who is to be led. It is this latter meaning that is intended here.

Atthasampattiyā sātthaṃ. Byañjanasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Saṅkāsanādichaatthapadasamāyogato vā sātthaṃ. Akkharādichabyañjanapadasamāyogato sabyañjanaṃ. Ayamevattho idhādhippeto. Upanetabbābhāvato ekantena paripuṇṇanti kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ. Apanetabbābhāvato parisuddhaṃ. Sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhapāripūriyā vā paripuṇṇaṃ. Caturoghanittharaṇāya pavattiyā lokāmisanirapekkhatāya ca parisuddhaṃ. Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ brahmūnaṃ vā seṭṭhānaṃ ariyānaṃ cariyaṃ sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsayissāmi paridīpayissāmīti attho.

It is 'with meaning' (sātthaṃ) due to its accomplishment in meaning. It is 'with phrasing' (sabyañjanaṃ) due to its accomplishment in phrasing. Or, it is 'with meaning' due to its connection with the six kinds of meaningful terms beginning with exposition; it is 'with phrasing' due to its connection with the six kinds of phrasing terms beginning with letters. And it is this latter meaning that is intended here. Because there is nothing to be added, it is 'entirely complete,' thus 'utterly complete' (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ). Because there is nothing to be removed, it is 'pure' (parisuddhaṃ). Or, it is 'complete' due to the fulfillment of the five aggregates of phenomena beginning with virtue. It is 'pure' because it proceeds for the purpose of crossing over the four floods and because of its non-reliance on worldly gain. The meaning is: I will proclaim and make clear the 'holy life' (brahmacariyaṃ)—the excellent, best, supreme conduct; or, the conduct of the holy, excellent, noble ones; the teaching that is the compendium of the threefold training.

Evaṃ [V 0.0174] bhagavatā desito pakāsito ca sāsanadhammo yesaṃ assādādīnaṃ dassanavasena pavatto, te assādādayo desanāhārassa visayabhūtā yattha yattha pāṭhe savisesaṃ vuttā, tato tato niddhāretvā udāharaṇavasena idhānetvā dassetuṃ “tattha katamo assādo”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kāmanti manāpiyarūpādiṃ tebhūmakadhammasaṅkhātaṃ vatthukāmaṃ. Kāmayamānassāti icchantassa. Tassa cetaṃ samijjhatīti tassa kāmayamānassa sattassa taṃ kāmasaṅkhātaṃ vatthu samijjhati ce, sace so taṃ labhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Addhā pītimano [M 0.0043] hotīti ekaṃsena tuṭṭhacitto hoti. Laddhāti labhitvā. Maccoti satto. Yadicchatīti yaṃ icchati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana niddese (mahāni. 1) vuttanayena veditabbo. Ayaṃ assādoti yāyaṃ adhippāyasamijjhanā icchitalābhe pītimanatā somanassaṃ, ayaṃ assādetabbato assādo.

Thus, the Dhamma of the Teaching, taught and illuminated by the Blessed One, proceeds by way of showing gratification and so forth. These gratifications and so on are the objects of the mode of teaching; wherever they are specifically stated in the text, having ascertained them from those places, they are brought here by way of example to show, beginning with 'Herein, what is gratification?' Herein, 'sensual pleasure' (kāma) refers to object-sensual pleasure, reckoned as phenomena of the three realms, such as agreeable forms and so forth. 'For one who desires' means 'for one who wishes.' 'If this succeeds for him' means if that object designated as sensual pleasure succeeds for that being who desires it, that is, if he obtains it. 'Surely, he becomes joyful' means he becomes unequivocally delighted in mind. 'Having obtained' means 'having gained.' 'A mortal' means 'a being.' 'Whatever he desires' means 'whatever he wishes.' This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the exposition (Mahāni. 1). This is gratification: whatever fulfillment of intention, joyful-mindedness, and gladness there is upon obtaining what is wished for. This is gratification because it is to be savored.

Tassa ce kāmayānassāti tassa puggalassa kāme icchamānassa, kāmena vā yāyamānassa. Chandajātassāti jātataṇhassa. Jantunoti sattassa. Te kāmā parihāyantīti te vatthukāmā kenaci antarāyena vinassanti ce. Sallaviddhova ruppatīti atha ayomayādinā sallena viddho viya pīḷiyatīti attho. Ayaṃ ādīnavoti yāyaṃ kāmānaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā kāmayānassa sattassa ruppanā domanassuppatti, ayaṃ ādīnavo.

‘If for him who is desirous’ means for that person who desires sensual pleasures, or who strives by means of sensual pleasure. ‘For one in whom desire has arisen’ means for one in whom craving has arisen. ‘For a creature’ means for a being. ‘Those sensual pleasures decline’ means if those object-sensual pleasures are destroyed by some obstacle. ‘Pierced by a dart, he is afflicted’ means then, as if pierced by a dart made of iron and so forth, he is afflicted; this is the meaning. This is the danger: whatever affliction and arising of displeasure there is for a being who desires sensual pleasures due to their change and alteration, this is the danger.

Yo kāme parivajjetīti yo bhikkhu yathāvutte kāme tattha chandarāgassa vikkhambhanena vā samucchindanena vā sabbabhāgena vajjeti. Yathā kiṃ? Sappasseva padā siroti, yathā koci puriso jīvitukāmo kaṇhasappaṃ paṭipathe passitvā attano pādena tassa siraṃ parivajjeti, somaṃ…pe… samativattatīti so bhikkhu sabbaṃ lokaṃ visaritvā ṭhitattā loke visattikāsaṅkhātaṃ imaṃ taṇhaṃ satimā hutvā samatikkamatīti. Idaṃ nissaraṇanti yadidaṃ visattikāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya nibbānārammaṇena ariyamaggena samativattanaṃ, idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

‘One who avoids sensual pleasures’ means a monk who, in regard to the aforesaid sensual pleasures, avoids desire and lust for them entirely, either by suppression or by eradication. How so? ‘Like a snake’s head with the foot’ means just as a person desiring to live, seeing a black snake on the path, avoids its head with his foot, so too... ‘he overcomes’ means that monk, because he stands having transcended the whole world, mindfully overcomes this craving, which is reckoned as attachment in the world. This is the escape: this overcoming of craving, which is reckoned as attachment, by means of the noble path that has Nibbāna as its object, this is the escape.

Khettanti kedārādikhettaṃ. Vatthunti gharavatthuādivatthuṃ. Hiraññaṃ vāti kahāpaṇasaṅkhātaṃ suvaṇṇasaṅkhātañca hiraññaṃ. Vā-saddo vikappanattho, so sabbapadesu yojetabbo. Gavāssanti gāvo ca asse cāti gavāssaṃ. Dāsaporisanti dāse ca porise cāti dāsaporisaṃ. Thiyoti itthiyo. Bandhūti ñātibandhavo. Puthū kāmeti aññepi vā manāpiyarūpādike bahū kāmaguṇe. Yo naro anugijjhatīti yo satto anu anu abhikaṅkhati patthetīti attho. Ayaṃ assādoti yadidaṃ khettādīnaṃ anugijjhanaṃ, ayaṃ assādeti vatthukāme etenāti assādo.

‘Field’ means a field such as a paddy field. ‘Site’ means a site such as a house site. ‘Or gold’ means gold reckoned as coins and gold reckoned as bullion. The word ‘or’ has the sense of an alternative; it should be applied in all instances. ‘Cattle and horses’ means both cows and horses. ‘Slaves and workmen’ means both slaves and male workers. ‘Women’ means females. ‘Relatives’ means kinsmen and relatives. ‘Many sensual pleasures’ means other numerous sensual qualities, such as agreeable forms and so on. ‘Whatever person is greedy for’ means whatever being again and again intensely desires and longs for; this is the meaning. This is gratification: this greediness for fields and so on. It is ‘gratification’ (assādo) because by this [greed] one savors (assādeti) object-sensual pleasures.

Abalā [V 0.0175][M 0.0044] naṃ balīyantīti khettādibhede kāme anugijjhantaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ kusalehi pahātabbattā abalasaṅkhātā kilesā balīyanti abhibhavanti, saddhābalādivirahena vā abalaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ abalā kilesā balīyanti, abalattā abhibhavantīti attho. Maddantenaṃ parissayāti enaṃ kāmagiddhaṃ kāme pariyesantaṃ rakkhantañca sīhādayo ca pākaṭaparissayā kāyaduccaritādayo ca apākaṭaparissayā maddanti. Tato naṃ…pe… dakanti tato tehi pākaṭāpākaṭaparissayehi abhibhūtaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ jātiādidukkhaṃ samudde bhinnanāvaṃ udakaṃ viya anveti anugacchatīti attho. Ayaṃ ādīnavoti yvāyaṃ taṇhāduccaritasaṃkilesahetuko jātiādidukkhānubandho, ayaṃ ādīnavo.

‘The weak overpower him’ means the defilements, which are reckoned as weak because they are to be abandoned by wholesome states, overpower and overwhelm that person who is greedy for the various sensual pleasures such as fields. Or, the weak defilements overpower that person who is weak due to the absence of the power of faith and so on; because he is weak, they overwhelm him. This is the meaning. ‘Dangers crush him’ means both manifest dangers such as lions and so on, and unmanifest dangers such as bodily misconduct and so on, crush that person who is greedy for sensual pleasures, who is seeking and guarding them. ‘Then suffering follows him... like water’ means then, the suffering of birth and so on follows that person who has been overwhelmed by those manifest and unmanifest dangers, just as water follows a broken boat in the ocean; this is the meaning. This is the danger: this sequence of the suffering of birth and so on, which is caused by craving, misconduct, and defilement, this is the danger.

Tasmāti yasmā kāmagiddhassa vuttanayena dukkhānubandho vijjati, tasmā. Jantūti satto. Sadā satoti pubbarattāpararattaṃ jāgariyānuyogena sato hutvā. Kāmāni parivajjayeti vikkhambhanavasena samucchedavasena ca rūpādīsu vatthukāmesu sabbappakāraṃ kilesakāmaṃ anuppādento kāmāni parivajjaye pajaheyya. Te pahāya tare oghanti evaṃ te kāme pahāya tappahānakaraariyamaggeneva catubbidhampi oghaṃ tareyya, tarituṃ sakkuṇeyyāti attho. Nāvaṃ sitvāva pāragūti yathā puriso udakaggahaṇena garubhāraṃ nāvaṃ udakaṃ bahi siñcitvā lahukāya nāvāya appakasireneva pāragū bhaveyya, pāraṃ gaccheyya, evameva attabhāvanāvaṃ kilesūdakagarukaṃ siñcitvā lahukena attabhāvena pāragū bhaveyya, pāraṃ nibbānaṃ arahattappattiyā gaccheyya anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānenāti attho. Idaṃ nissaraṇanti yaṃ kāmappahānamukhena caturoghaṃ taritvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā nibbānaṃ, idaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaraṇato nissaraṇanti.

‘Therefore’ means: because for one who is greedy for sensual pleasures there is a sequence of suffering in the way stated, therefore... ‘A creature’ means a being. ‘Always mindful’ means being mindful throughout the night by the practice of wakefulness. ‘One should avoid sensual pleasures’ means by not giving rise to defilement-sensual desire of any kind in regard to object-sensual pleasures such as forms, etc., both by way of suppression and by way of eradication, one should avoid and abandon sensual pleasures. ‘Having abandoned them, one should cross the flood’ means thus, having abandoned those sensual pleasures, one should cross the fourfold flood by the very noble path that accomplishes their abandonment; one would be able to cross, this is the meaning. ‘Having bailed out the boat, one goes to the far shore’ means just as a person, having bailed the water out of a boat that is heavy from taking on water, would, with the light boat, reach the far shore with little effort, just as he would go to the far shore; even so, having bailed out the boat of individuality, which is heavy with the water of defilements, one would, with a light individuality, become one who goes to the far shore. One would go to the far shore which is Nibbāna through the attainment of Arahantship, through the final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue; this is the meaning. This is the escape: this Nibbāna by means of the Nibbāna-element without residue, having crossed the four floods with the abandoning of sensual pleasures as the principal means. This, because it is an escape from all conditioned things, is the escape.

Dhammoti dānādipuññadhammo. Haveti nipātamattaṃ. Rakkhati dhammacārinti yo taṃ dhammaṃ appamatto carati, taṃ dhammacāriṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikabhedena duvidhatopi anatthato rakkhati pāleti. Chattaṃ mahantaṃ yatha vassakāleti vassakāle deve vassante yathā mahantaṃ chattaṃ kusalena purisena dhāritaṃ taṃ vassatemanato rakkhati. Tattha yathā taṃ chattaṃ appamatto hutvā attānaṃ rakkhantaṃ chādentañca vassādito rakkhati, evaṃ dhammopi attasammāpaṇidhānena appamatto hutvā dhammacariyāya attānaṃ rakkhantaṃyeva [M 0.0045] rakkhatīti adhippāyo. Esā…pe… cārīti etena vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ karoti, taṃ suviññeyyameva. Idaṃ phalanti diṭṭhadhammikehi samparāyikehi ca [V 0.0176] anatthehi yadidaṃ dhammassa rakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ rakkhāvasānassa ca abbhudayassa nipphādanaṃ, idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ anāmasitvā desanāya nibbattetabbatāya phalanti.

'Dhamma' refers to meritorious Dhamma such as giving. 'Haveti' is merely a particle. 'It protects the one who practices the Dhamma' means: whoever, being diligent, practices that Dhamma, it protects that practitioner of the Dhamma from harm of two kinds, namely, in the present life and in the future life. 'Like a great umbrella in the rainy season' means: just as in the rainy season when the sky rains, a great umbrella held by a skillful person protects that person from being soaked by the rain; just as that umbrella protects from being soaked by rain and so on the one who, being diligent, protects and covers oneself, so too the Dhamma protects only the one who, having rightly directed oneself and being diligent, protects oneself by the practice of Dhamma. This is the intended meaning. 'This… practitioner…'—by this, it makes the meaning already stated clearer; that statement is indeed easy to understand. 'This is the fruit' means: whatever protection by the Dhamma from harms in the present and future lives, and the accomplishment of prosperity which is the culmination of that protection, has been stated—this, because it is to be brought about by the teaching without touching upon liberation, is called the fruit.

Sabbe dhammāti sabbe saṅkhatā dhammā. Anattāti natthi etesaṃ attā kārakavedakasabhāvo, sayaṃ vā na attāti anattāti. Itīti evaṃ. Yadā paññāya passatīti yasmiṃ kāle vipassanaṃ ussukkāpento anattānupassanāsaṅkhātāya paññāya passati. Atha nibbindati dukkheti atha anattānupassanāya pubbe eva aniccatādukkhatānaṃ suparidiṭṭhattā nibbidānupassanāvasena vipassanāgocarabhūte pañcakkhandhadukkhe nibbindati nibbedaṃ āpajjati. Esa maggo visuddhiyāti yā vuttalakkhaṇā nibbidānupassanā sabbakilesavisujjhanato visuddhisaṅkhātassa ariyamaggassa accantavisuddhiyā vā amatadhātuyā maggo upāyo. Ayaṃ upāyoti yadidaṃ anattānupassanāmukhena sabbasmiṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ nibbindanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ visuddhiyā adhigamahetubhāvato upāyo.

'All phenomena' means all conditioned phenomena. 'Not-self' means: for these, there is no self which has the nature of an agent or an experiencer, therefore it is called not-self; or, they themselves are not a self, therefore it is called not-self. 'Thus' means in this way. 'When one sees with wisdom' means: at which time, while striving at insight meditation, one sees with the wisdom called the contemplation of not-self. 'Then one grows disenchanted with suffering' means: then, because the nature of impermanence and suffering has already been clearly seen beforehand through the contemplation of not-self, by way of the contemplation of disenchantment, one becomes disenchanted with the suffering of the five aggregates which has become the object of insight; one attains disenchantment. 'This is the path to purity' means: that contemplation of disenchantment with the aforesaid characteristic is the path, the means, to the noble path called 'purity' because of the purification from all defilements, or to the deathless element, which is utter purity. 'This is the means' means: whatever disenchantment in the entire round of existence through the approach of the contemplation of not-self has been stated, that disenchantment is called the means because it is a cause for the attainment of purity.

“Cakkhumā…pe… parivajjaye”ti imissā gāthāya ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yathā cakkhumā puriso sarīre vahante visamāni bhūmippadesāni caṇḍatāya vā visame hatthiādayo parivajjeti, evaṃ loke sappañño puriso sappaññatāya hitāhitaṃ jānanto pāpāni lāmakāni duccaritāni parivajjeyyāti. Ayaṃ āṇattīti yā ayaṃ “pāpāni parivajjetabbānī”ti dhammarājassa bhagavato āṇā, ayaṃ āṇattīti.

'The one with vision... should avoid': of this verse, this is the concise meaning: Just as a person with vision, while the body is functioning, avoids uneven places of ground or fierce and unruly elephants and so on, so too in the world, a wise person, due to being wise and knowing what is beneficial and non-beneficial, should avoid evil, base misconducts. 'This is the command' means: whatever this command of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, 'Evil things are to be avoided,' is, this is called a command.

Evaṃ visuṃ visuṃ suttesu āgatā phalūpāyāṇattiyo udāharaṇabhāvena dassetvā idāni tā ekato āgatā dassetuṃ “suññato”ti gāthamāha.

Thus, having shown by way of example the fruit, the means, and the command that have appeared separately in various suttas, now, in order to show them as they have appeared together in a single verse, he spoke the verse beginning 'suññato'.

Tattha suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu, mogharājāti āṇattīti “mogharāja, sabbampi saṅkhāralokaṃ avasavattitāsallakkhaṇavasena vā tucchabhāvasamanupassanavasena vā suññoti passā”ti idaṃ dhammarājassa vacanaṃ vidhānabhāvato āṇatti. Sabbadā satikiriyāya taṃsuññatādassanaṃ sampajjatīti “sadā satoti upāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhaccāti vīsativatthukaṃ [M 0.0046] sakkāyadassanaṃ uddharitvā samucchinditvā. Evaṃ maccutaro siyāti. Idaṃ phalanti yaṃ evaṃ vuttena vidhinā maccutaraṇaṃ maccuno visayātikkamanaṃ tassa yaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāpaṭipajjanaṃ, idaṃ desanāya phalanti attho. Yathā pana assādādayo sutte katthaci [V 0.0177] sarūpato katthaci niddhāretabbatāya katthaci visuṃ visuṃ katthaci ekato dassitā, na evaṃ phalādayo. Phalādayo pana sabbattha sutte gāthāsu vā ekato dassetabbāti imassa nayassa dassanatthaṃ visuṃ visuṃ udāharitvāpi puna “suññato loka”ntiādinā ekato udāharaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In that context, 'Look upon the world as empty, Mogharāja' is the command. This means: 'Mogharāja, see the entire world of formations as empty, either by way of its own characteristic of being uncontrollable or by way of contemplating its nature as void.' This word of the King of Dhamma, because it is an injunction, is a command. Because that seeing of emptiness is accomplished by the constant application of mindfulness, it is said, 'Always mindful' is the means. 'Having uprooted the view of self' means having lifted out and cut off completely the identity-view based on twenty grounds. 'Thus one may cross beyond death. This is the fruit' means: whatever crossing beyond death—the transcending of the sphere of death—by the method thus stated, and whatever practice of the preliminary path for that there is, this practice of the preliminary path is the fruit of the teaching. This is the meaning. Just as gratification and so on are shown in the suttas sometimes in their own nature, sometimes for determination, sometimes separately, and sometimes together, the fruit and so on are not shown thus. But the fruit and so on should be shown together everywhere, whether in a sutta or in verses. To show this principle, even after having given examples separately, an example is given together again with 'Look upon the world as empty,' and so on. Thus it should be understood.

6. Evaṃ assādādayo udāharaṇavasena sarūpato dassetvā idāni tattha puggalavibhāgena desanāvibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

6. Having thus shown gratification and so forth by way of example in their own nature, now, in order to show the division of the teaching therein according to the division of persons, it is said, 'Therein, the Blessed One,' and so forth.

Tattha ugghaṭitaṃ ghaṭitamattaṃ uddiṭṭhamattaṃ yassa niddesapaṭiniddesā na katā, taṃ jānātīti ugghaṭitaññū. Uddesamattena sappabhedaṃ savitthāramatthaṃ paṭivijjhatīti attho, ugghaṭitaṃ vā uccalitaṃ uṭṭhapitanti attho, taṃ jānātīti ugghaṭitaññū. Dhammo hi desiyamāno desakato desanābhājanaṃ saṅkamanto viya hoti, tamesa uccalitameva jānātīti attho, calitameva vā ugghaṭitaṃ. Sassatādiākārassa hi veneyyānaṃ āsayassa buddhāveṇikā dhammadesanā taṅkhaṇapatitā eva calanāya hoti, tato paramparānuvattiyā, tatthāyaṃ ugghaṭite calitamatteyeva āsaye dhammaṃ jānāti avabujjhatīti ugghaṭitaññū, tassa ugghaṭitaññussa nissaraṇaṃ desayati, tattakeneva tassa atthasiddhito. Vipañcitaṃ vitthāritaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū, vipañcitaṃ vā mandaṃ saṇikaṃ dhammaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū, tassa vipañcitaññussa ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca desayati, nātisaṅkhepavitthārāya desanāya tassa atthasiddhito. Netabbo dhammassa paṭiniddisena atthaṃ pāpetabboti neyyo, mudindriyatāya vā paṭilomaggahaṇato netabbo anunetabboti neyyo, tassa neyyassa assādaṃ ādīnavaṃ nissaraṇañca desayati, anavasesetvāva desanena tassa atthasiddhito. Tatthāyaṃ pāḷi –

Herein, one who understands what is merely stated, merely pointed out, for which an explanation and counter-explanation have not been made, is an ugghaṭitaññū (one who understands upon a brief statement). The meaning is that by a mere brief indication, one penetrates the meaning with its divisions and details. Alternatively, ugghaṭitaṃ means stirred or raised up; one who knows that is an ugghaṭitaññū. For when the Dhamma is being taught, it is as if it moves from the teacher to the recipient of the teaching; this person knows that Dhamma that is merely stirred—that is the meaning. Alternatively, ugghaṭitaṃ is merely the stirring [of a latent disposition]. For the Buddha's unique Dhamma teaching, falling upon [the mind] at that very moment, serves to stir the latent disposition of trainable beings characterized by [views such as] eternalism and so forth; thereafter, it leads to complete severance. In this context, this person knows and understands the Dhamma when the latent disposition is merely stirred—hence, an ugghaṭitaññū. For such an ugghaṭitaññū, the escape is taught, because for him the goal is accomplished by just that much. One who knows what is elaborated, expanded, and explained in detail is a vipañcitaññū (one who understands through explanation). Alternatively, one who knows the Dhamma slowly and gradually is a vipañcitaññū. For such a vipañcitaññū, the drawback and the escape are taught, because for him the goal is accomplished by a teaching that is neither too brief nor too detailed. One who is to be led, who is to be made to arrive at the meaning by means of a counter-explanation of the Dhamma, is a neyyo (one to be guided). Alternatively, because of dull faculties or because of grasping in a contrary way, one who is to be led, to be repeatedly instructed, is a neyyo. For such a neyyo, the allure, the drawback, and the escape are taught, because for him the goal is accomplished by teaching completely, without leaving anything out. Herein, this is the Pāli:

“Katamo ca puggalo ugghaṭitaññū? Yassa puggalassa saha udāhaṭavelāya dhammābhisamayo hoti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ugghaṭitaññū.

“And which person is an ugghaṭitaññū? The person for whom there is comprehension of the Dhamma simultaneously with the time of the utterance. This person is called an ugghaṭitaññū.

“Katamo [M 0.0047] ca puggalo vipañcitaññū? Yassa puggalassa saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne dhammābhisamayo hoti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo vipañcitaññū.

“And which person is a vipañcitaññū? The person for whom there is comprehension of the Dhamma when the meaning of what was stated in brief is analyzed in detail. This person is called a vipañcitaññū.

“Katamo [V 0.0178] ca puggalo neyyo? Yassa puggalassa uddesato paripucchato yonisomanasikaroto kalyāṇamitte sevato bhajato payirupāsato evaṃ anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hoti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo neyyo”ti (pu. pa. 148-150).

“And which person is a neyyo? The person for whom there is a gradual comprehension of the Dhamma through learning the text, inquiring into the meaning, applying wise attention, and associating with, attending on, and serving good friends. This person is called a neyyo.”

Padaparamo panettha nettiyaṃ paṭivedhassa abhājananti na gahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca assādo, ādīnavo, nissaraṇaṃ, assādo ca ādīnavo ca, assādo ca nissaraṇañca, ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañca, assādo ca ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañcāti ete satta paṭṭhānanayā.

The padaparama person (one for whom the text is the highest attainment), it should be understood, is not included here in the Netti because he is not a vessel for penetration. And herein, there are these seven foundational modes: allure; drawback; escape; allure and drawback; allure and escape; drawback and escape; and allure, drawback, and escape.

Tesu tatiyachaṭṭhasattamā veneyyattayavinayane samatthatāya gahitā, itare cattāro na gahitā. Na hi kevalena assādena ādīnavena tadubhayena vā kathitena veneyyavinayanaṃ sambhavati, kilesānaṃ pahānāvacanato. Pañcamopi ādīnavāvacanato nissaraṇassa anupāyo eva. Na hi vimuttirasā bhagavato desanā vimuttiṃ tadupāyañca anāmasantī pavattati. Tasmā ete cattāro nayā anuddhaṭā. Sace pana padaparamassa puggalassa vasena pavattaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ tadubhayabhāge ṭhitaṃ desanaṃ suttekadesaṃ gāthaṃ vā tādisaṃ etesaṃ nayānaṃ udāharaṇabhāvena uddharati, evaṃ sati sattannampi nayānaṃ gahaṇaṃ bhaveyya. Veneyyavinayanaṃ pana tesaṃ santāne ariyamaggassa uppādanaṃ. Taṃ yathāvuttehi eva nayeti, nāvasesehīti itare idha na vuttā. Yasmā pana peṭake (peṭako. 23) –

Among these, the third, sixth, and seventh are included for their capability in training the three types of trainable persons; the other four are not included. For the training of trainable persons is not possible merely by speaking of allure, or of drawback, or of both, because the abandoning of defilements is not stated. The fifth mode too, because it does not state the drawback, is not a means for escape. For the Blessed One's teaching, which has the taste of liberation, does not proceed without touching upon liberation and the means to it. Therefore, these four modes are not extracted. However, if one were to extract, as examples of these modes, a teaching—such as a portion of a sutta or a verse—that pertains to a padaparama person, or is connected with defilement, connected with latent tendencies, or established in both, then in that case, the inclusion of all seven modes would be possible. But the training of trainable persons is the production of the noble path in their mental continuum. That occurs only through the modes already mentioned, not through the remaining ones. Therefore, the others are not stated here. Because in the Peṭaka:

“Tattha katamo assādo ca ādīnavo ca?

“Therein, what are the allure and the drawback?

Yāni karoti puriso, tāni attani passati;

Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpaka”nti.

Whatever deeds a person does, those he sees in himself; the doer of good sees good, and the doer of evil, evil.”

Tattha yaṃ kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ paccanubhoti, ayaṃ assādo. Yaṃ pāpakārī pāpaṃ paccanubhoti, ayaṃ ādīnavo.

Therein, the good that the doer of good experiences is the allure. The evil that the doer of evil experiences is the drawback.

Aṭṭhime[M 0.0048], bhikkhave, lokadhammā. Katame aṭṭha? Lābhotiādi (a. ni. 8.6). Tattha [V 0.0179] lābho yaso sukhaṃ pasaṃsā, ayaṃ assādo. Alābho ayaso dukkhaṃ nindā, ayaṃ ādīnavo.

“Monks, there are these eight worldly conditions…,” and so on. Therein, gain, fame, pleasure, and praise are the allure. Loss, disrepute, pain, and blame are the drawback.

Tattha katamo assādo ca nissaraṇañca?

“Therein, what are the allure and the escape?

“Sukho vipāko puññānaṃ, adhippāyo ca ijjhati;

Khippañca paramaṃ santiṃ, nibbānamadhigacchatī”ti. (peṭako. 23);

“Pleasant is the result of meritorious deeds, and one's intention is fulfilled; and one quickly attains the supreme peace, Nibbāna.”

Ayaṃ assādo ca nissaraṇañca.

This is the allure and the escape.

Dvattiṃsimāni, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā…pe… vivaṭacchadoti sabbaṃ lakkhaṇasuttaṃ, (dī. ni. 3.199) ayaṃ assādo ca nissaraṇañca.

“Monks, these are the thirty-two marks of a great man, endowed with which a great man has only two destinies, no other…,” up to “…one with the veil removed”—the entire Lakkhaṇa Sutta. This is the allure and the escape.

Tattha katamo ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañca?

“Therein, what are the drawback and the escape?

“Bhārā have pañcakkhandhā, bhārahāro ca puggalo;

Bhārādānaṃ dukhaṃ loke, bhāranikkhepanaṃ sukhaṃ.

“Truly, the five aggregates are burdens, and the person is the burden-bearer. Taking up the burden is suffering in the world; laying down the burden is happiness.

“Nikkhipitvā garuṃ bhāraṃ, aññaṃ bhāraṃ anādiya;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, nicchāto parinibbuto”ti. (saṃ. ni. 3.22);

Having laid down the heavy burden and not taking up another burden, having uprooted craving together with its root, being without craving, one is fully extinguished.”

Ayaṃ ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañca.

This is the drawback and the escape.

Tattha katamo assādo ca ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañca?

“Therein, what are the allure, the drawback, and the escape?

“Kāmā hi citrā madhurā manoramā, virūparūpena mathenti cittaṃ;

Tasmā ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rāja, apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyoti. (ma. ni. 2.307; theragā. 787-788; peṭako. 23);

“For sensual pleasures—varied, sweet, and delightful—torment the mind with their diverse forms. Therefore, O king, I have gone forth; the unerring ascetic life is indeed better.”

Ayaṃ assādo ca ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañcā”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā tepi nayā idha niddhāretvā veditabbā. Phalādīsupi ayaṃ nayo labbhati eva. Yasmā peṭake (peṭako. 22) “tattha [V 0.0180] katamaṃ phalañca upāyo ca? Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti gāthā (saṃ. ni. 1.23), idaṃ phalañca upāyo ca.

'This is gratification, danger, and escape,' it is said. Therefore, these methods should also be determined and known here. This method is indeed obtained in the case of fruit and so on as well. Because in the Peṭaka it is said: 'Therein, what is the fruit and the means? The verse, “A wise person established in virtue…”' This is the fruit and the means.

Tattha [M 0.0049] katamaṃ phalañca āṇatti ca?

Therein, what is the fruit and the command?

“Sace bhāyatha dukkhassa, sace vo dukkhamappiyaṃ;

Mākattha pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, āvi vā yadi vā rahoti. (udā. 44);

If you fear suffering, if suffering is not dear to you, do not perform an evil action, whether openly or in secret.

Idaṃ phalañca āṇatti ca.

This is the fruit and the command.

Tattha katamo upāyo ca āṇatti ca?

Therein, what is the means and the command?

“Kumbhūpamaṃ kāyamimaṃ viditvā, nagarūpamaṃ cittamidaṃ ṭhapetvā;

Yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhena, jitañca rakkhe anivesano siyā”ti. (dha. pa. 40);

Having known this body to be like a pot, having established this mind to be like a fortified city, one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom. One should guard what has been conquered and be without attachment.

Ayaṃ upāyo ca āṇatti ca. Evaṃ phalādīnaṃ dukavasenapi udāharaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca yo nissaraṇadesanāya vinetabbo, so ugghaṭitaññūtiādinā yathā desanāvibhāgena puggalavibhāgasiddhi hoti, evaṃ ugghaṭitaññussa bhagavā nissaraṇaṃ desetītiādinā puggalavibhāgena desanāvibhāgo sambhavatīti so tathā dassito.

This is the means and the command. Thus, an example should be known by way of the dyad of fruit and so on. And here, just as the accomplishment of the division of persons occurs through the division of the teaching, by the principle 'the person who is to be trained by the teaching on escape is one of quick understanding,' and so on, so too, the division of the teaching is possible through the division of persons, by the principle 'the Blessed One teaches escape to one of quick understanding,' and so on. Therefore, it is shown in that way.

Evaṃ yesaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena desanāvibhāgo dassito, te puggale paṭipadāvibhāgena vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “catasso paṭipadā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭipadābhiññākato vibhāgo paṭipadākato hotīti āha – “catasso paṭipadā”ti. Tā panetā ca samathavipassanāpaṭipattivasena duvidhā honti. Kathaṃ? Samathapakkhe tāva paṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya yāva tassa tassa jhānassa upacāraṃ uppajjati, tāva pavattā samathabhāvanā “paṭipadā”ti vuccati. Upacārato pana paṭṭhāya yāva appanā tāva pavattā paññā “abhiññā”ti vuccati.

Thus, the division of the teaching has been shown by way of certain persons. To show those persons, having divided them by the division of the path, 'four paths,' etc., is said. Therein, the division, which is made in terms of the path and direct knowledge, is a division of the path; therefore, it says, 'four paths.' And these are twofold by way of the practice of serenity and insight. How? In the aspect of serenity, to begin with: from the first application of mind onwards, for as long as the access concentration of each respective jhāna arises, the development of serenity that has occurred up to that point is called 'the path.' Then, from access concentration onwards, for as long as absorption arises, the wisdom that has occurred up to that point is called 'direct knowledge.'

Sā [V 0.0181] panāyaṃ paṭipadā ekaccassa dukkhā hoti nīvaraṇādipaccanīkadhammasamudācāragahaṇatāya kicchā asukhasevanāti attho, ekaccassa tadabhāvena sukhā. Abhiññāpi ekaccassa dandhā hoti mandā asīghappavatti, ekaccassa khippā amandā sīghappavatti. Tasmā yo ādito kilese vikkhambhento dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilamanto vikkhambheti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti. Yo pana vikkhambhitakileso appanāparivāsaṃ [M 0.0050] vasanto cirena aṅgapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa dandhābhiññā nāma hoti. Yo khippaṃ aṅgapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa khippābhiññā nāma hoti. Yo kilese vikkhambhento sukhena akilamanto vikkhambheti, tassa sukhā paṭipadā nāma hoti.

Now, this path is painful for a certain person due to grasping the occurrence of opposing states such as the hindrances; the meaning is that it is difficult, an unpleasant undertaking. For another person, due to the absence of that, it is pleasant. Direct knowledge, too, is slow for a certain person—sluggish, not proceeding swiftly; for another, it is swift—not sluggish, proceeding swiftly. Therefore, for the person who from the beginning suppresses the defilements with difficulty, with effort, with application, and with fatigue, for him the path is painful. But as for the person who, having suppressed the defilements, dwells cultivating absorption and attains the manifestation of the factors after a long time, for him this is called slow direct knowledge. For the person who attains the manifestation of the factors quickly, for him this is called swift direct knowledge. For the person who suppresses the defilements with ease and without fatigue, for him this is called the pleasant path.

Vipassanāpakkhe pana yo rūpārūpamukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisanto cattāri mahābhūtāni pariggahetvā upādārūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti arūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti, rūpārūpaṃ pana pariggaṇhanto dukkhena kasirena kilamanto pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā nāma hoti. Pariggahitarūpārūpassa pana vipassanāparivāse maggapātubhāvadandhatāya dandhābhiññā nāma hoti. Yopi rūpārūpaṃ pariggahetvā nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapento dukkhena kasirena kilamanto vavatthapeti, vavatthapite ca nāmarūpe vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkoti. Tassāpi dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti.
