In the aspect of insight, however, a person who, applying himself to insight by means of materiality and immateriality, having comprehended the four great elements, comprehends derived materiality and comprehends immateriality; but while comprehending materiality and immateriality, is able to comprehend them only with difficulty, with hardship, and with fatigue—for that person, this is called the painful path. For one who has comprehended materiality and immateriality, however, due to the slowness of the path's manifestation while cultivating insight, this is called slow direct knowledge. And also for the person who, having comprehended materiality and immateriality, determines mind-and-materiality with difficulty, with hardship, and with fatigue; and having determined mind-and-materiality, while cultivating insight, is able to generate the path only after a long time—for that person also, this is called the painful path and slow direct knowledge.

Aparo nāmarūpampi vavatthapetvā paccaye pariggaṇhanto dukkhena kasirena kilamanto pariggaṇhāti, paccaye ca pariggahetvā vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ uppādeti. Evampi dukkhā [V 0.0182] paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti.

Another person, having determined mind-and-materiality, comprehends its conditions with difficulty, with hardship, and with fatigue; and having comprehended the conditions, while cultivating insight, he generates the path after a long time. In this way, too, this is called the painful path and slow direct knowledge.

Aparo paccayepi pariggahetvā lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhanto dukkhena kasirena kilamanto paṭivijjhati, paṭividdhalakkhaṇo ca vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ uppādeti. Evampi dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti.

Another person, having comprehended the conditions, penetrates the characteristics with difficulty, with hardship, and with fatigue; and having penetrated the characteristics, while cultivating insight, he generates the path after a long time. In this way, too, this is called the painful path and slow direct knowledge.

Aparo lakkhaṇānipi paṭivijjhitvā vipassanāñāṇe tikkhe sūre suppasanne vahante uppannaṃ vipassanānikantiṃ pariyādiyamāno dukkhena kasirena kilamanto pariyādiyati, nikantiñca pariyādiyitvā vipassanāparivāsaṃ vasanto cirena maggaṃ uppādeti. Evampi dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti. Imināvupāyena itarāpi tisso paṭipadā veditabbā. Vipassanāpakkhikā eva panettha catasso paṭipadā daṭṭhabbā.

Another person, having penetrated the characteristics, when the insight-knowledge is sharp, keen, very clear, and flowing, exhausts the arisen delight in insight with difficulty, with hardship, and with fatigue; and having exhausted the delight, while cultivating insight, he generates the path after a long time. In this way, too, this is called the painful path and slow direct knowledge. By this same means, the other three paths should be known. Here, however, the four paths should be seen as pertaining only to the aspect of insight.

Cattāro puggalāti yathāvuttapaṭipadāvibhāgena cattāro paṭipannakapuggalā. Taṃ pana paṭipadāvibhāgaṃ saddhiṃ hetupāyaphalehi dassetuṃ “taṇhācarito”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Four persons' means four practicing persons according to the aforesaid division of the path. To show that division of the path together with cause, means, and fruit, 'one of craving-temperament,' etc., is said.

Tattha caritanti cariyā, vuttīti attho. Taṇhāya nibbattitaṃ caritaṃ etassāti taṇhācarito, taṇhāya vā pavattito carito taṇhācarito, [M 0.0051] lobhajjhāsayoti attho. Diṭṭhicaritoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Mandoti mandiyaṃ vuccati avijjā, tāya samannāgato mando, mohādhikoti attho.

Therein, 'carita' means conduct (cariyā), behavior (vutti). 'Taṇhācarito' is one for whom there is a temperament produced by craving; or, 'taṇhācarito' is one whose temperament is set in motion by craving. The meaning is one with a greedy disposition. In the case of 'diṭṭhicarito,' too, this same method should be seen. As for 'mando': dullness (mandiyaṃ) is called ignorance (avijjā). One endowed with that is 'mando.' The meaning is one with excessive delusion.

Satindriyenāti satiyā ādhipaccaṃ kurumānāya. Satindriyameva hissa visadaṃ hoti. Yasmā taṇhācaritatāya pubbabhāge kosajjābhibhavena na vīriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, mohādhikatāya na paññā balavatī. Tadubhayenāpi na samādhi balavā hoti, tasmā “satindriyameva hissa visadaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “satipaṭṭhānehi nissayehī”ti. Taṇhācaritatāya cassa kilesavikkhambhanaṃ na sukaranti dukkhā paṭipadā, avisadañāṇatāya dandhābhiññāti pubbe vuttanayaṃ ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Niyyātīti ariyamaggena vaṭṭadukkhato niggacchati.

By the faculty of mindfulness (satindriyena) means by mindfulness that exercises mastery. For this person, only the faculty of mindfulness becomes clear. Because, due to having a nature inclined to craving, in the preliminary stage energy is not strong, being overcome by sloth; and due to an excess of delusion, wisdom is not strong. Due to both of these, concentration is also not strong; therefore, it was said, 'For this person, only the faculty of mindfulness becomes clear.' For that very reason, he said: 'by the foundations of mindfulness, as supports.' And for this person, due to having a nature inclined to craving, the suppression of defilements is not easy; thus, the practice is painful. Due to unclear knowledge, direct knowledge is slow—thus, the previously stated method should be brought in and connected. 'Leads out' (niyyāti) means one escapes from the suffering of the round of existence by means of the noble path.

Udatthoti udaattho, uḷārapaññoti attho. Paññāsahāyapaṭilābhena cassa samādhi tikkho hoti sampayuttesu ādhipaccaṃ pavatteti. Tenevāha – “samādhindriyenā”ti. Visadañāṇattā “khippābhiññāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Samādhipadhānattā jhānānaṃ jhānehi nissayehīti ayaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Diṭṭhicarito aniyyānikamaggampi niyyānikanti maññamāno tattha ussāhabahulattā vīriyādhiko hoti. Vīriyādhikatāyeva cassa kilesavikkhambhanaṃ sukaranti sukhā paṭipadā, avisadañāṇatāya pana dandhābhiññāti imamatthaṃ dasseti “diṭṭhicarito mando”tiādinā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

'Udattha' means one of expansive wisdom, one of vast wisdom. And by gaining wisdom as a companion, this person's concentration becomes keen and exercises mastery over associated states. For that very reason, he said: 'by the faculty of concentration.' Because of having clear knowledge, it was said: 'for quick direct knowledge.' Because concentration is predominant for the jhānas, it was said, 'by the jhānas, as supports'—this is the distinction. The rest is just like the preceding. A person of speculative temperament, thinking even a path that does not lead out to be one that does lead out, has an excess of energy due to having much exertion therein. And precisely because of having an excess of energy, the suppression of defilements is easy for him; therefore, the practice is pleasant. However, due to unclear knowledge, direct knowledge is slow. Thus, this meaning is shown by the text beginning with 'a person of speculative temperament is slow.' The rest is according to the method already stated.

Saccehīti ariyasaccehi. Ariyasaccāni hi lokiyāni pubbabhāgañāṇassa sammasanaṭṭhānatāya lokuttarāni adhimuccanatāya maggañāṇassa abhisamayaṭṭhānatāya ca nissayāni hontīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ettha ca diṭṭhicarito udattho ugghaṭitaññū. Taṇhācarito mando [V 0.0183] neyyo. Itare dvepi vipañcitaññūti evaṃ yena veneyyattayena pubbe desanāvibhāgo dassito, tadeva veneyyattayaṃ iminā paṭipadāvibhāgena dassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By 'truths' (saccehi) is meant by the noble truths. For the noble truths—the mundane ones are supports for the knowledge of the preliminary stage because of being the ground for comprehension; and the supramundane ones are supports for the path-knowledge because of being the ground for conviction and the ground for realization. The rest is according to the method already stated. And here, the person of speculative temperament, of expansive wisdom, is one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū). The person of craving temperament, of slow wisdom, is one who is to be led (neyyo). The other two persons as well are ones of detailed understanding (vipañcitaññū). Thus, it should be seen that the very triad of persons to be trained, by which the division of the teaching was previously shown, is shown by this division of the path.

Idāni taṃ veneyyupuggalavibhāgaṃ atthanayayojanāya visayaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “ubho taṇhācaritā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṇhāya samādhipaṭipakkhattā taṇhācarito visujjhamāno samādhimukhena visujjhatīti āha [M 0.0052] – “samathapubbaṅgamāyā”ti. “Samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (a. ni. 4.170; paṭi. ma. 2.1, 3) vacanato pana sammādiṭṭhisahiteneva sammāsamādhinā niyyānaṃ, na sammāsamādhinā evāti āha – “samathapubbaṅgamāya vipassanāyā”ti. “Rāgavirāgā cetovimuttīti arahattaphalasamādhī”ti saṅgahesu vuttaṃ. Idha pana anāgāmiphalasamādhīti vakkhati. So hi samādhismiṃ paripūrakārīti. Tattha rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo. So virajjati etāyāti rāgavirāgā, tāya rāgavirāgāya, rāgappahāyikāyāti attho.

Now, in order to show that division of persons to be trained by making it the subject for the application of the method of meaning, what begins with 'Both persons of craving temperament...' was said. Because craving is the opposite of concentration, a person of craving temperament, when being purified, is purified by means of concentration. Therefore, he said: 'with serenity as its forerunner.' However, because of the statement, 'one develops serenity and insight yoked together,' the leading out occurs only by right concentration accompanied by right view, not by right concentration alone. Therefore, he said: 'by insight that has serenity as its forerunner.' In the commentaries, it is said: 'The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship.' Here, however, it will be said to be the concentration of the fruit of non-returning, for that person is one who fulfills the practice of concentration. Therein, the meaning of the words should be seen thus: It is called 'lust' (rāga) in the sense of attachment. By this, that lust fades away, therefore it is 'the fading away of lust' (rāgavirāgā). By that 'fading away of lust' means by that which abandons lust—this is the meaning.

Cetovimuttiyāti cetoti cittaṃ, tadapadesena cettha samādhi vuccati “yathā cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23). Paṭippassaddhivasena paṭipakkhato vimuccatīti vimutti, tena vā vimutto, tato vimuccananti vā vimutti, samādhiyeva. Yathā hi lokiyakathāyaṃ saññā cittañca desanāsīsaṃ. Yathāha – “nānattakāyā nānattasaññino”ti (dī. ni. 3.332, 341, 357; a. ni. 7.44; 9.24) “kiṃ citto tvaṃ, bhikkhū”ti (pārā. 135) ca, evaṃ lokuttarakathāyaṃ paññā samādhi ca. Yathāha – “pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhī”ti (vibha. 804) ca “samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti ca. Tesu idha rāgassa ujuvipaccanīkato samathapubbaṅgamatāvacanato ca cetoggahaṇena samādhi vutto. Tathā vimuttivacanena. Tena vuttaṃ “samādhiyevā”ti. Ceto ca taṃ vimutti cāti cetovimutti. Atha vā vuttappakārasseva cetaso paṭipakkhato vimutti vimokkhoti cetovimutti, cetasi vā phalaviññāṇe vuttappakārāva vimuttīti cetovimutti, cetaso vā phalaviññāṇassa paṭipakkhato vimutti vimokkho etasminti cetovimutti, samādhiyeva. Paññāvimuttiyāti etthāpi ayaṃ nayo yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo.

In the phrase 'liberation of mind' (cetovimuttiyā): 'ceto' means mind (citta), and by that designation, concentration (samādhi) is meant here, as in 'developing mind and wisdom.' 'Liberation' (vimutti) is so called because one is liberated from the opposite by way of pacification; or one is liberated by it; or it is the act of being liberated from it—it is concentration itself. For just as in worldly discourse, perception and mind are the chief topics of the teaching—as it is said: 'beings of diverse bodies and diverse perceptions' and 'What is your mind, monk?'—so in supramundane discourse, wisdom and concentration are the chief topics. As it is said: 'right concentration is endowed with five kinds of knowledge' and 'one develops serenity and insight yoked together.' Among these, here, concentration is meant by the term 'ceto' because it is the direct opposite of lust and because of the statement that serenity is the forerunner. Likewise, by the word 'vimutti,' concentration is meant. Therefore, it was said, 'it is concentration itself.' It is 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti) because it is both mind (ceto) and that liberation (vimutti). Or, it is 'liberation of mind' because it is the liberation or release of the mind, of the kind described, from its opposite. Or, it is 'liberation of mind' because it is the liberation, of the kind described, in the mind or in the fruit-consciousness. Or, it is 'liberation of mind' because in it there is liberation or release of the mind or of the fruit-consciousness from its opposite—it is concentration itself. In the phrase 'liberation by wisdom' (paññāvimuttiyā) also, this method should be applied as is suitable.

Diṭṭhiyā savisaye paññāsadisī pavattīti diṭṭhicarito visujjhamāno paññāmukhena visujjhatīti āha – “ubho diṭṭhicaritā vipassanā”tiādi. Avijjāvirāgā paññāvimuttīti arahattaphalapaññā[V 0.0184]. Samathaggahaṇena tappaṭipakkhato taṇhaṃ vipassanāggahaṇena avijjañca niddhāretvā paṭhamanayassa bhūmiṃ sakkā sukhena dassetunti āha – “ye samatha…pe… hātabbā”ti.

Because the process of view (diṭṭhi) in its own domain is similar to that of wisdom, a person of speculative temperament, when being purified, is purified by means of wisdom. Therefore, he said: 'Both persons of speculative temperament, insight...' and so on. 'Liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance' is the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship. By taking up serenity and determining craving as its opposite, and by taking up insight and determining ignorance as its opposite, the ground of the first method can be easily shown. Therefore, he said: 'Those of serenity... are to be conveyed.'

Tattha [M 0.0053] samathapubbaṅgamā paṭipadāti purimā dve paṭipadā, itarā vipassanāpubbaṅgamāti daṭṭhabbā. Hātabbāti gametabbā, netabbāti attho. Vipassanāya aniccadukkhaanattasaññābhāvato dukkhasaññāparivārattā ca asubhasaññāya imā catasso saññā dassitā honti. Tappaṭipakkhena ca cattāro vipallāsāti sakalassa sīhavikkīḷitanayassa bhūmiṃ sukhena sakkā dassetunti āha – “ye vipassanā…pe… hātabbā”ti.

Therein, 'the path with serenity as its forerunner' refers to the former two paths; the others should be seen as 'the path with insight as its forerunner.' 'To be conveyed' (hātabbā) means 'to be made to arrive,' 'to be made to be known.' Because insight consists of the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, and because the perception of foulness is an accompaniment of the perception of suffering, these four perceptions are shown. And by their opposite, the four perversions are also shown. Therefore, the ground of the entire Lion's Sport method can be easily shown. Therefore, he said: 'Those of insight... are to be conveyed.'

7. Evaṃ paṭipadāvibhāgena veneyyapuggalavibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ ñāṇavibhāgena dassento yasmā bhagavato desanā yāvadeva veneyyavinayanatthā, vinayanañca nesaṃ sutamayādīnaṃ tissannaṃ paññānaṃ anukkamena nibbattanaṃ, yathā bhagavato desanāya pavattibhāvavibhāvanañca hāranayabyāpāro, tasmā imassa hārassa samuṭṭhitappakāraṃ tāva pucchitvā yena puggalavibhāgadassanena desanābhājanaṃ vibhajitvā tattha desanāyaṃ desanāhāraṃ niyojetukāmo taṃ dassetuṃ “svāyaṃ hāro kattha sambhavatī”tiādimāha.

7. Thus, having shown the classification of individuals to be trained by means of the classification of the path of practice, now, wishing to show that classification by means of the classification of knowledge—since the Blessed One’s teaching is solely for the purpose of training those who are to be trained, and their training is the successive arising of the three kinds of wisdom beginning with that born of learning, and since the clarification of the mode of occurrence of the Blessed One's teaching is the function of the methods of exposition—therefore, having first asked about the manner in which this method of exposition arises, and having classified the receptacle of the teaching by means of that showing of the classification of individuals, wishing to apply the method of exposition to the teaching therein, in order to show that classification of individuals, the Teacher said, 'Where does this method arise?' and so on.

Tattha yassāti yo so aṭṭhahi akkhaṇehi vimutto sotāvadhānapariyosānāhi ca sampattīti samannāgato yassa. Satthāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ anusāsanato satthā. Dhammanti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo, taṃ dhammaṃ. Desayatīti saṅkhepavitthāranayehi bhāsati katheti. Aññataroti bhagavato sāvakesu aññataro. Garuṭṭhānīyoti sīlasutādiguṇavisesayogena garukaraṇīyo. Sabrahmacārīti brahmaṃ vuccati seṭṭhaṭṭhena sakalaṃ satthusāsanaṃ. Samaṃ saha vā brahmaṃ carati paṭipajjatīti sabrahmacārī. Saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā yo evarūpassa dhammassa desetā”ti tathāgate, “svākkhāto vatāyaṃ dhammo yo evaṃ ekantaparipuṇṇo ekantaparisuddho”tiādinā dhamme ca saddhaṃ labhati uppādetīti attho.

Herein, 'of whom' (yassa) refers to that person who is freed from the eight inopportune moments and is endowed with the accomplishments that culminate in attentive listening. 'Teacher' (satthā) refers to one who instructs in a fitting way with the ultimate benefits pertaining to the present life and the future life; hence, he is the Teacher. Regarding 'Dhamma' (dhammaṃ), it upholds those who practice as instructed, preventing them from falling into the states of woe; therefore, it is the Dhamma. 'Teaches' (desayati) means he speaks and explains by means of concise and extensive methods. 'A certain one' (aññataro) means one or another among the Blessed One’s disciples. 'Worthy of respect' (garuṭṭhānīyo) means one who should be respected due to being endowed with the special qualities of virtue, learning, and so on. Regarding 'fellow practitioner of the holy life' (sabrahmacārī), the entire teaching of the Teacher is called 'brahma' in the sense of 'supreme'; one who fares or practices that 'brahma'—the noble teaching—equally or together is a 'sabrahmacārī'. 'Gains faith' (saddhaṃ paṭilabhati) means he obtains or produces faith in the Tathāgata, thinking, 'Truly, that Blessed One is a Sammāsambuddha, who is the teacher of such a Dhamma,' and in the Dhamma, with thoughts such as, 'Truly, this Dhamma is well-proclaimed, which is thus utterly complete and utterly pure.' This is the meaning.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ yathāsute yathāpariyatte dhamme. Vīmaṃsāti pāḷiyā pāḷiatthassa ca vīmaṃsanapaññā[V 0.0185]. Sesaṃ tassā eva vevacanaṃ. Sā hi yathāvuttavīmaṃsane saṅkocaṃ anāpajjitvā ussahanavasena ussāhanā, tulanavasena tulanā, upaparikkhaṇavasena upaparikkhāti ca vuttā. Atha vā [M 0.0054] vīmaṃsatīti vīmaṃsā, sā padapadatthavicāraṇā paññā. Ussāhanāti vīriyena upatthambhitā dhammassa dhāraṇaparicayasādhikā paññā. Tulanāti padena padantaraṃ, desanāya vā desanantaraṃ tulayitvā saṃsanditvā gahaṇapaññā. Upaparikkhāti mahāpadese otāretvā pāḷiyā pāḷiatthassa ca upaparikkhaṇapaññā. Attahitaṃ parahitañca ākaṅkhantehi suyyatīti sutaṃ, kālavacanicchāya abhāvato, yathā duddhanti. Kiṃ pana tanti? Adhikārato sāmatthiyato vā pariyattidhammoti viññāyati. Atha vā savanaṃ sutaṃ, sotadvārānusārena pariyattidhammassa upadhāraṇanti attho. Sutena hetunā nibbattā sutamayī. Pakārena jānātīti paññā. Yā vīmaṃsā, ayaṃ sutamayī paññāti paccekampi yojetabbaṃ. Tathāti yathā sutamayī paññā vīmaṃsādipariyāyavatī vīmaṃsādivibhāgavatī ca, tathā cintāmayī cāti attho. Yathā vā sutamayī oramattikā anavaṭṭhitā ca, evaṃ cintāmayī cāti dasseti.

Herein (tatthā) means in that Dhamma as it has been heard and as it has been learned. Investigation (vīmaṃsā) is the wisdom that investigates the Pāli text and the meaning of the Pāli. The remaining terms are synonyms for it. For that wisdom is called 'striving' (ussāhanā) by way of endeavoring, because it proceeds without hesitation in the aforesaid investigation; it is called 'weighing' (tulanā) by way of weighing; and it is called 'scrutiny' (upaparikkhā) by way of close examination. Alternatively, it investigates (vīmaṃsati), thus it is 'investigation' (vīmaṃsā); that is the wisdom that examines a term and the meaning of the term. 'Striving' (ussāhanā) is the wisdom, supported by energy, that accomplishes the retention and practice of the Dhamma. 'Weighing' (tulanā) is the wisdom of grasping the meaning after having weighed and compared one term with another term, or one teaching with another teaching. 'Scrutiny' (upaparikkhā) is the wisdom of closely examining the Pāli text and the meaning of the Pāli after applying them to the Great References. It is heard (suyyati) by those who desire their own welfare and the welfare of others, thus it is 'what is heard' (sutaṃ); this is due to the absence of an intention to denote past time, like 'duddha' (milked). What, then, is that which is heard? It is known as the scriptural Dhamma by virtue of its relevance and its capacity. Alternatively, hearing (savanaṃ) is what is heard (sutaṃ); the meaning is the retention of the scriptural Dhamma by way of the ear-door. That which is produced with 'what is heard' as its cause is 'born of hearing' (sutamayī). It knows (jānāti) by way of its aspects (pakārena), thus it is 'wisdom' (paññā). The connection 'That which is investigation is this wisdom born of hearing' should be applied to each term individually. 'Likewise' (tathā) means: just as the wisdom born of hearing has synonyms such as 'investigation' and divisions such as 'investigation', so too does the wisdom born of reflection. This is the meaning. Or, it shows that just as the wisdom born of hearing is of a lesser measure and is unfixed, so too is the wisdom born of reflection.

Sutena nissayenāti sutena pariyattidhammena pariyattidhammassavanena vā upanissayena itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ sutaṃ upanissāyāti attho. Vīmaṃsātiādīsu “idaṃ sīlaṃ, ayaṃ samādhi, ime rūpārūpadhammā, ime pañcakkhandhā”ti tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvavīmaṃsanabhūtā paññā vīmaṃsā. Tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ vacanatthaṃ muñcitvā sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇassa tulayitvā viya gahaṇapaññā tulanā. Tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ salakkhaṇaṃ avijahitvā aniccatādiruppanasappaccayādiākāre ca takketvā vitakketvā ca upaparikkhaṇapaññā upaparikkhā, tathā upaparikkhite dhamme saviggahe viya upaṭṭhahante evametehi nijjhānakkhame katvā cittena anu anu pekkhaṇā manasānupekkhaṇā. Ettha ca yathā sutamayī paññā yathāsutassa dhammassa dhāraṇaparicayavasena pavattanato ussāhajātā “ussāhanā”ti vattabbataṃ arahati, na evaṃ cintāmayīti idha “ussāhanā”ti padaṃ na vuttaṃ. Cintanaṃ cintā, nijjhānanti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

'By means of what is heard, as a support' (sutena nissayena) means: by means of what is heard—that is, the scriptural Dhamma or the hearing of the scriptural Dhamma—as a supportive condition. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of denoting a specific state. The meaning is 'relying on what has been heard as aforesaid'. In the section beginning with 'investigation' (vīmaṃsā), the wisdom that is the investigation of the intrinsic nature of those various phenomena—such as 'This is virtue,' 'This is concentration,' 'These are the phenomena of form and the formless,' 'These are the five aggregates'—is 'investigation' (vīmaṃsā). The wisdom of grasping that, having set aside the verbal meaning of those same phenomena, weighs, as it were, their intrinsic nature, essence, and specific characteristic is 'weighing' (tulanā). The wisdom of close examination that, without abandoning the specific characteristic of those same phenomena, thinks and reflects upon them in their aspects of impermanence, etc., and of being subject to affliction, conditioned, etc., is 'scrutiny' (upaparikkhā). When the phenomena have been thus scrutinized, they appear as if embodied; having made them fit for realization, the repeated contemplation of them with the mind is 'mental contemplation' (manasānupekkhaṇā). And here, just as the wisdom born of hearing—because it proceeds by way of retaining and practicing the Dhamma as it was heard—is born of endeavor and deserves to be called 'striving' (ussāhanā), the wisdom born of reflection is not so. Therefore, the term 'striving' is not stated here. Thinking (cintanaṃ) is thought (cintā); the meaning is contemplation (nijjhāna). The remainder is in the same way as has been stated.

Imāhi dvīhi paññāhīti yathāvuttāhi dvīhi paññāhi kāraṇabhūtāhi. Sutacintāmayañāṇesu hi patiṭṭhito vipassanaṃ ārabhatīti. “Imāsu dvīsu paññāsū”tipi paṭhanti. “Tehi jātāsu uppannāsū”ti vā vacanaseso [M 0.0055] yojetabbo. Manasikārasampayuttassāti rūpārūpapariggahādimanasikāre yuttappayuttassa. Yaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjatīti vuttanayena manasikārappayogena diṭṭhivisuddhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhimaggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhipaṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhīnaṃ [V 0.0186] sampa ādanena vipassanaṃ ussukkantassa yaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhisaṅkhātaṃ ariyamaggañāṇaṃ uppajjati, ayaṃ bhāvanāmayī paññāti sambandho. Taṃ pana dassanaṃ bhāvanāti duvidhanti āha – “dassanabhūmiyaṃ vā bhāvanābhūmiyaṃ vā”ti. Yadi dassananti vuccati, kathaṃ tattha paññā bhāvanāmayīti? Bhāvanāmayameva hi taṃ ñāṇaṃ, paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato pana “dassana”nti vuttanti saphalo paṭhamamaggo dassanabhūmi. Sesā sekkhāsekkhadhammā bhāvanābhūmi.

"By these two wisdoms" means by the two wisdoms previously mentioned, which are causal factors. Indeed, one established in the knowledge born of hearing and the knowledge born of reflection undertakes insight. Some also recite, "In these two wisdoms." For them, the remainder of the statement should be connected as "born" or "arisen." "Associated with attention" means for one who is engaged and applied in attention, such as the grasping of material and immaterial phenomena. "What knowledge arises"—in the manner already stated, through the application of attention, by accomplishing the purification of view, the purification of overcoming doubt, the purification of knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, and the purification of knowledge and vision of the way, for one striving for insight, what noble path-knowledge, called the purification of knowledge and vision, arises, this is the wisdom born of mental development. This is the connection. That knowledge, however, is twofold: seeing and development. Therefore, he said: "either in the ground of seeing or in the ground of development." If it is called "seeing," how then is the wisdom there born of development? Indeed, that knowledge is itself born of development, but because it is the first seeing of Nibbāna, it is called "seeing." The first path, together with its fruit, is the ground of seeing. The remaining phenomena of trainees and non-trainees are the ground of development.

8. Idāni imā tisso paññā pariyāyantarena dassetuṃ “paratoghosā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paratoti na attato, aññato satthuto sāvakato vāti attho. Ghosāti tesaṃ desanāghosato, desanāpaccayāti attho. Atha vā parato ghoso etissāti paratoghosā, yā paññā, sā sutamayīti yojetabbaṃ. Paccattasamuṭṭhitāti paccattaṃ tassa tassa attani sambhūtā. Yonisomanasikārāti tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvapariggaṇhanādinā yathāvuttena upāyena pavattamanasikārā. Parato ca ghosenāti paratoghosena hetubhūtena. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

8. Now, to show these three wisdoms by another method, "from another's voice," etc., is said. Herein, "from another" means not proceeding from oneself, but from another—whether from the Teacher or from a disciple. "Voice" means because of the sound of their teaching, because of the teaching as a condition. Alternatively, `paratoghosā` means 'for which there is a voice from another'; whatever wisdom that is, that is wisdom born of hearing. Thus it should be connected. "Arisen individually" means arisen individually in the personal continuity of this or that person, or in oneself. "From wise attention" means because of attention that proceeds by the appropriate means as stated before, such as grasping the intrinsic nature of those respective phenomena. "And from another's voice" means because of the voice from another, which is a cause. The rest is just as has been stated.

Idāni yadatthaṃ imā paññā uddhaṭā, tameva veneyyapuggalavibhāgaṃ yojetvā dassetuṃ “yassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha imā dveti gaṇanavasena vatvā puna tā sutamayī cintāmayī cāti sarūpato dasseti. Ayaṃ ugghaṭitaññūti ayaṃ sutamayacintāmayañāṇehi āsayapayogapabodhassa nipphāditattā uddesamatteneva jānanato “ugghaṭitaññū”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ vipañcitaññūti cintāmayañāṇena āsayassa aparikkhatattā uddesaniddesehi jānanato vipañcitaññū. Ayaṃ neyyoti sutamayañāṇassāpi abhāvato niravasesaṃ vitthāradesanāya netabbato neyyo.

Now, for the purpose for which these wisdoms were adduced, namely the classification of individuals to be trained, to show that very classification by connecting it, "for whom," etc., is said. Therein, having said "these two" by way of enumeration, he again shows them by their nature as "wisdom born of hearing and wisdom born of reflection." This one is called an `ugghaṭitaññū` because, through the knowledge born of hearing and reflection, the awakening of their disposition and application is accomplished, and because they know by a mere summary. This one is a `vipañcitaññū` because their disposition is not prepared by the knowledge born of reflection, and because they know through summary and detail. This one is a `neyya` because of the absence of even the knowledge born of hearing, and because they must be led without remainder by an extensive teaching.

9. Evaṃ desanāpaṭipadāñāṇavibhāgehi desanābhājanaṃ veneyyattayaṃ vibhajitvā idāni tattha pavattitāya bhagavato dhammadesanāya desanāhāraṃ niddhāretvā yojetuṃ “sāyaṃ dhammadesanā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

9. Thus, having divided the triad of individuals to be trained, who are the recipients of the teaching, by means of the classifications of teaching, practice, and knowledge, now, in order to determine and apply the method of conveying the teaching within the Blessed One's Dhamma-teaching that was set in motion for them, "This Dhamma-teaching," etc., is begun.

Tattha [M 0.0056] sāyanti sā ayaṃ. Yā pubbe “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādinā (netti. 5) paṭiniddesavārassa ādito desanāhārassa visayabhāvena nikkhittā pāḷi, tamevettha desanāhāraṃ niyojetuṃ “sāyaṃ dhammadesanā”ti paccāmasati. Kiṃ desayatīti kathetukamyatāvasena [V 0.0187] desanāya piṇḍatthaṃ pucchitvā taṃ gaṇanāya paricchinditvā sāmaññato dasseti “cattāri saccānī”ti. Saccavinimuttā hi bhagavato desanā natthīti. Tassā ca cattāri saccāni piṇḍattho. Pavattipavattakanivattitadupāyavimuttassa neyyassa abhāvato cattāri aviparītabhāvena saccānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tāni “dukkhaṃ samudayaṃ nirodhaṃ magga”nti sarūpato dasseti.

Therein, `sāyaṃ` is `sā ayaṃ`. The Pāḷi text that was previously set down at the beginning of the section on specific explanation with "Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma," etc., as the domain for the method of conveying the teaching—that very Pāḷi text is referred to here as "This Dhamma-teaching" in order to apply the method of conveying the teaching. With "What does he teach?", having asked for the summary meaning of the teaching out of a desire to speak, and having defined it by way of enumeration, he shows it in general terms with "the four truths." For there is no teaching of the Blessed One that is devoid of the truths. And for that teaching, the four truths are the summary meaning. Because there is no knowable thing that is devoid of what occurs, what makes it occur, its cessation, and the means to that cessation, there are four. Because of their unfailing nature, they are truths. Thus it should be seen. He shows them by their intrinsic nature as "suffering, origination, cessation, and path."

Tattha anekupaddavādhiṭṭhānabhāvena kucchitattā bālajanaparikappitadhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahena tucchattā ca dukkhaṃ. Avasesapaccayasamavāye dukkhassa uppattikāraṇattā samudayo. Sabbagatisuññattā natthi ettha saṃsāracārakasaṅkhāto dukkharodho, etasmiṃ vā adhigate saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa abhāvotipi nirodho, anuppādanirodhapaccayattā vā. Mārento gacchati, nibbānatthikehi maggiyatīti vā maggo. Tattha samudayena assādo, dukkhena ādīnavo, magganirodhehi nissaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ yasmiṃ sutte cattāri saccāni sarūpato āgatāni, tattha yathārutavasena. Yattha pana sutte cattāri saccāni sarūpato na āgatāni, tattha atthato cattāri saccāni uddharitvā tesaṃ vasena assādādayo niddhāretabbā. Yattha ca assādādayo sarūpato āgatā, tattha vattabbameva natthi. Yattha pana na āgatā, tattha atthato uddharitvā tesaṃ vasena cattāri saccāni niddhāretabbāni. Idha pana assādādayo udāharaṇavasena sarūpato dassitāti tehi saccāni niddhāretuṃ “ādīnavo cā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Therein, because it is the basis for many dangers, because it is contemptible, and because it is empty, being devoid of the state of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self as imagined by foolish people, it is `dukkha` (suffering). When there is a conjunction of the remaining conditions, because it is the cause for the arising of suffering, it is `samudaya` (origination). Because it is void of all destinations, herein there is no arising of suffering, which is called the prison of saṃsāra; or, when it is attained, there is an absence of the arising of suffering, which is called the prison of saṃsāra; for this reason also, it is `nirodha` (cessation). Or, because it is the condition for the cessation that is non-arising. Killing the defilements, it goes, or it is sought by those who desire Nibbāna; therefore, it is `magga` (path). Therein, with origination there is gratification; with suffering there is danger; with the path and cessation there is escape. Thus, in whatever sutta the four truths appear in their intrinsic nature, there gratification, etc., should be determined according to the literal text. But in whatever sutta the four truths do not appear in their intrinsic nature, there, having extracted the four truths by way of their meaning, gratification, etc., should be determined based on them. And where gratification, etc., appear in their intrinsic nature, there is nothing more to be said. But where they do not appear, there, having extracted them by way of their meaning, the four truths should be determined based on them. Here, however, gratification, etc., are shown in their intrinsic nature by way of example; therefore, in order to determine the truths from them, "and danger," etc., is said.

Tattha “saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (dī. ni. 2.387; ma. ni. 1.120; 3.373; vibha. 202) vacanato taṇhāvajjā tebhūmakadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, te ca aniccādisabhāvattā ādīnavo, phalañca desanāya sādhetabbaṃ. Tattha yaṃ lokiyaṃ, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “phalañca dukkha”nti. Assādoti taṇhāvipallāsānampi icchitattā te sandhāya “assādo samudayo”ti vuttaṃ. Saha vipassanāya ariyamaggo desanā ca [M 0.0057] desanāphalādhigamassa upāyoti katvā “upāyo āṇatti ca maggo”ti vuttaṃ. Nissaraṇapade cāpi ariyamaggo niddhāretabbo, na cāyaṃ saccavibhāgo ākuloti daṭṭhabbo. Yathā hi saccavibhaṅge (vibha. 208) “taṇhā avasiṭṭhā kilesā avasiṭṭhā akusalā dhammā sāsavāni kusalamūlāni sāsavā ca kusalā dhammā samudayasaccabhāvena vibhattā”ti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ naye taṃtaṃavasiṭṭhā tebhūmakadhammā dukkhasaccabhāvena vibhattā, evamidhāpi daṭṭhabbanti. Imāni cattāri saccānīti nigamanaṃ[V 0.0188]. Idaṃ dhammacakkanti yāyaṃ bhagavato catusaccavasena sāmukkaṃsikā dhammadesanā, idaṃ dhammacakkaṃ.

Herein, from the statement, “In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering,” the phenomena of the three planes, excluding craving, are the truth of suffering. And because they have the nature of impermanence and so on, they are a danger. The fruit, too, is to be accomplished by the teaching. Herein, with reference to that which is mundane, it is said, “and the fruit is suffering.” As for ‘gratification,’ with reference to craving and distortions, because they are desired, it is said, “gratification is the origin.” Because the noble path together with insight, and the teaching, are the means for attaining the fruit of the teaching, it is said, “the means and the instruction are the path.” In the term ‘escape,’ the noble path should also be determined. And it should be seen that this analysis of the truths is not confused. For just as in the Analysis of the Truths it is said, “Craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome phenomena, the wholesome roots that are subject to taints, and the wholesome phenomena with taints are classified by way of the truth of origin,” so in each of those methods, the remaining phenomena of the three planes are classified by way of the truth of suffering. In the same way, it should be seen here also. “These are the four truths” is the conclusion. “This is the Dhamma Wheel” means that this pre-eminent teaching of the Blessed One in terms of the four truths is the Dhamma Wheel.

Idāni tassā dhammadesanāya dhammacakkabhāvaṃ saccavibhaṅgasuttavasena (ma. ni. 3.371 ādayo) dassetuṃ “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha idaṃ dukkhanti idaṃ jātiādivibhāgaṃ saṅkhepato pañcupādānakkhandhasaṅgahaṃ taṇhāvajjaṃ tebhūmakadhammajātaṃ dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvena dukkhadukkhādibhāvena ca dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti attho. Meti bhagavā attānaṃ niddisati. Bārāṇasiyanti bārāṇasīnāmakassa nagarassa avidūre. Paccekabuddhaisīnaṃ ākāsato otaraṇaṭṭhānatāya isipatanaṃ. Migānaṃ tattha abhayassa dinnattā migadāyanti ca laddhanāme assame. Uttarati atikkamati, abhibhavatīti vā uttaraṃ, natthi etassa uttaranti anuttaraṃ. Anatisayaṃ appaṭibhāgaṃ vā. Kiñcāpi bhagavato dhammadesanā anekāsu devamanussaparisāsu anekasatakkhattuṃ tesaṃ ariyasaccappaṭivedhasampādanavasena pavattitā, tathāpi sabbapaṭhamaṃ aññāsikoṇḍaññappamukhāya aṭṭhārasaparimāṇāya brahmakoṭiyā catusaccappaṭivedhavibhāvanīyā dhammadesanā, tassā sātisayā dhammacakkasamaññāti “dhammacakkaṃ pavattita”nti vuttaṃ.

Now, to show that this Dhamma teaching is the Dhamma Wheel by way of the Discourse on the Analysis of the Truths, the passage beginning “As the Blessed One said” is stated. Therein, “this is suffering” means: this class of phenomena of the three planes—which has the division beginning with birth, is briefly comprised of the five aggregates of clinging, and excludes craving—is the noble truth called suffering because of being a basis for suffering and because of being suffering-as-suffering, etc. By ‘me,’ the Blessed One indicates himself. ‘At Bārāṇasī’ means not far from the city named Bārāṇasī. It is called Isipatana because it is the place of descent from the sky for the seers who are Paccekabuddhas, and it is in the hermitage that obtained the name Migadāya because safety was given to the deer there. ‘Superior’ (uttara) means it surpasses, it overcomes; ‘unsurpassed’ (anuttara) means there is nothing superior to it. It is unexcelled or incomparable. Although the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching was set forth more than a hundred times in many assemblies of devas and humans by way of accomplishing for them the penetration of the noble truths, nevertheless, the very first Dhamma teaching, which revealed the penetration of the four truths for the eighteen crores of brahmās headed by Aññāsikoṇḍañña, has the pre-eminent designation ‘Dhamma Wheel.’ Therefore, it is said, “the Dhamma Wheel was set in motion.”

Tattha satipaṭṭhānādidhammo eva pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ, cakkanti vā āṇā. Dhammato anapetattā dhammañca taṃ cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ. Dhammena ñāyena cakkantipi dhammacakkaṃ. Yathāha – “dhammañca pavatteti cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, cakkañca pavatteti dhammañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammena pavattetīti dhammacakka”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 2.41-42). Appaṭivattiyanti dhammissarassa bhagavato sammāsambuddhabhāvato dhammacakkassa ca anuttarabhāvato appaṭisedhanīyaṃ. Kena pana appaṭivattiyanti āha “samaṇena vā”tiādi. Tattha samaṇenāti pabbajjaṃ upagatena. Brāhmaṇenāti [M 0.0058] jātibrāhmaṇena. Paramatthasamaṇabrāhmaṇānañhi paṭilomanacittaṃyeva natthi. Devenāti kāmāvacaradevena. Kenacīti yena kenaci avasiṭṭhapārisajjena. Ettāvatā aṭṭhannampi parisānaṃ anavasesapariyādānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Lokasminti sattaloke.

Therein, the Dhamma of the foundations of mindfulness and so on, because of its nature of proceeding, is a wheel; hence, it is the ‘Dhamma Wheel.’ Or, ‘wheel’ means command. Because it is not separate from the Dhamma, it is the Dhamma, and that is the wheel; hence, it is the ‘Dhamma Wheel.’ Because it is a wheel that proceeds rightly, by the method of Dhamma, it is also the ‘Dhamma Wheel.’ As it is said: “It sets the Dhamma in motion and the wheel, thus it is the Dhamma Wheel; it sets the wheel in motion and the Dhamma, thus it is the Dhamma Wheel; it sets it in motion by means of the Dhamma, thus it is the Dhamma Wheel,” and so on. ‘That cannot be turned back’ means it cannot be stopped, because the Blessed One is the lord of the Dhamma and is a perfectly self-enlightened one, and because the Dhamma Wheel is unsurpassed. But by whom can it not be turned back? To this, he said, “by an ascetic,” and so on. Therein, ‘by an ascetic’ means by one who has gone forth. ‘By a brahmin’ means by a brahmin by birth. Indeed, for ascetics and brahmins in the ultimate sense, there is not even an opposing thought. ‘By a deva’ means by a deva of the sense sphere. ‘By anyone’ means by any remaining member of the assembly. By this much, the complete inclusion of all eight assemblies should be seen. ‘In the world’ means in the world of beings.

Tatthāti tissaṃ catusaccadhammadesanāyaṃ. Aparimāṇā padā, aparimāṇā akkharāti uppaṭipāṭivacanaṃ yebhuyyena padasaṅgahitāni akkharānīti dassanatthaṃ. Padā akkharā byañjanāti liṅgavipallāso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atthassāti catusaccasaṅkhātassa atthassa. Saṅkāsanāti saṅkāsitabbākāro. Esa nayo sesesupi. Atthassāti ca sambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Itipidanti [V 0.0189] itīti pakārattho, pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, imināpi imināpi pakārena idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ veditabbanti attho. Tena jātiādibhedena yathāvuttassa dukkhasaccassa anekabhedataṃ taṃdīpakānaṃ akkharapadādīnaṃ vuttappakāraṃ aparimāṇatañca samattheti.

‘Therein’ means in that Dhamma teaching of the four truths. “Immeasurable words, immeasurable syllables” is a statement in reverse order, in order to show that, for the most part, syllables are included in words. In “Words, syllables, consonants,” it should be seen that a change of gender has been made. ‘Of the meaning’ means of the meaning called the four truths. ‘Explanation’ means the manner of explanation. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. And ‘of the meaning’ is the genitive case in the sense of relation. In ‘itipidaṃ,’ the word ‘iti’ has the meaning of ‘manner,’ and the word ‘pi’ has the meaning of summing up. The meaning is: ‘In this manner and in that manner, this noble truth of suffering should be known.’ By this, it establishes the manifold nature of the truth of suffering, as stated before with its divisions beginning with birth, and the immeasurability, in the manner stated, of the syllables, words, and so on, that illuminate it.

Ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti ayaṃ kāmataṇhādibhedā taṇhāvaṭṭassa mūlabhūtā yathāvuttassa dukkhassa nibbattihetubhāvato dukkhasamudayo. Ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti ayaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭā asaṅkhatadhātu yathāvuttassa dukkhassa anuppādanirodhapaccayattā dukkhanirodho. Ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhiādiaṭṭhaṅgasamūho dukkhanirodhasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ gacchati ārammaṇavasena tadabhimukhībhūtattā paṭipadā ca hoti dukkhanirodhappattiyāti dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Itipidanti padassa pana samudayasacce aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritehi, nirodhasacce madanimmadanādipariyāyehi, maggasacce sattattiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammehi attho vibhajitvā veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

As for 'This is the origin of suffering': this craving, which has divisions such as sensual craving and is the root of the cycle, is the origin of suffering because it is the cause for the arising of the aforementioned suffering. As for 'This is the cessation of suffering': this unconditioned element, liberated from all conditioned things, is the cessation of suffering because it is the condition for the non-arising cessation of the aforementioned suffering. As for 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering': this collection of the eight factors beginning with right view goes to Nibbāna, which is called the cessation of suffering, by way of taking it as an object, because it is directed towards it; and it is the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering. Therefore, it is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, as for the term `itipidaṃ`, the meaning should be known by distinguishing it in the truth of the origin by the one hundred and eight applications of craving, in the truth of cessation by the synonyms such as 'the crushing of intoxication,' and in the truth of the path by the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The remainder is just as has been explained.

Evaṃ “dvādasa padāni sutta”nti gāthāya sakalassa sāsanassa channaṃ atthapadānaṃ channañca byañjanapadānaṃ vasena yā dvādasapadatā vuttā, tameva “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādinā desanāhārassa visayadassanavasena chachakkapariyāyaṃ (ma. ni. 3.420 ādayo) ekadesena uddisitvā dhammacakkappavattanasuttena (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 2.30) tadatthassa saṅgahitabhāvadassanamukhena sabbassāpi bhagavato vacanassa catusaccadesanābhāvaṃ tadatthassa ca catusaccabhāvaṃ vibhāvento “idaṃ dukkhanti [M 0.0059] me, bhikkhave, bārāṇasiya”ntiādinā saccavibhaṅgasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.371 ādayo) uddesato dassetvā “tattha aparimāṇā padā”tiādinā byañjanatthapadāni vibhajanto dvādasapadabhāvaṃ dīpetvā idāni tesaṃ aññamaññavisayivisayabhāvena sambandhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā akkharehi saṅkāsetī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus, by the verse, 'The Sutta of Twelve Terms,' the state of being twelve terms for the entire teaching was stated, by way of six meaning-terms and six expression-terms. And wishing to clarify that all the Blessed One's speech is a teaching of the Four Truths and that its meaning is the Four Truths—by means of showing how its meaning is encompassed by the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, after having first pointed out in part the Discourse on the Six Sixes by way of showing the scope of the teaching method with the passage beginning, 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma,' and having shown in summary the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta with the passage beginning, 'This is suffering, monks, for me in Bārāṇasī'—and while analyzing the expression-terms and meaning-terms with the passage beginning, 'Therein, the terms are immeasurable,' having explained that very state of being twelve terms, now, in order to show the state of their connection through their mutual relationship of domain and that which has a domain, the passage beginning, 'Therein, the Blessed One indicates with letters,' was stated.

Tattha padāvayavaggahaṇamukhena padaggahaṇaṃ, gahite ca pade padatthāvabodho gahitapubbasaṅketassa hoti. Tattha ca padāvayavaggahaṇena viya padaggahaṇassa, padatthāvayavaggahaṇenāpi padatthaggahaṇassa visesādhānaṃ jāyatīti āha – “akkharehi saṅkāsetī”ti. Yasmā pana akkharehi saṃkhittena dīpiyamāno attho padapariyosāne vākyassa apariyositattā padeneva pakāsito dīpito hoti, tasmā “padehi pakāsetī”ti vuttaṃ. Vākyapariyosāne pana so attho vivarito vivaṭo [V 0.0190] kato hotīti vuttaṃ “byañjanehi vivaratī”ti. Yasmā ca pakārehi vākyabhede kate tadattho vibhatto nāma hoti, tasmā “ākārehi vibhajatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā vākyāvayavānaṃ paccekaṃ nibbacanavibhāge kate so attho pākaṭo hotīti vuttaṃ “niruttīhi uttānīkarotī”ti. Katanibbacanehi vākyāvayavehi vitthāravasena niravasesato desitehi veneyyānaṃ cittaparitosanaṃ buddhinisānañca kataṃ hotīti āha – “niddesehi paññapetī”ti. Ettha ca akkharehi eva saṅkāsetīti avadhāraṇaṃ akatvā akkharehi saṅkāsetiyevāti evaṃ avadhāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañhi sati atthapadānaṃ nānāvākyavisayatāpi siddhā hoti. Tena ekānusandhike sutte chaḷeva atthapadāni, nānānusandhike pana anusandhimhi anusandhimhi cha cha atthapadāni niddhāretabbāni.

Therein, the grasping of a term is by means of grasping the components of the term, and when a term is grasped, understanding of its meaning arises for one who has previously grasped the convention. And therein, just as a special distinction in the grasping of a term arises from grasping the components of the term, so too a special distinction in the grasping of the term's meaning arises from grasping the components of the term's meaning. Therefore, he said: 'He indicates with letters.' Because a meaning being indicated briefly by letters is, at the end of the term, revealed and illuminated by the term itself, as the sentence is not yet complete, therefore it is said: 'He makes clear with terms.' But at the end of the sentence, that meaning is made disclosed and opened, so it is said: 'He discloses with expressions.' And because when a division of the sentence is made by modes, its meaning is called 'analyzed,' therefore it is said: 'He analyzes by modes.' Similarly, when an individual etymological analysis of the sentence's components is made, that meaning becomes manifest, so it is said: 'He makes manifest with etymologies.' Because the satisfaction of the minds and the sharpening of the intellect of the disciples are accomplished by the components of the sentence that are taught extensively and without remainder through established derivations, he said: 'He makes known with expositions.' And here, without making the exclusive emphasis 'he indicates only with letters,' the emphasis should be seen thus: 'he indeed indicates with letters.' For when this is so, the applicability of meaning-terms to various sentences is also established. Therefore, in a sutta with a single connection, only six meaning-terms are to be determined; but in a sutta with multiple connections, six meaning-terms are to be determined for each and every connection.

“Akkharehi ca padehi ca ugghaṭetī”tiādinā byañjanapadānaṃ kiccasādhanaṃ dasseti. Veneyyattayavinayameva hi tesaṃ byāpāro. Aṭṭhānabhāvato pana saccappaṭivedhassa padaparamo na idha vutto. Neyyaggahaṇeneva vā tassāpi idha gahaṇaṃ sekkhaggahaṇena viya kalyāṇaputhujjanassāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Akkharehītiādīsu karaṇasādhane karaṇavacanaṃ, na hetumhi. Akkharādīni hi ugghaṭanādiatthāni, na ugghaṭanādiakkharādiatthaṃ. Yadatthā ca kiriyā [M 0.0060] so hetu, yathā “annenavasatī”ti. Ugghaṭetīti sotāvadhānaṃ katvā samāhitacittānaṃ veneyyānaṃ saṅkāsanavasena akkharehi visesaṃ ādahanto yathā padapariyosāne āsayappaṭibodho hoti, tathā yathādhippetaṃ atthaṃ saṅkhepena katheti uddisatīti attho. Vipañcayatīti yathāuddiṭṭhaṃ atthaṃ niddisati. Vitthāretīti vitthāraṃ karoti, vitthāraṃ katvā ācikkhati vā, paṭiniddisatīti attho. Yasmā cettha ugghaṭetīti uddisanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Uddeso ca desanāya ādi, tasmā vuttaṃ – “ugghaṭanā ādī”ti. Tathā vipañcanaṃ niddisanaṃ, vittharaṇaṃ paṭiniddisanaṃ, niddesapaṭiniddesā ca desanāya majjhapariyosānāti. Tena vuttaṃ – “vipañcanā majjhe, vitthāraṇā pariyosāna”nti.

With the passage beginning, 'He opens up with letters and with terms,' he shows the accomplishment of the function of the expression-terms. For their business is solely the disciplining of the triad of disciples. However, because it is not the place for the penetration of the truths, the `padaparama` person is not mentioned here. Alternatively, it should be seen that he is also included here by the grasping of the `neyya` person, just as the virtuous worldling is included by the grasping of the trainee. In 'by letters,' etc., it is an instrumental expression in the sense of means, not in the sense of cause. For letters, etc., have the purpose of opening up, etc., not that opening up, etc., has the purpose of letters, etc. And that for the sake of which an action is, that is the cause, as in 'he lives by food.' 'He opens up' means: having made the disciples with composed minds attentive, while imparting a distinction with letters by way of indication, he speaks or points out the intended meaning concisely, in such a way that there is an awakening to the intention at the end of the term. 'He elaborates' means he expounds the meaning that was pointed out. 'He expands' means he makes an expansion, or having made an expansion, he declares it; he expounds it in detail again. This is the meaning. And because here 'he opens up' is intended as 'pointing out,' and pointing out is the beginning of a teaching, therefore it is said: 'Opening up is the beginning.' Likewise, elaborating is expounding (`niddesana`), and expanding is detailed exposition (`paṭiniddesana`); and expounding and detailed exposition are the middle and end of a teaching. Therefore it is said: 'Elaborating is the middle, expanding is the end.'

Evaṃ “akkharehi saṅkāsetī”tiādinā channaṃ byañjanapadānaṃ byāpāraṃ dassetvā idāni atthapadānaṃ byāpāraṃ dassetuṃ “soyaṃ dhammavinayo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sīlādidhammo eva pariyattiatthabhūto veneyyavinayanato dhammavinayo. Ugghaṭīyantoti uddisiyamāno. Tenāti ugghaṭitaññūvinayanena. Vipañcīyantoti niddisiyamāno. Vitthārīyantoti paṭiniddisiyamāno.

Thus, having shown the function of the six expression-terms by that which begins with 'he makes known with letters,' now, in order to show the function of the meaning-terms, that which begins with 'this is the Dhamma-Vinaya' is said. Therein, the Dhamma itself, consisting of virtue and so on, which is the meaning of the scriptural learning, is called the Dhamma-Vinaya because it disciplines the trainable beings. 'Ugghaṭīyanto' means being stated in brief. 'Tena' means by the disciplining of the person who understands concisely. 'Vipañcīyanto' means being explained in medium detail. 'Vitthārīyanto' means being explained again in detail.

10. Ettāvatā [V 0.0191] “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”ti uddiṭṭhāya pāḷiyā tividhakalyāṇataṃ dassetvā idāni atthabyañjanasampattiṃ dassetuṃ “cha padāni attho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyaṃ. “Tenāha bhagavā”tiādinā desanāhārassa visayabhāvena uddiṭṭhaṃ pāḷiṃ nigamanavasena dasseti. Lokuttarantiādi “kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddha”nti padānaṃ atthavivaraṇaṃ. Tattha upaṭṭhitaṃ sabbavisesānanti sabbesaṃ uttarimanussadhammasaṅkhātānaṃ visesānaṃ adhisīlasikkhādivisesānaṃ vā upatiṭṭhanaṭṭhānaṃ. “Idaṃ nesaṃ padakkanta”ntiādīnaṃ viya etassa saddasiddhi veditabbā. “Idaṃ vuccati tathāgatapadaṃ itipī”tiādīsu idaṃ sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ tathāgatagandhahatthino paṭipattidesanāgamanehi kilesagahanaṃ ottharitvā gatamaggotipi. Tena gocarabhāvanāsevanāhi nisevitaṃ bhajitantipi. Tassa mahāvajirañāṇasabbaññutaññāṇadantehi ārañjitaṃ tebhūmakadhammānaṃ ārañjanaṭṭhānantipi vuccatīti attho. Ato cetanti yato tathāgatapadādibhāvena vuccati, ato aneneva kāraṇena brahmuno sabbasattuttamassa bhagavato, brahmaṃ vā sabbaseṭṭhaṃ cariyanti paññāyati yāvadeva [M 0.0061] manussehi suppakāsitattā yathāvuttappakārehi ñāyati. Tenāha bhagavāti yathāvuttatthaṃ pāḷiṃ nigamanavasena dasseti.

10. By this much, having shown the threefold excellence of the Pāḷi that was stated in brief as 'I will teach you the Dhamma, O monks,' now, in order to show the perfection of meaning and phrasing, that which begins with 'six terms are the meaning' is said. That is easily understood. By that which begins with 'Thus said the Blessed One,' he shows the Pāḷi, which was stated in brief as the domain of the teaching method, by way of a conclusion. That which begins with 'supramundane' is an explanation of the meaning of the terms 'completely perfect and pure.' Therein, 'the foundation for all special qualities' means the place of establishment for all special qualities called the higher human states, or for the special qualities beginning with the training in higher virtue. The grammatical formation of this term should be known like that of terms beginning with 'this is their step.' In such phrases as 'This is called the Tathāgata's path,' this holy life of the teaching, which is comprised of the threefold training, is also called the path traveled by the Tathāgata, the noble fragrant elephant, having overcome the thicket of defilements by means of the goings of practice and teaching. It is also that which is constantly resorted to and frequented by him through the cultivation of the domain and of development. It is also called the place for penetrating the phenomena of the three planes with his tusks, which are the great diamond knowledge and the knowledge of omniscience. This is the meaning. 'Ato cetaṃ' means: since it is called the state of being the Tathāgata's path and so on, for this very reason it is known as the conduct of the Brahmā, the Blessed One, who is supreme among all beings; or, it is the supreme, the best conduct. It is known in the aforesaid ways because it is well-proclaimed by gods and humans. By 'Thus said the Blessed One,' he again shows the Pāḷi with its aforesaid meaning by way of a conclusion.

Anupādāparinibbānatthatāya bhagavato desanāya yāvadeva ariyamaggasampāpanattho desanāhāroti dassetuṃ “kesaṃ ayaṃ dhammadesanā”ti pucchitvā “yogīna”nti āha. Catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāya yuttappayuttāti yogino. Te hi imaṃ desanāhāraṃ payojentīti. Idaṃ vacanaṃ desanāhāravibhaṅgassa yathānusandhinā sammā ṭhapitabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ pakaraṇaṃ saṅgāyantehi ṭhapitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “tenāha āyasmā mahākaccāyano”ti. Niyuttoti pāḷito assādādipadatthe niddhāretvā yojitoti attho.

In order to show that because the Blessed One's teaching has the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging, the teaching method has the purpose of leading all the way to the noble path, having asked, 'For whom is this Dhamma teaching?', he said, 'For yogis.' They are called 'yogis' because they are diligently engaged in the development of the meditation subject of the four truths. For they apply this teaching method. It should be seen that this statement was placed by the elders who compiled the treatise in order to show that the Analysis of the Teaching Method was correctly placed in accordance with its sequence. For so it was said: 'Thus said the Venerable Mahākaccāyana.' 'Niyutto' means: having determined the meanings of the terms beginning with 'gratification' from the Pāḷi, he has applied them. This is the meaning.

Desanāhāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Analysis of the Teaching Method is concluded.

2. Vicayahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Analysis of the Investigation Method

11. Tattha katamo vicayo hārotiādi vicayahāravibhaṅgo. Tatthāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – kiṃ vicinatīti ettha “vicinatī”ti etena vicayasaddassa kattuniddesataṃ dasseti. Kinti panatthassa hārassa visayo pucchitoti taṃ tassa visayaṃ dassetuṃ “padaṃ vicinatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha padaṃ vicinatīti ādito paṭṭhāya yāva nigamanā suttassa sabbaṃ [V 0.0192] padaṃ vicinati. Ayañca vicayo duvidho saddato atthato ca. Tesu “idaṃ nāmapadaṃ, idaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ, idaṃ upasaggapadaṃ, idaṃ nipātapadaṃ, idaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ, idaṃ purisaliṅgaṃ, idaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, idaṃ atītakālaṃ, idaṃ anāgatakālaṃ, idaṃ vattamānakālaṃ, idaṃ kattusādhanaṃ, idaṃ karaṇasādhanaṃ, idaṃ kammasādhanaṃ, idaṃ adhikaraṇasādhanaṃ, idaṃ paccattavacanaṃ, idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, yāva idaṃ bhummavacanaṃ, idaṃ ekavacanaṃ, idaṃ anekavacana”nti evamādivibhāgavacanaṃ, ayaṃ saddato padavicayo. So panāyaṃ padavicayo aviparītasabhāvaniruttisallakkhaṇeneva sampajjatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atthato pana vicayo tena tena padena vattabbaatthasaṃvaṇṇanā. Sace pana padaṃ pucchādivasena pavattaṃ, tassa tadatthassa ca pucchādibhāvo vicetabboti imamatthaṃ dassento “pañhaṃ vicinatī”tiādimāha.

11. Therein, the passage beginning with 'Which is the Investigation Method?' is the Analysis of the Investigation Method. Therein, this is the sequential explanation of the terms. In the text 'What does one investigate?', by this term 'investigates' (vicinati), it shows the state of the word 'investigation' (vicaya) as indicating the agent. But by this term 'what' (kiṃ), the domain of this method is questioned. Therefore, to show the domain of that method, it is said, 'One investigates the term,' and so on. Therein, 'One investigates the term' means that from the beginning up to the conclusion, one investigates every term of the discourse. And this investigation is twofold: by way of grammar and by way of meaning. Among these, the statements of division such as: 'This is a noun-term, this is a verb-term, this is a prefix-term, this is a particle-term; this is feminine gender, this is masculine gender, this is neuter gender; this is past tense, this is future tense, this is present tense; this is derived in the agent sense, this is derived in the instrumental sense, this is derived in the objective sense, this is derived in the locative sense; this is the nominative case, this is the accusative case, up to this is the locative case; this is singular, this is plural'—this is the investigation of the term by way of grammar. This investigation of the term, however, should be understood to be accomplished only by discerning the uncorrupted natural etymology. The investigation by way of meaning, on the other hand, is the explanation of the meaning to be conveyed by each respective term. If, however, a term occurs by way of a question and so on, the nature of that term and its meaning as a question and so on must be investigated. Showing this meaning, he said, 'One investigates the question,' and so on.

Yasmā [M 0.0062] ca sabbo desanāhāro vicayahārassa visayo suttassa vicayoti katvā, tasmā vuttaṃ – “assādaṃ vicinatī”tiādi. Yasmā pana anugītīti ettha anurūpā gīti anugītīti ayampi attho icchito, tasmā viciyamānassa suttapadassa anurūpato suttantarapadānipi atthuddhāravasena vā paduddhāravasena vā ānetvā vicetabbānīti dassento “sabbe nava suttante vicinatī”ti āha. Nava suttanteti suttageyyādike nava sutte, yathāsambhavatoti adhippāyo. Ayaṃ vicayahārassa padatthaniddeso.

And because the entire Teaching Method is the domain of the Investigation Method, as it is an investigation of the discourse, therefore it is said, 'One investigates gratification,' and so on. Furthermore, because in the term 'anugīti', the meaning 'a corresponding recitation is anugīti' is also intended, therefore, showing that in correspondence with the discourse-term being investigated, terms from other discourses should also be brought—either by way of extracting the meaning or by way of extracting the term—and investigated, he said, 'One investigates all nine types of discourses.' 'Nine types of discourses' means one investigates the nine discourses beginning with Sutta, Geyya, etc., as is appropriate; this is the intention. This is the explanation of the meaning of the terms of the Investigation Method.

Evaṃ niddesavāre vicayahāro saṅkhepato niddiṭṭhoti taṃ vibhāgena niddisitvā paṭiniddesavasena vibhajanto yasmā padavicayo suttassa anupadaṃ pavattetabbatāya atibhāriko na sukaro cāti taṃ anāmasitvā pañhavissajjanavicaye tāva dassento “yathā kiṃ bhave”tiādimāha. Tattha yathā kiṃ bhaveti yena pakārena so vicayo pavattetabbo, taṃ pakārajātaṃ kiṃ bhave, kīdisaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. “Yathā kiṃ bhaveyyā”tipi pāṭho. Puna yathāti nipātamattaṃ. Āyasmāti piyavacanaṃ ajitoti bāvarībrāhmaṇassa paricārakabhūtānaṃ soḷasannaṃ aññataro. Pārāyaneti pāraṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ, tassa adhigamūpāyadesanattā kiñcāpi sabbaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ “pārāyana”nti vattabbataṃ arahati, saṅgītikārehi pana vatthugāthānugītigāthādīhi saddhiṃ ajitasuttādīnaṃ (su. ni. 1038 ādayo; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchā 57 ādayo, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 1 ādayo) soḷasannaṃ suttānaṃ idaṃ nāmaṃ katanti tesaññeva pārāyanasamaññāti āha “pārāyane”ti. Keci “pārāyaniko”ti paṭhanti. Te kira tāpasapabbajjūpagamanato pubbe pārāyanaṃ adhīyantā vicariṃsu. Tasmā ayampi [V 0.0193] pārāyanaṃ vattetīti pārāyanikoti vutto. Pucchatīti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu pucchānibbattattā atītāti? Saccametaṃ, pucchanākāraṃ pana buddhiyaṃ viparivattamānaṃ katvā evamāha.

Thus, in the section on exposition, the Investigation Method has been explained in brief. Therefore, having explained it in detail and analyzing it by way of re-exposition—because the term-by-term investigation, having to be conducted sequentially for each term of the discourse, is very burdensome and not easy—he sets it aside and first shows the investigation of question and answer, saying, 'In what way might it be?' and so on. Therein, the meaning of `yathā kiṃ bhave` is: by what manner should that investigation be conducted? What sort of thing might that collection of manners be? What kind might it be? There is also the reading `yathā kiṃ bhaveyyā`. Furthermore, `yathā` is merely a particle. `Āyasmā` is a term of affection. `Ajita` is one of the sixteen attendants of the brahmin Bāvarī. In `Pārāyana`, Nibbāna is called the 'far shore' (`pāra`). Because it is a teaching on the means to attain it, although all the Blessed One's speech deserves to be called 'Pārāyana', the Elders of the council gave this name to the sixteen discourses beginning with the Ajita Sutta, along with the introductory verses (Vatthugāthā), recitation verses (Anugītigāthā), and so on. Therefore, it is their designation as 'Pārāyana' that is meant when he says, 'in the Pārāyana.' Some read `pārāyaniko`. It is said that they, before going forth into the ascetic life, wandered while practicing the way to the far shore. Therefore, this one too practices the way to the far shore, thus he is called `pārāyaniko`. Why is it said, 'he asks'? Is the question not past, since it has already been completed? This is true. However, having considered the manner of questioning as revolving in his wisdom, he speaks thus.

Pucchā ca nāmesā adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā diṭṭhasaṃsandanā vimaticchedanā anumatipucchā kathetukamyatāpucchā ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyā vibhajjabyākaraṇīyā paṭipucchābyākaraṇīyā ṭhapanīyā dhammādhiṭṭhānā sattādhiṭṭhānāti anekavidhā. Tasmā “kimayaṃ pucchā adiṭṭhajotanā”tiādinā yathāsambhavaṃ pucchā vicetabbā. Yathā cettha pucchāvibhāgo, evaṃ vissajjanavibhāgopi [M 0.0063] vissajjanavicaye yathāsambhavaṃ vattabbo. Pucchāsabhāgena hi vissajjananti. Idha pana vimaticchedanaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ pucchaṃ udāharitvā tattha vicayanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “kenassu nivuto loko”tiādimāha.

And this thing called a question is of many kinds: a question illuminating the unseen, a question comparing the seen, a question cutting off doubt, a question for approval, a question from a desire to speak, a question to be answered categorically, a question to be answered analytically, a question to be answered with a counter-question, a question to be set aside, a question established on the Dhamma, and a question established on a being. Therefore, the question should be investigated as is appropriate, with such thoughts as, 'Is this a question illuminating the unseen?' and so on. And just as the classification of questions is stated here, so too the classification of answers should be stated in the investigation of answers, as is appropriate. For the answer is in accordance with the nature of the question. Here, however, having cited a question that cuts off doubt and is established on a being, in order to show the manner of investigation therein, he said, 'By what is the world enveloped?' and so on.

Tattha kenāti kattari karaṇavacanaṃ. Sūti nipātamattaṃ, sūti vā saṃsaye nipāto, tenassa pañhassa vimaticchedanapucchābhāvaṃ dasseti. Nivutoti paṭicchādito. Lokoti sattaloko. Iccāyasmā ajitoti saṅgītikārakavacanaṃ. Nappakāsatīti na paññāyati. Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsīti kiṃ assa lokassa abhilepanaṃ vadasi. “Kiṃ svābhilepana”ntipi pāṭho, tassa kiṃ su abhilepananti padavibhāgo.

Therein, in `kena`, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the agent. The term `su` is merely a particle, or `su` is a particle that occurs in the sense of doubt; by it, it shows the nature of this question as being one that cuts off doubt. `Nivuto` means enveloped. `Loko` means the world of beings. 'Thus the venerable Ajita'—this is a statement of the Elders of the council. `Nappakāsati` means it is not apparent. `Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsi` means: 'What do you declare to be the defilement of this world?' There is also the reading `kiṃsvābhilepanaṃ`; its word-division is `kiṃ su abhilepanaṃ`.

Padānīti pajjati etehi atthoti padāni, vākyāni. Pucchitānīti pucchābhāvena vuttānīti attho. Eko pañhoti yadipi cattāri padāni pucchanavasena vuttāni, ñātuṃ icchito pana attho eko evāti “eko pañho”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha kāraṇamāha “ekavatthupariggahā”ti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kiñcāpi nivāraṇaappakāsanaabhilepanamahābhayasaṅkhātā pucchāya gahitā cattāro ete atthā, te panekaṃ lokaṃ patiguṇabhūtā, loko padhānabhāvena gahitoti tabbasena ekovāyaṃ pañhoti. Tenevāha “lokādhiṭṭhāna”ntiādi. Ko pana so lokoti? Āha “loko tividho”tiādi.

Padāni means: by these, the meaning is known; that is, sentences. Pucchitāni means: spoken in the manner of a question; this is the meaning. Regarding Eko pañho (one question): although four sentences are spoken by way of questioning, the meaning desired to be known is only one; hence, it is said, "one question." Therein, he states the reason: "because it encompasses a single object." This is what is meant: Although these four meanings taken up in the question—termed covering, non-manifestation, smearing, and great fear—are taken up, they are subordinate with respect to the one world, and the world is taken as the primary focus. Therefore, by its power, this is just one question. For that very reason, he said, "founded on the world," and so forth. But what is that world? He said, "the world is threefold," and so forth.

Tattha rāgādikilesabahulatāya kāmāvacarasattā kilesaloko. Jhānābhiññāparibuddhiyā rūpāvacarasattā bhavaloko. Āneñjasamādhibahulatāya visadindriyattā arūpāvacarasattā indriyaloko. Atha vā kilissanaṃ kileso, vipākadukkhanti attho. Tasmā dukkhabahulatāya apāyesu sattā kilesaloko. Tadaññe sattā sampattibhavabhāvato bhavaloko. Tattha ye vimuttiparipācakehi [V 0.0194] indriyehi samannāgatā sattā, so indriyalokoti veditabbaṃ. Pariyāpannadhammavasena lokasamaññāti ariyapuggalā idha na saṅgayhanti.

Therein, due to the abundance of defilements such as lust, sense-sphere beings are the world of defilements. Due to the development of jhānas and supernormal knowledges, form-sphere beings are the world of existence. Due to the abundance of imperturbable concentration and because of having purified faculties, formless-sphere beings are the world of faculties. Alternatively, kilesa is defiling, meaning the suffering of result. Therefore, due to the abundance of suffering, beings in the states of deprivation are the world of defilements. Other beings, due to having a prosperous existence, are the world of existence. Among them, those beings endowed with faculties that bring liberation to maturity are to be known as the world of faculties. The designation 'world' is by way of phenomena included in the round of existence; therefore, noble individuals are not included here.

Avijjāya nivuto lokoti caturaṅgasamannāgatena andhakārena viya rathaghaṭādidhammasabhāvappaṭicchādanalakkhaṇāya avijjāya nivuto paṭicchādito [M 0.0064] loko. Vivicchāti vicikicchāhetu. “Vivicchā macchariya”nti saṅgahe vuttaṃ. Pamādāti pamādahetu. Jappābhilepananti jappā taṇhā assa lokassa makkaṭālepo viya makkaṭassa abhilepanaṃ silesoti brūmi. Dukkhanti jātiādikaṃ vaṭṭadukkhanti ayaṃ padattho. Sesaṃ pāḷiyā eva viññāyati. Imāni cattāri padāni pucchāgāthāyaṃ vuttāni “imehī”ti vissajjanagāthāyaṃ vuttehi imehi catūhi padehi vissajjitāni. Kathanti āha “paṭhama”ntiādiṃ. Tena yathākkamaṃ pucchāvissajjanāni veditabbānīti dasseti.

Avijjāya nivuto loko means: the world is covered, concealed by ignorance, which has the characteristic of concealing the true nature of phenomena, just as a darkness endowed with four factors covers an old chariot, etc. Vivicchā is because of the cause, which is doubt. "Stinginess is vivicchā" is said in the commentary. Pamādā is because of the cause, which is negligence. Jappābhilepanaṃ means: jappā is craving; it smears this world just as monkey-lime smears a monkey; it sticks. Thus I say. Dukkhaṃ is the suffering of the round, such as birth, etc.; this is the meaning of the word. The rest is understood from the Pāḷi itself. These four terms spoken in the question verse are answered by these four terms spoken in the answer verse, indicated by imehīti. Because the objection, "How?" arises, he said, "the first," etc. By that, he shows that the questions and answers should be understood in sequence.

Idāni taṃ yathākkamaṃ pucchaṃ vissajjanañca sarūpato dassetuṃ gāthāya ca atthaṃ vivarituṃ “kenassū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “nīvaraṇehī”ti padena vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “avijjānīvaraṇā hi sabbe sattā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “yathāhā”tiādinā suttantaradassanena imasmiṃ pañhavissajjanavicaye anugītivicayaṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha pariyāyatoti kāraṇato. Nīvaraṇasaṅkhātānaṃ kāmacchandādīnampi kāraṇabhāvato paṭicchādanabhāvato ca ekaṃyeva nīvaraṇaṃ vadāmi, na pana aññesaṃ nīvaraṇasabhāvānaṃ abhāvāti attho. Yathā ca avijjāya sati nīvaraṇānaṃ bhāvo, evaṃ avijjāya asati na santi nīvaraṇānīti dassetuṃ “sabbaso”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, in order to show that question and answer in their essence and in sequence, and to explain the meaning of the verse, 'By what?' etc., was said. Therein, to show clearly the meaning already stated by the word 'by the hindrances,' 'For all beings are hindered by ignorance,' etc., was said. And here, it should be understood that by showing another sutta with 'as it is said,' etc., he shows the analysis of the Anugīti in this investigation of the question and answer. Therein, 'pariyāyato' means 'from a cause.' Because it is the cause of the so-called hindrances such as sensual desire, and because of its nature of covering, I say that ignorance alone is the hindrance; it is not, however, because of the absence of other things that have the nature of a hindrance. This is the meaning. And to show that just as when ignorance exists, the hindrances exist, so too when ignorance does not exist, the hindrances do not exist, 'altogether,' etc., was said.

Tenāti “avijjāya nivuto loko”ti padena. Paṭhamassa padassāti “kenassu nivuto loko”ti padassa. Yuttāti yojitā, anurūpāti vā attho. Etena pucchānurūpatā vissajjanassa dassitāti pubbāparavicayo vuttoti veditabbaṃ. “Yo puggalo nīvaraṇehi nivuto”tiādinā vivicchāpamādānaṃ avijjāya paccayabhāvaṃ dasseti. Nivuto eva hi nappakāsati. Vivicchāti vicikicchā. Tenevāha – “vivicchā nāma vuccati vicikicchā”ti. Tatrāyaṃ padasiddhi – yathā micchādiṭṭhisammādiṭṭhiyo “niccaṃ anicca”ntiādinā ekaṃsaggāhabhāvena pavattanti, na evamayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana anekaṃsaggāhabhāvato “niccaṃ nu kho aniccaṃ nu kho”tiādinā vividhaṃ viruddhaṃ vā icchati esatīti vivicchāti[V 0.0195]. “So vicikicchanto”tiādinā appakāsanassa vivicchāpamādānaṃ kāraṇabhāvaṃ vivarati. Sukke dhamme na uppādiyatīti na samādāya vattati. Nappakāsantīti te attano santāne anuppādiyamānā kusalā dhammā taṃ puggalaṃ pakāsaṃ [M 0.0065] loke abhiññātaṃ na karontīti attho. Abhilimpatīti makkaṭālepo viya makkaṭaṃ dārusilādīsu purisaṃ rūpādivisaye allīyāpetīti attho. Āsattibahulassāti āsaṅgabahulassa. Evaṃ abhijappāti karitvāti evaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyinīti iminā kāraṇena. Tatthāti tāya taṇhāya. Loko abhilitto silesena makkhito viya hotīti attho.

‘Tena’ refers to the phrase 'the world is covered by ignorance.' ‘Paṭhamassa padassa’ refers to the phrase 'by what is the world covered?'. ‘Yuttā’ means connected or suitable. By this, the suitability of the answer to the question is shown; thus, it should be understood that the investigation of the former and latter parts is stated. With 'A person who is covered by the hindrances,' etc., he shows that ignorance is the condition for doubt and negligence. For, being covered, one is not manifest. ‘Vivicchā’ is doubt. For that very reason, he said: 'Vivicchā is called vicikicchā.' Therein, this is the word-formation: just as wrong view and right view proceed by way of taking a definite side, with 'permanent,' 'impermanent,' etc., this does not proceed so. This, however, because of not taking a definite side, desires or seeks the varied or contradictory, with 'Is it permanent, I wonder? Is it impermanent, I wonder?,' etc.; therefore, it is ‘vivicchā’. With 'He, being doubtful,' etc., he explains that doubt and negligence are the cause of non-manifestation. 'Does not produce bright qualities' means: he does not undertake and practice them. 'They are not manifest' means: those wholesome qualities, not being produced in his own mental continuum, do not make that person manifest or renowned in the world. ‘Abhilimpati’ (smears) means: just as monkey-lime causes a monkey to stick to wood, stone, etc., so it causes a person to stick to objects such as form, etc. ‘Āsattibahulassa’ means: of one with much clinging. The phrase ‘evaṃ abhijappā’ is explained as: for this reason, it is of an obsessing nature. ‘Tattha’ means: by that craving, the world is smeared, as if smeared with resin.

Bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ. Mahantaṃ bhayaṃ mahabbhayaṃ. Tenevāha – “dukkhamassa mahabbhaya”nti. Dukkhaṃ domanassanti dukkhameva vibhattanti sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “tisso dukkhatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Odhasoti kadāci attūpakkamamūlāya kadāci parūpakkamamūlāyātiādinā vibhāgena dukkhadukkhatāya muccanakā visesena rūpāvacarā. Tathāti odhaso kadāci karahacīti evaṃ ākaḍḍhati. Vipariṇāmadukkhatāya muccanakā upekkhāsamāpattibahulā visesena arūpāvacarasattā. Appābādhāti padaṃ dukkhadukkhatāya muccanassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Dīghāyukāti vipariṇāmadukkhatāya. Arūpadevā hi loke visesato dīghāyukāti. Idañca muccanamaccantikaṃ. Yasmā ca dukkhā vedanāpi saṅkhatattā aniccatādisaṅkhāradukkhasabhāvā eva, tasmā yato muccanamaccantikaṃ, taṃ anavasesapariyādānavasena saṅgaṇhitvā dassetuṃ “saṅkhāradukkhatāya panā”tiādimāha.

One fears this, therefore it is called ‘bhaya’ (fear). Great fear is ‘mahabbhaya’. For that very reason, it was said: 'Suffering is its great fear.' By the words ‘dukkhaṃ’ (suffering) and ‘domanassaṃ’ (mental pain), suffering itself is analyzed. Therefore, to show all suffering by dividing it, 'the three kinds of suffering,' etc., was said. Regarding ‘odhaso’ (partially): those who are freed from the suffering of pain—by the distinction of 'sometimes from that which is rooted in one's own exertion, sometimes from that which is rooted in another's exertion,' etc.—are especially the beings of the form realm. By the word ‘tathā’ (so), it implies thus: one is freed partially (‘odhaso’), sometimes, at some time. Those who are freed from the suffering due to change are those abounding in the attainment of equanimity, especially the beings of the formless realm. The word ‘appābādhā’ (of little illness) is a word stating the cause for being freed from the suffering of pain. The word ‘dīghāyukā’ (long-lived) is a word stating the cause for being freed from the suffering due to change. For the formless devas are especially long-lived in the world. And this liberation is not absolute. And since even painful feeling, because it is conditioned, has the very nature of the suffering of formations, such as impermanence, etc.; therefore, to show that liberation which is absolute, by way of taking it up through complete consumption without remainder, he said, 'But as for the suffering of formations,' etc.

Tattha upādiyatīti upādi, vipākakkhandhā kaṭattā ca rūpaṃ. Upādissa sesaṃ upādisesaṃ, taṃ natthi etissāti anupādisesā, nibbānadhātu, tāya anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cāyaṃ karaṇaniddeso. Nibbānadhātūti ca nibbāyanamattaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā sakalalokabyāpinī sabbasaṅgāhinī ca saṅkhāradukkhatā, tasmā. Lokassāti sambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Tena “dukkhamassā”ti padassa atthaṃ dasseti. Evamettha lokassa nīvaraṇādīni ajānantena, samayantaraparicayena vā tattha saṃsayapakkhandena ekaṃseneva byākātabbattā sattādhiṭṭhānā pucchā katā, sā ca ajānanassa, saṃsayassa vā nīvaraṇādivisayatāya catubbidhā.
