Pāḷiyaṃ pana nīvaraṇādīnaṃ loko ādhārabhāvena gāthāyaṃ vuttoti eko pañhoti dassitanti. Ayamettha pucchāvicayo. Vissajjanavicayopi adiṭṭhajotinī vissajjanā vimaticchedinī cātiādinā pucchāvicaye vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

Herein, it is clung to, therefore it is ‘upādi’; this refers to the resultant aggregates and kamma-born form. The remainder of that which is clung to is ‘upādisesa’. She for whom that remainder does not exist is ‘anupādisesā’, the Nibbāna-element. 'By that anupādisesā nibbānadhātu (Nibbāna-element with no remainder of what is clung to)'; and this is an instrumental designation in the sense of indicating a specific state. And ‘nibbānadhātu’ is merely extinguishment. 'Therefore': because the suffering of formations pervades the entire world and includes all suffering, 'therefore'. ‘Lokassa’ is a genitive in the sense of relation. Thereby, it shows the meaning of the phrase ‘dukkhamassā’. Thus, herein, a question founded on beings was asked—which has the nature of being answered definitively—by one who does not know the hindrances, etc., of the world, or who has plunged into doubt about them due to familiarity with other doctrines. And that question, because its subject matter is the hindrances, etc., is fourfold for one who does not know or has doubt. In the Pāḷi, however, because the world is stated in the verse as the basis for the hindrances, etc., it is shown that it is one question. This, herein, is the analysis of the question. The analysis of the answer, too, should be understood according to the method stated in the analysis of the question, by way of 'it is an answer that illuminates what has not been seen and an answer that cuts off uncertainty,' etc.

Evaṃ [V 0.0196][M 0.0066] ekādhāraṃ pucchaṃ dassetvā idāni anekādhāraṃ dassetuṃ “savanti sabbadhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha savantīti sandanti. Sabbadhīti sabbesu rūpādīsu āyatanesu. Sotāti taṇhādisotā. Kiṃ nivāraṇanti tesaṃ kiṃ āvaraṇaṃ kā rakkhā. Saṃvaraṃ brūhīti taṃ nesaṃ nīvaraṇasaṅkhātaṃ saṃvaraṃ kathehi. Kena sotā pidhīyareti kena dhammena taṇhādisotā pidhiyyanti pacchijjantīti ayamettha padattho. Sesaṃ pāḷivaseneva āvi bhavissati.

Having thus shown a question with a single basis, now to show one with multiple bases, 'They flow everywhere,' etc., was said. Herein, ‘savanti’ (they flow) means they stream. ‘Sabbadhī’ (everywhere) means in all the sense bases such as form, etc. ‘Sotā’ (streams) means the streams of craving, etc. ‘Kiṃ nivāraṇaṃ’ (What is their restraint?) means: what is their obstruction, what is their protection? ‘Saṃvaraṃ brūhi’ (Declare the restraint) means: speak of that restraint for them, which is called an obstruction (‘nīvaraṇa’). ‘Kena sotā pidhīyare’ (By what are the streams blocked?) means: by what principle are the streams of craving, etc., blocked and cut off? This is the meaning of the words herein. The rest will become clear by the Pāḷi itself.

Te dve pañhāti yadipi imissā gāthāya pucchāvasena pavattāya cattāri padāni cattāri vākyāni. Ñātuṃ icchitassa pana atthassa duvidhattā te dve pañhā. Kasmāti ce? “Imehi bahvādhivacanena pucchitā”ti āha. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – ime etāya gāthāya gahitā atthā yasmā bahūni adhikicca pavattavacanena pucchitā, tasmā te dve pañhāti. Ekato upari bahūti hi sāsanavohāro, tameva pucchāya duvidhatthavisayataṃ vivarituṃ “eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – yāhi ñātibyasanādisaṅkhātāhi pāṇavadhādīhi eva vā duggatihetubhūtāhi āpadāhi samaṃ saha, sabbathā vā ayaṃ loko āpanno ajjhotthaṭo. Taṃnimittehi dasahi kilesavatthūhi saṃkiliṭṭho ca, tassa taṃ āpannākāraṃ saṃkiliṭṭhākārañca buddhiyaṃ katvā āha – “evaṃ samāpannassa evaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhassā”ti. Vodāyati sujjhati etenāti vodānaṃ, samathavipassanā. Vuṭṭhāti etena nimittato pavattato cāti vuṭṭhānaṃ, ariyamaggo.

Regarding 'Those two questions': although in this verse, which proceeds by way of a question, there are four phrases, four sentences, they are two questions because of the twofold nature of the meaning wished to be known. If it is asked, 'Why?', he said, 'These are asked with a term signifying many.' Herein, this is the brief meaning: because these meanings taken by this verse are asked with speech that occurs concerning many things, therefore they are two questions. For 'many' is the usage in the Dispensation for what is more than one. To explain that very twofold nature of the question's subject matter, 'thus,' and so forth, was said. Its meaning is: this world is afflicted and overwhelmed by those adversities called 'destruction of relatives,' and so forth, or by those adversities which are the cause of a bad destination, namely, the killing of living beings, and so forth, or in every way. And it is defiled by the ten bases of defilements which are the cause of that. Having placed in his wisdom its manner of being afflicted and its manner of being defiled, he said: 'of one thus afflicted, of one thus defiled.' One is cleansed, becomes pure, by this; therefore it is `vodāna` (cleansing): calm and insight. One emerges by this from the sign and from the process; therefore it is `vuṭṭhāna` (emergence): the noble path.

Asamāhitassāti nānārammaṇesu vikkhittacittassa. Savantīti pavattanti. Abhijjhātiādi asamādhānahetudassanaṃ. Tenevāha – “evaṃ asamāhitassā”ti. “Yathāha bhagavā”tiādinā idhāpi anugītivicayaṃ dasseti. Sotānaṃ savanaṃ yebhuyyena anurodhavasenevāti āha – “savati manāpikesu rūpesū”ti. Ettha ca cakkhādayo sotānaṃ dvārabhāvena pavattamānā upacāravasena sayaṃ savantā viya vuttā. Itīti evaṃ. Sabbāti sabbasmā. Sabbathāti sabbappakārena. Idaṃ vodānanti idaṃ “pariyuṭṭhānavighāta”nti vuttaṃ pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ vodānaṃ.

`Asamāhitassa` (of one unconcentrated) means: of one whose mind is scattered among various objects. `Savanti` (they flow) means they proceed. Covetousness and so forth is a showing of the cause for non-concentration. For that very reason, he said: 'Thus, for one who is unconcentrated.' By 'As the Blessed One has said,' and so forth, he shows here also the analysis of the recitation. The flowing of the streams is for the most part by way of fondness, therefore he said: 'It flows towards agreeable forms.' And herein, the eye and so forth, which proceed as the doors for the streams, are spoken of metaphorically as if they themselves were flowing. `Iti` means thus. `Sabbā` means from all. `Sabbathā` means in every way. Regarding `idaṃ vodānaṃ` (this cleansing): this abandoning of the obsessions, which was called 'the destruction of obsessions,' is the cleansing.

Vissajjanagāthāya [M 0.0067] sati tesaṃ nivāraṇanti vipassanāsampayuttā sati kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesamānā tesaṃ sotānaṃ nivāraṇanti. Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmīti tameva satiṃ sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi. Paññāyete pidhīyareti rūpādīsu aniccatādipaṭivedhasādhikāya maggapaññāya [V 0.0197] ete sotā sabbaso pidhiyyanti, uppajjituṃ appadānavasena samucchijjantīti attho.

In the verse of reply, regarding 'mindfulness is their restraint': mindfulness associated with insight, while investigating the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, is the restraint of those streams. Regarding 'I declare the restraint of the streams': I declare that very mindfulness to be the restraint of the streams. Regarding 'By wisdom they are blocked': by the wisdom of the path which accomplishes the penetration of impermanence and so forth in form and so forth, these streams are blocked in every way. The meaning is that they are cut off by way of not giving an opportunity to arise.

Nāviñchatīti abhijjhādippavattidvārabhāvena cittasantānaṃ, puggalaṃ vā nākaḍḍhati. Anusayappahānaṃ idha pidhānaṃ adhippetanti āha – “paññāya anusayā pahīyantī”ti. Yasmā anusayanimittaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ anusayābhāve na hotīti āha “anusayesū”tiādi. Idāni tamevatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvento “taṃ yathā khandhavantassā”tiādimāha. Etthāpi sotānaṃ nivāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ saṃvaraṃ pidhānañca ajānantena tattha vā saṃsayitena ekaṃsikattā dhammādhiṭṭhānā pucchā katāti idha pucchāvicayo vuttanayeneva vissajjanavicayo ca veditabbo.

`Nāviñchati` (it does not pull) means that, by being the doorway for the arising of covetousness and so forth, it does not draw in the stream of consciousness or the person. The abandonment of latent tendencies is intended here as a covering; therefore, he said: 'Latent tendencies are abandoned by wisdom.' Because an obsession, which is caused by a latent tendency, does not occur in the absence of the latent tendency, he said: 'in regard to latent tendencies,' and so on. Now, wishing to clarify that very meaning by way of a simile, he says: 'Just as for a tree with a trunk,' and so on. Here too, the question, which is definite and has the Dhamma as its foundation, was asked by one who did not know or was doubtful about the restraint and covering designated as the prevention of the streams. Therefore, here the analysis of the question and the analysis of the reply should be understood in the way already stated.

Ettha ca yena adhippāyena “kenassu nivuto loko”ti gāthāya (su. ni. 1038; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchā 57, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 1; netti. 45) satipi nivāraṇādīnaṃ catunnaṃ pucchitabbabhāve eko pañhoti vuttaṃ. Tena tāva sotānaṃyeva saṃvaro pidhānañca pucchitanti sote ekatthavasena gahetvā pucchāya ekādhiṭṭhānabhāvato eko pañhoti vattabbaṃ siyā. Sotānaṃ vā bahubhāvato bahūti yattakā sotā, tattakā pañhāti. Yena pana adhippāyena “savanti sabbadhi sotā”ti gāthāyaṃ (su. ni. 1040; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchā 59, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 3; netti. 45) sote anāmasitvā saṃvarapidhānānaṃ vasena “dve pañhā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena paṭhamagāthāyaṃ satipi nivāraṇādīnaṃ lokādhārabhāve lokaṃ anāmasitvā nivāraṇādīnaṃ vibhāgena cattāro pañhātipi vattabbanti ayaṃ nayo dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And here, with the intention by which, in the verse 'By what is the world covered?', it is said to be one question even though there are four things to be asked about, beginning with the hindrances. By that intention, then, since only the restraint and covering of the streams are asked about, taking the streams as a single entity, it should be said to be one question because the question has a single foundation. Or, because the streams are many, they are 'many,' thus it should be said: 'As many streams as there are, so many questions there are.' But with the intention by which, in the verse 'The streams flow everywhere,' without referring to the streams, it is said to be 'two questions' by way of restraint and covering. By that intention, in the first verse, even though the hindrances and so on have the world as their support, without referring to the world, by the division of the hindrances and so on, it can also be said that there are four questions. This method is thus shown, it should be understood.

Idāni yasmā pucchanto na kevalaṃ pubbe attanā racitaniyāmeneva pucchati, atha kho desanākāle vuttadhammassa anusandhiṃ gahetvāpi pucchati, tasmā tassa anusandhiṃ pucchāya vicetabbākāraṃ dassento “yāni sotānī”ti gāthāya anantaraṃ “paññā ceva sati cā”ti gāthamāha. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yāyaṃ bhagavatā vuttā paññā, yā ca [M 0.0068] sati yañca tadavasesaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, etaṃ sabbampi kattha nirujjhati, etaṃ me puṭṭho pabrūhīti.

Now, because the questioner does not ask merely according to the arrangement composed by himself beforehand, but rather also asks by grasping the connection to the Dhamma spoken at the time of the discourse, therefore, showing the manner in which the connection in the question should be investigated, immediately after the verse 'Whatever streams there are...,' he speaks the verse 'Wisdom and mindfulness....' This is its condensed meaning: This wisdom spoken by the Blessed One, and this mindfulness, and this name-and-form which is the remainder—where does all this cease? Being asked this by me, please declare it in detail.

Vissajjanagāthāyaṃ panassa yasmā paññāsatiyo nāmeneva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, tasmā tā visuṃ na vuttā. Ayañcettha saṅkhepattho – yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ, ajita, etaṃ pañhaṃ apucchi – “katthetaṃ uparujjhatī”ti [V 0.0198] anantaragāthāyaṃ (su. ni. 1042; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchā 61, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 5; netti. 11, 45), yattha taṃ asesaṃ uparujjhati, taṃ te vadāmi. Tassa tassa hi viññāṇassa nirodhena saheva apubbaṃ acarimaṃ etthetaṃ uparujjhati, ettheva viññāṇassa nirodhena nirujjhati, etaṃ viññāṇanirodhaṃ tassa nirodho nātivattatīti vuttaṃ hotīti. Ayaṃ pañhe anusandhiṃ pucchatīti anantaragāthāyaṃ sotānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānānusayappahānakiccena saddhiṃ sati paññā ca vuttā, taṃ sutvā tappahāne paññāsatīsu tiṭṭhantīsu tāsaṃ sannissayena nāmarūpena bhavitabbaṃ, tathā ca sati vaṭṭati eva. Kattha nu kho imāsaṃ sanissayānaṃ paññāsatīnaṃ asesanirodhoti iminā adhippāyena ayaṃ pucchā katāti āha – “ayaṃ pañhe…pe… dhātu”nti. Tattha anusandhīyati desanā etāyāti anusandhi.

But in the reply-verse to this, because wisdom and mindfulness are included only under 'name,' they are not spoken of separately. And this is the condensed meaning here: Ajita, that question you asked me in the immediately following verse—'Where does this cease?'—I will declare to you where that ceases without remainder. Indeed, with the very cessation of each consciousness, this ceases right here, simultaneously. Right here it ceases with the cessation of consciousness; the cessation of that name-and-form does not go beyond this cessation of consciousness. Thus it is said. 'This one asks the connection in the question' means: in the immediately following verse, mindfulness and wisdom are spoken of together with the task of abandoning the obsessions and latent tendencies of the streams. Having heard that, he thinks: 'When wisdom and mindfulness are established in abandoning them, there must be name-and-form as their support, and that being so, the round of existence just turns. Where, indeed, is the cessation without remainder of this wisdom and mindfulness together with their support?' With this intention, this question was asked. Therefore, it is said: 'This one in the question... element.' Therein, 'connection' (anusandhi) is so called because the teaching is connected (anusandhīyati) by it.

Yāya paṭipadāya anupādisesaṃ nibbānadhātuṃ adhigacchanti, taṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāsaṅkhātaṃ paṭipadaṃ saha visayena dassetuṃ “tīṇi ca saccānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saṅkhatānīti samecca sambhūya paccayehi katānīti saṅkhatāni. Nirodhadhammānīti nirujjhanasabhāvāni. Dukkhaṃ samudayo maggoti tesaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ. Nirodho pana kathanti āha “nirodho asaṅkhato”ti. So hi kenaci paccayena na saṅkhatoti asaṅkhato. Saha visayena pahātabbapahāyakasabhāvesu ariyasaccesu pahāyakavibhāgamukhena pahātabbavibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha samudayo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

To show the practice by which they attain the Nibbāna-element without residue—that practice designated as the development of the meditation subject of the Four Truths—together with its object, it is said: 'And the three truths,' and so on. Therein, 'conditioned' means made by causes having come together and assembled; therefore, they are called 'conditioned.' 'Subject to cessation' means having the nature of ceasing. 'Suffering, origin, path' is the showing of their individual nature. But of what nature is cessation? To this, he says: 'Cessation is unconditioned.' For it is not conditioned by any cause; therefore, it is called 'unconditioned.' To show the division of that which is to be abandoned by means of the division of that which abandons, among the Noble Truths which have the nature of that which is to be abandoned and that which abandons, together with their object, it is said: 'Therein, the origin,' and so on.

Tattha avijjāvasesāti dassanamaggena pahīnāvasesā avijjāti attho. Ayañca sesa-saddo kāmacchando byāpādo māno uddhaccanti etthāpi yojetabbo. Yathā hi avijjā, evaṃ etepi dhammā apāyagamanīyasabhāvā paṭhamamaggena pahīyanti evāti. “Avijjāniravasesā”tipi pāṭho, etthāpi yathāvuttesu kāmacchandādipadesupi niravasesa-saddo yojetabbo[M 0.0069]. Sāvasesañhi purimamaggadvayena kāmacchandādayo pahīyanti, itarehi pana niravasesanti. Tedhātuke imāni dasa saṃyojanānīti ettha tedhātuketi saṃyojanānaṃ visayadassanaṃ. Tattha hi tāni saṃyojanavasena pavattanti.

Therein, 'with ignorance remaining' means the ignorance that remains from what was abandoned by the path of seeing. And this word 'remaining' should also be applied here to sensual desire, ill will, conceit, and restlessness. For just as ignorance, these states too, having the nature of leading to the planes of misery, are indeed abandoned by the first path. There is also the reading 'with ignorance not remaining'; here too, the word 'without remainder' should be applied to the terms mentioned, sensual desire and so on. For sensual desire and the like are abandoned with a remainder by the first two paths, but by the other two higher paths, they are abandoned without remainder. In 'These ten fetters in the three realms,' the term 'in the three realms' is a showing of the domain of the fetters. For it is there that they occur by way of fettering.

12. Anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ adhiṭṭhāyāti taṃ pahāyakaṃ patvā. Yaṃ panāti ettha yanti hetuatthe nipāto. Idaṃ khaye ñāṇanti yena ñāṇena hetubhūtena “khīṇā me jātī”ti attano jātiyā khīṇabhāvaṃ jānāti, idaṃ evaṃ paccavekkhaṇassa nimittabhūtaṃ arahattaphalañāṇaṃ khaye [V 0.0199] ñāṇaṃ nāma. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātīti etthāpi yanti ānetabbaṃ “yaṃ nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Idaṃ anuppāde ñāṇanti idhāpi pubbe vuttanayeneva arahattaphalañāṇavasena attho yojetabbo. Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. cittuppādakkaṇḍa 135-142) pana “khaye ñāṇaṃ kilesakkhayakare ariyamagge ñāṇanti vuttaṃ. Anuppāde ñāṇaṃ paṭisandhivasena anuppādabhūte taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesānaṃ anuppādapariyosāne uppanne ariyaphale ñāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Idha pana ubhayampi arahattaphalañāṇavaseneva vibhattaṃ. Tenevāha – “imāni dve ñāṇāni aññātāvindriya”nti, “ārammaṇasaṅketena dve nāmāni labbhantī”ti ca.

12. 'Having established the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown'' means having attained that which abandons. In `yaṃ pana`, `yaṃ` is a particle in the sense of cause. 'This is knowledge of destruction'—by which knowledge, being the cause, one knows the state of destruction of one's own birth, thinking, 'Destroyed is my birth.' This knowledge of the fruit of arahantship, which is the basis for such reflection, is called the knowledge of destruction. In 'He understands that there is no more of this state,' `yaṃ` should also be supplied: 'that which he understands as "there is no more of this state."' 'This is knowledge of non-arising'—here too, the meaning should be applied in the same way as stated before, by way of the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship. In the Aṭṭhasālinī, however, it is said: 'Knowledge of destruction is knowledge in the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of defilements. Knowledge of non-arising is knowledge in the Noble Fruit that arises at the conclusion of the non-arising of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, which has become non-arising with respect to rebirth.' Here, however, both are distinguished solely by way of the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, it is said: 'These two knowledges are the faculty of final knowledge,' and 'two names are obtained by the designation of the object.'

Aññindriyaṃ heṭṭhimesu tīsu phalesu, uparimesu ca tīsu maggesu uppattiyā punappunaṃ uppajjamānampi anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ viya paṭhamaphaluppattiyā aggaphaluppattiyā anuppādanirodhena nirujjhatīti āha – “yañca anaññātaññassāmītindriya”ntiādi. Etena pahātabbadhammā viya dassanabhāvanāhi aggaphaluppattiyā tadavasesaphaladhammāpi anuppādanirodhena nirujjhanti. Ko pana vādo tebhūmakadhammānanti dasseti, ekā paññā aññātāvindriyattā. Yadi ekā, kathaṃ dvidhā vuttāti āha “api cā”tiādi. Ārammaṇasaṅketenāti khaye anuppādeti imāya ārammaṇasamaññāya. Sā pajānanaṭṭhena paññāti yā pubbe sotānaṃ pidhānakiccā vuttā paññā, sā pajānanasabhāvena paññā. Itarā pana yathādiṭṭhaṃ yathāgahitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ apilāpanaṭṭhena ogāhanaṭṭhena satīti.

The faculty of knowledge, although arising repeatedly in the lower three fruits and the upper three paths, ceases with cessation by non-arising upon the attainment of the highest fruit, just as the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' ceases, as it were, with cessation by non-arising upon the attainment of the first fruit. Therefore, he said: 'And the faculty of "I shall know the unknown,"' etc. By this, he shows that, like the states to be abandoned by vision and development, upon the attainment of the highest fruit, the remaining fruition-states also cease with cessation by non-arising. What then is to be said of the cessation of states pertaining to the three planes? Because it is the faculty of final knowledge, it is one wisdom. If it is one, how is it said to be twofold? Thus he said 'Moreover,' etc. 'By the designation of the object' means: by this conventional name for the object, namely 'in destruction' and 'in non-arising'. 'That is wisdom in the sense of understanding' means: the wisdom previously described as performing the function of closing the streams. That is wisdom because of its nature of understanding. The other, however, is mindfulness in the sense of not forgetting and immersing itself in the object as seen and grasped.

13. Evaṃ [M 0.0070] “paññā ceva sati cā”ti padassa atthaṃ vivaritvā idāni “nāmarūpa”nti padassa atthaṃ vivaranto “tattha ye pañcupādānakkhandhā, idaṃ nāmarūpa”nti āha. Nāmarūpañca vibhāgena dassento sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ pākaṭanāmarūpameva vibhāvetuṃ “tattha ye”tiādimāha. Taggahaṇeneva hi sahacaraṇādinā tadaññe cittacetasikā rūpadhammā ca gahitā hontīti. Nāmaggahaṇena cettha khandhattayameva gahitanti “nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇasampayutta”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana rūpaṃ sampayuttanti? Nayidaṃ sampayuttapaccayavasena vuttaṃ. Pacurajanassa pana avibhāgena gahaṇīyasabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

13. Having thus explained the meaning of the phrase 'wisdom and mindfulness,' now, in explaining the meaning of the phrase 'name-and-form,' it is said: 'Therein, whatever are the five aggregates of clinging, this is name-and-form.' And in showing name-and-form by way of analysis, for the sake of easy comprehension, only the evident name-and-form is explained, as in the phrase 'Therein, whatever,' and so on. For by the grasping of that, other consciousness, mental factors, and material phenomena are also grasped by way of co-nascence, etc. And here, by the term 'name,' only the three aggregates are grasped; therefore it is said 'name-and-form associated with consciousness.' But is that form associated? This is not said in the sense of the associated-condition. Rather, it should be understood as said with reference to its nature of being grasped undifferentiatedly by the common person.

Gāthāya anupādisesā nibbānadhātu pucchitāti taṃ caturiddhipādamukhena ariyamaggādhigamena pattabbanti dassento iddhipādabhāvanāmūlabhūtāni indriyāni satipaññāhi niddhāretuṃ “tattha sati ca paññā ca cattāri indriyānī”ti āha. Kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo [V 0.0200] samanvesamānā sati sijjhantī ekantena samādhiṃ nipphādeti. Satiggahaṇena cettha pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ idhādhippetanti āha – “sati dve indriyāni, satindriyañca samādhindriyañcā”ti. Tathā anusayasamugghātavidhāyinī paññā sijjhamānā na vinā catubbidhasammappadhānavīriyaṃ sijjhatīti vuttaṃ – “paññā dve indriyāni paññindriyañca vīriyindriyañcā”ti.

Since the verse asks about the Nibbāna-element without residue of aggregates, in order to show that it is attainable through the Noble Path by means of the four bases of spiritual power, and to specify through mindfulness and wisdom the faculties that are the root for developing the bases of spiritual power, it is said: 'Therein, mindfulness and wisdom are four faculties.' Mindfulness, investigating the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, when accomplished, certainly produces concentration. Here, by the inclusion of mindfulness, the abandoning of mental obsessions is intended; thus it is said: 'Mindfulness is two faculties: the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration.' Likewise, wisdom, which uproots the latent tendencies, does not succeed when being accomplished without the energy of the fourfold right exertion; thus it is said: 'Wisdom is two faculties: the faculty of wisdom and the faculty of energy.'

Yā imesu catūsu indriyesūti imesu satiādīsu catūsu indriyesu nissayapaccayatāya adhiṭṭhānabhūtesu taṃsahajātā eva yā saddahanā. “Imehi catūhi indriyehī”tipi pāḷi, tassā imehi catūhi indriyehi sampayuttāti vacanaseso, ārammaṇe abhippasādalakkhaṇā saddhā kattukāmatāsabhāvassa chandassa visesapaccayo hotīti āha – “yā saddhādhipateyyā cittekaggatā, ayaṃ chandasamādhī”ti. Samāhite citteti vipassanāsamādhinā samāhite citte. Idaṃ pahānanti vikkhambhanappahānasādhako samādhi pahānanti vutto pajahati etenāti katvā. “Padhāna”ntipi pāṭho, aggoti attho. Tathā hi “samādhi ekodī”ti vuccati.

That which is in these four faculties—that is, in these four faculties beginning with mindfulness, which are a foundation by way of being a support-condition—is the faith co-nascent with them. 'By these four faculties' is also a reading; for that, the ellipsis to be supplied is 'associated with these four faculties.' Faith, which has the characteristic of clear confidence in the object, is a specific condition for desire, which has the nature of a wish to do. Therefore, it is said: 'That one-pointedness of mind which has faith as its dominant factor, this is concentration due to desire.' With the mind concentrated—that is, with the mind concentrated by insight-concentration. This is abandonment—the concentration that accomplishes abandonment by suppression is called 'abandonment' because 'one abandons by means of it.' 'Exertion' is also a reading; the meaning is 'supreme.' For thus it is said, 'concentration is unified.'

“Assāsapassāsā”tiādinā kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārasīsena taṃsamuṭṭhāpakā vīriyasaṅkhārāva gahitā. Te hi yāva bhāvanānipphatti tāva ekarasena saraṇato saṅkappetabbato ca sarasaṅkappā”ti vuttā “evaṃ [M 0.0071] me bhāvanā hotū”ti yathā icchitā, tathā pavattiyā hetubhāvato. Tadubhayanti chandasamādhisaṅkhātañca padhānasaṅkhārasaṅkhātañca vīriyanti taṃ ubhayaṃ. Ubhayameva hi upacāravasena aññaṃ viya katvā “chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipāda”nti vuttaṃ. Abhinnampi hi upacāravasena bhinnaṃ viya katvā voharanti, yathā “silāputtakassa sarīra”nti.

By 'in-breaths and out-breaths,' etc., under the heading of bodily, verbal, and mental formations, what is taken are the very formations of energy that produce them. For until the accomplishment of the development, they are called 'memories and intentions' because they are of a single function, and because they are to be remembered and intended. And they are the cause of occurring as one desires, as in 'May my development be like this.' That pair is the pair of energy: that designated as concentration due to desire and that designated as the formation of exertion. For it is just this pair that, having been made to seem different by way of figurative speech, is called 'the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to desire and the formation of exertion.' For even what is undifferentiated is spoken of as if it were differentiated by way of figurative speech, as in 'the body of a stone doll.'

Tattha ijjhatīti iddhi, samijjhati nipphajjatīti attho. Ijjhanti vā tāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi, pajjati etenāti pādo, paṭhamena atthena iddhi eva pādo iddhipādo, iddhikoṭṭhāsoti attho. Dutiyena atthena iddhiyā pādo patiṭṭhā adhigamūpāyoti iddhipādo. Tena hi uparūparivisesasaṅkhātaṃ iddhiṃ pajjanti pāpuṇanti. Vivekanissitanti tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ samucchedavivekanissitaṃ nissaraṇavivekanissitañca iddhipādaṃ bhāvetīti attho. Tathā hi ayaṃ iddhipādabhāvanānuyutto yogī vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ. Maggakkhaṇe pana kiccato [V 0.0201] samucchedavivekanissitaṃ ārammaṇato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāvetīti. Esa nayo virāganissitantiādīsu.

Herein, 'iddhi' is so called because it succeeds (ijjhati); the meaning is that it is accomplished, it is brought to fruition. Or, beings succeed through it—they become accomplished, developed, and have reached excellence—hence, it is called 'iddhi'. By this one attains (pajjati), hence it is a 'pāda' (basis). In the first sense, 'iddhi' itself is the 'pāda', thus 'iddhipāda'; the meaning is 'a constituent part of success'. In the second sense, it is the 'pāda' of 'iddhi' because it is its foundation, the means for its attainment, hence 'iddhipāda'. For by this, they attain and reach success, which is reckoned as higher and higher distinction. 'Based on seclusion' means one develops the basis of power that is based on seclusion by substitution of opposites, based on seclusion by cutting off, and based on seclusion as escape. For indeed, this yogī, devoted to the development of the basis of power, at the moment of insight, develops the basis of power that is functionally based on seclusion by substitution of opposites and, by inclination, based on seclusion as escape. But at the moment of the path, one develops the basis of power that is functionally based on seclusion by cutting off and, by way of object, based on seclusion as escape. This same method is to be applied to 'based on dispassion' and so on.

Vivekattā eva hi virāgādayo, kevalañcettha vossaggo duvidho pariccāgavossaggo ca pakkhandanavossaggo cāti. Tattha pariccāgavossaggo vipassanākkhaṇe tadaṅgavasena, maggakkhaṇe samucchedavasena kilesappahānaṃ. Pakkhandanavossaggo vipassanākkhaṇe tanninnabhāvena, maggakkhaṇe ārammaṇakaraṇavasena nibbānapakkhandanaṃ. Tadubhayampi imasmiṃ lokiyalokuttaramissake atthasaṃvaṇṇanānaye yujjati. Tathā hi ayaṃ paṭhamiddhipādo yathāvuttena pakārena kilese pariccajati nibbānañca pakkhandati. Vossaggapariṇāminti iminā pana vacanena vossaggatthaṃ pariṇamantaṃ pariṇatañca paripaccantaṃ paripakkañcāti attho. Ayañhi iddhipādabhāvanānuyutto yogī yathā paṭhamo iddhipādo kilesapariccāgavossaggatthaṃ nibbānapakkhandanavossaggatthañca paripaccati, yathā ca paripakko hoti, tathā naṃ bhāvetīti. Sesiddhipādesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattito samādhi chandasamādhi. Evaṃ vīriyaṃ cittaṃ vīmaṃsaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattito samādhi vīmaṃsāsamādhīti.

Indeed, dispassion and so on have the very meaning of seclusion. Here, however, relinquishment (vossagga) is twofold: relinquishment as abandonment (pariccāgavossagga) and relinquishment as plunging forward (pakkhandanavossagga). Therein, relinquishment as abandonment is the abandoning of defilements at the moment of insight by way of substitution of opposites, and at the moment of the path by way of cutting off. Relinquishment as plunging forward is the plunging into Nibbāna at the moment of insight by being inclined towards it, and at the moment of the path by way of making it an object. Both of these are suitable in this expository method of meaning that mixes the mundane and supramundane. For indeed, this first basis of power, in the way described, abandons defilements and plunges into Nibbāna. But by this phrase 'maturing in relinquishment,' the meaning is: for the sake of relinquishment, that which is inclining and inclined, and that which is ripening and ripened. For this yogī, devoted to the development of the basis of power, develops it in such a way that the first basis of power ripens for the sake of relinquishment as abandoning defilements and for the sake of relinquishment as plunging into Nibbāna, and in such a way that it becomes fully ripe. This very same method is to be applied to the remaining bases of power. This, however, is the distinction: just as the concentration that proceeds having made desire foremost is desire-concentration, so too the concentration that proceeds having made energy, mind, or investigation foremost is investigation-concentration.

14. Na [M 0.0072] kevalaṃ catutthaiddhipādo eva samādhiñāṇamūlako, atha kho sabbopīti dassetuṃ “sabbo samādhi ñāṇamūlako ñāṇapubbaṅgamo ñāṇānuparivattī”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā so eva vīmaṃsāsamādhīti vuttoti? Vīmaṃsaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattitattāti vuttovāyamattho. Tattha pubbabhāgapaññāya ñāṇamūlako. Adhigamapaññāya ñāṇapubbaṅgamo. Paccavekkhaṇapaññāya ñāṇānuparivatti. Atha vā pubbabhāgapaññāya ñāṇamūlako. Upacārapaññāya ñāṇapubbaṅgamo. Appanāpaññāya ñāṇānuparivatti. Upacārapaññāya vā ñāṇamūlako. Appanāpaññāya ñāṇapubbaṅgamo. Abhiññāpaññāya ñāṇānuparivattīti veditabbaṃ.

14. To show that not only the fourth basis of power has knowledge as the root of its concentration, but that all of them do, it was said: 'All concentration has knowledge as its root, is preceded by knowledge, and revolves in accordance with knowledge.' If so, why is only that one called investigation-concentration? This meaning has already been stated: because it proceeds having made investigation foremost. Therein, it has knowledge as its root through preliminary-part wisdom; it is preceded by knowledge through attainment wisdom; it revolves in accordance with knowledge through reviewing wisdom. Or, it has knowledge as its root through preliminary-part wisdom; it is preceded by knowledge through access wisdom; it revolves in accordance with knowledge through absorption wisdom. Or, it has knowledge as its root through access wisdom; it is preceded by knowledge through absorption wisdom; it should be understood that it revolves in accordance with knowledge through direct-knowledge wisdom.

Yathā [V 0.0202] pureti yathā samādhissa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇānuparivattibhāvena pure pubbe atītāsu jātīsu asaṅkhyeyyesupi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu attano paresañca khandhaṃ khandhūpanibaddhañca duppaṭivijjhaṃ nāma natthi, tathā pacchā samādhissa anāgataṃsañāṇānuparivattibhāvena anāgatāsu jātīsu asaṅkhyeyyesupi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu attano paresañca khandhaṃ khandhūpanibaddhañca duppaṭivijjhaṃ nāma natthīti attho.

As to 'as before': Just as, due to concentration's revolving in accordance with the knowledge of recollecting past lives, there is nothing called the aggregates nor anything connected with the aggregates of oneself and others that is difficult to penetrate, before, in past existences, even in innumerable cycles of contraction and expansion; so too, afterwards, due to concentration's revolving in accordance with the knowledge of future events, there is nothing called the aggregates nor anything connected with the aggregates of oneself and others that is difficult to penetrate in future existences, even in innumerable cycles of contraction and expansion. This is the meaning.

Yathā pacchāti yathā samādhissa cetopariyañāṇānuparivattibhāvena anāgatesu sattasu divasesu parasattānaṃ cittaṃ duppaṭivijjhaṃ nāma natthi, tathā pure atītesu sattasu divasesu parasattānaṃ cittaṃ duppaṭivijjhaṃ nāma natthīti attho. Yathā divāti yathā divasabhāge sūriyālokena andhakārassa vidhamitattā cakkhumantānaṃ sattānaṃ āpāthagataṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ suviññeyyaṃ. Tathā rattinti tathā rattibhāge caturaṅgasamannāgatepi andhakāre vattamāne samādhissa dibbacakkhuñāṇānuparivattitāya duppaṭivijjhaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ natthi.

As to 'as afterwards': Just as, due to concentration's revolving in accordance with the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others, there is nothing called the mind of other beings in the future seven days that is difficult to penetrate, so too, there is nothing called the mind of other beings in the past seven days that is difficult to penetrate. This is the meaning. As to 'as by day': Just as in the daytime, due to darkness having been dispelled by sunlight, a visible form cognizable by the eye that has come into the range of beings with sight is easily cognized. So too, 'as by night': So too, in the nighttime, even when a darkness endowed with four factors is present, due to concentration's revolving in accordance with the divine eye knowledge, there is no visible-form-base that is difficult to penetrate.

Yathā rattiṃ tathā divāti yathā ca rattiyaṃ tathā divāpi atisukhumaṃ kenaci tirohitaṃ yañca atidūre, taṃ sabbarūpaṃ duppaṭivijjhaṃ nāma natthi. Yathā ca rūpāyatane vuttaṃ, tathā samādhissa dibbasotañāṇānuparivattitāya saddāyatane ca netabbaṃ. Tenevāha “iti vivaṭena cetasā”tiādi. Tattha apariyonaddhenāti abhiññāñāṇassa pāribandhakakilesehi anajjhotthaṭena, apariyonaddhattā eva sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ. Eteneva samādhissa iddhividhañāṇānuparivattitāpi vuttā evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pañcindriyānīti iddhipādasampayuttāni sekkhassa pañcindriyāni adhippetānīti āha [M 0.0073] “kusalānī”ti. Cittasahabhūnītiādi tesaṃ viññāṇanirodhena nirodhadassanatthaṃ āraddhaṃ. Tathā “nāmarūpañcā”tiādi. Tenetaṃ dasseti “na kevalaṃ pañcindriyāni eva, atha kho nāmarūpañca viññāṇahetukaṃ viññāṇassa nirodhā nirujjhatī”ti.

As to 'as by night, so by day': Just as by night, so too by day, whatever form is extremely subtle, or concealed by something, or at a great distance—all such form is not something difficult to penetrate. And as was said regarding the visible-form-base, so too it should be applied to the sound-base, due to concentration's revolving in accordance with the divine ear knowledge. For that very reason, he said, 'Thus with an uncovered mind,' etc. Therein, 'uncovered' means not being overwhelmed by the defilements that are obstacles to direct knowledge; precisely because of not being covered, the mind is luminous. It should be seen that by this very thing, the fact of concentration's revolving in accordance with the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power is also stated. By 'the five faculties,' the five faculties of a learner-on-the-path associated with the bases of power are intended; therefore, he said 'wholesome.' 'Arising together with consciousness,' etc., was begun in order to show their cessation with the cessation of consciousness. Likewise for 'and name-and-form,' etc. By that, this meaning is shown: 'Not only do the five faculties cease with the cessation of consciousness, but also name-and-form, which has consciousness as its cause, ceases with the cessation of consciousness.'

Tassāti viññāṇassa. Hetūti taṇhāavijjādiko. Anāhāranti padassa atthavivaraṇaṃ. Anabhinanditanti abhinandanabhūtāya taṇhāya pahīnattā eva apatthitaṃ. Tato eva appaṭisandhikaṃ viññāṇaṃ taṃ nirujjhati. Yathā ca viññāṇaṃ, evaṃ nāmarūpampi viññāṇasaṅkhātassa hetuno paccayassa ca abhāvā tappaccayānaṃ saṅkhārādīnaṃ abhāvā ahetu appaccayaṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva. Pucchāvissajjanavicayopi vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

“Of that” means of consciousness. “The cause” means craving, ignorance, and so forth. The word “without sustenance” is an explanation of the meaning of the term. “Not delighted in” means not longed for, precisely because of the abandonment of craving, which is the nature of delight. From that very reason, that consciousness, not causing rebirth-linking, ceases. Just as consciousness [ceases], so too name-and-form is without cause and without condition, due to the absence of the cause and condition called consciousness, and due to the absence of formations and so on which are the conditions for that consciousness. The rest is evident. The analysis of questions and answers should also be understood in accordance with the method already stated.

Evaṃ anusandhipucchampi dassetvā heṭṭhā sattādhiṭṭhānā dhammādhiṭṭhānā ca pucchā visuṃ visuṃ dassitāti idāni tā saha dassetuṃ “ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ padattho – saṅkhātadhammāti aniccādivasena parivīmaṃsitadhammā, arahataṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sekkhāti sīlādīni sikkhamānā avasesā ariyapuggalā. Puthūti bahū sattajanā. Tesaṃ me nipako iriyaṃ, puṭṭho pabrūhīti tesaṃ sekhāsekhānaṃ nipako paṇḍito tvaṃ bhagavā paṭipattiṃ puṭṭho me brūhīti. Sesaṃ pāḷivaseneva viññāyati.

Thus, having shown the question by way of connection, and because the questions based on beings and the questions based on phenomena were shown separately below, now, to show them together, the passage beginning with “ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse” is commenced. Herein, this is the meaning of the terms: “saṅkhātadhammā” means those who have investigated phenomena by way of impermanence, etc.—this is a designation for Arahants. “Sekkhā” refers to the remaining noble individuals who are training in virtue, etc. “Puthū” means many, that is, the seven persons. “Tesaṃ me nipako iriyaṃ, puṭṭho pabrūhi” means: “You, the Blessed One, who are skilled and wise, having been asked about the practice of those trainees and non-trainees, explain it to me.” The rest is to be understood from the Pāli text itself.

15. Kissāti [V 0.0203] kissa hetu, kena kāraṇenāti attho. Sekhāsekhavipassanā pubbaṅgamappahānayogenāti sekhe asekhe vipassanāpubbaṅgamappahāne ca pucchanayogena, pucchāvidhināti attho.

15. “Kissā” means “for what reason, by what cause”—this is the meaning. “Sekhāsekhavipassanāpubbaṅgamappahānayogena” means by the method of questioning concerning trainees and non-trainees, and concerning abandonments preceded by insight; that is, by the method of questioning.

Vissajjanagāthāyaṃ kāmesu nābhigijjheyyāti vatthukāmesu kilesakāmena na abhigijjheyya. Manasānāvilo siyāti byāpādavitakkādayo kāyaduccaritādayo ca manaso āvilabhāvakare dhamme pajahanto cittena anāvilo bhaveyya. Yasmā pana asekkho aniccatādivasena sabbadhammānaṃ paritulitattā kusalo sabbadhammesu kāyānupassanāsatiādīhi ca sato sabbakilesānaṃ bhinnattā uttamabhikkhubhāvaṃ patto ca hutvā sabbairiyāpathesu pavattati, tasmā “kusalo…pe… paribbaje”ti āhāti ayaṃ saṅkhepattho.

In the reply verse, “kāmesu nābhigijjheyya” means one should not be greedy for objects of sensual pleasure with the defilement of sensual craving. “Manasā’nāvilo siyā” means, while abandoning states that make the mind troubled—such as thoughts of ill will and bodily misconduct—one should become untroubled in mind. Because a non-trainee, being skilled in all phenomena due to having weighed all phenomena by way of impermanence, etc., and being mindful through mindfulness of the body, etc., and having attained the state of an excellent bhikkhu due to all defilements having been destroyed, conducts himself in all postures, therefore, He said, “kusalo… paribbaje”—this is the condensed meaning.

Tattha [M 0.0074] yaṃ pucchāgāthāyaṃ “nipako”ti padaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ bhagavantaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, bhagavato ca nepakkaṃ ukkaṃsapāramippattaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇadassanena dīpetabbanti anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ tāva kammadvārabhedehi vibhajitvā sekhāsekhapaṭipadaṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakamma”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tena sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇadassanena tathāgatassa sekhāsekhapaṭipattidesanākosallameva vibhāveti. Tattha ko cāti kva ca, kasmiṃ visayeti attho. Taṃ visayaṃ dasseti “yaṃ anicce dukkhe anattani cā”ti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ñāṇadassanaṃ nāma uppajjamānaṃ “sabbaṃ saṅkhataṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ sabbe dhammā anattā”ti uppajjati, tassa pana tasmiṃ visaye yena appavatti, so paṭighātoti, etena lakkhaṇattayappaṭivedhassa durabhisambhavataṃ anaññasādhāraṇatañca dasseti. Lakkhaṇattayavibhāvanena hi bhagavato catusaccappaṭivedhaṃ sammāsambodhiñca paṇḍitā paṭijānanti.

Therein, the word “nipako” spoken in the question verse was spoken in reference to the Blessed One. And because the Blessed One's discernment, which has reached the highest perfection, should be illuminated by means of the unobstructed knowledge and vision, therefore, in order to show the practice of the trainee and non-trainee by first analyzing the unobstructed knowledge according to the divisions of the doors of action, the passage beginning “bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ” was spoken. By that, it clearly shows only the Tathāgata's skill in teaching the practice of the trainee and non-trainee through his unobstructed knowledge and vision in all respects. Therein, “kva ca” means “where?” or “in what sphere?”. It shows that sphere with the words “that which is in the impermanent, suffering, and non-self.” This is what is said: knowledge and vision, when arising, arises with the thought, “All conditioned things are impermanent and suffering; all phenomena are non-self.” However, that by which its non-arising in that sphere occurs, that is obstruction. By this, it shows the difficulty of penetrating the three characteristics and their non-ordinary nature. For it is through the explanation of the three characteristics that the wise acknowledge the Blessed One’s penetration of the Four Truths and perfect full enlightenment.

Aññāṇaṃ adassananti taṃ paṭighātaṃ sarūpato dasseti. Chaḷārammaṇasabhāvappaṭicchādako hi sammoho ñāṇadassanassa paṭighātoti. Yasmiṃ visaye ñāṇadassanaṃ uppattirahaṃ, tattheva tassa paṭighātena bhavitabbanti āha – “yaṃ anicce dukkhe anattani cā”ti. Yathā idha purisotiādi upamādassanaṃ. Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – puriso viya sabbo loko, tārakarūpāni viya cha ārammaṇāni, tassa purisassa tārakarūpānaṃ dassanaṃ viya lokassa cakkhuviññāṇādīhi yathārahaṃ chaḷārammaṇajānanaṃ, tassa purisassa tārakarūpāni passantassāpi “ettakāni [V 0.0204] satāni, ettakāni sahassānī”tiādinā gaṇanasaṅketena ajānanaṃ viya lokassa rūpādiārammaṇaṃ kathañci jānantassāpi aniccādilakkhaṇattayānavabodhoti. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

“Ignorance and non-seeing”—by this text, it shows that obstruction by its intrinsic nature. For delusion, which conceals the inherent nature of the six sense objects, is the obstruction to knowledge and vision. In whatever sphere knowledge and vision is fit to arise, in that very sphere there must be an obstruction to it. Therefore, He said, “that which is in the impermanent, suffering, and non-self.” The passage beginning “Just as a man here...” is the showing of a simile. Herein, this is the application of the simile: the whole world should be seen as the man; the six sense objects should be seen as the starry forms; the world's knowing of the six sense objects appropriately by means of eye-consciousness and so on should be seen as that man's seeing of the starry forms; and the world's non-comprehension of the three characteristics of impermanence and so on, even while knowing the sense objects of form and so on in some way, should be seen as that man's not knowing by way of numerical designation—“so many hundreds, so many thousands”—even while seeing the starry forms. The rest is evident.

Idāni yehi padehi bhagavatā āyasmato ajitassa sekhāsekhapaṭipadā vuttā, tesaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ vibhajituṃ “tattha sekhenā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti nipātamattaṃ, tasmiṃ vā vissajjane. Sekhenāti sikkhā etassa sīlanti sekho, tena sekhena. Dvīsu dhammesūti duvidhesu dhammesūti adhippāyo. Pariyuṭṭhānīyesūti dosena pariyuṭṭhitena yattha parivattitabbaṃ, tesu āghātavatthūsūti attho. “Paṭighaṭṭhānīyesū”tipi pāṭho, soyevattho.

Now, in order to analyze the meaning of those words by which the practice of the trainee and non-trainee was spoken by the Blessed One to the Venerable Ajita, he said the passage beginning “tattha sekhena…”. Therein, “tattha” is merely a particle, or it means “in that explanation.” “By the trainee” (sekhena): he is a “trainee” (sekho) because his practice is training (sikkhā); thus, by that trainee. “In two phenomena” means “in two kinds of phenomena.” “In things liable to obsession” means in those grounds for resentment wherein one might be engaged through overwhelming hatred. There is also the reading “in things liable to resistance” (paṭighaṭṭhānīyesu); the meaning is the very same.

Ettha [M 0.0075] ca gedhapaṭisedhacodanāyaṃ gedhanimitto doso gedhe sati hotīti tatopi cittassa rakkhitabbatā niddhāretvā vuttā. Yasmā pana bhagavatā “kāmesu nābhigijjheyyā”ti (su. ni. 1045; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchā 64, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 8; netti. 15-17) vuttaṃ, tasmā “tattha yā icchā”tiādinā gedhavasena niddeso kato. Atha vā dosato cittassa rakkhitabbatā gāthāya dutiyapādena vuttāyevāti daṭṭhabbā. Dutiyapādena hi sesakilesavodānadhammā dassitā. Tathā hi uppannānuppannabhedato sammāvāyāmassa visayabhāvena sabbe saṃkilesavodānadhamme catudhā vibhajitvā sammappadhānamukhena sekhapaṭipadaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassetuṃ “sekho abhigijjhanto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha anāvilasaṅkappoti āvilānaṃ kāmasaṅkappādīnaṃ abhāvena anāvilasaṅkappo. Tato eva ca anabhigijjhanto vāyamati, vīriyaṃ pavatteti. Kathaṃ vāyamatīti āha – “so anuppannāna”ntiādi.

And here, in the exhortation to prohibit greed, it is determined and stated that the mind should be guarded even from that fault, since the fault that has greed as its cause arises when greed is present. But since the Blessed One has said, 'One should not be greedy for sensual pleasures,' therefore the exposition is made in terms of greed with the words 'therein, whatever desire...'. Alternatively, it should be seen that the guarding of the mind from aversion is indeed stated by the second line of the verse. For by the second line, the remaining defiling and cleansing qualities are shown. For thus, in order to show the trainee's path brought to its culmination by means of the right exertions—having divided all defiling and cleansing qualities into four as the domain of right effort by the distinction of arisen and unarisen—it is said, 'the trainee, not being greedy...' and so on. Therein, 'with unclouded thoughts' means one has unclouded thoughts due to the absence of clouded thoughts such as sensual thoughts. And precisely because of that, not being greedy, one strives, one arouses energy. As to how one strives, He said: 'He, for the unarisen...' and so on.

Tattha soti uttarivisesatthāya paṭipajjamāno sekkho. Anuppannānanti anibbattānaṃ. Pāpakānanti lāmakānaṃ. Akusalānaṃ dhammānanti akosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Anuppādāyāti na uppādanatthāya. Chandaṃ janetīti kattukamyatāsaṅkhātaṃ kusalacchandaṃ uppādeti. Vāyamatīti payogaparakkamaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ karoti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti teneva sahajātavīriyena cittaṃ ukkhipati. Padahatīti padhānavīriyaṃ karoti. Vāyamatītiādīni pana cattāri padāni āsevanābhāvanābahulīkammasātaccakiriyāhi yojetabbāni. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānanti anuppannāti avattabbataṃ āpannānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ. Pahānāyāti pajahanatthāya. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānanti anibbattānaṃ kosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Uppādāyāti uppādanatthāya. Uppannānanti nibbattānaṃ. Ṭhitiyāti ṭhitatthaṃ. Asammosāyāti anassanatthaṃ[V 0.0205]. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti punappunaṃ bhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Bhāvanāyāti vaḍḍhiyā. Pāripūriyāti paripūraṇatthāyāti ayaṃ tāva padattho.

Therein, 'he' is the trainee who is practicing for the sake of attaining a higher distinction. 'Of the unarisen' means of those not yet come into being. 'Of the evil' means of the base. 'Of unwholesome states' means of states not born of skill. 'For non-arising' means for the purpose of not causing to arise. 'He generates desire' means he produces the wholesome desire termed the wish to do. 'He strives' means he makes a powerful effort. 'He arouses energy' means he makes bodily and mental energy. 'He exerts the mind' means he uplifts the mind by that very co-nascent energy. 'He makes an effort' means he makes the chief energy. But the four terms beginning with 'He strives' should be connected with cultivating, developing, making much of, and continuous action. 'Of arisen evil states' means of evil states that have reached a state where they cannot be called 'unarisen'. 'For abandoning' means for the purpose of abandoning. 'Of unarisen wholesome states' means of states born of skill that have not yet come into being. 'For arising' means for the purpose of causing to arise. 'Of the arisen' means of those that have come into being. 'For stability' means for the purpose of establishing. 'For non-confusion' means for the purpose of not losing. 'For increase' means for repeated becoming. 'For expansion' means for becoming extensive. 'For development' means for growth. 'For fulfillment' means for the purpose of completion. This, for now, is the meaning of the terms.

16. “Katame anuppannā”tiādi akusaladhammā kusaladhammā ca yādisā anuppannā yādisā ca uppannā, te dassetuṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha ime anuppannāti ime kāmavitakkādayo asamudācāravasena vā ananubhūtārammaṇavasena [M 0.0076] vā anuppannā nāma. Aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā nāma akusalā dhammā natthi. Vitakkattayaggahaṇañcettha nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Akusalamūlānīti anusayā eva sabbesaṃ akusalānaṃ mūlabhāvato evaṃ vuttā, na lobhādayo eva. Ime uppannā anusayā bhūmiladdhuppannā asamugghāṭituppannātiādiuppannapariyāyasabbhāvato nāmavasena uppannā nāma, na vattamānabhāvenāti attho. Ime anuppannā kusalā dhammāti ime sotāpannassa saddhādayo sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannassa anuppannā kusalā dhammā nāma, ko pana vādo puthujjanānanti dasseti. Kusalasaddo cettha bāhitikasutte (ma. ni. 2.358 ādayo) viya anavajjapariyāyo daṭṭhabbo. Ime uppannā kusalā dhammāti ime paṭhamamagge saddhādayo sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannassa uppannā kusalā dhammā nāma.

16. ‘Which are the unarisen?’ and so on, is begun in order to show what kind of unwholesome and wholesome states are unarisen, and what kind are arisen. Therein, 'these are unarisen' means these, such as sensual thoughts, are called unarisen either by way of not having occurred or by way of having an unexperienced object. For otherwise, in this beginningless saṃsāra, there are truly no unwholesome states that have not arisen before. And the inclusion of the three kinds of thoughts here should be seen as merely an illustration. 'Roots of the unwholesome'—the underlying tendencies alone are so called because they are the root of all unwholesome states, not greed and so on alone. The underlying tendencies are called 'arisen' by way of designation, due to the existence of descriptive terms for 'arisen' such as 'arisen by having obtained a plane' and 'arisen by not having been eradicated'; the meaning is that they are not 'arisen' in the sense of being in the present moment. By the phrase 'These are unarisen wholesome states,' he shows this meaning: for one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, these states such as faith of a stream-enterer are called 'unarisen wholesome states'—what then to say of worldlings? And here the word 'wholesome' should be seen as a synonym for 'blameless', as in the Bāhitika Sutta. 'These are arisen wholesome states' means these states such as faith, in the first path for one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, are called 'arisen wholesome states'.

Satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya suniggahito kāmavitakkoti āha – “yena kāmavitakkaṃ vāreti, idaṃ satindriya”nti. Anavajjasukhapadaṭṭhānena avikkhepena cetodukkhasannissayo vikkhepapaccayo byāpādavitakko suniggahitoti vuttaṃ – “yena byāpādavitakkaṃ vāreti, idaṃ samādhindriya”nti. Kusalesu dhammesu āraddhavīriyo parāparādhaṃ sukhena sahatīti vīriyena vihiṃsāvitakko suniggahitoti āha – “yena vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vāreti, idaṃ vīriyindriya”nti. Samādhiādīnampi yathāsakaṃpaṭipakkhappahānaṃ paññavantasseva ijjhatīti imamatthaṃ dassento āha – “yena uppannuppanne”tiādi.

Because sensual thought is well-restrained by the development of the establishments of mindfulness, he said: 'By which one restrains sensual thought, this is the faculty of mindfulness.' Because the thought of ill will—which is dependent on mental suffering and is a condition for distraction—is well-restrained by non-distraction, which has blameless happiness as its proximate cause, it is said: 'By which one restrains the thought of ill will, this is the faculty of concentration.' Because a person who has aroused energy in wholesome states easily endures the faults of others, the thought of cruelty is well-restrained by energy; therefore, he said: 'By which one restrains the thought of cruelty, this is the faculty of energy.' Showing this meaning, that the abandoning of their respective opposing states, even of concentration and so on, succeeds only for one with wisdom, he said: 'by which the arisen and unarisen...' and so on.

Etesaṃ yathāniddhāritānaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ savisaye jeṭṭhakabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “saddhindriyaṃ kattha daṭṭhabba”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva. Imesañca saddhādīnaṃ sekhānaṃ indriyānaṃ nibbattiyā sabbepi sekhā dhammā matthakappattā hontīti dassento “evaṃ sekho”tiādinā sekhapaṭipadaṃ nigameti.

In order to show the state of being chief in their own domain for these five faculties, which were determined in such a way, it was said: 'Where should the faculty of faith be seen?' and so on. That is indeed very easy to understand. And showing that with the accomplishment of these faculties of faith and so on, which belong to the trainees, all the qualities of the trainees reach culmination, he concludes the trainee's path with the words 'Thus the trainee...' and so on.

17. Evaṃ sekhapaṭipadaṃ vibhajitvā idāni asekhapaṭipadaṃ vibhajituṃ “kusalo sabbadhammāna”ntiādimāha[V 0.0206]. Tattha sabbadhammānanti iminā padena vuttadhamme tāva vibhajitvā tattha asekkhassa kosallaṃ dassetuṃ “loko nāmā”tiādi [M 0.0077] vuttaṃ. Taṃ vuttatthameva. Kilesalokena bhavaloko samudāgacchatīti kāmāvacaradhammaṃ nissāya rūpārūpāvacaradhamme samudāgametīti attho. Soti so mahaggatadhammesu, parittamahaggatadhammesu vā ṭhito. Indriyāni nibbattetīti sīlasamādhayo nibbedhabhāgiye katvā vimuttiparipācanīyāni saddhādīni indriyāni uppādeti. Indriyesu bhāviyamānesūti yathāvuttaindriyesu vaḍḍhiyamānesu rūpārūpapariggahādivasena neyyassa pariññā bhavati.

17. Having thus analyzed the path of the trainee, now, in order to analyze the path of the adept, He spoke the words beginning with, “skilled in all phenomena.” Therein, by this phrase “of all phenomena,” having first analyzed the phenomena that have been mentioned, in order to show the adept’s skill therein, the words beginning with, “the world is called…” were spoken. That has a meaning that has already been stated. “The world of existence arises through the world of defilements” means: depending on sense-sphere phenomena, one brings about form-realm and formless-realm phenomena. This is the meaning. “He” means: that person is established in exalted phenomena, or in limited and exalted phenomena. “He brings forth the faculties” means: having made virtue and concentration conducive to penetration, he produces the faculties beginning with faith, which are conducive to the ripening of liberation. “When the faculties are being developed” means: when the aforementioned faculties are being augmented, comprehension of what is to be known occurs by way of grasping material and immaterial phenomena, and so forth.

Dassanapariññāti ñātapariññā. Bhāvanāpariññāti tīraṇapariññā pahānapariññā ca. “Sā duvidhenā”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ “yadā hi sekho”tiādinā vivarati. Tattha “nibbidāsahagatehi saññāmanasikārehī”ti iminā balavavipassanaṃ dasseti. Yadā hi sekhoti cettha sikkhanasīlatāya kalyāṇaputhujjanopi sekhapadena saṅgahitoti katvā “dve dhammā kosallaṃ gacchanti dassanakosallañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ayamettha adhippāyo – yadā kalyāṇaputhujjano pubbabhāgasikkhaṃ sikkhanto nibbidāsahagatehi saññāmanasikārehi ñeyyaṃ parijānāti, tadā tassa te vipassanādhammā dassanakosallaṃ paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ gacchanti sampāpuṇanti tena saddhiṃ ghaṭenti. Yadā pana sotāpannādisekho vuttanayena neyyaṃ parijānāti, tadā tassa te vipassanādhammā bhāvanākosallaṃ gacchantīti.

Comprehension by seeing is comprehension by knowing. Comprehension by development is comprehension by thorough investigation and comprehension by abandonment. He explains the meaning stated concisely by the words beginning with, “It is twofold,” with the words beginning with, “When indeed a trainee.” Therein, by these words, “with perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by revulsion,” He shows powerful insight. And here in the phrase, “When indeed a trainee,” because of the nature of training, even a virtuous ordinary person is included by the term “trainee.” Holding this, the words beginning with, “two phenomena… go to skill, and skill in seeing…” were spoken. This is the intention here: when a virtuous ordinary person, while practicing the preliminary training, fully understands what is to be known through perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by revulsion, then for him, those insight-phenomena go to and arrive at the knowledge of the first path, which is skill in seeing; they connect with it. But when a trainee, such as a stream-enterer, fully understands what is to be known in the manner stated, then for him, those insight-phenomena go to skill in development.

Taṃ ñāṇanti yā pubbe neyyassa pariññā vuttā, taṃ neyyaparijānanañāṇaṃ. Pañcavidhena veditabbanti visayabhedena tassa bhedaṃ dasseti. Dhammānaṃ salakkhaṇe ñāṇanti rūpārūpadhammānaṃ kakkhaḷaphusanādisalakkhaṇe ñāṇaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā sabbaṃ neyyaṃ hetuhetuphalabhedato duvidhameva hoti, tasmā “dhammapaṭisambhidā ca atthapaṭisambhidā cā”ti niddiṭṭhaṃ.

“That knowledge” means: that which was previously stated as the comprehension of what is to be known, that is the knowledge that fully understands what is to be known. By the phrase, “it should be known in five ways,” He shows the division of that knowledge according to the distinction of its object. “Knowledge in the individual characteristics of phenomena” means: knowledge in the individual characteristics of material and immaterial phenomena, such as hardness, contact, and so forth. However, because all that is to be known is invariably twofold according to the distinction of cause and effect, therefore it is designated as, “the analytical knowledge of phenomena and the analytical knowledge of meaning.”

Pariññāti tīraṇapariññā adhippetā. Yasmā panassa rūpārūpadhamme salakkhaṇato paccayato ca abhijānitvā kusalādivibhāgehi te pariggahetvā aniccādivasena jānanā hoti, tasmā “evaṃ abhijānitvā yā parijānanā, idaṃ kusala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha evaṃgahitāti evaṃ aniccādito kalāpasammasanādivasena gahitā sammasitā. Idaṃ phalaṃ nibbattentīti idaṃ udayabbayañāṇādikaṃ phalaṃ paṭipāṭiyā uppādenti[M 0.0078], nimittassa kattubhāvena upacaraṇato yathā ariyabhāvakarāni saccāni ariyasaccānīti. Tesanti udayabbayañāṇādīnaṃ[V 0.0207]. Evaṃgahitānanti evaṃpavattitānaṃ. Ayaṃ atthoti ayaṃ saccānaṃ anubodhapaṭivedho attho. Yathā hi pariññāpaññā sammasitabbadhamme sammasanadhamme tattha sammasanākāraṃ parijānāti, evaṃ sammasanaphalampi parijānātīti katvā ayaṃ nayo dassito.

In this phrase “comprehension,” comprehension by thorough investigation is intended. Because for him, having directly known the material and immaterial phenomena by their individual characteristics and by their conditions, and having grasped them through classifications such as wholesome, there is the knowing of them by way of impermanence, and so forth, therefore the words beginning with, “Thus having directly known, the full understanding, this is wholesome,” were spoken. Therein, “thus grasped” means: grasped and contemplated in this way, by way of impermanence, etc., and by way of contemplation of groups, etc. “They bring forth this fruit” means: they sequentially produce this fruit, namely, the knowledge of arising and passing away, and so forth. This is because of the metaphorical usage of the object of contemplation as the agent, just as the truths that make one a noble one are called “Noble Truths.” “Of them” means: of the knowledge of arising and passing away, and so forth. “Thus grasped” means: of those that have thus occurred. “This is the meaning” means: this awakening and penetration of the truths is the result. For just as the wisdom of comprehension fully understands the phenomena to be contemplated, the contemplating phenomena, and the mode of contemplation therein, so too does it fully understand the fruit of contemplation. For this reason, this method was shown.

Ye akusalāti samudayasaccamāha. Sabbe hi akusalā samudayapakkhiyāti. Ye kusalāti maggadhammā sammādiṭṭhiādayo. Yadipi phaladhammāpi sacchikātabbā, catusaccappaṭivedhassa pana adhippetattā “katame dhammā sacchikātabbā, yaṃ asaṅkhata”nti vuttaṃ. Atthakusaloti paccayuppannesu atthesu kusalo. Dhammakusaloti paccayadhammesu kusalo. Pāḷiatthapāḷidhammā vā atthadhammā. Kalyāṇatākusaloti yuttatākusalo, catunayakovidoti attho, desanāyuttikusalo vā. Phalatākusaloti khīṇāsavaphalakusalo. “Āyakusalo”tiādīsu āyoti vaḍḍhi. Sā anatthahānito aṭṭhuppattito ca duvidhā. Apāyāti avaḍḍhi. Sāpi atthahānito anaṭṭhuppattito ca duvidhā. Upāyoti sattānaṃ accāyike kicce vā bhaye vā uppanne tassa tikicchanasamatthaṃ ṭhānuppattikāraṇaṃ, tattha kusaloti attho. Khīṇāsavo hi sabbaso avijjāya pahīnattā paññāvepullappatto etesu āyādīsu kusaloti. Evaṃ asekhassa kosallaṃ ekadesena vibhāvetvā puna anavasesato dassento “mahatā kosallena samannāgato”ti āha.

By the phrase, “Whatever unwholesome states,” He spoke of the truth of origination. For all unwholesome states belong to the side of origination. “Whatever wholesome states” means: the path-phenomena beginning with right view. Although fruition-phenomena are also to be realized, nevertheless, because the penetration of the Four Truths is intended, it was said, “Which phenomena are to be realized? That which is unconditioned.” “Skilled in meaning” means: skilled in the effects that have arisen from a condition. “Skilled in phenomena” means: skilled in the phenomena that are conditions. Alternatively, the meaning of the Pāḷi and the phenomena of the Pāḷi are called “meaning” and “phenomena.” “Skilled in the state of the good” means: skilled in suitability; the meaning is: expert in the four methods. Or, skilled in the suitability of teaching. “Skilled in the state of fruition” means: skilled in the fruition of one whose taints are destroyed. In the words beginning with, “skilled in income,” “income” means growth. It is twofold: from the non-diminution of what is not beneficial and from the arising of what is beneficial. “Expense” means non-growth. It too is twofold: from the diminution of what is beneficial and from the arising of what is not beneficial. “Means” means: when an urgent task or a danger has arisen for beings, it is the cause for an immediate response that is able to remedy it; skilled therein is the meaning. For one whose taints are destroyed, having attained the fullness of wisdom because of the complete abandonment of ignorance, is said to be skilled in these things beginning with income. Having thus clarified the adept’s skill in part, then, showing it without remainder, He said, “endowed with great skill.”

Pariniṭṭhitasikkhassa asekhassa satokāritāya aññaṃ payojanaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ “diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārattha”nti. Idāni yathāniddiṭṭhaṃ sekhāsekhapaṭipadaṃ nigamento “imā dve cariyā”tiādimāha. Tattha bojjhanti bujjhitabbaṃ. Taṃ catubbidhanti taṃ bojjhaṃ catubbidhaṃ, catusaccabhāvato. Evaṃ jānātīti evaṃ pariññābhisamayādivasena yo jānāti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ asekho sativepullappatto nippariyāyena “sato abhikkamatī”tiādinā vuccatīti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Idhāpi pucchāvissajjanavicayā pubbe vuttanayānusārena veditabbā.

For the adept whose training is completed, there is no other purpose for acting with mindfulness; therefore, it was said, “for the sake of dwelling happily in the present life.” Now, concluding the path of the trainee and the adept as it has been explained, He spoke the words beginning with, “these two conducts.” Therein, “that which is to be awakened to” means what is to be understood. That which is to be awakened to is fourfold because of being the Four Truths. “He knows thus” means: a person who knows in this way, by means of full understanding, penetration, and so forth. “This one is called” means: this adept, having attained the fullness of mindfulness, is called definitively by the words beginning with, “mindful, he goes forward.” Thus it should be understood. The rest has a plain meaning. Here too, the investigations of the questions and answers should be known in accordance with the method previously stated.

Ettāvatā [M 0.0079] ca mahāthero vicayahāraṃ vibhajanto ajitasuttavasena (su. ni. 103 ādayo; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchā 57 ādayo, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 1 ādayo) pucchāvicayaṃ vissajjanavicayañca dassetvā idāni suttantaresupi pucchāvissajjanavicayānaṃ nayaṃ dassento “evaṃ pucchitabbaṃ, evaṃ vissajjitabba”nti āha. Tattha evanti iminā nayena. Pucchitabbanti pucchā kātabbā, ācikkhitabbā vā, vivecetabbāti attho. Evaṃ vissajjitanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Suttassa cātiādi anugītivicayanidassanaṃ. Anugīti atthato [V 0.0208] ca byañjanato ca samānetabbāti suttantaradesanāsaṅkhātā anugīti atthato byañjanato ca saṃvaṇṇiyamānena suttena samānā sadisī kātabbā, tasmiṃ vā sutte sammā ānetabbā. Atthāpagatanti atthato apetaṃ, asambandhatthaṃ vā dasadāḷimādivacanaṃ viya. Tenevāha “samphappalāpaṃ bhavatī”ti. Etena atthassa samānetabbatāya kāraṇamāha. Dunnikkhittassāti asammāvuttassa. Dunnayoti dukkhena netabbo, netuṃ vā asakkuṇeyyo. Byañjanupetanti sabhāvaniruttisamupetaṃ.

With this much discourse, the Great Elder, while analyzing the section on investigation, demonstrated the investigation of questions and the investigation of answers by means of the Ajita Sutta. Now, to show the method for the investigation of questions and answers in other suttas as well, he said, 'It should be questioned thus; it should be answered thus.' Therein, 'thus' means by this method. 'It should be questioned' means a question should be made, or it should be stated, or it should be analyzed; this is the meaning. In 'it should be answered thus' as well, this is the very same method. The words beginning with 'And of the sutta' are an illustration of the investigation of the subsequent recitation. 'The subsequent recitation should be made similar in meaning and in phrasing' means: the subsequent recitation, which is known as a teaching of another sutta, should be made similar and identical in meaning and in phrasing with the sutta that is being expounded; or, it should be properly brought into that sutta. 'Departed from meaning' means devoid of meaning, or having an unconnected meaning, like the words 'ten pomegranates,' etc. For that very reason, he said, 'It becomes frivolous talk.' With this, he states the reason why the meaning must be made similar. 'Of the poorly placed' means of the incorrectly spoken. 'Of difficult inference' means to be understood with difficulty, or impossible to understand. 'Endowed with phrasing' means endowed with natural expression.

Evaṃ anugītivicayaṃ dassetvā niddesavāre “suttassa yo pavicayo”ti saṃkhittena vuttamatthaṃ vibhajituṃ “suttañca pavicinitabba”nti vatvā tassa vicinanākāraṃ dassento “kiṃ idaṃ suttaṃ āhaccavacana”ntiādimāha. Tattha āhaccavacananti bhagavato ṭhānakaraṇāni āhacca abhihantvā pavattavacanaṃ, sammāsambuddhena sāmaṃ desitasuttanti attho. Anusandhivacananti sāvakabhāsitaṃ. Tañhi bhagavato vacanaṃ anusandhetvā pavattanato “anusandhivacana”nti vuttanti. Nītatthanti yathārutavasena ñātabbatthaṃ. Neyyatthanti niddhāretvā gahetabbatthaṃ. Saṃkilesabhāgiyantiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho paṭṭhānavāravaṇṇanāyaṃ āvi bhavissati. Yasmā pana bhagavato desanā soḷasavidhe sāsanapaṭṭhāne ekaṃ bhāgaṃ abhajantī nāma natthi, tasmā sopi nayo vicetabbabhāvena idha nikkhitto.

Having thus shown the investigation of the subsequent recitation, in order to analyze the meaning stated concisely in the Niddesa section as 'whatever is the investigation of the sutta,' he said, 'and the sutta should be investigated.' Then, showing the manner of its investigation, he stated the words beginning with, 'Is this sutta an authoritative statement?' Therein, 'authoritative statement' (āhaccavacana) means a statement spoken by striking upon the grounds and reasons of the Blessed One; the meaning is: a sutta taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself. 'Connected statement' (anusandhivacana) means spoken by a disciple. Indeed, because it proceeds by connecting with the word of the Blessed One, it is called a 'connected statement.' 'Of definitive meaning' (nītattha) means having a meaning to be known by way of what is directly heard. 'Of interpretable meaning' (neyyattha) means having a meaning to be grasped by drawing it out. The meaning of the terms beginning with 'conducive to defilements' will become clear in the commentary on the Paṭṭhānavāra. And since there is no teaching of the Blessed One that does not partake of one portion in the sixteenfold foundations of the Dispensation, therefore, that method, too, is included here as something to be investigated.

Kuhiṃ imassa suttassāti imassa suttassa kasmiṃ padese ādimajjhapariyosānesu. Sabbāni saccāni passitabbānīti dukkhasaccaṃ suttassa “kuhiṃ kasmiṃ padese kasmiṃ vā pade passitabbaṃ niddhāretvā vicetuṃ, samudayasaccaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ maggasaccaṃ kuhiṃ passitabbaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ niddhāretvā vicetu”nti evaṃ sabbāni saccāni uddharitvā vicetabbānīti adhippāyo. Ādimajjhapariyosāneti evaṃ suttaṃ pavicetabbanti ādito majjhato pariyosānato [M 0.0080] ca evaṃ iminā pucchāvicayādinayena suttaṃ pavicitabbanti attho. Ettha ca pucchāvissajjanapubbāparānugītivicayā pāḷiyaṃ sarūpeneva dassitā. Assādādivicayo pana saccaniddhāraṇamukhena nayato dassito, so niddesavāre vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tabbicayeneva ca padavicayo siddhoti.

'Where of this sutta?' means: in what part of this sutta, among the beginning, middle, and end. 'All truths should be seen' means: 'Where, in what part or in what verse of the sutta, is the truth of suffering to be seen, so as to determine and investigate it? Where are the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path to be seen and noted, so as to determine and investigate them?' The intention is that in this way, all the truths should be extracted and investigated. 'At the beginning, middle, and end, the sutta should be thus investigated'—the meaning is: the sutta should be investigated at the beginning, at the middle, and at the end, thus, by this method beginning with the investigation of questions. And here, the investigations of question, answer, sequence, and subsequent recitation are shown in the Pāḷi in their own form. The investigation of gratification and so forth, however, is shown by way of method through the means of determining the truths; that should be understood by the very method stated in the Niddesa section. And by that very investigation, the investigation of terms is accomplished.

Vicayahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Analysis of the Section on Investigation is concluded.

3. Yuttihāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Analysis of the Application of Reasoning

18. Tattha [V 0.0209] katamo yuttihārotiādi yuttihāravibhaṅgo. Tattha kiṃ yojayatīti yuttihārassa visayaṃ pucchati. Ko panetassa visayo? Atathākārena gayhamānā suttatthā visayo, te hi tena sātisayaṃ yāthāvato yuttiniddhāraṇena yojetabbā. Itaresupi ayaṃ hāro icchito eva. Taṃ pana bhūtakathanamattaṃ hoti. Yasmā panāyaṃ yuttigavesanā nāma na mahāpadesena vinā, tasmā yuttihāraṃ vibhajanto tassa lakkhaṇaṃ tāva upadisituṃ “cattāro mahāpadesā”tiādimāha.

18. Herein, 'What is the application of reasoning?' and so forth is the Analysis of the Application of Reasoning. Therein, 'What does it connect?' asks about the scope of the application of reasoning. And what is its scope? The scope is the meanings of the suttas that are grasped in an incorrect manner, for they must be connected by it exceedingly, in a truthful manner, through the ascertainment of reasoning. This application is desired in the other applications as well. However, that is merely a statement of fact. Since this so-called investigation of reasoning does not occur without the great references, therefore, while analyzing the application of reasoning, in order to first point out its characteristic, he said, 'the four great references,' and so forth.

Tattha mahāpadesāti mahāapadesā, buddhādayo mahante apadisitvā vuttāni mahākāraṇānīti attho. Atha vā mahāpadesāti mahāokāsā, mahantāni dhammassa patiṭṭhānānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – apadissatīti apadeso, buddho apadeso etassāti buddhāpadeso. Esa nayo sesesupi. “Sammukhā metaṃ bhagavato suta”ntiādinā kenaci ābhatassa ganthassa dhammoti vā adhammoti vā vinicchayane kāraṇaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Tassa tathā ābhatassa suttotaraṇādi eva. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ cattāroti? Apadisitappabhedato. Dhammassa hi dve sampadāyo bhagavā sāvakā ca. Tesu sāvakā saṅghagaṇapuggalavasena tividhā. “Evamamumhā mayāyaṃ dhammo paṭiggahito”ti apadisitabbānaṃ bhedena cattāro. Tenāha – “buddhāpadeso…pe… ekattherāpadeso”ti. Tāni padabyañjanānīti kenaci ābhatasuttassa padāni byañjanāni ca, atthapadāni ceva byañjanapadāni cāti attho. Saṃvaṇṇakena vā saṃvaṇṇanāvasena āhariyamānāni [M 0.0081] padabyañjanāni. Sutte otārayitabbānīti sutte anuppavesitabbāni. Sandassayitabbānīti saṃsandetabbāni. Upanikkhipitabbānīti pakkhipitabbāni.

Therein, 'mahāpadesā' means great references (mahā-apadesā); the meaning is great reasons (mahā-kāraṇāni) spoken by referring to great ones such as the Buddha. Alternatively, 'mahāpadesā' means great opportunities (mahā-okāsā); it is said to mean great foundations (patiṭṭhānāni) of the Dhamma. Therein, this is the word-meaning: it is referred to (apadissati), therefore it is a reference (apadeso); the Buddha is the reference for this, hence 'Buddhāpadeso.' This is the method in the remaining cases as well. For a text brought by someone—beginning with 'This was heard by me in the presence of the Blessed One'—it is the reason for deciding whether it is Dhamma or not-Dhamma. But what is that reason? It is precisely the descending into the Sutta, etc., of that text thus brought. If so, how are there four? Due to the distinction of what is referred to. Indeed, there are two sources of the Dhamma: the Blessed One and the disciples. Among them, the disciples are of three kinds: by way of the Saṅgha, a group, and an individual. By the distinction of those who are to be referred to—as in 'Thus was this Dhamma received by me from so-and-so'—there are four. Therefore, he said: 'Reference to the Buddha... up to... reference to a single elder.' Regarding 'those words and phrases,' the meaning is: the words and phrases of a sutta brought by someone, that is, both the words of meaning and the words of phrasing. Or, the words and phrases being brought forward by a commentator by way of explanation. 'Should be made to descend into the Sutta' means they should be entered into the Sutta. 'Should be shown together' means they should be compared. 'Should be placed down beside' means they should be placed.

Suttādīni dassetuṃ “katamasmi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmā bhagavato vacanaṃ ekagāthāmattampi saccavinimuttaṃ natthi, tasmā sutteti padassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “catūsu ariyasaccesū”ti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tīṇi piṭakāni suttanti vuttaṃ, taṃ iminā nettivacanena aññadatthu saṃsandati ceva sameti cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yāvadeva anupādāparinibbānatthā bhagavato [V 0.0210] desanā, sā ekantena rāgādikilesavūpasamaṃ vadatīti vinayetipadassa atthaṃ dassento “rāgavinaye”tiādimāha. Vinayoti hi kāraṇaṃ rāgādivūpasamanimittaṃ idhādhippetaṃ. Yathāha –

To show the Sutta and so forth, the passage beginning 'In what?' was spoken. Therein, because not even a single verse of the Blessed One's word is devoid of the truths, therefore, to show the meaning of the word 'in the Sutta,' it was said, 'in the Four Noble Truths.' In the commentary, however, it is said that the three Piṭakas are the Sutta; it should be understood that this statement indeed compares with and agrees with this statement of the Netti. The Blessed One's teaching is for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging, and that teaching exclusively speaks of the stilling of defilements such as lust; thus, showing the meaning of the word 'in the Vinaya,' he said the passage beginning 'in the removal of lust.' For 'Vinaya' is here intended as the cause which is the reason for the stilling of defilements such as lust. As it is said:

“Ye kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi, ime dhammā sarāgāya saṃvattanti no virāgāya, saññogāya saṃvattanti no visaññogāya, ācayāya saṃvattanti no apacayāya, mahicchatāya saṃvattanti no appicchatāya, asantuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti no santuṭṭhiyā, saṅgaṇikāya saṃvattanti no pavivekāya, kosajjāya saṃvattanti no vīriyārambhāya, dubbharatāya saṃvattanti no subharatāya, ekaṃsena gotami dhāreyyāsi ‘neso dhammo, neso vinayo, netaṃ satthusāsana’nti.
