Ye ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi ime dhammā virāgāya saṃvattanti no sarāgāya, visaññogāya saṃvattanti no saññogāya, apacayāya saṃvattanti no ācayāya, appicchatāya saṃvattanti no mahicchatāya, santuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti no asantuṭṭhiyā pavivekāya saṃvattanti no saṅgaṇikāya, vīriyārambhāya saṃvattanti no kosajjāya, subharatāya saṃvattanti no dubbharatāya, ekaṃsena gotami dhāreyyāsi ‘eso dhammo, eso vinayo, etaṃ satthusāsana’”nti (cūḷava. 406).

“Gotamī, of whatever teachings you might know, ‘These teachings lead to passion, not to dispassion; they lead to bondage, not to detachment; they lead to accumulation, not to dispersal; they lead to great desire, not to little desire; they lead to discontent, not to contentment; they lead to association, not to seclusion; they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy; they lead to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support’—you should hold it for certain, Gotamī, that ‘This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction.’ And of whatever teachings you might know, ‘These teachings lead to dispassion, not to passion; they lead to detachment, not to bondage; they lead to dispersal, not to accumulation; they lead to little desire, not to great desire; they lead to contentment, not to discontent; they lead to seclusion, not to association; they lead to the arousal of energy, not to laziness; they lead to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support’—you should hold it for certain, Gotamī, that ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.’”

Dhammatāyantipadassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭiccasamuppāde”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭiccasamuppādo hi ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatāti (a. ni. 3.137) vutto. “Dhammatāyaṃ [M 0.0082] upanikkhipitabbānī”ti idaṃ pāḷiyaṃ natthi, atthadassanavasena pana idha vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca pavattiṃ nivattiṃ tadupāyañca bādhakādibhāve niyataṃ paridīpento sutte otarati nāma. Ekantena rāgādikilesavinayaṃ vadanto vinaye sandissati nāma. Tathā sassataṃ ucchedañca vajjetvā ekattanayādiparidīpanena sabhāvadhammānaṃ paccayapaccayuppannabhāvaṃ vibhāvento dhammataṃ na vilometi nāma.

To show the meaning of the word 'in the natural law,' it was said, 'in dependent origination.' For dependent origination is said to be 'that element is fixed, a stability of phenomena, a regularity of phenomena.' The statement 'should be placed in the natural law' is not in the Pāḷi, but it should be understood that it is said here by way of showing the meaning. And here, when one clearly illuminates occurrence, cessation, and the means to them, which are fixed in their state of being afflicting, etc., it is called 'descending into the Sutta.' When one speaks exclusively of the removal of defilements such as lust, it is called 'being comparable to the Vinaya.' Likewise, having avoided eternalism and annihilationism, by making clear the state of being condition and conditioned of natural phenomena through the demonstration of the method of unity, etc., one is said to 'not violate the natural law.'

Evaṃvidho ca kāmāsavādikaṃ āsavaṃ na uppādetīti imamatthaṃ dassento “yadi catūsu ariyasaccesū”tiādimāha. Nanu ca anulomato paṭiccasamuppādo pavatti, paṭilomato nivattīti so cattāri ariyasaccāni anupaviṭṭho kasmā idha visuṃ gahitoti? Saccametaṃ. Idha pana visuṃ gahaṇaṃ dhammānaṃ paccayāyattavuttidassanena aniccapaccayalakkhaṇaṃ asamatthapaccayalakkhaṇaṃ nirīhapaccayalakkhaṇañca vibhāvetvā tesaṃ udayavantatā tato eva vayavantatā tadubhayena [V 0.0211] aniccatā udayabbayapaṭipīḷanena dukkhatā anattatāti tilakkhaṇasamāyogaparidīpanī sabbadiṭṭhigatakumatividdhaṃsanī anaññasādhāraṇā sāsanasampatti pakāsitā hotīti dassanatthaṃ.

And showing this meaning—that such a thing does not cause the taints beginning with the taint of sensual desire to arise—he said the passage beginning with, “If in the Four Noble Truths…” Is it not so that dependent origination in forward order is occurrence, and in reverse order is cessation? Therefore, since it has already been included in the Four Noble Truths, why is it taken up separately here? This is true. However, the taking of it up separately here is for the purpose of showing this: by demonstrating that the occurrence of phenomena is dependent on conditions, and having made clear the characteristic of conditions as impermanent, the characteristic of conditions as incapable, and the characteristic of conditions as being without effort, their state of having an arising aspect is made clear. And precisely from that, their state of having a passing away aspect is made clear. By means of both of these, impermanence is made clear. By the oppression of arising and passing away, suffering and not-self are made clear. Thus, the accomplishment of the Teaching—which explains the conjunction with the three characteristics, which destroys all wrong views and perverse theories, and which is not shared with others—is made manifest.

Ettha ca suttaṃ suttānulomaṃ ācariyavādo attanomatīti idaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ – tattha suttaṃ nāma tisso saṅgītiyo āruḷhāni tīṇi piṭakāni. Suttānulomaṃ nāma mahāpadesā, yaṃ “anulomakappiya”nti vuccati. Ācariyavādo nāma aṭṭhakathā. Attanomati nāma nayaggāhena anubuddhiyā attano paṭibhānaṃ. Tattha suttaṃ appaṭibāhiyaṃ, taṃ paṭibāhantena satthāva paṭibāhito hoti. Anulomakappiyaṃ pana suttena samentameva gahetabbaṃ, na itaraṃ. Ācariyavādopi suttena samento eva gahetabbo, na itaro. Tathā attanomati, sā pana sabbadubbalāti.

And here, this group of four should be known: the Sutta, that which is in conformity with the Sutta, the doctrine of the teachers, and one's own opinion. Among these, what is called the Sutta is the Three Piṭakas that were established in the Three Councils. What is called that which is in conformity with the Sutta is the Great References, which are called 'conforming and permissible.' What is called the doctrine of the teachers is the commentaries. What is called one's own opinion is one's own understanding, through grasping a method and through subsequent knowing. Among these, the Sutta is not to be rejected; by one who rejects it, the Teacher himself is rejected. However, that which is conforming and permissible should be accepted only when it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. The doctrine of the teachers, too, should be accepted only when it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. Likewise for one's own opinion; but that is the weakest of all.

Idāni yadatthaṃ idha cattāro mahāpadesā ābhatā, taṃ dassetuṃ “catūhi mahāpadesehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ yanti yaṃ yaṃ atthajātañca dhammajātañca. Yujjatīti yathāvuttehi catūhi mahāpadesehi yujjati. Yena yenāti yena yena kāraṇena. Yathā yathāti yena yena pakārena. Taṃ taṃ gahetabbanti saṃvaṇṇiyamāne sutte ābhatena kāraṇena pasaṅgena pakārena ca suttato uddharitvā saṃvaṇṇanāvasena gahetabbanti [M 0.0083] attho. Tena catumahāpadesāviruddhāya yuttiyā suttato atthe niddhāretvā yuttihārayojanā kātabbāti dasseti.

Now, to show for what purpose the four Great References have been brought here, the passage beginning with “by the four Great References” was spoken. Therein, 'whatever' means whatever collection of effects and whatever collection of causes. 'It is consistent' means it is consistent with the four aforementioned Great References. 'By whatever' means by whatever reason. 'In whatever way' means in whatever manner. The meaning of “that should be accepted” is this: when a sutta is being explained, the meaning should be accepted by way of explanation, having been extracted from the sutta by a reason and by a manner that has been brought forth, or by way of relevance. By this, it shows that having determined the meanings from the Sutta by a reasoning that does not conflict with the four Great References, the application of the method of reasoning should be done.

19. Idāni taṃ yuttiniddhāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “pañhaṃ pucchitenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kati padānīti kittakāni padāni. Pariyogāhitabbanti padassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “vicetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Yattakāni padāni yathādhippetaṃ atthaṃ abhivadanti, tattakāni padāni tadatthassekassa ñātuṃ icchitattā “eko pañho”ti vuccati, tāni pana ekagāthāyaṃ yadi vā sabbāni padāni yāva yadi vā ekaṃ padaṃ ekaṃ atthaṃ abhivadati, ekoyeva so pañhoti imamatthaṃ dasseti “yadi sabbānī”tiādinā. Tanti taṃ pañhaṃ. Aññātabbanti ājānitabbaṃ. Kiṃ ime dhammātiādi ājānanākāradassanaṃ. Tattha dhammāti pariyattidhammā. Nānatthāti nānā atthā.

19. Now, to show that determination of reasoning, the passage beginning with “a question having been asked” is commenced. Therein, kati padāni means: how many words? To show the meaning of the word pariyogāhitabbaṃ, the word vicetabbaṃ [it should be investigated] was spoken. However many words express the intended meaning, because the knowing of that one meaning is desired, those many words are called “one question.” But as for those words, whether it is all the words in one verse or even just one word that expresses one meaning, that question is just one. This meaning is shown by the words beginning with “If all…” Taṃ means: that question. Aññātabbaṃ means: it should be made known. The words beginning with “What are these phenomena?” show the mode of knowing. Therein, dhammā means the teachings of the scripture. Nānatthā means: do they have different meanings?

Pucchāgāthāyaṃ ayaṃ padattho – kenassubbhāhato lokoti ayaṃ sattaloko coro viya coraghātakena [V 0.0212] kena abhihato vadhīyatīti attho. Kenassu parivāritoti māluvalatāya viya nissitarukkho kena loko ajjhotthaṭo. Kena sallena otiṇṇoti kena visapītakhurappena viya sarīrabbhantaranimuggena sallena anupaviṭṭho. Kissa dhūpāyitoti kissa kena kāraṇena dhūpāyito santāpito loko. Sadāti padaṃ sabbattha yojetabbaṃ. Teti cattāri padāni. Pañhasaddāpekkhāya pulliṅganiddeso. “Vissajjetī”ti etena vissajjanato tayo pañhāti ñāyatīti dasseti.

In the question verse, this is the meaning of the words: Regarding “By what is the world struck down?”—by what is this world of beings struck down and killed, like a thief by a thief-killer? This is the meaning. Regarding “By what is it enveloped?”—by what is the world enveloped, like a tree that is its support is enveloped by a māluva creeper? Regarding “By what dart is it pierced?”—by what dart that has sunk into the interior of the body is it pierced, like by a poison-smeared arrow? Regarding “By what is it tormented?”—for what reason is the world tormented and afflicted with heat? The word sadā [always] should be connected with every phrase. Te refers to these four phrases. With reference to the word pañha [question], the masculine gender is indicated. By the word vissajjeti [he answers], it shows that from the answering, it is known that there are three questions.

20. Tatthāti vissajjanagāthāyaṃ dutiyapāde vuttā jarā ca paṭhamapāde vuttaṃ maraṇañcāti imāni dve saṅkhatassa pañcakkhandhassa “saṅkhato”ti lakkhīyati etehīti saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, saṅkhatassa saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni. Katamāni tīṇi? Uppādo paññāyati, vayo paññāyati, ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatī”ti (a. ni. 3.47; kathā. 214). Tena vuttaṃ – “jarāyaṃ ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ, maraṇaṃ vayo”ti. Ettha ca “ṭhitassa aññathatta”nti etena khandhappabandhassa pubbāparaviseso idha jarā, na khaṇaṭṭhitīti dasseti. “Maraṇaṃ vayo”ti iminā ca “tisso mato, phusso [M 0.0084] mato”ti evaṃ loke vuttaṃ sammutimaraṇaṃ dasseti, na khaṇikamaraṇaṃ, samucchedamaraṇaṃ vā.

20. Tattha means: in the answer verse. Aging, spoken of in the second line, and death, spoken of in the first line—these two are characteristics of the conditioned (saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni) because by them the five aggregates, which are conditioned, are marked as “conditioned.” For this was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, these are the three characteristics of the conditioned. What three? Arising is apparent, passing away is apparent, and the alteration of that which is established is apparent.” Therefore it was said: “Aging is the alteration of that which is established; death is passing away.” And here, by this phrase “alteration of that which is established,” it shows that here jarā (aging) is the distinction between prior and posterior in the continuity of the aggregates, not momentary duration. And by this, “death is passing away,” it shows conventional death (sammutimaraṇa), spoken of in the world thus: “Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead”; it does not show momentary death or death as final cutting off.

Idāni “te tayo pañhā”ti vuttamatthaṃ yuttivasena dassetuṃ “jarāya cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yebhuyyena jiṇṇassa maraṇadassanato jarāmaraṇānaṃ nānattaṃ asampaṭicchamānaṃ pati tesaṃ nānattadassanatthaṃ “gabbhagatāpi hi mīyantī”ti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathādhippetajarāvirahitassa maraṇassa dassanato aññā jarā aññaṃ maraṇanti. Tenevāha – “na ca te jiṇṇā bhavantī”ti. Kiñca bhiyyo? Kevalassa maraṇassa diṭṭhattā aññāva jarā aññaṃ maraṇaṃ, yathā taṃ devānanti imamatthaṃ dasseti “atthi ca devāna”ntiādinā. Anuttarimanussadhammena ca tikicchanena sakkā jarāya paṭikāraṃ kātuṃ, na tathā maraṇassāti evampi jarāmaraṇānaṃ atthato nānattaṃ sampaṭicchitabbanti dassetuṃ “sakkatevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sakkateti sakyate, sakkāti attho. Paṭikammanti paṭikaraṇaṃ. Nanu ca maraṇassāpi paṭikāraṃ kātuṃ sakkā iddhipādabhāvanāya vasibhāve satīti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha – “aññatreva iddhimantānaṃ iddhivisayā”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Now, to show by way of reasoning the meaning stated as 'those three questions,' the passage beginning 'And with aging...' was spoken. Therein, with respect to one who, for the most part, does not accept the difference between aging and death because of seeing the death of the aged, the following was said in order to show the difference between them: 'Indeed, even those in the womb die.' This is what is said: because death is seen without the intended aging, aging is one thing and death is another. For that reason, he said: 'And they do not become aged.' What is more? Because death alone is seen, aging is one thing and death is another, just as for the devas. He shows this meaning with the passage beginning 'And for the devas there is...'. Furthermore, to show that it is possible to counteract aging by a superhuman state and by medical treatment, but not so for death, and that thus the difference in meaning between aging and death should be accepted, the passage beginning 'It is indeed possible...' was spoken. Therein, sakkateti means sakyate, that is, sakkā; the meaning is 'it is possible.' Paṭikammaṃ means paṭikaraṇaṃ (counteraction). Having kept in mind the objection, 'But is it not possible to counteract even death, when there is mastery in the development of the bases of psychic power?', he said: 'Except indeed from the sphere of psychic power of those possessing psychic power.' For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Yassa kassaci, ānanda, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā [V 0.0213] anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, so ākaṅkhamāno kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā”ti (dī. ni. 2.166, 182; saṃ. ni. 5.822; kathā. 623; udā. 51).

“Ānanda, if anyone has developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power, made them a vehicle, made them a foundation, established them, consolidated them, and properly undertaken them, he could, if he wished, remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.”

Ko panettha kappo, ko vā kappāvasesoti? Kappoti āyukappo, yasmiṃ tasmiñhi kāle yaṃ manussānaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ, taṃ paripuṇṇaṃ karonto kappaṃ tiṭṭhati nāma. “Appaṃ vā bhiyyo”ti (dī. ni. 2.7; a. ni. 7.74) vuttaṃ pana vassasatādito atirekaṃ tiṭṭhanto kappāvasesaṃ tiṭṭhati nāma. Yadi evaṃ kasmā iddhimanto cetovasippattā khīṇāsavā lokahitatthaṃ tathā na tiṭṭhantīti? Khandhasaṅkhātassa dukkhabhārassa pariññātattā anussukkatāya ca. Paṭippassaddhasabbussukkā hi te uttamapurisāti. Vuttañhetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā –

What here is an eon, and what is the remainder of an eon? 'Eon' means the life-span eon. For at any given time, whatever the life-span of humans is, one who makes that complete is said to remain for an eon. But, regarding what was said, 'a little or more,' one who remains in excess of one hundred years and so on is said to remain for the remainder of an eon. If so, why do those with psychic power, who have attained mastery of mind, the taint-destroyed ones, not remain so for the welfare of the world? Because of having fully understood the burden of suffering, designated as the aggregates, and because of a lack of eagerness. For those supreme persons have all eagerness calmed. This was said by the General of the Dhamma:

“Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhikaṅkhāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, vetanaṃ bhatako yathā”ti. (theragā. 654; mi. pa. 2.2.4);

“I do not delight in death, I do not long for life; I await the time, just as a hired servant awaits his wages.”

Yathā [M 0.0085] jarāmaraṇānaṃ aññamaññaṃ atthato nānattaṃ, evaṃ tehi taṇhāya ca nānatte dassite “tayo pañhā”ti idaṃ sijjhatīti taṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ panā”tiādimāha.

Just as there is a difference in meaning between aging and death, so too, when the difference between them and craving is shown, this statement 'three questions' is established. Thus, to show that, he said the passage beginning 'But as to...'

Tattha yasmā taṇhāya abhāvepi sati jarāmaraṇaṃ labbhati khīṇāsavasantāne, tasmā aññaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ aññā taṇhāti imamatthamāha “dissanti vītarāgā jīrantāpi mīyantāpī”ti. Nanu ca taṇhāpi jīraṇabhijjanasabhāvāti? Saccaṃ, na idaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ idhādhippetanti vuttovāyamattho. “Yadi cā”tiādinā jarāmaraṇato taṇhāya anaññatte dosaṃ dasseti. Yobbanaṭṭhāpi vigatataṇhā siyuṃ, na idaṃ yuttanti adhippāyo. Jarāmaraṇampi siyā dukkhassa samudayo taṇhāya anaññatte satīti adhippāyo. Na ca siyā taṇhā dukkhassa samudayo jarāmaraṇato anaññatte satīti bhāvo. Na hi jarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhassa samudayo, taṇhā dukkhassa samudayo, tasmā veditabbaṃ etesamatthato nānattanti adhippāyo. Yathā ca taṇhā maggavajjhā, evaṃ jarāmaraṇampi siyā maggavajjhaṃ taṇhāya anaññatte sati. Yathā ca jarāmaraṇaṃ na maggavajjhaṃ, tathā taṇhāpi siyāti ayampi nayo vutto evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imāya yuttiyāti [V 0.0214] imāya yathāvuttāya upapattiyā. Aññamaññehīti aññāhi aññāhi kāraṇūpapattīhi atthato ce aññattaṃ, tadaññampi byañjanato gavesitabbanti attho.

Herein, because even in the absence of craving, aging and death are found in the continuum of the taint-destroyed ones, therefore aging and death are one thing and craving is another—this meaning is stated with 'those free from passion are seen aging and dying.' But is not craving also of a nature to decay and break apart? True, but this momentary aging and death is not what is intended here—this meaning has already been stated. With the phrase beginning 'And if,' the flaw in craving not being different from aging and death is shown. The intention is: if they were the same, then those in their youth would also be free from craving, which is not logical. The intention is that aging and death would also be the origin of suffering if they were not different from craving. And the meaning is that craving would not be the origin of suffering if it were not different from aging and death. For aging and death are not the origin of suffering, whereas craving is the origin of suffering; therefore, the intention is that their difference in meaning should be known. And just as craving is to be eliminated by the path, so too would aging and death be eliminated by the path if they were not different from craving. And just as aging and death are not eliminated by the path, so too craving would not be eliminated by the path—this method, too, should be understood as having been stated. 'By this reasoning' means by this afore-stated justification. 'From each other' means: if a difference in meaning is seen through various distinct reasons and justifications, then a difference should also be sought in the phrasing. Such is the meaning.

Imesaṃ dhammānaṃ atthato ekattanti imamevatthaṃ “na hi yujjatī”tiādinā vivarati. Taṇhāya adhippāye aparipūramāneti icchitālābhamāha. Tena icchātaṇhānaṃ atthato ekattaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti. Etena na hi yujjati icchāya ca taṇhāya ca atthato aññattanti. Yathā idaṃ vacanaṃ samatthanaṃ hoti, evaṃ icchāvipariyāye āghātavatthūsu kodho ca upanāho ca uppajjatīti idampi samatthanaṃ hoti, na tathā jarāmaraṇavipariyāyeti jarāmaraṇataṇhānaṃ atthato aññattampi samatthitaṃ hotīti etamatthaṃ dasseti “imāya yuttiyā”tiādinā.

This very meaning—'the oneness in meaning of these phenomena'—he explains with the passage beginning 'for it is not fitting.' By 'when the intention of craving is not fulfilled,' he speaks of the non-attainment of what is desired. By that, it is said that desire and craving are one in meaning. By this, the statement 'for it is not fitting for desire and craving to be different in meaning' is supported. Just as this statement is supported, so too is the statement 'when desire is thwarted, anger and resentment arise in the grounds for vexation' also supported. But it is not so in the case of the absence of aging and death. Therefore, the difference in meaning between aging, death, and craving is also supported. This meaning is shown by the passage beginning 'by this reasoning'.

Yadi icchātaṇhānaṃ atthato anaññattaṃ, atha kasmā bhagavatā imissā gāthāya dvidhā vuttāti? Tattha parihāramāha “yaṃ panida”ntiādinā. Tattha yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ. Abhilapitanti vuttaṃ yaṃ idaṃ abhilapanaṃ[M 0.0086], idaṃ bāhirānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ ārammaṇavasena, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena vā yojetabbaṃ. Dvīhi dhammehīti dvīhi pakatīhi. Kā pana tā pakatiyoti? Appattassa visayassa esanavasena icchā, pattassa appattassa vā pātukāmatāvasena taṇhā, ayametāsaṃ viseso. Yadipi evaṃ, tathāpi sabbā taṇhā rūpādivisayaṃ gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā gahaṇena ekasabhāvā evāti dassento “sabbā hi taṇhā ajjhosānalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇā”ti āha. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya pakāsento “sabbo aggī”tiādimāha, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

If desire (icchā) and craving (taṇhā) are not different in meaning, then why were they spoken of twofold by the Blessed One in this verse? Concerning that, he states the refutation with 'yaṃ panida,' and so on. Therein, 'yaṃ' is a reference to the action. 'Abhilapitaṃ' means 'spoken.' This speaking should be connected either by way of the object—external things such as forms—or by way of making them an object. 'By two things' means by two natures. What, then, are those natures? 'Icchā' is by way of seeking an unattained object. 'Taṇhā' is by way of wishing to consume an attained or unattained object. This is the distinction between them. Although this is so, nevertheless, showing that all craving is of a single nature by swallowing, finishing, and grasping objects such as forms, he said, 'For all craving has the single characteristic of devouring.' Now, clarifying that meaning with a simile, he said, 'All fire,' and so on. That is very easy to understand.

Ayaṃ pana na kevalaṃ taṇhā ārammaṇe pavattivisesena dvīhi eva nāmehi vuttā, atha kho anekehipi pariyāyehīti dassanatthaṃ “icchāitipī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Moreover, this craving is spoken of not only by these two names based on the distinction of its occurrence in relation to its object, but also in many other ways. To illustrate this, it is said: 'icchā iti pi' (also called desire), and so on.

Tattha icchanti tāya ārammaṇānīti icchā. Taṇhāyanaṭṭhena taṇhā. Pīḷājananato duruddhāraṇato ca visapītaṃ sallaṃ viyāti sallaṃ. Santāpanaṭṭhena dhūpāyanā. Ākaḍḍhanaṭṭhena sīghasotā saritā viyāti saritā, allaṭṭhena vā saritā, “saritāni sinehitāni ca, somanassāni bhavanti jantuno”ti (dha. pa. 341) hi vuttaṃ. Allāni ceva siniddhāni cāti ayamettha attho. Visattikāti visatāti visattikā. Visaṭāti visattikā. Visamāti visattikā. Visālāti visattikā. Visakkatīti visattikā. Visaṃvādikāti visattikā[V 0.0215]. Visaṃharatīti visattikā. Visamūlāti visattikā. Visaphalāti visattikā. Visaparibhogāti visattikā. Visatā vā pana sā taṇhā rūpe sadde gandhe rase phoṭṭhabbe dhamme kule gaṇe visatā vitthatāti visattikā.

Therein, 'icchā' (desire) is so called because they desire objects by it. 'Taṇhā' (craving) is so called because of its nature of thirsting. Because it generates affliction and is difficult to extract, like a poisoned dart, it is called 'sallaṃ' (dart). Because of its nature of causing torment, it is called 'dhūpāyanā' (fuming). Because of its nature of dragging down, like a swift-flowing river, it is called 'saritā' (stream); or, because of its nature of being wet, it is 'saritā,' for it is said: 'For a being, there are streams and affections, which are states of mental pleasure' (Dhp. 341). The meaning here is 'both wet and sticky.' 'Visattikā' is so called because it spreads (visatā). It is 'visattikā' because it is diffused (visaṭā). It is 'visattikā' because it is uneven (visamā). It is 'visattikā' because it is vast (visālā). It is 'visattikā' because it clings (visakkati). It is 'visattikā' because it is deceptive (visaṃvādikā). It is 'visattikā' because it confuses (visaṃharati). It is 'visattikā' because it is rooted in suffering (visamūlā). It is 'visattikā' because its fruit is suffering (visaphalā). It is 'visattikā' because its consumption is of suffering (visaparibhogā). Or else, that craving is called 'visattikā' because it spreads (visatā) and is diffused (vitthatā) in relation to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, mental objects, families, and groups.

Sinehanavasena sineho. Nānāgatīsu kilamathuppādanena kilamatho. Paliveṭhanaṭṭhena latā viyāti latā. “Latā uppajja tiṭṭhatī”ti (dha. pa. 340) hi vuttaṃ. Mamanti maññanavasena maññanā. Dūragatampi ākaḍḍhitvā bandhanaṭṭhena bandho. Āsīsanaṭṭhena āsā. Ārammaṇarasaṃ pātukāmatāvasena pipāsā. Abhinandanaṭṭhena abhinandanā. Itīti evaṃ ārammaṇe pavattivisesena anekehi nāmehi gayhamānāpi sabbā taṇhā ajjhosānalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇāti yathāvuttamatthaṃ nigameti.

By way of producing affection, it is 'sineho' (affection). By producing weariness in various destinations, it is 'kilamatho' (weariness). Because of its nature of entwining, like a creeper, it is 'latā' (creeper). For it is said: 'A creeper springs up and remains' (Dhp. 340). By way of thinking 'mine,' it is 'maññanā' (conceiving). Because of its nature of binding by drawing in even what is far away, it is 'bandho' (bond). Because of its nature of wishing, it is 'āsā' (hope). By way of desiring to consume the savor of an object, it is 'pipāsā' (thirst). Because of its nature of greatly delighting, it is 'abhinandanā' (rejoicing). Thus, he concludes the aforementioned meaning: although craving is taken up by many names according to its specific way of occurring in relation to an object, all craving has the single characteristic of devouring.

Puna [M 0.0087] taṇhāya anekehi nāmehi gahitabhāvameva “yathā cā”tiādinā upacayena dasseti. Tattha vevacaneti vevacanahāravibhaṅge. “Āsā ca pihā”ti gāthāya (netti. 37; peṭako. 11) atthaṃ tattheva vaṇṇayissāma. Avigatarāgassātiādīsu rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo, chandanaṭṭhena chando, piyāyanaṭṭhena pemaṃ, paridahanaṭṭhena paridāhoti taṇhāva vuttā. Tenevāha – “taṇhāyetaṃ vevacana”nti. Evaṃ yujjatīti evaṃ icchātaṇhānaṃ atthato anaññattā “tayo pañhā”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ yujjati yuttiyā saṅgacchatīti attho.

Furthermore, the fact that craving is taken up by many names is shown by the phrase beginning 'yathā cā', which includes the cumulative particle `ca`. Here, 'synonyms' refers to the section on the analysis of synonyms. The meaning of the verse 'Āsā ca pihā' will be explained in that very context. In phrases like 'for one whose passion is not removed,' craving itself is stated as 'rāga' (passion) in the sense of coloring, 'chanda' (desire) in the sense of wishing, 'pema' (love) in the sense of endearment, and 'paridāha' (torment) in the sense of tormenting. Therefore, it is said: 'This is a synonym for craving.' Thus, 'it is fitting' means: because desire and craving are not different in meaning, what was said as 'three questions' is fitting; it accords with reason. This is the meaning.

21. Evaṃ “kenassubbhāhato loko”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.66) gāthāya “tayo pañhā”ti pañhattayabhāve yuttiṃ dassetvā idāni aññehi pakārehi yuttigavesanaṃ dassento “sabbo dukkhūpacāro”tiādimāha. Tattha dukkhūpacāroti dukkhappavatti. Kāmataṇhāsaṅkhāramūlakoti kāmataṇhāpaccayasaṅkhārahetukoti yujjatīti adhippāyo. Nibbidūpacāroti nibbidāpavatti kāmānaṃ vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjamānā anabhirati ñāṇanibbidā ca. Kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlakoti kāmataṇhāya parikkhārabhūtavatthukāmahetuko. Tattha anabhiratisaṅkhātā nibbidā kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlikā, na ñāṇanibbidāti sabbo nibbidūpacāro kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlakoti na pana yujjatīti vuttaṃ. Imāya yuttiyāti nayaṃ dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā pañhattayabhāve yutti vuttā, yathā ca dukkhūpacāranibbidūpacāresu, evaṃ imāya yuttiyā iminā yogena nayena aññamaññehi kāraṇehi taṃtaṃpāḷippadese anurūpehi aññathā aññehi hetūhi yutti gavesitabbāti.

21. Thus, having shown the reason for there being 'three questions' in the verse 'By what is the world afflicted?', now, showing the search for reason by other modes, he said, 'All is the process of suffering,' and so on. Therein, 'the process of suffering' means the occurrence of suffering. 'Rooted in the formations of craving for sensual pleasure' means it has formations as its cause, which are conditioned by craving for sensual pleasure; that this is suitable is the intention. 'The process of disenchantment' means the occurrence of disenchantment, which is the non-delight and the knowledge-disenchantment that arise because of the alteration and change of sensual pleasures. 'Rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasure' means it is caused by the objects of sensual pleasure which are the accessories of craving for sensual pleasure. Therein, the disenchantment called non-delight is rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasure, but the knowledge-disenchantment is not. Therefore, it was said that the statement 'all processes of disenchantment are rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasure' is not suitable. 'By this reason' shows the method. This is what is said: Just as the reason was stated regarding the three questions, and just as it was stated regarding the processes of suffering and disenchantment, so too, by this reason, by this application and method, reason should be sought through various distinct causes appropriate to each particular passage of the text, and otherwise through other grounds.

Idāni [V 0.0216] taṃ nayadassanaṃ saṃkhittanti vitthārato vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “yathā hi bhagavā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – rāgadosamohacaritānaṃ yathākkamaṃ asubhamettāpaccayākārakathā rāgādivinayanato sappāyāti ayaṃ sāsanayutti. Evamavaṭṭhite yadi rāgacaritassa mettācetovimuttiṃ deseyya, sā desanā na yujjati asappāyabhāvato. Tathā sukhāpaṭipadādayoti. Nanu ca sukhāpaṭipadādayo paṭipattiyā sambhavanti, na desanāyāti? Saccametaṃ, idha pana rāgacaritoti tibbakileso rāgacaritoti adhippeto. Tassa dukkhāya paṭipadāya bhāvanā [M 0.0088] samijjhati. Yassa ca dukkhāya paṭipadāya bhāvanā samijjhati, tassa garutarā asubhadesanā sappāyā, yassa garutarā asubhadesanā sappāyā, na tassa mandakilesassa viya lahukatarāti imamatthaṃ dassento āha – “sukhaṃ vā paṭipadaṃ…pe… deseyya na yujjati desanā”ti. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi yathāsambhavaṃ attho vattabbo. Ettha ca ayuttaparihārena yuttisamadhigamoti yuttivicāraṇāya ayuttipi gavesitabbāti vuttaṃ – “yadi hi…pe… na yujjati desanā”ti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ yaṃ kiñcītiādi yuttihārayojanāya nayadassanameva.

Now, because that showing of the method is concise, the passage beginning with 'yathā hi bhagavā' is commenced in order to show it by analyzing it in detail. Therein, this is the concise meaning: for persons of lustful, hateful, and deluded temperaments, respectively, the discourse on foulness, loving-kindness, and the structure of conditions is suitable because it subdues lust, etc. This is the rationale of the teaching. This being established, if one were to teach the liberation of mind through loving-kindness to a person of lustful temperament, that teaching would not be suitable, due to its unsuitability. The same applies to the easy paths of practice, etc. Is it not that the easy paths of practice, etc., arise in the practice, not in the teaching? This is true. However, here, by 'a person of lustful temperament' is intended one with intense defilements. For that person, cultivation through the difficult path of practice succeeds. And for whom cultivation through the difficult path of practice succeeds, for that person a more severe discourse on foulness is suitable. For the one for whom a more severe discourse on foulness is suitable, a lighter teaching is not suitable, as it would be for one with milder defilements. To show this meaning, it is said: 'If he were to teach the easy path of practice... the teaching would not be fitting.' By this method, the meaning should be stated in the remaining passages as is possible. And here, the understanding of the suitable occurs by rejecting the unsuitable; therefore, in the investigation of the rationale, even the unsuitable should be sought. Thus it is said: 'For if... the teaching would not be fitting.' In the remaining cases, this is the same method. Thus, the passage beginning with 'whatever it may be' is only a showing of the method for the application of the method of rationale.

Tattha evanti iminā nayena. Yaṃ kiñcīti aññampi yaṃ kiñci. Anulomappahānanti pahānassa anurūpaṃ, pahānasamatthanti attho. Sutte anavasesānaṃ padatthānaṃ anupadavicāraṇā vicayo hāro, vicayahārasaṃvaṇṇanāya niddhāritesu atthesu yuttigavesanaṃ sukaranti āha – “sabbaṃ taṃ vicayena hārena vicinitvā yuttihārena yojetabba”nti. Yāvatikā ñāṇassa bhūmīti saṃvaṇṇentassa ācariyassa yaṃ ñāṇaṃ yaṃ paṭibhānaṃ, tassa yattako visayo, tattako yuttihāravicāroti attho. Taṃ kissa hetu? Anantanayo samantabhaddako vimaddakkhamo vicittadesano ca saddhammoti.

Therein, 'evaṃ' means 'by this method.' 'Yaṃ kiñci' means any other thing whatsoever. 'Anulomappahāna' means 'suitable for abandonment,' that is, 'capable of abandoning'; this is the meaning. In the sutta, the word-by-word investigation of the meanings of all words without remainder is the Vicaya hāra (method of analysis). Because when the meanings have been determined in the commentary on the Vicaya hāra, the seeking of the rationale is easy, it is said: 'All that should be examined through the method of analysis and connected through the method of rationale.' The phrase 'as far as the ground of knowledge extends' means this: whatever is the knowledge and inspiration of the commentating teacher, whatever its range, that is the extent of the investigation of the Yutti hāra. What is the reason for that? Because the true Dhamma has endless methods, is auspicious all around, is able to withstand refutation, and has varied teachings.

Evaṃ nayadassanavaseneva yuttihārayojanā dassitāti taṃ brahmavihāraphalasamāpattinavānupubbasamāpattivasibhāvehi vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “mettāvihārissa sato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha mettāvihārissāti mettāvihāralābhino. Satoti samānassa, tathābhūtassāti attho. Byāpādoti padoso. Cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti cittaṃ abhibhavissati. Yasmā pana kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ apubbaṃ acarimaṃ pavatti nāma natthi, tasmā samāpattito vuṭṭhānassa aparabhāgeti dassanatthaṃ “ṭhassatī”ti vuttaṃ. Na yujjati desanāti byāpādapaṭipakkhattā mettāya tādisī kathā na yuttāti attho. Byāpādo pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti yujjati desanāti yathāvuttakāraṇato [V 0.0217] eva ayaṃ kathā yuttāti. Sesavāresupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Anuttānaṃ eva vaṇṇayissāma.

Thus, the application of the method of rationale has been shown by the power of showing the method alone. Therefore, in order to show that application by analyzing it through mastery in the divine abidings, the fruition attainments, and the nine successive attainments, the passage beginning with 'mettāvihārissa sato' is commenced. Therein, 'mettāvihārissa' means for one who has obtained the abiding in loving-kindness. 'Sato' means for one who is, that is, for one who has become thus. 'Byāpādo' means ill will. 'Cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti' means it will overwhelm the mind. And since there is no such thing as an occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states that is not preceded or not followed, 'ṭhassatī' is said in order to show that this occurs in the period after emerging from attainment. 'The teaching is not fitting' means that because loving-kindness is the opponent of ill will, such a discourse is not suitable; this is the meaning. 'The teaching is fitting that ill will is abandoned, goes to destruction' means that for the reason already stated, this discourse is suitable. In the remaining instances, the meaning should be understood by this same method. We will comment only on what is not obvious.

Animittavihārissāti aniccānupassanāmukhena paṭiladdhaphalasamāpattivihārassa. Nimittānusārīti saṅkhāranimittānusārī. Tena tenevāti niccādīsu [M 0.0089] yaṃ yaṃ pahīnaṃ, tena teneva nimittena. Asmīti vigatanti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu diṭṭhimānavasena yaṃ asmīti maññitaṃ, taṃ vigataṃ. Tamevatthaṃ vivarati “ayamahamasmīti na samanupassāmī”ti. Vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallanti vinayakukkuccassāpi kathaṃ kathanti pavattisabbhāvato vicikicchāpadena visesitaṃ. Na yujjati desanāti vicikicchāya pahānekaṭṭhabhāvato na yuttāyaṃ kathā.

‘Animittavihārissa’ means: for one who abides in the fruition attainment obtained through the gateway of the contemplation of impermanence. ‘Nimittānusārī’ means: one who follows after the sign of formations. ‘Tena teneva’ means: by that very sign among [signs such as] permanence, etc., that has been abandoned. ‘Asmīti vigataṃ’ means: the conceiving ‘I am’ by the power of view and conceit in the five aggregates of clinging is gone. It explains this very meaning with the text: “I do not perceive, ‘This I am.’” In ‘the dart of doubt and wavering,’ even scruples regarding the Vinaya are specified by the term ‘doubt’ (vicikicchā) because they have the nature of occurring as ‘how? how?’. ‘The teaching is not fitting’ means: this discourse is not suitable because doubt has the same basis for abandonment as view.

Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassāti paṭhamajjhānasamaṅgino. Kāmarāgabyāpādā visesāya saṃvattantīti na yujjatīti yasmā nīvaraṇesu appahīnesu paṭhamajjhānassa upacārampi na sampajjati, pageva jhānaṃ, tasmā kāmarāgabyāpādā visesāya dutiyajjhānāya saṃvattantīti na yuttāyaṃ kathā. Yathāladdhassa pana paṭhamajjhānassa kāmarāgabyāpādā pariyuṭṭhānappattā hānāya saṃvattantīti yujjati desanā yuttā kathāti, evaṃ sabbattha yojetabbaṃ. Avitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā nāma saha upacārena dutiyajjhānadhammā, ārammaṇakaraṇattho hettha sahagata-saddo. Hānāyāti paṭhamajjhānato parihānāya. Visesāyāti dutiyajjhānāya. Iminā nayena tattha tattha hānanti, visesoti ca vuttadhammā veditabbā. Vitakkavicārasahagatāti paṭhamajjhānadhammā, kāmāvacaradhammā eva vā. Upekkhāsukhasahagatāti upacārena saddhiṃ dutiyajjhānadhammā, tatramajjhattupekkhā hi idha upekkhāti adhippetā. Pītisukhasahagatāti saha upacārena tatiyajjhānadhammā. Upekkhāsatipārisuddhisahagatāti catutthajjhānadhammā.

‘Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa’ means: for one endowed with the first jhāna. The statement ‘sensual desire and ill will conduce to distinction’ is not suitable, because when the hindrances are not abandoned, even the access of the first jhāna is not accomplished, let alone the jhāna itself. Therefore, the discourse that sensual desire and ill will conduce to distinction, that is, to the second jhāna, is not suitable. However, for one who has obtained the first jhāna, when sensual desire and ill will have reached the state of obsession, they conduce to decline. Thus, the teaching is fitting, the discourse is suitable. In this way, it should be applied everywhere. ‘Perception and attention accompanied by what is without initial thought’ are the factors of the second jhāna together with access; here the word ‘sahagata’ has the meaning of making an object. ‘Hānāya’ means: for the decline from the first jhāna. ‘Visesāya’ means: for the second jhāna. By this method, the states called ‘decline’ and ‘distinction’ should be known in those various instances. ‘Accompanied by initial and sustained thought’ refers to the factors of the first jhāna, or just the sense-sphere states. ‘Accompanied by equanimity and happiness’ refers to the factors of the second jhāna together with access; for here by ‘equanimity’ is intended equanimity as neutrality. ‘Accompanied by rapture and happiness’ refers to the factors of the third jhāna together with access. ‘Accompanied by the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity’ refers to the factors of the fourth jhāna.

Saññūpacārāti paṭusaññākiccaṃ karontā eva ye keci cittuppādā, “ākiñcaññāyatanadhammā”tipi vadanti. Saññāvedayitanirodhasahagatāti “saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharissāmī”ti tassa parikammavasena pavattadhammā. Te pana yasmā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyaṃ ṭhiteneva sakkā saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ, na tato parihīnena, tasmā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā hānāya saṃvattantīti na yuttā kathā. Visesāya saṃvattantīti pana yuttā kathāti āha – “hānāya…pe… desanā”ti. Kallatāparicitanti [V 0.0218] samatthabhāvena paricitaṃ, yathāvuttasamāpattīsu vasibhāvena paricitanti attho. Tenevāha – “abhinīhāraṃ khamatī”ti. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ uttānameva.

‘Saññūpacārā’ means: any arisings of consciousness that perform the function of clear perception. They are also called ‘states of the base of nothingness.’ ‘Saññāvedayitanirodhasahagatā’ refers to: the states that arise by way of preliminary work for that [cessation], with the thought, ‘I will attain and abide in the cessation of perception and feeling.’ However, since it is possible to attain and abide in the cessation of perception and feeling only for one who is established in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and not for one who has fallen away from it, the statement that these states lead to decline from the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not correct. Rather, the statement that they lead to distinction is correct. Therefore, he said: ‘For decline… the teaching.’ ‘Kallatāparicitaṃ’ means: practiced by way of capability; that is, practiced by way of mastery in the aforementioned attainments. For that very reason, it is said: ‘it is capable of directing.’ The rest is all self-evident.

Api [M 0.0090] cettha appaṭikkūlasaññāmukhena kāmacchando vañcetīti yujjati. Paṭikkūlasaññāpatirūpatāya byāpādo vañcetīti yujjati. Samādhimukhena thinamiddhaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Vīriyārambhamukhena uddhaccaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Sikkhākāmatāmukhena kukkuccaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Ubhayapakkhasantīraṇamukhena vicikicchā vañcetīti yujjati. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhasamupekkhanamukhena sammoho vañcetīti yujjati. Attaññutāmukhena attani aparibhavane māno vañcetīti yujjati. Vīmaṃsāmukhena hetupatirūpakapariggahena micchādiṭṭhi vañcetīti yujjati. Virattatāpatirūpakena sattesu adayāpannatā vañcetīti yujjati. Anuññātapaṭisevanapatirūpatāya kāmasukhallikānuyogo vañcetīti yujjati. Ājīvapārisuddhipatirūpatāya asaṃvibhāgasīlatā vañcetīti yujjati. Saṃvibhāgasīlatāpatirūpatāya micchājīvo vañcetīti yujjati. Asaṃsaggavihāritāpatirūpatāya asaṅgahasīlatā vañcetīti yujjati. Saṅgahasīlatāpatirūpatāya ananulomikasaṃsaggo vañcetīti yujjati. Saccavāditāpatirūpatāya pisuṇavācā vañcetīti yujjati. Apisuṇavāditāpatirūpatāya anatthakāmatā vañcetīti yujjati. Piyavāditāpatirūpatāya cāṭukamyatā vañcetīti yujjati. Mitabhāṇitāpatirūpatāya asammodanasīlatā vañcetīti yujjati. Sammodanasīlatāpatirūpatāya māyā sāṭheyyañca vañcetīti yujjati. Niggayhavāditāpatirūpatāya pharusavācatā vañcetīti yujjati. Pāpagarahitāpatirūpatāya paravajjānupassitā vañcetīti yujjati. Kulānuddhayatāpatirūpatāya kulamacchariyaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Āvāsaciraṭṭhitikāmatāmukhena āvāsamacchariyaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Dhammaparibandhapariharaṇamukhena dhammamacchariyaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Dhammadesanābhiratimukhena bhassārāmatā vañcetīti yujjati. Apharusavācatāgaṇānuggahakaraṇamukhena saṅgaṇikārāmatā vañcetīti yujjati. Puññakāmatāpatirūpatāya kammārāmatā vañcetīti yujjati. Saṃvegapatirūpena cittasantāpo vañcetīti yujjati. Saddhālutāpatirūpatāya aparikkhatā vañcetīti yujjati. Vīmaṃsanāpatirūpena assaddhiyaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Attādhipateyyapatirūpena garūnaṃ anusāsaniyā appadakkhiṇaggāhitā vañcetīti yujjati. Dhammādhipateyyapatirūpena sabrahmacārīsu agāravaṃ vañcetīti yujjati. Lokādhipateyyapatirūpena attani dhamme ca paribhavo vañcetīti yujjati. Mettāyanāmukhena rāgo vañcetīti yujjati. Karuṇāyanāpatirūpena soko vañcetīti yujjati. Muditāvihārapatirūpena [V 0.0219] pahāso [M 0.0091] vañcetīti yujjati. Upekkhāvihārapatirūpena kusalesu dhammesu nikkhittachandatā vañcetīti yujjati. Evaṃ āgamapatirūpakaadhigamapatirūpakādīnampi tathā tathā vañcanasabhāvo yuttito veditabbo. Evaṃ āgamānusārena yuttigavesanā kātabbāti.

Furthermore, herein, it is correct that sensual desire deceives by means of the perception of the non-repulsive. It is correct that ill will deceives with the appearance of the perception of the repulsive. It is correct that sloth and torpor deceive by means of concentration. It is correct that restlessness deceives by means of the undertaking of effort. It is correct that worry deceives by means of the desire for the training. It is correct that doubt deceives by means of examining both sides. It is correct that delusion deceives by means of equanimity towards the agreeable and disagreeable. It is correct that conceit deceives by means of self-knowledge and non-disparagement of oneself. It is correct that wrong view deceives by means of investigation through grasping what appears to be a cause. It is correct that lack of compassion towards beings deceives with the appearance of dispassion. It is correct that indulgence in sensual pleasures deceives with the appearance of using what is permitted. It is correct that a nature of not sharing deceives with the appearance of purity of livelihood. It is correct that wrong livelihood deceives with the appearance of a sharing nature. It is correct that a nature of not being supportive deceives with the appearance of living in seclusion. It is correct that unsuitable association deceives with the appearance of a supportive nature. It is correct that divisive speech deceives with the appearance of truthfulness. It is correct that desiring what is not beneficial deceives with the appearance of non-divisive speech. It is correct that flattery deceives with the appearance of pleasant speech. It is correct that an uncongenial nature deceives with the appearance of measured speech. It is correct that deceit and craftiness deceive with the appearance of a congenial nature. It is correct that harsh speech deceives with the appearance of speaking censoriously. It is correct that seeing the faults of others deceives with the appearance of censuring evil. It is correct that stinginess regarding families deceives with the appearance of compassion for one's clan. It is correct that stinginess regarding dwellings deceives by means of desiring a long-term residence in a dwelling. It is correct that stinginess regarding the Dhamma deceives by means of warding off dangers to the Dhamma. It is correct that delight in talk deceives by means of delight in teaching the Dhamma. It is correct that delight in company deceives by means of non-harsh speech and supporting a group. It is correct that delight in activity deceives with the appearance of desiring merit. It is correct that mental agitation deceives with the appearance of spiritual urgency. It is correct that lack of investigation deceives with the appearance of much faith. It is correct that lack of faith deceives with the appearance of investigation. It is correct that not respectfully accepting the instruction of revered ones deceives with the appearance of self-sovereignty. It is correct that disrespect towards spiritual companions deceives with the appearance of Dhamma-sovereignty. It is correct that disparagement of oneself and the Dhamma deceives with the appearance of world-sovereignty. It is correct that lust deceives by means of loving-kindness. It is correct that sorrow deceives with the appearance of compassion. It is correct that frivolity deceives with the appearance of abiding in sympathetic joy. It is correct that having given up desire for wholesome states deceives with the appearance of abiding in equanimity. In this way, the deceptive nature of counterfeit causes, counterfeit effects, and so on, should be understood by way of reason in each respective case. Thus, the search for reason should be undertaken in accordance with the scriptures.

Yuttihāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Method of Reason is concluded.

4. Padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Analysis of the Method of the Proximate Cause

22. Tattha katamo padaṭṭhāno hārotiādi padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgo. Tattha yasmā “idaṃ imassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ imassa padaṭṭhāna”nti tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānabhūtadhammavibhāvanalakkhaṇo padaṭṭhāno hāro, tasmā pavattiyā mūlabhūtaṃ avijjaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabhāvadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ niddhārento avijjāya sabhāvaṃ niddisati “sabbadhammayāthāvaasampaṭivedhalakkhaṇā avijjā”ti. Tassattho – sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvo na sampaṭivijjhīyati etenāti sabbadhammayāthāvaasampaṭivedho. So lakkhaṇaṃ etissāti sā tathā vuttā. Etena dhammasabhāvappaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā avijjāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā sammā paṭivedho sampaṭivedho. Tassa paṭipakkho asampaṭivedho. Kattha pana so sampaṭivedhassa paṭipakkhoti āha – “sabba…pe… lakkhaṇā”ti. Yasmā pana asubhe subhantiādivipallāse sati tattha sammoho uparūpari jāyatiyeva na hāyati, tasmā “tassā vipallāsā padaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ.

4. Herein, the analysis of the method of proximate cause begins with 'What is the method of proximate cause?' Herein, because it is said, 'This is the proximate cause of this, this is the proximate cause of that,' the method of proximate cause is characterized by clarifying the phenomena that are the proximate causes for those various phenomena. Therefore, taking ignorance, which is the root of the round of existence, as the beginning, he, determining the proximate cause—the immediate reason—of natural phenomena, indicates the nature of ignorance thus: 'Ignorance has the characteristic of non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena.' Its meaning is: 'non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena' is so called because by this, the unperverted nature of all phenomena is not penetrated. That is its characteristic; therefore, it is so stated. By this, it is said that ignorance has the characteristic of concealing the nature of phenomena. Alternatively, right penetration is sampaṭivedha. Its opposite is asampaṭivedha. But where is that the opposite of sampaṭivedha? To this, he said: '...all... characteristic.' Furthermore, because when there is the perversion such as perceiving the attractive in the unattractive, delusion arises therein again and again and does not diminish, therefore it is said: 'The perversions are its proximate cause.'

Piyarūpaṃ sātarūpanti piyāyitabbajātiyaṃ iṭṭhajātiyañca padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133; vibha. 203) hi vuttaṃ. Adinnādānanti adinnādānacetanā. Sā hi ekavāraṃ uppannāpi anādīnavadassitāya lobhassa uppattikāraṇaṃ hotīti tassa padaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Dosassa pāṇātipāto padaṭṭhānaṃ, mohassa micchāpaṭipadā padaṭṭhānanti etthāpi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānabyañjanaggahaṇalakkhaṇāti nimittānubyañjanaggahaṇalakkhaṇā. Sukhasaññāya phassassa upagamanalakkhaṇatā phassapaccayatāva vuttā. “Phuṭṭho sañjānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.93) hi vuttaṃ[M 0.0092]. Assādoti taṇhā. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni uppādavayaññathattāni. Yebhuyyena niccaggahaṇaṃ viññāṇādhīnanti niccasaññāya viññāṇapadaṭṭhānatā vuttā. Tathā hi so bhikkhu taṃyeva viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsaratīti viññāṇavisayameva attano niccaggāhaṃ pavedesi. Pañcannaṃ [V 0.0220] khandhānaṃ yadi aniccatā dukkhatā ca sudiṭṭhā, attasaññā sukhasaññā anavakāsāti āha – “aniccasaññādukkhasaññāasamanupassanalakkhaṇā attasaññā”ti. “Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) hi vuttaṃ.

As for 'dear form and agreeable form,' that which is of a nature to be loved and that which is of a nature to be desired are the proximate cause. For it is said: 'Whatever in the world is dear form and agreeable form, it is here that this craving, when arising, arises.' As for 'taking what is not given,' it is the volition for taking what is not given. For that volition, even if it has arisen only once, through not seeing the danger, becomes a cause for the arising of greed; therefore, it is said to be the proximate cause of that greed. The volition for killing living beings is the proximate cause of hatred; wrong practice is the proximate cause of delusion. Here too, the meaning should be understood in this same way. As for 'the characteristic of grasping color, shape, and detail,' it has the characteristic of grasping the sign and the secondary sign. For the perception of pleasure, the characteristic of contact's approach is said to be simply its conditionality by contact. For it is said: 'Having been contacted, one perceives.' As for 'gratification,' it is craving. Arising, passing away, and otherwiseness are the characteristics of the conditioned. Because for the most part the grasping of permanence is dependent on consciousness, the state of consciousness being the proximate cause for the perception of permanence is stated. For that monk runs on and transmigrates to that very consciousness; thus, he taught that his own grasping of permanence has consciousness itself as its object. If the impermanence and suffering of the five aggregates are well seen, the perception of self and the perception of pleasure have no opportunity to arise; therefore, he said: 'The perception of self has the characteristic of not contemplating the perception of impermanence and the perception of suffering.' For it is said: 'What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is not-self.'

Yebhuyyena attābhiniveso arūpadhammesūti āha – “tassā nāmakāyo padaṭṭhāna”nti. Sabbaṃ neyyanti cattāri saccāni catusaccavinimuttassa ñeyyassa abhāvato. Cittavikkhepapaṭisaṃharaṇaṃ uddhaccavikkhambhanaṃ. Asubhāti asubhānupassanā, paṭibhāganimittabhūtā asubhā eva vā, taṇhāpaṭipakkhattā samathassa asubhā padaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ. Abhijjhāya tanukaraṇato adinnādānāveramaṇī alobhassa padaṭṭhānanti vuttā. Tathā byāpādassa tanukaraṇato pāṇātipātāveramaṇī adosassa padaṭṭhānanti vuttā. Vatthuavippaṭipatti visayasabhāvapaṭivedho, sammāpaṭipatti sīlasamādhisampadānaṃ nibbidāñāṇena anabhiratiñāṇameva vā tathā pavattaṃ. Sabbāpi vedanā dukkhadukkhatādibhāvato dukkhanti katvā vuttaṃ – “dukkhasaññāya vedanā padaṭṭhāna”nti. Dhammasaññāti dhammamattanti saññā.

Because for the most part adherence to self is in immaterial phenomena, he said: 'The mental body is its proximate cause.' As for 'all is to be known,' it means the four truths, because of the absence of anything to be known apart from the four truths. The suppression of restlessness is the removal of the mind's distraction. As for 'the foul,' it is the contemplation of the foul, or it is simply the foul things that have become the counterpart sign; because it is the opponent of craving, it is said that the foul is the proximate cause of serenity. Because it diminishes covetousness, abstinence from taking what is not given is said to be the proximate cause of non-greed. Similarly, because it diminishes ill will, abstinence from killing living beings is said to be the proximate cause of non-hatred. Non-perversion regarding the object is the penetration of the nature of the sense-field. Right practice is the accomplishment of virtue and concentration. Disenchantment is non-delight by means of knowledge, or it is simply the knowledge that proceeds in such a way. Having considered that all feeling is suffering because of its being suffering-as-suffering and so on, it was said: 'Feeling is the proximate cause for the perception of suffering.' As for 'perception of phenomena,' it is the perception 'it is mere phenomena.'

Sattānaṃ kāye avītarāgatā pañcannaṃ ajjhattikāyatanānaṃ vasena hotīti āha – “pañcindriyāni rūpīni rūparāgassa padaṭṭhāna”nti. Kāyo hi idha rūpanti adhippeto. Visesato jhānanissayabhūte manāyatane ca nikanti hotīti āha – “chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ bhavarāgassa padaṭṭhāna”nti. Edisaṃ mā rūpaṃ nibbattatu, mā edisī vedanāti evaṃ pavattā rūpādiabhinandanā nibbattabhavānupassitā. Ñāṇadassanassāti kammassakataññāṇadassanassa. Yonisomanasikāravato hi pubbenivāsānussati kammassakataññāṇassa kāraṇaṃ hoti, na ayoniso ummujjantassa. Imassa ca atthassa vibhāvanatthaṃ mahānāradakassapajātakaṃ (jā. 2.22.1153 ādayo), brahmajāle (dī. ni. 1.38 ādayo) ekaccasassatavādo ca udāharitabbo. “Okappanalakkhaṇā”tiādinā saddhāpasādānaṃ visesaṃ dasseti. So pana saddhāyayeva avatthāviseso daṭṭhabbo. Tattha okappanaṃ saddahanavasena ārammaṇassa ogāhaṇaṃ nicchayo. Anāvilatā [M 0.0093] assaddhiyāpagamena cittassa akālussiyatā. Abhipatthiyanā saddahanameva. Aveccapasādo paññāsahito āyatanagato abhippasādo. Apilāpanaṃ asammoso nimujjitvā viya ārammaṇassa ogāhaṇaṃ vā, ettha ca saddhādīnaṃ pasādasaddhāsammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānajhānaṅgāni yathākkamaṃ padaṭṭhānanti vadantena avatthāvisesavasena padaṭṭhānabhāvo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Satisamādhīnaṃ vā kāyādayo satipaṭṭhānāti. Vitakkādayo ca jhānānīti padaṭṭhānabhāvena vuttā.

The non-departure of lust in the body of beings is due to the five internal sense bases, thus it is said: 'The five material faculties are the proximate cause for lust for form.' For here, 'body' is intended as 'form.' Specifically, delight arises in the mind-base, which has become the support for jhāna, thus it is said: 'The sixth sense-base is the proximate cause for craving for existence.' The delight in form and so on, which proceeds as 'May such a form not arise, may such a feeling not arise,' is the contemplation of produced existence. 'Of knowledge and vision' means of the knowledge and vision that kamma is one's own property. For one who has wise attention, the recollection of past lives is a cause for the knowledge that kamma is one's own property; it is not for one who emerges with unwise attention. For the clarification of this meaning, the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka and the doctrine of some eternalists in the Brahmajāla Sutta should be cited. By 'characterized by confidence,' etc., it shows the distinction between faith and serenity. But that serenity should be seen as just a specific state of faith. Therein, confidence is the entering into and deciding upon the object by way of trust. Non-turbidity is the non-muddiness of the mind through the removal of disbelief. Aspiration is just trust. Unwavering confidence is profound serenity accompanied by wisdom, which has the Three Jewels as its object. Non-floating is non-confusion, or it is the entering into the object as if diving into it. And here, it should be understood that by the one who says that for faith and so on, serenity, faith, right effort, the foundations of mindfulness, and the jhāna factors are the proximate causes respectively, the state of being a proximate cause is spoken of by way of specific states. Or, the body and so on are called the foundations of mindfulness, and applied thought and so on are called the jhānas; they are spoken of as the proximate cause for mindfulness and concentration.

Assādamanasikāro [V 0.0221] saṃyojanīyesu dhammesu assādānupassitā. Punabbhavavirohaṇāti punabbhavāya virohaṇā, punabbhavanibbattanārahatā vipākadhammatāti attho. Opapaccayikanibbattilakkhaṇanti upapattibhavabhāvena nibbattanasabhāvaṃ. Nāmakāyarūpakāyasaṅghātalakkhaṇanti arūparūpakāyānaṃ samūhiyabhāvaṃ. Indriyavavatthānanti cakkhādīnaṃ channaṃ indriyānaṃ vavatthitabhāvo. Opapaccayikanti upapattikkhandhanibbattakaṃ. Upadhīti attabhāvo. Attano piyassa maraṇaṃ cintentassa bālassa yebhuyyena soko uppajjatīti maraṇaṃ sokassa padaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ. Ussukkaṃ cetaso santāpo. Odahananti avadahanaṃ. Attano nissayassa santapanameva bhavassāti vuttaṃ bhavaṃ dassetuṃ “imānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bhavassa aṅgāni bhavasaṅkhātāni ca aṅgāni bhavaṅgāni. Tesu kilesā bhavassa aṅgāni. Kammavipākavaṭṭaṃ bhavasaṅkhātāni aṅgāni. Samaggānīti sabbāni. Khandhāyatanādīnaṃ aparāparuppattisaṃsaraṇaṃ saṃsāro. Tassa purimapurimajātinipphannaṃ kilesādivaṭṭaṃ kāraṇanti āha – “bhavo saṃsārassa padaṭṭhāna”nti. Sampāpakahetubhāvaṃ sandhāya “maggo nirodhassa padaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ.

Attention to gratification is the contemplation of gratification in things that are bases for fetters. 'Sprouting of renewed existence' means sprouting for renewed existence; the meaning is the fitness to produce renewed existence, the nature of being a result. 'The characteristic of spontaneous arising' means the nature of arising through the state of rebirth-existence. 'The characteristic of the aggregate of the mental body and the physical body' means the state of being a collection of the formless body and the form body. 'The establishment of the faculties' is the defined state of the six faculties, such as the eye. 'Spontaneous' means productive of the rebirth-aggregates. 'Substratum' is individual existence. Because for a fool who thinks about the death of his own beloved one, sorrow generally arises, it is said that 'death is the proximate cause of sorrow.' 'Anxiety' is the torment of the mind. 'Putting down' is intense burning, the very tormenting of one's own support. To show the 'existence' that was spoken of as 'bhavassa' (of existence), the passage beginning 'these' was stated. Therein, the causes of existence and the parts designated as existence are the 'constituents of existence.' Among them, the defilements are the causes of existence. The round of kamma and the round of results are the parts designated as existence. 'United' means all. Saṃsāra is the wandering on through the successive arising of the aggregates, sense bases, and so on. Because the round of defilements, etc., produced in former and former births is its cause, he said: 'Existence is the proximate cause of saṃsāra.' With reference to its state of being a cause that brings one to it, it is said: 'The path is the proximate cause of cessation.'

Kammaṭṭhānogāhakassa otaraṇaṭṭhānatāya bahussuto titthaṃ nāma, tassa sammāpayirupāsanā titthaññutā. Dhammūpasañhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ pītaṃ nāma, sappāyadhammassavanena taṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānassa brūhanā pītaññutā, bhāvanāya thokampi layāpattiyā uddhaṃpattiyā ca jānanā pattaññutā. Attano pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgatassa jānanā attaññutā, tesu purimānaṃ purimānaṃ pacchimassa pacchimassa padaṭṭhānabhāvo suviññeyyo eva. Katapuññasseva patirūpadesavāso sambhavati[M 0.0094], na itarassāti “pubbekatapuññatā patirūpadesavāsassa padaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ saha adhiṭṭhānena taruṇavipassanā. Nibbidāti balavavipassanā. Virāgoti maggo. Vimuttīti phalaṃ. Evanti yadidaṃ “tassā vipallāsā padaṭṭhāna”ntiādinā avijjādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ, iminā nayena athāpi yo koci upanissayo balavapaccayoti yo koci avasesapaccayo, sabbo so padaṭṭhānaṃ kāraṇanti veditabbaṃ. “Evaṃ yā kāci upanisā yogato ca paccayato cā”tipi paṭhanti. Tattha upanisāti kāraṇaṃ, yogatoti yuttito, paccayatoti paccayabhāvamattatoti attho veditabbo. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

Because he is a place of descent for one who undertakes a meditation subject, a learned person is called a 'ford'; properly attending on him is 'knowledge of the ford.' Gladness connected with the Dhamma is called 'joy' (pīti); having generated that by hearing the suitable Dhamma, the cultivation of the meditation subject is 'knowledge of joy.' Knowing even a slight falling into laxity or into agitation in the development is 'knowledge of what is attained.' Knowing oneself to be endowed with the five factors of striving is 'knowledge of self.' Among these, that the former and former factors are the proximate cause for the latter and latter factors is very easy to understand. Only for one who has made merit is dwelling in a suitable place possible, not for another; therefore it is said: 'The making of merit in the past is the proximate cause for dwelling in a suitable place.' Knowledge and vision of things as they really are is tender insight together with its basis. 'Disenchantment' is powerful insight. 'Dispassion' is the path. 'Liberation' is the fruit. Thus: just as the proximate cause of ignorance and so on was shown by the passage beginning, 'its distortions are the proximate cause,' so too by this method it should be understood that whatever strong support condition and whatever remaining condition there is, all that is a proximate cause, a reason. They also recite: 'Thus, whatever condition there is, both through fitness and through causality.' Therein, the meaning should be understood thus: 'condition' means cause; 'through fitness' means through suitability; 'through causality' means merely through the state of being a condition. Whatever statement herein is not analyzed in terms of its meaning, that is very easy to understand.

Padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Proximate Cause is finished.

5. Lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Characteristics

23. Tattha [V 0.0222] katamo lakkhaṇo hārotiādi lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgo. Tattha kiṃ lakkhayatīti lakkhaṇahārassa visayaṃ pucchati. “Ye dhammā”tiādinā lakkhaṇahāraṃ saṅkhepato dassetvā taṃ udāharaṇehi vibhajituṃ “cakkhu”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha “vadhakaṭṭhena ekalakkhaṇānī”ti iminā anavaṭṭhitabhāvādināpi ekalakkhaṇatā vuttā evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

23. Therein, the passage beginning 'Which is the mode of characteristics?' is the Analysis of the Mode of Characteristics. Therein, by 'What does it characterize?' he asks about the scope of the mode of characteristics. Having shown the mode of characteristics in brief with 'Whatever phenomena,' etc., the passage beginning 'the eye,' etc., is begun in order to analyze it with examples. Therein, it should be understood that by this: 'they have a single characteristic in the sense of being a killer,' the state of having a single characteristic is also stated by way of the state of instability and so on.

Evaṃ āyatanavasena ekalakkhaṇataṃ dassetvā idāni khandhādivasena dassetuṃ “atīte, rādha, rūpe anapekkho hotī”tiādi suttaṃ ābhataṃ. Yamakovādasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.85) vadhakaṭṭhena ekalakkhaṇā vuttāti tasmiṃ sutte “vadhakaṃ rūpaṃ vadhakaṃ rūpanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī”tiādinā āgatattā vuttaṃ. Itīti evaṃ, imissaṃ gāthāyaṃ kāyagatāya satiyā vuttāya sati vedanāgatā sati cittagatā sati dhammagatā ca sati vuttā bhavati satipaṭṭhānabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattāti adhippāyo. Diṭṭhantiādīnaṃ atthaṃ parato vaṇṇayissāma.

Having thus shown the single characteristic by way of the sense bases, now, to show it by way of the aggregates and so on, the sutta beginning, 'Rādha, be without expectation regarding past form,' and so forth is introduced. In the Yamakovāda Sutta, it is said that [the aggregates] have a single characteristic in the sense of being a slaughterer, because in that sutta it is said: 'One does not understand as it really is, "Form is a slaughterer, form is a slaughterer,"' and so forth. Thus, in this way, in this verse, when mindfulness directed to the body has been stated, mindfulness directed to feeling, mindfulness directed to mind, and mindfulness directed to mental objects are also stated, the intention being that they are of a single characteristic in terms of being foundations of mindfulness. The meaning of 'seen' and so forth will be explained later.

Kāye [M 0.0095] kāyānupassī viharāhīti ettha kāyeti rūpakāye. Rūpakāyo hi idha aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kesādīnañca samūhaṭṭhena kāyoti adhippeto. Yathā ca samūhaṭṭhena, evaṃ kucchitānaṃ āyaṭṭhena. Kucchitānañhi paramajegucchānaṃ so āyotipi kāyo, āyoti uppattideso. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – āyanti tatoti āyo. Ke āyanti? Kucchitā kesādayo, iti kucchitānaṃ āyoti kāyo.

In the phrase 'Dwell contemplating the body in the body,' 'in the body' here means in the physical body. For the physical body is here intended as 'body' in the sense of being a collection of limbs major and minor, and of hair and so on. And just as it is in the sense of a collection, so too is it in the sense of being a source (āya) of repulsive things. For of repulsive, extremely loathsome things, it is the source (āya); for this reason also it is called 'kāya'. 'Āya' means place of origin. Herein is the word-meaning: They come (āyanti) from that (tato), therefore it is a source (āyo). What things come? Repulsive things, such as hair and so on. Thus, because it is the source (āya) of repulsive things, it is 'kāya' (body).

Kāyānupassīti kāyaṃ anupassanasīlo, kāyaṃ vā anupassamāno. “Kāye”ti ca vatvā puna “kāyānupassī”ti dutiyaṃ kāyaggahaṇaṃ asammissato vavatthānaghanavinibbhogādidassanatthaṃ. Tena na kāye vedanānupassī cittadhammānupassī vā, atha kho kāyānupassī evāti kāyasaṅkhāte vatthusmiṃ kāyānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā na kāye aṅgapaccaṅgavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, nāpi kesalomādivinimuttaitthipurisānupassī.

‘Contemplating the body’ means one who is in the habit of contemplating the body, or one who is contemplating the body. And having said ‘in the body,’ then saying again ‘contemplating the body’—this second taking up of the word ‘body’ is for the purpose of showing, by way of non-admixture, demarcation, the analysis of solidity, and so on. Therefore, one is not a contemplator of feeling in the body, or a contemplator of mind and mental objects, but rather one is solely a contemplator of the body. Thus, by showing the very mode of body-contemplation in the object designated as the body, demarcation by way of non-admixture is shown. Likewise, one is not a contemplator of a single phenomenon in the body apart from its limbs major and minor, nor a contemplator of a woman or man apart from hair, body hair, and so on.

Yopi cettha kesalomādiko bhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhāto kāyo, tatthapi na bhūtupādāyavinimuttaekadhammānupassī[V 0.0223], atha kho rathasambhārānupassako viya aṅgapaccaṅgasamūhānupassī, nagarāvayavānupassako viya kesalomādisamūhānupassī, kadalikkhandhapattavaṭṭivinibbhujjako viya rittamuṭṭhiviniveṭhako viya ca bhūtupādāyasamūhānupassī evāti nānappakārato samūhavaseneva kāyasaṅkhātassa vatthuno dassanena ghanavinibbhogo dassito hoti. Na hettha yathāvuttasamūhavinimutto kāyo vā añño vā koci dhammo dissati, yathāvuttadhammasamūhamatte eva pana tathā tathā sattā micchābhinivesaṃ karonti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

And whatever body there is here, designated as a collection of primary and derived matter, consisting of hair, body hair, and so on, in that too one is not a contemplator of a single phenomenon apart from the primary and derived matter. But rather, like one who inspects the components of a chariot, one contemplates the collection of limbs major and minor; like one who inspects the parts of a city, one contemplates the collection of hair, body hair, and so on; and like one who peels off the sheaths of a plantain trunk or like one who unclasps an empty fist, one is solely a contemplator of the collection of primary and derived matter. Thus, in various ways, by showing the object designated as 'body' solely by way of being a collection, the analysis of solidity is shown. For here, neither a body nor any other phenomenon is seen apart from the aforementioned collection. But it is on just this mere collection of phenomena as described that beings, in various ways, form a wrong adherence. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Yaṃ passati na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passati;

Apassaṃ bajjhate mūḷho, bajjhamāno na muccatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.36; mahāni. aṭṭha. 3);

“What one sees is not the seen; what is seen, that one does not see. Not seeing, the deluded one is bound; being bound, one is not freed.”

Ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthanti ādisaddena ayamattho veditabbo. Ayañhi etasmiṃ kāye kāyānupassīyeva, na aññadhammānupassī.

In the phrase 'for the purpose of showing the analysis of solidity, etc.,' this meaning should be understood by the word 'etc.': For this one is, in this body, solely a contemplator of the body, not a contemplator of other phenomena.

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā anudakabhūtāyapi marīciyā udakānupassino honti, na evaṃ aniccadukkhānattaasubhabhūte eva imasmiṃ kāye niccasukhaattasubhabhāvānupassī[M 0.0096], atha kho kāyānupassī aniccadukkhaanattaasubhākārasamūhānupassīti attho. Atha vā yvāyaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhāne (dī. ni. 2.374 ādayo) assāsapassāsādicuṇṇikajātaaṭṭhikapariyosāno kāyo vutto, yo ca “idhekacco pathavīkāyaṃ aniccato anupassati, āpokāyaṃ tejokāyaṃ vāyokāyaṃ kesakāyaṃ…pe… aṭṭhimiñjakāya”nti paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.34 ādayo) kāyo vutto, tassa sabbassa imasmiṃyeva kāye anupassanato kāye kāyānupassīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

This is what is said: Just as there are those who perceive water in a mirage, although it is not water, it is not so that in this body, which is in fact impermanent, suffering, not-self, and impure, one contemplates a state of permanence, pleasure, self, and beauty. But rather, one is a contemplator of the body, a contemplator of the collection of characteristics of impermanence, suffering, not-self, and impurity—this is the meaning. Alternatively, there is the body described in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Dī. Ni. 2.374 ff.), from the in-and-out breaths ending with bones become scattered powder; and there is the body described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 3.34 ff.) thus: “Here, someone contemplates the earth-body as impermanent, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, the hair-body… up to the bone-marrow-body.” Because all of that is contemplated in this very body, the meaning here should also be understood as: one contemplates the body in the body.

Atha vā kāye ahanti vā mamanti vā gahetabbassa kassaci ananupassanato, tassa pana kesalomādikassa nānādhammasamūhassa anupassanato kāye kesādidhammasamūhasaṅkhāte kāyānupassīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Api ca “imasmiṃ kāye aniccato anupassati no niccato”tiādinā anukkamena paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.34 ādayo) āgatanayassa sabbasseva [V 0.0224] aniccalakkhaṇādikassa ākārasamūhasaṅkhātassa kāyassa anupassanato kāye kāyānupassīti attho.

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as: one is a contemplator of the body in the body designated as a collection of phenomena such as hair, because of not contemplating anything in the body to be grasped as “I” or “mine,” but because of contemplating that collection of various phenomena such as hair, body hair, and so on. Moreover, according to the method that has come down sequentially in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 3.34 ff.), beginning with “one contemplates this body as impermanent, not as permanent,” the meaning is that one is a contemplator of the body in the body because of contemplating the body designated as a collection of characteristics such as impermanence.

Viharāhīti vattāhi. Ātāpīti tīsu bhavesu kilese ātāpetīti ātāpo, so assa atthīti ātāpī. Sampajānoti sampajaññasaṅkhātena ñāṇena samannāgato. Satimāti kāyapariggāhikāya satiyā samannāgato. Ayaṃ pana yasmā satiyā ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā paññāya anupassati, na hi sativirahitā anupassanā atthi, tenevāha – “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Anātāpino ca anto saṅkoco antarāyakaro hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sampajjati. Tasmā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ānubhāvena taṃ sampajjati, taṃ dassanatthaṃ “ātāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Dwell' (viharāhi) means 'abide' (vattāhi). 'Ardent' (ātāpī): Ardor (ātāpa) is that which scorches the defilements in the three existences; because one possesses that ardor, one is called ardent. 'Clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) means endowed with the knowledge designated as clear comprehension. 'Mindful' (satimā) means endowed with mindfulness that grasps the body. But since this one grasps the object with mindfulness and then contemplates it with wisdom—for there is no contemplation without mindfulness—therefore He said: “Mindfulness, bhikkhus, I declare to be beneficial everywhere” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.234). And for one who is not ardent, inner constriction is an obstacle; the meditation subject is not accomplished. Therefore, to show those qualities by the power of which it is accomplished, the words “ardent,” etc., are stated.

Tattha vineyyāti tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā vinayitvā. Loketi tasmiṃyeva kāye. Kāyo hi idha lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti adhippeto. Abhijjhāggahaṇena cettha kāmacchando, domanassaggahaṇena byāpādo gahitoti nīvaraṇesu balavadhammadvayappahānadassanena nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttanti kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānassa pahānaṅgaṃ [M 0.0097] dassitaṃ. “Ātāpī”tiādinā pana sampayogaṅgaṃ dassitanti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “ātāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha abhijjhādomanassānaṃ samatho ujupaṭipakkhoti abhijjhādomanassavinayo vuccamāno samādhindriyaṃ dīpetīti āha – “vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti samādhindriya”nti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.367). Ekalakkhaṇattā catunnaṃ indriyānanti yathā vīriyapaññāsamādhindriyehi kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ ijjhati, evaṃ vedanācittadhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānānipi tehi ijjhantīti catusatipaṭṭhānasādhane imesaṃ indriyānaṃ sabhāvabhedābhāvato samānalakkhaṇattā itarāni satipaṭṭhānānipi vuttāni eva hontīti attho.

Herein, “having subdued” (vineyya) means having subdued either by subduing by substitution (tadaṅgavinaya) or by subduing by suppression (vikkhambhanavinaya). “In the world” (loke) refers to that very body. For here, the body is intended as “world” in the sense of perishing and crumbling. And here, by the taking up of “covetousness” (abhijjhā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is taken; by the taking up of “grief” (domanassa), ill will (byāpāda) is taken. Therefore, by showing the abandoning of the pair of strong states among the hindrances, the abandoning of the hindrances is stated. Thus, the factor of abandoning of the establishment of mindfulness through contemplation of the body is shown. But by “ardent,” etc., the factor of association is shown. To show this meaning, “ardent,” etc., is stated. Therein, the calming of covetousness and grief is the direct opposite. Therefore, when the subduing of covetousness and grief is being spoken of, it illuminates the faculty of concentration. Thus, it is said: “Having subdued covetousness and grief in the world—this is the faculty of concentration.” Because the four faculties have a single characteristic: just as the establishment of mindfulness through contemplation of the body is accomplished by the faculties of energy, wisdom, and concentration, so too the establishments of mindfulness through contemplation of feelings, mind, and dhammas are accomplished by them. Therefore, in the accomplishment of the four establishments of mindfulness, because of the non-difference in the intrinsic nature of these faculties and because of their similar characteristic, the other establishments of mindfulness are also indeed spoken of. This is the meaning.

24. Idāni satipaṭṭhānesu gahitesu sabbesaṃ bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ gahitabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “catūsu satipaṭṭhānesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bodhaṅgamāti bodhaṃ ariyamaggañāṇaṃ gacchantīti bodhaṅgamā. Yathāvuttassa bodhassa pakkhe bhavāti bodhipakkhiyā. Neyyānikalakkhaṇenāti ettha nimittato pavattato ca vuṭṭhānaṃ niyyānaṃ, niyyāne niyuttāti neyyānikā, yathā dovārikoti. Niyyānasaṅkhātaṃ vā phalaṃ arahantīti neyyānikā. Niyyānaṃ payojanaṃ etesanti vā neyyānikā. “Niyyānikā”tipi pāṭho, tattha niyyānaṃ etesaṃ atthīti niyyānikāti [V 0.0225] attho. “Niyyāniyā”tipi pāṭho, tassa niyyantīti niyyāniyāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Niyyānikalakkhaṇenāti niyyānikasabhāvena.

24.
