Now, to show that when the establishments of mindfulness are taken up, all the qualities pertaining to enlightenment are also taken up, it is said, “In the four establishments of mindfulness,” and so on. Herein, as for ‘factors of enlightenment’: they go to enlightenment, the knowledge of the Noble Path, therefore they are factors of enlightenment. They are ‘qualities pertaining to enlightenment’ because they are on the side of the aforesaid enlightenment. As for ‘by the characteristic of leading out’: herein, emergence from the sign and from the process of existence is ‘leading out.’ They are engaged in leading out, therefore they are ‘leading out,’ just as a doorkeeper. Or, they are ‘leading out’ because they are worthy of the fruit designated as ‘leading out.’ Or, they are ‘leading out’ because leading out is their purpose. There is also the reading ‘niyyānikā’; therein, the meaning is ‘they have leading out, therefore they are niyyānikā.’ There is also the reading ‘niyyāniyā’; its meaning should be understood as ‘they lead out, therefore they are niyyāniyā.’ ‘By the characteristic of leading out’ means by the nature of leading out.

Evaṃ akusalāpi dhammāti yathā kusalā dhammā ekalakkhaṇabhāvena niddhāritā, evaṃ akusalāpi dhammā ekalakkhaṇaṭṭhena niddhāretabbā. Kathaṃ? Pahānekaṭṭhatāvasenāti dassento “pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchantī”ti āha. Idāni taṃ pahānaṃ dassetuṃ “catūsu satipaṭṭhānesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kāyānupassanādīsu catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu bhāviyamānesu asubhe subhantiādayo cattāro vipallāsā pahīyanti, kabaḷīkārāhārādayo cattāro āhārā cassa pariññaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ parijānanassa paribandhino kāmarāgādayo byantīkatā hontīti attho, kasmā? Tehi pahātabbabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattāti. Evaṃ sabbattha attho yojetabbo. Tenevāha – “evaṃ akusalāpi dhammā ekalakkhaṇattā pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchantī”ti.

Thus, regarding unwholesome states: just as wholesome states are determined by way of having a single characteristic, so too, unwholesome states should be determined by way of having a single characteristic. How? Showing that it is by way of having the single state of being abandoned, he said, “they go to the setting of abandonment.” Now, to show that abandonment, it is said, “in the four establishments of mindfulness,” and so on. Therein, when the four establishments of mindfulness, such as contemplation of the body, are being developed, the four perversions, such as perceiving the attractive in the unattractive, are abandoned; and the four kinds of nutriment, such as physical food, go to full understanding for that person. The meaning is that sensual lust and so on, which are obstacles to the full understanding of them, are brought to an end. Why? Because of having the single characteristic of being that which should be abandoned by them. Thus, the meaning should be applied everywhere. For that very reason, he said: “Thus, unwholesome states, too, due to their single characteristic, go to the setting of abandonment.”

Idāni [M 0.0098] aññenapi pariyāyena lakkhaṇahārassa udāharaṇāni dassetuṃ “yattha vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yatthāti yassaṃ desanāyaṃ. Vā-saddo vikappattho. Panāti padapūraṇo. Rūpindriyanti ruppanasabhāvaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ indriyaṃ. Tatthāti tassaṃ desanāyaṃ. Rūpadhātūti ruppanasabhāvā dasa dhātuyo. Rūpāyatananti ruppanasabhāvaṃ dasāyatanaṃ, rūpīni dasāyatanānīti attho. Ruppanalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā imāni desitānīti adhippāyo. Desitaṃ tattha sukhindriyaṃ somanassindriyaṃ sukhavedanābhāvena ekalakkhaṇattāti adhippāyo.

Now, to show examples of the characteristic mode by another method, it is said, “or wherever,” and so on. Therein, ‘wherever’ means in whichever teaching. The word ‘vā’ has the meaning of an alternative. ‘Pana’ is a particle for filling out the meter. ‘The faculty of form’ means the eightfold faculty with the nature of being afflicted. ‘Therein’ means in that teaching. ‘The element of form’ means the ten elements with the nature of being afflicted. ‘The base of form’ means the ten bases with the nature of being afflicted; the meaning is the ten physical bases. The intention is that these are taught because they have the single characteristic of being afflicted. The intention is that the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy are taught therein because they have the single characteristic of being pleasant feeling.

Dukkhasamudayo ca ariyasaccanti idaṃ akusalassa somanassassa vasena vuttaṃ, sāsavakusalassāpi vasena yujjati eva. Sabbo ca paṭiccasamuppādo desitoti sambandho. Avijjānusayitattā adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya. Vuttañhetaṃ – “adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo anusetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.465). Tathā ca vuttaṃ “adukkhamasukhāya hi vedanāya avijjā anusetī”ti. Etena adukkhamasukhāvedanāggahaṇena avijjā gahitāti dasseti. Sati ca avijjāggahaṇe sabbo paṭiccasamuppādo desitoti dassetuṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādi vuttaṃ. So cāti ettha ca-saddo byatirekattho, tena so paṭiccasamuppādo anulomapaṭilomavasena duvidhoti imaṃ vakkhamānavisesaṃ joteti. Tesu anulomato paṭiccasamuppādo yathādassito sarāgasadosasamohasaṃkilesapakkhena hātabboti vutto, paṭilomato pana paṭiccasamuppādo yo “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā”tiādinā pāḷiyaṃ [V 0.0226] (ma. ni. 3.126; mahāva. 1) vutto, taṃ sandhāya “vītarāgavītadosavītamohaariyadhammehi hātabbo”ti vuttaṃ.

This phrase, ‘and the noble truth of the origin of suffering,’ is stated by way of unwholesome joy; it is indeed also applicable by way of wholesome joy connected with cankers. The connection is: ‘and all of dependent origination is taught.’ This is because of the underlying tendency of ignorance in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. For this has been said: ‘In neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency of ignorance lies latent.’ And so it is said: ‘Indeed, in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, ignorance lies latent.’ By this, he shows that through the taking up of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, ignorance is taken up. And to show that when ignorance is taken up, all of dependent origination is taught, it is said: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations arise,’ and so on. Herein, in ‘so ca,’ the word ‘ca’ has the meaning of distinction; by that, it illuminates this following distinction: that dependent origination is twofold, by way of forward order and reverse order. Among these, dependent origination in forward order, as shown, is said to be that which is to be grasped as on the side of defilement with lust, with hate, and with delusion. But dependent origination in reverse order, which is stated in the Pali text as ‘With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance…,’ and so on, referring to that, it is said, ‘is to be grasped by means of the noble Dhamma free from lust, free from hate, and free from delusion.’

Idāni ekalakkhaṇatāvibhāvanena lakkhaṇahārayojanāya nayaṃ dassetuṃ “evaṃ ye dhammā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kiccatoti pathavīādīnaṃ phassādīnañca rūpārūpadhammānaṃ sandhāraṇasaṅghaṭṭanādikiccato, tesaṃ tesaṃ vā paccayadhammānaṃ taṃtaṃpaccayuppannadhammassa paccayabhāvasaṅkhātakiccato. Lakkhaṇatoti kakkhaḷaphusanādisabhāvato. Sāmaññatoti ruppananamanādito aniccatādito khandhāyatanādito ca. Cutūpapātatoti saṅkhatadhammānaṃ bhaṅgato uppādato ca, samānanirodhato samānuppādato cāti [M 0.0099] attho. Ettha ca sahacaraṇaṃ samānahetutā samānaphalatā samānabhūmitā samānavisayatā samānārammaṇatāti evamādayopi ca-saddena saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

Now, to show the method for the application of the characteristic mode by explaining the state of having a single characteristic, the passage beginning with ‘Thus, those phenomena…’ is stated. Therein, ‘by function’ refers to the function of the material and immaterial phenomena, such as the earth element and contact, in terms of supporting, colliding, and so on; or, it refers to the function of the respective conditioning phenomena, which is designated as being a condition for the respective conditioned phenomenon. ‘By characteristic’ refers to their intrinsic nature, such as hardness and touching. ‘By generality’ refers to being afflicted, bending, and so on; to impermanence and so on; and to the aggregates, sense bases, and so on. ‘By passing away and arising’ means by the dissolution and arising of conditioned phenomena; the meaning is by simultaneous cessation and simultaneous arising. Herein, it should be understood that such terms as ‘co-occurrence,’ ‘having the same cause,’ ‘having the same result,’ ‘having the same plane,’ ‘having the same scope,’ and ‘having the same object’ are also included by the particle ‘ca.’ The rest has a clear meaning.

Lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Characteristic Mode is completed.

6. Catubyūhahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Analysis of the Fourfold Array Mode

25. Tattha katamo catubyūho hāroti catubyūhahāravibhaṅgo. Tattha byañjanena suttassa neruttañca adhippāyo ca nidānañca pubbāparasandhi ca gavesitabboti saṅkhepena tāva catubyūhaṃ dasseti. “Byañjanenā”ti iminā hārānaṃ suttassa byañjanavicayabhāvato byañjanamukheneva ete catubyūhahārapadatthā niddhāretabbāti dasseti. Neruttanti niruttaṃ nibbacananti attho. Niruttameva neruttaṃ. Tenevāha – “yā niruttipadasaṃhitā”ti. Tassattho – yā nirutti, idaṃ neruttaṃ. Kā pana sā nirutti? Padasaṃhitāti padesu saṃhitā yuttā, liṅgavacanakālasādhanapurisādivisesayogena yo yo attho yathā yathā vattabbo, tathā tathā pavattasabhāvaniruttīti attho. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “yaṃ dhammānaṃ nāmaso ñāṇa”nti.

25. Herein, 'What is the fourfold array mode?' is the analysis of the fourfold array mode. Therein, with the passage, 'By the expression, the etymology, the intention, the basis, and the sequential connection of the sutta should be investigated,' he first shows the fourfold array mode in brief. By the phrase 'By the expression,' he shows that because, among the modes, this one has the nature of investigating the expression of a sutta, the meanings of the terms of this fourfold array mode should be determined only through the expression as the entry point. 'Neruttaṃ' means niruttaṃ (etymology) or nibbacanaṃ (derivation); this is the meaning. Nirutta itself is nerutta. For that very reason, he said: 'That nirutti which is connected to the terms.' Its meaning is: that which is nirutti, this is nerutta. But what is that nirutti? 'Connected to the terms' means connected to or suitable for the terms. The meaning is: the natural derivation that occurs in such and such a way, according to whatever meaning is to be expressed in whatever way by connection with distinctions such as gender, number, tense, instrument, and person. For so it was said: 'The knowledge of phenomena by name.'

Tattha yanti hetuatthe nipāto, yāya kāraṇabhūtāyāti attho. Dhammānanti ñeyyadhammānaṃ. Nāmasoti pathavī phasso khandhā dhātu tisso phussoti evamādināmavisesena ñāṇaṃ pavattati, ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti nāma. Pathavīti hi evamādikaṃ saddaṃ gahetvā tato paraṃ saṅketadvārena tadatthapaṭipatti taṃtaṃaniyatanāmapaññattiggahaṇavaseneva hotīti. Atha vā padasaṃhitāti padena saṃhitā[V 0.0227]. Padato hi padatthāvabodho. So panassa atthe pavattinimittabhūtāya paññattiyā gahitāya eva hotīti sā pana paññatti niruttisaṅkhātapadena saṃhitā padatthaṃ bodhetīti padasaṃhitāti vuttā. “Yadā hi bhikkhū”tiādinā “dhammānaṃ nāmaso ñāṇa”nti padassa atthaṃ vivarati.

Therein, 'yaṃ' is a particle in the sense of cause; the meaning is 'by which nirutti that is the cause.' 'Dhammānaṃ' means of knowable phenomena. 'Nāmaso' means knowledge arises through the distinction of names such as earth, contact, aggregates, element, Tissa, Phussa, and so on; this is called natural derivation. For, having taken a word such as 'earth,' the subsequent understanding of its meaning through convention occurs only by the power of grasping the respective unfixed name-concept. Alternatively, 'padasaṃhitā' means connected with the term. For the understanding of the meaning of a term comes from the term. But that understanding occurs only when the concept, which is the ground for its occurrence in that meaning, has been grasped. That concept, being connected with the term called nirutti, makes known the meaning of the term; therefore, it is called 'padasaṃhitā.' With the passage beginning 'Yadā hi bhikkhū...,' he explains the meaning of the phrase 'the knowledge of phenomena by name.'

Tattha atthassāti saddābhidheyyassa atthassa. Nāmaṃ jānātīti nāmapaññattivasena ayaṃ nāmāti nāmaṃ jānāti. Dhammassāti sabhāvadhammassa. Tathā [M 0.0100] tathā naṃ abhiniropetīti yo yo attho dhammo ca yathā yathā ca voharitabbo, tathā tathā naṃ nāmaṃ vohāraṃ abhiniropeti desetīti attho. Ettāvatā ca ayaṃ bhikkhu atthakusalo yāva anekādhivacanakusaloti vuccatīti sambandhitabbaṃ.

Herein, 'of the meaning' means of the meaning expressed by the word. 'He knows the name' means that by way of name-concept, he knows the name thus: 'This is the name.' 'Of the phenomenon' means of the natural phenomenon. 'He applies it accordingly' means: whatever meaning and whatever natural phenomenon is to be designated in whatever way, he applies that name and designation accordingly; he teaches it. This is the meaning. And to this extent, it should be connected that this bhikkhu is said to be 'skilled in meaning' up to 'skilled in various designations.'

Tattha atthakusaloti pāḷiatthe kusalo. Dhammakusaloti pāḷiyaṃ kusalo. Byañjanakusaloti akkharesu ca vākyesu ca kusalo. Niruttikusaloti nibbacane kusalo. Pubbāparakusaloti desanāya pubbāparakusalo. Desanākusaloti dhammassa desanāya kusalo. Atītādhivacanakusaloti atītapaññattikusalo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Evaṃ sabbāni kātabbāni, janapadaniruttānīti yattakāni sattavohārapadāni, tāni sabbāni yathāsambhavaṃ sutte nibbacanavasena kātabbāni vattabbānīti attho. Sabbā ca janapadaniruttiyoti sabbā ca lokasamaññāyo yathārahaṃ kātabbā. “Samaññaṃ nātidhāveyyā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Tathā hi sammutisaccamukheneva paramatthasaccādhigamo hotīti.

Herein, 'skilled in meaning' means skilled in the meaning of the Pāḷi. 'Skilled in the Dhamma' means skilled in the Pāḷi. 'Skilled in expression' means skilled in letters and in sentences. 'Skilled in etymology' means skilled in derivation. 'Skilled in the before and after' means skilled in the before and after of the teaching. 'Skilled in teaching' means skilled in teaching the Dhamma. 'Skilled in past designations' means skilled in past concepts. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. Regarding 'Thus all regional expressions should be employed,' the meaning is that however many terms of worldly parlance there are, all those terms should be treated and spoken of in the sutta by way of derivation as is suitable. And 'all regional expressions' means all worldly conventions should be treated appropriately. For it is said, 'One should not transgress convention.' For it is only through conventional truth as the entry point that the attainment of ultimate truth occurs.

26. Adhippāyakaṇḍe anuttānaṃ nāma natthi.

26. In the section on intention, there is no such thing as an unclear term.

27. Nidānakaṇḍe iminā vatthunāti iminā puttagavādikittanasaṅkhātena kāraṇena. Kāraṇañhettha vatthu nidānanti ca vuttaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbattha nidānaniddhāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

27. In the section on basis, 'by this matter' means by this cause, which is designated as the mention of sons, cattle, and so on. And herein, a cause is also called a 'matter' and a 'basis.' In this way, the determination of the basis should be understood in all cases.

Kāmandhāti kilesakāmena andhā. Jālasañchannāti taṇhājālapaliguṇṭhitā. Taṇhāchadanachāditāti taṇhāsaṅkhātena andhakārena pihitā. Bandhanābaddhāti kāmaguṇasaṅkhātena bandhanena baddhā. “Pamattabandhanā”tipi pāṭho, pamādenāti attho. Pubbāparenāti pubbena vā aparena vā desanantarenāti adhippāyo. Yujjatīti yogaṃ upeti, sametīti attho. Imehi padehi [V 0.0228] pariyuṭṭhānehīti imehi yathāvuttehi gāthāpadehi taṇhāpariyuṭṭhānadīpakehi. Sāyeva taṇhāti yā purimagāthāya vuttā, sāyeva taṇhā. “Yañcāhā”tiādinā dvinnampi gāthānaṃ atthasaṃsandanena pubbāparaṃ vibhāveti. Payogenāti samudācārena. Tasmāti yattha sayaṃ uppannā, taṃ santānaṃ nissarituṃ adentī nānārammaṇehi [M 0.0101] palobhayamānā kilesehi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Tasmā kilesavasena ca pariyuṭṭhānavasena ca taṇhābandhanaṃ vuttā.

‘Blinded by lust’ means blinded by the defilement of sensual pleasure. ‘Covered by a net’ means enveloped by the net of craving. ‘Shrouded by craving’ means covered by the darkness that is craving. ‘Bound by fetters’ means bound by the bondage that is sensual qualities. There is also the reading ‘bound by heedlessness’; the meaning is ‘by heedlessness.’ ‘Earlier and later’ means the implication is by another discourse, either preceding or succeeding. ‘Fits’ means it connects, it agrees; this is the meaning. ‘By these obsessions’ means by these lines of the verse, as stated, which illuminate the obsession of craving. ‘That very craving’ is the craving that was mentioned in the previous verse. Through ‘and what was said,’ and so on, he clarifies the preceding and succeeding teachings by connecting the meaning of both verses. ‘By application’ means by conduct. ‘Therefore’—because, in whatever mental continuum it has arisen, not allowing that continuum to escape, enticing it with various objects, it stands, having completely taken over the mind with defilements. Therefore, craving is called a bondage, both by way of defilements and by way of obsession.

Papañcenti saṃsāre ciraṃ ṭhapentīti papañcā. Tiṭṭhanti etāhīti ṭhitī. Bandhanaṭṭhena sandānaṃ viyāti sandānaṃ. Nibbānanagarappavesassa paṭisedhanato palighaṃ viyāti palighaṃ. Anavasesataṇhāpahānena nittaṇho. Attahitaparahitānaṃ idhalokaparalokānañca munanato munīti evaṃ gāthāya padattho veditabbo. Papañcādiatthā pana pāḷiyaṃ vibhattā evāti. Tattha yassete papañcādayo abbhatthaṃ gatā, tassa taṇhāya lesopi na bhavati. Tena vuttaṃ – “yo etaṃ sabbaṃ samatikkanto, ayaṃ vuccati nittaṇho”ti.

They cause one to delay for a long time in saṃsāra; hence, they are called 'papañcā' (proliferations). By these they stand; thus, they are called 'ṭhitī' (stabilities). Because of the nature of binding, like a tether, it is called 'sandānaṃ' (tether). Because it obstructs entry into the city of Nibbāna, like a crossbar, it is called 'palighaṃ' (crossbar). By the abandoning of craving without remainder, one is 'nittaṇho' (craving-free). Because he knows the welfare of oneself and others, and of this world and the next, he is called 'munī' (sage). Thus, the meaning of the words of the verse should be understood. The meanings of 'papañcā' and so on, however, are already explained in the Pāḷi text. Therein, for whichever sage these proliferations and so on have gone to cessation, for him not even a trace of craving exists. Therefore, it is said: 'He who has completely overcome all this is called craving-free.'

28. Pariyuṭṭhānanti “taṇhāya pariyuṭṭhāna”nti vuttāni taṇhāvicaritāni. Saṅkhārāti “tadabhisaṅkhatā saṅkhārā”ti vuttā taṇhādiṭṭhimānahetukā saṅkhārā. Te pana yasmā sattasu javanacetanāsu paṭhamacetanā sati paccayasamavāye imasmiṃyeva attabhāve phalaṃ deti. Pacchimacetanā anantare attabhāve. Ubhinnaṃ vemajjhacetanā yattha katthaci phalaṃ deti, tasmā vipaccanokāsavasena vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana taṃtaṃcetanāsampayuttā taṇhāpi cetanā viya diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādivasena tidhā hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ – “evaṃ taṇhā tividhaṃ phalaṃ detī”ti. Pubbāparena yujjatīti yaṃ pubbaṃ purimaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyatādivacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ iminā aparena kammassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyatādivacanena yujjati gaṅgodakaṃ viya yamunodakena saṃsandati sametīti attho.

28. ‘Pariyuṭṭhāna’ (obsessions) are the misconducts of craving, which are spoken of as ‘the obsession of craving.’ ‘Saṅkhārā’ (formations) are the formations, spoken of as ‘formations conditioned by that,’ which have craving, views, and conceit as their cause. Now, concerning these, because among the seven javana-volitions, the first volition, when there is a conjunction of conditions, gives its fruit in this very existence; the last volition gives its fruit in the immediately following existence; and the volitions between those two give their fruit anywhere at all—therefore, to show this division by way of the opportunity for ripening, it is said: ‘to be experienced in the here-and-now,’ and so on. Moreover, because craving associated with those respective volitions is also threefold, like volition, by way of being experienced in the here-and-now, and so on, it is therefore said: ‘Thus, craving gives a threefold fruit.’ ‘It fits with the preceding and succeeding’ means: the preceding, earlier statement that was made about formations being experienced in the here-and-now, and so on, fits with this succeeding statement about kamma being experienced in the here-and-now, and so on, just as the water of the Ganges connects and combines with the water of the Yamunā; this is the meaning.

Saṅkhārā dassanabalenāti catūsu diṭṭhigatasampayuttesu vicikicchāsampayutte cāti pañcasu cittuppādesu saṅkhārā paṭhamamaggapaññābalena. Chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritāni bhāvanābalenāti paṭhamamaggena pahīnāvasesavasena vuttaṃ, na sabbesaṃ vasena.

‘Formations by the power of vision’ means: the formations in the five arisings of consciousness—that is, in the four associated with wrong view and the one associated with doubt—are abandoned by the power of the wisdom of the first path. ‘The thirty-six misconducts of craving by the power of development’—this is said by way of what remains after having been abandoned by the first path, not by way of all of them.

Anubandhoti taṇhādīnaṃ anuppabandhena pavatti. Yo cāpi papañcotiādinā “papañcetī”tiādinā vuttaṃ rādhasuttañcasaṃsandati. Tenevāha – “idaṃ ekattha”nti. Yadipi atthato [V 0.0229] ekaṃ, desanāya pana viseso [M 0.0102] vijjatīti dassetuṃ “api cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evanti iminā vuttappakārena. Suttenāti saṃvaṇṇiyamānena suttena. Suttanti suttantaraṃ. Saṃsandayitvāti vimissitvā atthato abhinnaṃ katvā. Pubbāparena saddhiṃ yojayitvāti pubbena vā aparena vā suttena saddhiṃ atthato sambandhaṃ yojetvā. Vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti tena suttassa attho niddiṭṭho hoti vitthārito suttantaradassanena.

‘Following’ means the proceeding by way of the uninterrupted sequence of craving and so on. By the phrase ‘And what is proliferation,’ and so on, he connects the sutta spoken of with the phrase ‘one proliferates,’ and so on, and the Rādha Sutta. For that very reason, he said: ‘This is one in meaning.’ To show that although it is one in meaning, there is a difference in the teaching, ‘Moreover,’ and so on, was said. ‘Thus’ means in this stated manner. ‘By the sutta’ means by the sutta that is being commented upon. ‘Sutta’ means another sutta. ‘Having connected’ means having mixed, having made it not different in meaning. ‘Having joined with the preceding and succeeding’ means having joined in a connection of meaning with either the preceding or the succeeding sutta. He makes clear the very meaning that was stated. By that, the meaning of the sutta becomes pointed out and is expanded by the showing of another sutta.

Na kevalaṃ suttantarasaṃsandanameva pubbāparasandhi, atha kho aññopi atthīti dassetuṃ “so cāya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha atthasandhīti kiriyākārakādivasena atthassa sambandho. So pana yasmā saṅkāsanādīnaṃ channaṃ atthapadānaṃyeva hoti, sabbassāpi padatthassa tadavarodhato.

The connection of preceding and succeeding is not merely the connecting of another sutta; but to show that there is also another kind, ‘so cāyaṃ,’ and so on, was said. Therein, ‘connection of meaning’ is the connection of meaning by way of action, agent, and so on. That connection, however, belongs only to the six terms of meaning, such as elucidation, because all word-meanings are included in them.

Sambandho ca nāma na koci attho. Tasmā “atthasandhi chappadānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Byañjanasandhīti padassa padantarena sambandho. Yasmā pana sabbampi nāmādipadaṃ chahi byañjanapadehi asaṅgahitaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā “byañjanasandhi chappadānī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

And the term ‘connection’ is not a meaning in itself. Therefore, ‘the connection of meaning is sixfold,’ and so on, was said. ‘Grammatical connection’ is the connection of a word with another word. Moreover, because there is no word, such as a noun, that is not included within the six grammatical terms, ‘grammatical connection is sixfold,’ and so on, was said.

Desanāsandhīti yathāvuttadesanantarena desanāya saṃsandanaṃ. Na ca pathaviṃ nissāyāti pathaviṃ visayasaṅkhātaṃ nissayaṃ katvā, pathaviṃ ālambitvāti attho. Jhāyīti phalasamāpattijhānena jhāyī. So hi sabbasaṅkhāranissaṭaṃ nibbānaṃ ālambitvā samāpajjanavasena jhāyati, na pathaviṃ nissāya jhāyatīti vutto. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca catūhi mahābhūtehi rūpappaṭibaddhavuttitāya sabbo kāmabhavo rūpabhavo ca gahitā. Arūpabhavo pana sarūpeneva gahitoti sabbaṃ lokaṃ pariyādiyitvā puna aññenapi pariyāyena taṃ dassetuṃ “na ca imaṃ loka”ntiādimāha. Sabbo hi loko idhaloko paraloko cāti dveva koṭṭhāsā honti. Yasmā pana “idhaloko”ti visesato diṭṭhadhammabhūto sattasantāno vuccati. “Paraloko”ti bhavantarasaṅkhepagato sattasantāno tadubhayavinimutto anindriyabaddho rūpasantāno. Tasmā taṃ sandhāya “yamidaṃ ubhayamantarenā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Connection of the Teaching’ is the connection of a teaching with a previously stated teaching. ‘And not depending on earth’ means: having made the earth element, which is called an object, a support, and having taken the earth element as an object. ‘One who enters jhāna’ refers to one who enters jhāna by means of the jhāna of fruition attainment. For that person enters jhāna by way of attaining absorption, taking as object Nibbāna which is liberated from all formations; he does not enter jhāna by depending on the earth element—thus it is said. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Herein, the entire sense-sphere existence and form-sphere existence are included because their existence is connected with form through the four great elements. The formless existence, however, is included by its own nature. Having encompassed the entire world, to show it by another method, it is said, ‘and not this world,’ and so on. For the entire world consists of only two divisions: this world and the other world. However, by ‘this world’ is specifically meant the continuum of beings that is the presently visible life. By ‘the other world’ is meant the continuum of beings that has passed into another existence. There is a continuum of form, liberated from both of these and not bound to the faculties. Therefore, with reference to that, it is said, ‘that which is between both,’ and so on.

Ye pana “ubhayamantarenā”ti vacanaṃ gahetvā antarābhavaṃ icchanti, tesaṃ taṃ micchā. Antarābhavo hi abhidhamme paṭikkhittoti. Diṭṭhanti rūpāyatanaṃ[M 0.0103]. Sutanti saddāyatanaṃ. Mutanti patvā gahetabbato gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanañca. Viññātanti avasiṭṭhaṃ dhammārammaṇapariyāpannarūpaṃ. Pattanti pariyesitvā vā apariyesitvā vā pattaṃ. Pariyesitanti pattaṃ [V 0.0230] vā appattaṃ vā pariyesitaṃ. Vitakkitaṃ vicāritanti vitakkanavasena anumajjanavasena ca ālambitaṃ. Manasānucintitanti cittena anu anu cintitaṃ. Ayaṃ sadevake…pe… anissitena cittena na ñāyati jhāyantoti ayaṃ khīṇāsavo phalasamāpattijhānena jhāyanto pubbeva taṇhādiṭṭhinissayānaṃ suṭṭhu pahīnattā sadevake loke…pe… manussāya yattha katthacipi anissitena cittena jhāyati nāma. Tato eva loke kenacipi na ñāyati “ayaṃ idaṃ nāma nissāya jhāyatī”ti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But as for those who, taking the phrase ‘between both,’ desire an intermediate existence, that is wrong. For the intermediate existence is rejected in the Abhidhamma. ‘Seen’ is the form base. ‘Heard’ is the sound base. ‘Sensed’ refers to the odor base, taste base, and tangible base, because they are to be grasped by contact. ‘Cognized’ is the remaining form included in the mental-object base. ‘Attained’ is that which is reached, whether sought or not sought. ‘Sought’ is that which is sought, whether attained or not attained. ‘Thought upon and pondered’ is that which is taken as an object by way of initial thought and sustained application. ‘Reflected upon by mind’ is that which is repeatedly thought of by the mind. As for ‘This one… is not known while entering jhāna with an unattached mind’: this one whose taints are destroyed, entering jhāna by means of the jhāna of fruition attainment, is said to enter jhāna with an unattached mind anywhere at all in the world with its devas… among the generation with its devas and humans, because the supports of craving and views have already been well abandoned. For that very reason, it is not known by anyone in the world, ‘This person enters jhāna depending on such-and-such.’ For this was said:

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te nābhijānāma, kiṃ tvaṃ nissāya jhāyasī”ti. (netti. 104);

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men; homage to you, O supreme man. We do not know what you rely upon to enter jhāna.”

Idāni khīṇāsavacittassa katthacipi anissitabhāvaṃ godhikasuttena (saṃ. ni. 1.159) vakkalisuttena (saṃ. ni. 3.87) ca vibhāvetuṃ “yathā māro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Viññāṇaṃ samanvesantoti parinibbānato uddhaṃ viññāṇaṃ pariyesanto. “Papañcātīto”tiādinā adassanassa kāraṇamāha. Anissitacittā na ñāyanti jhāyamānāti na kevalaṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā khīṇāsavassa cittagatiṃ mārādayo na jānanti, api ca kho saupādisesāyapi nibbānadhātuyā tassa taṃ na jānantīti attho. Ayaṃ desanāsandhīti godhikasuttavakkalisuttānaṃ viya suttantānaṃ aññamaññaatthasaṃsandanā desanāsandhi nāma.

Now, to clarify by means of the Godhika Sutta and the Vakkali Sutta the unattached state anywhere of the mind of one whose taints are destroyed, the text beginning 'yathā māro' was stated. 'Viññāṇaṃ samanvesanto' (searching for consciousness) means seeking the consciousness that is beyond parinibbāna. With the text beginning 'papañcātīto' (gone beyond proliferation), the reason for not seeing is stated. Regarding 'Anissitacittā na ñāyanti jhāyamānā' (Those with unattached minds are not known while meditating), the meaning is this: it is not only that Māra and others do not know the course of the mind of one whose taints are destroyed in the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, but rather, they do not know it even in the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining. This is desanāsandhi (Connection of the Teaching): like the mutual connection of meaning of the Godhika Sutta and the Vakkali Sutta, the mutual connection of meaning of suttas is called desanāsandhi.

Niddesasandhīti niddesassa sandhi niddesasandhi, niddesena vā sandhi niddesasandhi. Purimena suttassa niddesena tasseva pacchimassa niddesassa, pacchimena vā purimassa sambandhananti attho. Taṃ dassetuṃ yasmā bhagavā yebhuyyena paṭhamaṃ vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā pacchā vivaṭṭaṃ dasseti, tasmā “nissitacittā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nissitaṃ cittaṃ etesanti nissitacittā, puggalā, niddisitabbā puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāyāti adhippāyo. Dhammādhiṭṭhānāya pana nissitaṃ cittaṃ etthāti nissitacittā, nissitacittavanto taṇhādiṭṭhinissayavasena pavattā suttapadesā. Sesamettha sabbaṃ pākaṭameva.

'Niddesasandhi' (Connection of the Exposition) is the connection of an exposition, or the connection with an exposition. The meaning is: the connection of the latter exposition of a sutta with its former exposition, or of the former with the latter. To show this, because the Blessed One for the most part first shows the round of existence and afterwards shows the ending of the round, therefore the text beginning 'nissitacittā' (those with dependent minds) was stated. Therein, 'nissitacittā' means 'those who have a dependent mind'; the intention is that individuals are to be indicated by means of a teaching founded on individuals. But in the case of a teaching founded on phenomena, 'nissitacittā' means 'wherein there is a dependent mind'; this refers to the passages of the sutta which proceed by way of the supports of craving and views, and which possess dependent minds. The rest here is all clear.

Catubyūhahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Analysis of the Fourfold Array is finished.

7. Āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Analysis of the Reversion Application

29. Tattha [V 0.0231][M 0.0104] katamo āvaṭṭo hāroti āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgo. Tattha ārambhathāti ārambhadhātusaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ karotha. Nikkamathāti kosajjapakkhato nikkhantattā nikkamadhātusaṅkhātaṃ taduttarivīriyaṃ karotha. Yuñjatha buddhasāsaneti yasmā sīlasaṃvaro indriyesu guttadvāratā bhojane mattaññutā satisampajaññanti imesu dhammesu patiṭṭhitānaṃ jāgariyānuyogavasena ārambhanikkamadhātuyo sampajjanti, tasmā tathābhūtasamathavipassanāsaṅkhāte bhagavato sāsane yuttappayuttā hotha. Dhunātha maccuno senaṃ, naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaroti evaṃ paṭipajjantā ca tedhātuissarassa maccurājassa vasaṃ satte netīti tassa senāsaṅkhātaṃ abalaṃ dubbalaṃ yathā nāma balūpapanno kuñjaro naḷehi kataṃ agāraṃ khaṇeneva viddhaṃseti, evameva kilesagaṇaṃ dhunātha vidhamatha viddhaṃsethāti attho (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.185).

29. Herein, 'What is the reversion application?' is the Analysis of the Reversion Application. Therein, 'ārambhatha' (begin) means: undertake the effort called the element of initiating. 'Nikkamatha' (exert) means: because of having departed from the side of laziness, undertake the further effort called the element of exertion. 'Yuñjatha buddhasāsane' (Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching) means: because for those established in these things—moral restraint, guardedness of the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, mindfulness, and clear comprehension—the elements of initiating and exertion are accomplished by way of devotion to wakefulness, therefore, be diligently engaged in the Blessed One's teaching, which is called serenity and insight of such a kind. 'Dhunātha maccuno senaṃ, naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaro' (Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant a reed hut) means: for those practicing thus, just as a powerful elephant in a moment destroys a house made of reeds, even so, shake off, dispel, and destroy the mass of defilements, which is called the weak and feeble army of the King of Death, the lord of the three realms, who leads beings under his power. This is the meaning.

Idāni yadatthaṃ ayaṃ gāthā nikkhittā, taṃ yojetvā dassetuṃ “ārambhatha nikkamathāti vīriyassa padaṭṭhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ārambhatha nikkamathāti idaṃ vacanaṃ vīriyassa padaṭṭhānaṃ vīriyapayogassa kāraṇaṃ vīriyārambhe niyojanato, “yogā ve jāyatī bhūrī”ti (dha. pa. 282) vacanato yogo bhāvanā. Tattha vipassanābhāvanāya vakkhamānattā samādhibhāvanā idhādhippetāti vuttaṃ – “yuñjatha buddhasāsaneti samādhissa padaṭṭhāna”nti. “Maccuno sena”nti vuttāya kilesasenāya sammā dhunanaṃ ñāṇeneva hotīti āha – “dhunātha…pe… padaṭṭhāna”nti. Puna yathāvuttavīriyasamādhipaññāsampayuttesu ādhipaccakiccatāya papañcappahānasamatthā vaṭṭamūlaṃ chinditvā vivaṭṭaṃ pāpenti cāti dassanatthaṃ “ārambhatha nikkamathāti vīriyindriyassa padaṭṭhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Imāni padaṭṭhānāni desanāti “yānimāni vīriyassa padaṭṭhāna”ntiādinā vīriyādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānāni vuttāni, sā ārambhatha nikkamathāti ādidesanā, na vīriyārambhavatthuādīnīti attho. Tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ.

Now, to show for what purpose this verse was set forth by connecting it, the text beginning with 'ārambhatha nikkamathāti vīriyassa padaṭṭhānaṃ' (Begin, strive—this is the foundation of energy) was stated. Therein, the statement 'Begin, strive' is the foundation of energy, the cause for the application of energy, because it enjoins the undertaking of energy. In accordance with the saying, 'From exertion, indeed, wisdom arises' (Dhp. 282), 'exertion' means 'cultivation.' Therein, because insight cultivation will be spoken of later, concentration cultivation is intended here; therefore, it was stated: 'Apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching—this is the foundation of concentration.' Because the proper shaking off of the army of defilements—which is what is meant by 'the army of Death'—is accomplished only by wisdom, he said: 'Shake off… the foundation of wisdom.' Furthermore, to show that energy, concentration, and wisdom, as previously described, through their function of dominance among associated states, are capable of abandoning proliferation, and having cut off the root of the round, they lead to the ending of the round, the text beginning with 'Begin, strive—this is the foundation of the faculty of energy' was stated. Regarding the phrase 'These foundations are the teaching': by the phrase 'the foundation of energy,' etc., the foundations of energy and so on are stated. That foundation is the teaching beginning with 'Begin, strive,' and not the grounds for undertaking energy, etc. This is the meaning. And it is explained in just that way.

Evaṃ yathānikkhittāya desanāya padaṭṭhānavasena atthaṃ niddhāretvā idāni taṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammavasena āvaṭṭetukāmo tassa bhūmiṃ dassetuṃ [M 0.0105] “ayuñjantānaṃ vā sattānaṃ yoge yuñjantānaṃ vā ārambho”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yoge bhāvanāyaṃ taṃ ayuñjantānaṃ vā sattānaṃ [V 0.0232] aparipakkañāṇānaṃ vāsanābhāgena āyatiṃ vijānanatthaṃ ayaṃ desanārambho yuñjantānaṃ vā paripakkañāṇānanti.

Thus, having determined the meaning of the teaching as it was set forth by way of its foundations, now, wishing to expound upon it by way of similar and dissimilar states, and in order to show the basis for this, he stated the text beginning with: 'The beginning of this teaching is for beings who are not applying themselves to the exertion, or for those who are applying themselves.' The meaning of this is: this beginning of the teaching is for the future understanding, through the portion of their latent tendencies, of beings who are not applying themselves to that exertion—that is, cultivation—and whose knowledge is immature; or it is for the attainment of distinction for beings who are applying themselves and whose knowledge is mature.

So pamādo duvidhoti yena pamādena bhāvanaṃ nānuyuñjanti, so pamādo attano kāraṇabhedena duvidho. Aññāṇenāti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇapaṭicchādakena sammohena. Nivutoti chādito. Ñeyyaṭṭhānanti ñeyyañca taṃ “iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo”tiādinā ñāṇassa pavattanaṭṭhānañcāti ñeyyaṭṭhānaṃ. Anekabhedattā pāpadhammānaṃ tabbasena anekabhedopi pamādo mūlabhūtāya avijjāya vasena eko evāti āha – “ekavidho avijjāyā”ti. Lābhavinicchayapariggahamacchariyāni pariyesanāārakkhāparibhogesu antogadhāni. Chandarāgajjhosānā taṇhā evāti taṇhāmūlakepi dhamme ettheva pakkhipitvā “tividho taṇhāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'That heedlessness is twofold': the heedlessness by which they do not engage in cultivation, that heedlessness is twofold by way of the distinction of its causes. 'By ignorance' means by the delusion that conceals the specific and general characteristics of the five aggregates. 'Covered' means veiled. 'The basis for knowledge' means it is both that which is to be known and, by way of 'this is form, this is the origin of form,' etc., it is the basis for the arising of knowledge; therefore, it is called the 'basis for knowledge.' Although heedlessness is of many kinds by way of evil states, which are of many kinds, he says, 'onefold by way of ignorance,' because it is only one by way of fundamental ignorance. Gain, deciding, possessing, and stinginess are included in seeking, guarding, and using. Desire, lust, and clinging are craving itself; therefore, having included even states rooted in craving right here, it was said: 'threefold by way of craving.'

Rūpīsu bhavesūti rūpadhammesu. Ajjhosānanti taṇhābhiniveso. Etena “taṇhāya rūpakāyo padaṭṭhāna”nti padassa atthaṃ vivarati. Anādimati hi saṃsāre itthipurisā aññamaññarūpābhirāmā, ayañcattho cittapariyādānasuttena (a. ni. 1.1-10) dīpetabbo. Arūpīsu sammohoti phassādīnaṃ atisukhumasabhāvattā santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanavinibbhogassa dukkarattā ca arūpadhammesu sammoho, sattānaṃ patiṭṭhitoti vacanaseso. Evaṃ niddhārite rūpakāyanāmakāyasaṅkhāte upādānakkhandhapañcake ārammaṇakaraṇavasena pavattaṃ taṇhañca avijjañca avisesena vuttaṃ catupādānānaṃ vasena vibhajitvā tesaṃ khandhānaṃ upādānānañca dukkhasamudayabhāvena sahapariññeyyapahātabbabhāvaṃ dasseti “tattha rūpakāyo”tiādinā.

‘In existences with form’ means in form-states. ‘Clinging’ means adherence through craving. By this, he explains the meaning of the phrase, ‘the body of form is the foundation of craving.’ For in beginningless saṃsāra, men and women delight in each other's forms; this meaning should be illustrated by the Cittapariyādāna Sutta. ‘Confusion regarding the formless’ means that because of the extremely subtle nature of contact and other formless states, and because of the difficulty of analyzing separately the continuity-mass, the group-mass, the function-mass, and the object-mass, confusion regarding formless states is established for beings—this is the remainder of the statement to be supplied. Thus, with regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging—designated as the ‘body of form’ and the ‘body of name’—which have been determined in this way, he takes craving and ignorance, which were stated without distinction as occurring by way of taking them as object, and, having divided them by way of the four kinds of clinging, he shows, with the text beginning ‘Therein, the body of form...,’ the state of those aggregates as things to be fully understood along with their nature as suffering, and the state of those clingings as things to be abandoned along with their nature as the origin of suffering.

30. Evaṃ pamādamukhena purimasaccadvayaṃ niddhāretvā pamādamukheneva aparampi saccadvayaṃ niddhāretuṃ “tattha yo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tassāti tassa pamādassa. Sampaṭivedhenāti sammā parijānanena assādādīnaṃ jānanena. Rakkhaṇā paṭisaṃharaṇāti attano cittassa rakkhaṇasaṅkhātā pamādassa paṭisaṃharaṇā, tappaṭipakkhena saṅkocanā appamādānuyogena yā [M 0.0106] khepanā. Ayaṃ samathoti kiccena samādhiṃ dasseti. Ayaṃ vodānapakkhavisabhāgadhammavasena āvaṭṭanā. “Yadā jānāti kāmānaṃ…pe… ānisaṃsa”nti iminā samathādhigamassa upāyaṃ dasseti.

30. Thus, having determined the first pair of truths through the gateway of heedlessness, the text beginning with ‘Therein, whoever...’ is stated in order to determine the latter pair of truths also through the gateway of heedlessness. Therein, ‘of that’ means of that heedlessness. ‘Through penetration’ means through proper understanding, by knowing the gratification, and so on. ‘Protection and withdrawal’ means the withdrawal of heedlessness, which is described as the protection of one's own mind; it is the shrinking back by means of its opposite, the elimination that occurs through the application of heedfulness. By ‘This is serenity,’ he shows concentration by its function. This is the exposition by way of a dissimilar state belonging to the side of purification. By the text ‘When one knows the gratification of sensual pleasures... the benefit,’ he shows the means for the attainment of serenity.

Tattha [V 0.0233] kāmānanti vatthukāmānañca kilesakāmānañca. Assādañca assādatoti kāme paṭicca uppajjamānaṃ sukhasomanassasaṅkhātaṃ assādaṃ assādatāya assādamattato. Ādīnavanti “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.236) vuttaṃ ādīnavaṃ dosaṃ. Nissaraṇanti paṭhamajjhānaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhamma”nti (itivu. 72). Okāranti lāmakabhāvaṃ. Saṃkilesanti saṃkilissanaṃ. Kāmahetu hi sattā saṃkilissanti. Vodānanti visujjhanaṃ. Nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsanti nīvaraṇappahānādiguṇavisesayogaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ yathāvutte samathe sati. Yā vīmaṃsāti yā paññā. “Samāhito, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1071) hi vuttaṃ. Yathā taṇhāsahitāva avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo, evaṃ avijjāsahitāva taṇhā upādānānaṃ paccayo. Tāsu niruddhāsu upādānādīnaṃ abhāvo evāti taṇhāavijjāpahānena sakalavaṭṭadukkhanirodhaṃ dassento “imesu dvīsu dhammesu pahīnesū”tiādimāha. Imāni cattāri saccāni visabhāgasabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavasena niddhāritānīti adhippāyo.

Herein, ‘of sensual pleasures’ means: of both object-sensual-pleasures and defilement-sensual-pleasures. ‘And gratification as gratification’ means: the gratification, described as pleasure and joy, that arises dependent on sensual pleasures, is known by way of its gratifying nature and as mere gratification. ‘The danger’ means: the danger, the fault, spoken of as ‘sensual pleasures have little gratification and much suffering,’ and so on. ‘The escape’ means: the first jhāna. For it has been said: ‘This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation.’ ‘Degradation’ means: the state of being base. ‘Defilement’ means: the state of being defiled. For beings are defiled on account of sensual pleasures. ‘Purification’ means: cleansing. ‘And the benefit in renunciation’ means: the connection with special qualities such as the abandoning of the hindrances. ‘Therein’ means: when that aforementioned serenity exists. ‘What investigation’ means: what wisdom is. For it has been said: ‘A monk who is concentrated, O monks, understands things as they truly are.’ Just as ignorance accompanied by craving is a condition for formations, so too, craving accompanied by ignorance is a condition for clinging. When these have ceased, there is only the non-arising of clinging and so on. Thus, showing the cessation of all the suffering of the round of existence through the abandoning of craving and ignorance, he says, ‘When these two states are abandoned,’ and so on. The meaning is that these four truths have been determined by way of the revolving of dissimilar and similar states.

Evaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ nikkhipitvā tassa visabhāgadhammavasena sabhāgadhammavasena ca āvaṭṭanaṃ dassetvā idāni saṃkilesapakkhaṃ nikkhipitvā tassa visabhāgadhammavasena sabhāgadhammavasena ca āvaṭṭanaṃ dassetuṃ “yathāpi mūle”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho – yathā nāma patiṭṭhāhetubhāvena mūlanti laddhavohāre bhūmigate rukkhassa avayave pharasuchedādiantarāyābhāvena anupaddave tato eva daḷhe thire sati khandhe chinnepi assatthādirukkho ruhati, evameva taṇhānusayasaṅkhāte attabhāvarukkhassa mūle maggañāṇapharasunā anupacchinne tayidaṃ dukkhaṃ punappunaṃ aparāparabhāvena nibbattati na nirujjhatīti. Kāmataṇhādinivattanatthaṃ “bhavataṇhāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Etassa dhammassa paccayoti etassa bhavataṇhāsaṅkhātassa dhammassa bhavesu ādīnavappaṭicchādanādivasena assādaggahaṇassa paccayo. Vuttañhetaṃ – “saṃyojanīyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino [M 0.0107] taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.57). Tenevāha – “avijjāpaccayā hi bhavataṇhā”ti. Idha samatho vipassanā ca maggasamādhi maggapaññā ca adhippetāti āha – “yena taṇhānusayaṃ samūhanatī”tiādi. Imāni cattāri saccānīti visabhāgasabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavasena niddhāritānīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, having set aside the section on purification and shown its revolving by way of dissimilar and similar states, now, having set aside the section on defilement, in order to show its revolving by way of dissimilar and similar states, he spoke the verse ‘Just as with the root.’ Its meaning is this: Just as, when the part of a tree that is in the ground, which has received the designation ‘root’ because it is the cause of its establishment, is unharmed by the absence of dangers such as being cut by an axe, and is thereby firm and stable, even if the trunk is cut, a tree such as an assattha regrows; so too, when the root of the tree of individual existence, called the latent tendency of craving, is not cut off by the axe of path-knowledge, this suffering arises again and again in succession and does not cease. For the purpose of averting craving for sensual pleasures and so on, ‘by craving for existence’ was said. ‘A condition for this state’ means: it is a condition for the grasping of gratification by way of concealing the danger in states of existence, and so on, for this state called craving for existence. For this has been said: ‘Bhikkhus, for one who repeatedly sees gratification in things that are bases for fetters, craving increases.’ Therefore he said: ‘For craving for existence is conditioned by ignorance.’ Herein, serenity and insight, and path-concentration and path-wisdom are intended. Therefore, he said, ‘by which one uproots the latent tendency of craving,’ and so on. These four truths have been determined by way of the revolving of dissimilar and similar states. The rest is just as has been explained.

Idāni na kevalaṃ niddhāriteheva visabhāgasabhāgadhammehi āvaṭṭanaṃ, atha kho pāḷiāgatehipi tehi āvaṭṭanaṃ āvaṭṭahāroti dassanatthaṃ “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti gāthamāha[V 0.0234]. Tattha sabbapāpassāti sabbākusalassa. Akaraṇanti anuppādanaṃ. Kusalassāti catubhūmakakusalassa. Upasampadāti paṭilābho. Sacittapariyodāpananti attano cittavodānaṃ, taṃ pana arahattena hoti. Iti sīlasaṃvarena sabbapāpaṃ pahāya samathavipassanāhi kusalaṃ sampādetvā arahattaphalena cittaṃ pariyodapetabbanti etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ ovādo anusiṭṭhīti ayaṃ saṅkhepattho, vitthārato pana attho pāḷito eva viññāyati.

Now, in order to show that the Method of Revolving is not merely the revolving by means of dissimilar and similar states that have been determined, but rather the revolving by means of those that have come in the Pāli text, he spoke the verse ‘The non-doing of all evil.’ Therein, ‘of all evil’ means: of all that is unwholesome. ‘Non-doing’ means: non-production. ‘Of the wholesome’ means: of the wholesome of the four planes. ‘Accomplishment’ means: acquisition. ‘The purification of one’s own mind’ means: the cleansing of one’s own mind, and that comes about through Arahantship. Thus: having abandoned all evil through restraint in virtue, having accomplished the wholesome through serenity and insight, the mind is to be purified with the fruit of Arahantship. This is the teaching, advice, and instruction of the Buddhas. This is the brief meaning; but the detailed meaning is to be understood from the Pāli itself.

Tattha “sabbapāpaṃ nāmā”tiādīsu dosasamuṭṭhānanti doso samuṭṭhānameva etassāti dosasamuṭṭhānaṃ, na doso eva samuṭṭhānanti. Lobhasamuṭṭhānāyapi pisuṇavācāya sambhavato. Kāyaduccaritanti padaṃ apekkhitvā “dosasamuṭṭhāna”nti napuṃsakaniddeso. Lobhasamuṭṭhānaṃ mohasamuṭṭhānanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Samphappalāpo uddhaccacittena pavattayatīti adhippāyena tassa mohasamuṭṭhānatā vuttā.

Therein, in 'all evil is named,' and so on, 'rooted in aversion' means it has aversion as its origin; it should not be understood as 'aversion alone is its origin,' because of the possibility of divisive speech that is also rooted in greed. With reference to the term 'bodily misconduct,' the neuter designation 'rooted in aversion' occurs. Here too, in 'rooted in greed' and 'rooted in delusion,' this is the same method. With the intention that frivolous talk is produced by a restless mind, its state of being rooted in delusion was stated.

Evaṃ duccaritaakusalakammapathakammavibhāgena “sabbapāpa”nti ettha vuttapāpaṃ vibhajitvā idānissa akusalamūlavasena agatigamanavibhāgampi dassetuṃ “akusalamūla”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha akusalamūlaṃ payogaṃ gacchantanti lobhādiakusalāni kāyavacīpayogaṃ gacchantāni, kāyavacīpayogaṃ samuṭṭhāpentānīti attho. Chandāti chandahetu. Yaṃ chandā agatiṃ gacchati, idaṃ lobhasamuṭṭhānanti chandā agatiṃ gacchatīti yadetaṃ agatigamanaṃ, idaṃ lobhasamuṭṭhānanti. Evaṃ sesesupi attho daṭṭhabbo. Ettāvatā “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti ettha pāpaṃ dassetvā idāni tassa akaraṇaṃ dassento “lobho…pe… paññāyā”ti tīhi kusalamūlehi [M 0.0108] tiṇṇaṃ akusalamūlānaṃ pahānavasena sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ anuppādanamāha. Tathā lobho upekkhāyātiādinā brahmavihārehi. Tattha aratiṃ vūpasamentī muditā tassā mūlabhūtaṃ mohaṃ pajahatīti katvā vuttaṃ – “moho muditāya pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatī”ti.

Thus, having analyzed the evil spoken of in 'all evil' by way of the division of misconduct, unwholesome courses of action, and kamma, now, in order to also show its division as wrong courses by way of unwholesome roots, 'unwholesome root,' and so on, was said. Therein, 'an unwholesome root going to application' means: unwholesome states such as greed going to bodily and verbal application; the meaning is: giving rise to bodily and verbal application. 'From desire' means: on account of desire. 'That which goes to a wrong course from desire, this is rooted in greed' means: this going to a wrong course which is on account of desire, this is rooted in greed. Thus the meaning should be understood in the remaining cases as well. To this extent, having shown the evil in 'the non-doing of all evil,' now, showing its non-doing, he speaks of the non-doing, the non-production, of all evil by way of abandoning the three unwholesome roots by means of the three wholesome roots, with the words 'greed... by wisdom.' Likewise, with 'greed by equanimity,' and so on, he speaks of this by means of the divine abidings. Therein, since appreciative joy, by pacifying discontent, abandons the delusion that is its root, it was said: 'Delusion goes to abandonment and destruction by means of appreciative joy.'

31. Idāni aññenapi pariyāyena pāpaṃ tassa akaraṇañca dassetvā sesapadānañca atthavibhāvanamukhena sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbapāpaṃ nāma aṭṭha micchattānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Akiriyā akaraṇaṃ anajjhācāroti tīhipi padehi micchattānaṃ anuppādanameva vadati. Tathā kiriyā karaṇaṃ ajjhācāroti tīhipi padehi uppādanameva vadati. Ajjhācāroti adhiṭṭhahitvā ācaraṇaṃ. Atītassāti cirakālappavattivasena purāṇassa. Maggassāti ariyamaggassa. Vuttañhetaṃ – “purāṇamaggaṃ purāṇaṃ añjasanti kho ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa [V 0.0235] maggassa adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.65 atthato samānaṃ). Atītena vā vipassinā bhagavatā yathādhigataṃ desitabhāvaṃ sandhāya “atītassa maggassā”ti vuttaṃ. Vipassino hi ayaṃ bhagavato sammāsambuddhassa pātimokkhuddesagāthāti.

31. Now, by another method, having shown evil and its non-doing, and in order to show the revolving of similar and dissimilar states by means of elucidating the meaning of the remaining terms, the text beginning with, “All evil, namely, the eight wrongnesses,” was spoken. By the three terms 'non-action,' 'non-doing,' and 'non-transgression,' it speaks only of the non-arising of wrongnesses. Likewise, by the three terms 'action,' 'doing,' and 'transgression,' it speaks only of their arising. 'Transgression' means acting after having undertaken it. 'Of the past' means of the ancient, by way of its prevalence for a long time. 'Of the path' means of the Noble Path. For this was said: “The ancient path, the ancient highway—this, indeed, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path.” Or, 'of the past path' is said with reference to the fact that it was taught by the Blessed One Vipassī in the past according to how it was realized. For this is the Pātimokkha recitation verse of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Fully Enlightened Buddha.

Yaṃ paṭivedhenāti yassa pariññābhisamayena. Yaṃ pariyodāpitaṃ, ayaṃ nirodhoti yadipi asaṅkhatā dhātu kenaci saṃkilesena na saṃkilissati, adhigacchantassa pana puggalassa vasena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa hi yāva saṃkilesā na vigacchanti, tāva asaṅkhatā dhātu apariyodapitāti vuccati. Yathā nibbānādhigamena ye khandhā vūpasametabbā, tesaṃ sesabhāvena asesabhāvena ca “saupādisesā”ti ca, “anupādisesā”ti ca vuccati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'By means of the penetration of which' means by the full understanding and comprehension of which. Regarding the statement, 'That which is purified, this is cessation'—although the unconditioned element is not defiled by any defilement, it is spoken of in this way from the perspective of the person who attains it. For, as long as defilements have not departed from that person, the unconditioned element is said to be unpurified. Just as, through the attainment of Nibbāna, concerning the aggregates that are to be pacified, it is called 'with residue remaining' and 'without residue remaining' based on whether there is a residue of them or no residue, so should this successful application be understood.

Imāni pāḷiāgatadhammānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavasena niddhāritāni cattāri saccāni punapi pāḷiāgatadhammānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanena āvaṭṭahāraṃ dassetuṃ “dhammo have rakkhatī”ti gāthamāha. Tassā padattho pubbe vutto eva. Dhammoti puññadhammo idhādhippeto. Taṃ vibhajitvā dassento “dhammo nāma duvidho indriyasaṃvaro maggo cā”ti āha. Indriyasaṃvarasīsena cettha sabbampi sīlaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ[M 0.0109]. Sabbā upapattiyo duggati dukkhadukkhatādiyogena dukkhā gatiyoti katvā. Yathāvutte duvidhe dhamme paṭhamo dhammo yathā suciṇṇo hoti, yato ca so rakkhati, yattha ca patiṭṭhāpeti, taṃ sabbaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha yā saṃvarasīle akhaṇḍakāritā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idāni tassa dhammassa apāyato rakkhaṇe ekantikabhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ gāmaṇisaṃyutte (saṃ. ni. 4.358) asibandhakaputtasuttaṃ ābhataṃ.

These Four Truths have been determined by way of the revolving of similar and dissimilar phenomena among the teachings found in the Pāli. Again, to demonstrate the Revolving Method by the revolving of similar and dissimilar phenomena among the teachings found in the Pāli, he stated the verse, “Dhamma truly protects.” The meaning of its words has already been stated before. Here, by 'Dhamma' is intended meritorious Dhamma. Analyzing and showing it, he said: “Dhamma is twofold: restraint of the senses and the Path.” And here, it should be understood that by the heading 'restraint of the senses,' all virtue is included. All states of existence are miserable destinations because they are painful destinations due to their connection with the suffering of suffering, etc. Regarding the aforementioned twofold Dhamma, to show all of this—how the first Dhamma is well-practiced, from what it protects, and where it establishes—the text beginning with, “Therein, the unbroken practice in the virtue of restraint,” was stated. Now, to clarify the certainty of that Dhamma's protection from the lower realms, the Asibandhakaputta Sutta from the Gāmaṇisaṃyutta is brought forth.

Tattha evanti pakārena. Ca-saddo sampiṇḍane, imināpi pakārena ayamattho veditabboti adhippāyo. Asibandhakaputtoti asibandhakassa nāma putto. Gāme jeṭṭhakatāya gāmaṇī. Pacchābhūmakāti pacchābhūmivāsino. Kāmaṇḍalukāti sakamaṇḍaluno. Sevālamālikāti pātova udakato sevālañceva uppalādīni ca gahetvā udakasuddhibhāvajānanatthaṃ mālaṃ katvā piḷandhanakā. Udakorohakāti sāyaṃ pātaṃ udakaṃ orohaṇakā. Uyyāpentīti upariyāpenti. Saññāpentīti sammā yāpenti. Saggaṃ nāma okkāmentīti parivāretvā ṭhitāva “gaccha, bho, brahmalokaṃ, gaccha, bho, brahmaloka”nti vadantā saggaṃ pavesenti.

Therein, 'evaṃ' is in the sense of 'manner.' The particle 'ca' is for aggregation; the intention is that this meaning should be understood in this manner also. 'Asibandhakaputta' means the son of one named Asibandhaka. He is called a 'gāmaṇī' (headman) because of his position as chief in the village. 'Pacchābhūmakā' means dwellers in the western land. 'Kāmaṇḍalukā' means those with their own water pots. 'Sevālamālikā' means those who wear garlands, having made them in the early morning after taking moss and lotuses, etc., from the water in order to know the state of the water's purity. 'Udakorohakā' means those who descend into the water in the evening and morning. 'Uyyāpenti' means they cause to go up. 'Saññāpenti' means they guide well. 'Saggaṃ nāma okkāmenti' means they usher into heaven, having surrounded him and while standing there, saying, “Go, good sir, to the Brahma-world! Go, good sir, to the Brahma-world!”

Anuparisakkeyyāti [V 0.0236] anuparigaccheyya. Ummujjāti uṭṭhaha. Uplavāti jalassa upariplava. Thalamuplavāti thalaṃ abhiruha. Tatra yāssāti tatra yaṃ assa, yaṃ bhaveyya. Sakkharakaṭhalanti sakkharā vā kaṭhalā vā. Sā adhogāmī assāti sā adho gaccheyya, heṭṭhāgāmī bhaveyya. Adho gaccheyyāti heṭṭhā gaccheyya. Maggassāti ariyamaggassa. Tikkhatāti tikhiṇatā. Sā ca kho na satthakassa viya nisitakaraṇatā, atha kho indriyānaṃ paṭubhāvoti dassetuṃ “adhimattatā”ti āha. Nanu ca ariyamaggo attanā pahātabbakilese anavasesaṃ samucchindatīti atikhiṇo nāma natthīti? Saccametaṃ, tathāpi no ca kho “yathā diṭṭhippattassā”ti vacanato saddhāvimuttadiṭṭhippattānaṃ kilesappahānaṃ pati atthi kāci visesamattāti sakkā vattuṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso na idhādhippeto, sabbupapattisamatikkamanassa adhippetattā. Yasmā pana ariyamaggena odhiso kilesā pahīyanti, tañca nesaṃ tathāpahānaṃ maggadhammesu indriyānaṃ [M 0.0110] apāṭavapāṭavatarapāṭavatamabhāvena hotīti yo vajirūpamadhammesu matthakappattānaṃ aggamaggadhammānaṃ paṭutamabhāvo. Ayaṃ idha maggassa tikkhatāti adhippetā. Tenevāha – “ayaṃ dhammo suciṇṇo sabbāhi upapattīhi rakkhatī”ti. “Tasmā rakkhitacittassā”tiādinā suttantarena (udā. 32) sugatisaññitānampi upapattīnaṃ duggatibhāvaṃ sādheti.

'It would follow along' means it would go along after. 'Emerge' means rise up. 'Float' means float on the surface of the water. 'Come to shore' means climb onto the land. 'Whatever might be there' means whatever would be there, whatever might exist there. 'A pebble or potsherd' means a pebble or a potsherd. 'It would go downwards' means it would go down, it would be one that goes below. 'It would go down' means it would go below. 'Of the path' means of the Noble Path. 'Sharpness' means keenness. And that keenness is not a matter of being sharpened like a knife; rather, to show that it is the acuity of the faculties, he said 'adhimattatā' (excellence). Is it not so that, since the Noble Path eradicates without remainder the defilements to be abandoned by it, there is no such thing as a path that is not sharp? This is true. Nevertheless, because of the statement 'but not like that of one who has attained to view,' it can be said that with respect to the abandoning of defilements, there is some measure of difference between one liberated by faith and one who has attained to view. This difference, however, is not intended here, because what is intended is the transcending of all states of existence. But since defilements are abandoned in stages by the Noble Path, and their abandonment as such occurs through the faculties in the path-factors being dull, acute, more acute, or most acute, therefore, that which is the supreme acuity of the supreme path-factors which have reached the pinnacle among the diamond-like factors—this is what is intended here by the 'sharpness' of the path. For that very reason, he said: “This Dhamma, well-practiced, protects from all states of existence.” By means of another sutta passage beginning with, “Therefore, for one with a guarded mind,” he establishes the miserable nature even of those states of existence considered to be happy destinations.

32. Idāni yathāvuttassa dhammassa visabhāgadhammānaṃ taṇhāvijjādīnaṃ sabhāgadhammānañca samathavipassanādīnaṃ niddhāraṇavasena āvaṭṭahāraṃ yojetvā dassetuṃ “tattha duggatīnaṃ hetu taṇhā ca avijjā cā”tiādimāha. Taṃ pubbe vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva. Idaṃ vuccati brahmacariyanti idaṃ ariyaṃ samathavipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ maggabrahmacariyanti vuccati. Yaṃ rakkhatīti sabbāhi duggatīhi rakkhantassa ariyamaggassa ārammaṇabhūto nirodho rakkhanto viya vutto, nimittassa kattubhāvena upacaritattā. Imāni cattāri saccāni visabhāgasabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavasena niddhāritānīti adhippāyo.

32. Now, in order to demonstrate the revolving method (āvaṭṭahāra) by way of determining the dissimilar phenomena of the aforementioned Dhamma, such as craving and ignorance, and the similar phenomena, such as serenity and insight, he said, beginning with: “Therein, the cause of miserable destinations is craving and ignorance.” That, being a method previously stated, is indeed easily understood. “This is called the holy life” means this noble Dhamma, known as serenity and insight, is called the holy life of the path. “That which protects” means that cessation, which is the object of the noble path that protects from all miserable destinations, is spoken of as if it protects, due to the figurative usage of the sign as the agent. The meaning is that these Four Truths are determined by way of the revolving of dissimilar and similar phenomena.

Āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the analysis of the revolving method is concluded.

8. Vibhattihāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Analysis of the Division Method

33. Tattha [V 0.0237] katamo vibhattihāroti vibhattihāravibhaṅgo. Tattha dhammavibhattibhūmivibhattipadaṭṭhānavibhattīti tividhā vibhatti. Tāsu yasmā dhammesu vibhāgato niddiṭṭhesu tattha labbhamāno bhūmivibhāgo padaṭṭhānavibhāgo ca niddisiyamāno suviññeyyo hoti, tasmā dhammavibhattiṃ tāva niddisanto soḷasavidhe paṭṭhāne yesaṃ suttānaṃ vasena visesato vibhajitabbā, tāni suttāni dassetuṃ “dve suttāni vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañcā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha vāsanā puññabhāvanā, tassā bhāgo koṭṭhāso vāsanābhāgo, tassa hitanti vāsanābhāgiyaṃ, suttaṃ. Nibbijjhanaṃ lobhakkhandhādīnaṃ padālanaṃ nibbedho, tassa bhāgoti sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Yasmiṃ sutte tīṇi puññakiriyavatthūni desitāni, taṃ suttaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ. Yasmiṃ pana sekkhāsekkhā desitā, taṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ. Ayañca attho pāḷiyaṃyeva āgamissati.

33. “Therein, what is the division method (vibhattihāra)?” is the analysis of the division method. Therein, the division is threefold: division of phenomena, division of planes, and division of proximate causes. Among these, because when phenomena are specified in detail, the division of planes and the division of proximate causes that are found therein become easily understood when they are indicated, therefore, first indicating the division of phenomena, in order to show those suttas by means of which the division should be particularly analyzed in the sixteenfold foundation of the teaching, it is said: “Two suttas, the Vāsanābhāgiya and the Nibbedhabhāgiya.” Therein, `vāsanā` is the cultivation of merit; its part or portion is `vāsanābhāga`; what is conducive to that is `vāsanābhāgiya`, a sutta. `Nibbedha` is penetration, the breaking up of the aggregates of greed, etc.; its part... the rest is just like the former. The sutta in which the three grounds for meritorious action are taught, that sutta is called `vāsanābhāgiya` (pertaining to the portion of cultivation). But the sutta in which trainees and non-trainees are taught, that is called `nibbedhabhāgiya` (pertaining to the portion of penetration). And this meaning will come in the Pāḷi itself.

Puññabhāgiyāti [M 0.0111] puññabhāge bhavā. Tathā phalabhāgiyā veditabbā. Phalanti pana sāmaññaphalaṃ. Saṃvarasīlanti pātimokkhasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti pañca saṃvarā saṃvarasīlaṃ. Pahānasīlanti tadaṅgappahānaṃ, vikkhambhanappahānaṃ, samucchedappahānaṃ, paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ, nissaraṇappahānanti pañcappahānāni. Tesu nissaraṇappahānavajjānaṃ pahānānaṃ vasena pahānasīlaṃ veditabbaṃ. Soti yo vāsanābhāgiyasuttasampaṭiggāhako, so. Tena brahmacariyenāti tena saṃvarasīlasaṅkhātena seṭṭhacariyena kāraṇabhūtena brahmacārī bhavati. Ettha ca aṭṭhasamāpattibrahmacariyassa na paṭikkhepo, keci pana “teneva brahmacariyenā”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ matena siyā tassa paṭikkhepo.

`Puññabhāgiya` means the practice that occurs in the portion of merit. Similarly, `phalabhāgiyā` should be understood. `Phala` (fruit), however, is the fruit of recluseship. `Saṃvarasīla` (virtue of restraint) is the five restraints: Pātimokkha restraint, mindfulness restraint, knowledge restraint, patience restraint, and energy restraint. `Pahānasīla` (virtue of abandonment) is the five abandonments: abandonment by substitution, abandonment by suppression, abandonment by eradication, abandonment by tranquillization, and abandonment by escape. Among these, virtue of abandonment should be understood by way of the abandonments excluding abandonment by escape. `So` (he) is the person who is the recipient of the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta. `Tena brahmacariyena` (by that holy life) means: by that excellent conduct called virtue of restraint, which is the cause, one becomes a practitioner of the holy life. And here, there is no rejection of the holy life of the eight attainments; however, some recite `teneva brahmacariyenā` (“by that very holy life”), and according to their view, there would be a rejection of it.

Pahānasīle ṭhitoti samucchedapaṭippassaddhippahānānaṃ vasena pahānasīle ṭhito. Tena brahmacariyenāti tena pahānasīlena visesabhūtena maggabrahmacariyena. Ye pana “teneva brahmacariyenā”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ ayaṃ pāṭho “vāsanābhāgiyaṃ nāma suttaṃ dānakathā, sīlakathā, saggakathā, puññavipākakathā”ti. Ye pana “tena brahmacariyenā”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ ayaṃ pāṭho – “vāsanābhāgiyaṃ nāma suttaṃ dānakathā, sīlakathā, saggakathā kāmānaṃ ādīnavo nekkhamme [V 0.0238] ānisaṃso”ti. Tattha katamo pāṭho yuttataroti? Pacchimo pāṭhoti niṭṭhaṃ gantabbaṃ. Yasmā “nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ nāma suttaṃ yā catusaccappakāsanā”ti vakkhati, na hi mahāthero sāvasesaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desesīti.

“Established in the virtue of abandonment” means being established in the virtue of abandonment by way of abandonment by eradication and abandonment by tranquillization. “By that holy life” means by that holy life of the path, which is distinguished by that virtue of abandonment. For those who recite `teneva brahmacariyenā` (“by that very holy life”), this is the reading: “A sutta called `vāsanābhāgiya` is a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, a talk on heaven, a talk on the result of merit.” But for those who recite `tena brahmacariyenā` (“by that holy life”), this is the reading: “A sutta called `vāsanābhāgiya` is a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, a talk on heaven, the danger in sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation.” Therein, which reading is more suitable? It should be concluded that the latter reading is more suitable. Because it will be said: “A sutta called `nibbedhabhāgiya` is the exposition of the Four Truths,” and indeed, the Great Elder did not teach the Dhamma leaving it incomplete.

“Natthi pajānanā”tiādinā ubhinnaṃ suttānaṃ sātisayaṃ asaṅkarakāraṇaṃ dasseti. Tattha pajānanāti ariyamaggassa padaṭṭhānabhūtā vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanāpaññā. Imāni cattāri suttānīti imesaṃ suttānaṃ vāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyānaṃ vakkhamānānañca saṃkilesabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyānaṃ vasena cattāri suttāni. Desanāyāti desanānayena. Sabbato vicayena hārena vicinitvāti sabbatobhāgena ekādasasu ṭhānesu pakkhipitvā vicayena hārena vicinitvā. “Yuttihārena yojetabbānī”ti etena vicayahārayuttihārā vibhattihārassa parikammaṭṭhānanti dasseti. “Yāvatikā ñāṇassa bhūmī”ti iminā vibhattihārassa mahāvisayataṃ dasseti.

Beginning with “There is no understanding,” he shows the excellent reason for the non-confusion of the two suttas. Therein, `pajānanā` (understanding) is the insight-wisdom leading to emergence, which is the proximate cause of the noble path. `Imāni cattāri suttāni` (these four suttas) means there are four suttas by way of these suttas—the one partaking of habitual tendencies (`vāsanābhāgiya`) and the one partaking of penetration (`nibbedhabhāgiya`)—and those to be spoken of, the one partaking of defilement (`saṃkilesabhāgiya`) and the one partaking of the non-trainee (`asekkhabhāgiya`). `Desanāya` (by teaching) means by the method of teaching. `Sabbato vicayena hārena vicinitvā` (having investigated with the method of inquiry from all sides) means having placed them in the eleven locations in all aspects and investigated with the method of inquiry. By this, “They should be connected by the method of reasoning,” he shows that the method of inquiry and the method of reasoning stand in the place of preliminary work for the division method. By this, “As far as the ground of knowledge extends,” he shows the vast scope of the division method.

34. Evaṃ [M 0.0112] vāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyabhāvehi dhamme ekadesena vibhajitvā idāni tesaṃ kilesabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyabhāvehi sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇabhāvehi vibhajituṃ “tattha katame dhammā sādhāraṇā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha katame dhammāti katame sabhāvadhammā. Sādhāraṇāti avisiṭṭhā, samānāti attho. Dve dhammāti duve pakatiyo. Pakatiattho hi ayaṃ dhamma-saddo “jātidhammānaṃ sattāna”ntiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.33) viya. Nāmasādhāraṇāti nāmena sādhāraṇā, kusalākusalāti samānanāmāti attho. Vatthusādhāraṇāti vatthunā nissayena sādhāraṇā, ekasantatipatitatāya samānavatthukāti attho. Visesato saṃkilesapakkhe pahānekaṭṭhā nāmasādhāraṇā, sahajekaṭṭhā vatthusādhāraṇā. Aññampi evaṃ jātiyanti kiccapaccayapaṭipakkhādīhi samānaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Micchattaniyatānaṃ aniyatānanti idaṃ puthujjanānaṃ upalakkhaṇaṃ. Tasmā sassatavādā ucchedavādāti ādiko sabbo puthujjanabhedo āharitvā vattabbo. Dasanappahātabbā kilesā sādhāraṇā micchattaniyatānaṃ aniyatānaṃ eva ca sambhavato sammattaniyatānaṃ asambhavato ca. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi attho veditabbo.

34. Having thus analyzed the phenomena in part by their state of partaking of habitual tendencies and their state of partaking of penetration, now, in order to analyze those phenomena by their state of partaking of defilement and their state of partaking of the non-trainee, as well as by their state of being common and uncommon, the passage beginning with 'Therein, what phenomena are common?' is introduced. Therein, 'what phenomena?' means what phenomena of the same nature. 'Common' means undistinguished, the same; this is the meaning. 'Two phenomena' means two natures, for this word 'dhamma' has the meaning of 'nature', as in 'for beings subject to birth' and so on. 'Common by name' means common by name; that is, having the same name, such as 'wholesome' and 'unwholesome'. 'Common by basis' means common by basis, by support; that is, having the same basis due to occurring in a single continuity. Especially on the side of defilement, those that have the same standing with respect to abandonment are common by name; those that have the same standing with respect to co-arising are common by basis. By 'and also others in this way by birth,' it includes what is the same in terms of function, condition, opposition, and so on. The phrase 'for those of fixed wrongness and for the undetermined' is a characteristic mark of worldlings. Therefore, every division of worldlings, beginning with eternalists and annihilationists, should be brought forward and stated. The defilements to be abandoned by seeing are common to those of fixed wrongness and the undetermined because they occur in them, and because they do not occur in those of fixed rightness. In this way, the meaning should be understood in the remaining passages as well.

Ariyasāvakoti sekkhaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sabbā sā avītarāgehi sādhāraṇāti lokiyasamāpatti rūpāvacarā arūpāvacarā dibbavihāro brahmavihāro paṭhamajjhānasamāpattīti evamādīhi pariyāyehi sādhāraṇā. Kusalasamāpatti pana iminā pariyāyena siyā asādhāraṇā[V 0.0239], imaṃ pana dosaṃ passantā keci “yaṃ kiñci…pe… sabbā sā avītarāgehi sādhāraṇā”ti paṭhanti. Kathaṃ te odhiso gahitā, atha odhiso gahetabbā, kathaṃ sādhāraṇāti? Anuyogaṃ manasikatvā taṃ visodhento āha – “sādhāraṇā hi dhammā evaṃ aññamañña”ntiādi. Tassattho – yathā micchattaniyatānaṃ aniyatānañca sādhāraṇāti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sādhāraṇā dhammā na sabbasattānaṃ sādhāraṇatāya sādhāraṇā, kasmā? Yasmā aññamaññaṃ paraṃ paraṃ sakaṃ sakaṃ visayaṃ nātivattanti. Paṭiniyatañhi tesaṃ pavattiṭṭhānaṃ, itarathā tathā vohāro eva na siyāti adhippāyo. Yasmā ca ete eva dhammā evaṃ [M 0.0113] niyatā visayā, tasmā “yopi imehi dhammehi samannāgato na so taṃ dhammaṃ upātivattatī”ti āha. Na hi micchattaniyatānaṃ aniyatānañca dassanena pahātabbā kilesā na santi, aññesaṃ vā santīti evaṃ sesepi vattabbaṃ.

By 'noble disciple', he speaks with reference to the trainee. 'All that is common to those who are not free from passion' means it is common in terms of such designations as mundane attainment, form-sphere attainment, formless-sphere attainment, divine abiding, Brahmā abiding, and the first jhāna attainment. But in terms of the designation 'wholesome attainment', it may be uncommon. Seeing this fault, some recite, 'Whatever... all that is common to those who are not free from passion.' 'How are those phenomena taken with limitation? Or should they be taken with limitation? If so, how are they common?' Having considered this inquiry and clarifying it, he said, 'For common phenomena are thus mutually...' and so on. Its meaning is this: Just as it was said that they are common to those of fixed wrongness and the undetermined, so these phenomena are common only to these two; they are not common in the sense of being common to all beings. Why? Because they do not mutually transcend their own respective spheres. For their sphere of occurrence is specifically fixed; otherwise, such a designation would not be possible—this is the intention. And because these very phenomena are thus of a fixed sphere, he said, 'Whoever is endowed with these phenomena does not overstep that phenomenon.' For it is not that for those of fixed wrongness and the undetermined there are no defilements to be abandoned by seeing; they certainly exist. But for others, they do not exist. In this way, it should be stated for the remaining cases as well.

Asādhāraṇo nāma dhammo tassa tassa puggalassa paccattaniyato ariyesu sekkhāsekkhadhammavasena anariyesu sabbābhabbapahātabbavasena gavesitabbo, itarassa tathā niddisitabbabhāvābhāvato. So ca kho sādhāraṇāvidhuratāya taṃ taṃ upādāya tathāvuttadesanānusārenāti imamatthaṃ dasseti “katame dhammā asādhāraṇā yāva desanaṃ upādāya gavesitabbā sekkhāsekkhā bhabbābhabbā”ti iminā. Aṭṭhamakassāti sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannassa. Dhammatāti dhammasabhāvo paṭhamassa maggaṭṭhatā dutiyassa phalaṭṭhatā. Paṭhamassa vā pahīyamānakilesatā. Dutiyassa pahīnakilesatā. Puna aṭṭhamakassāti anāgāmimaggaṭṭhassa. Nāmanti sekkhāti nāmaṃ. Dhammatāti taṃtaṃmaggaṭṭhatā heṭṭhimaphalaṭṭhatā ca. Paṭipannakānanti maggasamaṅgīnaṃ. Nāmanti paṭipannakāti nāmaṃ. Evaṃ “aṭṭhamakassā”tiādinā ariyapuggalesu asādhāraṇadhammaṃ dassetvā itaresu nayadassanatthaṃ “evaṃ visesānupassinā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Lokiyadhammesu eva hi hīnādibhāvo. Tattha visesānupassināti asādhāraṇadhammānupassinā. Micchattaniyatānaṃ aniyatā dhammā sādhāraṇā micchattaniyatā dhammā asādhāraṇā. Micchattaniyatesupi niyatamicchādiṭṭhikānaṃ aniyatā dhammā sādhāraṇā. Niyatamicchādiṭṭhi asādhāraṇāti iminā nayena visesānupassinā veditabbā.

A phenomenon called 'uncommon' is to be sought as that which is personally specific to each individual: among noble ones, by way of the phenomena of the trainee and the non-trainee; among non-nobles, by way of the capable and the incapable. This is because for any other phenomenon, there is no state of being designated as such. And that personally specific phenomenon, being the opposite of common, is to be understood by taking up this or that phenomenon in accordance with the teaching thus stated. He shows this meaning with the phrase: 'What phenomena are uncommon... to be sought by taking up the teaching... trainees and non-trainees, capable and incapable.' 'For the eighth person' means for one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. 'Nature' means the intrinsic nature of the phenomenon: for the first, the state of being on the path; for the second, the state of being in the fruit. Or, for the first, the state of having defilements being abandoned; for the second, the state of having defilements abandoned. Again, 'for the eighth person' means for one on the non-returner's path. 'Name' means the name 'trainee' is common. 'Nature' means the state of being on this or that path and the state of being in a lower fruit are uncommon. 'For those practicing' means for those endowed with the path. 'Name' means the name 'one practicing' is common. Thus, having shown the uncommon phenomenon among noble individuals with the passage beginning 'for the eighth person', the passage beginning 'thus by one who sees distinctions' was stated to show the method for the others. For it is only in worldly phenomena that there is the state of being inferior, and so on. Therein, 'by one who sees distinctions' means by one who sees uncommon phenomena. For those of fixed wrongness, the undetermined phenomena are common; the phenomena of fixed wrongness are uncommon. Even among those of fixed wrongness, for those with fixed wrong view, the undetermined phenomena are common; the fixed wrong view is uncommon.
