Yena ca pariḍayhatīti yena kupitena ayaṃ kāyo ḍayhati, so ca puggalo “ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī”ti kandanto satadhotasappigosītacandanādilepanaṃ tālavaṇṭavātañca paccāsīsati. Yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatīti asitaṃ vā odanādi, pītaṃ vā pānakādi, khāyitaṃ vā piṭṭhakhajjakādi, sāyitaṃ vā ambapakkamadhuphāṇitādi sammā paripākaṃ gacchati, rasādibhāvena vivekaṃ gacchatīti attho. Ettha ca purimā tayo tejodhātū catusamuṭṭhānā. Pacchimo kammasamuṭṭhānova.

Herein, 'kesā' means hair of the head, which is situated in the appropriated body, has the characteristic of hardness, and is a distinct portion of the earth element in this body. 'Lomā' means… and so on… 'matthaluṅgaṃ' means the brain, which is situated in the body, has the characteristic of hardness, and is a distinct portion in this body—this is diversity. In the portions beginning with the water element, such as bile and so on, this is the same method. This, however, is the distinction: 'and by which' means by which agitated fire element. 'Is heated' means this body is heated; it becomes feverish with conditions such as an intermittent fever. 'And by which it ages' means by which this body ages. It attains impairment of the faculties, loss of strength, wrinkled skin, grey hair, and so on. 'And by which it is consumed by fever' means by which agitated fire element this body is consumed by fever; and that person, crying, “I am burning, I am burning,” longs for anointment with hundred-times-washed ghee, gosīta sandalwood, and so on, and for the breeze of a palm-leaf fan. 'And by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested' means that what is eaten, such as boiled rice; or what is drunk, such as beverages; or what is chewed, such as flour-based foods; or what is tasted, such as ripe mangoes, honey, molasses, and so on, is properly digested; the meaning is that it is resolved into essences and so on. And herein, the first three fire elements are of fourfold origin. The last is of kamma-origin only.

Uddhaṅgamā vātāti uggārahikkārādipavattakā uddhaṃ ārohanavātā. Adhogamā vātāti uccārapassāvādinīharaṇakā adho orohanavātā. Kucchisayā vātāti antānaṃ bahivātā. Koṭṭhāsayā vātāti antānaṃ antovātā. Aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātāti dhamanijālānusārena sakalasarīre aṅgamaṅgāni anusaṭā samiñjanapasāraṇādinibbattakā vātā. Assāsoti antopavisananāsikavāto. Passāsoti bahinikkhamananāsikavāto. Ettha ca purimā sabbe catusamuṭṭhānā. Assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānā eva. Evaṃ vemattatādassanavasena vibhāgena udāhaṭā catasso dhātuyo paṭikkūlamanasikāravasena upasaṃharanto “imehi dvācattālīsāya ākārehī”tiādimāha. Tattha na gayhūpaganti na gahaṇayoggaṃ. Sabhāvabhāvatoti sabhāvalakkhaṇato.

'Upward-going winds' are the winds that ascend, causing belching, hiccuping, and so on. 'Downward-going winds' are the winds that descend, causing the expulsion of feces, urine, and so on. 'Winds in the belly' are the winds outside the intestines. 'Winds in the bowels' are the winds inside the intestines. 'Winds that course through the limbs' are the winds that, following the network of vessels, pervade the major and minor limbs throughout the entire body, causing bending, stretching, and so on. 'In-breath' is the wind of the nose that enters. 'Out-breath' is the wind of the nose that exits. And herein, all the former winds are of fourfold origin. In-breaths and out-breaths are of mind-origin only. Thus, summarizing the four elements—which were set forth by way of analysis, by showing their diversity—through attention to their repulsiveness, he stated the passage beginning, “by these forty-two aspects…”. Therein, 'na gayhūpaganti' means not fit for grasping. 'Sabhāvabhāvato' means by its intrinsic characteristic.

Evaṃ [V 0.0256] paṭikkūlamanasikāraṃ dassetvā puna tattha sammasanacāraṃ pāḷivaseneva dassetuṃ “tenāha bhagavā yā ceva kho panā”tiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ suviññeyyaṃ.

Thus, having shown the attention to repulsiveness, in order to then show the section on comprehension concerning them in accordance with the Pāli itself, he stated the passage beginning, “Therefore the Blessed One said: ‘Whatever, however…’”. All of this is easy to understand.

48. Evaṃ saccamaggarūpadhammavasena adhiṭṭhānahāraṃ dassetvā idāni avijjāvijjādīnampi vasena taṃ dassetuṃ “avijjāti ekattatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādīsu yasmā avijjā dukkhasaccassa yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0131] jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “dukkhe aññāṇa”nti vuccati. Tathā yasmā dukkhasamudayassa dukkhanirodhassa dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya aññāṇa”nti vuccati. Pubbanto atītaddhabhūtā khandhāyatanadhātuyo. Aparanto anāgataddhabhūtā. Pubbantāparanto tadubhayaṃ. Idappaccayatā saṅkhārādīnaṃ kāraṇāni avijjādīni. Paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā avijjādīhi nibbattā saṅkhārādidhammā.

48. Thus, having shown the method of resolution by way of the truths, the path, and material phenomena, now, in order to show it also by way of ignorance, knowledge, and so on, the passage beginning, “'Ignorance' is unity,” is stated. Therein, concerning “ignorance of suffering,” and so on: because ignorance, by covering and enveloping, stands so as not to allow the knowing and penetrating of the true, own characteristic of the truth of suffering, it is therefore called “ignorance of suffering.” Similarly, because, by covering and enveloping, it stands so as not to allow the knowing and penetrating of the true, own characteristic of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering, it is therefore called “ignorance of… the path leading to the cessation of suffering.” The past end is the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements that have arisen in the past. The future end is those that will arise in the future. The past and future ends are both of these. Specific conditionality is the causes of formations and so on, namely ignorance and so on. Dependently arisen phenomena are the phenomena of formations and so on, which are produced by ignorance and so on.

Tatthāyaṃ avijjā yasmā atītānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ yāva paṭiccasamuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “pubbante aññāṇaṃ yāva paṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu aññāṇa”nti vuccati, evāyaṃ avijjā kiccato jātitopi kathitā. Ayañhi imāni aṭṭha ṭhānāni jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na detīti kiccato kathitā. Uppajjamānāpi imesu aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu uppajjatīti jātito kathitā. Evaṃ kiccato jātito ca kathitāpi lakkhaṇato kathite eva sukathitā hotīti lakkhaṇato dassetuṃ “aññāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Herein, this ignorance is called “ignorance of the past end… up to… ignorance concerning dependently arisen phenomena” because, by covering and enveloping, it stands so as not to allow the knowing and penetrating of the true, own characteristic of past aggregates and so on, up to dependently arisen phenomena. Thus this ignorance is described in terms of its function and also its origin. For it is described in terms of its function because it does not allow the knowing or penetrating of these eight instances. It is described in terms of its origin because, when arising, it arises in these eight instances. Although it is thus described in terms of function and origin, it is well-described only when described in terms of its characteristic. Therefore, to show its characteristic, the passage beginning, “non-knowledge,” is stated.

Tattha ñāṇaṃ atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ pana avijjā uppajjitvā taṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ na detīti ñāṇapaccanīkato aññāṇaṃ. Dassanantipi paññā, sā hi taṃ ākāraṃ passati. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā passituṃ na detīti adassanaṃ. Abhisamayotipi paññā, sā taṃ ākāraṃ abhisameti. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ abhisametuṃ na detīti anabhisamayo. Anubodho sambodho paṭivedhotipi paññā, sā taṃ ākāraṃ anubujjhati sambujjhati paṭivijjhati. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ anubujjhituṃ sambujjhituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na detīti ananubodho asambodho appaṭivedho. Tathā sallakkhaṇaṃ upalakkhaṇaṃ paccupalakkhaṇaṃ samapekkhaṇantipi paññā, sā taṃ ākāraṃ sallakkhati [V 0.0257] upalakkhati paccupalakkhati samaṃ sammā ca apekkhati. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā tassa tathā kātuṃ na detīti asallakkhaṇaṃ anupalakkhaṇaṃ apaccupalakkhaṇaṃ asamapekkhaṇanti ca vuccati.

Therein, knowledge makes known and manifest what is beneficial and unbeneficial, cause and non-cause, and the Dhamma of the Four Truths. But this ignorance, having arisen, does not allow that to be made known and manifest; therefore, because it is the opposite of knowledge, it is non-knowledge. Seeing is also wisdom, for it sees that aspect. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to see; thus, it is non-seeing. Comprehension is also wisdom, for it comprehends that aspect. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to comprehend; thus, it is non-comprehension. Understanding, complete understanding, and penetration are also wisdom, for they understand, completely understand, and penetrate that aspect. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to understand, completely understand, or penetrate; thus, it is non-understanding, non-complete understanding, and non-penetration. Similarly, marking, observing, repeatedly observing, and reflecting are also wisdom, for they mark, observe, repeatedly observe, and consider that aspect evenly and rightly. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow that wisdom to do so; thus, it is called non-marking, non-observing, non-repeatedly observing, and non-reflecting.

Nāssa [M 0.0132] kiñci paccakkhakammaṃ atthi, sayañca appaccavekkhitvā katakammanti appaccakkhakammaṃ. Dummedhānaṃ bhāvo dummejjhaṃ. Bālānaṃ bhāvo bālyaṃ. Sampajaññanti paññā, sā atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ sampajānāti. Avijjā pana uppajjitvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ pajānituṃ na detīti asampajaññaṃ. Mohanavasena moho. Pamohanavasena pamoho. Sammohanavasena sammoho. Avindiyaṃ vindati, vindiyaṃ na vindatīti avijjā. Vaṭṭasmiṃ ohanati otaratīti avijjogho. Vaṭṭasmiṃ yojetīti avijjāyogo. Appahīnaṭṭhena ceva punappunaṃ uppajjanato ca avijjānusayo. Magge pariyuṭṭhitacorā viya addhike kusalacittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti viluppatīti avijjāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā nagaradvāre palighasaṅkhātāya laṅgiyā patitāya manussānaṃ nagarappaveso pacchijjati, evameva yassa sakkāyanagare ayaṃ patitā, tassa nibbānasampāpakaṃ ñāṇagamanaṃ pacchijjatīti avijjālaṅgī nāma hoti. Akusalañca taṃ mūlañca, akusalānaṃ vā mūlanti akusalamūlaṃ. Taṃ pana na aññaṃ, idhādhippeto mohoti moho akusalamūlanti ayaṃ ekapadiko avijjāya atthuddhāro. Ayaṃ vemattatāti ayaṃ avijjāya vemattatā.

For it [ignorance], there is no act that is directly perceived. And because it is an act done without reflection, it is called an act not directly perceived. The state of the unwise is foolishness (`dummejjha`). The state of fools is folly (`bālya`). Clear comprehension (`sampajañña`) is wisdom; it clearly knows what is beneficial and not beneficial, what is a cause and not a cause, and the Dhamma of the Four Truths. But ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to know that cause; therefore, it is called lack of clear comprehension (`asampajañña`). By way of delusion, it is delusion (`moha`). By way of intense delusion, it is bewilderment (`pamoha`). By way of complete delusion, it is confusion (`sammoha`). It obtains what should not be obtained and does not obtain what should be obtained; therefore, it is ignorance (`avijjā`). It causes one to sink and descend into the round of existence; therefore, it is the flood of ignorance (`avijjogha`). It yokes one to the round of existence; therefore, it is the yoke of ignorance (`avijjāyoga`). Because it is not yet abandoned and because it arises again and again, it is the latent tendency of ignorance (`avijjānusayo`). Like robbers who plunder travelers on the road, it assails and plunders the wholesome mind; therefore, it is the obsession of ignorance (`avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna`). Just as when the crossbar called a `paligha` has fallen at a city gate, the entry of people into the city is cut off, so too, for whomever this [ignorance] has fallen in the city of personality-belief, their journey of knowledge that leads to Nibbāna is cut off; therefore, it is called the bar of ignorance (`avijjālaṅgī`). It is both unwholesome and a root, or it is the root of unwholesome states; therefore, it is an unwholesome root (`akusalamūla`). But that is nothing else; here, delusion is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'Delusion is an unwholesome root.' This is the single-term exposition of the meaning of ignorance. 'This is the diversity' means this is the diversity of ignorance.

Vijjāti vindiyaṃ vindatīti vijjā, vijjhanaṭṭhena vijjā, viditakaraṇaṭṭhena vijjā. “Dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādīsu dukkhasaccassa yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ jānāti passati paṭivijjhatīti dukkhe ariyasacce visayabhūte ñāṇaṃ “dukkhe ñāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Paññāti tassa tassa atthassa pākaṭakaraṇasaṅkhātena paññāpanaṭṭhena paññā, tena tena vā aniccādinā pakārena dhamme jānātīti paññā. Pajānanākāro pajānanā. Aniccādīni vicinatīti vicayo. Pakārehi vicinatīti pavicayo. Catusaccadhamme vicinatīti dhammavicayo. Aniccādīnaṃ sallakkhaṇavasena sallakkhaṇā. Tesaṃyeva pati pati upalakkhaṇavasena paccupalakkhaṇā. Paṇḍitabhāvo paṇḍiccaṃ. Kusalabhāvo kosallaṃ. Nipuṇabhāvo nepuññaṃ. Aniccādīnaṃ vibhāvanavasena vebhabyā. Tesaṃyeva cintanavasena cintā. Aniccādīni upaparikkhatīti upaparikkhā. Bhūrīti pathaviyā nāmaṃ, ayampi saṇhaṭṭhena vitthataṭṭhena ca bhūrī viyāti bhūrī. Tena vuttaṃ – “bhūrī vuccati pathavī, tāya pathavisamāya vitthatāya paññāya samannāgatoti [V 0.0258] bhūripañño”ti [M 0.0133] (mahāni. 27). Api ca bhūrīti paññāyevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhūte atthe ramatīti bhūrī.

Knowledge (`vijjā`) is so called because it obtains what is to be obtained; it is `vijjā` because of its nature of piercing, and because of its nature of making known. In phrases such as 'knowledge of suffering,' it is the knowledge that knows, sees, and penetrates the true, intrinsic characteristic of the Noble Truth of suffering, which has become its object; thus it is called 'knowledge of suffering.' The same method applies to the remaining terms. Wisdom (`paññā`) is so called because of its nature of making known, which is described as making clear the meaning of this and that; or, it is `paññā` because it knows phenomena in various ways, such as impermanence. The mode of discerning is discernment (`pajānanā`). It investigates impermanence and so on; therefore, it is investigation (`vicayo`). It investigates by way of aspects; therefore, it is thorough investigation (`pavicayo`). It investigates the Dhamma of the Four Truths; therefore, it is investigation of phenomena (`dhammavicayo`). By way of carefully noting impermanence and so on, it is careful noting (`sallakkhaṇā`). By way of repeatedly and closely noting those very things, it is repeated close noting (`paccupalakkhaṇā`). The state of being wise is wisdom (`paṇḍicca`). The state of being skillful is skillfulness (`kosalla`). The state of being subtle is subtlety (`nepuñña`). By way of elucidating impermanence and so on, it is elucidation (`vebhabyā`). By way of thinking about those very things, it is thought (`cintā`). It examines impermanence and so on; therefore, it is examination (`upaparikkhā`). `Bhūrī` is a name for the earth; this [wisdom] also, by its nature of being subtle and extensive, is like the earth; therefore, it is called `bhūrī`. Thus it is said: 'The earth is called `bhūrī`; one endowed with that wisdom which is extensive, like the earth, is called `bhūripañño`.' Furthermore, `bhūrī` is a designation for wisdom itself. It delights in what is true; therefore, it is `bhūrī`.

Kilese medhati hiṃsatīti medhā, khippaṃ gahaṇadhāraṇaṭṭhena vā medhā. Yassuppajjati, taṃ sattaṃ hitapaṭipattiyaṃ sampayuttaṃ vā yāthāvalakkhaṇapaṭivedhe pariṇetīti pariṇāyikā. Aniccādivasena dhamme vipassatīti vipassanā. Sammā pakārehi aniccādīni jānātīti sampajaññaṃ. Uppathapaṭipanne sindhave vīthiāropanatthaṃ patodo viya uppathe dhāvanakūṭacittaṃ vīthiāropanatthaṃ vijjhatīti patodo viyāti patodo. Dassanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ, paññāsaṅkhātaṃ indriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ. Avijjāya na kampatīti paññābalaṃ. Kilesacchedanaṭṭhena paññāva satthaṃ paññāsatthaṃ. Accuggataṭṭhena paññāva pāsādo paññāpāsādo. Ālokanaṭṭhena paññāva āloko paññāāloko.

It crushes and destroys the defilements; therefore, it is intelligence (`medhā`). Or, by its nature of quickly grasping and retaining, it is `medhā`. When it arises in a being, it leads that being to beneficial practice, or it leads its associated states to the penetration of characteristics as they truly are; therefore, it is a guide (`pariṇāyikā`). It sees phenomena in various distinct ways by way of impermanence and so forth; therefore, it is insight (`vipassanā`). It knows impermanence and so forth rightly and in various ways; therefore, it is clear comprehension (`sampajañña`). Just as a goad pierces Sindhava horses that have gone astray from the path in order to bring them onto the path, so too it pierces the deceitful mind that runs astray in order to bring it onto the path; as it is like a goad, it is called a goad (`patodo`). It exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of seeing; therefore, it is a faculty (`indriya`). The faculty called wisdom is the faculty of wisdom (`paññindriya`). It is not shaken by ignorance; therefore, it is the power of wisdom (`paññābala`). By its nature of cutting off the defilements, wisdom itself is a weapon, the weapon of wisdom (`paññāsattha`). By its nature of being lofty, wisdom itself is a palace, the palace of wisdom (`paññāpāsāda`). By its nature of illuminating, wisdom itself is light, the light of wisdom (`paññāloka`).

Obhāsanaṭṭhena paññāva obhāso paññāobhāso. Pajjotanaṭṭhena paññāva pajjoto paññāpajjoto. Ratikaraṇaṭṭhena ratidāyakaṭṭhena ratijanakaṭṭhena cittīkataṭṭhena dullabhapātubhāvaṭṭhena atulaṭṭhena anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhena ca paññāva ratanaṃ paññāratanaṃ. Na tena sattā muyhanti, sayaṃ vā ārammaṇe na muyhatīti amoho. Dhammavicayapadaṃ vuttatthameva. Kasmā panetaṃ puna vuttanti? Amohassa mohapaṭipakkhabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Tenetaṃ dīpeti – yvāyaṃ amoho, so na kevalaṃ mohato añño dhammo, mohassa paṭipakkho dhammavicayasaṅkhāto amohova idhādhippetoti. Sammādiṭṭhīti yāthāvaniyyānikakusaladiṭṭhi. Dhammavicayasaṅkhāto pasattho sundaro vā bojjhaṅgoti dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo. Maggaṅganti ariyamaggassa aṅgaṃ kāraṇanti maggaṅgaṃ. Ariyamaggassa antogadhattā maggapariyāpannanti.

By its nature of being a radiance, wisdom itself is radiance, the radiance of wisdom. By its nature of shining, wisdom itself is a light, the light of wisdom. By its nature of causing delight, giving delight, generating delight, being revered, being rare of appearance, being incomparable, and being for the use of noble beings, wisdom itself is a jewel, the jewel of wisdom. Beings are not deluded by it, or it itself is not deluded regarding its object; therefore, it is non-delusion. The term 'investigation of phenomena' has the meaning already stated. Why then is it stated again? To show that non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. By this it is shown: whatever non-delusion there is, it is not merely a state different from delusion, but it is non-delusion itself, designated as 'investigation of phenomena,' the opposite of delusion, that is intended here. Right view is the wholesome view that is true and leads to deliverance. The enlightenment factor designated as 'investigation of phenomena,' being praised or excellent, is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. A path factor is a constituent or cause of the Noble Path; therefore, it is a path factor. Because it is included within the Noble Path, it is said to be 'included in the path'.

Asaññāsamāpattīti saññāvirāgabhāvanāvasena pavattitā asaññabhavūpapattinibbattanasamāpatti. Anuppanne hi buddhe ekacce titthāyatane pabbajitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya saññāya dosaṃ passanti, saññāya sati hatthacchedādidukkhañceva sabbabhayāni [M 0.0134] ca honti, “alaṃ imāya saññāya, saññābhāvo santo”ti evaṃ saññāya dosaṃ passitvā saññāvirāgavasena catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhānā kālaṃ katvā asaññīsu nibbattanti. Cittaṃ nesaṃ cuticittanirodheneva idha nivattati, rūpakkhandhamattameva tattha nibbattati.

The attainment of the non-percipient state is the attainment that brings about rebirth in the non-percipient realm, brought about by the power of developing dispassion toward perception. Indeed, when a Buddha has not yet appeared, some, having gone forth in the domain of other sects and performed the preliminary work on the air kasiṇa, produce the fourth jhāna. Upon emerging from that jhāna, they see the fault in perception: “When perception exists, there is the suffering of having hands cut off and so forth, and all dangers arise. Enough of this perception! The absence of perception is peaceful.” Thus, having seen the fault in perception, they produce the fourth jhāna by the power of dispassion toward perception. With their jhāna undiminished, they pass away and are reborn among the non-percipient beings. Their consciousness ceases here only with the cessation of the death-consciousness, and only the aggregate of form arises there.

Te [V 0.0259] yathā nāma jiyāvegukkhitto saro yattako jiyāvego, tattakameva ākāse gacchati, evamevaṃ jhānavegukkhittā upapajjitvā yattako jhānavego, tattakameva kālaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Jhānavege pana parikkhīṇe tattha rūpakkhandho antaradhāyati, idha paṭisandhisaññā uppajjati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “asaññabhavūpapattinibbattanasamāpattī”ti. Vibhūtasaññāsamāpattīti viññāṇañcāyatanasamāpatti. Sā hi paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa paṭhamāruppasaññāyapi vibhāvanato “vibhūtasaññā”ti vuccati. Keci “vibhūtarūpasaññā”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ matena vibhūtarūpasamāpatti nāma sesāruppasamāpattiyo. Sesā samāpattiyo suviññeyyāva.

Just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring travels in the sky only as far as the force of the bowstring, in the same way, they, cast up by the force of jhāna, are reborn and remain for only as long as the force of that jhāna lasts. But when the force of the jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of form there vanishes, and here rebirth-perception arises. Regarding this, it is said: “the attainment that brings about rebirth in the non-percipient realm.” The attainment with manifest perception is the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness. For it is called “manifest perception” because it makes manifest the first immaterial perception for one who has the first immaterial consciousness. Some recite it as “manifest form-perception.” According to their view, the attainment with manifest form-perception refers to the remaining immaterial attainments. The remaining attainments are easily understood.

Nevasekkhanāsekkho jhāyīti jhānalābhī puthujjano. Ājāniyo jhāyīti arahā, sabbepi vā ariyapuggalā. Assakhaluṅko jhāyīti khaluṅkassasadiso jhāyī. Tathā hi khaluṅko asso damathaṃ na upeti ito cito ca yathāruci dhāvati, evamevaṃ yo puthujjano abhiññālābhī, so abhiññā assādetvā “alamettāvatā, katamettāvatā”ti uttaridamathāya aparisakkanto abhiññācittavasena ito cito ca dhāvati pavattati, so “assakhaluṅko jhāyī”ti vutto. Diṭṭhuttaro jhāyīti jhānalābhī diṭṭhigatiko. Paññuttaro jhāyīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena jhāyī, sabbo eva vā paññādhiko jhāyī.

The meditator who is neither a learner nor a non-learner is an ordinary person who has attained jhāna. The thoroughbred meditator is an Arahant, or indeed all Noble Persons. The wild colt meditator is a meditator like a wild colt. For just as a wild colt does not submit to taming but runs here and there as it pleases, in the same way, an ordinary person who has gained higher knowledges, having relished those knowledges, thinks, “This much is enough; with this much, the task is done,” and does not strive for the higher taming. By the power of the mind of higher knowledge, he runs and proceeds here and there; such a one is called “the wild colt meditator.” The view-supreme meditator is one who has attained jhāna and holds wrong views. The wisdom-supreme meditator is one who meditates by closely contemplating the characteristics, or indeed any meditator who is pre-eminent in wisdom.

Saraṇo samādhīti akusalacittekaggatā, sabbopi vā sāsavo samādhi. Araṇo samādhīti sabbo kusalābyākato samādhi, lokuttaro eva vā. Savero samādhīti paṭighacittesu ekaggatā. Avero samādhīti mettācetovimutti. Anantaradukepi eseva nayo. Sāmiso samādhīti lokiyasamādhi. So hi anatikkantavaṭṭāmisalokāmisatāya sāmiso. Nirāmiso samādhīti lokuttaro samādhi. Sasaṅkhāro samādhīti dukkhāpaṭipado dandhābhiñño sukhāpaṭipado ca dandhābhiñño. So hi sasaṅkhārena sappayogena cittena paccanīkadhamme kicchena [M 0.0135] kasirena niggahetvā adhigantabbo. Itaro asaṅkhāro samādhi. Ekaṃsabhāvito samādhīti sukkhavipassakassa samādhi. Ubhayaṃsabhāvito samādhīti samathayānikassa samādhi. Ubhayato bhāvitabhāvano samādhīti kāyasakkhino ubhatobhāgavimuttassa ca samādhi. So hi ubhayato bhāgehi ubhayato bhāvitabhāvano.

The concentration with conflict is one-pointedness of unwholesome mind, or indeed all concentration with taints. The concentration without conflict is all wholesome or indeterminate concentration, or exclusively supramundane concentration. The concentration with enmity is one-pointedness in minds associated with aversion. The concentration without enmity is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. The same method applies to the immediately following pair. The concentration with baits is mundane concentration. Indeed, it is with baits because it has not transcended the baits of the round of existence and worldly baits. The concentration without baits is supramundane concentration. The concentration with prompting is that with painful progress and slow direct knowledge, and that with pleasant progress and slow direct knowledge. Indeed, this is to be attained by suppressing opposing states with difficulty and exertion, with a mind that has prompting and effort. The other—that with painful progress and swift direct knowledge, and that with pleasant progress and swift direct knowledge—is the concentration without prompting. The one-sidedly developed concentration is the concentration of a dry-insight practitioner. The two-sidedly developed concentration is the concentration of one who takes serenity as their vehicle. The concentration developed from both sides is the concentration of a body-witness and of one liberated in both ways. Indeed, for such a one, the development is cultivated from both sides: by means of the two parts, the form-body and the mind-body, and through the two liberations, by suppression and by cutting off.

Āgāḷhapaṭipadāti kāmānaṃ orohanapaṭipatti, kāmasukhānuyogoti attho. Nijjhāmapaṭipadāti kāmassa nijjhāpanavasena khedanavasena pavattā paṭipatti, attakilamathānuyogoti [V 0.0260] attho. Akkhamā paṭipadātiādīsu padhānakaraṇakāle sītādīni asahantassa paṭipadā, tāni nakkhamatīti akkhamā. Sahantassa pana tāni khamatīti khamā. “Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.14; 6.58) nayena micchāvitakke sametīti samā. Manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni dametīti damā paṭipadā.

The indulgent practice is the practice of descending into sensual pleasures; the meaning is indulgence in sensual pleasures. The mortifying practice is the practice that proceeds by way of burning and tormenting sensual desire; the meaning is the practice of self-mortification. In the case of the unbearable practice and so on, at the time of striving, it is the practice of one who does not endure cold and other things; because they cannot endure them, it is called unbearable. The practice of one who endures, however, is called bearable because it endures them. By the method beginning, “He does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought,” he pacifies wrong thoughts; therefore, it is called the calmed practice. It tames the faculties with the mind as the sixth; therefore, it is the tamed practice.

Evanti iminā vuttanayena. Yo dhammoti yo koci jātiādidhammo. Yassa dhammassāti tato aññassa jarādidhammassa. Samānabhāvoti dukkhādibhāvena samānabhāvo. Ekattatāyāti samānatāya dukkhādibhāvānaṃ ekībhāvena. Ekī bhavatīti anekopi “dukkha”ntiādinā ekasaddābhidheyyatāya ekī bhavati. Etena ekattatāya lakkhaṇamāha. Yena yena vā pana vilakkhaṇoti yo dhammo yassa dhammassa yena yena bhāvena visadiso. Tena tena vemattaṃ gacchatīti tena tena bhāvena so dhammo tassa dhammassa vemattataṃ visadisattaṃ gacchati, dukkhabhāvena samānopi jātiādiko abhinibbattiādibhāvena jarādikassa visiṭṭhataṃ gacchatīti attho. Iminā vemattatāya lakkhaṇamāha.

'Thus' means: by this stated method. 'Whatever phenomenon' means: any phenomenon such as birth and so on. 'Of whatever phenomenon' means: of another phenomenon such as aging and so on, other than that. 'Sameness of nature' means: sameness of nature by way of being suffering and so on. 'By unity' means: by sameness, through the oneness of states such as suffering and so on. 'It becomes one' means: though many, it becomes one by being designated by a single term such as 'suffering.' By this, he states the characteristic of unity. 'Or by whatever distinction' means: by whatever nature a phenomenon is dissimilar to another phenomenon. 'By that, it becomes distinct' means: by that nature, that phenomenon attains distinctness, dissimilarity, from that other phenomenon. The meaning is: although similar in being suffering, a phenomenon such as birth becomes distinct from a phenomenon such as aging by way of its nature as arising, and so on. By this, he states the characteristic of distinction.

Idāni tāva ekattavemattatāvisaye niyojetvā dassetuṃ “sutte vā veyyākaraṇe vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pucchitanti pucchāvasena desitasuttavasena vuttaṃ, na pana adhiṭṭhānahārassa pucchāvisayatāya. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

Now, firstly, in order to demonstrate by applying it to the subject of unity and diversity, the passage beginning “in the Sutta or in the exposition” is stated. Therein, the phrase beginning with “pucchitaṃ” is stated by way of a question, by way of a sutta that was taught, but it is not stated as being a subject of inquiry for the Adhiṭṭhānahāra. The rest is self-evident.

Adhiṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Adhiṭṭhānahāra is finished.

15. Parikkhārahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

15. Commentary on the Analysis of the Requisite Mode

49. Tattha [M 0.0136] katamo parikkhāro hāroti parikkhārahāravibhaṅgo. Tattha yo dhammo yaṃ dhammaṃ janayati, tassa so parikkhāroti saṅkhepato parikkhāralakkhaṇaṃ vatvā taṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “kiṃlakkhaṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha hinoti attano phalaṃ paṭikāraṇabhāvaṃ gacchatīti hetu. Paṭicca etasmā phalaṃ etīti paccayo. Kiñcāpi hetupaccayasaddehi kāraṇameva vuccati, tathāpi tattha visesaṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “asādhāraṇalakkhaṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabhāvo hetūti samānabhāvo [V 0.0261] bījaṃ hetu. Nanu ca bījaṃ aṅkurādisadisaṃ na hotīti? No na hoti, aññato hi tādisassa anuppajjanato.

49. Herein, 'What is the requisite mode?' refers to the Analysis of the Requisite Mode. Therein, after briefly stating the characteristic of a requisite—'Whatever phenomenon generates another phenomenon, that is its requisite'—in order to explain it in detail, the passage beginning, 'What is its characteristic?' was stated. In that passage, a 'hetu' (cause) is so called because it goes to (hinoti), i.e., reaches, the state of being a cause with respect to its own fruit. A 'paccaya' (condition) is so called because dependent (paṭicca) on this, the fruit arises (eti). Although by the words 'hetu' and 'paccaya' only a cause is meant, nevertheless, to show the distinction therein in detail, the passage beginning, 'with an uncommon characteristic' was stated. 'Its own nature is the hetu' means: the similar nature, the seed, is the hetu. But is it not so that the seed is not similar to the sprout and so forth? It is not that it is not so; indeed it is. For from anything else, a thing of such a nature does not arise.

“Yathā vā panā”tiādināpi udāharaṇantaradassanena hetupaccayānaṃ visesameva vibhāveti. Tattha duddhanti khīraṃ. Dadhi bhavatīti ekattanayena abhedopacārena vā vuttaṃ, na aññathā. Na hi khīraṃ dadhi hoti. Tenevāha – “na catthi ekakālasamavadhānaṃ duddhassa ca dadhissa cā”ti. Atha vā ghaṭe duddhaṃ pakkhittaṃ dadhi bhavati, dadhi tattha kālantare jāyati paccayantarasamāyogena, tasmā na catthi ekakālasamavadhānaṃ duddhassa ca dadhissa ca rasakhīravipākādīhi bhinnasabhāvattā. Evamevanti yathā hetubhūtassa khīrassa phalabhūtena dadhinā na ekakālasamavadhānaṃ, evamaññassāpi hetussa phalena na ekakālasamavadhānaṃ, na tathā paccayassa, na hi paccayo ekantena phalena bhinnakālo evāti. Evampi hetupaccayānaṃ viseso veditabboti adhippāyo.

Also by the passage beginning, 'Or just as,' by showing another example, he explains the very distinction between causes and conditions. Herein, 'duddhaṃ' means milk. 'It becomes curd' is stated either by the method of oneness or by the metaphor of non-difference, and not otherwise. For milk does not become curd. For that very reason, he said: 'There is no co-existence at a single time of milk and of curd.' Alternatively: milk placed in a pot becomes curd; the curd arises there at a later time through association with other conditions. Therefore, there is no co-existence at a single time of milk and of curd, because their natures are different with respect to taste, physical state, ripening, and so on. 'Just so' means: just as there is no co-existence at a single time of the milk which is the cause with the curd which is the fruit, so also there is no co-existence at a single time of any other cause with its fruit. It is not so with a condition, for a condition is not necessarily of a different time from its fruit. 'In this way also, the distinction between causes and conditions should be known'—this is the intended meaning.

Evaṃ bāhiraṃ hetupaccayavibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni ajjhattikaṃ dassetuṃ “ayañhi saṃsāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “avijjā avijjāya hetū”ti vutte kiṃ ekasmiṃ cittuppāde anekā avijjā vijjantīti? Āha “purimikā avijjā pacchimikāya avijjāya hetū”ti. Tena ekasmiṃ kāle hetuphalānaṃ samavadhānaṃ natthīti etamevatthaṃ samattheti. Tattha “purimikā avijjā”tiādinā hetuphalabhūtānaṃ avijjānaṃ vibhāgaṃ dasseti. “Bījaṅkuro viyā”tiādinā imamatthaṃ dasseti – yathā bījaṃ aṅkurassa hetu hontaṃ samanantarahetutāya hetu hoti. Yaṃ pana bījato phalaṃ nibbattati, tassa bījaṃ paramparahetutāya hetu hoti. Evaṃ avijjāyapi hetubhāve daṭṭhabbanti.

Having thus shown the external division of causes and conditions, now, to show the internal division, the passage beginning, 'For this is the round of existence,' was stated. Herein, when it is said, 'Ignorance is a cause for ignorance,' the question arises: 'Do many instances of ignorance exist in a single mind-moment?' He said: 'The preceding ignorance is a cause for the subsequent ignorance.' By this, he establishes this very meaning: that there is no co-existence of cause and fruit at one time. Therein, by the passage beginning 'the preceding ignorance,' he shows the division of ignorances that are cause and fruit. By the passage beginning 'like a seed and a sprout,' he shows this meaning: just as a seed, being a cause for the sprout, is a cause by way of being an immediate cause; but for the fruit that is produced from the seed, the seed is a cause by way of being a remote cause. Thus it should also be seen in the case of the causal nature of ignorance.

Puna [M 0.0137] “yathā vā panā”tiādināpi hetupaccayavibhāgameva dasseti. Tattha thālakanti dīpakapallikā. Anaggikanti aggiṃ vinā. Dīpetunti jāletuṃ. Iti sabhāvo hetūti evaṃ padīpujjālanādīsu aggiādipadīpasadisaṃ kāraṇaṃ sabhāvo hetu. Parabhāvo paccayoti tattheva kapallikāvaṭṭitelādisadiso aggito añño sabhāvo paccayo. Ajjhattikoti niyakajjhattiko niyakajjhatte bhavo. Bāhiroti tato bahibhūto. Janakoti nibbattako. Pariggāhakoti upatthambhako. Asādhāraṇoti āveṇiko. Sādhāraṇoti aññesampi paccayuppannānaṃ samāno.

Again, by the passage beginning 'Or just as,' he shows the very division of causes and conditions. Herein, 'thālakaṃ' means a lamp saucer. 'Anaggikaṃ' means without fire. 'Dīpetuṃ' means to light. Thus, 'Its own nature is the cause' means: in such cases as the lighting of a lamp, the cause that is similar to the lamp-flame, such as the fire, is the cause by way of having a similar nature. 'Another nature is the condition' means: in that same case, a nature different from the fire, such as the saucer, wick, and oil, is the condition. 'Internal' means one's own internal, that which arises in one's own person. 'External' means that which is external to that. 'Generative' means productive. 'Supportive' means upholding. 'Uncommon' means specific. 'Common' means common to other conditionally arisen phenomena as well.

Idāni [V 0.0262] yasmā kāraṇaṃ “parikkhāro”ti vuttaṃ, kāraṇabhāvo ca phalāpekkhāya, tasmā kāraṇassa yo kāraṇabhāvo yathā ca so hoti, yañca phalaṃ yo ca tassa viseso, yo ca kāraṇaphalānaṃ sambandho, taṃ sabbaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “avupacchedattho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kāraṇaphalabhāvena sambandhatā santati. Ko ca tattha sambandho, ko kāraṇaphalabhāvo ca? So eva avupacchedattho. Yo phalabhūto aññassa akāraṇaṃ hutvā nirujjhati, so vupacchinno nāma hoti, yathā taṃ arahato cuticittaṃ. Yo pana attano anurūpassa phalassa hetu hutvā nirujjhati, so anupacchinno eva nāma hoti, hetuphalasambandhassa vijjamānattāti āha – “avupacchedattho santatiattho”ti.

Now, since a cause is called a 'requisite,' and the state of being a cause is dependent on a fruit, therefore, in order to explain all of this—what the nature of a cause is and how it comes to be, what the fruit is and what its distinction is, and what the connection between cause and fruit is—the passage beginning 'having the meaning of non-severance' was stated. Herein, continuity is the state of being connected by way of the nature of cause and fruit. And what, in this context, is the connection, and what is the nature of cause and fruit? It is precisely the meaning of non-severance. A phenomenon which, being a fruit, ceases without becoming a cause for another is called 'severed'—such as the death-consciousness of an Arahant. But a phenomenon which ceases after having been a cause for its corresponding fruit is called 'unsevered,' because the connection between cause and fruit exists. Therefore, he said: 'The meaning of non-severance is the meaning of continuity.'

Yasmā ca kāraṇato nibbattaṃ phalaṃ nāma, na anibbattaṃ, tasmā “nibbattiattho phalattho”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana purimabhavena anantarabhavapaṭisandhānavasena pavattā upapattikkhandhā punabbhavo, tasmā vuttaṃ – “paṭisandhiattho punabbhavattho”ti. Tathā yassa puggalassa kilesā uppajjanti, taṃ palibundhenti sammā paṭipajjituṃ na denti. Yāva ca maggena asamugghātitā, tāva anusenti nāma, tena vuttaṃ – “palibodhattho pariyuṭṭhānattho, asamugghātattho anusayattho”ti. Pariññābhisamayavasena pariññāte na kadāci taṃ nāmarūpaṅkurassa kāraṇaṃ hessatīti āha – “apariññātattho viññāṇassa bījattho”ti. Yattha avupacchedo tattha santatīti yattha rūpārūpappavattiyaṃ yathāvutto avupacchedo, tattha santativohāro[M 0.0138]. Yattha santati tattha nibbattītiādi paccayaparamparadassanaṃ hetuphalasambandhavibhāvanameva.

And because that which is produced from a cause is called 'fruit,' and that which is not produced is not, therefore it is said: 'The meaning of production is the meaning of fruit.' Moreover, because the aggregates of existence that proceed by way of linking the immediately subsequent existence with the prior existence are 'renewed existence,' therefore it is said: 'The meaning of linking is the meaning of renewed existence.' Likewise, when defilements arise in a person, they obstruct them and do not allow them to practice rightly. And as long as they are not eradicated by the path, they are said to 'lie latent'; therefore it is said: 'The meaning of obstruction is the meaning of obsession, the meaning of not being eradicated is the meaning of latent tendency.' When it is fully known by means of the full understanding that is comprehension, that consciousness will never again be a cause for the sprout of name-and-form; therefore, he said: 'The meaning of not being fully known is the meaning of seed for consciousness.' 'Where there is non-severance, there is continuity' means: wherein the process of material and immaterial phenomena there is non-severance as described, therein is the designation 'continuity.' The showing of the succession of conditions, such as 'Where there is continuity, there is production,' is simply the clarification of the cause-fruit connection.

“Yathā vā pana cakkhuñca paṭiccā”tiādinā “sabhāvo hetū”ti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāgena dasseti. Tattha sannissayatāyāti upanissayapaccayatāya. Manasikāroti kiriyāmanodhātu. Sā hi cakkhuviññāṇassa viññāṇabhāvena samānajātitāya sabhāvo hetu. Saṅkhārā viññāṇassa paccayo sabhāvo hetūti puññādiabhisaṅkhārā paṭisandhiviññāṇassa paccayo, tattha yo sabhāvo, so hetūti. Saṅkhārāti cettha sabbo lokiyo kusalākusalacittuppādo adhippeto. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi attho veditabbo. Evaṃ yo koci upanissayo sabbo so parikkhāroti yathāvuttappabhedo yo koci paccayo, so sabbo attano phalassa parikkharaṇato abhisaṅkharaṇato parikkhāro. Tassa niddhāretvā kathanaṃ parikkhāro hāroti.

By the text beginning with, “Just as, depending on the eye…,” the meaning already stated as “intrinsic nature is the cause” is shown in detail. Therein, 'by way of dependence' means by way of the decisive support condition. 'Attention' means the functional mind-element. For, being of the same kind as eye-consciousness by way of being consciousness, it is the cause which is its intrinsic nature. 'Formations are a condition for consciousness, an intrinsic nature, a cause' means that meritorious and other volitional formations are a condition for rebirth-linking consciousness; therein, whatever is the intrinsic nature, that is the cause. And here, by 'formations,' all mundane wholesome and unwholesome arisings of consciousness are intended. By this method, the meaning should be understood in the remaining terms as well. 'Thus, whatever decisive support there is, all that is a requisite' means: whatever condition there is of the kind already mentioned, all that condition, because it prepares and fabricates its own fruit, is a requisite. The statement that defines this is the Requisite Mode.

Parikkhārahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Requisite Mode is concluded.

16. Samāropanahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

16. The Commentary on the Analysis of the Application Mode

50. Tattha [V 0.0263] katamo samāropano hāroti samāropanahāravibhaṅgo. Tattha ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāneti yasmiṃ kismiñci ekasmiṃ kāraṇabhūte dhamme suttena gahite. Yattakāni padaṭṭhānāni otarantīti yattakāni aññesaṃ kāraṇabhūtāni tasmiṃ dhamme samosaranti. Sabbāni tāni samāropayitabbānīti sabbāni tāni padaṭṭhānāni padaṭṭhānabhūtā dhammā sammā niddhāraṇavasena ānetvā desanāya āropetabbā, desanāruḷhe viya katvā kathetabbāti attho. Yathā āvaṭṭe hāre “ekamhi padaṭṭhāne, pariyesati sesakaṃ padaṭṭhāna”nti (netti. 4 niddesavāra) vacanato anekesaṃ padaṭṭhānānaṃ pariyesanā vuttā, evamidhāpi bahūnaṃ padaṭṭhānānaṃ samāropanā kātabbāti dassento “yathā āvaṭṭe hāre”ti āha. Na kevalaṃ padaṭṭhānavaseneva samāropanā, atha kho vevacanabhāvanāpahānavasenapi samāropanā kātabbāti dassento “tattha samāropanā catubbidhā”tiādimāha.

50. Therein, what is the Application Mode? It is the analysis of the Application Mode. Therein, 'in one basis' means: when any single causal phenomenon is taken up by the discourse. 'As many bases as descend' means: as many phenomena that are causes for others converge in that phenomenon. 'All those should be applied' means: all those bases—the phenomena that are bases—having been brought by way of proper determination, should be applied to the teaching; they should be stated as if they were placed upon the teaching. This is the meaning. Just as in the Turning Mode, because of the statement, “In one basis, one seeks the remaining bases,” the search for many bases is stated, so too here the application of many bases should be done. To show this, he said, “as in the Turning Mode.” The application should not be done only by way of the basis, but rather, the application should also be done by way of synonyms, development, and abandonment. To show this, he said the words beginning with, “Therein, the application is fourfold.”

Kasmā [M 0.0139] panettha padaṭṭhānavevacanāni gahitāni, nanu padaṭṭhānavevacanahāre eva ayamattho vibhāvitoti? Saccametaṃ, idha pana padaṭṭhānavevacanaggahaṇaṃ bhāvanāpahānānaṃ adhiṭṭhānavisayadassanatthañceva tesaṃ adhivacanavibhāgadassanatthañca. Evañhi bhāvanāpahānāni suviññeyyāni honti sukarāni ca paññāpetuṃ. Idaṃ padaṭṭhānanti idaṃ tividhaṃ sucaritaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanassa ovādassa visayādhiṭṭhānabhāvato padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha “kāyika”ntiādinā tīhi sucaritehi sīlādayo tayo khandhe samathavipassanā tatiyacatutthaphalāni ca niddhāretvā dasseti, taṃ suviññeyyameva. Vanīyatīti vanaṃ, vanati, vanute iti vā vanaṃ. Tattha yasmā pañca kāmaguṇā kāmataṇhāya, nimittaggāho anubyañjanaggāhassa, ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni tappaṭibandhachandarāgādīnaṃ, anusayā ca pariyuṭṭhānānaṃ kāraṇāni honti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “pañca kāmaguṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

But why are the basis and synonyms taken up here? Has not this meaning already been clarified in the Basis Mode and the Synonym Mode? This is true. Nevertheless, here the taking up of the basis and synonyms is for the purpose of showing the domain of the foundation for development and abandonment, and for showing the classification of their designations. For in this way, development and abandonment become easy to understand and easy to explain. 'This is the basis' means: this threefold good conduct is the basis because it is the domain and foundation of the teaching and instruction of the Buddhas. Therein, by the three kinds of good conduct beginning with “bodily,” he defines and shows the three aggregates beginning with virtue, as well as serenity, insight, and the third and fourth fruits. That is indeed easy to understand. It is called vana (a wood) because it is frequented (vanīyati); or it is vana because one frequents it (vanati), or because one desires it (vanute). Therein, because the five strands of sensual pleasure are causes for sensual craving, the grasping of signs is a cause for the grasping of details, the internal and external sense bases are causes for the desire, passion, etc., connected with them, and the underlying tendencies are causes for the active defilements—therefore, to show that meaning, the passage beginning with “the five strands of sensual pleasure” was stated.

51. Ayaṃ vevacanena samāropanāti yo “rāgavirāgā cetovimutti sekkhaphalaṃ, anāgāmiphalaṃ, kāmadhātusamatikkamana”nti etehi pariyāyavacanehi tatiyaphalassa niddeso, tathā yo “avijjāvirāgā paññāvimutti asekkhaphalaṃ, aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ, tedhātukasamatikkamana”nti [V 0.0264] etehi pariyāyavacanehi catutthaphalassa niddeso, yo ca “paññindriya”ntiādīhi pariyāyavacanehi paññāya niddeso, ayaṃ vevacanehi ca samāropanā.

51. This is application by way of synonyms: whatever designation there is of the third fruit by these synonymous terms—“liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, the fruit of a trainee, the fruit of a non-returner, the transcending of the sense-sphere realm”; and likewise, whatever designation there is of the fourth fruit by these synonymous terms—“liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance, the fruit of one beyond training, the supreme fruit, arahantship, the transcending of the three realms”; and whatever designation there is of wisdom by synonymous terms beginning with “the faculty of wisdom”—this is the application by way of synonyms.

Tasmātiha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, kāye kāyānupassī viharāhītiādi lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Kevalaṃ tattha ekalakkhaṇattā avuttānampi vuttabhāvadassanavaseneva āgataṃ, idha bhāvanāsamāropanavasenāti ayameva viseso. Kāyānupassanā visesato asubhānupassanā eva kāmarāgatadekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ ekantapaṭipakkhāti asubhasaññā kabaḷīkārāhārapariññāya paribandhakilesā kāmupādānaṃ kāmayogo abhijjhākāyagantho kāmāsavo kāmogho rāgasallaṃ rūpadhammapariññāya paṭipakkhakilesā rūpadhammesu rāgo chandāgatigamananti etesaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahānāya saṃvattatīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “kāye kāyānupassī viharanto”tiādinā.

The passage beginning with, “Therefore, bhikkhu, you should dwell contemplating the body in the body,” should be understood according to the method stated in the Commentary on the Analysis of the Characteristic Mode. The only difference is this: there, because of the single characteristic, it is presented by way of showing even what was unstated as having been stated; here, it is presented by way of application as development. He shows this meaning by the passage beginning with, “dwelling contemplating the body in the body”: that the contemplation of the body, especially the contemplation of unattractiveness, is the absolute opposite of sensual lust and the defilements that share its foundation, and that it conduces to the abandonment of these evil states, namely: the perception of beauty; the defilements that obstruct the full understanding of physical nutriment; sensual clinging; the yoke of sensuality; the bodily knot of covetousness; the taint of sensuality; the flood of sensuality; the dart of lust; the defilements that are the opposite of the full understanding of material phenomena; lust for material phenomena; and proceeding on a wrong course due to desire.

Tathā [M 0.0140] vedanānupassanā visesato dukkhānupassanāti, sā –

Likewise, the contemplation of feeling is especially the contemplation of suffering. That contemplation—

“Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, adakkhi naṃ aniccato”ti. (saṃ. ni. 4.253; itivu. 53) –

“One who saw pleasant feeling as suffering, saw painful feeling as a dart, and saw the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent…”

Ādivacanato sabbaṃ vedanaṃ “dukkha”nti passantī sukhasaññāya vedanāhetupariññāya paribandhakilesānaṃ gosīlādīhi bhavasuddhi hotīti vedanāssādena pavattassa bhavupādānasaṅkhātassa sīlabbatupādānassa vedanāvasena “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādinayappavattassa (dī. ni. 3.340; a. ni. 9.29; 10.79; dha. sa. 1237; vibha. 909, 960) byāpādakāyaganthassa dosasallassa vedanāssādavaseneva pavattassa bhavayogabhavābhavabhavoghasaṅkhātassa bhavarāgassa bhavapariññāya paribandhakakilesānaṃ vedanāvisayassa rāgassa dosāgatigamanassa ca pahānāya saṃvattatīti etamatthaṃ dasseti “vedanāsu vedanānupassī”tiādinā.

Because of the initial statement, seeing all feeling as 'suffering,' it conduces to the abandonment of: the perception of pleasure; the defilements that are an obstacle to the full understanding of the cause of feeling; the clinging to precepts and vows, which is called the clinging to existence, arising from delight in feeling with the view that 'purity of existence is through the practices of cows, etc.'; the bodily knot of ill will and the dart of aversion, which arise by way of feeling in the manner of 'he has done me harm,' etc.; the craving for existence, which is called the yoke of existence, the taint of existence, and the flood of existence, arising solely through the power of delight in feeling; the defilements that are an obstacle to the full understanding of existence; lust for which feeling is the object; and going on a wrong course through aversion. He shows this meaning by 'contemplating feelings in feelings,' etc.

Tathā cittānupassanā visesato aniccānupassanāti, sā cittaṃ “anicca”nti passantī tattha yebhuyyena sattā niccasaññinoti niccasaññāya viññāṇāhārapariññāya paribandhakilesānaṃ niccābhinivesapaṭipakkhato eva diṭṭhupādānaṃ diṭṭhiyogasīlabbataparāmāsakāyaganthadiṭṭhāsavadiṭṭhoghasaṅkhātāya diṭṭhiyā niccasaññānimittassa “seyyohamasmī”tiādinayappavattassa [V 0.0265] (dha. sa. 1239; vibha. 832, 866, 962) mānasallassa saññāpariññāya paṭipakkhakilesānaṃ saññāya rāgassa diṭṭhābhinivesassa appahīnattā uppajjanakassa bhayāgatigamanassa ca pahānāya saṃvattatīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “citte cittānupassī”tiādinā.

Similarly, the contemplation of mind is especially the contemplation of impermanence. Therefore, seeing the mind as 'impermanent' (for beings for the most part have the perception of permanence therein), it conduces to the abandonment of: the perception of permanence; the defilements that are an obstacle to the full understanding of consciousness-nutriment; the view—which is called the clinging to views, the yoke of views, the bodily knot of adherence to precepts and vows, the taint of views, and the flood of views, and which is the very opposite of adherence to impermanence; the dart of conceit, which has the perception of permanence as its sign and arises in the manner of 'I am superior,' etc.; the defilements that are opposed to the full understanding of perception; lust for perception; and going on a wrong course through fear, which is liable to arise because of the non-abandonment of adherence to views. He shows this meaning by 'contemplating mind in mind,' etc.

Tathā dhammānupassanā visesato anattasaññāti, sā saṅkhāresu attasaññāya manosañcetanāhārapariññāya paṭipakkhakilesānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā “idameva sacca”nti (ma. ni. 2.187, 202-203; 3.27) pavattassa micchābhinivesassa micchābhinivesahetukāya avijjāyogaavijjāsavaavijjoghamohasallasaṅkhātāya avijjāya saṅkhārapariññāya paribandhakilesānaṃ saṅkhāresu rāgassa mohāgatigamanassa [M 0.0141] ca pahānāya saṃvattatīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “dhammesu dhammānupassī viharanto”tiādinā. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

Similarly, the contemplation of phenomena is especially the perception of not-self. Therefore, it conduces to the abandonment of: the perception of self in formations; the defilements that are opposed to the full understanding of mental-volition-nutriment; the identity view; wrong adherence which arises as 'this alone is true'; ignorance—which has wrong adherence as its cause and is called the yoke of ignorance, the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, and the dart of delusion; the defilements that are an obstacle to the full understanding of formations; lust for formations; and going on a wrong course through delusion. He shows this meaning by 'dwelling contemplating phenomena in phenomena,' etc. The rest is indeed clear.

Samāropanahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Application is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca hāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā.

And the Explanation of the Analysis of the Modes of Interpretation is concluded.

1. Desanāhārasampātavaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Combination of the Modes of Interpretation: The Mode of Discourse

Evaṃ suparikammakatāya bhūmiyā nānāvaṇṇāni muttapupphāni pakiranto viya susikkhitasippācariyavicāritesu surattasuvaṇṇālaṅkāresu nānāvidharaṃsijālasamujjalāni vividhāni maṇiratanāni bandhanto viya mahāpathaviṃ parivattetvā pappaṭakojaṃ khādāpento viya yojanikamadhugaṇḍaṃ pīḷetvā sumadhurasaṃ pāyento viya ca āyasmā mahākaccāno nānāsuttapadese udāharanto soḷasa hāre vibhajitvā idāni te ekasmiṃyeva sutte yojetvā dassento hārasampātavāraṃ ārabhi. Ārabhanto ca yāyaṃ niddesavāre –

Thus, like one scattering pearl-flowers of various colors on well-prepared ground; and like one setting various jewel-gems—glittering with diverse networks of rays—in ornaments of the finest red gold fashioned by a master craftsman of well-learned skill; and like one, having turned over the great earth, causing others to eat the essence of its surface; and like one, having pressed a honeycomb a yojana in size, causing others to drink the sweet honey-juice—even so, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, having brought forth and divided the sixteen modes in various sutta passages, now, showing them combined in a single sutta, began the section on the Combination of Modes. And in beginning, in the section on Exposition—

52.

52.

“Soḷasa hārā paṭhamaṃ, disalocanato disā viloketvā;

Saṅkhipiya aṅkusena hi, nayehi tīhi niddise sutta”nti. –

“Sixteen modes first, having surveyed the directions with the directional eye; indeed, having summarized with the hook, the sutta should be expounded by three ways.”

Gāthā vuttā. Yasmā taṃ hāravibhaṅgavāro nappayojeti, vippakiṇṇavisayattā, nayavicārassa ca antaritattā[V 0.0266]. Anekehi suttapadesehi hārānaṃ vibhāgadassanameva hi hāravibhaṅgavāro. Hārasampātavāro pana taṃ payojeti, ekasmiṃyeva suttapadese soḷasa hāre yojetvāva tadanantaraṃ nayasamuṭṭhānassa kathitattā. Tasmā “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”nti gāthaṃ paccāmasitvā “tassā niddeso kuhiṃ daṭṭhabbo, hārasampāte”ti āha. Tassattho – “tassā gāthāya niddeso kattha daṭṭhabbo”ti. Etena suttesu hārānaṃ yojanānayadassanaṃ hārasampātavāroti dasseti. Hārasampātapadassa attho vutto eva.

The verse was spoken. Because the section on the analysis of modes does not apply to it, due to its scattered subject matter and its being separated from the examination of methods. Indeed, the section on the analysis of modes is merely the showing of the division of modes by means of many sutta passages. However, the section on the combination of modes does apply to it, because the arising of a method is discussed immediately after having combined the sixteen modes in a single sutta passage. Therefore, having reflected upon the verse, “Sixteen modes first,” he said, “Where should its exposition be seen? In the combination of modes.” Its meaning is: “Where should the exposition of that verse be seen?” By this, he shows that the section on the combination of modes is the showing of the method of applying the modes in the suttas. The meaning of the term “combination of modes” has already been stated.

Arakkhitena [M 0.0142] cittenāti cakkhudvārādīsu satiārakkhābhāvena aguttena cittena. Micchādiṭṭhihatenāti sassatādimicchābhinivesadūsitena. Thinamiddhābhibhūtenāti cittassa kāyassa ca akalyatālakkhaṇehi thinamiddhehi ajjhotthaṭena. Vasaṃ mārassa gacchatīti kilesamārādīnaṃ yathākāmaṃ karaṇīyo hotīti ayaṃ tāva gāthāya padattho.

“With an unguarded mind” means with a mind unguarded due to the absence of the guard of mindfulness at the eye-door and so forth. “Destroyed by wrong view” means defiled by wrong adherence such as to eternalism and so forth. “Overcome by sloth and torpor” means overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, which have the characteristic of unfitness of mind and body. “One falls under the sway of Māra” means one becomes one who can be dealt with as they wish by the Māra of defilements and so forth. This, then, is the word-meaning of the verse.

Pamādanti “arakkhitena cittenā”ti idaṃ padaṃ chasu dvāresu sativosaggalakkhaṇaṃ pamādaṃ katheti. Taṃ maccuno padanti taṃ pamajjanaṃ guṇamāraṇato maccusaṅkhātassa mārassa vasavattanaṭṭhānaṃ, tena “arakkhitena cittena, vasaṃ mārassa gacchatī”ti paṭhamapādaṃ catutthapādena sambandhitvā dasseti. So vipallāsoti yaṃ aniccassa khandhapañcakassa “nicca”nti dassanaṃ, so vipallāso vipariyesaggāho. Tenevāha – “viparītaggāhalakkhaṇo vipallāso”ti. Sabbaṃ vipallāsasāmaññena gahetvā tassa adhiṭṭhānaṃ pucchati “kiṃ vipallāsayatī”ti. Sāmaññassa ca viseso adhiṭṭhānabhāvena voharīyatīti āha – “saññaṃ cittaṃ diṭṭhimitī”ti. Taṃ “vipallāsayatī”ti padena sambandhitabbaṃ. Tesu saññāvipallāso sabbamuduko, aniccādikassa visayassa micchāvasena upaṭṭhitākāraggahaṇamattaṃ migapotakānaṃ tiṇapurisakesu purisoti uppannasaññā viya. Cittavipallāso tato balavataro, amaṇiādike visaye maṇiādiākārena upaṭṭhahante tathā sanniṭṭhānaṃ viya niccādito sanniṭṭhānamattaṃ. Diṭṭhivipallāso pana sabbabalavataro yaṃ yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ yathā yathā upaṭṭhāti, tathā tathā naṃ sassatādivasena “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti abhinivisanto pavattati. Tattha saññāvipallāso cittavipallāsassa kāraṇaṃ, cittavipallāso diṭṭhivipallāsassa kāraṇaṃ hoti.

“Negligence”—this phrase, “with an unguarded mind,” speaks of negligence, which has the characteristic of the release of mindfulness at the six doors. “That is the domain of death”—that negligence, because it destroys virtues, is the basis for coming under the sway of Māra, who is known as death. By this, it shows the connection of the first line, “with an unguarded mind,” with the fourth line, “one falls under Māra’s sway.” “That is a distortion”—whatever seeing of the impermanent five aggregates as “permanent” is a distortion, a perverted grasping. For that very reason, it is said: “Distortion has the characteristic of perverted grasping.” Taking all distortions in terms of distortion-in-general, he asks about their basis: “What does it distort?” And the particular of the general is designated as the basis; thus, he said: “perception, mind, and view.” That should be connected with the phrase “it distorts.” Among these, the distortion of perception is the very mildest: it is merely the grasping of the presented aspect of an object such as the impermanent, by way of error, like the perception that arises in young deer of a grass-man as a man. The distortion of mind is stronger than that: it is merely the deciding about permanence and so forth, like the conclusion that an object is a jewel when, in an object that is not a jewel, it appears with the aspect of a jewel. But the distortion of view is the very strongest of all: whatever object appears in whatever way, one adheres to it by way of eternalism and so forth, clinging with the thought, “This alone is true, the other is futile.” Therein, the distortion of perception is the cause of the distortion of mind, and the distortion of mind is the cause of the distortion of view.

Idāni vipallāsānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānaṃ visayaṃ dassetuṃ “so kuhiṃ vipallāsayati, catūsu attabhāvavatthūsū”ti āha. Tattha attabhāvavatthūsūti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu. Te hi āhito ahaṃ [V 0.0267] māno etthāti attā, “attā”ti bhavati ettha buddhi vohāro cāti attabhāvo, so eva subhādīnaṃ vipallāsassa ca adhiṭṭhānabhāvato vatthu cāti “attabhāvavatthū”ti vuccati. “Rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādinā tesaṃ sabbavipallāsamūlabhūtāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā pavattiṭṭhānabhāvena attabhāvavatthutaṃ dassetvā puna vipallāsānaṃ pavattiākārena saddhiṃ [M 0.0143] visayaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “rūpaṃ paṭhamaṃ vipallāsavatthu asubhe subha”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ suviññeyyaṃ. Puna mūlakāraṇavasena vipallāse vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “dve dhammā cittassa saṃkilesā”tiādimāha. Tattha kiñcāpi avijjārahitā taṇhā natthi, avijjā ca subhasukhasaññānampi paccayo eva, tathāpi taṇhā etāsaṃ sātisayaṃ paccayoti dassetuṃ “taṇhānivutaṃ…pe… dukkhe sukha”nti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhinivutanti diṭṭhisīsena avijjā vuttāti avijjānivutanti attho. Kāmañcettha taṇhārahitā diṭṭhi natthi, taṇhāpi diṭṭhiyā paccayo eva. Taṇhāpi “niccaṃ attā”ti ayoniso ummujjantānaṃ tathāpavattamicchābhinivesassa moho visesapaccayoti dassetuṃ “diṭṭhinivutaṃ…pe… attā”ti vuttaṃ.

Now, to show the domain, the place of occurrence of the distortions, he said, “Where does it distort? In the four foundations of individuality.” Therein, “foundations of individuality” means in the five aggregates of clinging. For in them the conceit ‘I am’ is placed, and thus they are ‘self’ (attā); the notion and usage “self” occurs in them, and thus they are ‘individuality’ (attabhāvo); and that very individuality, because it is the basis for distortions of beauty and so on, and for distortion in general, is also a ‘foundation’ (vatthu). Therefore, it is called ‘foundation of individuality’ (attabhāvavatthu). Having shown, by means of “One regards form as self,” etc., that they are the foundation of individuality by being the place of occurrence for identity view, which is the root of all distortions, again, to show the domain by dividing it together with the mode of occurrence of the distortions, it was said: “Form is the first foundation of distortion: the unattractive as attractive.” All this is easily understood. Again, to show the distortions by dividing them according to their root cause, he said: “Two things are defilements of the mind,” etc. Therein, although there is no craving devoid of ignorance, and ignorance is indeed a condition for perceptions of beauty and pleasure, nevertheless, to show that craving is an exceedingly strong condition for them, it was said: “Shrouded by craving… in suffering, pleasure.” “Shrouded by view” means that ignorance is stated with view as the head, so the meaning is “shrouded by ignorance.” Moreover, although there is no view devoid of craving, and craving is indeed a condition for view, nevertheless, to show that for those who inappropriately conceive “permanent, self,” delusion is a special condition for such wrong adherence, it was said: “Shrouded by view… [perceiving] non-self as self.”

Yo diṭṭhivipallāsoti “anicce niccaṃ, anattani attā”ti pavattampi vipallāsadvayaṃ sandhāyāha – “so atītaṃ rūpaṃ…pe… atītaṃ viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti. Etena aṭṭhārasavidhopi pubbantānukappikavādo pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ vipallāsānaṃ vasena hotīti dasseti. Taṇhāvipallāsoti taṇhāmūlako vipallāso. “Asubhe subhaṃ, dukkhe sukha”nti etaṃ vipallāsadvayaṃ sandhāya vadati. Anāgataṃ rūpaṃ abhinandatīti anāgataṃ rūpaṃ diṭṭhābhinandanavasena abhinandati. Anāgataṃ vedanaṃ, saññaṃ, saṅkhāre, viññāṇaṃ abhinandatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Etena catucattālīsavidhopi aparantānukappikavādo yebhuyyena purimānaṃ dvinnaṃ vipallāsānaṃ vasena hotīti dasseti. Dve dhammā cittassa upakkilesāti evaṃ paramasāvajjassa vipallāsassa mūlakāraṇanti visesato dve dhammā cittassa upakkilesā taṇhā ca avijjā cāti te sarūpato dasseti. Tāhi visujjhantaṃ cittaṃ visujjhatīti paṭipakkhavasenapi tāsaṃ upakkilesabhāvaṃyeva vibhāveti, na hi taṇhāavijjāsu pahīnāsu koci saṃkilesadhammo na pahīyatīti. Yathā ca vipallāsānaṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ taṇhāvijjā, evaṃ sakalassāpi vaṭṭassa mūlakāraṇanti yathānusandhināva gāthaṃ niṭṭhapetuṃ “tesa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tesanti yesaṃ arakkhitaṃ cittaṃ micchādiṭṭhihatañca, tesaṃ. “Avijjānīvaraṇāna”ntiādinā mārassa vasagamanena anādimatisaṃsāre saṃsaraṇanti dasseti.

Regarding “The distortion of views”: he says this referring to the two distortions that occur as “permanent in the impermanent, self in the non-self”—“He regards past form… past consciousness as self.” By this, he shows that even the eighteen kinds of prior-end speculation arise by way of the latter two distortions. Regarding “The distortion of craving”: this is the distortion that has craving as its root. He speaks referring to these two distortions: “the attractive in the unattractive, the pleasant in the painful.” Regarding “He delights in future form”: this means he delights in future form by way of the delight that is a view. The same principle applies to “He delights in future feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.” By this, he shows that the forty-four kinds of posterior-end speculation mostly arise by way of the former two distortions. Regarding “Two things are defilements of the mind”: as they are the root cause of such a supremely blameworthy distortion, he specifically shows that two things are defilements of the mind, indicating them by their intrinsic nature as “craving and ignorance.” Regarding “The mind, being purified from them, becomes pure”: by this, he clarifies their very nature as defilements even by way of their opposite, for when craving and ignorance are abandoned, no defiling state is not abandoned. And just as craving and ignorance are the root cause of the distortions, so too are they the root cause of the entire round of existence. Thus, to complete the verse in accordance with the sequential connection, “for them,” etc., is stated. Therein, “for them” refers to those whose mind is unguarded and struck by wrong view. By the text beginning with “Of those hindered by ignorance,” he shows that by going under the power of Māra, they wander in beginningless saṃsāra.

Thinamiddhābhibhūtenāti [V 0.0268] ettha “thinaṃ nāmā”tiādinā thinamiddhānaṃ sarūpaṃ dasseti. Tehi cittassa abhibhūtatā suviññeyyāvāti taṃ anāmasitvā kilesamāraggahaṇeneva [M 0.0144] taṃnimittā abhisaṅkhāramārakhandhamāramaccumārā gahitā evāti “kilesamārassa ca sattamārassa cā”ti ca-saddena vā tesampi gahaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. So hi nivuto saṃsārābhimukhoti so māravasaṃ gato, tato eva nivuto kilesehi yāva na mārabandhanaṃ chijjati, tāva saṃsārābhimukhova hoti, na visaṅkhārābhimukhoti adhippāyo. Imāni bhagavatā dve saccāni desitāni. Kathaṃ desitāni?

Regarding “overcome by sloth and torpor”: here, by the text beginning with “what is called sloth,” he shows the intrinsic nature of sloth and torpor. Because the mind’s state of being overcome by them is easily understood, without touching upon that, by the very grasping of the defilement-Māra, the formations-Māra, the aggregates-Māra, and the death-Māra, which have that as their cause, are indeed grasped. Therefore, it is stated “of the defilement-Māra and of the being-Māra.” Or, it should be understood that by the word “ca,” the grasping of those others is also done. Regarding “For he, being obstructed, is turned toward saṃsāra”: he has come under Māra’s power; because of that, being obstructed by defilements, as long as the bond of Māra is not cut, he remains turned only toward saṃsāra, not toward the unconditioned. This is the meaning. These two truths were taught by the Blessed One. How were they taught?

Tattha duvidhā kathā abhidhammanissitā ca suttantanissitā ca. Tāsu abhidhammanissitā nāma arakkhitena cittenāti rattampi cittaṃ arakkhitaṃ, duṭṭhampi cittaṃ arakkhitaṃ, mūḷhampi cittaṃ arakkhitaṃ. Tattha rattaṃ cittaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ lobhasahagatacittuppādānaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ, duṭṭhaṃ cittaṃ dvinnaṃ paṭighacittuppādānaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ, mūḷhaṃ cittaṃ dvinnaṃ momūhacittuppādānaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ. Yāva imesaṃ cittuppādānaṃ vasena indriyānaṃ agutti agopāyanā apālanā anārakkhā sativosaggo pamādo cittassa asaṃvaro, evaṃ arakkhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Micchādiṭṭhihataṃ nāma cittaṃ catunnaṃ diṭṭhisampayuttacittuppādānaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ, thinamiddhābhibhūtaṃ nāma cittaṃ pañcannaṃ sasaṅkhārikākusalacittuppādānaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ sabbepi aggahitaggahaṇena dvādasa akusalacittuppādā honti. Te “katame dhammā akusalā? Yasmiṃ samaye akusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”tiādinā cittuppādakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 365) akusalacittuppādadesanāvasena vitthārato vattabbā. Mārassāti ettha pañca mārā. Tesu kilesamārassa catunnaṃ āsavānaṃ catunnaṃ oghānaṃ catunnaṃ yogānaṃ catunnaṃ ganthānaṃ catunnaṃ upādānānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ dasannaṃ kilesavatthūnaṃ vasena āsavagocchakādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 14-19, 1102) vuttanayena, tathā “jātimado gottamado ārogyamado”tiādinā khuddakavatthuvibhaṅge (vibha. 832) āgatānaṃ sattannaṃ kilesānañca vasena vibhāgo vattabbo. Ayaṃ tāvettha abhidhammanissitā kathā.

Herein, the discussion is twofold: that which is based on the Abhidhamma and that which is based on the Suttanta. Among them, the discussion based on the Abhidhamma is as follows. Regarding “with an unguarded mind”: a mind with greed is unguarded, a mind with hate is unguarded, and a mind with delusion is unguarded. Therein, a mind with greed should be understood by way of the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed; a mind with hate should be understood by way of the two types of consciousness of aversion; a mind with delusion should be understood by way of the two types of consciousness of strong delusion. For as long as, by way of these types of consciousness, there is non-guarding, non-protecting, non-maintaining, and non-watching over of the faculties, letting go of mindfulness, negligence, and non-restraint of the mind, for that long the mind is unguarded. A mind struck by wrong view should be understood by way of the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view. A mind overcome by sloth and torpor should be understood by way of the five types of prompted unwholesome consciousness. Thus, without double-counting, there are in all twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. They should be spoken of in detail according to the discourse on unwholesome consciousness in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Dhs § 365), beginning with, “Which things are unwholesome? At the time when an unwholesome consciousness has arisen…” Regarding “of Māra”: here, there are five Māras. Among them, the analysis of the defilement-Māra should be understood according to the method stated in the sections on the corruptions, etc., (Dhs Dukamātikā §§ 14-19, § 1102) by way of the four corruptions, four floods, four yokes, four bonds, four clingings, eight hindrances, and ten bases of defilements. Similarly, the analysis should be understood by way of the seven defilements that come in the Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga (Vibh § 832), beginning with “intoxication with birth, intoxication with clan, intoxication with health.” This, for now, is the discussion based on the Abhidhamma.

Suttantanissitā (ma. ni. 1.347; a. ni. 11.17) pana arakkhitena cittenāti cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā nimittaggāhī hoti anubyañjanaggāhī, yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa [M 0.0145] saṃvarāya na paṭipajjati, na rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye na saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Sotena [V 0.0269] …pe… ghānena… jivhāya… kāyena… manasā…pe… manindriyena saṃvaraṃ āpajjati (ma. ni. 1.347, 411, 421; 2.419; 3.15, 75). Evaṃ arakkhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Micchādiṭṭhihatena cāti micchādiṭṭhihataṃ nāma cittaṃ pubbantakappanavasena vā aparantakappanavasena vā pubbantāparantakappanavasena vā micchābhinivisantassa ayoniso ummujjantassa “sassato lokoti vā…pe… neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti (vibha. 937; paṭi. ma. 1.140) vā yā diṭṭhi, tāya hataṃ upahataṃ. Yā ca kho “imā cattāro sassatavādā…pe… pañca paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā”ti brahmajāle (dī. ni. 1.30 ādayo) pañcattaye (ma. ni. 3.21 ādayo) ca āgatā dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo, tāsaṃ vasena cittassa micchādiṭṭhihatabhāvo kathetabbo.

The Suttanta-based explanation, however, should be understood thus. Regarding 'with an unguarded mind': having seen a form with the eye, one grasps the sign and grasps the secondary characteristics. Because of that cause, while one dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure would flow in upon him. One does not practice for its restraint, does not guard the eye faculty, and does not achieve restraint in the eye faculty. With the ear... with the nose... with the tongue... with the body... with the mind... one does not achieve restraint in the mind faculty. Thus the mind is unguarded. And regarding 'with a mind struck by wrong view': a mind said to be struck by wrong view is that of one who wrongly adheres and emerges without wise attention, based on speculations about the past, the future, or both the past and future, holding such views as: 'The world is eternal,' or... 'After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist.' By whatever such view there is, by that the mind is struck and damaged. Furthermore, the state of the mind being struck by wrong view should be explained by means of the sixty-two views that are found in the Brahmajāla Sutta and the Pañcattaya Sutta, such as 'these four eternalist views... and the five views of supreme Nibbāna in this very life.'

Thinamiddhābhibhūtenāti thinaṃ nāma cittassa akammaññatā. Middhaṃ nāma vedanādikkhandhattayassa akammaññatā. Tathā thinaṃ anussāhasaṃhananaṃ. Middhaṃ asattivighāto. Iti thinena middhena ca cittaṃ abhibhūtaṃ ajjhotthaṭaṃ upaddutaṃ saṅkocanappattaṃ layāpannaṃ. Vasaṃ mārassa gacchatīti vaso nāma icchā lobho adhippāyo ruci ākaṅkhā āṇā āṇatti. Māroti pañca mārā – khandhamāro abhisaṅkhāramāro maccumāro devaputtamāro kilesamāroti. Gacchatīti tesaṃ vasaṃ icchaṃ…pe… āṇattiṃ gacchati upagacchati upeti vattati anuvattati nātikkamatīti. Tena vuccati – “vasaṃ mārassa gacchatī”ti.

Regarding 'overcome by sloth and torpor': sloth is the name for the unworkability of the mind. Torpor is the name for the unworkability of the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Likewise, sloth is a lack of exertion and shrinking. Torpor is the impairment of energy. Thus, by this sloth and by this torpor, the mind is overcome, overwhelmed, afflicted, has reached a state of contraction, and has fallen into sluggishness. Regarding 'one goes under the sway of Māra': 'sway' is a name for desire, greed, intention, liking, longing, command, and order. Regarding 'Māra': there are five Māras—the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of karmic formations, the Māra of death, the Māra who is the son of a deva, and the Māra of defilements. Regarding 'goes': one goes to, approaches, draws near to, follows, conforms to, and does not transgress their sway, that is, their desire... order. Therefore it is said: 'one goes under the sway of Māra.'

Tattha yathāvuttā akusalā dhammā, taṇhāvijjā eva vā samudayasaccaṃ. Yo so “vasaṃ mārassa gacchatī”ti vutto, so ye pañcupādānakkhandhe upādāya paññatto, te pañcakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ. Evaṃ bhagavatā idha dve saccāni desitāni. Tenevāha – “dukkhaṃ samudayo cā”ti. Tesaṃ bhagavā pariññāya ca pahānāya ca dhammaṃ desetīti vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “dukkhassa pariññāya samudayassa pahānāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ desetīti ce –

Herein, the unwholesome states as described, or indeed craving and ignorance, are the truth of the origin. The person who is said to 'go under the sway of Māra' is the one who is designated in dependence on the five aggregates of clinging; those five aggregates are the truth of suffering. In this way, the Blessed One has taught two truths here. Therefore, he said: 'suffering and the origin.' To make clearer the meaning already stated—that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding and for the abandonment of these—it is said: 'for the full understanding of suffering, for the abandonment of the origin.' If it were asked, 'How does he teach?'—

“Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro;

Sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā, ñatvāna udayabbayaṃ;

Thinamiddhābhibhū bhikkhu, sabbā duggatiyo jahe”ti. (udā. 32) –

By the verse: 'Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, whose range is right intention, having placed right view foremost, having known rise and fall, a monk, overcoming sloth and torpor, should abandon all miserable destinations.'

Gāthāya[M 0.0146]. Tassattho – yasmā arakkhitena cittena vasaṃ mārassa gacchati, tasmā satisaṃvarena manacchaṭṭhānaṃ [V 0.0270] indriyānaṃ rakkhaṇena rakkhitacitto assa. Sammāsaṅkappagocaroti yasmā kāmasaṅkappādimicchāsaṅkappagocaro tathā tathā ayoniso vikappetvā nānāvidhāni micchādassanāni gaṇhāti. Tato eva ca micchādiṭṭhihatena cittena vasaṃ mārassa gacchati, tasmā yonisomanasikārena kammaṃ karonto nekkhammasaṅkappādisammāsaṅkappagocaro assa. Sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvāti sammāsaṅkappagocaratāya vidhutamicchādassano kammassakatālakkhaṇaṃ yathābhūtañāṇalakkhaṇañca sammādiṭṭhiṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā sīlasamādhīsu yuttappayutto. Tato eva ca ñatvāna udayabbayaṃ pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu samapaññāsāya ākārehi uppādaṃ nirodhañca ñatvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā anukkamena ariyamagge gaṇhanto aggamaggena thinamiddhābhibhū bhikkhu sabbā duggatiyo jaheti evaṃ sabbaso bhinnakilesattā bhikkhu khīṇāsavo yathāsambhavaṃ tividhadukkhatāyogena duggatisaṅkhātā sabbāpi gatiyo jaheyya, tāsaṃ parabhāge nibbāne tiṭṭheyyāti attho.

Its meaning is as follows: because one with an unguarded mind goes under the sway of Māra, therefore, by restraint through mindfulness and by the protection of the six sense faculties, one should have a guarded mind. Regarding 'whose range is right intention': because one whose range is wrong intentions, such as sensual intention, conceives improperly in various ways and adopts various kinds of wrong views, and precisely because of that, with a mind struck by wrong view, one goes under the sway of Māra, therefore, while undertaking the [meditation] work with wise attention, one should have as their range right intentions, such as the intention of renunciation.
