The Blessed One has knowledge of the process, in a classified way, regarding demeritorious kamma, meritorious kamma, and the kamma that brings about the destruction of kamma, all of which are reckoned as the path. This is the Tathāgata's power called the knowledge of the path leading everywhere. For with this knowledge, the Blessed One knows every path as it really is.

Kathaṃ? Sakalagāmavāsikesupi ekaṃ sūkaraṃ vā migaṃ vā mārentesu sabbesaṃ cetanā parassa jīvitindriyārammaṇāva hoti, taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva nānā hoti. Tesu hi eko ādarena karoti, eko “tvampi karohī”ti parehi nippīḷito karoti[M 0.0163], eko samānacchando viya hutvā appaṭibāhamāno vicarati. Tesu eko teneva kammena niraye nibbattati, eko tiracchānayoniyaṃ, eko pettivisaye, taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇe eva “iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa niraye nibbattissati, esa tiracchānayoniyaṃ, esa pettivisaye”ti jānāti. Niraye nibbattanakampi “esa aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu nibbattissati, esa soḷasasu ussadesū”ti jānāti. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattanakampi “esa apādako bhavissati, esa dvipādako, esa catuppādako, esa bahuppādako”ti jānāti. Pettivisaye nibbattanakampi “esa nijjhāmataṇhiko bhavissati, esa khuppipāsiko, esa paradattūpajīvī”ti jānāti.

How? Even when all the villagers are killing a single pig or a deer, the volition of all has the life faculty of another as its object. But that kamma of theirs becomes different at the very moment of exertion. For among them, one does it with eagerness; one, being oppressed by others saying, 'You do it too,' does it; one moves about without obstructing, as if having the same wish. Among them, one is reborn in hell by that very kamma, one in the animal womb, and one in the sphere of petas. The Tathāgata knows this at the very moment of exertion: 'Because of having been exerted in this manner, this person will be reborn in hell, this one in the animal womb, this one in the sphere of petas.' Also regarding the one to be reborn in hell, He knows: 'This one will be reborn in the eight great hells, this one in the sixteen Ussada hells.' Also regarding the one to be reborn in the animal womb, He knows: 'This one will become footless, this one two-footed, this one four-footed, this one many-footed.' Also regarding the one to be reborn in the sphere of petas, He knows: 'This one will become a `nijjhāmataṇhika` peta (one consumed by thirst), this one a `khuppipāsika` peta (one afflicted by hunger and thirst), this one a `paradattūpajīvī` peta (one who subsists on what is given by others).'

“Tesu ca kammesu idaṃ kammaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhissati, idaṃ nākaḍḍhissati dubbalaṃ dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkamattaṃ bhavissatī”ti jānāti. Tathā sakalagāmavāsikesu ekato [V 0.0286] dānaṃ dadamānesu sabbesampi cetanā deyyadhammārammaṇāva hoti, taṃ pana kammaṃ tesaṃ āyūhanakkhaṇe eva nānaṃ hoti. Tesu hi keci devaloke nibbattanti, keci manussaloke, taṃ tathāgato āyūhanakkhaṇe eva “iminā nīhārena āyūhitattā esa manussaloke nibbattissati, esa devaloke”ti jānāti. Tatthapi “esa paranimmitavasavattīsu nibbattissati, esa bhummadevesu nibbattissati, esa jeṭṭhakadevarājā hutvā, esa tassa dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ vā ṭhānantaraṃ karonto paricārako hutvā nibbattissatī”ti jānāti.

And among those kammas, he knows: 'This kamma will draw forth rebirth-linking; this one will not. Being weak, when rebirth-linking has been given (by another kamma), it will only be for the maturing of the personality-group.' Likewise, when all the villagers are giving a gift together, the volition of all has the gift-object as its object. But that kamma of theirs becomes different at the very moment of exertion. For among them, some are reborn in the deva world, and some in the human world. The Tathāgata knows this at the very moment of exertion: 'Because of having been exerted in this manner, this person will be reborn in the human world, this one in the deva world.' Therein also, he knows: 'This one will be reborn among the Paranimmitavasavattī devas; this one will be reborn among the Bhumma devas; this one will be reborn having become the chief deva-king; this one will be reborn having become an attendant performing the second or third rank for that deva-king.'

“Tesu ca kammesu idaṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ sakkhissati, idaṃ na sakkhissati dubbalaṃ dinnāya paṭisandhiyā upadhivepakkamattaṃ bhavissatī”ti jānāti. Tathā “vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapentesu ca esa iminā nīhārena vipassanāya āraddhattā arahā bhavissati, esa anāgāmī, esa sakadāgāmī, esa sotāpanno, ekabījī kolaṃkolo sattakkhattuparamo, esa maggaṃ pattuṃ na sakkhissati lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāyameva ṭhassati, esa paccayapariggahe, esa nāmarūpapariggahe, arūpapariggahe ca ṭhassati, esa mahābhūtamattameva vavatthapessati, esa kiñci sallakkhetuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti jānāti. “Kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontesupi esa parikammamatte eva ṭhassati, esa nimittaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkhissati, na appanaṃ. Esa appanampi uppādessati, esa [M 0.0164] jhānaṃ adhigamissati, na uparivisesaṃ. Esa uparivisesampi adhigamissatī”ti jānāti.

And among those actions, he knows: 'This kamma will be able to draw forth rebirth-linking; this one will not be able. A weak kamma, once rebirth-linking has been given, will merely be a result that ripens during the course of existence.' Similarly, among those establishing insight, he knows: 'This one, because of having undertaken insight in this manner, will become an Arahant; this one, a non-returner; this one, a once-returner; this one, a stream-enterer—a one-seeder, a family-to-family goer, or a seven-times-at-most goer. This one will not be able to attain the path; he will remain only in insight that has the characteristics as its object. This one will remain in the comprehension of conditions, this one in the comprehension of name-and-form, and in the comprehension of the formless. This one will only determine the great elements. This one will not be able to discern anything at all.' He also knows: 'Among those performing the kasiṇa preliminary work, this one will remain only in the preliminary work itself; this one will be able to produce the sign, but not absorption. This one will produce absorption as well; this one will attain jhāna, but not a higher distinction. This one will attain a higher distinction as well.'

Anekadhātūti anekā cakkhādayo pathavādayo ca dhātuyo etassāti anekadhātu, bahudhātūti attho. Lokoti khandhāyatanādiloko. Cakkhudhātūtiādi yāhi dhātūhi “anekadhātū”ti loko vutto, tāsaṃ sarūpato dassanaṃ. Tattha sabhāvaṭṭhena nissattaṭṭhena ca dhātu. Cakkhu eva dhātu cakkhudhātu. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Kāmadhātūti ettha dve kāmā kilesakāmo ca vatthukāmo ca. Kilesakāmapakkhe kāmapaṭisaṃyutto dhātu kāmadhātu, kāmavitakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vatthukāmapakkhe pana kāmāvacaradhammā kāmo uttarapadalopena, kāmo ca so dhātu cāti kāmadhātu. Byāpādapaṭisaṃyutto dhātu byāpādadhātu, byāpādavitakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Byāpādova dhātu byāpādadhātu, dasaāghātavatthuvisayassa paṭighassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto dhātu vihiṃsādhātu, vihiṃsāvitakko. Vihiṃsā eva vā dhātu vihiṃsādhātu, parasattavihesanassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Nekkhammaabyāpādaavihiṃsādhātuyo nekkhammavitakkādayo sabbakusaladhammā mettākaruṇā cāti veditabbaṃ. Rūpadhātūti rūpabhavo, sabbe vā rūpadhammā. Arūpadhātūti [V 0.0287] arūpabhavo, arūpadhammā vā. Nirodhadhātūti nirodhataṇhā. Saṅkhāradhātūti sabbe saṅkhatadhammā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyaṃ.

'Manifold elements' (anekadhātu) means: because this world has many elements, such as the eye and so forth, and the earth element and so forth, it is called 'manifold elements'; the meaning is 'having numerous elements.' 'The world' (loka) refers to the world of aggregates, sense bases, and so forth. 'Eye-element' (cakkhudhātu) and so forth is a presentation, according to their intrinsic nature, of those elements by which the world is called 'of manifold elements.' Herein, 'element' (dhātu) signifies intrinsic nature and the absence of a being. The eye itself is an element, thus 'eye-element.' The same method applies to the remaining terms. In the case of 'sensual element' (kāmadhātu), there are two kinds of sensual desire: defilement-sensual desire (kilesakāma) and object-sensual desire (vatthukāma). In the case of defilement-sensual desire, the element associated with sensual desire is the 'sensual element'; this is a name for sensual thought (kāmavitakka). But in the case of object-sensual desire, phenomena of the sense sphere are called 'sensual desire' by elision of the latter term, and that is both sensual desire and an element, thus 'sensual element.' The element associated with ill will is the 'ill-will element' (byāpādadhātu); this is a name for ill-willed thought (byāpādavitakka). Ill will itself is the 'ill-will element'; this is a name for resentment (paṭigha) that has the ten bases of malice as its object. The element associated with harmfulness is the 'harmfulness element' (vihiṃsādhātu); this is harmful thought (vihiṃsāvitakka). Or, harmfulness itself is the 'harmfulness element'; this is a name for harming other beings. The 'renunciation element' (nekkhamma-dhātu), the 'non-ill-will element' (abyāpāda-dhātu), and the 'non-harmfulness element' (avihiṃsā-dhātu) should be understood as thoughts of renunciation and so forth, all wholesome states, and loving-kindness and compassion. The 'form element' (rūpadhātu) is the form existence, or all form phenomena. The 'formless element' (arūpadhātu) is the formless existence, or formless phenomena. The 'cessation element' (nirodhadhātu) is craving for cessation. The 'formations element' (saṅkhāradhātu) is all conditioned phenomena. The rest is easily understood.

Aññamaññavilakkhaṇattā nānappakārā dhātuyo etasminti nānādhātu, loko. Tenevāha – “aññā cakkhudhātu yāva aññā nibbānadhātū”ti, yathā ca idaṃ ñāṇaṃ cakkhudhātuādibhedena upādinnakasaṅkhāralokassa vasena anekadhātunānādhātulokaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ anupādinnakasaṅkhāralokassapi vasena taṃ pajānāti. Paccekabuddhā hi dve ca aggasāvakā upādinnakasaṅkhāralokasseva nānattaṃ jānanti, tampi ekadeseneva, na nippadesato. Anupādinnakasaṅkhāralokassa pana nānattaṃ na jānanti. Bhagavā pana “imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya imassa rukkhassa khandho seto hoti, imassa kāḷo, imassa maṭṭho, imassa pharuso, imassa bahalo, imassa tanuttaco. Imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya imassa rukkhassa pattaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena evarūpaṃ nāma hoti, imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannattā imassa rukkhassa pupphaṃ nīlaṃ hoti pītakaṃ lohitakaṃ odātaṃ [M 0.0165] sugandhaṃ duggandhaṃ, imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya phalaṃ khuddakaṃ mahantaṃ dīghaṃ vaṭṭaṃ susaṇṭhānaṃ dussaṇṭhānaṃ maṭṭhaṃ pharusaṃ sugandhaṃ duggandhaṃ tittaṃ madhuraṃ kaṭukaṃ ambilaṃ kasāvaṃ hoti, imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya imassa rukkhassa kaṇṭako tikhiṇo hoti, atikhiṇo ujuko kuṭilo kaṇho nīlo odāto hotī”ti evaṃ anupādinnasaṅkhāralokassāpi vasena anekadhātunānādhātubhāvaṃ jānāti. Sabbaññubuddhānaṃ eva hi etaṃ balaṃ, na aññesaṃ.

Because in this world there are elements of various kinds due to their being distinct from one another, it is called 'of diverse elements'; this refers to the world. For that reason, he said: 'The eye-element is one... up to the Nibbāna-element is another.' And just as this knowledge understands the world of manifold and diverse elements by way of the world of conditioned phenomena that are clung to, classified by the eye-element and so forth, so too does it understand it by way of the world of conditioned phenomena that are not clung to. For Paccekabuddhas and the two chief disciples know only the diversity of the world of conditioned phenomena that are clung to, and that too only partially, not exhaustively. But they do not know the diversity of the world of conditioned phenomena that are not clung to. The Blessed One, however, knows: 'When such-and-such an element is predominant, the trunk of this tree is white; of this one, black; of this one, smooth; of this one, rough; of this one, thick-barked; of this one, thin-barked. When such-and-such an element is predominant, the leaf of this tree becomes of such a nature by way of color, shape, and so on. Because such-and-such an element is predominant, the flower of this tree is blue, yellow, red, or white; fragrant or foul-smelling. When such-and-such an element is predominant, the fruit is small or large; long or round; well-formed or ill-formed; smooth or rough; fragrant or foul-smelling; bitter, sweet, pungent, sour, or astringent. When such-and-such an element is predominant, the thorn of this tree is sharp or not sharp; straight or crooked; black, blue, or white.' In this way, he understands the state of being of manifold and diverse elements even by way of the world of conditioned phenomena that are not clung to. For this is the power of the Omniscient Buddhas alone, not of others.

60. Yaṃ yadeva dhātunti yaṃ kiñci hīnādisabhāvaṃ. Yasmā adhimutti nāma ajjhāsayadhātu, tasmā adhimuccanaṃ ajjhāsayassa hīnādisabhāvena pavattanaṃ. Taṃ pana tassa taṃ taṃ adhiṭṭhahanaṃ abhinivisanañca hotīti āha – “adhimuccanti, taṃ tadeva adhiṭṭhahanti abhinivisantī”ti. Adhimuccanassa visayaṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “keci rūpādhimuttā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva. Nānādhimuttikatāñāṇanti hīnādivasena nānādhimuttikatāya ñāṇaṃ.

60. 'Whatever element' means whatever has an inferior nature and so forth. Since 'disposition' (adhimutti) is the element of inclination (ajjhāsayadhātu), therefore 'being disposed' (adhimuccanaṃ) is the functioning of inclination with an inferior nature and so forth. And that, for that inclination, is its determination and adherence to that very thing. Therefore he said: 'They are disposed, they determine that very thing, they adhere to it.' To show the object of being disposed by way of classification, 'some are disposed towards form,' etc., was said. That is easily understood. 'The knowledge of the state of diverse dispositions' is the knowledge of the state of having diverse dispositions by way of the inferior and so forth.

Te yathādhimuttā ca bhavantīti te hīnādhimuttikā paṇītādhimuttikā sattā yathā yathā adhimuttā honti. Taṃ taṃ kammasamādānaṃ samādiyantīti adhimuttianurūpaṃ taṃ taṃ attanā samādiyitabbaṃ kattabbaṃ kammaṃ karonti, tāni kammasamādānāni samuṭṭhānavasena vibhajanto “te chabbidhaṃ kamma”ntiādimāha. Tattha keci lobhavasena kammaṃ samādiyantīti sambandhitabbaṃ. Esa nayo [V 0.0288] sesesupi. Taṃ vibhajjamānanti taṃ samuṭṭhānavasena chabbidhaṃ puna pavattinivattivasena vibhajjamānaṃ duvidhaṃ.

'They are as they are disposed' means: those beings, whether of inferior disposition or superior disposition, are disposed in whatever way. 'They undertake such and such an undertaking of kamma' means: in accordance with their disposition, they perform such and such kamma that is to be undertaken and done by themselves. Dividing those undertakings of kamma by way of their origin, he said, 'Those kammas are sixfold,' and so on. Therein, it should be connected thus: 'Some undertake kamma by way of greed.' This is the method in the remaining cases as well. 'That which is being divided' means: that kamma, which is sixfold by way of origin, when divided again by way of the continuation and cessation of the round of existence, is twofold.

Yaṃ lobhavasena dosavasena mohavasena ca kammaṃ karotīti dasaakusalakammapathakammaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tañhi saṃkiliṭṭhatāya kāḷakanti kaṇhaṃ. Apāyesu nibbattāpanato kāḷakavipākanti kaṇhavipākaṃ. Yaṃ saddhāvasena kammaṃ karotīti dasakusalakammapathakammaṃ. Tañhi asaṃkiliṭṭhattā paṇḍaranti sukkaṃ. Sagge nibbattāpanato paṇḍaravipākattā sukkavipākaṃ. Yaṃ lobhavasena dosavasena mohavasena saddhāvasena ca kammaṃ karoti, idaṃ kaṇhasukkanti vomissakakammaṃ. Kaṇhasukkavipākanti sukhadukkhavipākaṃ. Missakakammañhi katvā akusalavalena tiracchānayoniyaṃ maṅgalahatthibhāvaṃ upapanno kusalena pavatte sukhaṃ anubhavati, kusalena rājakule [M 0.0166] nibbattopi akusalena dukkhaṃ vedayati. Yaṃ vīriyavasena paññāvasena ca kammaṃ karoti, idaṃ kammaṃ akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākanti kammakkhayakarā catumaggacetanā. Tañhi yadi kaṇhaṃ bhaveyya, kaṇhavipākaṃ dadeyya. Yadi sukkaṃ bhaveyya, sukkaupapattipariyāpannaṃ vipākaṃ dadeyya. Ubhayavipākassa pana appadānato akaṇhaasukkavipākanti ayamettha attho.

'The kamma one performs by way of greed, hatred, and delusion' refers to the kamma of the ten unwholesome courses of action. Indeed, because it is defiled, it is dark, thus it is called black. Because it causes rebirth in the woeful states, it has a dark result, thus it is called 'of black result.' 'The kamma one performs by way of faith' refers to the kamma of the ten wholesome courses of action. Indeed, because it is undefiled, it is bright, thus it is called white. Because it causes rebirth in heaven and has a bright result, it is called 'of white result.' 'The kamma one performs by way of greed, hatred, delusion, and faith' is 'black-and-white,' which refers to mixed kamma. 'Of black-and-white result' means having a result of pleasure and pain. For, having performed mixed kamma, by the power of the unwholesome, one is reborn in the animal realm, becoming a state elephant, and in the course of that existence experiences pleasure due to the wholesome; or, by the power of the wholesome, one is reborn in a royal family, yet experiences pain due to the unwholesome. 'The kamma one performs by way of energy and wisdom'—this kamma is 'neither black nor white' with a 'neither black nor white result'; this refers to the volition of the four paths which brings about the exhaustion of kamma. For if that kamma were black, it would give a black result. If it were white, it would give a white result included in the rebirth process. But since it gives neither of the two kinds of result, it is 'of neither black nor white result.' This is the meaning here.

Kammasamādāne paṭhamaṃ acelakapaṭipadā kāmesu pātabyatā, dutiyaṃ tibbakilesassa assumukhassāpi rudato parisuddhabrahmacariyacaraṇaṃ, tatiyaṃ kāmesu apātabyatā acelakapaṭipadā, catutthaṃ paccaye alabhamānassāpi jhānavipassanāsukhasamaṅgino sāsanabrahmacariyacaraṇaṃ. Yaṃ evaṃ jātiyaṃ kammasamādānanti yaṃ aññampi evaṃpakāraṃ kammaṃ. Iminā puggalenātiādi tasmiṃ kammavipāke bhagavato ñāṇassa pavattanākāradassanaṃ. Tattha upacitanti yathā kataṃ kammaṃ phaladānasamatthaṃ hoti, tathā kataṃ upacitaṃ. Avipakkanti na vipakkavipākaṃ. Vipākāya paccupaṭṭhitanti vipākadānāya katokāsaṃ. Na ca bhabbo abhinibbidhā gantunti kilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ abhinibbijjhanato abhinibbidhāsaṅkhātaṃ ariyamaggaṃ adhigantuṃ na ca bhabbo. Taṃ bhagavā na ovadatīti taṃ vipākāvaraṇena nivutaṃ puggalaṃ bhagavā saccapaṭivedhaṃ purakkhatvā na ovadati, vāsanatthaṃ pana tādisānampi dhammaṃ deseti eva, ajātasattuādīnaṃ viya.

In the undertaking of kamma: first is the practice of naked asceticism, which is indulgence in sensual pleasures; second is the practice of the pure holy life by one with intense defilements, even while weeping with a tearful face; third is the practice of naked asceticism, which is non-indulgence in sensual pleasures; fourth is the practice of the holy life of the Dispensation by one endowed with the bliss of jhāna and insight, even when not receiving the requisites. 'Whatever undertaking of kamma is of this kind' means whatever other kamma is of this sort. The passage beginning with 'by this person' shows the mode of occurrence of the Blessed One's knowledge regarding that kamma-result. Therein, 'accumulated' means kamma done in such a way that it becomes capable of giving a result. 'Unripened' means it does not have a ripened result. 'Present for ripening' means the opportunity has been created for it to give its result. 'And he is not capable of going to disenchantment' means he is not capable of attaining the noble path, which is called 'disenchantment' because it pierces through the defilements and formations. 'The Blessed One does not advise him' means the Blessed One does not advise that person, who is obstructed by the obstruction of result, by placing the penetration of the truths at the forefront. However, for the sake of implanting a tendency, he does indeed teach the Dhamma even to such persons, as in the case of Ajātasattu and others.

Upacitanti kātuṃ āraddhaṃ. Tenevāha – “na ca tāva pāripūriṃ gata”nti. Tena micchattaniyāmassa asamatthataṃ dasseti. Purā pāripūriṃ gacchatīti pāripūriṃ phalanipphādanasamatthataṃ gacchati purā adhigaccheyya. Micchattaniyatatāya sajjukaṃ phaladhammassa abhājanabhāvaṃ nibbattayati [V 0.0289] purā. Tenevāha – “purā veneyyattaṃ samatikkamatī”ti. “Purā aniyataṃ samatikkamatī”tipi pāṭho, so evattho. Asamatteti kamme asampuṇṇe, te asampuṇṇe vā.

'Accumulated' means it has been started to be done. For that reason he said, 'But it has not yet reached completion.' By this, he shows the incompletion of the fixed course of wrongness. 'Before it reaches completion' means: before it reaches completion, that is, the capability of producing the fruit, it might be attained beforehand. Beforehand, due to its fixed wrongness, it produces on that very day the state of not being a receptacle for the fruit-Dhamma. For that reason he said, 'Before it transcends the state of being trainable.' There is also the reading, 'Before it transcends the indeterminate,' which has the same meaning. 'When incomplete' means: when the kamma is incomplete, or when they have incomplete kamma.

61. Evaṃ kilesantarāyamissakaṃ kammantarāyaṃ dassetvā idāni amissakaṃ kammantarāyaṃ dassetuṃ “imassa ca puggalassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ vuttanayameva.

61. Having thus shown the kamma-obstruction mixed with the defilement-obstruction, now, in order to show the unmixed kamma-obstruction, the passage beginning with 'And for this person...' was stated. That is just in the way already stated.

Sabbesanti imasmiṃ balaniddese vuttānaṃ sabbesaṃ kammānaṃ. Mudumajjhādhimattatāti mudumajjhatibbabhāvo. Kammānañhi muduādibhāvena taṃvipākānaṃ mudumajjhatikkhabhāvo [M 0.0167] viññāyatīti adhippāyo. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyantiādīsu diṭṭhadhamme imasmiṃ attabhāve veditabbaṃ phalaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ. Upapajje anantare attabhāve veditabbaṃ phalaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ. Aparasmiṃ attabhāve ito aññasmiṃ yasmiṃ kasmiñci attabhāve veditabbaṃ phalaṃ aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ. Ekajavanavārasmiñhi sattasu cetanāsu paṭhamacetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ nāma. Pariyosānacetanā upapajjavedanīyaṃ nāma. Majjhe pañca cetanā aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ nāma. Vipākavemattatāñāṇanti vipākavemattatāya vipākavisese ñāṇaṃ. Imassa pana kammavipākassa gatisampatti gativipatti, upadhisampatti upadhivipatti, kālasampatti kālavipatti, payogasampatti payogavipattiyo kāraṇaṃ. So ca nesaṃ kāraṇabhāvo “atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānāni gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantī”tiādipāḷivasena (vibha. 810) veditabbo.

'Of all' means: of all the kammas mentioned in this exposition of powers. 'Mild, medium, and intense' means the state of being mild, medium, or strong. For the intended meaning is that the mild, medium, or sharp nature of their results is known through the mild, etc., nature of the kammas. In the phrases beginning with 'to be experienced in the here-and-now': a result to be experienced in this very existence is 'to be experienced in the here-and-now.' A result to be experienced in the next existence is 'to be experienced upon rebirth.' A result to be experienced in some other existence apart from this one, in any existence whatsoever, is 'to be experienced in a subsequent period.' For, in a single course of impulsion, among the seven volitions, the first volition is called 'to be experienced in the here-and-now.' The final volition is called 'to be experienced upon rebirth.' The five volitions in the middle are called 'to be experienced in a subsequent period.' 'The knowledge of the diversity of results' means knowledge of the distinctions in results due to their diversity. Furthermore, the causes for this kamma-result are: accomplishment and failure of destination, accomplishment and failure of substratum, accomplishment and failure of time, and accomplishment and failure of means. And their nature as causes should be understood by way of the Pāḷi text beginning: 'There are certain evil undertakings of kamma which, being obstructed by accomplishment of destination, do not ripen,' etc.

62. Anantarabalaniddese vuttakammasamādānapadeneva jhānādīni saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “tathā samādinnānaṃ kammāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sekkhaputhujjanasantānesu pavattāni jhānādīni kammaṃ honti. Tattha tathā samādinnānanti “sukkaṃ sukkavipākaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ, āyatiṃ sukhavipāka”nti evamādippakārehi samādinnesu kammesu. Saṃkilesoti paṭipakkhadhammavasena kiliṭṭhabhāvo. Vodānaṃ paṭipakkhadhammehi visujjhanaṃ. Vuṭṭhānaṃ paguṇavodānaṃ bhavaṅgavuṭṭhānañca. Evaṃ saṃkilissatītiādīsu ayamevattho – iminā ākārena jhānādi saṃkilissati vodāyati vuṭṭhahatīti jānanañāṇaṃ bhagavato anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ, na tassa āvaraṇaṃ atthīti.

62. In the exposition of the immediately following power, in order to include and show the jhānas, etc., by means of the very term 'undertaking of kamma' mentioned there, the phrase 'of kammas thus undertaken,' etc., is stated. The jhānas, etc., occurring in the continuities of trainees and ordinary people are kamma. Herein, 'thus undertaken' refers to kammas undertaken in such ways as: 'bright, with bright result; presently pleasant, with pleasant result in the future,' etc. 'Defilement' is the state of being defiled by the power of opposing states. 'Purification' is cleansing from opposing states. 'Emergence' is accomplished purification and emergence from the life-continuum. In the phrases 'thus it becomes defiled,' etc., this is the meaning: The knowledge of knowing that jhāna, etc., becomes defiled, is purified, and emerges in this way, is the Blessed One's unobstructed knowledge; there is no obstruction to it.

Kati jhānānītiādi jhānādayo vibhāgena dassetuṃ āraddhaṃ. Cattāri jhānānīti catukkanayavasena rūpāvacarajjhānāni sandhāyāha. Ekādasāti “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādinā [V 0.0290] (dī. ni. 2.129, 174; 3.339, 358; ma. ni. 2.248; 3.312) aṭṭhannaṃ tiṇṇañca suññatavimokkhādīnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhāti tesu ṭhapetvā lokuttare vimokkhe aṭṭha. Sattāti tesu eva nirodhasamāpattiṃ ṭhapetvā satta. Tayoti suttantapariyāyena suññatavimokkhādayo tayo. Dveti abhidhammapariyāyena animittavimokkhassāsambhavato avasesā dve. Ettha ca paṭipāṭiyā satta appitappitakkhaṇe vikkhambhanavasena paccanīkadhammehi vimuccanato[M 0.0168], ārammaṇe adhimuccanato ca vimokkhā. Nirodhasamāpatti pana sabbaso saññāvedayitehi vimuttattā apagamavimokkho nāma. Lokuttarā ca taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesehi samucchedavasena vimuttattā vimokkhoti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo.

The section beginning 'How many jhānas?' is commenced in order to show the jhānas, etc., by way of analysis. 'Four jhānas' refers to the form-sphere jhānas by way of the fourfold method. 'Eleven' is stated by way of the eight beginning with 'One with form sees forms' and the three, such as the emptiness liberation. 'Eight' means eight among those, excluding the supramundane liberations. 'Seven' means seven among those, excluding the attainment of cessation. 'Three' means the three, such as the emptiness liberation, according to the Suttanta method. 'Two' means the remaining two, since the signless liberation is impossible according to the Abhidhamma method. Here, in sequence, the seven are called liberations because they are freed from opposing states by way of suppression at the moment of attainment and because of resolving upon the object. The attainment of cessation, however, is called the liberation by removal because it is entirely freed from perception and feeling. And the supramundane liberations are called liberations because they are freed from the defilements to be vanquished by the respective paths by way of cutting off. This distinction should be understood.

Samādhīsu catukkanayapañcakanayesu paṭhamajjhānasamādhi savitakko savicāro samādhi nāma. Pañcakanaye dutiyajjhānasamādhi avitakko vicāramatto samādhi nāma. Catukkanaye pañcakanayepi sesajhānesu samādhi avitakko avicāro samādhi nāma.

Among the concentrations, in both the fourfold and fivefold methods, the concentration of the first jhāna is called 'concentration with initial application and sustained application.' In the fivefold method, the concentration of the second jhāna is called 'concentration without initial application but with only sustained application.' In both the fourfold and fivefold methods, the concentration in the remaining jhānas is called 'concentration without initial application and without sustained application.'

Samāpattīsu paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ “samādhī”tipi nāmaṃ “samāpattī”tipi. Kasmā? Cittekaggatāsabbhāvato. Nirodhasamāpattiyā tadabhāvato na “samādhī”ti nāmaṃ. Saññāsamāpattiādi heṭṭhā vuttameva.

Among the attainments, the eight attainments in sequence are named both 'samādhi' and 'samāpatti.' Why? Because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind. The attainment of cessation, however, is not named 'samādhi' because of the absence of that. As for the attainment of perception, etc., that has already been stated below.

Hānabhāgiyo samādhīti appaguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ kāmādianupakkhandanaṃ paṭhamajjhānādisamādhissa hānabhāgiyatā. “Paṭhamajjhānassa kāmarāgabyāpādā saṃkileso”ti vuttattā dutiyajjhānādivasena yojetabbaṃ. Kukkuṭaṃ vuccati ajaññājigucchanamukhena tapparamatā. Kukkuṭajhāyīti puggalādhiṭṭhānena jhānāni vuttāni, dve paṭhamadutiyajjhānānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo paṭhamaṃ dutiyaṃ vā jhānaṃ nibbattetvā “alamettāvatā”ti saṅkocaṃ āpajjati, uttari na vāyamati, tassa tāni jhānāni cattāripi “kukkuṭajhānānī”ti vuccanti, taṃsamaṅgino ca kukkuṭajhāyī. Tesu purimāni dve āsannabalavapaccatthikattā visesabhāgiyatābhāvato ca saṃkilesabhāvena vuttāni. Itarāni pana visesabhāgiyatābhāvepi mandapaccatthikattā vodānabhāvena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding 'concentration partaking of decline': for one who has emerged from the unproficient first jhāna, etc., the running of perceptions and mental attention towards sensual pleasures, etc., is the state of partaking of decline for the concentration of the first jhāna, etc. Since it is said, “The defilement of the first jhāna is sensual desire and ill will,” this should be applied by way of the second jhāna, etc. 'Kukkuṭa' (stunted) is said of being satisfied with that much, by way of not being disgusted with what is ignoble. 'Kukkuṭajhāyī' (one who practices stunted jhāna) is stated where the jhānas are spoken of with reference to a person; it means the first and second jhānas. Whoever, having produced the first or second jhāna, falls into contraction, thinking “This is enough,” and makes no further effort—for such a person, those jhānas, even all four, are called 'kukkuṭa-jhānas,' and one endowed with them is a 'kukkuṭajhāyī.' Among those, the first two are spoken of as being in the portion of defilement because they have near and strong adversaries and because of the absence of a state partaking of distinction. The latter ones, however, even with the absence of a state partaking of distinction, should be seen as spoken of as being in the portion of purification because of their weak adversaries.

Visesabhāgiyo samādhīti paguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ dutiyajjhānādipakkhandanaṃ, paguṇavodānaṃ bhavaṅgavuṭṭhānañca “vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimañhi paguṇajjhānaṃ [V 0.0291] uparimassa uparimassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tasmā vodānampi “vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Bhavaṅgavasena sabbajhānehi vuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti bhavaṅgañca vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ. Yasmā pana vuṭṭhānavasibhāvena yathāparicchinnakālaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmā samāpattivuṭṭhānakosallaṃ idha “vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'concentration partaking of distinction': for one who has emerged from the proficient first jhāna, etc., the plunging of perceptions and mental attention into the second jhāna, etc., is the state of partaking of distinction. Proficient purification and emergence from the life-continuum are called 'emergence.' For each lower proficient jhāna is the proximate cause for each higher one. Therefore, purification is also called 'emergence.' Since emergence from all jhānas occurs by way of the life-continuum, both the life-continuum and purification are 'emergence.' However, since emergence from an attainment occurs at a predetermined time by means of mastery over emergence, skill in emerging from an attainment is here called 'emergence.'

63. Tasseva [M 0.0169] samādhissāti tassa anantarabalaniddese jhānādipariyāyehi vuttasamādhissa. Parivārāti parikkhārā. Indriyānīti saddhāsatipaññindriyāni. Balānīti hirottappehi saddhiṃ tāniyeva. Vīriyassa visuṃ gahaṇaṃ balānaṃ bahūpakāradassanatthaṃ. Vīriyupatthambhena hi saddhādayo paṭipakkhena akampanīyā honti. Tenevāha – “vīriyavasena balāni bhavantī”ti. Tesanti indriyānaṃ. Mudumajjhādhimattatāti avisadaṃ mudu. Nātivisadaṃ majjhaṃ. Ativisadaṃ adhimattaṃ balavaṃ “tikkha”nti vuccati.

63. ‘Of that very concentration’ refers to that concentration spoken of by way of jhāna, etc., in the exposition of the immediately following power. ‘Entourage’ means requisites. ‘The faculties’ are the faculties of faith, mindfulness, and wisdom. ‘The powers’ are those very same faculties together with moral shame and moral dread. The separate mention of energy is to show its great helpfulness to the powers. For through the support of energy, faith and the others become unshakeable by opposing forces. For that very reason, it is said: “Through energy, they become powers.” ‘Of these’ refers to the faculties. ‘Mild, medium, and intense’ means: not clear is mild; not excessively clear is medium; extremely clear is intense, and strong is called ‘sharp.’

Veneyyānaṃ indriyānurūpaṃ bhagavato desanāpavattīti dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saṃkhittavitthārenāti saṃkhittassa vitthārena. Atha vā saṃkhittenāti uddiṭṭhamattena. Saṃkhittavitthārenāti uddesena niddesena ca. Vitthārenāti uddesaniddesapaṭiniddesehi. Mudukanti lahukaṃ apāyabhayavaṭṭabhayādīhi santajjanavasena bhāriyaṃ akatvā. Mudutikkhanti nātitikkhaṃ. Saṃvegavatthūhi saṃvegajananādivasena bhāriyaṃ katvā. Samathaṃ upadisatīti samathaṃ adhikaṃ katvā upadisati, na tathā vipassananti adhippāyo. Na hi kevalena samathena saccappaṭivedho sambhavati. Samathavipassananti samadhuraṃ samathavipassanaṃ. Vipassananti sātisayaṃ vipassanaṃ upadisati. Yasmā cettha tikkhindriyādayo ugghaṭitaññuādayova, tasmā “tikkhindriyassa nissaraṇaṃ upadisatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha adhipaññāsikkhāyāti adhipaññāsikkhaṃ.

To show that the Blessed One’s teaching proceeds in accordance with the faculties of those to be trained, it is said, ‘Here the Blessed One,’ and so forth. Here, ‘briefly and in detail’ means the detailed explanation of what is brief. Alternatively, ‘briefly’ means merely by way of a heading. ‘Briefly and in detail’ means by way of both summary and exposition. ‘In detail’ means by way of summary, exposition, and counter-exposition. ‘Gentle’ means light, not made heavy by threats involving the dangers of the lower realms, the cycle of existence, and so forth. ‘Gentle and sharp’ means not too sharp, having made it weighty by generating urgency, and so forth, by means of grounds for urgency. ‘He teaches serenity’ means he teaches, emphasizing serenity, not so much insight—this is the intention. For the realization of truth does not come about through serenity alone. ‘Serenity and insight’ means serenity and insight in due proportion. ‘Insight’ means he teaches insight to a surpassing degree. Because here those with sharp faculties, and so forth, are precisely those who understand quickly, and so forth, therefore it is said, ‘For one with sharp faculties, he teaches escape,’ and so forth. Here, ‘in the training in higher wisdom’ means the training in higher wisdom.

Yaṃ ettha ñāṇanti ettha indriyānaṃ mudumajjhādhimattatāya yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, idaṃ vuccati parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattavemattatāñāṇanti sambandhitabbaṃ. Tassa ñāṇassa pavattanākāraṃ dassetuṃ “ayaṃ imaṃ bhūmi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ayaṃ imaṃ bhūmiṃ bhāvanañca gatoti ayaṃ puggalo evamimaṃ saṃkilesavāsanaṃ vodānaṃ bhavaṅgañca gato gacchati gamissati ca, kālavacanicchāya abhāvato, yathā duddhanti. Imāya velāya imasmiṃ samaye imāya mudumajjhatikkhabhedāya anusāsaniyā. Evaṃdhātukoti hīnādivasena evaṃajjhāsayo evaṃadhimuttiko. Ayañcassa āsayoti imassa puggalassa ayaṃ sassatucchedappakāro, yathābhūtañāṇānulomakhantippakāro [V 0.0292] vā āsayo. Idañhi catubbidhaṃ āsayanti ettha sattā vasantīti āsayoti vuccati. Imaṃ pana bhagavā sattānaṃ āsayaṃ [M 0.0170] jānanto tesaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ vipassanāñāṇakammassakataññāṇānañca appavattikkhaṇepi jānāti eva. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “kāmaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo kāmagaruko kāmāsayo kāmādhimutto’ti. Kāmaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo nekkhammagaruko nekkhammāsayo nekkhammādhimutto’ti. Nekkhammaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti… byāpādaṃ… abyāpādaṃ… thinamiddhaṃ… ālokasaññaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo thinamiddhagaruko thinamiddhāsayo thinamiddhādhimutto’”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.113).

‘The knowledge here’ refers to the knowledge regarding the mild, medium, and intense nature of the faculties here; this should be connected as the knowledge of the diversity in the maturity of the faculties of other beings and other individuals. To show the manner in which that knowledge arises, it is said, ‘This one has attained this level,’ and so forth. Here, ‘this one has attained this level and this development’ means that this individual has gone, goes, or will go to this kind of defilement-tendency, purification, or the life-continuum, because there is no restriction of tense, just as with ‘milked’. At this time, on this occasion, by this instruction with its division into mild, medium, and sharp. ‘Of such a nature’ means with such a disposition and such an inclination by way of being inferior, and so forth. ‘And this is his inclination’ means that this individual’s inclination is either of the kind of eternalism or annihilationism, or it is of the kind of patience conforming to knowledge of what actually is. For this is fourfold. It is called ‘inclination’ (āsayo) because ‘beings dwell (āsayanti) in it’. But the Blessed One, knowing the inclination of beings, knows their wrong views, insight-knowledge, and knowledge of kamma as one’s own even in moments when these do not arise. And this has been said: “While one is indulging in sensual pleasures, he knows: ‘This person is heavily inclined to sensual pleasures, has an inclination for sensual pleasures, is intent on sensual pleasures.’ While one is indulging in sensual pleasures, he knows: ‘This person is heavily inclined to renunciation, has an inclination for renunciation, is intent on renunciation.’ While one is indulging in renunciation, he knows… while indulging in ill-will… good-will… sloth and torpor… the perception of light, he knows: ‘This person is heavily inclined to sloth and torpor, has an inclination for sloth and torpor, is intent on sloth and torpor.’”

Ayaṃ anusayoti ayaṃ imassa puggalassa kāmarāgādiko appahīnoyeva anusayitakileso. Appahīnoyeva hi thāmagato kileso anusayo. Parasattānanti padhānasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti tato paresaṃ sattānaṃ, hīnasattānanti attho. Ekatthameva vā etaṃ padadvayaṃ veneyyavasena dvidhā vuttaṃ. Indriyaparopariyattavemattatāñāṇanti parabhāvo ca aparabhāvo ca paropariyattaṃ a-kārassa okāraṃ katvā, tassa vemattatā paropariyattavemattatā. Saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ paropariyattavemattatāya ñāṇaṃ indriyaparopariyattavemattatāñāṇanti padavibhāgo veditabbo.

‘This latent tendency’ means that this individual’s sensual desire and similar defilements, which have not been abandoned, are the defilement that lies latent. For indeed, a defilement that has not been abandoned, having become strong, is a latent tendency. ‘Other beings’ refers to principal beings. ‘Other individuals’ means beings other than those, that is, inferior beings. Alternatively, these two terms may be considered as having the same meaning, spoken of in two ways according to those to be trained. ‘The knowledge of the diversity in the maturity of the faculties’—here, ‘paropariyatta’ is formed by ‘parabhāva’ (superior state) and ‘aparabhāva’ (inferior state) with the vowel ‘a’ changed to ‘o’; the diversity in that is ‘paropariyattavemattatā.’ The knowledge of the diversity in the maturity of faculties such as faith is called ‘indriyaparopariyattavemattatāñāṇa.’ The division of the terms should be understood thus.

Tattha yanti yaṃ anekavihitassa pubbenivāsassa anussaraṇavasena bhagavato ñāṇaṃ, idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ tathāgatabalanti sambandho. Anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ, anekehi vā pakārehi pavattitaṃ. Pubbenivāsanti anussarituṃ icchitaṃ attano paresañca samanantarātītaṃ bhavaṃ ādiṃ katvā tattha tattha nivutthasantānaṃ. Anussaratīti “ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo”ti evaṃ jātipaṭipāṭiyā anugantvā sarati, anudeva vā sarati, citte abhininnāmitamatte eva saratīti attho. Bhagavato hi parikammakiccaṃ natthi, āvajjanamatteneva sarati. Seyyathidanti āraddhappakāranidassanatthe nipāto. Ekampi jātinti ekampi paṭisandhimūlaṃ cutipariyosānaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannaṃ khandhasantānaṃ. Esa nayo dvepi jātiyotiādīsupi.

Therein, the knowledge of the Blessed One by way of recollecting diverse past abodes—this is the eighth power of the Tathāgata. This is the connection. 'Diverse' (anekavihitaṃ) means of many kinds or occurring in many ways. 'Past abodes' (pubbenivāsaṃ) refers to the continuity of dwelling in various places, beginning with one's own and others' immediately past existence, which is desired to be recollected. 'He recollects' (anussarati) means he recalls following the sequence of births, such as 'one birth, two births,' and so on; or he recollects immediately, that is, he recollects merely upon the mind being directed—this is the meaning. For the Blessed One, there is no need for preparatory work; he recollects merely by adverting. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is a particle used to illustrate the kinds of things undertaken. 'One birth' (ekampi jātiṃ) means one continuum of aggregates, comprising a single existence, beginning with rebirth-linking and ending with death. The same method applies to 'two births' and so on.

Anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappetiādīsu pana parihāyamāno kappo saṃvaṭṭakappo, vaḍḍhamāno vivaṭṭakappoti veditabbo. Tattha saṃvaṭṭena saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī [M 0.0171] gahito taṃmūlattā, vivaṭṭena ca vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. Evañhi sati yāni “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyāni. Katamāni cattāri? Saṃvaṭṭo saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī vivaṭṭo vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī”ti (a. ni. 4.156) vuttāni[V 0.0293], tāni sabbāni pariggahitāni honti. Amutrāsintiādi saraṇākāradassanaṃ. Tattha amutrāsinti amumhi saṃvaṭṭakappe, amumhi bhave vā yoniyaṃ vā gatiyaṃ vā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyaṃ vā sattāvāse vā sattanikāye vā. Evaṃnāmoti tisso vā phusso vā. Evaṃgottoti bhaggavo vā gotamo vā. Evaṃvaṇṇoti odāto vā sāmo vā. Evamāhāroti sālimaṃsodanāhāro vā pavattaphalabhojano vā. Evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedīti anekappakārena kāyikacetasikānaṃ sāmisanirāmisappabhedānaṃ vā sukhadukkhānaṃ paṭisaṃvedī. Evamāyupariyantoti evaṃ vassasataparamāyupariyanto vā caturāsītikappasahassaparamāyupariyanto vā. So tato cuto amutra udapādinti so tato bhavato, sattanikāyato vā cuto puna amukasmiṃ nāma sattanikāye udapādiṃ. Atha vā tatrāpi bhave vā sattanikāye vā ahosiṃ. Evaṃnāmotiādi vuttatthameva.

In the case of terms like 'many eons of contraction' (anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe), it should be understood that a declining eon is a 'contracting eon' (saṃvaṭṭakappa), and an increasing eon is an 'expanding eon' (vivaṭṭakappa). Here, by the contracting eon is taken the eon of remaining in contraction, because it has that as its root; and by the expanding eon, the eon of remaining in expansion. For when this is so, all those incalculable eons which were spoken of thus: 'Monks, there are these four incalculable eons of a world cycle. Which four? The contracting eon, the eon of remaining in contraction, the expanding eon, and the eon of remaining in expansion' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.156), are thereby included. The phrase 'I was there' (amutrāsiṃ) and so on, shows the mode of recollection. Here, 'I was there' (amutrāsiṃ) means: in that contracting eon, or in that existence, or womb, or destination, or station of consciousness, or abode of beings, or group of beings. 'Of such a name' (evaṃnāmo) means: such as Tissa or Phussa. 'Of such a clan' (evaṃgotto) means: such as Bhaggava or Gotama. 'Of such an appearance' (evaṃvaṇṇo) means: such as fair or dark. 'With such food' (evamāhāro) means: having a diet of fine rice with meat, or living on fallen fruits. 'Experiencing such pleasure and pain' (evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī) means: experiencing, in many ways, bodily and mental pleasures and pains, whether worldly or unworldly. 'With such a lifespan' (evamāyupariyanto) means: with a lifespan limited to a maximum of one hundred years, or a lifespan limited to a maximum of eighty-four thousand eons. 'Having passed away from there, I arose there' (so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ) means: having passed away from that existence or that group of beings, I was reborn in such-and-such a group of beings. Or alternatively: I was there, in that existence or group of beings. 'Of such a name, etc.' (evaṃnāmotiādi) has the same meaning as already stated.

64. Dibbenātiādīsu dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ. Devatānañhi sucaritakammanibbattampi pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhaṃ upakkilesavimuttattā dūrepi ārammaṇaggahaṇasamatthaṃ dibbaṃ pasādacakkhu hoti. Idampi vīriyabhāvanābalanibbattaṃ ñāṇacakkhu tādisamevāti dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ, dibbavihāravasena vā paṭiladdhattā, attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattāpi dibbaṃ, ālokapariggahena mahājutikattāpi dibbaṃ, tirokuṭṭādigatarūpadassanena mahāgatikattāpi dibbaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ saddasatthānusārena veditabbaṃ. Dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu. Cakkhukiccakaraṇena cakkhumivātipi cakkhu. Cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddhaṃ. Yo hi cutimattameva passati, na upapātaṃ, so ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo upapātamattameva passati na cutiṃ, so navasattapātubhāvadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo pana tadubhayaṃ passati, so yasmā duvidhampi taṃ diṭṭhigataṃ ativattati. Tasmāssa taṃ dassanaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhihetu hoti. Tadubhayañca bhagavā passati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddha”nti.

64. In 'divine' (dibba) and so on, it is called 'divine' because it is similar to the divine. For the divine sensitive eye of deities, produced by their wholesome kamma, is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and being free from defilements, is capable of grasping objects even from a distance. This knowledge-eye (ñāṇacakkhu), produced by the power of the development of energy, is just like that, and so it is called 'divine' because it is similar to the divine; or because it is attained by means of the divine abidings; or because it is itself dependent on the divine abidings; or because it is greatly radiant through the grasping of light; or because it has great scope by seeing forms beyond walls, etc. All this should be understood according to the grammatical treatises. It is an 'eye' (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing. It is also an 'eye' because it performs the function of an eye, as it were. It is 'purified' (visuddhaṃ) because it is the cause for the purification of view by seeing the passing away and rebirth of beings. For one who sees only the passing away and not the rebirth grasps the view of annihilation. One who sees only the rebirth and not the passing away grasps the view of the appearance of a new being. But one who sees both overcomes both kinds of wrong view. Therefore, that seeing of theirs is the cause for the purification of view. And the Blessed One sees both. Hence it was said: 'Purified because it is the cause for the purification of view by seeing the passing away and rebirth of beings.'

Ekādasaupakkilesavirahato [M 0.0172] vā visuddhaṃ. Yathāha –

Or, it is purified because it is free from the eleven defilements. As he said:

“So kho ahaṃ anuruddhā ‘vicikicchā cittassa upakkileso’ti iti viditvā vicikicchaṃ cittassa upakkilesaṃ pajahiṃ. ‘Amanasikāro cittassa upakkileso… thinamiddhaṃ… chambhitattaṃ… uppilaṃ… duṭṭhullaṃ… accāraddhavīriyaṃ… atilīnavīriyaṃ… abhijappā… nānattasaññā… atinijjhāyitattaṃ rūpānaṃ cittassa upakkileso’ti [V 0.0294] iti viditvā atinijjhāyitattaṃ rūpānaṃ cittassa upakkilesaṃ pajahi”nti (ma. ni. 3.242) evamādi.

'Anuruddhas, having known, 'Doubt is a defilement of the mind,' I abandoned doubt, a defilement of the mind. Having known, 'Inattention is a defilement of the mind... sloth and torpor... fright... elation... grossness... excessive exertion... deficient exertion... longing... perception of diversity... excessive contemplation of forms is a defilement of the mind,' I abandoned excessive contemplation of forms, a defilement of the mind.' (Majjhima Nikāya 3.242) And so on.

Tadevaṃ ekādasaupakkilesavirahato vā visuddhaṃ. Manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā rūpadassanena atikkantamānusakaṃ, maṃsacakkhuṃ atikkantattā vā atikkantamānusakaṃ. Tena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena.

Thus, it is purified in this way, and also because it is free from the eleven defilements. It is 'transcending the human' (atikkantamānusakaṃ) because it sees forms by transcending the human sphere, or because it has transcended the fleshly eye. With that divine eye, purified and transcending the human...

Satte passatīti manusso manussaṃ maṃsacakkhunā viya satte passati oloketi. Cavamāne upapajjamāneti ettha cutikkhaṇe upapattikkhaṇe vā dibbacakkhunāpi daṭṭhuṃ na sakkā. Ye pana āsannacutikā idāni cavissanti, ye ca gahitapaṭisandhikā sampati nibbattā, te “cavamānā upapajjamānā”ti adhippetā. Te evarūpe cavamāne upapajjamāne. Hīneti mohanissandayuttattā hīnajātikulabhogādivasena hīḷite paribhūte. Paṇīteti amohanissandayuttattā tabbiparīte. Suvaṇṇeti adosanissandayuttattā iṭṭhakantamanāpavaṇṇayutte. Dubbaṇṇeti dosanissandayuttattā aniṭṭhākantāmanāpavaṇṇayutte abhirūpe virūpe vāti attho. Sugateti sugatigate, alobhanissandayuttattā vā aḍḍhe mahaddhane. Duggateti duggatigate, lobhanissandayuttattā vā dalidde appannapānabhojane. Yathākammūpageti yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ upacitaṃ, tena tena upagate. Tattha purimehi “cavamāne”tiādīhi dibbacakkhukiccaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā pana padena yathākammūpagañāṇakiccaṃ. Yathākammūpagañāṇaanāgataṃsañāṇāni ca dibbacakkhupādakāneva dibbacakkhunā saheva ijjhanti.

'One sees beings' (satte passati) means one sees and observes beings just as a person sees a human with the fleshly eye. In 'passing away and being reborn' (cavamāne upapajjamāne), it is not possible to see with the divine eye at the very moment of death or the moment of rebirth. However, those beings who are near death and are now about to pass away, and those who have taken rebirth-linking and are now arisen, are intended by 'passing away and being reborn.' Those beings of such a kind, passing away and being reborn. 'Inferior' (hīne) means, by way of low birth, family, wealth, and so on, despised and scorned, due to being connected with the consequence of delusion. 'Superior' (paṇīte) means the opposite, due to being connected with the consequence of non-delusion. 'Of good color' (suvaṇṇe) means endowed with a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable appearance, due to being connected with the consequence of non-hatred. 'Of bad color' (dubbaṇṇe) means endowed with an undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable appearance, due to being connected with the consequence of hatred; or in other words, of beautiful form or of ugly form—this is the meaning. 'Gone to a good destination' (sugate) means gone to a good destination, or, due to being connected with the consequence of non-greed, wealthy and of great means. 'Gone to a bad destination' (duggate) means gone to a bad destination, or, due to being connected with the consequence of greed, poor and with little food and drink. 'Faring according to their kamma' (yathākammūpage) means they fare according to whatever kamma has been accumulated. Therein, the former terms, 'passing away,' etc., state the function of the divine eye. This term, however, states the function of the knowledge of the faring of beings according to their kamma. The knowledges of the faring of beings according to their kamma and of the future are accomplished only as having the divine eye for their basis, together with the divine eye.

Kāyaduccaritenātiādīsu duṭṭhu caritaṃ, duṭṭhaṃ vā caritaṃ kilesapūtikattā duccaritaṃ. Kāyena duccaritaṃ, kāyato vā pavattaṃ duccaritaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ. Evaṃ vacīmanoduccaritānipi daṭṭhabbāni. Samannāgatāti samaṅgībhūtā. Ariyānaṃ [M 0.0173] upavādakāti buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ, antamaso gihisotāpannānampi antimavatthunā vā guṇaparidhaṃsanena vā upavādakā akkosakā garahakā. Micchādiṭṭhikāti viparītadassanā. Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānāti micchādiṭṭhihetubhūtasamādinnanānāvidhakammā. Ye ca micchādiṭṭhimūlakesu kāyakammādīsu aññepi samādapenti. Tattha vacīmanoduccaritaggahaṇena ariyūpavādamicchādiṭṭhīsu gahitāsupi tesaṃ puna vacanaṃ mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Mahāsāvajjo hi ariyūpavādo ānantariyasadiso. Yathāha –

In the text beginning with 'by bodily misconduct,' misconduct (duccarita) is bad conduct (duṭṭhu caritaṃ), or it is corrupt conduct (duṭṭhaṃ caritaṃ) because of being putrid with defilements. Bodily misconduct (kāyaduccarita) is misconduct by the body, or misconduct proceeding from the body. In this way, verbal and mental misconduct should also be understood. 'Endowed with' (samannāgatā) means being possessed of (samaṅgībhūtā). 'Disparagers of the noble ones' (ariyānaṃ upavādakā) refers to those who disparage the noble ones such as the Buddhas, down to even lay stream-enterers, either by means of the final matter (a pārājika offense) or by destroying their virtue; they are accusers, revilers, and censurers. 'Those of wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhikā) means those with perverted views. 'Those who undertake actions of wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā) refers to those who have various kinds of actions undertaken with wrong view as their cause, and also those who cause others to undertake bodily actions and so on that are rooted in wrong view. Herein, although disparaging the noble ones and wrong view are included by the mention of verbal and mental misconduct, mentioning them again is for the purpose of showing their state of great fault. Indeed, disparaging the noble ones is of great fault, similar to an act with immediate result. As it is said:

“Seyyathāpi[V 0.0295], sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃsampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye”ti (ma. ni. 1.149).

‘Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom might accomplish the fruit of Arahantship in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, I declare this to be an inevitable outcome: that without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, without relinquishing that view, one is placed in hell as if brought and deposited there.’

Micchādiṭṭhito ca mahāsāvajjataraṃ nāma aññaṃ natthi. Yathāha –

And there is nothing else more greatly at fault than wrong view. As it is said:

“Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi evaṃ mahāsāvajjataraṃ, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, micchādiṭṭhi. Micchādiṭṭhiparamāni, bhikkhave, vajjānī”ti (a. ni. 1.310).

‘Monks, I do not see even one other thing so greatly at fault as this, monks: wrong view. Monks, faults have wrong view as their utmost.’

Kāyassa bhedāti upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā. Paraṃ maraṇāti tadanantaraṃ abhinibbattakkhandhaggahaṇe. Atha vā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassa upacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cutito uddhaṃ. Apāyantiādi sabbaṃ nirayavevacanaṃ. Nirayo hi saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasammatā ayā apetattā, sukhānaṃ vā āyassa abhāvā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati, dosabahulatāya vā duṭṭhena kammunā nibbattā gati duggati. Vivasā nipatanti tattha dukkaṭakārinoti vinipāto. Natthi ettha assādasaññito ayoti nirayo.

'The breakup of the body' means the abandoning of the clung-to aggregates. 'After death' means at the time of grasping newly arisen aggregates immediately after that. Or, 'the breakup of the body' means because of the cutting off of the life faculty. 'After death' means after the death-consciousness. 'State of deprivation' and so on are all synonyms for hell. Indeed, hell is called a 'state of deprivation' (apāya) because it is devoid of the merit which is the cause of heaven and liberation, or because of the absence of the enjoyment of pleasures. It is a 'bad destination' (duggati) because it is the destination and resort of suffering, or it is a destination produced by bad kamma due to an abundance of aversion. It is a 'downfall' (vinipāta) because evildoers fall there helplessly. It is 'hell' (niraya) because here there is no enjoyment known as pleasure.

Atha vā apāyaggahaṇena tiracchānayoniṃ dīpeti, tiracchānayoni hi apāyo, sugatito apetattā. Na duggati, mahesakkhānaṃ nāgarājādīnaṃ sambhavato. Duggatiggahaṇena pettivisayaṃ dīpeti, so hi apāyo ceva duggati ca sugatito apetattā, dukkhassa ca gatibhūtattā. Na tu vinipāto asurasadisaṃ avinipatitattā. Petamahiddhikānañhi [M 0.0174] vimānānipi nibbattanti. Vinipātaggahaṇena asurakāyaṃ dīpeti, so hi yathāvuttenatthena apāyo ceva duggati ca sukhasamussayehi vinipātattā vinipātoti vuccati. Nirayaggahaṇena avīciādianekappakāraṃ nirayameva dīpeti. Upapannāti upagatā, tattha abhinibbattāti adhippāyo. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

Alternatively, by the term 'state of deprivation' (apāya), it indicates the animal realm. For the animal realm is a state of deprivation because it is devoid of a good destination. It is not a 'bad destination' (duggati) because of the existence of powerful beings like nāga kings. By the term 'bad destination', it indicates the realm of spirits (petas). For that is both a state of deprivation and a bad destination, being devoid of a good destination and being a destination of suffering. But it is not a 'downfall' (vinipāta) because it is not a complete falling away like that of the asuras; indeed, even mansions arise for powerful petas. By the term 'downfall', it indicates the host of asuras. For that is both a state of deprivation and a bad destination, and it is called a 'downfall' because it is a falling away from the collections of happiness. And by the term 'hell' (niraya), it indicates only hell of many kinds, such as Avīci. 'Arisen' (upapannā) means gone to, newly arisen there; this is the intended meaning. The bright side should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been said.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – ettha sugatiggahaṇena manussagatimpi saṅgaṇhāti. Saggaggahaṇena devagatiṃ eva. Tattha sundarā gatīti sugati. Rūpādīhi visayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo. So [V 0.0296] sabbopi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti ayaṃ vacanattho. Amukāya kappakoṭiyaṃ upacitaṃ tenāyaṃ etarahi, anāgate vā saggūpago apāyūpago cāti aṭṭhamanavamabalañāṇakiccaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā dassitaṃ. Tathā kappasatasahassevātiādīsupi. Tenevāha – “imāni bhagavato dve ñāṇānī”ti.

This, however, is the distinction: here, by the term 'good destination' (sugati), the human destination is also included. By the term 'heaven' (sagga), only the divine destination is included. Therein, a 'good destination' is a beautiful destination. 'Heaven' is what is supremely excellent with respect to sense objects such as form. All of that is 'world' (loka) in the sense of perishing and dissolving. This is the meaning of the word. The passage shows, by combining them as one, the function of the eighth and ninth powers of knowledge: that by kamma accumulated in such-and-such a koṭi of kappas, this person is now, or will be in the future, one who goes to heaven or one who goes to a state of deprivation. It is likewise for the text beginning with 'for a hundred thousand kappas.' Therefore, He said: ‘These are the two knowledges of the Blessed One.’

Nihato māro bodhimūleti nihato samucchinno kilesamāro bodhirukkhamūle. Idaṃ bhagavato dasamaṃ balanti idaṃ kilesamārassa hananaṃ samucchindanaṃ bhagavato dasamaṃ balaṃ. Tenevāha – “sabbāsavaparikkhayaṃ ñāṇa”nti. Yasmā pana yadā arahattamaggena savāsanā sabbe āsavā khepitā, tadā bhagavatā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ adhigataṃ nāma, tasmā “yaṃ sabbaññutā pattā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Māra was defeated at the root of the Bodhi tree' means: the Māra of defilements was defeated, utterly cut off, at the root of the Bodhi tree. 'This is the tenth power of the Blessed One' means: this knowledge, which is the defeating and utter cutting off of the Māra of defilements, is the tenth power of the Blessed One. Therefore, He said: ‘the knowledge of the destruction of all taints.’ Moreover, since it was when all taints together with their latent tendencies were destroyed by the path of Arahantship that the Blessed One is said to have attained the knowledge of omniscience, therefore it was said: ‘that omniscience was attained,’ and so forth.

Ayaṃ tāvettha ācariyānaṃ samānatthakathā. Paravādī panāha – “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma pāṭiekkaṃ natthi, yasmā ‘sabbaññutā pattā viditā sabbadhammā’ti vuttaṃ, tasmā sabbaññutaññāṇassevāyaṃ pabhedo”ti, taṃ na tathā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññameva hi dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Dasabalañāṇañhi sakasakakiccameva jānāti, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ tampi tato avasesampi jānāti. Dasabalañāṇesu hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti. Dutiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva, tatiyaṃ dhātunānattakāraṇameva, catutthaṃ ajjhāsayādhimuttimeva, pañcamaṃ kammavipākantarameva, chaṭṭhaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva, sattamaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva, aṭṭhamaṃ pubbenivutthakkhandhasantatimeva, navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutūpapātameva, dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttariñca pajānāti. Etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ sabbaṃ na karoti[M 0.0175]. Tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti, iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkoti, maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti.

This, for now, is the teachers' uniform explanation. But an opponent says: 'There is no separate knowledge called the ten powers, because it is said, "Having attained omniscience, all things are known," therefore this is a division of the knowledge of omniscience itself.' That should not be regarded thus. For the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another. The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective function, whereas the knowledge of omniscience knows that and also what remains beyond that. For among the knowledges of the ten powers: the first knows only cause and non-cause; the second knows only the demarcation of kamma; the third knows only the diversity of elements; the fourth knows only inclinations and resolutions; the fifth knows only the distinction in the results of kamma; the sixth knows only, together with the jhānas and so forth, their defilement and the like; the seventh knows only the acuteness or obtuseness of faculties; the eighth knows only the continuity of aggregates previously abided in; the ninth knows only the passing away and rebirth of beings; the tenth knows only the demarcation of the truths. The knowledge of omniscience, however, knows what is to be known by these and what is beyond that. But it does not perform all of their functions. For it cannot, being jhāna, enter absorption; nor, being psychic power, perform transformations; nor, being the path, destroy the defilements.

Apica paravādī evaṃ pucchitabbo “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāmetaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ avitakkavicāramattaṃ avitakkaavicāraṃ kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttara”nti. Jānanto “paṭipāṭiyā satta savitakkasavicārānī”ti vakkhati, tato parāni dve avitakkaavicārānīti, āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ siyā savitakkasavicāraṃ, siyā avitakkavicāramattaṃ, siyā avitakkaavicāranti. Tathā paṭipāṭiyā satta kāmāvacarāni, tato [V 0.0297] dve rūpāvacarāni, avasāne ekaṃ lokuttaranti vakkhati. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana savitakkasavicārameva kāmāvacarameva lokiyamevāti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked thus: "Is this knowledge of the ten powers with initial and sustained thought, without initial thought but with sustained thought only, or without initial and sustained thought? Is it of the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, the formless-sphere, mundane, or supramundane?" One who knows will say: "In sequence, seven are with initial and sustained thought; the two after that are without initial and sustained thought; and the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers may be with initial and sustained thought, may be without initial thought but with sustained thought only, or may be without initial and sustained thought." Similarly, he will say: "In sequence, seven are of the sense-sphere, then two are of the form-sphere, and the one at the end is supramundane." But the knowledge of omniscience is only with initial and sustained thought, only of the sense-sphere, and only mundane—this is the conclusion to be reached here.

Vicayahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Investigation is finished.

3. Yuttihārasampātavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Reasoning

65. Evaṃ nānānayehi vicayahārasampātaṃ vitthāretvā idāni yuttihārasampātādīni dassetuṃ “tattha katamo yuttihārasampāto”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha “tasmā rakkhitacittassā”ti gāthāya padattho vitthāritoyeva. Rakkhitacittassa sammāsaṅkappagocaro bhavissatīti yujjatīti manacchaṭṭhāni dvārāni satikavāṭena pidahitvā viharantassa kāmavitakkādīnaṃ micchāsaṅkappānaṃ avasaro eva natthīti nekkhammavitakkādiko sammāsaṅkappo eva tassa gocaro pavattiṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatīti ayamattho yujjati. Yuttiyā ghaṭeti saṃsandati sametīti attho. Sammāsaṅkappagocaro sammādiṭṭhi bhavissatīti vuttanayena sammāsaṅkappagocaro puggalo aviparītameva vitakkato sammādiṭṭhi bhavissati. Sammādiṭṭhisaṅkhātaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ purakkhatvā viharanto maggañāṇena pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ asammohato paṭivijjhissati. Tathā paṭivijjhanto ca dukkhasabhāvattā duggatisaṅkhātā sabbā bhavagatiyo jahissati, tato eva sabbaṃ vinipātabhayaṃ saṃsārabhayañca samatikkamissatīti sabbopi cāyamattho yutto evāti.

65. Having thus elaborated the Convergence of the Mode of Investigation through various methods, now, to show the Convergence of the Mode of Reasoning and so on, the passage beginning with, 'Therein, what is the Convergence of the Mode of Reasoning?' has been started. Therein, the word-meaning of the verse 'Therefore, for one with a guarded mind...' has already been explained in detail. The meaning of the phrase 'For one with a guarded mind, the resort will be right intention—this is fitting' is that for one who dwells having closed the six doors, with mind as the sixth, with the bolt of mindfulness, there is no opportunity for wrong intentions such as sensual thoughts; therefore, only right intention, beginning with thoughts of renunciation, will be his resort and sphere of activity. This meaning is fitting. The meaning is that it connects, corresponds, and agrees with reason. As for 'One whose resort is right intention will have right view': in the aforesaid manner, a person whose resort is right intention, because he thinks without distortion, will have right view. Dwelling with the insight-knowledge designated as 'right view' placed foremost, he will penetrate with path-knowledge the arising and passing away of the five aggregates without delusion. And penetrating thus, due to their nature of suffering, he will abandon all destinations of existence designated as woeful states. From that very reason, he will transcend all fear of downfall and the peril of saṃsāra. Thus, this entire meaning is indeed fitting.

Yuttihārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Reasoning is finished.

4. Padaṭṭhānahārasampātavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Proximate Cause

66. Sakasampattiyā [M 0.0176] viya susaṃvihitasaṅkappo bhavati. Indriyesu guttadvāratā sucaritapāripūriyā āsannakāraṇanti āha – “rakkhitacittassāti tiṇṇaṃ sucaritānaṃ padaṭṭhāna”nti. Tassattho – “rakkhitacittassā”ti idaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sucaritānaṃ padaṭṭhānavacananti. Nekkhammasaṅkappādibahulassa kāmacchandādinīvaraṇappahānaṃ sukaranti nekkhammasaṅkappādayo samathassa āsannakāraṇanti āha – “sammāsaṅkappagocaroti samathassa padaṭṭhāna”nti. Kammassakatāsammādiṭṭhiyaṃ sappaccayanāmarūpadassanasammādiṭṭhiyañca ṭhito attādhīnaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ passanto tadatikkamanupāyaṃ vipassanaṃ ārabhatīti sammādiṭṭhivipassanāya visesakāraṇanti āha – “sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāroti vipassanāya padaṭṭhāna”nti. Udayabbayadassanaṃ ussukkāpento sammattaniyāmaṃ [V 0.0298] okkamatīti taṃ paṭhamamaggādhigamassa kāraṇanti āha – “ñatvāna udayabbayanti dassanabhūmiyā padaṭṭhāna”nti. Ālokasaññāmanasikārādīhi thinamiddhassa abhibhavanaṃ vīriyassa āsannakāraṇanti āha – “thinamiddhābhibhū bhikkhūti vīriyassa padaṭṭhāna”nti. Yadipi ariyamaggakkhaṇe pahānabhāvanā samānakālā ekābhisamayassa icchitattā, tathāpi pahātabbassa pahānābhāve bhāvanāpāripūrī natthīti pahānanimittā viya katvā bhāvanā vuttā “sabbā duggatiyo jaheti bhāvanāya padaṭṭhāna”nti. Atha vā “sabbā duggatiyo jahe”ti idaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ yogīnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ ānisaṃsakittanaṃ hotīti bhāvanāya visesakāraṇanti vuttaṃ “sabbā…pe… padaṭṭhāna”nti.

66. As with one's own success, one's intention becomes well-composed. Guarding the sense doors is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of good conduct; thus, he said: “For one with a guarded mind, this is the proximate cause of the three good conducts.” Its meaning is: The phrase “for one with a guarded mind” is the statement of the proximate cause for the three good conducts. For one who abounds in thoughts of renunciation and so on, abandoning hindrances such as sensual desire becomes easy. Therefore, thoughts of renunciation and so on are the proximate cause of serenity; thus, he said: “The domain of right thought is the proximate cause of serenity.” Established in the right view of the ownership of kamma and in the right view that sees name-and-form with its conditions, one perceives the suffering of saṃsāra as dependent on oneself and undertakes insight as the means to transcend it. Therefore, right view is a special cause of insight; thus, he said: “Having right view as a forerunner is the proximate cause of insight.” One who strives by means of the vision of arising and passing away enters the fixed course of rightness. Therefore, that vision is the cause for attaining the first path; thus, he said: “Having known arising and passing away, this is the proximate cause for the stage of vision.” Overcoming sloth and torpor through attention to the perception of light and so on is a proximate cause for energy; thus, he said: “A monk who has overcome sloth and torpor is the proximate cause of energy.” Although at the moment of the noble path, abandoning and development occur simultaneously because a single penetration is desired, still, without the abandonment of what is to be abandoned, the fulfillment of development does not occur. Therefore, treating abandoning as if it were the cause, development is spoken of thus: “One abandons all bad destinations; this is the proximate cause of development.” Alternatively, this statement of the Blessed One, “One should abandon all bad destinations,” is a declaration of the benefits for the purpose of generating diligence in yogis. Therefore, it is a special cause for development; thus, it is said: “All… pe… proximate cause…”

Padaṭṭhānahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Proximate Cause is concluded.

5. Lakkhaṇahārasampātavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Characteristics

67. Indriyesu guttadvāratā satisaṃvaro, satibalena ca nekkhammavitakkādibahulo hotīti vuttaṃ – “tasmā rakkhitacittassa sammāsaṅkappagocaroti idaṃ satindriya”nti. Tassattho – “tasmā rakkhitacittassa sammāsaṅkappagocaro”ti ettha rakkhitacittatāya ca sammāsaṅkappagocaratā kāraṇūpacārena [M 0.0177] idaṃ satindriyaṃ, gahitāni bhavanti pañcindriyāni indriyalakkhaṇena vimuttiparipācanabhāvena vā ekalakkhaṇattāti adhippāyo. Gahito bhavatīti ettha maggalakkhaṇena gahaṇaṃ suviññeyyanti taṃ ṭhapetvā kāraṇato gahaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “sammādiṭṭhito hi sammāsaṅkappo pabhavatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tato eva gahito bhavati ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggoti vatvā vimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanānipi vuttāni.

67. Guarding the sense doors is restraint by mindfulness, and by the power of mindfulness one abounds in thoughts of renunciation and so on; thus it was said: “Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, the domain of right thought—this is the faculty of mindfulness.” Its meaning is: Herein, in “Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, the domain of right thought,” both the state of having a guarded mind and the state of having right thought as its domain—this is the faculty of mindfulness by way of metaphorical extension from the cause. The five faculties are included because they have a single characteristic, either by the characteristic of a faculty or by their nature of maturing one for liberation; this is the intention. Herein, in “it is included,” inclusion by way of the characteristic of the path is easy to understand. Therefore, setting that aside, in order to show the inclusion by way of cause, it was said: “For right thought arises from right view,” and so on. Having said, “Precisely from that the noble eightfold path is included,” liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation are also spoken of.

Lakkhaṇahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Characteristics is concluded.

6. Catubyūhahārasampātavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of the Fourfold Array

68. Rakkhīyatīti rakkhitaṃ. Idaṃ padavasena nibbacanaṃ. Yasmā pana atthavasena nibbacane vutte padavasena nibbacanaṃ vuttameva hoti, tasmā “rakkhitaṃ paripālīyatīti esā niruttī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha iti-saddo ādyattho, pakāre vā. Tena evamādikā evaṃpakārā vā esā niruttīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā cintetīti cittaṃ. Attano santānaṃ cinotīti cittaṃ, paccayehi [V 0.0299] citanti cittaṃ, cittavicittaṭṭhena cittaṃ, cittakaraṇaṭṭhena cittaṃ. Sammā saṅkappetīti sammāsaṅkappotiādinā nirutti veditabbā.

68. Because it is guarded (rakkhīyati), it is 'rakkhitaṃ'. This is the etymological explanation by way of the word. However, since when the etymological explanation by way of the meaning is stated, the etymological explanation by way of the word is indeed already stated, therefore it is said: 'It is guarded (rakkhitaṃ), it is protected (paripālīyati)—this is the derivation (nirutti)'. Therein, the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'ādi' (and so on), or it occurs in the sense of 'manner'. By that, this is what is meant: 'This derivation is of this sort (beginning with this) or of this manner'. Therefore, 'because it thinks (cinteti), it is cittaṃ (mind)'; 'because it accumulates (cinoti) its own continuity (santānaṃ), it is cittaṃ'; 'because it is accumulated (citaṃ) by conditions (paccayehi), it is cittaṃ'; 'by the meaning of being variegated (cittavicittaṭṭhena), it is cittaṃ'; 'by the meaning of making things variegated (cittakaraṇaṭṭhena), it is cittaṃ'. 'Because it rightly conceives (sammā saṅkappeti), it is sammāsaṅkappa (right thought)'—in this way and so on, the derivation should be understood.

Ayaṃ ettha bhagavato adhippāyoti “rakkhitacitto assā”tiādinā indriyasaṃvarādayo duggatipahānañca vadato bhagavato ettha gāthāyaṃ adhippāyo. Kokāliko hītiādi nidānaniddeso. Tattha hi-saddo kāraṇe. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā kokāliko (saṃ. ni. 1.181; a. ni. 10.89; su. ni. kokālikasutta) arakkhitacittatāya aggasāvakesu cittaṃ padosetvā padumanirayaṃ upapanno, tasmā duggatiyo jahitukāmo rakkhitacitto assāti bhagavā satiārakkhena cetasā samannāgato sabbā duggatiyo jahatīti attho. Suttamhi vuttaṃ “satiyā cittaṃ rakkhitabba”nti desanānusandhidassanaṃ.

This is the Blessed One’s intention here in this verse: of the Blessed One who speaks, by way of 'one should have a guarded mind' and so on, of restraint of the faculties and so on, and the abandoning of bad destinations, this is the intention. The passage beginning 'Kokālika hi' is the pointing out of the occasion. Therein, the word 'hi' is in the sense of 'reason'. This is what is meant: because Kokālika, due to having an unguarded mind, having corrupted his mind towards the foremost disciples, was reborn in the Paduma hell, therefore one who wishes to abandon bad destinations should have a guarded mind. The Blessed One, endowed with a mind that has mindfulness as its guard, abandons all bad destinations—this is the meaning. The statement made in the Sutta, 'The mind should be guarded by mindfulness,' is the showing of the connection of the teaching.

Catubyūhahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of the Fourfold Array is concluded.

7. Āvaṭṭahārasampātavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Turning

69. Nekkhammasaṅkappabahulo [M 0.0178] kasiṇavasena mettādivasena vā laddhāya cittekaggatāsaṅkhātāya cittamañjūsāya cittaṃ ṭhapetvā samādhiṃyeva vā yathāladdhaṃ saṃkilesato rakkhitacitto nāma hotīti vuttaṃ – “tasmā rakkhitacittassa sammāsaṅkappagocaroti ayaṃ samatho”ti. Paññāpadhānā vipassanāti āha – “sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāroti ayaṃ vipassanā”ti. Ariyamaggena dukkhasacce pariññāte udayabbayadassanaṃ matthakappattaṃ nāma hotīti vuttaṃ – “ñatvāna udayabbayanti dukkhapariññā”ti. “Yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti hi maggañāṇassa pavattidassanāti. Imāni cattāri saccānīti catusaccadhammavasena āvaṭṭanaṃ niṭṭhapeti. Tattha purimena saccadvayaṭṭhapanena visabhāgadhammavasena, pacchimena sabhāgadhammavasena āvaṭṭananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

69. A person abundant in thoughts of renunciation is called 'one with a guarded mind' by having placed the mind in the mind-casket called one-pointedness of mind—attained either by way of kasiṇa or by way of loving-kindness and so on—or by guarding from defilements concentration itself as it has been attained. Thus it is said: 'Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, right thought is the resort—this is serenity (samatha)'. Because insight has wisdom as its chief, he said: 'Having right view as a forerunner—this is insight (vipassanā)'. Because when the truth of suffering is fully understood by the noble path, the seeing of arising and passing away is said to have reached the summit, it is said: 'Having known arising and passing away is the full understanding of suffering'. For, 'Whatever has the nature to arise, all that has the nature to cease' is the seeing of the process of path-knowledge. By 'These are the four truths', he concludes the turning by way of the principle of the four truths. Therein, it should be understood that by the establishing of the first pair of truths, the turning occurs by way of dissimilar phenomena, and by the latter pair, by way of similar phenomena.

Āvaṭṭahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Turning is concluded.

8. Vibhattihārasampātavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Analysis

70. Kusalapakkho [V 0.0300] kusalapakkhena niddisitabboti rakkhitacittassāti satisaṃvaro, so chabbidho dvāravasena cakkhudvārasaṃvaro yāva manodvārasaṃvaroti. Sammāsaṅkappo tividho – nekkhammasaṅkappo, abyāpādasaṅkappo, avihiṃsāsaṅkappoti. Sammādiṭṭhi aṭṭhavidhā dukkhe ñāṇaṃ…pe… idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu ñāṇanti. Udayabbayañāṇaṃ paññāsavidhaṃ avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo…pe… vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi viññāṇakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Thinamiddhābhibhavanaṃ catubbidhaṃ catumaggavasena. Tattha satisaṃvaro lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidho. Tesu lokiyo kāmāvacarova, lokuttaro dassanabhāvanābhedato duvidho. Ekameko cettha catusatipaṭṭhānabhedato catubbidho. Esa nayo sammāsaṅkappādīsupi.

70. The wholesome side is to be designated by the wholesome side. Thus, 'of one whose mind is guarded' refers to mindfulness-restraint. It is sixfold by way of the doors: restraint of the eye-door up to restraint of the mind-door. Right thought is threefold: the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill-will, and the thought of non-cruelty.
