Right view is eightfold: knowledge in suffering... up to knowledge in phenomena that have arisen dependently from this condition. Knowledge of arising and passing away is fiftyfold: from the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form... up to one who, even while seeing the characteristic of change, sees the dissolution of the consciousness aggregate. Overcoming sloth and torpor is fourfold by way of the four paths. Herein, mindfulness-restraint is twofold by way of the mundane and the supramundane. Of these, the mundane is only of the sense sphere, while the supramundane is twofold by the distinction of vision and development. Each one of these is fourfold by the distinction of the four foundations of mindfulness. This is the method for right thought and the others as well.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – sammāsaṅkappo paṭhamajjhānavasena rūpāvacarotipi nīharitabbo. Padaṭṭhānavibhāgo padaṭṭhānahārasampāte vuttanayena vattabbo[M 0.0179]. Akusalapakkhe asaṃvaro cakkhuasaṃvaro…pe… kāyaasaṃvaro, copanakāyaasaṃvaro, vācāasaṃvaro, manoasaṃvaroti aṭṭhavidho. Micchāsaṅkappo kāmavitakkādivasena tividho. Aññāṇaṃ “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā aṭṭhavidhā vibhattaṃ. Sammādiṭṭhipaṭipakkhato micchādiṭṭhi dvāsaṭṭhividhena veditabbā. Thinamiddhaṃ uppattibhūmito pañcavidhanti evaṃ akusalapakkhe vibhatti veditabbā.

However, this is the distinction: right thought should also be extracted as belonging to the form sphere by way of the first jhāna. The analysis of the proximate cause should be explained in the manner stated in the convergence of the mode of proximate cause. In the unwholesome side, non-restraint is eightfold: non-restraint of the eye... up to non-restraint of the body, non-restraint of prompting the body, non-restraint of speech, and non-restraint of the mind. Wrong thought is threefold by way of sensual thought and so forth. Ignorance is analyzed as eightfold by way of 'ignorance in suffering' and so forth. As the opposite of right view, wrong view should be understood as sixty-twofold. Sloth and torpor are fivefold from the plane of arising. Thus, the analysis in the unwholesome side should be understood.

Vibhattihārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Analysis is concluded.

9. Parivattanahārasampātavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Convergence of the Mode of Transformation

71. Parivattanahāre āvaṭṭahāre vuttanayena samathavipassanāniddhāraṇaṃ akatvā “samathavipassanāya bhāvitāyā”ti āha. Lokiyā cettha samathavipassanā daṭṭhabbā. Paṭipakkhenāti “arakkhitena cittenā”ti gāthāya paṭipakkhenāti adhippāyo. Atha vā vibhattihāre niddiṭṭhassa akusalapakkhassa paṭipakkhenāti attho.

71. In the Mode of Transformation, without making a determination of serenity and insight according to the method stated in the Mode of Revolving, it is said, 'by means of serenity and insight having been developed.' And here, mundane serenity and insight should be understood. By 'as the opposite,' the intention is 'as the opposite' of the verse 'with an unprotected mind.' Alternatively, the meaning is 'as the opposite' of the unwholesome side that was specified in the Mode of Inflection.

Parivattanahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mode of Transformation is concluded.

10. Vevacanahārasampātavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mode of Synonyms

72. “Mānasaṃ [V 0.0301] hadayaṃ paṇḍaraṃ viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho manoviññāṇadhātū”ti (dha. sa. 6) ca cittassa vevacanaṃ. “Takko vitakko saṅkappo appanā byappanā cetaso abhiniropanā”ti ca sammāsaṅkappassa. “Paññā pajānanā vicayo pavicayo”tiādinā (dha. sa. 16) sammādiṭṭhiyā. “Thinaṃ thiyanā thiyitattaṃ cittassa akallatā akammaññatā onāho parināho antosaṅkoco”ti thinassa. “Akallatā akammaññatā kāyālasiyaṃ supyaṃ supyanā supitatta”nti (dha. sa. 1163) middhassa. “Bhikkhako bhikkhū”tiādinā (pārā. 45) bhikkhupadassa. “Duggati apāyo vinipāto vaṭṭadukkhaṃ saṃsāro”tiādinā duggatiyā vevacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

72. ‘Mind, the heart, the pure, consciousness, the consciousness aggregate, the mind-consciousness element’—these and others should be known as synonyms for mind. ‘Reasoning, thought, intention, application, sustained application, the directing of the mind’—these and others should be known as synonyms for right intention. By way of ‘Wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation,’ and so forth, the synonyms for right view should be known. ‘Sloth, the state of being rigid, the fact of being rigid, unfitness of mind, unworkability, envelopment, complete envelopment, inner contraction’—thus, the synonyms for sloth should be known. ‘Unfitness, unworkability, bodily laziness, sleepiness, the state of causing sleep, the fact of having slept’—thus are the synonyms for torpor. By way of ‘He begs, therefore he is a bhikkhu,’ and so forth, the synonyms for the word ‘bhikkhu’ should be known. By way of ‘A bad destination, a state of loss, a place of ruin, the suffering of the round of rebirth, transmigration,’ and so forth, the synonyms for a bad destination should be known.

Vevacanahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mode of Synonyms is concluded.

11. Paññattihārasampātavaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mode of Designation

73. Adhiṭṭhahitvā [M 0.0180] rakkhantiyā satiyā rakkhiyamānaṃ cittaṃ tassā adhiṭṭhānaṃ viya hotīti katvā vuttaṃ – “rakkhitacittassāti padaṭṭhānapaññatti satiyā”ti. Sesaṃ imasmiṃ paññattihārasampāte ito paresu otaraṇasodhanahārasampātesupi apubbaṃ natthi. Heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

73. Because the mind, being guarded by mindfulness which guards having resolved, becomes like the very foundation of that mindfulness, it is said: ‘For one with a guarded mind, the designation has mindfulness as its proximate cause.’ As for the rest, in this Concatenation of the Mode of Designation and also in the subsequent Concatenations of the Modes of Descent and Purification, there is nothing new. It is just according to the method stated previously.

Paññattihārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mode of Designation is concluded.

14. Adhiṭṭhānahārasampātavaṇṇanā

14. The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mode of Determination

76. Adhiṭṭhānahārasampāte sammādiṭṭhi nāma yaṃ dukkhe ñāṇantiādinā catusaccahetuhetusamuppannapaccayapaccayuppannasaṅkhātassa visayassa vasena vemattataṃ dassetvā puna yaṃ tattha tattha yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇadassananti pāḷipāḷiatthānaṃ avasiṭṭhavisayavaseneva vemattataṃ dīpeti. Tattha yaṃ saccāgamananti yaṃ saccato aviparītato visayassa āgamanaṃ, adhigamoti attho. “Yaṃ paccāgamana”ntipi pāṭho, tassa yaṃ paṭipāṭivisayassa āgamanaṃ, taṃtaṃvisayādhigamoti attho[V 0.0302]. Sesamettha parikkhārasamāropanahārasampātesu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ pubbe vuttanayattā uttānameva.

76. In the Concatenation of the Mode of Determination, by way of ‘Right view is knowledge of suffering,’ etc., having shown the diversity by way of the object designated as the four truths, cause, what arises from cause, condition, and what arises from condition, it again clarifies the diversity solely by way of the remaining objects of the Pali texts and their meanings, namely, ‘the knowledge and vision of things as they are in each respective case.’ Therein, ‘yaṃ saccāgamanaṃ’ (whatever arrival at the truth) means whatever knowing of the object there is truthfully, without perversion; the meaning is attainment. There is also the reading ‘yaṃ paccāgamanaṃ’ (whatever return); its meaning is: whatever knowing there is of the respective objects in order, that is the attainment of each particular object. As for the rest, whatever should be said here in the Concatenation of the Mode of Determination and in the Concatenations of the Modes of Requisite and Superimposition, that is already clear because of the method stated previously.

Adhiṭṭhānahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mode of Determination is concluded.

Missakahārasampātavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Concatenation of the Mixed Mode

Api cettha hārasampātaniddeso imināpi nayena veditabbo –

Furthermore, herein the exposition of the concatenation of the modes should be understood by this method also:

“Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā;

Manasā ce pasannena, bhāsati vā karoti vā;

Tato naṃ sukhamanveti, chāyāva anapāyinī”ti. (dha. pa. 2);

“Phenomena are preceded by mind, have mind as their chief, are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows one like a shadow that never departs.”

Tattha katamo desanāhārasampāto? Manopubbaṅgamā dhammāti manoti khandhavavatthānena viññāṇakkhandhaṃ deseti. Āyatanavavatthānena manāyatanaṃ[M 0.0181], dhātuvavatthānena viññāṇadhātuṃ, indriyavavatthānena manindriyaṃ. Katame dhammā pubbaṅgamā? Cha dhammā pubbaṅgamā, kusalānaṃ kusalamūlāni, akusalānaṃ akusalamūlāni, sādhipatikānaṃ adhipati, sabbacittuppādānaṃ indriyāni. Api ca imasmiṃ sutte mano adhippeto. Yathā balaggassa rājā pubbaṅgamo, evamevaṃ dhammānaṃ mano pubbaṅgamo. Tattha tividhena mano pubbaṅgamo nekkhammachandena abyāpādachandena avihiṃsāchandena. Tattha alobhassa nekkhammachandena manopubbaṅgamaṃ, adosassa abyāpādachandena manopubbaṅgamaṃ, amohassa avihiṃsāchandena manopubbaṅgamaṃ.

Herein, what is the concatenation of the mode of teaching? In ‘Phenomena are preceded by mind,’ ‘mind’ indicates the consciousness aggregate by way of the delimitation of aggregates. By way of the delimitation of sense bases, it indicates the mind base; by way of the delimitation of elements, the consciousness element; by way of the delimitation of faculties, the mind faculty. What phenomena are preceded? Six phenomena are preceded: for wholesome states, the wholesome roots; for unwholesome states, the unwholesome roots; for states with a dominant factor, the dominant factor; for all arisings of consciousness, the faculties. Moreover, in this discourse, mind is intended. Just as a king is the forerunner of an army, so too is mind the forerunner of phenomena. Herein, mind is the forerunner in three ways: through the desire for renunciation, the desire for non-ill will, and the desire for non-harming. Herein, for non-greed, mind is the forerunner through the desire for renunciation; for non-hatred, mind is the forerunner through the desire for non-ill will; for non-delusion, mind is the forerunner through the desire for non-harming.

Manoseṭṭhāti mano tesaṃ dhammānaṃ seṭṭhaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ pavaraṃ mūlaṃ pamukhaṃ pāmokkhaṃ, tena vuccati “manoseṭṭhā”ti. Manomayāti manena katā, manena nimmitā, manena nibbattā, mano tesaṃ paccayo, tena vuccati “manomayā”ti. Te pana dhammā chandasamudānitā anāvilasaṅkappasamuṭṭhānā phassasamodhānā vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho. Manasā ce pasannenāti yā saddhā saddahanā okappanā abhippasādo. Iti iminā pasādena upeto samupeto upagato samupagato sampanno samannāgato, tena vuccati “pasannenā”ti idaṃ manokammaṃ[V 0.0303]. Bhāsati vāti vacīkammaṃ. Karoti vāti kāyakammaṃ. Iti dasakusalakammapathā dassitā.

‘Have mind as their chief’ means the mind is the chief, distinguished, highest, excellent, root, foremost, and principal of those phenomena. Therefore, it is said ‘have mind as their chief.’ ‘Mind-made’ means made by mind, created by mind, produced by mind; mind is their condition. Therefore, it is said ‘mind-made.’ Those phenomena, moreover, are originated by desire, arise from unperturbed thought, and have contact as their convergence—they are the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and the formations aggregate. ‘If with a pure mind’ refers to that which is faith, conviction, confidence, and serene trust. Thus, one endowed with, possessed of, furnished with, and complete in this serenity is called ‘one with a pure mind.’ This is mental action. ‘Speaks’ indicates verbal action. ‘Acts’ indicates bodily action. Thus, the ten wholesome courses of action have been shown.

Tatoti dasavidhassa kusalakammassa katattā upacitattā. Nanti yo so katapuñño katakusalo katabhīruttāṇo, taṃ puggalaṃ. Sukhanti duvidhaṃ sukhaṃ kāyikaṃ cetasikañca. Anvetīti anugacchati.

‘From that’ (tato) is because the tenfold wholesome kamma has been done and accumulated. ‘One’ (naṃ) refers to that person who has made merit, done wholesome deeds, and created a refuge from fear. ‘Happiness’ (sukhaṃ) is twofold: bodily and mental. ‘Follows’ (anveti) means it follows along.

Idhassu puriso appahīnānusayo saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādaṃ anupassati, so saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādaṃ anupassanto yathādiṭṭhaṃ yathāsutaṃ sampattibhavaṃ pattheti. Iccassa avijjā ca bhavataṇhā ca anubaddhā honti, so yathādiṭṭhaṃ yathāsutaṃ sampattibhavaṃ patthento pasādanīyavatthusmiṃ cittaṃ pasādeti saddahati okappeti. So pasannacitto tividhaṃ puññakiriyavatthuṃ anutiṭṭhati dānamayaṃ sīlamayaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ kāyena vācāya manasā. So tassa vipākaṃ paccanubhoti diṭṭheva dhamme upapajje vā aparāpare vā pariyāye. Iti kho panassa avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ, saḷāyatanapaccayā sukhavedanīyo phasso, phassapaccayā [M 0.0182] vedanāti evaṃ santaṃ taṃ sukhamanveti. Tassevaṃ vedanāya aparāparaṃ parivattamānāya uppajjati taṇhā. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… samudayo hotīti.

Here, a person with unabandoned underlying tendencies repeatedly sees gratification in things that are fettering. Repeatedly seeing gratification in things that are fettering, they long for a prosperous becoming as seen and as heard. Thus, for this person, ignorance and craving for becoming follow in succession. Longing for a prosperous becoming as seen and as heard, they make their mind serene, have faith, and become confident in a basis for serenity. With a serene mind, they undertake the threefold basis of meritorious action—giving, virtue, and development—by body, speech, and mind. They experience its result either in this very life, or in the next life, or in a subsequent life. Thus, indeed, for this person: with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold sense base comes to be; with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact to be felt as pleasant comes to be; with contact as condition, feeling comes to be. This being so, happiness follows that person. For that person, with feeling thus repeatedly changing, craving arises. With craving as condition, clinging arises… and so on… the origin of this mass of suffering comes to be.

Tattha yaṃ mano, ye ca manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, yañca sukhaṃ, ime vuccanti pañcakkhandhā, te dukkhasaccaṃ. Tesaṃ purimakāraṇabhūtā avijjā bhavataṇhā ca samudayasaccaṃ. Tesaṃ pariññāya pahānāya bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti, dukkhassa pariññāya samudayassa pahānāya. Yena parijānāti, yena pajahati, ayaṃ maggo. Yattha ca maggo pavattati, ayaṃ nirodho. Imāni cattāri saccāni evaṃ āyatanadhātuindriyamukhenāpi niddhāretabbāni. Tattha samudayena assādo, dukkhena ādīnavo, magganirodhehi nissaraṇaṃ, sukhassa anvayo phalaṃ, manasā pasannena kāyavacīsamīhā upāyo, manopubbaṅgamattā dhammānaṃ attano sukhakāmena pasannena manasā vacīkammaṃ kāyakammañca pavattetabbanti ayaṃ bhagavato āṇatti. Ayaṃ desanāhārasampāto.

Herein, that which is mind, and those phenomena that are preceded by mind, and that which is happiness—these are called the five aggregates; they are the truth of suffering. Their prior causes, ignorance and craving for becoming, are the truth of the origin. For their full understanding and abandonment, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma—for the full understanding of suffering and the abandonment of its origin. That by which one fully understands and that by which one abandons, this is the path. And where the path operates, this is cessation. These four truths should be determined in this way also through the gateway of the sense bases, elements, and faculties. Herein, with the origin there is gratification; with suffering, danger; with the path and cessation, escape. The following of happiness is the fruit. With a serene mind, bodily and verbal endeavor is the means. Because phenomena are preceded by mind, one who desires one's own happiness should, with a serene mind, arouse verbal and bodily action—this is the Blessed One's instruction. This is the application of the mode of teaching.

Tattha katamo vicayahārasampāto? Mananato ārammaṇavijānanato mano. Mananalakkhaṇe sampayuttesu ādhipaccakaraṇato pubbaṅgamo īhābhāvato nissattanijjīvaṭṭhena dhammā. Gāmesu gāmaṇi [V 0.0304] viya padhānaṭṭhena mano seṭṭho etesanti manoseṭṭhā. Sahajātādipaccayabhūtena manasā nibbattāti manomayā. Akālussiyato, ārammaṇassa okappanato ca pasannena vacīviññattivipphārato tathā sādiyanato ca bhāsati. Copanakāyavipphārato tathā sādiyanato ca karoti. Tathā pasutattā anaññattā ca “tato”ti vuttaṃ. Sukhanato sātabhāvato iṭṭhabhāvato ca “sukha”nti vuttaṃ. Katūpacitattā avipakkavipākattā ca “anvetī”ti vuttaṃ. Kāraṇāyattavuttito asaṅkantito ca “chāyāva anapāyinī”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ anupadavicayato vicayahārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the mode of analysis? Mind (mano) is so called from 'minding,' from cognizing an object. It is the forerunner (pubbaṅgamo) because it exercises dominance among associated states in its characteristic of minding. Phenomena (dhammā) are so called due to the absence of striving, in the sense of being without a being, without a soul. Just as a village headman in the villages, in the sense of being primary, 'mind is their chief' (mano seṭṭho etesaṃ), thus they are called 'manoseṭṭhā' (having mind as their chief). Because they are produced by mind which is a condition such as co-nascence, they are called 'manomayā' (mind-made). 'With a pure (mind)' (pasannena) is because of its unclouded nature and because of its settling upon an object. One 'speaks' (bhāsati) because of the diffusion of verbal intimation and because of assenting thus. One 'acts' (karoti) because of the diffusion of bodily movement and because of assenting thus. 'From that' (tato) is said because of being thus engaged and because of not being other. 'Happiness' (sukhaṃ) is said because it makes happy, because of its agreeable nature, and because of its desirable nature. 'It follows' (anveti) is said because it has been done and accumulated and because its result has not yet ripened. 'Like a non-departing shadow' (chāyāva anapāyinī) is said because its occurrence is dependent on a cause and because it does not transmigrate. This is the application of the mode of analysis by way of word-by-word investigation.

Tattha katamo yuttihārasampāto? Manassa dhammānaṃ ādhipaccayogato pubbaṅgamatā yujjati. Tato eva tesaṃ manassa anuvattanato dhammānaṃ manoseṭṭhatā yujjati. Sahajātādipaccayavasena manasā nibbattattā dhammānaṃ manomayatā yujjati. Manasā pasannena samuṭṭhānānaṃ kāyavacīkammānaṃ kusalabhāvo yujjati. Yena kusalakammaṃ upacitaṃ, taṃ chāyā viya sukhaṃ anvetīti yujjati. Ayaṃ yuttihārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the mode of justification? The mind's precursorship of phenomena is justified due to its connection with dominance. Precisely from that, the mind's being chief among phenomena is justified due to their following the mind. The mind-made nature of phenomena is justified because they are produced by the mind by way of co-nascence and other conditions. The wholesome nature of bodily and verbal actions arising from a serene mind is justified. It is justified that happiness follows the one by whom wholesome kamma has been accumulated, just like a shadow. This is the application of the mode of justification.

Tattha [M 0.0183] katamo padaṭṭhāno hārasampāto? Mano manopavicārānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā sabbassa kusalapakkhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Bhāsatī”ti sammāvācā, “karotī”ti sammākammanto, te sammāājīvassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sammāvāyāmo sammāsatiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sammāsati sammāsamādhissa padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Manasā pasannenā”ti ettha pasādo saddhindriyaṃ, taṃ sīlassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sīlaṃ samādhissa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Samādhi paññāyāti yāva vimuttiñāṇadassanā yojetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ padaṭṭhānahārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the mode of proximate cause? The mind is the proximate cause of mental investigations. Phenomena preceded by mind are the proximate cause for the entire wholesome side. By 'speaks' is meant Right Speech; by 'acts' is meant Right Action; these are the proximate cause for Right Livelihood. Right Livelihood is the proximate cause for Right Effort. Right Effort is the proximate cause for Right Mindfulness. Right Mindfulness is the proximate cause for Right Concentration. Here, in 'with a serene mind,' serenity is the faculty of faith, and that is the proximate cause for virtue. Virtue is the proximate cause for concentration. Concentration is the proximate cause for wisdom, and so on, it should be connected up to the knowledge and vision of liberation. This is the application of the mode of proximate cause.

Tattha katamo lakkhaṇo hārasampāto? “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti manopubbaṅgamatāvacanena dhammānaṃ chandapubbaṅgamatāpi vīriyapubbaṅgamatāpi vīmaṃsāpubbaṅgamatāpi vuttā hoti ādhipateyyalakkhaṇena chandādīnaṃ manasā ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā nesaṃ saddhādipubbaṅgamatāpi vuttā hoti indriyalakkhaṇena saddhādīnaṃ manasā ekalakkhaṇattā. “Manasā ce pasannenā”ti yathā manassa pasādasamannāgamo taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ kāyavacīkammānaṃ anavajjabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ. Evaṃ cittassa satiādisamannāgamopi nesaṃ anavajjabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ yonisomanasikārasamuṭṭhānabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Sukhamanvetī”ti sukhānugamanavacanena sukhassa paccayabhūtānaṃ manāpiyarūpādīnaṃ [V 0.0305] anugamo vutto hoti tesampi kammapaccayatāya ekalakkhaṇattāti. Ayaṃ lakkhaṇahārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the mode of characteristics? By the statement 'Phenomena are preceded by mind,' it is also stated that phenomena are preceded by desire, preceded by energy, and preceded by investigation, due to the characteristic of dominance, since desire and the like share a single characteristic with the mind. Similarly, it is stated that they are preceded by faith and the like, due to the characteristic of faculties, since faith and the like share a single characteristic with the mind. Just as the mind's being endowed with serenity is the characteristic of blamelessness for bodily and verbal actions arising from it, so too the mind's being endowed with mindfulness and the like is also a characteristic of blamelessness for them, due to their having a single characteristic by way of arising from wise attention. By the statement 'happiness follows,' the following of pleasing forms and the like, which are conditions for happiness, is also stated, because they too share a single characteristic due to being conditioned by kamma. This is the application of the mode of characteristics.

Tattha katamo catubyūho hārasampāto? “Manopubbaṅgamā”tiādīsu “mano”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ nibbacanaṃ niruttaṃ, taṃ padatthaniddesavasena veditabbaṃ. Padattho ca vuttanayena suviññeyyova. Ye sukhena atthikā, tehi pasannena manasā kāyavacīmanokammāni pavattetabbānīti ayamettha bhagavato adhippāyo. Puññakiriyāya aññesampi pubbaṅgamā hutvā tattha tesaṃ sammā upanetāro imissā desanāya nidānaṃ. “Chadvārādhipatī rājā (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.181 erakapattanāgarājavatthu), cittānuparivattino dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 62; 1205-1206), cittassa ekadhammassa, sabbeva vasamanvagū”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.62) evamādisamānayanena imissā desanāya saṃsandanā desanānusandhi. Padānusandhiyo pana suviññeyyāvāti. Ayaṃ catubyūho hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of the fourfold array? In phrases such as 'Phenomena are preceded by mind,' the derivation and explanation of terms like 'mind' should be understood through the exposition of the meaning of the terms. The meaning of the terms is easily understood by the method already stated. The Blessed One's intention here is that those who desire happiness should engage in bodily, verbal, and mental actions with a serene mind. The origin of this teaching are those who, becoming forerunners for others in meritorious deeds, rightly guide them therein. The connection of the teaching is the correlation of this teaching with similar passages, such as: 'The king, lord of the six doors...'; 'Phenomena follow the mind...'; 'Of the mind, a single phenomenon, all come under its sway...'. The connections of the terms, however, are easily understood. This is the application of the method of the fourfold array.

Tattha [M 0.0184] katamo āvaṭṭo hārasampāto? “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti tattha yāni tīṇi kusalamūlāni, tāni aṭṭhannaṃ sammattānaṃ hetu. Ye sammattā, ayaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Yaṃ manosahajanāmarūpaṃ, idaṃ dukkhaṃ. Asamucchinnā purimanipphannā avijjā bhavataṇhā, ayaṃ samudayo. Yattha tesaṃ pahānaṃ, ayaṃ nirodhoti imāni cattāri saccāni. Ayaṃ āvaṭṭo hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of turning? In 'Phenomena are preceded by mind,' the three wholesome roots therein are the cause for the eight kinds of rightness. Those kinds of rightness are the Noble Eightfold Path. That name-and-form co-arising with mind is suffering. Ignorance and craving for existence, previously arisen and not yet eradicated, this is the origin. Where their abandoning occurs, that is cessation—these are the Four Noble Truths. This is the application of the method of turning.

Tattha katamo vibhattihārasampāto? “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manasā ce pasannena, tato naṃ sukhamanvetī”ti nayidaṃ yathārutavasena gahetabbaṃ. Yo hi samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā pāṇātipātimhi micchādiṭṭhike micchāpaṭipanne sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādeti, pasannena ca cittena abhūtaguṇābhitthavanavasena bhāsati vā nipaccakāraṃ vāssa yaṃ karoti, na tato naṃ sukhamanveti. Dukkhameva pana taṃ tato cakkaṃva vahato padamanveti. Iti hi idaṃ vibhajjabyākaraṇīyaṃ. Yaṃ manasā ce pasannena bhāsati vā karoti vā, tañce vacīkammaṃ kāyakammañca sukhavedanīyanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sammattagatehi sukhavedanīyaṃ micchāgatehi dukkhavedanīyanti. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ pasādo daṭṭhabbo? Nāyaṃ pasādo, pasādapatirūpako pana micchādhimokkhoti vadāmi. Ayaṃ vibhattihārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of analysis? This statement, 'Phenomena are preceded by mind... if with a serene mind... then happiness follows,' should not be taken literally. For if an ascetic or a brahmin generates serenity of mind towards one who takes life, holds wrong view, and is of wrong practice, and with that serene mind speaks in praise of non-existent virtues or performs an act of homage for him, happiness does not follow him from that. Rather, suffering follows him from that, just as the wheel follows the foot of the draught animal. For this should be explained with analysis. The statement, 'If what one speaks or does with a serene mind, that verbal and bodily action is to be experienced as pleasant,' is to be analyzed. For what reason? With regard to those who have gone to rightness, it is to be experienced as pleasant; with regard to those who have gone to wrongness, it is to be experienced as painful. But how is this serenity to be understood? This is not serenity; rather, I say it is a counterfeit of serenity, a wrong resolve. This is the application of the method of analysis.

Tattha [V 0.0306] katamo parivattano hārasampāto? Manopubbaṅgamātiādi. Yaṃ manasā paduṭṭhena bhāsati vā karoti vā dukkhassānugāmī. Idañhi suttaṃ etassa ujupaṭipakkho. Ayaṃ parivattano hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of reversal? The verse beginning, 'Phenomena are preceded by mind...' Whatever one speaks or does with a corrupted mind is followed by suffering. For this discourse is the direct opposite of that one. This is the application of the method of reversal.

Tattha katamo vevacano hārasampāto? “Manopubbaṅgamā”ti mano cittaṃ manāyatanaṃ manindriyaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇadhātūti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Pubbaṅgamā purecārino puregāminoti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Dhammā attā sabhāvāti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Seṭṭhaṃ padhānaṃ pavaranti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Manomayā manonibbattā manosambhūtāti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Pasannena saddahantena okappentenāti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Sukhaṃ sātaṃ vedayitanti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Anveti anugacchati anubandhatīti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Ayaṃ vevacano hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of synonyms? For 'mano' in 'Manopubbaṅgamā,' the terms 'cittaṃ,' 'manāyatanaṃ,' 'manindriyaṃ,' 'manoviññāṇaṃ,' and 'manoviññāṇadhātu' are synonyms. For 'pubbaṅgamā,' 'purecārino' and 'puregāmino' are synonyms. For 'dhammā,' 'attā' and 'sabhāvā' are synonyms. For 'seṭṭhaṃ,' 'padhānaṃ' and 'pavaraṃ' are synonyms. For 'manomayā,' 'manonibbattā' and 'manosambhūtā' are synonyms. For 'pasannena,' 'saddahantena' and 'okappentena' are synonyms. For 'sukhaṃ,' 'sātaṃ' and 'vedayitaṃ' are synonyms. For 'anveti,' 'anugacchati' and 'anubandhati' are synonyms. This is the application of the method of synonyms.

Tattha [M 0.0185] katamo paññattihārasampāto? Manopubbaṅgamāti ayaṃ manaso kiccapaññatti. Dhammāti sabhāvapaññatti, kusalakammapathapaññatti. Manoseṭṭhāti padhānapaññatti. Manomayāti sahajātapaññatti. Pasannenāti saddhindriyena samannāgatapaññatti, assaddhiyassa paṭikkhepapaññatti. Bhāsati vā karoti vāti sammāvācāsammākammantānaṃ nikkhepapaññatti. Tato naṃ sukhamanvetīti kammassa phalānubandhapaññatti, kammassa avināsapaññattīti. Ayaṃ paññattihārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of designations? The phrase 'Manopubbaṅgamā' is a designation of the mind's function. The word 'dhammā' is a designation of intrinsic nature and a designation of wholesome courses of action. The phrase 'Manoseṭṭhā' is a designation of primacy. The word 'Manomayā' is a designation of co-arising. The word 'pasannena' is a designation of being endowed with the faculty of faith and a designation of the rejection of faithlessness. The phrase 'bhāsati vā karoti vā' is a designation of the establishment of right speech and right action. The phrase 'tato naṃ sukhamanveti' is a designation of the consequence of kamma and a designation of the indestructibility of kamma. This is the application of the method of designations.

Tattha katamo otaraṇo hārasampāto? Manoti viññāṇakkhandho. Dhammāti vedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhā. Bhāsati vā karoti vāti kāyavacīviññattiyo. Tāsaṃ nissayā cattāro mahābhūtāti rūpakkhandhoti ayaṃ khandhehi otaraṇo. Manoti abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇanti manoggahaṇena avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā gahitāti. Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… samudayo hotīti ayaṃ paṭiccasamuppādena otaraṇoti. Ayaṃ otaraṇo hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of descent? 'Mano' is the aggregate of consciousness. 'Dhammā' are the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations. 'Bhāsati vā karoti vā' are bodily and verbal intimations; their basis, the four great elements, is the aggregate of form. This is the descent by way of the aggregates. 'Mano' is volitional consciousness; thus, by the taking up of 'mano', 'formations conditioned by ignorance' are grasped. 'Conditioned by formations, consciousness arises... [and so on]... thus there is origination'—this is the descent by way of dependent origination. This is the application of the method of descent.

Tattha katamo sodhano hārasampāto? Manoti ārambho neva padasuddhi, na ārambhasuddhi. Manopubbaṅgamāti padasuddhi, na ārambhasuddhi. Tathā dhammāti yāva sukhanti padasuddhi, na ārambhasuddhi. Sukhamanvetīti pana padasuddhi ceva ārambhasuddhi cāti. Ayaṃ sodhano hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of purification? 'Mano' is a beginning; it is neither a pure term nor a pure opening. 'Manopubbaṅgamā' is a pure term, but not a pure opening. Likewise, from 'dhammā' up to 'sukhaṃ' is a pure term, but not a pure opening. But 'sukhamanveti' is both a pure term and a pure opening. This is the application of the method of purification.

Tattha [V 0.0307] katamo adhiṭṭhāno hārasampāto? Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayāti ekattatā. Manasā ce pasannenāti vemattatā, tathā manasā ce pasannenāti ekattatā. Bhāsati vā karoti vāti vemattatā, tathā manasā ce pasannenāti ekattatā. So pasādo duvidho ajjhattañca byāpādavikkhambhanato, bahiddhā ca okappanato. Tathā sampattibhavahetubhūtopi vaḍḍhihetubhūtovāti ayaṃ vemattatā. Tayidaṃ suttaṃ dvīhi ākārehi adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ hetunā ca yo pasannamānaso, vipākena ca yo sukhavedanīyoti. Ayaṃ adhiṭṭhāno hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of determination? 'Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā, manomayā' is generality. 'Manasā ce pasannena' is particularity. Likewise, 'Manasā ce pasannena' is generality. 'Bhāsati vā karoti vā' is particularity. Likewise, 'Manasā ce pasannena' is generality. That serenity is twofold: internal, through the suppression of ill will, and external, through conviction. Likewise, being a cause for a fortunate becoming and also a cause for growth—this is particularity. This discourse should be determined in two aspects: by cause, which is 'one with a serene mind'; and by result, which is 'what is to be experienced as pleasant'. This is the application of the method of determination.

Tattha katamo parikkhāro hārasampāto? Manopubbaṅgamāti ettha manoti kusalaviññāṇaṃ. Tassa ca ñāṇasampayuttassa alobho adoso amohoti tayo sampayuttā hetū, ñāṇavippayuttassa alobho [M 0.0186] adosoti dve sampayuttā hetū. Sabbesaṃ avisesena yonisomanasikāro hetu, cattāri sampatticakkāni paccayo. Tathā saddhammassavanaṃ, tassa ca dānādivasena pavattamānassa deyyadhammādayo paccayo. Dhammāti cettha vedanādīnaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇādayo. Tathā tayo viññāṇassa, vedanādayo pasādassa, saddheyyavatthukusalābhisaṅkhāro vipākasukhassa paccayoti. Ayaṃ parikkhāro hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of requisites? In 'Manopubbaṅgamā', 'mano' is wholesome consciousness. For that which is associated with knowledge, the three associated factors—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are causes; for that which is dissociated from knowledge, the two associated factors—non-greed and non-hatred—are causes. For all without distinction, wise attention is a cause; the four wheels of accomplishment are a condition. Likewise, listening to the good Dhamma is a condition. And for that consciousness occurring by way of giving and so on, things to be given and so on are a condition. And here, in 'dhammā', desirable objects and so on are a condition for feeling and so on. Likewise, the three [roots] are a condition for consciousness; feeling and so on are a condition for serenity; and wholesome volitional formations regarding objects of faith are a condition for resultant happiness. This is the application of the method of requisites.

Tattha katamo samāropano hārasampāto? Manopubbaṅgamā dhammāti manoti puññacittaṃ, taṃ tividhaṃ – dānamayaṃ, sīlamayaṃ, bhāvanāmayanti. Tattha dānamayassa alobho padaṭṭhānaṃ, sīlamayassa adoso padaṭṭhānaṃ, bhāvanāmayassa amoho padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbesaṃ abhippasādo padaṭṭhānaṃ, “saddhājāto upasaṅkamati, upasaṅkamanto payirupāsatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.183) suttaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Kusalacittaṃ sukhassa iṭṭhavipākassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yonisomanasikāro kusalacittassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yoniso hi manasi karonto kusalacittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti kusalacittaṃ bhāveti, so anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti, uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ…pe… padahati. Tassevaṃ catūsu sammappadhānesu bhāviyamānesu cattāro satipaṭṭhānā yāva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchatīti ayaṃ bhāvanāya samāropanā. Sati ca bhāvanāya pahānañca siddhamevāti. Ayaṃ samāropano hārasampāto.

Herein, what is the application of the method of superimposition? In 'Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā', 'mano' is meritorious consciousness, and it is threefold: consisting of giving, of virtue, and of development. Herein, for that consisting of giving, non-greed is the proximate cause; for that consisting of virtue, non-hatred is the proximate cause; for that consisting of development, non-delusion is the proximate cause. For all of them, profound serenity is the proximate cause. The discourse should be elaborated: 'One in whom faith is born approaches; approaching, one attends upon him.' A wholesome mind is the proximate cause for a pleasant, desirable result. Wise attention is the proximate cause for a wholesome mind. For one who attends wisely establishes and develops a wholesome mind. Such a one generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states... and strives. For one who thus develops the four right strivings, the four establishments of mindfulness up to the noble eightfold path go to the culmination of development. This is the superimposition by way of development. And by development, both mindfulness and abandonment are indeed accomplished. This is the application of the method of superimposition.

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Dadato [V 0.0308] puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati, saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyati;

Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakaṃ, rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbuto”ti. (dī. ni. 2.197; udā. 75; peṭako. 16);

For one who gives, merit increases; through restraint, enmity is not accumulated. The skillful one abandons evil; through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, that one is extinguished.

Tattha dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu vuttaṃ. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti sīlamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu vuttaṃ. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti lobhassa ca dosassa ca mohassa ca pahānamāha. Tena bhāvanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu vuttaṃ. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti anupādāparinibbānamāha.

Herein, by 'For one who gives, merit increases,' the basis of merit-making consisting of giving is stated. By 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' the basis of merit-making consisting of virtue is stated. By 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion is spoken of. Therefore, the basis of merit-making consisting of mental development is stated. By 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the final Nibbāna without clinging is spoken of.

Dadato [M 0.0187] puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti alobho kusalamūlaṃ. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti adoso kusalamūlaṃ. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti amoho kusalamūlaṃ. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti tesaṃ nissaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ.

By 'For one who gives, merit increases,' the wholesome root of non-greed is stated. By 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' the wholesome root of non-hatred is stated. By 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the wholesome root of non-delusion is stated. By 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' their escape is stated.

Dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti sīlakkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti samādhikkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti paññākkhandhassa vimuttikkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Dānena oḷārikānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ, sīlena majjhimānaṃ, paññāya sukhumānaṃ. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti katāvībhūmiṃ dasseti.

'For one who gives, merit increases' is the proximate cause of the aggregate of virtue. 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated' is the proximate cause of the aggregate of concentration. 'And the skillful one abandons evil' is the proximate cause of the aggregate of wisdom and the aggregate of liberation. Through giving, the abandonment of gross defilements occurs; through virtue, of medium ones; through wisdom, of subtle ones. 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished' shows the plane of the Arahant.

Dadato puññaṃ…pe… jahāti pāpakanti sekkhabhūmi dassitā. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti aggaphalaṃ vuttaṃ.

By 'For one who gives, merit increases… and the skillful one abandons evil,' the plane of the trainee is shown. By 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the highest fruit is stated.

Tathā dadato puññaṃ…pe… na cīyatīti lokiyakusalamūlaṃ vuttaṃ. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti lokuttarakusalamūlaṃ vuttaṃ. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti lokuttarassa kusalamūlassa phalaṃ vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, by 'For one who gives, merit increases… enmity is not accumulated,' the mundane wholesome root is stated. By 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the supramundane wholesome root is stated. By 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the fruit of the supramundane wholesome root is stated.

Dadato…pe… na cīyatīti puthujjanabhūmi dassitā. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti sekkhabhūmi dassitā. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti asekkhabhūmi dassitā.

By 'For one who gives… enmity is not accumulated,' the plane of the worldling is shown. By 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the plane of the trainee is shown. By 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the plane of the one beyond training is shown.

Dadato [V 0.0309] …pe… na cīyatīti saggagāminī paṭipadā vuttā. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti sekkhavimutti. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti asekkhavimutti vuttā.

By 'For one who gives… enmity is not accumulated,' the practice leading to heaven is stated. By 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the liberation of the trainee is stated. By 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the liberation of the one beyond training is stated.

Dadato…pe… na cīyatīti dānakathaṃ sīlakathaṃ saggakathaṃ lokiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ desanamāha. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti loke ādīnavānupassanāya saddhiṃ sāmukkaṃsikaṃ dhammadesanamāha. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti tassā desanāya phalamāha.

By 'For one who gives… enmity is not accumulated,' the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue, the discourse on heaven, and the teaching of mundane phenomena are spoken of. By 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the exalted teaching of the Dhamma, together with the contemplation of danger in the world, is spoken of. By 'Through the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the fruit of that teaching is spoken of.

Dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti dhammadānaṃ āmisadānañca vadati. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti pāṇātipātā veramaṇiyā sattānaṃ abhayadānaṃ vadati. Evaṃ sabbānipi sikkhāpadāni vitthāretabbāni. Tena ca sīlasaṃyamena sīle patiṭṭhito cittaṃ saṃyameti, tassa samatho pāripūriṃ gacchati. Evaṃ so samathe ṭhito vipassanākosallayogato kusalo ca jahāti [M 0.0188] pāpakaṃ rāgaṃ jahāti, dosaṃ jahāti, mohaṃ jahāti, ariyamaggena sabbepi pāpake akusale dhamme jahāti. Evaṃ paṭipanno ca rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti rāgādīnaṃ parikkhayā dvepi vimuttiyo adhigacchatīti ayaṃ suttaniddeso.

'For one who gives, merit increases' speaks of the gift of the Dhamma and the gift of material things. 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated' speaks of the giving of fearlessness to beings through abstinence from the destruction of life. In this way, all the training precepts should be elaborated. And by that restraint of virtue, one established in virtue restrains the mind; for that one, serenity reaches fulfillment. Thus, one established in serenity, through the application of skill in insight, being skillful, abandons evil; one abandons lust, abandons hatred, abandons delusion; by the noble path, one abandons all evil, unwholesome states. And one who has practiced thus, by 'through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' attains both liberations through the complete destruction of lust and so on. This is the exposition of the sutta.

Tattha katamo desanāhārasampāto? Imasmiṃ sutte kiṃ desitaṃ? Dve sugatiyo devā ca manussā ca, dibbā ca pañca kāmaguṇā, mānusakā ca pañca kāmaguṇā, dibbā ca pañcupādānakkhandhā, mānusakā ca pañcupādānakkhandhā. Idaṃ vuccati dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ. Tassa kāraṇabhāvena purimapurimanipphannā taṇhā samudayo ariyasaccaṃ. Tayidaṃ vuccati assādo ca ādīnavo ca. Sabbassa purimehi dvīhi padehi niddeso “dadato…pe… na cīyatī”ti. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti maggo vutto. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti dve nibbānadhātuyo saupādisesā ca anupādisesā ca. Idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ. Phalādīni pana yathārahaṃ veditabbānīti. Ayaṃ desanāhārasampāto.

Herein, what is the Desanāhārasampāta? What is taught in this sutta? The two good destinations, that is, devas and humans; the five divine strands of sensual pleasure and the five human strands of sensual pleasure; the five divine aggregates of clinging and the five human aggregates of clinging. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering. As its cause, the craving produced in former existences is the Noble Truth of the Origin. This is called both gratification and danger. The exposition of all this is by the first two phrases: 'For one who gives… enmity is not accumulated.' By 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the Path is stated. By 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the two Nibbāna-elements are stated: that with residue remaining and that without residue remaining. This is the escape. But the fruits and so on should be understood as is appropriate. This is the Desanāhārasampāta.

Vicayoti “dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”ti iminā paṭhamena padena tividhampi dānamayaṃ sīlamayaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu vuttaṃ. Dasavidhassapi deyyadhammassa pariccāgo vutto. Tathā chabbidhassapi rūpādiārammaṇassa. “Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatī”ti dutiyena padena averā asapattā abyāpādā ca paṭipadā vuttā. “Kusalo ca jahāti pāpaka”nti tatiyena padena ñāṇuppādo aññāṇanirodho sabbopi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo sabbepi bodhipakkhiyā dhammā vuttā[V 0.0310]. “Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbuto”ti rāgakkhayena rāgavirāgā cetovimutti, mohakkhayena avijjāvirāgā paññāvimutti vuttāti. Ayaṃ vicayo hārasampāto.

Analysis: By this first phrase, 'For one who gives, merit increases,' the threefold basis of meritorious action—consisting of giving, virtue, and mental development—is stated. The relinquishing of the tenfold kinds of things to be given is stated. Likewise, of the sixfold kinds of objects beginning with forms. By the second phrase, 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' the practice that is without inner enmity, without outer enmity, and without ill will is stated. By the third phrase, 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the arising of knowledge, the cessation of ignorance, the entire Noble Eightfold Path, and all the qualities that are part of enlightenment are stated. By 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' through the destruction of lust, the liberation of mind through dispassion for lust is stated; through the destruction of delusion, the liberation by wisdom through dispassion for ignorance is stated. This is the Vicayo Hārasampāto.

Yuttīti dāne ṭhito ubhayaṃ paripūreti macchariyappahānañca puññābhisandañcāti atthesā yutti. Sīlasaṃyame ṭhito ubhayaṃ paripūreti upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhiñcāti atthesā yutti. Pāpake dhamme pajahanto dukkhaṃ parijānāti, nirodhaṃ sacchikaroti, maggaṃ bhāvetīti atthesā yutti. Rāgadosamohesu sabbaso parikkhīṇesu anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyatīti atthesā yuttīti. Ayaṃ yuttihārasampāto.

Reasoning: One established in giving fulfills both the abandonment of stinginess and the stream of merit—such is the reasoning. One established in the restraint of virtue fulfills both access concentration and absorption concentration—such is the reasoning. One abandoning evil states fully understands suffering, realizes cessation, and develops the path—such is the reasoning. When lust, hatred, and delusion are completely destroyed, one attains final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining—such is the reasoning. This is the Yutti Hārasampāto.

Padaṭṭhānanti [M 0.0189] dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti cāgādhiṭṭhānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti saccādhiṭṭhānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti paññādhiṭṭhānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti upasamādhiṭṭhānassa padaṭṭhānanti. Ayaṃ padaṭṭhāno hārasampāto.

The Proximate Cause: The statement, 'For one who gives, merit increases,' is the proximate cause of the foundation of relinquishment. The statement, 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' is the proximate cause of the foundation of truth. The statement, 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' is the proximate cause of the foundation of wisdom. The statement, 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' is the proximate cause of the foundation of peace. This is the Padaṭṭhāna Hārasampāto.

Lakkhaṇoti “dadato”ti etena peyyavajjaṃ atthacariyaṃ samānattatā ca dassitāti veditabbā saṅgahavatthubhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Saṃyamato”ti etena khantimettāavihiṃsāanuddayādayo dassitāti veditabbā verānuppādanalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Veraṃ na cīyatī”ti etena hirīottappaappicchatāsantuṭṭhitādayo dassitā verāvaḍḍhanena ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā ahirīkānottappādayo acetabbabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Kusalo”ti etena kosalladīpanena sammāsaṅkappādayo dassitā maggaṅgādibhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Jahāti pāpaka”nti etena pariññābhisamayādayopi dassitā abhisamayalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Rāgadosamohakkhayā”ti etena avasiṭṭhakilesādīnampi khayā dassitā khepetabbabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattāti ayaṃ lakkhaṇo.

The Characteristic: By the term 'dadato,' it should be known that pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality are shown, because they have the same characteristic of being bases of sympathy. By the term 'saṃyamato,' it should be known that patience, loving-kindness, non-harming, compassion, and so on, are shown, because they have the same characteristic of not giving rise to enmity. By the term 'veraṃ na cīyati,' moral shame, moral dread, fewness of wishes, contentment, and so on, are shown, because they have the same characteristic of not increasing enmity. Similarly, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, and so on, are shown, because they have the same characteristic of not being accumulated. By the term 'kusalo,' through the showing of skillfulness, right thought and so on are shown, because they have the same characteristic of being path factors and so on. By the term 'jahāti pāpakaṃ,' full understanding, realization, and so on, are also shown, because they have the same characteristic of realization. By 'rāgadosamohakkhayā,' the destruction of the remaining defilements and so on is also shown, because they have the same characteristic of being that which should be destroyed. This is the Characteristic.

Catubyūhoti dadatoti gāthāyaṃ bhagavato ko adhippāyo? Ye mahābhogataṃ patthayissanti, te dānaṃ dassanti dāliddiyappahānāya. Ye averataṃ icchanti, te pañca verāni pajahissanti. Ye kusaladhammehi chandakāmā, te aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvessanti. Ye nibbāyitukāmā, te rāgadosamohaṃ pajahissantīti ayamettha bhagavato adhippāyo. Evaṃ nibbacananidānasandhayo vattabbāti. Ayaṃ catubyūho.

The Fourfold Array: In the verse beginning 'dadato,' what is the Blessed One's intention? Those who will aspire to great wealth, they will give gifts in order to abandon poverty. Those who desire freedom from enmity, they will abandon the five enmities. Those who have desire for wholesome states, they will develop the eightfold path. Those who desire to be extinguished, they will abandon lust, hatred, and delusion. This is the Blessed One's intention here. Thus, the explanations, the reasons, and the connections should be stated. This is the Catubyūha.

Āvaṭṭoti [V 0.0311] yañca adadato macchariyaṃ, yañca asaṃyamato veraṃ, yañca akusalassa pāpassa appahānaṃ, ayaṃ paṭipakkhaniddesena samudayo. Tassa alobhena ca adosena ca amohena ca dānādīhi pahānaṃ, imāni tīṇi kusalamūlāni. Tesaṃ paccayo aṭṭha sammattāni, ayaṃ maggo. Yo rāgadosamohānaṃ khayo, ayaṃ nirodhoti. Ayaṃ āvaṭṭo.

The Turning: Whatever stinginess there is for one who does not give, whatever enmity for one who is unrestrained, and whatever non-abandoning of evil for one who is unskillful—this, shown by way of indicating the opposite, is the Origin. Its abandoning by means of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, through giving and so on—these are the three wholesome roots. Their condition is the eight rightnesses; this is the Path. Whatever is the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, this is Cessation. This is the Turning.

Vibhattīti dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti ekaṃsena yo bhayahetu deti, rāgahetu deti, āmisakiñcikkhahetu deti, na tassa puññaṃ vaḍḍhati. Yañca daṇḍadānaṃ satthadānaṃ paraviheṭhanatthaṃ apuññaṃ assa pavaḍḍhati. Yaṃ pana kusalena cittena anukampanto vā apacāyamāno vā annaṃ deti, pānaṃ vatthaṃ yānaṃ [M 0.0190] mālāgandhavilepanaṃ seyyāvasathaṃ padīpeyyaṃ deti, sabbasattānaṃ vā abhayadānaṃ deti, mettacitto hitajjhāsayo nissaraṇasaññī dhammaṃ deseti. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti ekaṃsena abhayūparatassa cīyati, kiṃkāraṇaṃ? Yaṃ asamattho, bhayūparato diṭṭhadhammikassa bhāyati “mā maṃ rājāno gahetvā hatthaṃ vā chindeyyuṃ…pe… jīvantampi sūle uttāseyyu”nti, tena saṃyamena averaṃ cīyati. Yo pana evaṃ samāno veraṃ na cīyati. Yo pana evaṃ samādiyati, pāṇātipātassa pāpako vipāko diṭṭhe ceva dhamme abhisamparāye ca, evaṃ sabbassa akusalassa, so tato āramati, iminā saṃyamena veraṃ na cīyati. Saṃyamo nāma sīlaṃ. Taṃ catubbidhaṃ cetanā sīlaṃ, cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīlanti. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti pāpapahāyakā sattattiṃsa bodhipakkhiyā dhammā vattabbāti. Ayaṃ vibhatti.

The Analysis: In the phrase 'For one who gives, merit increases,' it is definite that for one who gives out of fear, gives out of lust, or gives for the sake of some material gain, merit does not increase. And for one who gives a cudgel or a weapon for the purpose of harming others, demerit increases for them. But when one, with a wholesome mind, being compassionate or being respectful, gives food, drink, clothing, a vehicle, garlands, scents, ointments, lodging, or a lamp; or gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings; or, with a mind of loving-kindness, with a disposition for their welfare, and perceiving the escape, teaches the Dhamma—for them, merit increases. In the phrase 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' it is definite that for one who does not abstain out of fear, enmity is accumulated. For what reason? Because one who is incapable abstains out of fear. One fears the immediate consequences, thinking: 'Lest kings seize me and cut off my hand... or impale me alive on a stake.' Through that restraint, freedom from enmity is accumulated. But for one who is thus, enmity is not accumulated. Furthermore, one undertakes thus: 'The result of killing living beings is evil both in the present life and in the future,' and so it is for all that is unwholesome. That person refrains from it. Through this restraint, enmity is not accumulated. Restraint means virtue. That virtue is fourfold: virtue as volition, virtue as mental factors, virtue as restraint, and virtue as non-transgression. In the phrase 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that abandon evil should be stated. This is the Analysis.

Parivattanoti dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati, adadatopi puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati, na dānamayikaṃ. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyati asaṃyamatopi veraṃ na cīyati, yaṃ dānena paṭisaṅkhānabalena bhāvanābalena. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakaṃ, akusalo pana na jahāti. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbuto, tesaṃ aparikkhayā natthi nibbutīti. Ayaṃ parivattano.

The Reversal: For one who gives, merit increases. Even for one who does not give, merit increases, but not the merit consisting of giving. For one who is restrained, enmity is not accumulated. Even for one who is not restrained, enmity is not accumulated through giving, through the power of reflection, and through the power of development. And the skillful one abandons evil, but the unskillful one does not abandon it. Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished; through their non-destruction, there is no extinguishment. This is the Reversal.

Vevacanoti dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati. Pariccāgato kusalaṃ upacīyati. Anumodatopi puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati cittappasādatopi veyyāvaccakiriyāyapi. Saṃyamatoti sīlasaṃvarato soraccato. Veraṃ na cīyatīti pāpaṃ na vaḍḍhati, akusalaṃ na vaḍḍhati. Kusaloti paṇḍito nipuṇo medhāvī parikkhako. Jahātīti samucchindati samugghāṭeti. Ayaṃ vevacano.

The Synonym: 'For one who gives, merit increases' is synonymous with 'Through relinquishment, the wholesome is accumulated.' Merit also increases through appreciation, through confidence of mind, and through performing services. Synonyms for the term 'saṃyamato' (through restraint) are: 'sīlasaṃvarato' (through restraint by virtue) and 'soraccato' (through gentleness). Synonyms for the phrase 'veraṃ na cīyati' (enmity is not accumulated) are: 'pāpaṃ na vaḍḍhati' (evil does not increase) and 'akusalaṃ na vaḍḍhati' (the unwholesome does not increase). Synonyms for the term 'kusalo' (skillful) are: 'paṇḍito' (wise), 'nipuṇo' (subtle), 'medhāvī' (intelligent), and 'parikkhako' (investigator). Synonyms for the term 'jahāti' (abandons) are: 'samucchindati' (cuts off) and 'samugghāṭeti' (eradicates). This is the Synonym.

Paññattīti [V 0.0312] dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti lobhassa paṭinissaggapaññatti, alobhassa nikkhepapaññatti. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti dosassa vikkhambhanapaññatti, adosassa nikkhepapaññatti. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti mohassa samugghātapaññatti, amohassa bhāvanāpaññatti. Rāgadosamohassa pahānapaññatti, alobhādosāmohassa bhāvanāpaññatti. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti kilesānaṃ paṭippassaddhipaññatti, nibbānassa sacchikiriyapaññattīti. Ayaṃ paññatti.

The Designation: The designation, 'For one who gives, merit increases,' is the designation for the relinquishing of greed and the designation for the placing of non-greed. The designation, 'Through restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' is the designation for the suppression of hatred and the designation for the placing of non-hatred. The designation, 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' is the designation for the uprooting of delusion and the designation for the development of non-delusion. It is the designation for the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion, and the designation for the development of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. The designation, 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' is the designation for the pacification of the defilements and the designation for the realization of Nibbāna. This is the Designation.

Otaraṇoti [M 0.0191] dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti dānaṃ nāma saddhādīhi indriyehi hotīti ayaṃ indriyehi otaraṇo. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti saṃyamo nāma sīlakkhandhoti ayaṃ khandhehi otaraṇo. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti pāpappahānaṃ nāma tīhi vimokkhehi hoti. Tesaṃ upāyabhūtāni tīṇi vimokkhamukhānīti ayaṃ vimokkhamukhehi otaraṇo. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti vimuttikkhandho. So ca dhammadhātu dhammāyatanañcāti ayaṃ dhātūhi ca āyatanehi ca otaraṇoti. Ayaṃ otaraṇo.

The Penetration: In the phrase, 'For one who gives, merit increases,' giving, so-called, occurs through faculties such as faith. This is penetration by the faculties. In the phrase, 'By restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' restraint, so-called, is the aggregate of virtue. This is penetration by the aggregates. In the phrase, 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' the abandoning of evil, so-called, occurs through the three liberations. The means to them are the three gateways to liberation. This is penetration by the gateways to liberation. By the phrase, 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' the aggregate of liberation is stated. And that is the Dhamma-element and the Dhamma-sphere. This is penetration by the elements and by the spheres. This is the Penetration.

Sodhanoti dadatotiādikā padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti ayaṃ padasuddhi ca ārambhasuddhi cāti. Ayaṃ sodhano.

The Purification: 'For one who gives,' and so on, is purity of wording, but not purity of inception. The phrase, 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' is both purity of wording and purity of inception. This is the Purification.

Adhiṭṭhānoti dadatoti ayaṃ ekattatā, cāgo pariccāgo dhammadānaṃ āmisadānaṃ abhayadānaṃ, aṭṭha dānāni vitthāretabbāni. Ayaṃ vemattatā. Saṃyamoti ayaṃ ekattatā. Pātimokkhasaṃvaro satisaṃvaroti ayaṃ vemattatā. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti ayaṃ ekattatā. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati vicikicchaṃ pajahatītiādikā ayaṃ vemattatā. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti ayaṃ ekattatā. Saupādisesā nibbānadhātu anupādisesā nibbānadhātūti ayaṃ vemattatāti. Ayaṃ adhiṭṭhāno.

The Determination: By the phrase, 'For one who gives,' this is generality. Generosity, relinquishment, the gift of Dhamma, the gift of material things, the gift of fearlessness—eight kinds of giving should be elaborated. This is specificity. By the phrase, 'By restraint,' this is generality. Restraint of the Pātimokkha and restraint by mindfulness—this is specificity. By the phrase, 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' this is generality. 'One abandons personality view,' 'one abandons doubt,' and so on—this is specificity. By the phrase, 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' this is generality. The Nibbāna-element with residue remaining and the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining—this is specificity. This is the Determination.

Parikkhāroti dānassa pāmojjaṃ paccayo. Alobho hetu, saṃyamassa hirottappādayo paccayo. Yonisomanasikāro adoso ca hetu, pāpappahānassa samādhi yathābhūtañāṇadassanañca paccayo. Tisso anupassanā hetu, nibbutiyā maggasammādiṭṭhi hetu, sammāsaṅkappādayo paccayoti. Ayaṃ parikkhāro.

The Requisite: For giving, joy is a condition. Non-greed is a root-cause. For restraint, conscience, moral dread, and so on are a condition. Wise attention and non-hatred are a root-cause. For the abandoning of evil, concentration and knowledge and vision of things as they truly are are a condition. The three contemplations are a root-cause. For extinguishment, right view that is the path is a root-cause; right intention and so on are a condition. This is the Requisite.

Samāropano [V 0.0313] hārasampātoti dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu, taṃ sīlassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṃyamato veraṃ na cīyatīti sīlamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu, taṃ samādhissa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sīlena hi jhānenapi rāgādikilesā na cīyanti. Yepissa tappaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, tepissa na honti. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti pahānapariññā, taṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa [M 0.0192] nibbutoti rāgassapi khayā dosassapi khayā mohassapi khayā. Tattha rāgoti yo rāgo sārāgo cetaso sārajjanā lobho lubbhanā lubbhitattaṃ abhijjhā lobho akusalamūlaṃ. Dosoti yo doso dussanā dussitattaṃ byāpādo cetaso byāpajjanā doso akusalamūlaṃ. Mohoti yaṃ aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ anabhisamayo asambodho appaṭivedho dummejjhaṃ bālyaṃ asampajaññaṃ moho akusalamūlaṃ. Iti imesaṃ rāgādīnaṃ khayo nirodho paṭinissaggo nibbuti nibbāyanā parinibbānaṃ saupādisesā nibbānadhātu anupādisesā nibbānadhātūti. Ayaṃ samāropano hārasampāto.

The application of the method of transference is as follows: By the phrase, 'For one who gives, merit increases,' the basis for meritorious action consisting of giving is stated; that is the proximate cause for virtue. By the phrase, 'By restraint, enmity is not accumulated,' the basis for meritorious action consisting of virtue is stated; that is the proximate cause for concentration. For, by virtue or by jhāna, defilements such as lust are not accumulated. Whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise for him on account of that, they do not exist for him. By the phrase, 'And the skillful one abandons evil,' full understanding by abandoning is stated; that is the basis for meritorious action consisting of mental development. In the phrase, 'Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is extinguished,' this means: through the destruction of lust, through the destruction of hatred, and through the destruction of delusion. Therein, 'lust' is: whatever lust, passion, attachment of the mind, greed, greediness, state of being greedy, covetousness, which is the unwholesome root of greed. 'Hatred' is: whatever hatred, malevolence, state of being malevolent, ill will, ill will of the mind, which is the unwholesome root of hatred. 'Delusion' is: whatever ignorance, not seeing, non-realization, non-awakening, non-penetration, witlessness, folly, lack of clear comprehension, which is the unwholesome root of delusion. Thus, the destruction, cessation, relinquishment, extinguishment, calming, and final extinguishment of these—lust and so on—is the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining and the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. This is the application of the method of transference.

Missakahārasampātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the application of the mixed method is completed.

Nayasamuṭṭhānavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Origination of the Modes

79. Evaṃ nānāsuttavasena ekasuttavasena ca hāravicāraṃ dassetvā idāni nayavicāraṃ dassetuṃ “tattha katamaṃ nayasamuṭṭhāna”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Kasmā panettha yathā “tattha katamo desanāhāro, assādādīnavatāti gāthā. Ayaṃ desanāhāro kiṃ desayatī”tiādinā hāraniddeso āraddho, evaṃ “tattha katamo nandiyāvaṭṭo, taṇhañca avijjampi cāti gāthā, ayaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭo kiṃ nayatī”tiādinā anārabhitvā samuṭṭhānamukhena āraddhanti? Vuccate – hāranayānaṃ visayabhedato. Yathā hi hārā byañjanamukhena suttassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanā, na evaṃ nayā. Nayā pana nānāsuttato niddhāritehi taṇhāvijjādīhi mūlapadehi catusaccayojanāya nayato anubujjhiyamāno dukkhādiattho. So hi maggañāṇaṃ nayati sampāpetīti nayo. Paṭivijjhantānaṃ pana ugghaṭitaññuādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ veneyyānaṃ vasena mūlapadavibhāgato tidhā vibhattā. Ekameko cettha yato neti, yañca neti, tesaṃ saṃkilesavodānānaṃ vibhāgato dvisaṅgaho catuchaaṭṭhadiso cāti bhinno hāranayānaṃ visayo. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “hārā byañjanavicayo, suttassa nayā tayo ca suttattho”ti (netti. saṅgahavāra). Evaṃ visiṭṭhavisayattā hāranayānaṃ hārehi aññathā naye niddisanto “tattha katamaṃ nayasamuṭṭhāna”ntiādimāha.

79. Having thus shown the analysis of the methods by means of various suttas and by means of a single sutta, now, in order to show the analysis of the modes, the passage beginning, “Therein, what is the origination of the modes?” was undertaken. Why here, just as the exposition of the methods was undertaken with the passage beginning, “Therein, what is the method of teaching? The verse, ‘Delight, danger...’ This is the method of teaching. What does it teach?”, was it not similarly undertaken with a passage beginning, “Therein, what is the Nandiyāvaṭṭa? The verse, ‘Craving and ignorance...’ This is the Nandiyāvaṭṭa. To what does it lead?”, but was instead undertaken with origination as the entry point? It is said: because of the difference in scope between the methods and the modes. For just as the methods are explanations of the meaning of a sutta by way of the letter, the modes are not so. Rather, the modes are the meaning of suffering and so on, which is to be understood by way of the mode through the application of the Four Truths by means of root terms such as craving and ignorance, extracted from various suttas. For that meaning of suffering and so on leads to and causes the attainment of path-knowledge; therefore, it is called a 'mode'. Moreover, for those who penetrate—by way of the three types of individuals to be trained, such as the quick-to-understand—they are divided threefold according to the division of the root terms. And here, each one, by the division of those states of defilement from which it leads and those states of purification to which it leads, is twofold, and has four, six, and eight directions. Thus, the scope of the methods and the modes is different. For so it has been said: “The methods are the analysis of the letter; the three modes are the meaning of the sutta.” Thus, because the methods and the modes have a distinct scope, when expounding the modes differently from the methods, he said the passage beginning, “Therein, what is the origination of the modes?”

Tatthāyaṃ [V 0.0314][M 0.0193] vacanattho – samuṭṭhahanti etenāti samuṭṭhānaṃ. Ke samuṭṭhahanti? Nayā. Nayānaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ nayasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Kiṃ pana taṃ? Taṃtaṃmūlapadehi catusaccayojanā. Sā hi nandiyāvaṭṭādīnaṃ nayānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānatāya samuṭṭhānaṃ bhūmīti ca vuccati. Tathā ca vakkhati – “ayaṃ vuccati nandiyāvaṭṭassa nayassa bhūmī”ti (netti. 81). Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya ca bhavataṇhāya cātiādi nandiyāvaṭṭassa nayassa bhūmidassanaṃ. Tattha pubbā koṭi na paññāyatīti asukassa nāma buddhassa bhagavato, asukassa vā cakkavattino kāle avijjā bhavataṇhā ca uppannā. Tato pubbe nāhosīti evaṃ avijjābhavataṇhānaṃ na kāci purimā mariyādā upalabbhati. Kasmā? Anamataggattā saṃsārassa. Vuttañhetaṃ – “anamataggoyaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃsāro, pubbā koṭi na paññāyatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.124; kathā. 75) vitthāro. Tatthāti avijjābhavataṇhāsu. Yadipi avijjāya saṃyojanabhāvo, taṇhāya ca nīvaraṇabhāvo pāḷiyaṃ vutto, tathāpi avijjāya paṭicchāditādīnavehi bhavehi taṇhā saṃyojetīti imassa atthassa dassanatthaṃ “avijjānīvaraṇaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojana”nti vuttaṃ.

Herein, this is the meaning of the word: ‘They arise by this,’ hence ‘origination.’ What arise? The modes. The cause of arising for the modes is ‘origination of the modes.’ But what is that? It is the application of the Four Truths by means of their respective root terms. For that application, because it is the place of arising for modes such as Nandiyāvaṭṭa and others, is called ‘origination’ and also ‘ground.’ And so it will be said: “This is called the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa mode.” The passage beginning, “A prior point is not discerned for ignorance and craving for existence,” is the demonstration of the ground for the Nandiyāvaṭṭa mode. Therein, “a prior point is not discerned” means that a prior limit of ignorance and craving for existence—such that they arose at the time of a certain Buddha, the Blessed One, or a certain universal monarch, and did not exist before that—is not found. Why? Because of the unconceivable beginning of saṃsāra. For this has been said: “Monks, this saṃsāra has an unconceivable beginning; a prior point is not discerned”—the full text should be understood. ‘Therein’ means: regarding ignorance and craving for existence. Although it is stated in the Pāli that ignorance has the nature of a fetter and craving has the nature of a hindrance, it was nevertheless said, “ignorance is the hindrance, craving is the fetter,” in order to show this meaning: craving connects one with states of existence whose dangers are concealed by ignorance.

Avijjāsaṃyuttāti avijjāya missitā, avijjāya vā abhinivesavatthūsu baddhā. Avijjāpakkhena vicarantīti avijjāpakkhena avijjāsahāyena dvādasavidhena vipallāsena abhinivesavatthubhūte ārammaṇe pavattanti. Te vuccanti diṭṭhicaritāti te avijjābhibhūtā rūpādīni niccādito abhinivisantā diṭṭhicaritāti vuccanti, diṭṭhicaritā nāmāti attho. Taṇhāpakkhenāti aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritena. Diṭṭhivicarite taṇhāvicarite ca paṭipattiyā vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “diṭṭhicaritā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha attakilamathānuyoganti attano kāyassa kilissanapayogaṃ attaparitāpanapaṭipattiṃ. Kāmasukhallikānuyoganti kāmasukhassa allīyanapayogaṃ kāmesu pātabyataṃ.

'Conjoined with ignorance' means mixed with ignorance, or bound by ignorance to objects of adherence. 'They fare on the side of ignorance' means they proceed in an object that has become a ground for adherence, by means of the twelve kinds of perversion which have ignorance as their companion. 'They are called “of speculative temperament”' means: those beings, being overcome by ignorance and adhering to form, etc., as permanent, etc., are called 'of speculative temperament'; this is the meaning: they are named 'of speculative temperament.' 'On the side of craving' means by the conduct of the one hundred and eight kinds of craving. The passage beginning 'Those of speculative temperament...' was stated in order to show the division in practice between those of speculative conduct and those of craving-conduct. Therein, 'the pursuit of self-mortification' means the exertion that torments one's own body, the practice of self-torment. 'The pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasure' means the exertion of clinging to sensual pleasure, the state of being immersed in sensual pleasures.

Yadipi bāhirakā “dukkhaṃ taṇhā”ti ca jānanti “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkha”nti, “ayaṃ taṇhā, ayaṃ tassā virāgo”ti pariññeyyapahātabbabhāvena pana na jānanti, iti pavattipavattihetumattampi na jānanti. Kā pana kathā nivattinivattihetūsūti āha – “ito bahiddhā natthi saccavavatthāna”ntiādi. Tattha [M 0.0194] saccappakāsanāti saccadesanā. Samathavipassanākosallanti samathavipassanāsu bhāvanākosallaṃ, tāsu uggahaparipucchāsavanamanasikārakosallaṃ vā. Vipassanādhiṭṭhānañcettha samathaṃ adhippetaṃ. Upasamasukhappattīti [V 0.0315] kilesānaṃ vūpasamasukhādhigamo. Viparītacetāti micchābhiniviṭṭhacetā. Natthi sukhena sukhanti yaṃ anavajjapaccayaparibhogasukhena kāyaṃ cittañca paṭippassaddhadarathaṃ katvā ariyehi pattabbaṃ upasamasukhaṃ, taṃ paṭikkhipati. Dukkhenāti kāyakhedanadukkhena.

Although outsiders may know of ‘suffering’ and ‘craving,’ and that “this is suffering, this much is suffering,” and “this is craving, this is the fading away of it,” they do not know it in its aspect of being something to be fully understood and something to be abandoned. Thus, they do not know even the mere round of existence and the cause of the round of existence. What, then, is to be said of cessation and the cause of cessation? Therefore, he said the passage beginning, “Outside of this, there is no establishment of the truths.” Therein, ‘proclamation of the truths’ means the teaching of the truths. ‘Skill in serenity and insight’ means skill in the development of serenity and insight, or skill in learning, questioning, hearing, and reflecting upon them. And here, serenity as the foundation for insight is intended. ‘Attainment of the happiness of peace’ means the acquisition of the happiness that is the stilling of the defilements. ‘Of perverted mind’ means having a mind that adheres wrongly. By the statement, ‘There is no happiness through happiness,’ he rejects that happiness of peace to be attained by the noble ones, having made body and mind tranquil in their agitation through the happiness of using blameless requisites. ‘Through suffering’ means through the suffering of bodily fatigue.

So lokaṃ vaḍḍhayatīti so kāme paṭisevento attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ lokaṃ vaḍḍheti pīneti. Puttanattuparamparāya vā saṃsārassa anupacchedanato sattalokaṃ vaḍḍheti. Bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavatīti attano pañcahi kāmaguṇehi santappanena puttamukhadassanena ca bahuṃ puññaṃ uppādeti. Abhinivesassa nātidaḷhatāya evaṃsaññī. Daḷhatāya evaṃdiṭṭhī dukkhena sukhaṃ patthayamānā attakilamathānuyogamanuyuttā kāmesu puññasaññī kāmasukhallikānuyogamanuyuttā ca viharantīti yojetabbaṃ.

‘He increases the world’ means: that person, by indulging in sensual pleasures, increases and fattens the world designated as individual existence. Or, by not cutting off the cycle of rebirth through the succession of children and grandchildren, he increases the world of beings. ‘He generates much merit’ means: by satisfying himself with the five strands of sensual pleasures and by seeing the face of his child, he produces much merit. Because his adherence is not very firm, he has such a perception. Because of its firmness, he has such a view. It should be connected thus: desiring happiness through suffering, they dwell devoted to the practice of self-mortification; and, perceiving merit in sensual pleasures, they dwell devoted to the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasure.

Tadabhiññā santāti tathāsaññino samānā. Rogameva vaḍḍhayantīti attabhāvarogameva kilesarogameva vā aparāparaṃ vaḍḍhenti. Gaṇḍasallesupi eseva nayo. Rogābhitunnāti yathāvuttarogabyādhitā. Gaṇḍapaṭipīḷitāti yathāvuttagaṇḍabādhitā. Sallānuviddhāti yathāvuttasallena anupaviṭṭhā. Ummujjanimujjānīti upapajjanacavanāni. Ugghātanigghātanti uccāvacabhāvaṃ. Rogagaṇḍasallabhesajjanti yathāvuttarogāditikicchanaṃ, samathavipassanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tenevāha – “samathavipassanā roganigghātakabhesajja”nti. Tattha roganigghātakanti rogavūpasamanaṃ. “Saṃkileso dukkha”ntiādinā saccāni tesaṃ pariññeyyādibhāvena katheti.

‘Being of such knowledge’ means being of such perception. ‘They increase only the disease’ means they successively increase either the disease of individual existence or the disease of defilements. In the case of boils and darts, this is the same method. ‘Struck by disease’ means afflicted by the aforementioned disease. ‘Oppressed by a boil’ means afflicted by the aforementioned boil. ‘Pierced by a dart’ means penetrated by the aforementioned dart. ‘Emerging and submerging’ means arising and passing away. ‘Rising and falling’ means the state of being high and low. ‘The medicine for disease, boils, and darts’ refers to the cure for the aforementioned disease and so on; it is said with reference to serenity and insight. Therefore, he said: ‘Serenity and insight are the medicine that eradicates disease.’ Therein, ‘eradicating disease’ means the calming of disease. By the phrase beginning with ‘Defilement is suffering,’ he explains the truths in terms of their being things to be fully understood, and so on.

Tattha saṃkileso dukkhanti attakilamathānuyogakāmasukhallikānuyogasaṃkilesavanto, tehi vā saṃkilissamāno rūpārūpakāyo dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ. Tadabhisaṅgo taṇhāti tattha abhisaṅgo āsaṅgoti laddhanāmā taṇhā.

Therein, ‘defilement is suffering’ means: the form-body and formless-body possessing the defilements of the practice of self-mortification and the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasure, or the form-body and formless-body being defiled by them, is the noble truth of suffering. ‘Attachment to that is craving’ means: therein, craving, which has obtained the name ‘attachment’ or ‘clinging,’ is that attachment.

80. Idāni diṭṭhicaritataṇhācaritānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhidassane pavattibhedaṃ dassetuṃ “diṭṭhicaritā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha diṭṭhicaritā rūpaṃ attato upagacchantīti [M 0.0195] diṭṭhicaritā diṭṭhābhinivesassa balavabhāvato rūpaṃ “attā”ti gaṇhanti. Tesañhi attābhiniveso balavā, na tathā attaniyābhiniveso. Esa nayo vedanantiādīsupi. Taṇhācaritā rūpavantaṃ attānanti taṇhācaritā taṇhābhinivesassa balavabhāvato rūpaṃ attano kiñcanapalibodhabhāve ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ vedanādiṃ “attā”ti gaṇhanti. Attani vā rūpanti attādhāraṃ vā rūpaṃ. Rūpasmiṃ vā [V 0.0316] attānanti rūpādhāraṃ vā attānaṃ. Vedanāvantantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Etesañhi attaniyābhiniveso balavā, na tathā attābhiniveso. Tasmā yathāladdhaṃ attaniyanti kappetvā tadaññaṃ “attā”ti gaṇhanti. Ayaṃ vuccati vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhīti ayaṃ pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ekekasmiṃ catunnaṃ catunnaṃ gāhānaṃ vasena vīsativatthukā sati vijjamāne khandhapañcakasaṅkhāte kāye, satī vā vijjamānā tattha diṭṭhīti sakkāyadiṭṭhi.

80. Now, to show the difference in the arising of the view of personality for those with a speculative temperament and those with a craving temperament, the passage beginning with ‘those with a speculative temperament’ is stated. Therein, ‘those with a speculative temperament approach form as self’ means: those with a speculative temperament, due to the strength of their adherence to views, grasp form as ‘self.’ For them, indeed, adherence to ‘self’ is strong, but adherence to ‘what is mine’ is not so strong. This is the method in the cases of feeling and so on as well. ‘Those with a craving temperament [grasp] a self possessing form’ means: those with a craving temperament, due to the strength of their adherence to craving, having established form in the state of being a possession or impediment of their own, grasp the remaining [aggregates] such as feeling as ‘self.’ ‘Or form in self’ means or form having self as its support. ‘Or self in form’ means or self having form as its support. This is the same method in the cases of ‘possessing feeling’ and so on as well. For them, indeed, adherence to ‘what is mine’ is strong, but adherence to ‘self’ is not so strong.
