94. Cārikaṃ pakkamissatīti janapadacārikaṃ gamissati. Kasmā pana bhagavā janapadacārikaṃ caratīti? Sattahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto janapadacārikaṃ caranti – desantaragatānaṃ veneyyānaṃ vinayanattaṃ, tatra ṭhitānaṃ ussukkasamuppādanaṃ, bhāvakānaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nibaddhavāsapariharaṇaṃ attano ca tattha anāsaṅgadassanaṃ, sambuddhavasitaṭṭhānatāya desānaṃ cetiyabhāvasampādanaṃ, bahūnaṃ sattānaṃ dassanūpasaṅkamanādīhi puññoghappasavanaṃ, avuṭṭhiādiupaddavūpasamanañcāti imehi sattahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto janapadacārikaṃ carantīti veditabbaṃ.

94. ‘Will set out on a journey’ means he will go on a tour of the country. But why does the Blessed One tour the country? The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, tour the country for seven reasons: for the training of receptive beings who have gone to other regions; for generating enthusiasm in those staying there; for preventing disciples from becoming attached to a fixed residence in one place; for showing His own non-attachment to that place; for establishing regions as shrines by virtue of their being places where a Fully Enlightened Buddha has dwelt; for the growth of a flood of merit for many beings through seeing Him, approaching Him, and so on; and for the pacification of calamities such as drought. It should be understood that it is for these seven reasons that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, tour the country.

Isidattapurāṇāti isidatto ca purāṇo ca, tesu isidatto sakadāgāmī. Purāṇo sotāpanno. Sāketeti “sāketo”ti laddhanāme attano bhogagāmake. Magge purisaṃ ṭhapesunti tesaṃ kira gāmadvārena bhagavato gamanamaggo, tasmā “sace bhagavā amhākaṃ suttānaṃ vā pamattānaṃ vā gaccheyya, atha passituṃ na labheyyāmā”ti maggamajjhe purisaṃ ṭhapesuṃ. Anubandhiṃsūti na dūratova, piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhiṃsu. Bhagavā hi sakaṭamaggassa majjhe jaṅghamaggena agamāsi, itare ubhosu passesu anugacchantā agamaṃsu. Maggā okkammāti buddhā hi kenaci saddhiṃ gacchantāva paṭisanthāraṃ karonti kenaci saddhiṃ ṭhitā kenaci saddhiṃ divasabhāgampi nisinnā, tasmā bhagavā cintesi – “ime mayhaṃ sāsane vallabhā āgataphalā, imehi saddhiṃ nisīditvā divasabhāgaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karissāmī”ti. Maggato okkamitvā yenaññataraṃ [V 0.0347] rukkhamūlaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Paññatte āsane nisīdīti te kira chattupāhanakattaradaṇḍapādabbhañjanatelāni ceva aṭṭhavidhañca pānakaṃ sarabhapādapallaṅkañca gāhāpetvā āgamaṃsu. Atha naṃ pallaṅkaṃ paññapetvā adaṃsu. Satthā tattha nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsūti “chattupāhanādīni bhikkhusaṅghassa dethā”ti vatvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

Isidatta and Purāṇa—among them, Isidatta was a once-returner, and Purāṇa was a stream-enterer. Sāketa—this was the name given to their own village of sustenance. They placed a man on the road—it seems the path by which the Blessed One would pass went through their village gate. Therefore, thinking, “If the Blessed One goes while we are sleeping or heedless, we might not get to see him,” they stationed a man in the middle of the road. They followed—not from a distance, but right behind. The Blessed One walked along the foot-path in the middle of the cart-track, while the others followed on both sides. Stepping aside from the road—Buddhas exchange courtesies with someone while walking, while standing, and while sitting for even part of the day. Therefore, the Blessed One thought, “These are dear to me in the dispensation, having attained the fruits. I will sit with them and spend part of the day exchanging courtesies.” Stepping off the road, he approached the foot of a certain tree. He sat down on the prepared seat—it seems they had brought, having had them carried, a sunshade, sandals, a walking stick, and oils for anointing the feet, as well as eight kinds of beverages and a couch with legs shaped like a sarabha's. Then, having prepared the couch, they offered it. The Teacher sat there. They sat down to one side—having said, “Give the sunshade, sandals, and other things to the community of monks,” they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Sāvatthiyā [M 0.0229] kosalesu cārikaṃ pakkamissatītiādi sabbaṃ majjhimadesavaseneva vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Niyatāciṇṇattā. Bhagavato hi cārikacaraṇaṃ majjhimadeseyeva. Sacepi paccantadese gacchati, majjhimadeseyeva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetīti niyatāciṇṇaṃ, tasmā majjhimadesavaseneva vuttaṃ. Kāsīsūti kāsiraṭṭhato. Tathā magadhesūti magadharaṭṭhato. Āsanne no bhagavā bhavissatīti ettha na kevalaṃ āsannattā eva tesaṃ somanassaṃ hoti, atha kho “idāni dānaṃ dātuṃ gandhamālādipūjaṃ kātuṃ dhammaṃ sotuṃ pañhaṃ pucchituṃ labhissāmā”ti nesaṃ somanassaṃ hoti.

“He will set out on a wandering tour from Sāvatthī in the Kosala country,” and so on—all this is spoken in reference to the Middle Country. Why? Because it was his constant practice. For the Blessed One’s wandering was always in the Middle Country. Even if he went to the border regions, it was his fixed habit to have the dawn arise in the Middle Country. Therefore, it is spoken in reference to the Middle Country. “In Kāsī” means from the Kāsī country. Similarly, “in Magadha” means from the Magadha country. “Will the Blessed One be near us?”—here, their joy arises not merely from his proximity, but from the thought, “Now we shall be able to give alms, offer worship with perfumes and garlands, hear the Dhamma, and ask questions.” Thus, they have joy.

Tasmātiha thapatayo sambādho gharāvāsoti thapatayo yasmā tumhākaṃ mayi dūrībhūte anappakaṃ domanassaṃ āsanne anappakaṃ somanassaṃ hoti, tasmāpi veditabbametaṃ “sambādho gharāvāso”ti. Gharāvāsassa hi dosena tumhākaṃ evaṃ hoti. Sace pana gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajitā assatha, evaṃ vo mayā saddhiṃyeva gacchantānañca āgacchantānañca taṃ na bhaveyyāti imamatthaṃ dīpento evamāha. Tattha sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena sambādhatā veditabbā. Mahāghare vasantassāpi hi sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena gharāvāso sambādhova. Rajopathoti rāgādirajānaṃ āgamanapatho, āgamanaṭṭhānanti attho. Abbhokāso pabbajjāti pabbajjā pana akiñcanaapalibodhaṭṭhena abbhokāso. Caturatanikepi hi gabbhe dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pallaṅkena pallaṅkaṃ ghaṭṭetvā nisinnānampi akiñcanāpalibodhaṭṭhena pabbajjā abbhokāso nāma hoti. Alañca pana vo thapatayo appamādāyāti evaṃ sambādhagharāvāse vasantānaṃ tumhākaṃ appamādameva kātuṃ yuttanti attho.

Therefore, O carpenters, household life is crowded. O carpenters, because when I am far away from you, there is considerable sorrow, and when I am near, there is considerable joy, for this reason too it should be understood that ‘household life is crowded.’ Indeed, it is due to the fault of household life that this happens to you. But if you were to abandon household life and go forth, then as you go and come with me, that would not be the case. Explaining this meaning, he spoke thus. There, ‘crowdedness’ should be understood as being encumbered with possessions and attachments. Even for one living in a great house, household life is indeed crowded because of being encumbered with possessions and attachments. ‘A dusty path’ means it is the path for the coming of the dust of lust and other defilements, that is, the place of their arising. ‘The going forth is like the open air’—the going forth, however, is like the open air, being free from possessions and attachments. For even in a room of four cubits, if two monks sit with their couches touching, the going forth is called ‘the open air’ because it is free from possessions and attachments. And enough, O carpenters, for heedfulness—this means that while living in the crowded household life, it is fitting for you to practice heedfulness.

Nāgāti hatthino. Opavayhāti rañño ārohanayoggā. Ekaṃ purato ekaṃ pacchato nisīdāpemāti te kira dvepi janā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā dvīsu nāgesu tā itthiyo evaṃ nisīdāpetvā rañño nāgaṃ majjhe katvā ubhosu passesu gacchanti, tasmā evamāhaṃsu. Nāgopi rakkhitabboti yathā kiñci visesitaṃ na karoti, evaṃ rakkhitabbo hoti. Tāpi bhaginiyoti yathā pamādaṃ nāpajjanti, evaṃ rakkhitabbā honti. Attāpīti sitakathitavikkhepitādīni [V 0.0348] akarontehi attāpi rakkhitabbo hoti[M 0.0230]. Evaṃ karonto hi “sāmidubbhako eso”ti niggahetabbo hoti.

'Nāga' means elephants. 'Opavayha' means fit for the king to ride. 'We will seat one in front and one behind'—it is said that those two men, both adorned with all ornaments, seated those women on two elephants, placed the king's elephant in the middle, and proceeded on both sides. Therefore, they spoke thus. The elephant, too, must be guarded—so that it does nothing contrary, thus it must be protected. Those sisters, too—so that they do not fall into negligence, thus they must be guarded. Even oneself—by not doing things such as smiling, talking, and casting improper glances, oneself must be guarded. For one who acts thus should be reprimanded, 'This is one who betrays his master.'

Tasmātiha thapatayoti yasmā tumhe rājā niccaṃ rājabhaṇḍaṃ paṭicchāpeti, tasmāpi sambādho gharāvāso rajopatho. Yasmā pana paṃsukūlikaṃ bhikkhuṃ evaṃ paṭicchāpento natthi, tasmā abbhokāso pabbajjā, evaṃ sabbatthāpi. Alañca kho thapatayo appamādāya, appamādameva karothāti dasseti.

Therefore, O carpenters—since the king constantly entrusts you with royal goods, for that reason, too, household life is crowded, a path of dust. But since there is no one who entrusts a rag-robe-wearing monk in this way, for that reason, the going forth is like the open air. Thus it is in all cases. He shows (by the phrase) 'Indeed, carpenters, it is sufficient for heedfulness,' that you should practice heedfulness alone.

Muttacāgoti vissaṭṭhacāgo. Payatapāṇīti āgatāgatānaṃ dānatthāya dhotahattho. Vosaggaratoti vosaggasaṅkhāte cāge rato. Yācayogoti yācitabbayutto. “Yājayogo”tipi pāṭho, dānayuttoti attho. Dānasaṃvibhāgaratoti etena appamattakampi kiñci labhitvā tatopi saṃvibhāge rato. Appaṭivibhattanti “idaṃ amhākaṃ bhavissati, idaṃ ayyāna”nti evaṃ akatavibhāgaṃ, sabbaṃ dātabbameva hutvā ṭhitanti attho. Imehi kho thapatayo catūhi dhammehi samannāgato ariyasāvako sotāpanno hotīti sotāpanno imehi dhammehi samannāgato hotīti attho. Etena sotāpannena imesaṃ catunnaṃ dhammānaṃ ekantato labbhamānataṃ dasseti.

'Muttacāgo' means one of open-handed generosity. 'Payatapāṇī' means one who has hands washed, ready to give to all who come. 'Vosaggarato' means one who delights in generosity, which is termed 'vosagga'. 'Yācayogo' means one who is fit to be asked for gifts. There is also a variant reading, 'Yājayogo,' meaning one who is devoted to giving. 'Dānasaṃvibhāgarato'—by this is meant one who delights in sharing, even upon obtaining something small. 'Appaṭivibhatta' means not having made a division, thinking, 'This will be ours, this will belong to the noble ones,' but rather everything stands as being fit to be given away. 'Carpenters, when a noble disciple is endowed with these four qualities, he is a stream-enterer'—the meaning is that a stream-enterer is endowed with these qualities. By this, it is shown that these four qualities are certainly attainable by a stream-enterer.

Evaṃ tesaṃ thapatīnaṃ imehi catūhi dhammehi samannāgataṃ pariyāyena dassetvā idāni nippariyāyena taṃ dassetuṃ “tumhe kho thapatayo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus, having shown indirectly that those carpenters are endowed with these four qualities, now, in order to show it directly, the phrase 'You, O carpenters,' and so on, was spoken.

95. Sahassaṃ kappakoṭiyoti sahassaṃ attabhāvā ahesunti attho. “Asīti kappakoṭiyo”tipi pāṭho, asītiāyukappakoṭiyo ahesunti attho. Kattha pana te ahesunti? Āha “deve ceva manusse cā”ti, devesu ceva manussesu cāti attho. Saṃviruḷhamhīti samantato pallavaggahaṇena viruḷhe. Alabhiṃhanti alabhiṃ ahaṃ. Ajja tiṃsaṃ tato kappāti tato kappato ajja sampati ayaṃ kappo tiṃsatimo. Tassā saññāya vāsanāti tassa buddhagatāya saññāya vāsanato.

95. 'A thousand koṭi of aeons' means a thousand koṭi of existences occurred. The reading 'eighty koṭi of aeons' also exists, meaning eighty koṭi of life-aeons occurred. But where did those occur? He said, 'among gods and also humans,' meaning among gods and also among humans. 'I was well-grown' means grown all around by the taking of shoots. 'Alabhiṃhaṃ' means 'I obtained'. 'Today is the thirtieth aeon from then' means from that aeon, now at present, this aeon is the thirtieth. 'Due to the influence of that perception' means due to the influence of that perception which has the Buddha as its object.

Taṇhānighātakoti [M 0.0231] taṇhāya samucchedako. Vaṭaṃsakoti pupphamayakaṇṇiko. Sabbapupphehilaṅkatoti nānāpupphehi alaṅkato. Lapanantarāti uttarādharoṭṭhānaṃ antarato. Okkāti pabhā. Muddhanantaradhāyathāti muddhani antaradhāyatha. Kaṅkhaṃ vitarāti vimatiṃ vinodehi. Yassa taṃ sabbadhammesu[V 0.0349], sadā ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti tanti nipātamattaṃ. Yassa sabbadhammesu ākaṅkhappaṭibaddhattā sadā ñāṇaṃ pavattati. So sabbaññū bhagavā theraṃ ānandaṃ etadabravīti sambandho. Rājā raṭṭhe bhavissatīti sabbasmiṃ raṭṭhe rājā bhavissati. Carimanti carimabhavaṃ. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Dhammatanti catusaccadhammaṃ, paccekabodhiṃ vā.

'One who destroys craving' means one who eradicates craving. 'An ear-ornament' means a flower-made ear-ornament. 'Adorned with all flowers' means adorned with various flowers. 'From between the lips' means from between the upper and lower lips. 'Okkā' means radiance. 'Vanish on the head' means it vanishes on the head. 'Dispel doubt' means dispel uncertainty. In the phrase 'Yassa taṃ sabbadhammesu, sadā ñāṇaṃ pavattati' (For whom knowledge always arises in all phenomena), the word 'taṃ' is merely a particle. The connection should be made thus: 'For whom knowledge always arises in all phenomena because of its connection to his wish, that All-Knowing Blessed One spoke this to the Elder Ānanda.' 'A king will be in the country' means a king will be in the entire country. 'The final' means the final existence. 'Having realized' means having made it directly manifest. 'The nature of the Dhamma' means the Dhamma of the Four Truths, or the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.

96. Suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ nāvanti ubhosu passesu suvaṇṇālaṅkārehi paṭimaṇḍitavasena chāditaṃ suvaṇṇanāvaṃ. Pañhaṃ puṭṭhā viyākāsi, sakkassa iti me sutanti yathā sā devatā pañhaṃ puṭṭhā sakkassa byākāsi, evaṃ mayāpi sutanti āyasmā mahāmoggallāno attanā yathāsutaṃ taṃ bhagavato vadati.

96. 'A golden-roofed boat' means a golden boat covered by way of being adorned with golden ornaments on both sides. Regarding 'Having been asked a question, she explained it to Sakka; thus it has been heard by me': just as that deity, having been asked a question, explained it to Sakka, so too has it been heard by me. Thus the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna tells the Blessed One that which was heard by himself, just as it was heard.

Paṃsuthūpesūti sarīradhātuṃ abbhantare ṭhapetvā paṃsūhi katathūpesu. Evañhi te bhagavantaṃ uddissakatā nāma honti, tenevāha – “uddissakatesu dasabaladharāna”nti.

'In dust stūpas' means in stūpas made of dust after having placed bodily relics inside. For in this way they are indeed called 'made in dedication to the Blessed One'; therefore, he said, 'in those dedicated to the bearers of the ten powers.'

97. Devaputtasarīravaṇṇāti devaputtasarīrasadisavaṇṇā. Subhagasaṇṭhitīti sobhaggayuttasaṇṭhānā. Uḷāraṃ vata taṃ āsīti taṃ mayā kataṃ puññaṃ uḷāraṃ vata ahosi. Yāhanti yā ahaṃ. Satasahassaṃ kappe, mudito thūpaṃ apūjesīti thūpaṃ pūjetvā satasahassaṃ āyukappe ahaṃ muditoti attho. Anāgantuna vinipātanti apāyupapattiṃ anupagantvā. Yaṃ cakkhunti yaṃ paññācakkhuṃ. Paṇihitanti ṭhapitaṃ. Vimuttacittamhīti vimuttacitto amhi. Vidhūtalatoti vidhūtataṇhālato, samucchinnataṇhoti attho.

97. 'Having the complexion of a devaputta's body' means having a complexion similar to the body of a devaputta. 'Of beautiful form' means having a form endowed with beauty. 'Indeed, that was magnificent!' means that merit made by me was indeed magnificent. 'Yāhaṃ' means 'I who...'. 'For a hundred thousand aeons, joyful, I worshipped the stūpa' means: because of worshipping the stūpa, for a hundred thousand life-aeons, I was joyful. 'Not coming to the lower realms' means not having gone to a birth in the lower realms. 'Which eye' means which eye of wisdom. 'Aimed' means established. 'I am with a liberated mind' means I am one with a liberated mind. 'With the creeper shaken off' means one who has shaken off the creeper of craving; the meaning is one whose craving is cut off.

98. Sāmākapatthodanamattanti sāmākatiṇānaṃ nāḷikodanamattaṃ. Akhileti pañcannaṃ cetokhilānaṃ abhāvena akhile. Tasmiñca okappayi dhammamuttamanti tasmiṃ paccekabuddhe uttamadhammaṃ paccekabodhiṃ “uttamadhammena nāma imasmiṃ [M 0.0232] bhavitabba”nti saddahiṃ. “Tasmiñca dhamme paṇidhesiṃ mānasa”nti iminā paṭiladdhadhammaṃ ahampi sacchikareyyanti cittaṃ paṇidahiṃ. Bhave kudāsupi ca mā apekkhavāti katthaci bhave apekkhavā mā bhaveyyanti ca paṇidhesiṃ mānasanti sambandho.

98. 'Just a pattha measure of rice from sāmāka grass' means a nāḷi measure of rice from sāmāka grass. 'Without barrenness' means without the five mental barrennesses due to their absence. 'And in him I placed faith in the supreme Dhamma' means I had faith in that Paccekabuddha regarding the supreme Dhamma, the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, thinking, 'In this venerable one, there must be what is called the supreme Dhamma.' 'And for that Dhamma I directed my mind' means I directed my mind, thinking, 'May I too realize the Dhamma attained by this one.' 'And may I not have longing for any existence whatsoever'—the connection is: and I directed my mind, thinking, 'May I not be one with longing for any existence whatsoever.'

Kurūsūti uttarakurūsu. Dīghāyukesūti tesaṃ vassasahassāyukatāya vuttaṃ. Amamesūti apariggahesu. Pāṇīsūti sattesu. Ahīnagāmīsūti yathāladdhasampattīhi yāvatāyukaṃ aparihīnasabhāvesu[V 0.0350]. Tidasopapajjathāti tāvatiṃso hutvā upapajjiṃ, tidase vā tāvatiṃsabhavane upapajjiṃ. Visiṭṭhakāyūpagatoti visiṭṭhakāyesu nānāvaṇṇakāyesu upagato. Yasassisūti parivāravantesu. Hitāhitāsihīti kusalākusale vītivattīhi. Paccakkhaṃ khvimanti paccakkhaṃ kho imaṃ vacananti adhippāyo.

“Among the Kurus” means among the Northern Kurus. “Among the long-lived” is said because of their having a lifespan of a thousand years. “Among those without possessions” means among those without grasping. “Among breathing beings” means among beings. “Among those who do not decline” means among those whose nature does not decline from whatever prosperity is gained, for as long as life lasts. “I was reborn among the Thirty-three” means I was reborn having become a Tāvatiṃsa deva, or I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm of the Thirty-three. “Having gone to distinguished bodies” means having gone to distinguished bodies, to bodies of various colors. “Among the famous” means among those with a retinue. “By those who have passed beyond benefit and harm” means by those who have transcended the wholesome and unwholesome. Regarding “Paccakkhaṃ khvimanti,” the intention is: “This word is indeed directly manifest.”

Sakāsīti so akāsi. Balimābhihārīti pūjābaliṃ abhihari. Patitassa ekanti tassa hatthato ekapupphaṃ patitaṃ.

“He did” means “he did.” “Bringing an offering” means he brought an offering of worship. “One fell from him” means one flower fell from his hand.

Upariṭṭhanti upari vehāse ṭhitaṃ. Ariṭṭhanti ariṭṭhaṃ nāma paccekasambuddhaṃ. Ajjhattañca bahiddhā cāti ajjhattavisayā ca bahiddhavisayā ca. Ye me vijjiṃsūti ye me pubbe vijjamānā ahesuṃ. Jātimaraṇasaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavoti punappunaṃ jāyanamīyanabhūto saṃsāro punabbhavoti ca vuccati, so ca dāni natthīti attho.

“Standing above” means standing above in the sky. “Ariṭṭha” means the Paccekasambuddha named Ariṭṭha. “Both internal and external” means those that have internal phenomena as their object and those that have external phenomena as their object. “Which existed for me” means which taints existed for me previously. “The saṃsāra of birth and death, now there is no renewed existence” means: the saṃsāra which consists of repeated birth and death is also called “renewed existence,” and that now does not exist; this is the meaning.

Idaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttanti idaṃ vāsanābhāgapuññavibhāvanānaṃ nānāsuttapadānaṃ udāharaṇavasena dassitaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttanti veditabbaṃ.

“This is a sutta connected with habitual tendencies” means: this sutta should be known as a sutta connected with habitual tendencies because it is shown by way of example of various sutta passages that explain the merit that is a portion of habitual tendencies.

99. “Uddhaṃ adho…pe… apunabbhavāyā”ti idaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttanti vuttaṃ oghataraṇassa ariyamaggakiccattā. Na cetanā karaṇīyāti na cittaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Dhammatāti dhammasabhāvo.

99. “‘Above, below… for the sake of no renewed existence’” is called a sutta pertaining to penetration, because the crossing of the flood is the task of the noble path. “No volition is to be made” means a thought is not to be produced. “The nature of phenomena” means the intrinsic nature of phenomena.

100. Yadā haveti yasmiṃ have kāle. Pātubhavantīti uppajjanti. Dhammāti anulomapaccayākārapaṭivedhasādhakā bodhipakkhiyadhammā. Pātubhavantīti vā pakāsenti, abhisamayavasena pākaṭā honti. Dhammāti catuariyasaccadhammā. Ātāpo vuccati kilesasantāpanaṭṭhena vīriyaṃ. Ātāpinoti [M 0.0233] sammappadhānavīriyavato. Jhāyatoti ārammaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇena lakkhaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇena ca jhānena jhāyantassa. Brāhmaṇassāti bāhitapāpassa khīṇāsavassa. Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbāti athassa evaṃ pātubhūtadhammassa yā tā “ko nu kho, bhante, phusatīti? No kallo pañhoti bhagavā avocā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.12) nayena “katamaṃ nu kho, bhante, jarāmaraṇaṃ, kassa panidaṃ jarāmaraṇanti? No kallo pañhoti bhagavā avocā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.35) ca nayena paccayākārakaṅkhā vuttā. Yā ca [V 0.0351] paccayākārasseva appaṭividdhattā “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”ntiādikā (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) soḷasakaṅkhā “buddhe kaṅkhati dhamme kaṅkhatī”tiādikā (dha. sa. 1008) aṭṭha ca kaṅkhā āgatā, tā sabbā vapayanti apagacchanti nirujjhanti, kasmā? Yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ, yasmā avijjādikena hetunā sahetukaṃ imaṃ saṅkhārādiṃ kevalaṃ dukkhakkhandhadhammaṃ pajānāti aññāsi paṭivijjhati.

100. “Yadā have” means: at which time, indeed. “Pātubhavanti” (they become manifest) means they arise. “Dhammā” (phenomena) means the factors of enlightenment that accomplish the penetration of dependent origination in forward order. Or, “pātubhavanti” means they are revealed; they become evident by means of realization. “Dhammā” also means the dhammas of the Four Noble Truths. “Ātāpa” (ardor) is the term for energy in the sense of tormenting the defilements. “Ātāpino” (of one with ardor) means of one who possesses the energy of the right exertions. “Jhāyato” (of one who meditates) means of one who meditates with the jhāna characterized by close contemplation of the object and close contemplation of the characteristics. “Brāhmaṇassa” (of the brahmin) means of one who has cast off evil, of one whose taints are destroyed. “Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā” (Then all his doubts vanish) means: then, for that person to whom the phenomena have thus become manifest, those doubts concerning dependent origination which were spoken of in the manner of “‘Who, venerable sir, has contact?’ ‘The question is not proper,’ the Blessed One said,” and so on, and in the manner of “‘What, venerable sir, is aging-and-death, and whose is this aging-and-death?’ ‘The question is not proper,’ the Blessed One said,” and so on; and also the sixteen doubts, beginning with “Did I exist in the past?”, that arise from not having penetrated dependent origination itself; and also the eight doubts that have been taught, beginning with “He has doubt about the Buddha, he has doubt about the Dhamma”—all these doubts vanish, depart, and cease. Why? “Yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ” (Because he understands the phenomenon with its cause), which means: because, with ignorance and so on as the cause, he understands, knows, and penetrates this entire aggregate of suffering, this phenomenon of formations and so on, as having a cause.

Yato khayaṃ paccayānaṃ avedīhi yasmā paccayānaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ avedi aññāsi paṭivijjhi, tasmā yadāssa ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa vuttappakārā dhammā pātubhavanti. Athassa yā nibbānassa aviditattā kaṅkhā uppajjeyyuṃ, sabbāpi tā kaṅkhā vapayantīti.

“Yato khayaṃ paccayānaṃ avedī” (Because he has known the destruction of conditions) means: because he knew, understood, and penetrated Nibbāna, which is called the destruction of conditions, therefore, when the aforementioned kinds of phenomena become manifest to that ardent, meditating brahmin, then whatever doubts might arise for him due to not having known Nibbāna, all those doubts vanish.

Āraññanti āraññakaṃ. Aññātuñchena yāpentanti kulesu aññāto niccanavoyeva hutvā uñchena piṇḍacariyāya yāpentaṃ. Atha vā abhilakkhitesu issarajanagehesu kaṭukabhaṇḍasambhāraṃ sugandhabhojanaṃ pariyesantassa uñchanaṃ ñātuñchanaṃ nāma, gharapaṭipāṭiyā pana dvāre ṭhitena laddhamissakabhojanaṃ aññātuñchanaṃ nāma. Idaṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Tena yāpentaṃ. Kāmesu anapekkhinanti vatthukāmakilesakāmesu nirapekkhaṃ.

“Āraññaṃ” (in the forest) means a forest-dweller. “Aññātuñchena yāpentaṃ” (subsisting on unknown gleanings) means subsisting by gleaning on the alms-round, having become unknown in families, as if always new. Alternatively, the gleaning of one who seeks pungent ingredients and fragrant food in marked, prominent houses of powerful people is called “known gleaning” (ñātuñchana). But seeking mixed food obtained by standing at the door according to the order of houses is called “unknown gleaning” (aññātuñchana). This latter is intended here. Subsisting by that. “Kāmesu anapekkhinaṃ” (unconcerned with sensual pleasures) means having no concern for sensual pleasures of the object-kind and sensual pleasures of the defilement-kind.

Chetvāti vadhitvā. Sukhaṃ setīti kodhapariḷāhena aparidayhamānattā sukhaṃ sayati. Na socatīti kodhavināsena vinaṭṭhadomanassattā na socati. Visamūlassāti dukkhavipākassa. Madhuraggassāti yaṃ akkuṭṭhassa paccakkositvā pahaṭassa paṭippaharitvā sukhaṃ uppajjati, taṃ sandhāya so “madhuraggo”ti vutto. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne pariyosānaṃ “agga”nti vuttaṃ. Ariyāti buddhādayo.

“Chetvā” (having cut) means having killed. “Sukhaṃ seti” (he sleeps happily) means he dwells happily, not being burned by the fever of anger. “Na socati” (he does not grieve) means he does not grieve, because with the destruction of anger, his displeasure is destroyed. “Visamūlassa” (of that with a poisonous root) means of that which has a painful result. “Madhuraggassa” (of that with a sweet tip) refers to the mental pleasure that arises for one who has been abused, by abusing in return, and for one who has been struck, by striking in return; with reference to this pleasure, that anger is called “sweet-tipped.” Indeed, in this context, the end (pariyosānaṃ) is called “tip” (agga). “Ariyā” (the noble ones) refers to the Buddhas and others.

Haneti [M 0.0234] haneyya. Uppatitanti asamugghāṭitaṃ avikkhambhituppannavasena samudācāruppannavasena samudācarantaṃ. Vinodayeti attano santānato nīhareyya.

“Hane” means one should kill. “Uppatitaṃ” (arisen) means that which is not uprooted, arisen by way of not being suppressed and by way of transgression. “Vinodaye” (one should dispel) means one should remove it from one's own mental continuity.

101. Sattiyāti desanāsīsametaṃ, ekatodhārādinā satthenāti attho. Omaṭṭhoti pahaṭo. Cattāro hi pahārā omaṭṭho ummaṭṭho maṭṭho vimaṭṭhoti. Tattha upari ṭhatvā adhomukhaṃ dinnappahāro omaṭṭho nāma, adho ṭhatvā uddhaṃ mukhaṃ dinnappahāro ummaṭṭho nāma, aggaḷasūci viya vinivijjhitvā kato maṭṭho nāma, seso sabbopi vimaṭṭho nāma. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne omaṭṭho [V 0.0352] gahito. So hi sabbadāruṇo duruddharaṇasallo duttikiccho antodoso antopubbalohito ca hoti. Pubbalohitaṃ anikkhamitvā vaṇamukhaṃ pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati. Pubbalohitaṃ nīharitukāmehi mañcena saddhiṃ bandhitvā adhosiro kātabbo hoti, maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Paribbajeti vihareyya.

101. “Sattiyā” (with a spear): this is a principal term in the teaching; the meaning is “with a weapon such as a single-edged one.” “Omaṭṭho” means struck downwards. Indeed, there are four kinds of strikes: “omaṭṭha” (a downward strike), “ummaṭṭha” (an upward strike), “maṭṭha” (a piercing strike), and “vimaṭṭha” (a strike of various kinds). Among them, a blow delivered downwards from above is called “omaṭṭha”; a blow delivered upwards from below is called “ummaṭṭha”; a blow made by piercing through like a door-bolt is called “maṭṭha”; and all the remaining kinds of blows are called “vimaṭṭha”. But in this context, “omaṭṭho” is taken. For that strike is the most cruel of all, has a dart that is difficult to extract, is difficult to treat, has an internal defect, and has internal pus and blood. The pus and blood, not coming out, cover the mouth of the wound and remain. Those who wish to remove the pus and blood must bind him together with a bed and make him head-downwards; he reaches death or suffering equivalent to death. “Paribbaje” means one should dwell.

Imāya gāthāya kiṃ kathitaṃ? Yathā sattiyā omaṭṭhapuriso sallubbāhanavaṇatikicchanānaṃ atthāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati payogaṃ karoti parakkamati. Yathā ca dayhamāne matthake ādittasiro tassa nibbāpanatthāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati payogaṃ karoti parakkamati, evamevaṃ bhikkhu kāmarāgappahānāya sato appamatto hutvā vihareyya bhagavāti kathesi.

What is said by this verse? Just as a man struck downwards by a spear arouses energy, makes an effort, and exerts himself for the sake of extracting the dart and treating the wound; and just as a man with his head on fire arouses energy, makes an effort, and exerts himself for the sake of extinguishing it; in the very same way, a bhikkhu, for the abandoning of sensual desire, should dwell mindful and diligent—thus the devatā spoke.

Evaṃ devatāya kathite atha bhagavā cintesi – “imāya devatāya upamā daḷhaṃ katvā ānītā, atthaṃ pana parittakaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā. Punappunaṃ kathentīpi hi esā kāmarāgassa vikkhambhanappahānameva katheyya, yāva ca kāmarāgo maggena na samugghāṭiyyati, tāva anubandhova hotī”ti tameva upamaṃ gahetvā paṭhamamaggavasena devatāya vinivaṭṭetvā dassento “sattiyā viya omaṭṭho”ti dutiyagāthamāha. Tassattho purimanayānusārena veditabbo.

When the devatā had spoken thus, the Blessed One thought: “This devatā has brought forth a strong simile, but she remains grasping only a little of the meaning. Indeed, even if she were to speak repeatedly, she would speak only of the abandoning of sensual desire by way of suppression. And as long as sensual desire is not uprooted by the path, it will continue to follow.” Taking up that very simile, turning it back to the devatā and showing it by way of the first path, he spoke the second verse: “As if struck by a spear…” Its meaning should be understood in accordance with the previous method.

Lokāmisanti kāmaguṇo. Santipekkhoti sabbasaṅkhārūpasamaṃ nibbānaṃ apekkhamāno. Paññavāti paññavanto. Pahitattoti nibbānaṃ patipesitacitto. Virato kāmasaññāyāti yāya kāyaci sabbato kāmasaññāya [M 0.0235] catutthamaggasampayuttāya samucchedaviratiyā virato. “Viratto”tipi pāṭho. Kāmasaññāyāti pana bhummavacanaṃ hoti. Sagāthāvagge (saṃ. ni. 1.96) “kāmasaññāsū”ti pāṭho. Catūhi maggehi dasannampi saṃyojanānaṃ atītattā sabbasaṃyojanātīto. Catutthamaggeneva vā uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanātīto tatra tatrābhinandanato nandisaṅkhātāya taṇhāya tiṇṇañca bhavānaṃ parikkhīṇattā nandibhavaparikkhīṇo. So tādiso khīṇāsavo bhikkhu gambhīre saṃsāraṇṇave na sīdati.

“Worldly pleasures” refers to the objects of sensual pleasure. “Looking for peace” means one who seeks Nibbāna, the pacification of all formations. “Wise” means possessing wisdom. “Resolute” means one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna. “Detached from sensual perceptions” means detached from any sensual perception whatsoever by the detachment of eradication associated with the fourth path. There is also a reading as “viratto” (dispassionate). In that case, “kāmasaññāya” is in the locative case. In the Sagāthāvagga (SN 1.96), the reading is “kāmasaññāsu”. Having transcended all ten fetters by means of the four paths, he has transcended all fetters. Or, having transcended the higher fetters by the fourth path alone, he has exhausted delight and becoming, because he has exhausted craving, which is called delight due to repeated rejoicing in those states, and the three kinds of becoming. Such a bhikkhu, whose taints are destroyed, does not sink in the deep ocean of saṃsāra.

Saddahānoti yena pubbabhāge kāyasucaritādibhedena, aparabhāge ca sattattiṃsabodhipakkhiyabhedena dhammena arahanto buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakā nibbānaṃ pattā. Taṃ saddahāno arahataṃ dhammaṃ nibbānappattiyā lokiyalokuttarapaññaṃ labhati, tañca kho na saddhāmattakeneva. Yasmā pana saddhājāto upasaṅkamati, upasaṅkamanto payirupāsati, payirupāsanto [V 0.0353] sotaṃ odahati, odahitasoto dhammaṃ suṇāti, tasmā upasaṅkamanato paṭṭhāya yāva dhammassavanena sussūsaṃ labhate paññaṃ.

“Faithful” (saddahāno) refers to one who has faith in the Dhamma by which Arahants, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha attain Nibbāna—by means of good bodily conduct and so forth in the earlier stage, and by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the later stage. Having faith in that Dhamma of the Arahants, for the attainment of Nibbāna, he gains mundane and supramundane wisdom—and that not merely by faith alone. For one born of faith approaches; approaching, he attends; attending, he lends an ear; and having lent an ear, he hears the Dhamma. Therefore, from the approach onward, up to hearing the Dhamma, by being attentive one obtains wisdom.

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Taṃ dhammaṃ saddahitvāpi ācariyupajjhāye kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvāpi vattakaraṇena payirupāsitvā yadā payirupāsanāya ārādhitacittā kiñci vattukāmā honti. Atha adhigatāya sotukāmatāya sotaṃ odahitvā suṇanto labhatīti evaṃ sussūsampi ca satiavippavāsena appamatto subhāsitadubbhāsitaññutāya vicakkhaṇo eva labhati, na itaro. Tenāha – “appamatto vicakkhaṇo”ti.

What is meant by this? Having faith in that Dhamma, and having approached teachers and preceptors from time to time, and having attended to them by performing one's duties, when their minds, pleased by such attendance, wish to say something, then, having acquired a desire to hear, lending an ear and listening, he obtains wisdom. Thus, even while being attentive, it is only the discerning one, who is diligent through unfailing mindfulness and who knows what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken, who obtains wisdom, not the other. Therefore, it is said: “The diligent and discerning one.”

Patirūpakārīti desakālādīni ahāpetvā lokiyassa lokuttarassa dhammassa patirūpaṃ adhigamūpāyaṃ karotīti patirūpakārī. Dhuravāti cetasikavīriyavasena anikkhittadhuro. Uṭṭhātāti kāyikavīriyavasena uṭṭhānasampanno asithilaparakkamo. Vindate dhananti lokiyalokuttaradhanaṃ adhigacchati. Saccenāti vacīsaccena paramatthasaccena ca. Buddhapaccekabuddhaariyasāvakā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇantā kittimpi pāpuṇantiyeva. Dadanti paresaṃ yaṃ kiñci icchitaṃ patthitaṃ dento mittāni ganthati sampādeti karotīti [M 0.0236] attho. Duddadaṃ vā dadanto ganthati, dānamukhena cattāripi saṅgahavatthūni gahitānīti veditabbāni. Tehi mittāni karonti. Asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ, sa ve pecca na socatīti yassa puggalassa ime saddhādayo dhammā vijjanti, so imasmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ gantvā na socati, sokakāraṇaṃ tassa natthīti attho.

“One who acts appropriately” (patirūpakārī) is one who, without neglecting place, time, and so forth, engages in the proper means for the attainment of mundane and supramundane Dhamma. “One who bears the burden” (dhuravā) is one who does not abandon the burden by means of mental energy. “One who is energetic” (uṭṭhātā) is one endowed with bodily energy, with unyielding effort. “One attains wealth” (vindate dhanaṃ) means one attains mundane and supramundane wealth. “Through truth” (saccena) means by means of verbal truth and ultimate truth. Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples, while attaining Nibbāna, also indeed attain renown. Giving to others whatever is wished for or desired, one forms, establishes, and makes friendships; this is the meaning. Or, giving what is hard to give, one establishes bonds; through generosity, all four bases of sympathy should be understood as included. By these, they make friendships. “From this world to the next, such a person, having passed away, does not grieve”—this means that for the person in whom these qualities of faith and so forth are found, having gone from this world to the next, he does not grieve. For that person there is no cause for sorrow; this is the meaning.

“Yassete caturo dhammā, saddhassa gharamesino;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, sa ve pecca na socatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 190) –

“For a faithful householder who possesses these four qualities—truth, wisdom, fortitude, and generosity—he, indeed, does not grieve after passing away.”

Gāthaṃ avasesaṃ katvā udāhaṭaṃ. Āḷavakasutte hi imā gāthā āḷavakena “kathaṃ su labhate pañña”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 187) puṭṭhena bhagavatā bhāsitāti.

The verse was cited, with the rest omitted. For in the Āḷavaka Sutta, these verses were spoken by the Blessed One when asked by Āḷavaka with questions such as, “How does one gain wisdom?” (SN 1.246; Sn 187).

Yena kenaci vaṇṇenāti yena kenaci kāraṇena, pakārena vā. Saṃvāsoti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sahavāso samāgamo. Tanti tathā samāgataṃ anukampitabbaṃ purisaṃ. Manasā ce pasannenāti karuṇāsamussāhitena [V 0.0354] pasādena pasannena manasā. Na tena hoti saṃyuttoti tena yathāvuttena anusāsanena kāmacchandādīnaṃ saṃyojanavasena saṃyutto nāma na hoti. Yānukampā anuddayāti yā ariyamaggasampāpanavasena karuṇāyanā, mettāyanā cāti attho.

“By whatever means” (yena kenaci vaṇṇena) means by whatever reason or manner. “Association” (saṃvāsa) means living together in one place, a coming together. “That person” (taṃ) refers to such a person who has come together and who should be regarded with compassion. “If one’s mind is pleased” (manasā ce pasannena) means with a mind pleased by serene confidence stirred by compassion. “One is not bound by that” (na tena hoti saṃyutto) means one is not bound by sensual desire and so forth, in the manner of fetters, through such instruction as described. “Compassion and sympathy” (yā anukampā anuddayā) refers to the compassion and loving-kindness as a means for causing the attainment of the noble path; this is the meaning.

102. Rāgo ca doso cāti rāgadosā heṭṭhā vuttanayāva. Kutonidānāti kiṃnidānā kiṃhetukā. Paccattavacanassa hi ayaṃ to-ādeso, samāse cassa lopābhāvo veditabbo. Aratī ratī lomahaṃso kutojāti yāyaṃ pantesu senāsanesu, adhikusalesu ca dhammesu arati ukkaṇṭhitā, yā ca pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rati abhirati āsatti kīḷanādi, yo ca lomahaṃsasamuṭṭhānato lomahaṃsasaṅkhāto cittutrāso, ime tayo dhammā kuto jātā kuto nibbattāti pucchā. Kuto samuṭṭhāyāti kuto uppajjitvā. Manoti kusalacittaṃ. Vitakkāti kāmavitakkādayo. Kumārakā dhaṅkamivosajantīti yathā kumārakā kīḷantā kākaṃ suttena pāde bandhitvā osajanti khipanti, evaṃ kusalamanaṃ akusalavitakkā kuto samuṭṭhāya osajantīti pucchā.

102. “Lust and hate” (rāgo ca doso ca) means lust and hate, as explained previously. “From what source?” (kutonidānā) means what is their origin, what is their cause? For this is the substitution of 'to' for the nominative case, and its non-elision in a compound should be understood. “Discontent, delight, and horror—from what are they born?” (arati ratī lomahaṃso kutojāti) means that discontent which is dissatisfaction in remote lodgings and in higher wholesome states; that delight which is great delight, attachment, and playfulness in the five strands of sensual pleasure; and that mental terror called 'horror' which arises from the bristling of hairs—from what are these three states born, from what do they arise?—this is the question. “From what do they originate?” (kuto samuṭṭhāya) means from what do they arise? “Mind” (mano) means the wholesome mind. “Thoughts” (vitakkā) means thoughts of sensual desire and the like. “Like boys releasing a crow” (kumārakā dhaṅkamivosajanti) means just as boys at play tie a string to a crow’s foot and release or throw it, so too, from where do unwholesome thoughts, having arisen, assail the wholesome mind?—this is the question.

Rāgo [M 0.0237] cāti dutiyagāthā tassā vissajjanaṃ. Tattha itoti attabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha. Attabhāvanidānā hi rāgadosā, arati rati lomahaṃsā ca attabhāvato jātā. Kāmavitakkādayo attabhāvato eva samuṭṭhāya kusalamanaṃ osajanti. Tena tadaññaṃ pakatiādikāraṇaṃ paṭikkhipanto āha – “itonidānā ito samuṭṭhāyā”ti. Purimagāthāya vuttanayenettha saddasiddhi veditabbā.

The second verse, “Lust and hate,” is the answer to that question. Therein, “from this” (ito) refers to individual existence (attabhāva). For lust and hate have individual existence as their source; discontent, delight, and horror are also born from individual existence. Thoughts of sensual desire and the like, arising from individual existence itself, assail the wholesome mind. Thus, rejecting other causes such as primordial nature, it is said: “From this as the source, from this arising.” The grammatical formation here should be understood in the same way as explained in the previous verse.

Idāni yvāyaṃ “itonidānā”tiādīsu attabhāvanidānā attabhāvato jātā attabhāvato samuṭṭhāyāti attho vutto, taṃ sādhento āha – “snehajā attasambhūtā”ti. Ete hi rāgādayo vitakkapariyosānā taṇhāsnehena jātā. Tathā jāyantā ca pañcupādānakkhandhabhede attabhāvasaṅkhāte attani sambhūtā. Tenāha – “snehajā attasambhūtā”ti. Idāni tadatthajotikaṃ upamaṃ dasseti “nigrodhasseva khandhajā”ti. Tattha khandhajāti khandhesu jātā pārohā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nigrodhassa khandhajasaṅkhātā pārohā āporasasaṅkhāte snehe sati jāyanti, jāyantā ca tasmiṃyeva nigrodhe tesu tesu sākhappadesesu sambhavanti, evaṃ ete rāgādayo ajjhattaṃ taṇhāsnehe sati jāyanti, jāyantā ca tasmiṃyeva attabhāve tesu tesu cakkhādippadesesu iṭṭhārammaṇesu sambhavanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “snehajā attasambhūtā”ti. Puthu visattā kāmesūti yasmā [V 0.0355] rāgopi pañcakāmaguṇikādivasena, dosopi āghātavatthuādivasena aratiādayopi tassa tassa bhedassa vasenāti sabbathā sabbepime kilesā puthu anekappakārā hutvā vatthudvārārammaṇādivasena tesu tesu kāmesu tathā tathā visattā laggā saṃsibbitvā ṭhitā. Kimiva? Māluvāva vitatā vane yathā vane vitatā māluvā tesu tesu rukkhasākhappasākhādibhedesu visattā hoti laggā saṃsibbitvā ṭhitā, evaṃ ete kilesā dhammā, tasmā ettha puthupabhedesu vatthukāmesu visattaṃ kilesagahanaṃ.

Now, regarding the meaning stated in such phrases as 'from this as the source'—that is, 'having individual existence as the source, born from individual existence, and arisen from individual existence'—to establish that meaning, he said: 'Born of affection, arisen from self.' For these states, from lust to thought, are born from the stickiness of craving. And being so born, they are produced in the self, which is designated as individual existence, differentiated as the five aggregates of clinging. Therefore, he said: 'Born of affection, arisen from self.' Now, he presents a simile that illuminates this meaning: 'like the trunk-born of a banyan tree.' Therein, 'trunk-born' means the aerial roots born on the trunks. This is what is said: Just as the aerial roots of a banyan tree, called 'trunk-born,' arise when there is sap, designated as water-essence, and having arisen, they manifest on that very banyan tree in its various branch-regions; so too, these states of lust and so on arise when there is the internal stickiness of craving, and having arisen, they manifest in that very individual existence in desirable objects in the various regions of the eye and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'Born of affection, arisen from self.' As for 'variously attached to sensual pleasures': because lust is of many kinds by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure, etc.; and aversion is of many kinds by way of the grounds for resentment, etc.; and discontent and so on are of many kinds by way of their respective distinctions; therefore, in every way, all these defilements, having become manifold and of many kinds, are in various ways attached and clinging to, stitched to and established in, those various sensual pleasures by way of their objects, doors, sense-objects, and so on. Like what? 'Like a māluvā vine spreading in the forest.' Just as a māluvā vine spreading in the forest is attached, clinging, stitched to and established in the various distinctions of tree branches, major and minor, and so on, so too are these defiled states. Therefore, here, in the sensual objects of various kinds, is the entangled thicket of defilements.

Ye naṃ pajānanti yatonidānaṃ, te naṃ vinodenti suṇohi yakkha. Tassattho – ye sattā naṃ kilesagahanaṃ “itonidānaṃ esa uppajjatī”ti jānanti, te naṃ taṇhāsinehasinehite attabhāve uppajjatīti [M 0.0238] ñatvā taṃ taṇhāsinehaṃ ādīnavānupassanādibhāvanāñāṇagginā visosentā vinodenti pajahanti, evaṃ amhākaṃ bhāsitaṃ suṇohi yakkhāti. Te duttaraṃ oghamimaṃ taranti, atiṇṇapubbaṃ apunabbhavāyāti ye hi saṃkilesagahanaṃ vinodenti, te ekantena maggaṃ bhāventi. Na hi maggabhāvanaṃ vinā kilesavinodanaṃ atthi. Evaṃ maggaṃ bhāventā te pakatiñāṇena duttaraṃ kāmoghādiṃ catubbidhaṃ oghaṃ iminā dīghena addhunā supinantenapi atiṇṇapubbaṃ anatikkantapubbaṃ apunabbhavāya nibbānāya taranti.

“Those who understand it and from what it is sourced, they eliminate it; listen, yakkha.” The meaning is this: Those beings who know that thicket of defilements, thinking, 'This arises from this as its source,' and knowing that it arises in the individual existence moistened by the stickiness of craving, they, drying up that stickiness of craving with the fire that is the wisdom of meditation, such as the contemplation of danger, eliminate and abandon it. Thus, listen to our speech, O yakkha. “They cross this flood so hard to cross, never crossed before, for the sake of no more becoming.” For those beings who eliminate the thicket of defilements, they certainly develop the path. Indeed, without the development of the path, there is no elimination of defilements. Thus, developing the path, those beings, by their natural wisdom, cross the fourfold flood—of sensual desire and so on—which is hard to cross, never before crossed or surpassed in this long course of time, not even in a dream, for the sake of no more becoming, for the sake of Nibbāna.

Dukkaraṃ bhagavāti eko kira devaputto pubbayogāvacaro bahalakilesatāya sappayogena kilese vikkhambhento samaṇadhammaṃ katvā pubbahetumandatāya ariyabhūmiṃ appatvāva kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatto, so tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā dukkarabhāvaṃ ārocento evamāha. Tattha dukkaranti dasapi vassāni…pe… saṭṭhipi vassāni ekantaparisuddhassa samaṇadhammassa karaṇaṃ nāmetaṃ dukkaraṃ. Sekkhāti satta sekkhā. Sīlasamāhitāti sīlena samāhitā samupetā. Ṭhitattāti patiṭṭhitasabhāvā. Evaṃ pucchitapañhaṃ vissajjitvā uparipañhaṃ samuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ “anagāriyupetassā”tiādimāha. Tattha anagāriyupetassāti anagāriyaṃ niggehabhāvaṃ upagatassa, pabbajitassāti attho. Tuṭṭhīti catupaccayasantoso.

'Difficult, O Blessed One!' A certain devaputta, it is said, who was formerly a practitioner of meditation, due to the thickness of his defilements, practiced the ascetic's duty while suppressing the defilements with effort, but due to the weakness of his past causes, he passed away without reaching the noble stage and was reborn in the deva world. He approached the Tathāgata and, declaring the state of difficulty, spoke thus. Herein, 'difficult' means: that which is called the practice of the perfectly pure ascetic's duty for ten years... up to sixty years, that practice is difficult. 'Trainees' means the seven trainees. 'Composed in virtue' means composed and endowed with virtue. 'Steadfast' means those of established nature. Having thus answered the question that was asked, in order to raise a further question, he said 'for one who has gone forth into homelessness,' and so on. Herein, 'for one who has gone forth into homelessness' means for one who has attained the homeless state, that is, for a renunciant. 'Contentment' means contentment with the four requisites.

Bhāvanāyāti cittavūpasamabhāvanāya. Te chetvā maccuno jālanti ye rattindivaṃ indriyūpasame ratā, te dussamādahaṃ cittaṃ samādahanti. Ye samāhitacittā, te catupaccayasantosaṃ pūrentā na kilamanti. Ye santuṭṭhā, te sīlaṃ pūrentā na kilamanti. Ye sīle patiṭṭhitā satta sekkhā, te ariyā maccuno jālasaṅkhātaṃ kilesajālaṃ chinditvā gacchanti.

'For development' means for the development of samatha and vipassanā which brings about the calming of the mind. As for 'They, having cut the net of Death': Those noble ones who delight day and night in the calming of the faculties, they compose the mind that is difficult to compose. Those noble ones with composed minds, fulfilling contentment with the four requisites, do not become weary. Those noble ones who are content, fulfilling virtue, do not become weary. Those seven trainees who are established in virtue, those noble ones, having cut the net of defilements, designated as the net of Death, go.

Duggamoti [V 0.0356] saccametaṃ, bhante, ye indriyūpasame ratā, te dussamādahaṃ cittaṃ samādahanti. Ye samāhitacittā, te catupaccayasantosaṃ pūrentā na kilamanti. Ye santuṭṭhā, te sīlaṃ pūrentā na kilamanti. Ye sīle paramaggāhino satta sekkhā, te ariyā maccuno jālasaṅkhātaṃ kilesajālaṃ chinditvā gacchanti. Kiṃ na gamissanti, ayaṃ pana duggamo “bhagavā [M 0.0239] visamo maggo”ti āha. Tattha kiñcāpi ariyamaggo neva duggamo na visamo, pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya panassa bahū parissayā honti, tasmā evaṃ vutto. Avaṃsirāti ñāṇasirena adhosirā hutvā papatanti. Ariyamaggaṃ ārohituṃ asamatthatāya eva te magge papatantīti vuccanti. Ariyānaṃ samo maggoti sveva maggo ariyānaṃ samo hoti. Visame samāti visamepi sattakāye samā eva.

'Hard to traverse.' This is true, venerable sir. Those noble ones who delight in the calming of the faculties, they compose the mind that is difficult to compose... Those seven trainees who hold virtue as supreme, those noble ones, having cut the net of defilements, designated as the net of Death, go. Why would they not go? 'But this path, Blessed One, is hard to traverse, it is an uneven path,' he said. Herein, although the noble path is indeed not hard to traverse nor uneven, yet in its preliminary practice there are many dangers. Therefore, it was said thus. 'Head-downward' means they fall headlong, with their head of wisdom facing downwards. It is because of their inability to ascend the noble path that they are said to fall on the path. 'The path is even for the noble ones' means that very path is even for the noble ones. 'Even amidst the uneven' means that even amidst the uneven assembly of beings, they are even.

103. Idañhi taṃ jetavananti anāthapiṇḍiko devaputto jetavanassa ceva buddhādīnañca vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ āgantvā evamāha. Isisaṅghanisevitanti bhikkhusaṅghanivesitaṃ. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya jetavanassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā idāni ariyamaggassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento “kammaṃ vijjā”tiādimāha. Tattha kammanti maggacetanā. Vijjāti maggapaññā. Dhammoti samādhi, samādhipakkhikā vā dhammā. Sīlaṃ jīvitamuttamanti sīle patiṭṭhitassa jīvitañca uttamanti dasseti. Atha vā vijjāti diṭṭhisaṅkappā. Dhammoti vāyāmasatisamādhayo. Sīlanti vācākammantājīvā. Jīvitamuttamanti etasmiṃ sīle patiṭṭhitassa jīvitaṃ nāma uttamanti. “Etena maccā sujjhantī”ti etena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena sattā visujjhanti.

103. 'This indeed is that Jetavana,' thus the devaputta Anāthapiṇḍika, having come for the purpose of speaking the praise of both the Jetavana monastery and of the Buddha and others, spoke. 'Frequented by the community of sages' means frequented by the community of monks. Having thus spoken the praise of Jetavana in the first verse, now, speaking the praise of the noble path, he spoke the words beginning with, 'Action and knowledge.' Therein, 'action' is the volition of the path. 'Knowledge' is the wisdom of the path. 'Dhamma' is concentration, or the states that are partisans of concentration. 'Virtue, the supreme life' shows that for one established in virtue, life is also supreme. Alternatively, 'knowledge' is right view and right intention. 'Dhamma' is right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. 'Virtue' is right speech, right action, and right livelihood. 'The supreme life' means that for one established in this virtue, life is indeed supreme. 'By this, mortals are purified' means: by this eightfold path, beings are purified.

Tasmāti yasmā maggena sujjhanti, na gottadhanehi, tasmā. Yoniso vicine dhammanti upāyena bodhipakkhiyadhammaṃ vicineyya. Evaṃ tattha visujjhatīti evaṃ tasmiṃ ariyamagge visujjhati. Atha vā yoniso vicine dhammanti upāyena ariyasaccadhammaṃ vicineyya. Evaṃ tattha visujjhatīti evaṃ tesu catūsu ariyasaccesu visujjhati. Idāni sāriputtattherassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento “sāriputtovā”tiādimāha. Tattha sāriputtovāti avadhāraṇavacanaṃ, etehi paññādīhi sāriputtova seyyoti vadati. Upasamenāti kilesavūpasamena. Pāraṅgatoti nibbānaṃ gato, yo koci nibbānapatto bhikkhu, na tādiso. Etāvaparamo siyā, na therā uttaritaro nāma sāvako atthīti vadati.

'Therefore' means: because they are purified by the path, not by lineage and wealth, therefore. 'One should wisely investigate the Dhamma' means: one should investigate the factors of enlightenment by a skillful means. 'Thus one is purified therein' means: thus one is purified in that noble path. Alternatively, 'one should wisely investigate the Dhamma' means: one should investigate the Dhamma of the noble truths by a skillful means. 'Thus one is purified therein' means: thus one is purified in those four noble truths. Now, speaking the praise of the Elder Sāriputta, he spoke the words beginning with, 'Sāriputta indeed.' Therein, 'Sāriputtova' is a word of emphasis; it is said that with these, wisdom and so on, Sāriputta alone is the best. 'With peacefulness' means: through the calming of defilements. 'Gone beyond' means: gone to Nibbāna. Any monk who has attained Nibbāna is not like him. He may be the utmost; it is said that there is no disciple more excellent than the Elder.

Atītanti atīte pañcakkhandhe. Nānvāgameyyāti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi nānugaccheyya. Nappaṭikaṅkheti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi na pattheyya. Yadatītanti idamettha kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā yaṃ atītaṃ, taṃ [V 0.0357] pahīnaṃ niruddhaṃ atthaṅgataṃ, tasmā [M 0.0240] taṃ nānugaccheyya. Yasmā ca yaṃ tattha anāgataṃ, taṃ appattaṃ ajātaṃ anibbattaṃ, tasmā tampi na pattheyya. Tattha tatthāti paccuppannampi dhammaṃ yattha yattheva so uppanno, tattha tattheva naṃ aniccānupassanādīhi sattahi anupassanāhi vipassati, araññādīsu vā tattha tattha vipassati. Asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppanti idaṃ vipassanāpaṭivipassanādassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Vipassanā hi rāgādīhi na saṃhirati na kuppatīti asaṃhīrā asaṃkuppā, taṃ anubrūhaye vaḍḍheyya paṭivipasseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā nibbānaṃ rāgādīhi na saṃhirati na kuppatīti asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ, taṃ vidvā paṇḍito bhikkhu anubrūhaye, punappunaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appento vaḍḍheyyāti attho.

'The past' means the past five aggregates. 'One should not pursue' means one should not follow with craving and views. 'One should not long for' means one should not yearn for with craving and views. 'What is past' is here a word of reason. Because what is past is abandoned, ceased, and has come to an end, therefore one should not follow it. And because what is future is not yet arrived, unborn, and not produced, therefore one should not yearn for it either. 'There and then' means: one contemplates the present phenomenon wherever it has arisen, right there and then, with the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence; or one contemplates in forests and so on, in those various places. 'Unshaken, unagitated' - this was said to show the re-contemplation of insight. Indeed, insight is not carried away, not agitated by lust and so on, therefore it is called 'unshaken, unagitated'; it is said that one should develop it, increase it, and re-contemplate it. Alternatively, Nibbāna is not carried away, not agitated by lust and so on, therefore it is called 'unshaken, unagitated'; a wise, learned monk should develop it. The meaning is: one should increase it by repeatedly entering the fruition attainment that has that as its object.

Tassa pana anubrūhanassa atthāya ajjeva kiccamātappanti kilesānaṃ ātāpanaparitāpanena “ātappa”nti laddhanāmaṃ vīriyaṃ ajjeva kātabbaṃ. Ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suveti sve jīvitaṃ vā maraṇaṃ vā ko jānāti. Ajjeva dānaṃ dassāmi, sīlaṃ vā rakkhissāmi, aññataraṃ vā pana kusalaṃ karissāmi, “ajja tāva papañco atthi, sve vā punadivase vā jānissāmī”ti cittaṃ anuppādetvā “ajjeva karissāmī”ti evaṃ vīriyaṃ kātabbanti dasseti. Mahāsenenāti ahivicchikavisasatthādīni hi anekāni maraṇakāraṇāni tassa senāti tāya mahatiyā senāya vasena mahāsenena evarūpena maccunā saddhiṃ “katipāhaṃ tāva āgamehi, yāvāhaṃ buddhapūjādiṃ attano avassayaṃ kammaṃ karomī”ti evaṃ mittasanthavākārasaṅkhāto vā “idaṃ sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā gahetvā katipāhaṃ āgamehī”ti evaṃ lañjānuppadānasaṅkhāto vā “iminā balarāsinā paṭibāhissāmī”ti evaṃ balarāsisaṅkhāto vā saṅgaro natthi. Saṅgaroti hi mittakaraṇalañjadānabalarāsisaṅkaḍḍhanānaṃ nāmaṃ, tasmā ayamattho vutto. Atanditanti analasaṃ uṭṭhāhakaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipannattā bhaddo ekaratto assāti bhaddekaratto. Itīti evaṃ paṭipannaṃ puggalaṃ “bhaddekaratto aya”nti rāgādisantatāya santo buddhamuni ācikkhati.

For the sake of that development, 'one must be ardent today itself.' The energy which has obtained the name 'ardor' (ātappa) because it scorches and torments the defilements should be applied today itself. 'Who knows of death tomorrow?' means: who knows whether there will be life or death tomorrow? It shows that one should apply energy thus: without giving rise to the thought, 'Today there is still delay; I will know tomorrow or the day after,' one should resolve, 'I will do it today itself,' whether it be giving alms, observing virtue, or doing some other wholesome act. Regarding 'with a great army': because the many causes of death—such as snakes, scorpions, poison, and weapons—are its army, therefore, on account of that great army, there is no bargaining with Death, who possesses such a great army. There is no bargaining in the form of making friends, saying, 'Wait for a few days while I perform an action that is my refuge, such as making offerings to the Buddha'; nor in the form of giving a bribe, saying, 'Take this hundred or thousand and wait for a few days'; nor in the form of amassing strength, saying, 'I will repel you with this mass of force.' Indeed, the term 'saṅgara' is a name for making friends, giving bribes, and amassing strength; therefore, this meaning was stated. 'Unremitting' means not lazy, energetic. Because of practicing thus, a fortunate single night is his, so he is called a 'bhaddekaratta' (one with a fortunate single night). Thus, the Buddha, the sage, who is calm through the pacification of lust and so on, declares a person who practices in this way to be a 'bhaddekaratta'.

Cakkhunā paññāya cāti cakkhunā ca paññāya ca. Cakkhubhūtāya vā paññāya. Satiyā paññāya cāti satiyā ca paññāya ca, sativisiṭṭhāya vā paññāya. Kāyenāti nāmakāyena.

'With the eye and with wisdom' means: with the eye and with wisdom, or with wisdom that has become the eye. 'With mindfulness and with wisdom' means: with mindfulness and with wisdom, or with wisdom distinguished by mindfulness. 'With the body' means: with the mental body.

Dibbacakkhu [M 0.0241] suvisuddhanti dibbaṃ cakkhu suvisuddhaṃ, yaṃ sacchikarotīti adhippāyo. Pubbenivāsāti purimāsu jātīsu nivutthakkhandhā. Iddhividhāti iddhikoṭṭhāsā. Nirodhoti nibbānaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'The divine eye is perfectly pure': the intended meaning concerns that which it realizes. 'Remembrance of past lives' means the aggregates that have been lived in previous births. 'Kinds of psychic power' means the divisions of psychic power. 'Cessation' means Nibbāna. The rest is very easy to understand.

104. Yassa [V 0.0358] selūpamaṃ cittanti ekaghanaṃ selaṃ viya pakativātehi lokadhammavātehi akampanīyato yassa cittaṃ selūpamaṃ. Tenāha – “ṭhitaṃ nānupakampatī”ti. Rajanīyesūti lābhādīsu. Kopaneyyeti alābhādike. Kuto naṃ dukkhamessatīti taṃ evaṃ bhāvitacittaṃ vītikkantalokadhammaṃ uttamapurisaṃ lokadhammahetukaṃ dukkhaṃ nānugamissati.

104. 'Whose mind is like a rock' means: because it is unshakeable by the winds of the worldly conditions, like a solid rock is by ordinary winds, that person’s mind is like a rock. Therefore, he said, 'Established, it does not tremble.' 'In things that arouse passion' means: in gain and so on. 'In things that provoke anger' means: in loss and so on. 'From where will suffering come to him?' means: suffering caused by worldly conditions will not follow that supreme person whose mind is thus developed and who has transcended the worldly conditions.

Yo brāhmaṇoti bāhitapāpadhammatāya brāhmaṇo, na diṭṭhamaṅgalikatāya huṃhuṅkārakasāvādipāpadhammayutto hutvā kevalaṃ jātimattena brāhmaṇoti paṭijānāti. So brāhmaṇo bāhitapāpadhammattā huṃhuṅkārappahānena nihuṃhuṅko. Rāgādikasāvābhāvena nikkabhāvo. Sīlasaṃvarena saṃyatacittatāya yatatto. Catumaggañāṇasaṅkhātehi vedehi antaṃ nibbānaṃ, vedānaṃ vā antaṃ gatattā vedantagū. Maggabrahmacariyassa vusitattā vūsitabrahmacariyo. Dhammena so brahmavādaṃ vadeyyāti so “brāhmaṇo aha”nti etaṃ vādaṃ vadeyya. Yassa sakalalokasannivāse kuhiñci ekārammaṇepi rāgussado dosussado mohussado mānussado diṭṭhussadoti ime ussadā natthīti attho.

Regarding 'Who is a brahmin?': One is a brahmin because of having banished evil qualities, not one who, being endowed with evil qualities such as making 'huṃ huṃ' sounds and the stain of defilements, and being one who relies on auspicious signs, merely claims to be a brahmin by birth. That brahmin, because of having banished evil qualities, is without the 'huṃ huṃ' sound through having abandoned it. Due to the absence of the stain of defilements such as lust, he is without stain. Through restraint in virtue, because of having a restrained mind, he is self-controlled. Because of having gone to the end, Nibbāna, by means of the knowledges called the four path-knowledges, or because of having gone to the end of the knowledges, he is a 'vedantagū' (one who has gone to the end of knowledge). Because the noble life of the path has been lived, he is one who has lived the noble life. Regarding 'Righteously, he would make the brahmin-claim': that person should make this claim, 'I am a brahmin.' The meaning is: that person for whom, in the entire assembly of the world, in any single object, these upsurges—the upsurge of lust, the upsurge of hatred, the upsurge of delusion, the upsurge of pride, and the upsurge of wrong views—do not exist.

Na gādhatīti na patiṭṭhahati. Sukkāti sukkasaṅkhātā gahā. Yadi candimasūriyādīnaṃ pabhā tattha natthi, tamo eva ca siyāti āsaṅkamāne sandhāyāha “tamo tattha na vijjatī”ti. Yadā ca attanāvedītiādīsu evaṃvidhaṃ nibbānaṃ attapaccakkhena ñāṇena yadā vindati, atha rūpārūpadhammato sukhadukkhato ca vippamutto hotīti.

Regarding 'does not get stuck': it means one is not established. Regarding 'the bright ones': it refers to the planets called 'the bright ones.' Referring to those who might doubt, 'If the light of the moon, sun, and so on is not there, then there would be only darkness,' he said, 'Darkness does not exist there.' Regarding 'And when one knows for oneself' and so on: when one attains such a Nibbāna with knowledge that is personally experienced, then one is liberated from material and immaterial phenomena, and from pleasure and pain.

Sakesu dhammesūti sakaattabhāvasaṅkhātesu upādānakkhandhesu. Yebhuyyena hi ajjhattaṃ vipassanābhiniveso hotīti. Etaṃ pisācanti ajakalāpaka, etaṃ tayā vuttaṃ pisācaṃ kilesapisācañca. Pakkulanti tayā kataṃ akkulaṃ pakkulakaraṇañca. Ativattatīti atikkamati.

Regarding 'in one's own phenomena': it means in the aggregates of clinging, which are called one's own individual existence. For, for the most part, the application of insight is internal. Regarding 'this goblin': it refers to the Ajakalāpaka goblin, this goblin spoken of by you, and the goblin of defilements. Regarding 'tangled': it refers to the tangling and the act of making tangled done by you. Regarding 'overcomes': it means transcends.

Nābhinandati [M 0.0242] āyantinti purāṇadutiyikaṃ āgacchantiṃ aññaṃ vā na abhinandati cittena na sampaṭicchati. Tameva pakkamantiṃ na socati. Saṅgā saṅgāmajiṃ muttanti pañcavidhāpi saṅgato muttaṃ saṅgāmajiṃ bhikkhuṃ.

Regarding 'does not delight in one who is coming': it means one does not delight in a former wife who is coming, or another woman; one does not accept her with the mind. One does not grieve for that very same one who is departing. Regarding 'freed, a victor in battle': it refers to a monk who is freed from the five kinds of association and who has conquered in battle.

Bahvetthāti bahu ettha nhāyati jano, na tena so suddho nāma hotīti adhippāyo.

Regarding 'many here': many people bathe here, but by that, one is not called pure. This is the intended meaning.

Jātibalaṃ [V 0.0359] nisedhanti jātibalassa nisedhakaṃ. Sahāyā vatāti samathavipassanābhāvanāya saha ayanavasena sahāyā vata. Kālena kālaṃ sappāyadhammassa savanavasena cirarattaṃ sameti samāgamo etesanti cirarattasametikā. Sithilamārabbhāti sithilaṃ vīriyaṃ katvā.

Regarding 'they prevent the power of birth': it means that which prevents the power of birth. Regarding 'truly, companions': they are indeed companions by way of proceeding together in the development of serenity and insight. Because their association lasts for a long time by way of listening to suitable teachings from time to time, they are 'long-standing associates.' Regarding 'having begun slackly': it means having made slack effort.

105. Tatra kho, bhikkhave, ko visesoti satthu sāvakassa ca pañcasveva upādānakkhandhesu nibbidādayoti pubbabhāgapaṭipattiyaṃ anupādāvimuttiyañca heṭṭhā upari ca visesābhāvaṃ dasseti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “natthi vimuttiyā nānatta”nti (a. ni. 5.31; kathā. 355 atthato samānaṃ). Tattha visesābhāvaṃ paccāmasati “tatra ko viseso”ti. Adhippayāsoti adhikapayogo. Nānākaraṇanti ca visesoyeva vutto.

105. Regarding 'Therein, O monks, what is the distinction?': it shows the absence of distinction between the Teacher and the disciple, both below and above, in the preliminary practice and in liberation without clinging, with respect to disenchantment and so forth towards the five aggregates of clinging. For this has been said: 'There is no diversity in liberation.' With the phrase 'Therein, what is the distinction?', it reflects upon the absence of distinction in that context. Regarding 'Adhippayāso': it means 'additional application.' And regarding 'Nānākaraṇa': it is the distinction itself that is spoken of.

Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, visesoti bhikkhave, yadipi sāvakassa satthu ca vimuttiyaṃ viseso natthi, sayambhuñāṇena pana savāsanasabbakilese khepetvā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā anuppannassa ariyamaggassa parasantāne uppādanādisakalasabbaññuguṇasamāyogo. Ayaṃ sammāsambuddhassa paññāvimuttato visesoti. Tattha anuppannassāti avattamānassa. Ariyamaggañhi kassapasammāsambuddho uppādesi. Antarā añño satthā uppādetā nāma nāhosi, tasmā ayaṃ bhagavā anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā nāma. Asañjātassāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Anakkhātassāti akathitassa. Maggaṃ jānātīti maggaññū. Maggaṃ viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsīti maggavidū. Magge ca amagge ca kovidoti maggakovido. Maggānugāti maggaṃ anugacchantā. Pacchāsamannāgatāti ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ samannāgato, sāvakā pacchā samannāgatā.

Regarding 'This, O monks, is the distinction': O monks, although there is no distinction in liberation between the disciple and the Teacher, yet by means of self-existent knowledge, having destroyed all defilements together with their latent tendencies and having fully awakened to perfect self-enlightenment, there is the endowment with all the qualities of an omniscient one, such as causing the unarisen noble path to arise in the mental continuum of others. This is the distinction of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One from one who is liberated by wisdom. Therein, regarding 'unarisen': it means not presently existing. For the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha Kassapa caused the noble path to arise. In the interim, no other teacher who could cause it to arise appeared; therefore, this Blessed One is the one who causes the unarisen path to arise. Regarding 'unproduced': it is a synonym for that very word. Regarding 'undeclared': it means 'untaught.' Because he knows the path, he is a 'knower of the path' (maggaññū). Because he made the path known and manifest, he is a 'discoverer of the path' (maggavidū). Because he is skilled in the path and the non-path, he is 'skilled in the path' (maggakovido). Regarding 'followers of the path': it means those who follow along the path. Regarding 'subsequently endowed': I was endowed first; the disciples were endowed afterwards.

106. “Nīce [M 0.0243] kule paccājāto”tiādinā (a. ni. 4.85; pu. pa. 168) tamena yuttoti tamo. Kāyaduccaritādīhi puna nirayatamupagamanato tamaparāyaṇo. Iti ubhayenapi khandhatamova kathito hoti. “Aḍḍhe kule paccājāto”tiādinā (a. ni. 4.85; pu. pa. 168) jotinā yuttoti joti, ālokabhūtoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyasucaritādīhi puna saggūpapattibhavūpagamanato jotiparāyaṇo. Iminā nayena itarepi dve veditabbā.

106. By the text beginning, 'Born in a low family,' because he is endowed with darkness (tamena), he is called 'darkness' (tamo). Furthermore, because of going to the darkness of hell through bodily misconduct and so on, he has darkness as his future destination (tamaparāyaṇo). Thus, by both terms, it is the darkness of the aggregates that is spoken of. By the text beginning, 'Born in a wealthy family,' because he is endowed with light (jotinā), he is called 'light' (joti); it is said that he has become light. Furthermore, because of going to the heavenly plane of existence through good bodily conduct and so on, he has light as his future destination (jotiparāyaṇo). In this way, the other two persons should also be understood.

Na taṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrāti ettha dhīrāti buddhādayo paṇḍitapurisā. Yaṃ saṅkhalikasaṅkhātaṃ [V 0.0360] ayena nibbattaṃ āyasaṃ addubandhanasaṅkhātaṃ dārumayañca pabbajatiṇehi rajjuṃ katvā katarajjubandhanañca, taṃ asiādīhi chindituṃ sakkuṇeyyatāya “thira”nti na vadantīti attho. Sārattarattāti rattā hutvā rattā. Balavarāgarattāti attho. Maṇikuṇḍalesūti maṇīsu ca kuṇḍalesu ca, maṇicittesu vā kuṇḍalesu. Etaṃ daḷhanti ye maṇikuṇḍalesu sārattarattā, tesu yo rāgo, yā ca puttadāresu apekkhā taṇhā, etaṃ kilesamayaṃ bandhanaṃ paṇḍitapurisā “daḷha”nti vadanti.

Regarding 'The wise do not call that a strong bond': here, 'the wise' means the Buddhas and other wise persons. The meaning is that they do not call 'firm' that which is called a chain made of iron, that which is called a fetter-stock made of wood, and a rope-bond made by making a rope from Pabbaja grass, because it can be cut with swords and so forth. Regarding 'deeply impassioned': it means being impassioned, they are impassioned. The meaning is 'impassioned with strong, excellent lust.' Regarding 'in jewels and earrings': it means in jewels and in earrings, or in earrings adorned with jewels. Regarding 'This is strong': the lust that those who are deeply impassioned for jewels and earrings have, and the longing and craving for children and wives—this bond made of defilements, the wise persons call 'strong'.

Ohārinanti ākaḍḍhitvā catūsu apāyesu pātanato avaharati heṭṭhā haratīti ohārinaṃ. Sithilanti bandhanaṭṭhāne chaviādīni akopetvā bandhanabhāvampi ajānāpetvā jalapathathalapathādīsu kammaṃ kātuṃ detīti sithilaṃ. Duppamuñcanti lobhavasena hi ekavārampi uppannaṃ kilesabandhanaṃ daṭṭhaṭṭhānato kacchapo viya dummocayaṃ hotīti duppamuñcaṃ. Etampi chetvānāti etaṃ daḷhampi kilesabandhanaṃ ñāṇakhaggena chinditvā anapekkhino hutvā kāmasukhaṃ pahāya paribbajanti pakkamanti pabbajanti cāti attho.

Regarding 'that which drags down' (ohārinaṃ): because by dragging down, it causes one to fall into the four states of woe; it carries one downwards, hence 'ohārinaṃ'. Regarding 'loose' (sithilaṃ): because at the place of binding, without damaging the skin and so on, and without making the state of bondage known, it allows one to perform actions on water paths, land paths, and so on; thus, it is 'loose'. Regarding 'hard to release' (duppamuñcaṃ): for a fetter of defilement that has arisen even once through the power of greed is hard to be released from, like a tortoise from its shell; thus, it is 'hard to release'. Regarding 'having cut even this': The meaning is that having severed even this firm fetter of defilement with the sword of wisdom, becoming unconcerned, having abandoned sensual pleasure, they wander forth, depart, and go forth into homelessness.

107. Cetetīti akusalacetanāvasena ceteti. Pakappetīti tameva akusalacetanaṃ kāyavacīkammabhāvaṃ pāpanavasena kappeti. Anusetīti rāgādianusayova santāne appahīnabhāvena anuseti. Ārammaṇametaṃ hoti viññāṇassa ṭhitiyāti yadetaṃ cetanaṃ pakappanaṃ anusayanañca, etaṃ abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa ṭhitiyā pavattiyā paccayo hotīti attho. Ārammaṇe sati patiṭṭhā viññāṇassa hotīti yathāvuttapaccaye sati abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa kammaṃ [M 0.0244] javāpetvā paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanasamatthatāsampādanato patiṭṭhā hoti. Āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti hotīti āyatiṃ punabbhavasaṅkhātā viññāṇādīnaṃ abhinibbatti hoti.

107. Regarding 'intends' (ceteti): one intends by the power of unwholesome volition. Regarding 'fashions' (pakappeti): by the power of causing it to arrive, one fashions that very unwholesome volition into the state of bodily and verbal kamma. Regarding 'lies dormant' (anuseti): the underlying tendency of lust and so on lies dormant in one's continuity through the state of not being abandoned. Regarding 'This becomes an object for the station of consciousness': The meaning is that this intending, fashioning, and lying dormant is a condition for the station and occurrence of kamma-forming consciousness. Regarding 'When there is an object, there is a foundation for consciousness': When the aforesaid condition exists, there is an establishment for kamma-forming consciousness by means of accomplishing the capability of drawing forth rebirth-linking, having impelled the kamma. Regarding 'In the future, there is the production of renewed existence': In the future, there is the arising of consciousness and so on, which are called renewed existence.

“No ce, bhikkhave, cetetī”tiādinā akusalakammameva paṭikkhipati. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho, yadipi kadāci yonisomanasikārā akusalacetanā nappavattati, anusayā pana appahīnāti, te kusalassa abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa patiṭṭhā honti yevāti. Sati ca abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇe āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti hotīti vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Tatiyavāro vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo.

By the text beginning with 'If, monks, one does not intend,' only unwholesome kamma is rejected. This is the concise meaning here: although sometimes, due to wise attention, unwholesome volition does not arise, nevertheless, the underlying tendencies are not yet abandoned. Therefore, they become a foundation for wholesome kamma-forming consciousness. And when there is kamma-forming consciousness, it is indeed proper to say that in the future there is the arising of renewed existence. The third section should be understood by the method opposite to what has been stated.

108. “Neso, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddo”tiādi yadi duppūraṇaṭṭhena saṃsīdanaṭṭhena [V 0.0361] duratikkamanaṭṭhena sāgaro “samuddo”ti vucceyya, tato satabhāgenapi sahassabhāgenapi cakkhuādīsveva ayaṃ nayo labbhatīti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha – “cakkhu, bhikkhave, purisassa samuddo, tassa rūpamayo vego”ti, rūpesu sattānaṃ āviñchanato rūpāyatanameva vego cakkhussa vegoti attho.

108. Regarding the text beginning, 'Monks, that is not the ocean in the Noble One's discipline': This was said to show that if the great ocean were to be called 'ocean' in the sense of being hard to fill, in the sense of causing sinking, and in the sense of being hard to cross, then this principle is found in the eye and so on to a greater degree by a hundredfold or a thousandfold. Therefore, He said: 'The eye, monks, is a person's ocean; its current is made of forms.' The meaning is: because it drags beings towards forms, the form-base itself is the current, the current of the eye.

Yo taṃ rūpamayaṃ vegaṃ sahatīti yo bhikkhu saha visayena cakkhuṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato sammasanto tattha ca nibbindanto virajjanto tappaṭibaddhato kilesajālato vimuccanto abhibhavati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, atari cakkhusamuddanti ayaṃ bhikkhu cakkhusaṅkhātaṃ samuddaṃ tiṇṇoti vuccati.

Regarding 'One who withstands that current made of forms': That is, a monk who, contemplating the eye together with its object as impermanent, as suffering, and as not-self, and thereby becoming disenchanted with it, becoming dispassionate towards it, and being liberated from the net of defilements connected with it, overcomes it. Regarding 'This one, monks, is said to have crossed the eye-ocean': This means this monk is said to be one who has crossed the ocean designated as the eye.

Aparo nayo – cakkhu, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddoti yadipi duppūraṇaṭṭhena yadi vā samudanaṭṭhena samuddo, cakkhumeva samuddo. Tassa hi pathavito yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā nīlādiārammaṇaṃ samosarantaṃ paripuṇṇabhāvaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Evaṃ duppūraṇaṭṭhenapi samuddo. Cakkhu ca tesu tesu nīlādiārammaṇesu samudeti asaṃvutaṃ hutvā osaramānaṃ kilesuppattiyā kāraṇabhāvena sadosabhāvena gacchatīti samudanaṭṭhenapi samuddo. Tathā cakkhuṃ taṇhāsotādīnaṃ uppattidvāratāya tehi santānassa samudanaṭṭhena temanaṭṭhena samuddo. Tassa rūpamayo vegoti samuddassa appamāṇo ūmimayo vego viya [M 0.0245] tassāpi cakkhusamuddassa samosarantassa nīlādibhedassa ārammaṇassa vasena appameyyo rūpamayo vego veditabbo. Yo taṃ rūpamayaṃ vegaṃ sahatīti yo taṃ cakkhusamudde samosarantaṃ rūpamayaṃ vegaṃ manāpe rūpe rāgaṃ, amanāpe dosaṃ, asamapekkhane mohanti evaṃ rāgādikilese anuppādento upekkhakabhāvena sahati.

Another method: 'The eye, monks, is an ocean in the Noble One's discipline'—the eye itself is an ocean, whether in the sense of being hard to fill or in the sense of moistening. For the blue and other objects gathering from the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā world cannot bring it to a state of fullness. Thus, it is an ocean also in the sense of being hard to fill. And the eye moistens (samudeti); when unrestrained and descending upon those various blue and other objects, it proceeds with a faulty nature, being a cause for the arising of defilements. Thus, it is an ocean also in the sense of moistening. Likewise, because the eye is a gateway for the arising of the currents of craving and so on, it is an ocean in the sense of moistening, of drenching the continuity of existence with them. 'Its current is made of forms': Just as the ocean has an immeasurable current made of waves, so too, for that eye-ocean, an immeasurable current made of forms, on account of the various blue and other objects that gather, should be understood. 'One who withstands that current made of forms': This is one who, with regard to that current made of forms gathering in the eye-ocean, does not generate lust for a pleasant form, hatred for an unpleasant form, or delusion in the case of what is not properly regarded, and thus withstands it with equanimity.

Saūmintiādīsu kilesaūmīhi saūmiṃ. Kilesavaṭṭehi sāvaṭṭaṃ. Kilesagahehi sagahaṃ. Kilesarakkhasehi sarakkhasaṃ. Kodhupāyāsassa vā vasena saūmiṃ. Kāmaguṇavasena sāvaṭṭaṃ. Mātugāmavasena sagahaṃ sarakkhasaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “ūmibhayanti kho, bhikkhave, kodhupāyāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ (itivu. 109; ma. ni. 2.162; a. ni. 4.122). Tathā āvaṭṭanti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ (itivu. 109; ma. ni. 2.164; a. ni. 4.122). Gaharakkhasoti kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (itivu. 109). Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo.
