In the phrases 'with waves' and so on, the meaning should be understood thus: 'with waves' (saūmiṃ) means with the waves of defilements. 'With whirlpools' (sāvaṭṭaṃ) means with the whirlpools of defilements. 'With grasping sea-monsters' (sagahaṃ) means with the grasping sea-monsters of defilements. 'With demons' (sarakkhasaṃ) means with the demons of defilements. Alternatively, 'with waves' is by way of anger and despair. 'With whirlpools' is by way of the strands of sensual pleasure. 'With grasping sea-monsters' and 'with demons' are by way of women. For this has been said: 'The fear of waves, monks, is a designation for anger and despair.' Likewise: 'The whirlpool, monks, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.' And: 'The grasping demon, monks, is a designation for a woman.' This same method applies to the remaining sense doors as well.

Saūmibhayaṃ [V 0.0362] duttaraṃ accatarīti aniccatādiūmibhayena sabhayaṃ duratikkamaṃ atikkami. Lokantagūti saṃsāralokassa antaṃ gato. Pāragatoti vuccatīti nibbānaṃ gatoti kathīyati.

Regarding 'He crossed over that which is with the fear of waves, hard to cross': He crossed over this fearful and hard-to-cross ocean of the senses by means of the fear of the waves of impermanence and so on. 'Gone to the world's end' (lokantagū): He has gone to the end of the world of saṃsāra. 'He is called one who has gone to the far shore' (pāragato): He is said to have gone to Nibbāna.

Baḷisāti sattānaṃ anatthahetutāya baḷisā viya baḷisā. Anayāyāti anatthāya. Byābādhāyāti dukkhāya. Iṭṭhāti pariyiṭṭhā vā apariyiṭṭhā vā sukhārammaṇatāya iṭṭhā. Kāmanīyaṭṭhena kantā. Manassa vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena manāpā. Piyasabhāvatāya piyarūpā. Kilesakāmasahitattā kāmūpasaṃhitā. Rāgajananaṭṭhena cittassa rañjanato rajanīyā. Tañceti taṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ, nīlādivasena anekabhedabhinnampi hi rūpāyatanaṃ rūpārammaṇabhāvena cakkhuviññeyyabhāvena ca ekavidhataṃ nātivattatīti taṃsabhāvasāmaññaṃ gahetvā “tañce”ti vuttaṃ. Abhinandatīti abhinandanabhūtāya sappītikataṇhāya abhimukho nandati. Abhivadatīti “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti vadāpentiyā taṇhāyanavasena abhivadati. Ajjhosāya tiṭṭhatīti gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā tiṭṭhati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gilitabaḷiso mārassāti ayaṃ, bhikkhu, kilesamārassa baḷisabhūtaṃ rūpataṇhaṃ gilitvā ṭhitoti vuccati. Sesavāresupi iminā nayena [M 0.0246] attho veditabbo. Abhedīti bhindi. Paribhedīti sabbabhāgena bhindi. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

'Fishhook' (baḷisa) means that because they are a cause of harm to beings, they are like fishhooks. 'For ruin' (anayāya) means for harm. 'For affliction' (byābādhāya) means for suffering. 'Pleasing' (iṭṭha) means that whether sought after or not, because of being a pleasant object or a cause of pleasure, they are called 'pleasing'. 'Charming' (kantā) in the sense of being desirable. 'Agreeable' (manāpā) in the sense of causing the mind to increase. 'Lovely' (piyarūpā) in the sense of having a pleasing nature. 'Associated with sensual desire' (kāmūpasaṃhitā) because it is accompanied by the defilement of sensual desire. 'Enchanting' (rajanīyā) because it generates lust, captivating the mind. And 'that' (tañce) refers to that form object. For although the form-base is divided into many types such as blue and so forth, it does not transcend its singular nature as a form-object and as something cognizable by eye-consciousness. Thus, taking the common characteristic of that nature, it is said, 'and that.' 'He delights in it' (abhinandati) means he delights in or accepts it, facing it with craving accompanied by joy that has become great delight. 'He welcomes it' (abhivadati) means he mentally attends to it under the influence of craving that causes one to say, 'Oh, happiness! Oh, happiness!' 'He remains clinging to it' (ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati) means he remains, having swallowed and settled it firmly. 'This, monks, is called a monk who has swallowed Māra's hook'—that is, this monk is said to have swallowed the craving for forms, which has become the fishhook of Māra the defiler, and to stand thus. In the remaining cases too, the meaning should be understood by this method. 'He shattered' (abhedi) means he broke. 'He utterly shattered' (paribhedi) means he broke completely. The rest is clear.

109. Ayaṃ loko santāpajātoti ayaṃ sattaloko jātasantāpo ñātibyasanādivasena uppannasokasantāpo ca rāgādivasena uppannapariḷāhasantāpo cāti attho. Phassaparetoti anekehi dukkhaphassehi abhibhūto. Rodaṃ vadati attatoti taṃ taṃ attanā phuṭṭhaṃ dukkhaṃ abhāvitakāyatāya adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto “aho dukkhaṃ, īdisaṃ dukkhaṃ mayhaṃ sattunopi mā hotū”tiādinā vilapanto vadati. Kasmā? Yena yena hi maññanti, tato taṃ hoti aññathā, yasmā ete sattā yena yena pakārena attano dukkhassa paṭikāraṃ maññanti āsīsanti, taṃ dukkhaṃ tato aññena pakārena tikicchitabbaṃ hoti. Yena vā pakārena attano vaḍḍhiṃ maññanti, tato aññathā avaḍḍhi eva pana hoti. Evaṃ aññathābhāvitaṃ icchāvighātaṃ eva pāpuṇāti. Ayaṃ bhavasatto kāmādibhavesu satto sattaloko, tathāpi bhavamevābhinandati, na tattha nibbindati. Yadabhinandati taṃ bhayanti yaṃ kāmādibhavaṃ abhinandati, taṃ jarāmaraṇādianekabyasanānubandhattā ativiya bhayānakaṭṭhena bhayaṃ. Yassa bhāyatīti yato jarāmaraṇādito bhāyati, taṃ dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato dukkhadukkhatāya ca dukkhanti.

109. 'This world is born of anguish'—this world of beings is born of anguish, meaning the anguish of sorrow arising from the loss of relatives and so forth, and the anguish of burning arising from lust and so forth. 'Overcome by contact' (phassapareto) means overwhelmed by many painful contacts. 'He weeps, speaking from the self' (Rodaṃ vadati attato)—that is, being unable to endure the various suffering that has befallen him due to his undeveloped body, he laments, saying, 'Alas, suffering! May such suffering not even befall my enemies!' and so forth. Why? 'For whatever they conceive, it turns out otherwise.' Because these beings, in whatever way they imagine and hope for a remedy for their suffering, that suffering must be treated in another way. Or, in whatever way they imagine their own growth, it turns out otherwise—only decline occurs. Thus, they only meet with the frustration of their desires. This world of beings, attached to existence—attached to sensual and other states of existence—still delights in existence and does not grow disenchanted with it. 'What one delights in is a danger' (Yadabhinandati taṃ bhayaṃ)—whatever sensual and other states of existence one delights in is a danger, in the sense of being extremely terrifying, due to being followed by many calamities like aging and death. 'That of which one is afraid' (Yassa bhāyati)—that from which one fears, such as aging and death, is called suffering because it is the basis of suffering and because of its nature as suffering-in-itself.

Bhavavippahānāyāti [V 0.0363] bhavassa pajahanatthāya. Khoti avadhāraṇatthe nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ekanteneva kāmādibhavassa samudayappahānena pahānatthaṃ idaṃ mayā adhigataṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ vussatīti.

'For the abandonment of existence' (Bhavavippahānāya) means for the purpose of abandoning existence. The word 'kho' is a particle used in the sense of emphasis. This is what is said: 'This holy life of the path, attained by me, is lived solely for the purpose of abandoning existence, such as sensual existence, by abandoning its origin.'

Evaṃ ariyassa maggassa ekaṃseneva niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni aññamaggassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipanto “ye hi kecī”tiādimāha. Tattha bhavenāti rūpabhavena vā arūpabhavena vā. Bhavassāti saṃsārassa. Vippamokkhanti bhavato vimuttiṃ, saṃsārasuddhinti attho. Kiñcāpi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā tattha nibbānasaññino, bhavagāmikammena pana rūpārūpajjhānena[M 0.0247], taṃnibbattena ca upapattibhavena bhavavisuddhiṃ vadantā bhavena bhavavippamokkhaṃ vadanti nāma. Tenāha – “sabbe te avippamuttā bhavasmāti vadāmī”ti. Atha vā bhavenāti bhavadiṭṭhiyā, bhavati tiṭṭhati sassatanti hi pavattanato sassatadiṭṭhi “bhavadiṭṭhī”ti vuccati. Bhavadiṭṭhi eva uttarapadalopena “bhavo”ti vuttā bhavataṇhātiādīsu viya. Bhavadiṭṭhivasena hi idhekacce bhavavisesaṃyeva bhavavippamokkhaṃ maññanti. Yathā taṃ bako brahmā āha – “idaṃ niccaṃ, idaṃ dhuvaṃ, idaṃ sassataṃ, idaṃ avipariṇāmadhamma”nti (ma. ni. 1.501; saṃ. ni. 1.175). Vibhavenāti ucchedadiṭṭhiyā. Vibhavati vinassati ucchijjatīti hi pavattanato ucchedadiṭṭhi vuttanayena “vibhavo”ti vuccati. Bhavassa nissaraṇamāhaṃsūti saṃsārasuddhiṃ vadiṃsu. Ucchedadiṭṭhivasena hi idhekacce saṃsārasuddhiṃ vadanti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

Having thus shown the Noble Path's nature as leading to liberation in one way only, now, wishing to reject the nature of other paths as leading to liberation, he said, 'Whatever those may be,' and so forth. Herein, 'by existence' (bhavena) means either by form existence or formless existence. 'Of existence' (bhavassa) refers to saṃsāra. 'Liberation' (vippamokkha) means freedom from existence; the meaning is purification from saṃsāra. Although those ascetics and brahmins have the perception of Nibbāna therein, by speaking of the purification of existence through the form and formless jhānas, which are kamma leading to existence, and through the resultant rebirth-existence, they are indeed speaking of liberation from existence by means of existence. Therefore, he said: 'I say that all those are not liberated from existence.' Alternatively, 'by existence' (bhavena) means by the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi); for the eternalist view is called 'the view of existence' because it proceeds as 'it exists, it persists, it is eternal.' The view of existence itself is called 'existence' (bhavo) by eliding the subsequent word, as in 'craving for existence' and so forth. For by means of the view of existence, some here consider a particular existence itself to be liberation from existence. As the Brahmā Baka said: 'This is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal, this is not subject to change' (MN 49; SN 6.4). 'By non-existence' (vibhavena) means by the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). For because it proceeds as 'it ceases to be, it perishes, it is annihilated,' the annihilationist view, in the way stated, is called 'non-existence' (vibhavo). 'They spoke of an escape from existence' means they spoke of purification from saṃsāra. For by means of the annihilationist view, some here speak of purification from saṃsāra. Thus it is said—

“Yato kho, bho, ayaṃ attā rūpī cātumahābhūtiko…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ettāvatā kho, bho, ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.91).

'When, friend, this self is material, composed of the four great elements... and so forth... having attained and dwelling in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. To this extent, friend, this self is rightly and completely annihilated' (DN 1).

Anissaṭāti anikkhantā. Tattha kāraṇamāha – “upadhiñhi paṭicca dukkhamidaṃ sambhotī”ti. Tattha upadhinti khandhādiupadhiṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yattha ime diṭṭhigatikā nibbānasaññino, tattha khandhūpadhikilesūpadhiabhisaṅkhārūpadhayo adhigatā ñātā. Kuto tassa dukkhanissaraṇatāti. Yaṃ pana paramatthato dukkhanissaraṇaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “sabbupādānakkhayā natthi dukkhassa sambhavo”ti vuttaṃ.

Not escaped (anissaṭā) means not gone forth. Therein he states the reason: 'For this suffering arises in dependence on the substrates of existence.' Therein, 'substrates of existence' (upadhi) refers to the substrates such as the aggregates. What is meant? Where those with wrong views have the perception of Nibbāna, there the substrates of existence—the aggregates, the defilements, and the volitional formations—are attained and known. How could the escape from suffering from that be known? But to show what the escape from suffering is in the ultimate sense, it is said: 'With the destruction of all clinging, there is no arising of suffering.'

Lokamimaṃ passāti bhagavā attano cittaṃ ālapati. Puthūti visuṃ visuṃ. Avijjāya paretanti [V 0.0364] mohena abhibhūtaṃ. Bhūtanti khandhapañcakaṃ. Bhūtaratanti itthī purise, puriso itthiyāti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ sattesu rataṃ, tato eva bhavā aparimuttā. Ye hi keci bhavāti ittarakhaṇā vā dīghāyukā vā sātavanto vā asātavanto vā bhavā. Sabbadhīti uddhaṃ adho tiriyanti sabbattha. Sabbatthatāyāti sabbabhāvena. Sabbe te bhavātiādīsu “sabbepi bhavā aniccā”tiādinā vipassanāsahitāya maggapaññāya aviparītaṃ passato bhavataṇhāpi pahīyati nirujjhati, vibhavaṃ ucchedampi nābhinandati na pattheti, tassa sabba [M 0.0248] taṇhānaṃ anavasesato maggena nirujjhanato nibbānaṃ nibbuti hoti. Tassa evaṃ nibbutassa bhikkhuno anupādā kilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ anupādānato aggahaṇato punabbhavo na hoti. Evaṃbhūtena ca abhibhūto pañcavidhopi māro vijito assa anena mārena saṅgāmo, sabbepi bhave samatikkanto iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīsu tādilakkhaṇappattoti.

The Blessed One addresses His own mind, saying, 'See this world!' 'Puthū' means 'separately, separately.' 'Avijjāya pareta' means 'overwhelmed by delusion.' 'Bhūta' means the five aggregates. 'Bhūtarata' means: a woman delights in a man, and a man delights in a woman; thus, it means delighting in one another among beings. Precisely because of this, they are not freed from existence. 'Ye hi keci bhavā' means whatever existences there are, whether of brief duration, or long-lived, or pleasant, or unpleasant. 'Sabbadhī' means 'everywhere': above, below, and across. 'Sabbatthatāya' means 'in every way.' Regarding 'Sabbe te bhavā,' etc., the meaning should be understood thus: For one who sees without distortion by means of the wisdom of the path associated with insight, thinking 'All existences are impermanent,' etc., the craving for existence is abandoned and ceases. He does not delight in nor desire non-existence, which is annihilationism. For him, because all cravings cease without remainder through the path, Nibbāna, which is extinguishment, occurs. For that monk who is thus extinguished, because of non-clinging—that is, due to not clinging to and not grasping the defilements and volitional formations—there is no future existence. And by such a one, the fivefold Māra is overcome; the battle with Māra has been won by him. Having transcended all existences, he has attained the characteristic of being 'such' (tādi) with regard to desirable, undesirable, and other objects.

Anusotagāmī andhaputhujjano paṭisotagāmī kalyāṇaputhujjano. Ṭhitatto sekkho. Itaro asekkho.

The blind worldling is one who goes with the stream; the virtuous worldling is one who goes against the stream. The trainee (sekha) is one of established nature. The other is the non-trainee (asekha).

110. Abhijātikoti jātiyo. Kaṇhābhijātikoti kaṇhe nīce kule jāto. Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyatīti kāḷakaṃ dasavidhaṃ dussīladhammaṃ pasavati karoti, so taṃ abhijāyitvā niraye nibbattati. Sukkaṃ dhammanti “ahaṃ pubbepi puññānaṃ akatattā nīce kule nibbatto, idāni puññaṃ karissāmī”ti puññasaṅkhātaṃ sukkaṃ paṇḍaraṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyati, so tena sagge nibbattati. Akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ nibbānanti nibbānañhi sace kaṇhaṃ bhaveyya, kaṇhavipākaṃ dadeyya. Sukkaṃ, sukkavipākaṃ dadeyya. Dvinnampi appadānato pana “akaṇhaṃ asukka”nti vuttaṃ. Nibbānanti cettha arahattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tañhi kilesanibbānante jātattā nibbānaṃ nāma. Taṃ esa abhijāyati pasavati karoti. Sukkābhijātikoti sukke ucce kule jāto. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. “Kaṇhaṃ kaṇhavipāka”ntiādikassa kammacatukkassa attho heṭṭhā hārasampātavāre vibhatto eva.

110. 'Abhijātiko' means lineages. 'Kaṇhābhijātiko' means one born in a dark, low family. 'Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyati' means he cultivates and performs the dark, tenfold immoral dhamma; and that person, having cultivated it, is reborn in hell. 'Sukkaṃ dhammaṃ' means: thinking, 'Because I did not perform meritorious deeds in the past, I was born in a low family; now I will perform merit,' he cultivates the bright, pure dhamma called 'merit'; and by that, that person is reborn in heaven. Regarding 'Akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ nibbānaṃ': Indeed, if Nibbāna were dark, it would give a dark result. If it were bright, it would give a bright result. But because it gives neither of the two results, it is called 'neither dark nor bright.' And here by 'Nibbāna,' the fruit of Arahantship is intended. For, because it arises at the end of the extinguishing of the defilements, it is called Nibbāna. This person cultivates, produces, and performs it. 'Sukkābhijātiko' means one born in a bright, high family. The remainder should be understood in the way already stated. The meaning of the fourfold kamma beginning with 'dark with a dark result' has already been analyzed below in the section on Hārasampāta.

111. Mānusattanti manussabhāvaṃ, manussayoninti attho. Dveti kiccaṃ akiccameva cāti dve. Kiccāni tveva kattabbāni, na cākiccaṃ kiñci kattabbanti dasseti. Sukiccantiādi “kicca”nti vuttānaṃ tesaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ.

111. 'Mānusattaṃ' means the human state, the human birth; this is the meaning. 'Dve' means two: what should be done and what should not be done. It shows that only what should be done is to be done, and nothing that should not be done is to be done. The phrase beginning with 'Sukiccaṃ' is a statement showing the nature of those things that were called 'what should be done'.

Padhānānīti [V 0.0365] uttamāni visiṭṭhāni. Purimasmiṃ pabbajitesūti visaye bhummaṃ. Dutiye adhikaraṇe. Tattha nibbānanti arahattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Kasmā panettha āmisapariccāgo arahattena samadhuro niddiṭṭhoti? Dakkhiṇeyyesu dakkhiṇāya mahapphalabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Yena yena vā pana vatthunāti ucchedādivatthunā. Ajjhositāti bhavataṇhādivasena ajjhositā. Dutiye yena yena vā pana vatthunāti amarāvikkhepavatthuādinā.

`Padhānāni` means supreme, distinguished. In the first instance of the word `pabbajitesu`, the locative case has the sense of 'sphere'; in the second, it has the sense of 'location'. Therein, by `nibbānaṃ`, Arahantship is intended. If one should object, 'Why here is the relinquishment of material things indicated as being on par with Arahantship?', it is so indicated in order to show the great fruitfulness of an offering to those worthy of offerings. `Yena yena vā pana vatthunā` means by some thing or other, such as the tenet of annihilationism, etc. `Ajjhositā` means clung to by way of craving for existence, etc. In the second instance, `yena yena vā pana vatthunā` means by some thing or other, such as the tenets of the eel-wrigglers, etc.

Iminā [M 0.0249] asubhena kammavipākenāti asubhassa kāyaduccaritādikammassa vipākattā asubhena asivena kammavipākena. Idaṃ bālalakkhaṇaṃ nibbattatīti purimasmiṃ bhave duccaritasamaṅgitāya bālo ayaṃ bhavatīti upalakkhaṇaṃ jāyati. Idaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttanti idaṃ evaṃ pavattaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ nāma suttaṃ.

`Iminā asubhena kammavipākena` means: by this foul, unpeaceful karmic result, because it is the result of foul kamma such as bodily misconduct, etc. `Idaṃ bālalakkhaṇaṃ nibbattati` means: a sign arises, indicating, 'This person is a fool because of being endowed with misconduct in a previous existence.' `Idaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ` means: this discourse, proceeding thus, is called the 'Discourse Pertaining to Defilement'.

Iminā subhenāti ettha vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Tattha mahāpurisalakkhaṇanti paṇḍitalakkhaṇaṃ. Kilesabhūmīhīti kilesaṭṭhānehi kilesāvatthāhi vā. Sānusayassa pariyuṭṭhānaṃ jāyatīti appahīnānusayassa paccayasamāyoge rāgādayo pariyuṭṭhānavasena pavattanti. Pariyuṭṭhito saṃyujjatīti yo rāgādīhi pariyuṭṭhitacitto, so kāmarāgādīhi saṃyujjati nāma. Saṃyujjanto upādiyatīti yo kāmarāgasaṃyojanādīhi saṃyutto, so kāmupādānādīni akusalakammāni ca upādiyati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

Regarding `Iminā subhena`, the meaning should be understood here according to the method already stated. Therein, `mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ` means the sign of a wise person. `Kilesabhūmīhi` means from the grounds of the defilements or from the states of the defilements. `Sānusayassa pariyuṭṭhānaṃ jāyati` means: for one whose underlying tendencies have not been abandoned, when the appropriate conditions come together, lust and so on arise by way of obsession. `Pariyuṭṭhito saṃyujjati` means: a person whose mind is obsessed by lust, etc., is indeed fettered by sensual lust, etc. `Saṃyujjanto upādiyati` means: one who is bound by the fetter of sensual lust, etc., clings firmly to sensual clinging, etc., and to unwholesome kammas. The remainder is clear everywhere.

112. Evaṃ soḷasavidhena sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ nānāsuttehi udāharaṇavasena vibhajitvā idāni aṭṭhavīsatividhena sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ dassentena yasmā ayampi paṭṭhānavibhāgo mūlapadehi saṅgahito, na imassāpi tehi asaṅgahito padeso atthi, tasmā mūlapadaṃ vibhajitabbatañca dassetuṃ “tattha katame aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā”ti pucchāya vasena mūlapadāni uddharitvā “lokiyaṃ lokuttara”ntiādinā navatikā, thavo cāti aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ. Tattha lokiyanti loke niyutto, loke vā vidito lokiyo. Idha pana lokiyo attho yasmiṃ sutte vutto, taṃ suttaṃ lokiyaṃ. Tathā lokuttaraṃ. Yasmiṃ pana sutte padesena lokiyo, padesena lokuttaro vutto, taṃ lokiyañca lokuttarañca. Yañca satte adhiṭṭhāya sattapaññattimukhena desitaṃ, taṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Dhammavaseneva desitaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Ubhayavasena desitaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānañca dhammādhiṭṭhānañca. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Buddhādīnaṃ pana guṇābhitthavanavasena pavattaṃ suttaṃ thavo nāma.

112. Having thus analyzed the foundation of the teaching in sixteen ways by way of examples from various discourses, now, by one who is showing the foundation of the teaching in twenty-eight ways: since this analysis of the foundation is also included in the root terms, and there is no part of it not included in them, therefore, to show the root term and its analyzability, having extracted the root terms by means of the question, 'Therein, what are the eighteen root terms?', the twenty-eight-fold foundation of the teaching is set forth in brief by means of 'mundane, supramundane,' etc., which are the nine triads, and 'praise.' Therein, 'mundane' means connected with the world, or known in the world. Here, however, a discourse in which a mundane meaning is spoken is a 'mundane' discourse. Similarly for 'supramundane.' But a discourse in which partly a mundane meaning is spoken and partly a supramundane meaning is spoken is 'both mundane and supramundane.' And that which is taught based on beings, with the designation of a being as its entry point, is 'founded on beings.' That which is taught solely by way of phenomena is 'founded on phenomena.' That which is taught by way of both is 'founded on beings and founded on phenomena.' By this method, the meaning should be understood in all the triads. However, a discourse that proceeds by way of extolling the virtues of the Buddha and others is called 'praise.'

Tattha [V 0.0366] sajjukhīranti taṅkhaṇaṃyeva dhenuyā thanehi nikkhantaṃ abbhuṇhakhīraṃ. Muccatīti pariṇamati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā dhenuyā thanato nikkhantaṃ khīraṃ [M 0.0250] taṅkhaṇaṃyeva na muccati na pariṇamati na dadhibhāvaṃ gacchati, takkādiambilasamāyogato pana parato kālantarena pakatiṃ jahati dadhibhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, evamevaṃ pāpakammampi kiriyakkhaṇeyeva na vipaccati. Yadi vipacceyya, nānāgatīnaṃ sabhāvaṭṭhānaṃ siyā, na koci pāpakammaṃ kātuṃ visaheyya. Yāva pana kusalābhinibbattakkhandhā caranti, tāva taṃ te rakkhanti, tesaṃ bhedā apāyesu nibbattāpanavasena vipaccati. Vipaccamānañca ḍahantaṃ bālamanveti, kiṃ viya? Bhasmacchannova pāvako. Yathā hi chārikāya paṭicchanno vītaccitaṅgāro akkantopi chārikāya paṭicchannattā na tāva ḍahati, chārikaṃ pana tāpetvā cammādīni ḍahanavasena yāva matthaluṅgā ḍahanto gacchati, evamevaṃ pāpakammampi yena kataṃ, taṃ bālaṃ dutiye vā tatiye vā attabhāve nirayādīsu nibbattaṃ ḍahantaṃ anugacchatīti.

Therein, `sajjukhīraṃ` means milk that has come from a cow's teats at that very moment, fresh and warm. `Muccati` means it transforms or curdles. This is what is said: Just as milk that has come from a cow's udder does not immediately curdle, does not transform, does not attain the state of yogurt, but later, after some time, due to contact with souring agents like buttermilk, it abandons its natural state and attains the state of yogurt; in the very same way, an evil deed also does not ripen at the moment it is performed. If it were to ripen, there would be a simultaneous existence of various destinies, and no one would dare to perform an evil deed. As long as the aggregates produced by wholesome kamma endure, they protect that person. Upon their breaking up, it ripens by way of causing rebirth in the woeful states. And while ripening, it follows the fool, burning him. Like what? Like a fire covered by ash. For just as a glowing ember covered by ash, though stepped upon, does not burn at once because it is covered by ash, but after heating the ash, it proceeds to burn things like hide, etc., burning all the way to the brain-marrow; in the very same way, the evil deed that was done by a fool follows that fool, burning him when he is reborn in a second or third existence in hell and other such states.

Yassindriyānīti tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yassa bhikkhuno chekena sārathinā sudantā assā viya cha indriyāni samathaṃ dantabhāvaṃ nibbisevanabhāvaṃ gatāni, tassa navavidhaṃ mānaṃ pahāya ṭhitattā pahīnamānassa catunnaṃ āsavānaṃ abhāvena anāsavassa tādibhāve ṭhitassa tathārūpassa devāpi pihayanti, manussāpi dassanañca āgamanañca patthentiyevāti. Āhāre satīti āhārapaṭibaddhe chandarāge appahīne sati.

Regarding 'Whose faculties...': here is the brief meaning. For whichever monk the six faculties have reached tranquility, a state of being tamed, and a state of non-indulgence, like the well-tamed horses of a skilled charioteer; for him, who stands having abandoned the ninefold conceit and thus has abandoned conceit, who is without taints due to the absence of the four taints, and who is established in such a state—for such a one, even the gods hold him dear, and humans indeed long for the sight of him and for his coming. 'When there is food' means: when the desire and lust connected with food has not been abandoned.

113. Sabbā disā anuparigamma cetasāti parito dasapi disā cittena anugantvā. Nevajjhagāti neva adhigaccheyya. Piyataranti atisayena piyaṃ. Attanāti attato. Evaṃ piyo puthu attā paresanti evaṃ kassacipi attanā piyatarassa anupalabbhanavasena visuṃ visuṃ paresaṃ sattānaṃ attā piyo. Yasmā ca etadeva, tasmā na hiṃse paraṃ attakāmo attano sukhakāmoti.

113. 'Having gone around all directions with the mind' means: having mentally traversed all ten directions round about. 'He would not find' means: he would not find. 'Dearer' means: exceedingly dear. 'Than oneself' means: than one's own self. 'Thus dear is the separate self to others' means: in this way, by virtue of not finding anyone dearer than oneself, for other beings, each one separately, their own self is dear. And because this is so, therefore, one who desires his own welfare, desiring his own happiness, should not harm another.

Bhūtāti jātā nibbattā. Bhavissantīti nibbattissanti. Bhūtāti vā khīṇāsavā. Te hi pahīnabhavattā bhūtā eva. Gamissantīti paralokaṃ gamissanti. Khīṇāsavā pana anupādisesaṃ nibbānaṃ.

'Those who have become' means those who have been born, who have arisen. 'Those who will be' means those who will come into being. Alternatively, 'those who have become' means the Arahants. For they, because they have abandoned becoming, are indeed 'those who have become.' 'They will go' means they will go to another world. The Arahants, however, will go to Nibbāna without remainder of aggregates.

Piyo [V 0.0367] ca hotīti suparisuddhāya sīlasampattiyā, suparisuddhāya ca diṭṭhisampattiyā samannāgato piyo piyāyitabbo hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘And he becomes dear’ means: being endowed with the accomplishment of perfectly pure virtue and the accomplishment of perfectly pure view, he becomes dear and worthy of being held dear. For this was said:

“Sīladassanasampannaṃ[M 0.0251], dhammaṭṭhaṃ saccavādinaṃ;

Attano kammakubbānaṃ, taṃ jano kurute piya”nti. (dha. pa. 217);

One who is accomplished in virtue and vision, established in the Dhamma, a speaker of truth, who does his own work—such a one the people hold dear.

Pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garukātabbatāya garu. Uttarimanussadhammavasena sambhāvetabbatāya bhāvanīyo. Sīlaguṇena vā piyagaruādibhāvā veditabbā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā’ti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”ti (ma. ni. 1.65).

He is respected because he is to be respected, like a stone umbrella. He is to be esteemed because he is to be esteemed by way of his superhuman states. Or, these states of being dear, respected, and so on, are to be understood as being due to the quality of his virtue. For so it was said: 'If, monks, a monk should wish: "May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow practitioners of the holy life, may I be respected and esteemed," he should be one who fulfills the precepts.'

Vattāti “kālena vakkhāmī”tiādipañcadhamme attani upaṭṭhāpetvā sabrahmacārīnaṃ ullumpanabhāve ṭhatvā vattā. Vacanakkhamoti sabrahmacārīhi yena kenaci vuccamāno subbaco hutvā padakkhiṇaggāhitāya tesaṃ vacanaṃ khamatīti vacanakkhamo. Vattāti vā dhammakathāvasena vacanasīlo. Vacanakkhamoti dhammaṃ saṃvaṇṇento parehi asaṃhīro hutvā tesaṃ pucchāvacanakkhamatāya vacanakkhamo. Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattāti saccapaṭiccasamuppādādiṃ, aññaṃ vā gambhīrakathaṃ kattā. Na caṭṭhāne niyojakoti dhammavinayādiṃ adhammāvinayādivasena avatvā dhammavinayādivaseneva dīpanato na ca aṭṭhāne niyojako.

He is a speaker: having established in himself the five qualities beginning with ‘I will speak at the right time,’ and standing in a state of uplifting his fellow practitioners, he is a speaker. He is patient with speech: when spoken to by any of his fellow practitioners, being easy to admonish, he endures their words by accepting them respectfully; thus he is patient with speech. Alternatively, he is a speaker: he is one whose nature is to speak by way of Dhamma-talk. He is patient with speech: when explaining the Dhamma, being unshaken by others, he is patient with speech because of his forbearance toward their questioning speech. He is a maker of profound talk: he is a maker of profound talk on such topics as the truths, dependent origination, or other profound subjects. And he is not one who engages in what is inappropriate: because he explains the Dhamma and Vinaya only by way of what is Dhamma and Vinaya, not speaking by way of what is not Dhamma and not Vinaya, he is not one who engages in what is inappropriate.

Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvāti ettha “taṇhā janeti purisa”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.55-57) vacanato tīsu bhavesu sattānaṃ jananato taṇhā mātā nāma. “Ahaṃ asukassa nāma rañño, rājamahāmattassa vā putto”ti pitaraṃ nissāya asmimānassa uppajjanato asmimāno pitā nāma. Loko viya rājānaṃ yasmā sabbadiṭṭhigatāni dve sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyo bhajanti, tasmā sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyo dve khattiyā rājāno nāma. Dvādasāyatanāni vitthataṭṭhena raṭṭhasadisattā raṭṭhaṃ nāma. Āyasādhako āyuttakapuriso viya taṃnissito nandirāgo anucaro nāma.

In the text ‘Having slain mother and father’: because it is said, “Craving begets a person,” craving is called the mother due to its generating beings in the three existences. Because the conceit ‘I am’ arises dependent on a father through the thought, “I am the son of such-and-such a king or a great royal minister,” the conceit ‘I am’ is called the father. Just as the world attends upon a king, because all wrong views attend upon the two views of eternalism and annihilationism, therefore the two views of eternalism and annihilationism are called the two warrior-kings. The twelve sense bases are called the country because of their similarity to a country in the sense of being extensive. Like an appointed official who collects revenue, the delight-lust that is dependent on them is called the attendant.

Anīghoti niddukkho. Brāhmaṇoti khīṇāsavo. Etena hi taṇhādayo arahattamaggañāṇāsinā hatā bāhitā. Yātīti so brāhmaṇo niddukkho hutvā yātīti.

‘Without trouble’ means free from suffering. ‘Brahmin’ means one whose taints are destroyed. For indeed, by this Arahant, craving and so on are slain and expelled with the sword that is the knowledge of the Arahantship path. ‘He goes’ means: that brahmin, having become free from suffering, goes.

Kāyeti [V 0.0368] karajakāye. Cittanti pādakajjhānacittaṃ. Samodahatīti pakkhipati. Yadā dissamānena kāyena gantukāmo hoti, tadā kāyagatikaṃ [M 0.0252] pādakajjhānacittaṃ adhiṭṭhahatīti attho. Cittepi kāyaṃ samodahatīti yadā sīghaṃ gantukāmo hoti, tadā pādakajjhānacitte kāyaṃ pakkhipati, cittagatikaṃ kāyaṃ adhiṭṭhahatīti attho. Kāye sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamitvāti “seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyyā”ti vuttanayena (mahāva. 8, 137; dī. ni. 2.66; ma. ni. 1.282; 2.338; saṃ. ni. 1.172) iddhimā kāye sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamitvā paresaṃ dissamānena kāyena ārāmarāmaṇeyyakādīni pekkhamāno cittakkhaṇeneva icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati.

‘In the body’ means: in the physical body. ‘Mind’ means: the basic jhāna-mind. ‘He places together’ means: he places. The meaning is: when he wishes to go with the visible body, he then resolves upon the basic jhāna-mind that is conformed to the body. ‘He also places the body in the mind’ means: when he wishes to go swiftly, he then places the body in the basic jhāna-mind; he resolves upon the body that is conformed to the mind. This is the meaning. ‘Having entered into the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness in the body’ means: in the way that has been taught, “Just as a strong man...”, the one with psychic power, having entered into the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness in the body, while looking at delightful parks and so on with a body visible to others, goes to the desired place in a single mind-moment.

114. Yaṃ taṃ lokuttaraṃ ñāṇanti sabbaṃ lokaṃ uttaritvā abhibhavitvā ṭhitattā vuttaṃ, na pana lokuttarabhūmikattā. Sabbakāle pavattatīti āvajjanapaṭibaddhavuttittā vuttaṃ, na satataṃ samitaṃ pavattatīti. Na hi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ bhagavato sabbasmiṃyeva kāle uppajjatīti sakkā vattunti.

114. The phrase ‘that which is world-transcending knowledge’ is said because it stands having transcended and overcome the entire world, and not because it belongs to the supramundane plane. The phrase ‘it occurs at all times’ is said because its occurrence is connected to adverting; it is not said because it occurs constantly and uninterruptedly. For indeed, it is not possible to say that the Blessed One's omniscience arises at all times.

Kittayissāmi te santinti sabbakilesavūpasamahetutāya santiṃ nibbānaṃ dassessāmi. Diṭṭhe dhammeti diṭṭhe dukkhādidhamme, imasmiṃ eva vā attabhāve. Anītihanti itihāsāti evaṃ na itikirāya pavattaṃ, attapaccakkhanti attho. Yaṃ viditvā sato caranti “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādinā (dha. pa. 277; theragā. 676; netti. 5) nayena sato hutvā caranto ariyamaggena yaṃ santiṃ viditvā. Tare loke visattikanti saṅkhāraloke visappanato visattikasaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ tare tareyya samatikkameyyāti attho.

‘I will declare peace to you’ means: I will teach Nibbāna, which is peace because it is the cause for the stilling of all defilements. ‘In this visible world’ means: when the phenomena of suffering and so on are seen, or in this very existence. ‘Not based on hearsay’ means: not occurring by way of hearsay as “it was thus,” but directly experienced by oneself. This is the meaning. ‘Knowing which, one fares on mindfully’ means: having known that peace by means of the noble path, faring on mindfully in accordance with the principle, “All formations are impermanent,” etc. ‘One should cross over attachment in the world’ means: one should cross, one should completely overcome craving, which is called ‘attachment’ because it spreads in the world of formations. This is the meaning.

Tañcāhaṃ abhinandāmīti taṃ vuttappakāraṃ santijotakaṃ tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ ahaṃ patthayāmi, taṃ eva vā santiṃ uttamaṃ abhinandāmīti dhotako vadati. Uddhaṃ adho tiriyañcāpi majjheti ettha uddhanti anāgataṃ upari ca. Adhoti atītaṃ heṭṭhā ca. Tiriyañcāpi majjheti paccuppannaṃ parito ca. Etaṃ viditvā saṅgotīti etaṃ anāgatādiṃ saṅgajananaṭṭhānanti ñatvā. Bhavābhavāyāti khuddakānañceva mahantānañca bhavānaṃ atthāya, sassatucchedāya vā.

‘And that I rejoice in’ means: I desire your words which illuminate peace in the manner described; or, I rejoice in that supreme peace itself. Thus Dhotaka speaks. In the text ‘Above, below, across, and also in the middle’: ‘above’ means the future and the upward direction. ‘Below’ means the past and the downward direction. ‘Across and also in the middle’ means the present and all around. ‘Having known this, it is attachment’ means: having known this—the future and so on—as a basis for the generation of attachment. ‘For existence and non-existence’ means: for the sake of minor and major existences, or for the sake of eternalism and annihilationism.

Ariyasaccānanti [M 0.0253] ariyabhāvakarānaṃ saccānaṃ. Ananubodhāti abujjhanena ajānanena. Appaṭivedhāti [V 0.0369] appaṭivijjhanena. Sandhāvitanti bhavato bhavassa gamanena sandhāvitaṃ. Saṃsaritanti punappunaṃ gamanavasena saṃsaritaṃ. Mamañceva tumhākañcāti mayā ceva tumhehi ca. Atha vā sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritanti sandhāvanaṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ mamañceva tumhākañca ahosīti attho. Bhavanettīti bhavābhavaṃ nayanasamatthā taṇhārajju. Saṃsitanti saṃsaritaṃ. Samūhatāti suṭṭhu hatā chinnā appavattikatā.

`Ariyasaccānaṃ` means: of the truths that make one noble. `Ananubodhā` means: through not awakening, through not knowing. `Appaṭivedhā` means: through not penetrating. `Sandhāvitaṃ` means: it has been run through by going from existence to existence. `Saṃsaritaṃ` means: it has been transmigrated by way of going again and again. `Mamañceva tumhākañca` means: by me and by you. Alternatively, `sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ` means: the running through and transmigrating of both me and you has occurred. This is the meaning. `Bhavanettī` means: the rope of craving, capable of leading to minor and major existences. `Saṃsitaṃ` means: it has been transmigrated. `Samūhatā` means: well destroyed, cut off, rendered unable to occur again.

Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccāti paccayehi saṅkharīyantīti “saṅkhārā”ti laddhanāmā pañcakkhandhā. Ādiantavantato aniccantikato tāvakālikato khaṇaparittato ca na niccāti aniccā. Yadā paññāya passatīti yadā vipassanāpaññāya passati. Atha imasmiṃ vaṭṭadukkhe nibbindati, nibbindanto dukkhaparijānanādivasena saccāni paṭivijjhati. Esa maggo visuddhiyāti yvāyaṃ vuttanayena saccappaṭivedho, esa visuddhatthāya maggo. Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhāti sabbe saṅkhārā abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena khayaṭṭhena ca dukkhāti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Sabbe dhammā anattāti sabbepi tebhūmakadhammā parato tucchato suññato asārato avasavattanato ca anattāti. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

`Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā` means: the five aggregates, which have obtained the name "formations" because they are formed by conditions. They are not permanent, and thus are impermanent, because they have a beginning and an end, because they have an impermanent aspect, because they are temporary, and because they have a short moment. `Yadā paññāya passati` means: when one sees with insight-wisdom. Then one becomes disenchanted with this suffering of the round. Becoming disenchanted, one penetrates the truths by way of fully understanding suffering and so on. `Esa maggo visuddhiyā` means: this penetration of the truths in the manner described, this is the path for the sake of purity. `Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā` means: all formations are suffering in the sense of constant oppression and in the sense of perishing. The rest is as stated. `Sabbe dhammā anattā` means: all phenomena of the three planes are not-self because they are other, empty, void, without substance, and not subject to one's will. The rest is similar to the foregoing.

Seyyoti visiṭṭho uttamo. Sadisoti samāno. Hīnoti lāmako. Omānopi hi attano avaṅkaraṇamukhenapi saṃpaggaṇhanavaseneva pavattati. Tena vuttaṃ “hīnohamasmī”ti. Kimaññatra yathābhūtassa adassanāti sarasapabhaṅgutāya ekanteneva anavaṭṭhitasabhāvehi rūpadhammehi seyyādivasena attano ukkhipanassa tesaṃ yathābhūtaṃ adassanaṃ aññāṇaṃ vinā kiṃ aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ siyā, aññaṃ kiñci kāraṇaṃ tassa natthīti attho. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

`Seyyo` means: distinguished, excellent. `Sadiso` means: similar. `Hīno` means: lowly. Indeed, even self-deprecation proceeds only by way of upholding oneself through the means of making oneself lowly. Therefore, it is said, 'I am inferior.' Regarding the text 'What else other than not seeing things as they really are?': For the elevating of oneself by way of being superior, etc., through material phenomena which are by nature utterly unstable due to their inherent fragility, what other cause could there be apart from not seeing them as they really are—that is, ignorance? There is no other cause for it. This is the meaning. This same method applies to feelings and so forth. The bright side should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.

115. Ye ariyasaccāni vibhāvayantīti dukkhādīni ariyasaccāni paññāobhāsena saccappaṭicchādakakilesandhakāraṃ vidhametvā attano pakāsāni pākaṭāni karonti. Gambhīrapaññenāti appameyyapaññatāya sadevakassapi lokassa ñāṇena alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhapaññena sabbaññunāti vuttaṃ [M 0.0254] hoti. Sudesitānīti saṅkhepavitthārādīhi tehi tehi nayehi suṭṭhu desitāni. Kiñcāpi te honti bhusaṃ pamattāti te vibhāvitaariyasaccā puggalā kāmaṃ devarajjacakkavattirajjādipamādaṭṭhānaṃ āgamma bhusaṃ pamattā honti, tathāpi sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena ṭhapetvā satta bhave anamatagge saṃsāre ye [V 0.0370] uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca, tesaṃ niruddhattā na aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ ādiyanti, sattamabhaveyeva pana vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇantīti attho.

115. `Ye ariyasaccāni vibhāvayanti` means: they, with the light of wisdom, dispel the darkness of defilements that conceals the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth, making them manifest and evident to themselves. `Gambhīrapaññena` means: due to immeasurable wisdom, with wisdom whose foundation cannot be obtained even by the knowledge of the world with its gods, he is called the 'All-Knower.' `Sudesitāni` means: well-taught by those various methods, such as the concise and the detailed. Regarding `Kiñcāpi te honti bhusaṃ pamattā`: Those persons who have made the Noble Truths manifest may indeed become greatly heedless, having come to a cause of heedlessness such as divine kingship or universal sovereignty. Nevertheless, through the cessation of the consciousness of formations by the knowledge of the stream-entry path, setting aside seven existences, they do not take up an eighth existence, because of the cessation of that name-and-form which would have arisen in the beginningless round of rebirth. Rather, in the seventh existence itself, having undertaken insight meditation, they attain Arahantship. This is the meaning.

Yathindakhīloti ettha yathāti upamāvacanaṃ. Indakhīloti nagaradvārathirakaraṇatthaṃ ummārabbhantare aṭṭha vā dasa vā hatthe pathaviṃ khaṇitvā ākoṭitassa sāradārumayassa thambhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pathavissito siyāti gambhīranemitāya anto pavisitvā bhūminissito siyā bhaveyya. Catubbhi vātehīti catūhi disāhi āgatavātehi. Asampakampiyoti kampetuṃ vā cāletuṃ vā asakkuṇeyyo. Tathūpamaṃ…pe… passatīti yo cattāri ariyasaccāni paññāya ajjhogāhetvā passati, taṃ sappurisaṃ uttamapurisaṃ tathā dassanato sabbatitthiyavādavātehi asampakampiyatāya tathūpamaṃ yathāvuttaindakhīlūpamaṃ vadāmīti attho.

In the phrase `Yathindakhīlo`, the word `yathā` is a term of comparison. `Indakhīlo` is a designation for a pillar made of heartwood, planted in a hole dug eight or ten cubits deep into the earth inside the threshold for the purpose of making the city gate firm. `Pathavissito siyā` means: having entered deep due to its deep foundation, it would be founded on the earth. `Catubbhi vātehi` means: by the winds coming from the four directions. `Asampakampiyo` means: unable to be made to tremble or to be moved. `Tathūpamaṃ… passati` means: whoever, having penetrated the Four Noble Truths with wisdom, sees them—that good person, that supreme person, because of seeing thus and due to being unshakeable by the winds of the doctrines of all sectarians, I declare to be of such a comparison, comparable to the aforementioned city-gate pillar. This is the meaning.

Sotāpattiyaṅgehīti ariyasotāpajjanassa aṅgabhūtehi. Ariyasāvakoti ariyassa buddhassa bhagavato saddhammassavanante jātattā ariyasāvako. Khīṇanirayomhīti khīṇanirayo amhi. Khīṇāpāyaduggativinipātoti idaṃ nirayādīnaṃyeva vevacanavasena vuttaṃ. Nirayādayo hi vaḍḍhisaṅkhātato ayato apetattā apāyā. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggatiyo. Dukkaṭakārino vivasā ettha nipatantīti vinipātā. Sotaṃ ariyamaggaṃ ādito patto adhigatoti sotāpanno. Akuppadhammatāya maggaphalānaṃ puthujjanabhāvasaṅkhāte virūpe na nipatanasabhāvoti avinipātadhammo. Tato eva dhammaniyāmena niyatatāya niyato. Uparimaggattayasaṅkhātā sambodhi avassaṃ pattabbatāya assa paraṃ ayanaṃ gati paṭisaraṇanti sambodhiparāyaṇo.

`Sotāpattiyaṅgehi` means: by the factors that constitute noble stream-attainment. `Ariyasāvako` is so called because one is born at the end of listening to the True Dhamma of the noble Buddha, the Blessed One. `Khīṇanirayomhi` means: 'I am one whose hell is exhausted.' `Khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto` is said by way of synonyms for hell and so forth. Indeed, hell and the other states are called 'planes of loss' (apāyā) because they are devoid of benefit, which is known as 'increase' (aya). They are 'bad destinations' (duggatiyo) because they are a destination and resort for suffering. They are 'the abyss' (vinipātā) because evil-doers, being helpless, fall into them. One is a 'stream-enterer' (sotāpanno) because one has first reached and attained the stream, which is the noble path. One is 'of an un-falling nature' (avinipātadhammo) because, due to the unshakeable nature of the path and fruit, one does not have the nature of falling into the contrary state known as the state of a worldling. For that very reason, one is 'fixed' (niyato) due to being fixed by the fixed principle of the Dhamma. One is 'bound for enlightenment' (sambodhiparāyaṇo) because enlightenment, known as the triad of higher paths, is inevitably to be attained and is for that person the supreme destination, goal, and resort.

Niviṭṭhātiādīni padāni aññamaññavevacanāneva. Sahadhammiyāti sabrahmacārino. Ariyakantehīti ariyānaṃ kantehi piyehi manāpehi. Pañca sīlāni [M 0.0255] hi ariyasāvakānaṃ kantāni honti, bhavantarepi avijahanato. Tāni sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbopi panettha saṃvaro labbhatiyeva. Sotāpannohamasmīti idaṃ desanāsīsameva. Sakadāgāmiādayopi “sakadāgāmīhamasmī”tiādinā nayena byākarontiyeva. Yato sabbesampi sikkhāpadāvirodhena yuttaṭṭhāne byākaraṇaṃ anuññātamevāti.

The words 'established' and so on are merely synonyms for one another. 'With fellow practitioners' means with those who share the holy life. 'By what is dear to the noble ones' means by what is liked, dear, and pleasing to the noble ones. Indeed, the five precepts are dear to noble disciples because they are not abandoned even in another existence. This was said with reference to them. Nevertheless, in this case, all restraint is indeed obtained. This statement, 'I am a stream-enterer,' is simply the pinnacle of the teaching. Indeed, once-returners and others also declare by the method of 'I am a once-returner,' and so forth. This is because for all of them, a declaration in a suitable situation, without contradicting the training rules, is indeed permitted.

Yassindriyānīti yassa ariyapuggalassa saddhādīni indriyāni. Subhāvitānīti ariyamaggabhāvanāvasena suṭṭhu bhāvitāni. Ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā cāti orambhāgiyānaṃ uddhambhāgiyānañca [V 0.0371] saṃyojanānaṃ pajahanavasena. Tenāha “sabbaloke”ti. Nibbijjhāti nibbijjhitvā paṭivijjhitvā.

'Whose faculties' means the faculties, such as faith and so forth, of whichever noble person. 'Are well-developed' means they are well-developed by means of the cultivation of the noble path. 'Internally and externally' refers to the faculties being well-developed by means of abandoning the lower and higher fetters. Therefore, he said, 'in all the world.' 'Having penetrated' means having pierced and penetrated.

Dhammapadānīti dhammakoṭṭhāsāni. Anabhijjhā dhammapadaṃ nāma alobho vā alobhasīsena adhigatajhānavipassanāmaggaphalanibbānāni vā dasaasubhavasena vā adhigatajhānādīni anabhijjhā dhammapadaṃ. Catubrahmavihāravasena adhigatāni abyāpādo dhammapadaṃ. Dasānussatiāhārepaṭikkūlasaññāvasena adhigatāni sammāsati dhammapadaṃ. Dasakasiṇaānāpānavasena adhigatāni sammāsamādhi dhammapadaṃ.

'Portions of the Dhamma' means sections of the Dhamma. Non-covetousness is called a portion of the Dhamma; this can be non-greed, or the jhāna, insight, path, fruit, and Nibbāna attained with non-greed as the head, or the jhānas and so forth attained by means of the ten kinds of foulness meditation. Non-ill will is a portion of the Dhamma; this refers to the states attained by means of the four divine abidings. Right mindfulness is a portion of the Dhamma; this refers to the states attained by means of the ten recollections and the perception of loathsomeness in food. Right concentration is a portion of the Dhamma; this refers to the states attained by means of the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing.

Pañca chindeti heṭṭhā apāyupapattisaṃvattanikāni pañca orambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni pāde baddharajjuṃ viya puriso satthena heṭṭhā maggattayena chindeyya. Pañca jaheti uparidevalokasampāpakāni pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni puriso gīvāya baddharajjuṃ viya arahattamaggena jaheyya chindeyyevāti attho. Pañca cuttari bhāvayeti uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ pahānatthāya saddhādīni pañcindriyāni uttari bhāveyya. Pañca saṅgātigoti evaṃ sante pañcannaṃ rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhisaṅgānaṃ atikkamanena pañcasaṅgātigo hutvā bhikkhu “oghatiṇṇo”ti vuccati, nittiṇṇacaturoghoti vuccatīti attho.

One should cut off five: the five lower fetters, which cause rebirth in the lower realms, should be cut off by means of the three lower paths, just as a man would cut a rope tied to his foot with a knife. One should abandon five: the five higher fetters, which lead to the upper celestial realms, should be abandoned by means of the path of Arahantship, just as a man would cut a rope tied to his neck; this is the meaning: one should cut them off. One should develop five further: for the sake of abandoning the higher fetters, one should further develop the five faculties, beginning with faith. One who has gone beyond the five attachments: this being so, by overcoming the five attachments—lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wrong views—and having become one who has gone beyond the five attachments, the monk is called 'one who has crossed the flood.' This is the meaning: he is called 'one who has crossed the four floods'.

Anaññātaṃ appaṭividdhaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ, amatapadaṃyeva vā ñassāmi jānissāmīti paṭipannassa paṭhamamaggaṭṭhassa indriyanti anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ. Paṭhamamaggañāṇañhi taṃpubbabhāgavasena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ājānāti paṭhamamaggena ñātamariyādaṃ anatikkamitvā jānātīti añño, tassa indriyanti aññindriyaṃ, heṭṭhā tīsu phalesu, upari tīsu maggesu ca ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aññātāvino catūsu saccesu niṭṭhitakiccassa arahato [M 0.0256] indriyanti aññātāvindriyaṃ, aggaphalañāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Anabhisametassāti appaṭividdhassa. Abhisamayāyāti paṭivedhāya.

The faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is the faculty of one who is practicing, established in the first path, with the thought, 'I shall know, I shall understand the Dhamma of the Four Truths, which is not yet known, not yet penetrated, or the deathless state itself.' Indeed, the first path-knowledge is so called in terms of its preliminary stage. 'He knows' (ājānāti) means he knows without transgressing the limit known through the first path; thus, he is a 'knower' (añña). His faculty is the faculty of knowing (aññindriya). This is a designation for the knowledge that occurs in the three lower fruitions and the three higher paths. The faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) is the faculty of the Arahant, who has known and whose task is finished with regard to the Four Truths. This is a designation for the knowledge of the highest fruition. 'Of one who has not fully understood' (anabhisametassa) means of one who has not penetrated. 'For full understanding' (abhisamayāya) means for penetration.

116. Bālalakkhaṇānīti bālassa upalakkhaṇakāraṇāni. Bālanimittānīti “bālo aya”nti gahetuṃ nimittāni kāraṇāni. Bālāpadānānīti bālassa porāṇāni viruḷhāni kammāni. “Duccintitacintī”tiādīsu duccintitaṃ abhijjhaṃ byāpādaṃ micchādassanañca cintetīti [V 0.0372] duccintitacintī. Dubbhāsitaṃ musāvādādiṃ bhāsatīti dubbhāsitabhāsī. Dukkaṭaṃ pāṇātipātādikammaṃ karotīti dukkaṭakammakārī. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

116. 'Characteristics of a fool' (bālalakkhaṇāni) means the causes for recognizing a fool. 'Signs of a fool' (bālanimittāni) means the signs, the causes for grasping, 'This is a fool.' 'Deeds of a fool' (bālāpadānāni) means the fool's ancient, developed actions. In 'one who thinks ill-thought thoughts' (duccintitacintī) and so on, he thinks an ill-thought thought, which is covetousness, ill will, and wrong view; thus, he is 'one who thinks ill-thought thoughts.' He speaks ill-spoken speech (dubbhāsita), such as false speech and so on; thus, he is 'one who speaks ill-spoken speech' (dubbhāsitabhāsī). He does an ill-done deed (dukkaṭa), an action such as killing living beings and so on; thus, he is 'one who does ill-done deeds' (dukkaṭakammakārī). The bright side should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been said.

Bhiyyoti uparūpari. Pakujjheyyunti virujjheyyuṃ. “Pakuppeyyu”ntipi pāṭho. Bhusenāti daḷhena. Daṇḍenāti daṇḍadānena. Dhīroti paṇḍito sappaññajātiko. Nisedhayeti paṭibāheyya. Puna kiñci kātuṃ vattuṃ vā asamatthaṃ kareyyāti attho.

'Further' (bhiyyo) means again and again. 'They would become angry' (pakujjheyyuṃ) means they would be hostile. There is also the reading 'pakuppeyyuṃ'. 'Strongly' (bhusena) means severely. 'With punishment' (daṇḍena) means by the giving of punishment. 'A wise person' (dhīro) means a learned person, one of an intelligent nature. 'He should prevent' (nisedhaye) means he should ward off. The meaning is: he should make him unable to do or say anything further.

Paranti paccatthikaṃ. Yo sato upasammatīti yo satimā hutvā upasammati, tassa upasamaṃyevāhaṃ bālassa paṭisedhanaṃ maññāmīti attho.

'Another' (paraṃ) means an enemy. The meaning of 'Who, being mindful, is calm' (yo sato upasammatī) is: one who, having become mindful, is calm; I consider his very calmness to be the prevention of the fool.

Vajjanti dosaṃ. Yadā naṃ maññatīti yasmā naṃ maññati. Ajjhāruhatīti ajjhottharati. Gova bhiyyo palāyinanti yathā goyūthe tāvadeva dve gāvo yujjhante gogaṇo olokento tiṭṭhati yāva na eko palāyati, yadā pana palāyati, atha taṃ palāyīnaṃ sabbo gogaṇo bhiyyo ajjhottharati, evaṃ dummedho khamantaṃ bhiyyo ajjhottharatīti attho.

'Fault' (vajjaṃ) means a fault (dosaṃ). 'When one thinks of him' (yadā naṃ maññati) means 'because one thinks of him' (yasmā naṃ maññati). 'He mounts upon' (ajjhāruhati) means he overwhelms (ajjhottharati). The meaning of 'like a cow, further, to one who flees' (gova bhiyyo palāyinaṃ) is: just as in a herd of cattle, while two cows are fighting, the herd stands watching only as long as one does not flee; but when one does flee, then the entire herd further overwhelms that fleeing one. So too, a person of little wisdom further overwhelms one who is patient.

Sadatthaparamāti sakatthaparamā. Khantyā bhiyyo na vijjatīti tesu sakatthaparamesu atthesu khantito uttaritaro añño attho na vijjati. Tamāhu paramaṃ khantinti yo balavā titikkhati, tassa taṃ khantiṃ paramaṃ āhu. Bālabalaṃ nāma aññāṇabalaṃ. Taṃ yassa balaṃ, abalameva taṃ, na taṃ balanti āhu kathenti dīpenti. Dhammaguttassāti dhammena rakkhitassa dhammaṃ vā rakkhantassa. Paṭivattāti paṭippharitvā vattā, paṭipparitvā vā yaṃ vā taṃ vā vadeyyāsi. Dhammaṭṭhaṃ pana cāletuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Tasseva tena pāpiyoti tena kodhena tasseva puggalassa pāpaṃ hoti. Katarassāti[M 0.0257]? Yo kuddhaṃ paṭikujjhati, tassa. Tattha kuddhanti sampadāne upayogavacanaṃ, kuddhassāti attho. Tikicchantānanti ekavacane bahuvacanaṃ, tikicchantanti attho. Janā maññantīti evarūpaṃ attano ca parassa cāti ubhinnaṃ atthaṃ tikicchantaṃ nipphādentaṃ puggalaṃ “bālo aya”nti andhabālaputhujjanā evaṃ maññanti. Ye dhammassa akovidāti ye catusaccadhamme akovidā acchekā, te evaṃ maññantīti attho.

'Having one's own welfare as supreme' (sadatthaparamā) means one's own welfare is supreme. 'There is nothing greater than patience' (khantyā bhiyyo na vijjati) means: among those benefits where one's own welfare is supreme, there exists no other benefit more excellent than patience. 'That they call the supreme patience' (tamāhu paramaṃ khantiṃ) means: he who is strong and endures—his patience they call supreme. The strength of a fool (bālabalaṃ) is called the strength of ignorance. For whomever that is strength, it is truly no strength at all; they do not call it, speak of it, or show it to be strength. 'Of one protected by Dhamma' (dhammaguttassa) means of one protected by the Dhamma, or of one who protects the Dhamma. 'A respondent' (paṭivattā) means one who can speak having overcome; or, having overcome, you might say whatever you please, but there is no one capable of shaking one who is established in the Dhamma. 'For him, through that, it is worse' (tasseva tena pāpiyo) means: through that anger, evil comes to that very person. To whom? To the one who gets angry in return at an angry person. Here, in the word 'kuddhaṃ', the accusative case is used in the sense of the dative; the meaning is 'to an angry person' (kuddhassa). 'Of those who are curing' (tikicchantānaṃ) is a plural form used for a singular; the meaning is 'one who is curing'. 'People think' (janā maññanti) means: blind, foolish worldlings think of such a person who is accomplishing the welfare of both himself and others, 'This is a fool.' 'Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma' (ye dhammassa akovidā) means: those people who are not skilled, not expert in the Dhamma of the Four Truths, they think in this way. This is the meaning.

117. Pattanti adhigataṃ etarahi anubhuyyamānaṃ kāmūpakaraṇaṃ pattabbanti tadeva anāgate adhigantabbaṃ anubhavitabbaṃ, ubhayametaṃ rajānukiṇṇanti tadubhayampi rāgarajādīhi avakiṇṇaṃ[V 0.0373]. Āturassāti rāgādikilesāturassa. Anusikkhatoti kilesabahulapuggale anusikkhato. Ye ca sikkhāsārāti ye yathāsamādinnaṃ sīlavatādisaṅkhātaṃ sikkhaṃ sārato gahetvā ṭhitā. Tenāha – “sīlaṃ vataṃ jīvitaṃ brahmacariya”nti. Tattha yaṃ “na karomī”ti oramati, taṃ sīlaṃ. Yaṃ vesabhojanakiccacaraṇādi, taṃ vataṃ. Jīvitanti ājīvo. Brahmacariyanti methunavirati. Upaṭṭhānasārāti etesaṃ sīlādīnaṃ anuṭṭhānasārā. Etehi eva saṃsārasuddhīti tāni sārato gahetvā ṭhitāti attho.

117. 'Attained' (pattaṃ) means the equipment for sensual pleasure that has been obtained and is now being experienced. 'To be attained' (pattabbaṃ) means that very same equipment that is to be obtained and experienced in the future. 'Both these are strewn with dust' (ubhayametaṃ rajānukiṇṇaṃ) means both of these are strewn with the dust of lust and so on. 'Of one who is afflicted' (āturassa) means of one afflicted by the defilements of lust and so on. 'Following' (anusikkhato) means following a person full of defilements. 'And those who take training as the essence' (ye ca sikkhāsārā) are those who, having undertaken the training known as virtue, observances, and so on, as prescribed, stand firm by taking its essence. Therefore it is said: 'virtue, observance, life, and the holy life.' Therein, that from which one refrains with the thought, 'I will not do it,' that is virtue (sīla). That which is the practice of eating like a dog, difficult conduct, and so on, that is an observance (vata). 'Life' (jīvitaṃ) means livelihood (ājīvo). 'The holy life' (brahmacariyaṃ) means abstinence from sexual intercourse. 'Taking attendance as the essence' (upaṭṭhānasārā) means they take the repeated practice of these things—virtue and so on—as the essence. The meaning is: thinking, 'Purification from saṃsāra comes through these alone,' they stand firm, having taken them as the essence.

Iccete ubho antāti iti sīlabbataparāmāsamukhena attakilamathānuyogo, kāmesu anavajjasaññitāmukhena kāmasukhallikānuyogo cāti ete ubho antā. Te ca kho yathākkamaṃ āyatiṃ pattabbe, etarahi patte ca rāgarajādiokiṇṇe kāmaguṇe allīnehi kilesāturānaṃ anusikkhantehi, sayañca kilesātureheva paṭipajjitabbā, tato eva ca te kaṭasivaḍḍhanā aparāparaṃ jarāmaraṇehi sivathikāya vaḍḍhanasīlā ekanteneva kaṭasiṃ vaḍḍhenti, sayaṃ vaḍḍhantā pare ca antadvaye samādapentā vaḍḍhāpenti cāti attho.

Thus, these are the two extremes: the practice of self-mortification by way of adherence to rules and observances, and the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasures by way of the perception of blamelessness in sensual pleasures. These are the two extremes. And these, respectively, are to be practiced by those who imitate the ones afflicted with defilements who are attached to sensual qualities—sullied by the dust of lust and so on, to be attained in the future and attained in the present—and by those who are themselves afflicted with defilements. For that very reason, they increase the charnel ground; being of a nature to increase the cemetery through aging and death again and again, they exclusively increase the charnel ground. The meaning is that while they themselves increase it, they also establish others in the two extremes and cause them to increase it.

Ubho ante anabhiññāyāti yathāvutte ubho ante ajānitvā. Olīyanti eketi “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti olīyanataṇhābhinivesavasena avalīyanti ekacce. Atidhāvanti eketi ekacce – “ucchijjati vinassati attā ca loko cā”ti atidhāvanābhinivesavasena atikkamanti.

'Not having fully known both extremes' means not having known both extremes as stated. Some fall short: some shrink back by way of the adherence of craving for existence and the view of existence that causes clinging, thinking, 'The self and the world are eternal.' Some overshoot: some transgress by way of the adherence of the annihilationist view that overshoots, thinking, 'The self and the world are annihilated and perish.'

Na [M 0.0258] amaññiṃsu tesañca taṇhādimaññanānaṃ pahīnattā. Tato eva anupādāparinibbānato tividhampi vaṭṭaṃ tesaṃ paññāpanāya natthīti.

They did not conceive, because their conceivings of craving and so on were abandoned. Because of that very attainment of parinibbāna without clinging, there is no designation of the threefold round for them.

Jaññāti jāneyya. Saṃyujeti saṃyojeyya. Mānusanti manussānaṃ idanti mānusaṃ, manussabhavapariyāpannaṃ. Kiñhi tassa sakaṃ hotīti tassa maccumukhaṃ pavisantassa sattassa kiṃ aññaṃ sakaṃ nāma aññatra kalyāṇakammato. Kammassakā hi sattā. Tenāha – “tasmā kareyya kalyāṇa”ntiādi. Tattha samparāyikanti samparāyaphalanibbattakaṃ.

'One should know' (jaññā) means one would know. 'One should unite' (saṃyuje) means one would unite. 'Human' (mānusaṃ): this belongs to humans, thus it is 'human'; it is included in human existence. For what is his own? For a being entering the mouth of death, what else is his own apart from good kamma? For beings are owners of their kamma. Hence it is said: 'Therefore one should do good,' and so on. Therein, 'for the future life' (samparāyikaṃ) means productive of a result in the future life.

118. Ime dhammāti ime kusalā vā akusalā vā dhammā. Evaṃgahitāti evaṃ samādinnā [V 0.0374] uppāditā. Idaṃ phalanti idaṃ iṭṭhavipākaṃ aniṭṭhavipākañca phalaṃ. Ayamatthoti ayaṃ vuḍḍhi, ayaṃ hānīti attho. Aññampi evaṃjātiyanti ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyaṃ vadati.

118. 'These phenomena' means these wholesome or unwholesome phenomena. 'Thus grasped' means thus undertaken, thus generated. 'This is the fruit' means this is the desirable and undesirable result as fruit. 'This is the meaning' means: this is growth, this is decline. 'Also other things of this kind' means he speaks of what is to be answered categorically.

Ākaṅkhato na jāneyyunti tattha yena hetunā bhagavato yā ākaṅkhā, sā aññesaṃ avisayoti āha – “kintaṃ bhagavā ākaṅkhatīti. Idaṃ avisajjanīya”nti.

Regarding 'They would not know of the aspiring one' (Ākaṅkhato na jāneyyuṃ): therein, for the reason that the Blessed One's aspiration is beyond the range of others, he said: 'What does the Blessed One aspire to? This is a question not to be answered.'

Ettakoti etaparimāṇo. Sīlakkhandheti sīlakkhandhahetu. “Sīlakkhandhenā”tipi pāṭho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Iriyāyanti kāyavacīsamācāre. Pabhāveti ānubhāve. Hitesitāyanti mettāya. Iddhiyanti iddhividhāya. Ettakā buddhaguṇā, te ca paccekaṃ evaṃpabhāvā. Tathā maggaphalanibbānāni evamānubhāvāni. Ariyasaṅgho evaṃvidhaguṇehi yuttoti.

'So much' (ettako) means of such a measure. 'In the aggregate of virtue' (sīlakkhandhe) means on account of the aggregate of virtue. 'By the aggregate of virtue' (sīlakkhandhena) is also a reading. This same method applies to the remaining terms. 'In deportment' (iriyāyaṃ) means on account of bodily and verbal conduct. 'In power' (pabhāve) means on account of influence. 'In desire for welfare' (hitesitāyaṃ) means on account of loving-kindness. 'In psychic power' (iddhiyaṃ) means on account of the kinds of psychic power. The Buddha's qualities are of such a measure, and each one individually is of such power. Similarly, the path, fruits, and Nibbāna are of such influence. The noble Sangha is endowed with such kinds of qualities.

Tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ mahānubhāvatā na sabbathā aññesaṃ visayo, bhagavato eva visayoti āha – “buddhavisayo avisajjanīyo”ti. Tena yo aññopi attho buddhavisayo, so avisajjanīyoti dasseti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “buddhavisayo acinteyyo na cintetabbo, yaṃ cintento ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77). Katamā pubbā koṭīti avisajjanīyanti “katamā pubbā koṭī”ti kenaci kataṃ pucchanaṃ avisajjanīyaṃ. Kasmā? Saṃsārassa purimāya koṭiyā abhāvato. Tenevāha – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyatī”ti (a. ni. 10.61). Tattha na paññāyatīti [M 0.0259] na dissati, na upalabbhatīti attho. Na paññāyatīti aññassa ñāṇavisayo na hotīti pana atthaṃ sandhāya “na paññāyatīti sāvakānaṃ ñāṇavekallenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha attūpanāyikāti attā upanetabbo etissāti attūpanāyikā. Natthi buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ avijānanāti etena purimāya koṭiyā abhāvato eva na paññāyati, na tattha ñāṇassa paṭighātoti dasseti.

The great power of the Three Jewels is not in every way the range of others, but is the range of the Blessed One alone; therefore he says: 'The range of a Buddha is a question not to be answered.' By this he shows that whatever other matter is the range of a Buddha, that is a question not to be answered. For this has been said by the Blessed One: 'The range of a Buddha is an inconceivable that should not be conceived, which if one conceived of it, one would be a partaker of madness and vexation.' 'What is the first point?' is a question not to be answered. The question 'What is the first point?' asked by someone is a question not to be answered. Why? Because of the non-existence of a first point of saṃsāra. Hence he said: 'Bhikkhus, a first point is not discerned.' Therein, 'is not discerned' means it is not seen, it is not found. However, with reference to the meaning that 'is not discerned' means it is not the range of another's knowledge, it is said: '"is not discerned" because of the disciples' deficiency in knowledge,' and so on. Therein, 'to be applied to oneself' (attūpanāyikā) means that oneself is to be brought to this teaching. By the words 'There is no not-knowing for the Blessed Buddhas,' he shows that it is not discerned simply because of the non-existence of a first point, not that there is any obstruction to his knowledge there.

Yaṃ pana atthi, taṃ aññesaṃ appameyyampi bhagavato na appameyyanti bhagavato sabbattha appaṭihataññāṇataṃ dassetuṃ “yathā bhagavā kokālikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbhā”tiādimāha. Tattha aññataraṃ bhikkhunti nāmagottena apākaṭaṃ. “Kīva dīghaṃ nu kho, bhante, padume niraye āyuppamāṇa”nti pañhaṃ pucchitvā nisinnaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ evamāhāti. Etthāyaṃ pāṭhaseso – dīghaṃ kho, bhikkhu, padume niraye āyuppamāṇaṃ, taṃ na sukaraṃ saṅkhātuṃ “ettakāni vassānī”ti vā “ettakāni vassasatānī”ti vā “ettakāni vassasahassānī”ti vā “ettakāni [V 0.0375] vassasatasahassānī”ti vāti. Sakkā pana, bhante, upamā kātunti. “Sakkā bhikkhū”ti bhagavā avoca. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhu, vīsatikhāriko kosalako tilavāho. Tato puriso vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena ekamekaṃ tilaṃ uddhareyya. Khippataraṃ kho so, bhikkhu, vīsatikhāriko kosalako tilavāho iminā upakkamena parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya, na tveva eko abbudo nirayo. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhu, vīsati abbudā nirayā, evameko nirabbudo nirayotiādi (saṃ. ni. 1.181; a. ni. 10.89; su. ni. kokālikasutta).

But whatever exists, though it may be immeasurable to others, is not immeasurable to the Blessed One. To show the Blessed One's unobstructed knowledge in all respects, he said: 'As the Blessed One, concerning the bhikkhu Kokālika,' and so on. Therein, 'a certain bhikkhu' means one not specified by name and clan. He spoke thus to a certain bhikkhu who was seated after asking the question: 'Venerable sir, for how long is the measure of the lifespan in the Paduma hell?' Herein, this is the remainder of the text: 'Long, O bhikkhu, is the lifespan in the Paduma hell. It is not easy to reckon it as “so many years,” or “so many hundreds of years,” or “so many thousands of years,” or “so many hundreds of thousands of years.”' 'But is it possible, venerable sir, to make a simile?' 'It is possible, bhikkhu,' the Blessed One said. 'Suppose, bhikkhu, there were a Kosalan cartload of twenty khāris of sesame seeds. From that a man would remove one sesame seed at the passing of every hundred years. That Kosalan cartload of twenty khāris of sesame seeds would by this endeavor be more quickly exhausted and consumed than a single Abbuda hell. Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Abbuda hells, so there is one Nirabbuda hell,' and so on.

Tattha vīsatikhārikoti māgadhakena patthena cattāro patthā kosalaraṭṭhe eko pattho hoti. Tena patthena cattāro patthā āḷhakaṃ, cattāri āḷhakāni doṇaṃ, catudoṇā mānikā, catumānikā khārī. Tāya khāriyā vīsatikhāriko tilavāho. Tilavāhoti tilasakaṭaṃ. Abbudo nirayoti abbudo nāma eko paccekanirayo natthi, avīcimhi eva pana abbudagaṇanāya paccanokāso “abbudo nirayo”ti vutto. Esa nayo nirabbudādīsupi.

Therein, regarding 'of twenty khāris': by the Magadhan measure, four patthas are one pattha in the Kosalan country. By that pattha, four patthas are an āḷhaka, four āḷhakas are a doṇa, four doṇas are a mānikā, and four mānikās are a khārī. By that khārī, twenty khāris is a cartload of sesame. 'A cartload of sesame' means a cart of sesame. Regarding 'Abbuda hell': there is no separate hell named Abbuda, but rather in Avīci itself, a place for being cooked for the duration of an abbuda reckoning is called the 'Abbuda hell.' This is the method also in the case of Nirabbuda and so on.

Tattha vassagaṇanāpi evaṃ veditabbā – yathā hi sataṃsatasahassāni koṭi hoti. Evaṃ sataṃsatasahassakoṭiyo pakoṭi nāma. Sataṃsatasahassapakoṭiyo [M 0.0260] koṭipakoṭi nāma. Sataṃsatasahassakoṭipakoṭiyo nahutaṃ. Sataṃsatasahassanahutāni ninnahutaṃ. Sataṃsatasahassāni ninnahutāni eko abbudo. Tato vīsatiguṇo nirabbudo. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ayañca gaṇanā aparicitānaṃ dukkarāti vuttaṃ – “taṃ na sukaraṃ saṅkhātu”nti. Keci pana “tattha tattha paridevanānattena kammakāraṇanānattenapi imāni nāmāni laddhānī”ti vadanti. Apare “sītanarakā ete”ti. Cittaṃ āghātetvāti cittaṃ padūsetvā.

Therein, the reckoning of years should also be understood thus: just as a hundred hundred-thousands is a koṭi, so a hundred hundred-thousands of koṭis is called a pakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousands of pakoṭis is a koṭipakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousands of koṭipakoṭis is a nahuta; a hundred hundred-thousands of nahutas is a ninnahuta; a hundred hundred-thousands of ninnahutas is one abbuda. Twenty times that is a nirabbuda. This is the method in all cases. And since this calculation is difficult for the unacquainted, it was said: 'It is not easy to reckon it.' Some, however, say: 'These names were obtained because of the diversity of lamentation in those places and also because of the diversity of the torment.' Others say: 'These are cold hells.' 'Having struck the mind' means having corrupted the mind.

119. Kathaṃ jinoti pakārapucchā. Kena jinoti kāraṇapucchā. Kena kāraṇena kena hetunā kāya paṭipattiyā jinoti pucchati. Kathanti pana kena pakārena kiṃ atītānaṃ, udāhu anāgatānaṃ paccuppannānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānena jinoti pucchati, tasmā taṃ “visajjanīya”nti vuttaṃ. Katamo jinoti kiṃ rūpaṃ jino, udāhu vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ jino. Rūpādivinimutto vā añño jino, yo “attā”ti vuccatīti imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “avisajjanīya”nti. Kittakoti pamāṇato kiṃparimāṇo.

119. 'How does one conquer?' is a question about the mode. 'By what does one conquer?' is a question about the cause. He asks: 'By what reason, by what cause, by what practice is one called a Jina?' But as to 'how,' he asks by what mode one is called a Jina—whether by the abandoning of past, or future, or present defilements. Therefore, that question is said to be 'a question to be answered.' Regarding 'Who is the conqueror?': Is form the conqueror, or are feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness the conqueror? Or is the conqueror another, liberated from form and so on, who is called 'self'? With reference to this meaning, he said it is 'a question not to be answered.' 'How much?' means: by measure, of what quantity?

Atthi [V 0.0376] tathāgatoti atthi satto. Yvāyamāyasmā “evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto”ti pañcakkhandhe upādāya paññapīyati, tassa puggalassa adhippetattā vuttaṃ “visajjanīya”nti. Rūpaṃ tathāgatoti rūpaṃ attāti sakkāyadiṭṭhivasena pucchatīti katvā vuttaṃ “avisajjanīya”nti. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

The question 'Does a Tathāgata exist?' means 'Does a being exist?'. Since this venerable one is designated as 'of such a name, of such a clan' in dependence on the five aggregates, and that person is intended, it is said to be 'a question to be answered.' Because one asks 'Is form the Tathāgata?'—which is to ask 'Is form the self?' by way of identity view—it is said to be 'a question not to be answered.' The meaning should be understood in all instances by this method.

120. Bālaṃ pīṭhasamāruḷhantiādīni sāmiatthe upayogavacanāni. Kāyena duccaritānīti kāyena duṭṭhu katāni. Olabbhantīti avalambanti avatthariyanti. Sesapadadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Olambanādiākārena hi tāni upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahatanti mahantānaṃ. Pathaviyaṃ olambantīti pathavitale pattharanti. Sesapadadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Pattharaṇākāroyeva hesa. Tatra, bhikkhave, bālassāti tasmiṃ upaṭṭhahanākāre bālassa evaṃ hoti.

120. 'A fool mounted on a seat,' and so on, are accusative expressions used in the sense of possession. 'Acts of misconduct by body' means things badly done by the body. 'They hang down' means they hang on, they cover over. The remaining two terms are synonyms for that. For those kamma-signs and destiny-signs appear in the manner of hanging down, etc.; therefore it is said thus. 'Great' means of the great ones. 'They hang down on the earth' means they spread over the surface of the earth. The remaining two terms are synonyms for that. For this is indeed the manner of spreading. 'Therein, bhikkhus, for a fool' means: when that mode of appearance is present, for a fool, displeasure arises thus.

Lābhā [M 0.0261] vo, bhikkhaveti bhikkhave, ye ime tumhehi paṭiladdhā manussattasaddhāpaṭilābhādayo, lābhā vo tumhākaṃ lābhā eva. Suladdhanti yampidaṃ pabbajitvā catupārisuddhisīlādisampādanaṃ laddhaṃ, tampi suladdhaṃ. Khaṇo vo paṭiladdhoti aṭṭhaakkhaṇavajjito navamoyaṃ khaṇo paṭiladdho maggabrahmacariyavāsāya. “Diṭṭhā mayā”tiādinā ekadesanidassanena aṭṭha akkhaṇe vibhāveti.

Regarding 'Gain is yours, monks': Monks, these things obtained by you, such as the attainment of human existence and faith, are a gain for you, truly a gain. Regarding 'Well-gained': that which has been gained by going forth, the accomplishment of the fourfold purity of virtue and so on, that too is well-gained. Regarding 'An opportunity has been gained by you': this moment of a Buddha's appearance, the ninth opportunity which is devoid of the eight inopportune moments, has been obtained for the purpose of dwelling in the path, the holy life. By means of the partial indication beginning, 'I have seen,' he explains the eight inopportune moments.

121. Yahiṃ yahinti yaṃ yaṃ duggatiṃ yo gacchati. So naṃ adhammoti yo adhammo tena carito, so naṃ adhammacāriṃ puggalaṃ. Hanātīti bādhati.

121. Regarding 'Whatever, whatever': whatever bad destination a person goes to. Regarding 'That unrighteousness harms him': the unrighteousness that was practiced by him, that unrighteousness harms that person, the practitioner of unrighteousness. 'Harms' means it afflicts.

Appesakkhatāti appānubhāvatā. Dubbaṇṇatāti virūpatā bībhacchatā. Duppaññatāti nippaññatā ahetukapaṭisandhivasena eḷamūgatā.

'Being of little influence' means having little power. 'Having a bad complexion' means deformity, loathsomeness. 'Having little wisdom' means lack of wisdom; by way of a rootless rebirth-linking, it is the state of being driveling or mute.

122. Vācānurakkhīti catunnaṃ vacīduccaritānaṃ parivajjanena vācānurakkhī. Abhijjhādīnaṃ anuppādanena manasā suṭṭhu saṃvuto. Pāṇātipātādayo pajahanto kāyena ca akusalaṃ na kayirā, ete tayo kammapathe visodhaye. Evaṃ visodhento hi sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ esakehi buddhādīhi isīhi paveditaṃ ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ ārādheyyāti. Dukkaṭanti kāyena vācāya manasā ca dukkaṭaṃ sāvajjaṃ dukkhudrayaṃ duggatisaṃvattaniyaṃ kammaṃ yassa natthi. Saṃvutaṃ tīhi [V 0.0377] ṭhānehīti etehi tīhi kāraṇehi kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ pavesanivāraṇato pihitaṃ, taṃ ahaṃ “brāhmaṇa”nti vadāmīti.

122. Regarding 'Guarding speech': one should guard speech by avoiding the four kinds of verbal misconduct. One should be 'well-restrained in mind' by not giving rise to covetousness and so on. Abandoning killing and so on, 'with the body one should not do what is unwholesome.' 'One should purify these three paths of action.' For by thus purifying them, one may accomplish the Noble Eightfold Path proclaimed by the sages, such as the Buddhas, who are seekers of the aggregates of virtue and so on. Regarding 'one for whom there is no wrongdoing': one for whom there is no kamma done badly by body, speech, or mind—which is blameworthy, has suffering as its result, and leads to a bad destination. Regarding 'restrained in the three places': by these three causes, one is closed off by preventing the entry of bodily misconduct and so on. Such a one I call a 'brahmin'.

Accantadussīlyanti ekantadussīlabhāvo. Gihī vāpi jātito paṭṭhāya dasa akusalakammapathe karonto, pabbajito vāpi upasampannadivasato paṭṭhāya garukāpattiṃ āpajjamāno accantadussīlo nāma. Idha pana yo dvīsu tīsu attabhāvesu dussīlo, tassa gatiyā āgataṃ dussīlabhāvaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Dussīlabhāvoti cettha dussīlassa cha dvārāni nissāya uppannā taṇhā veditabbā. Māluvā sālamivotthatanti yassa puggalassa taṃ taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyaṃ. Yathā nāma māluvā sālaṃ otthataṃ deve vassante pattehi udakaṃ paṭicchitvā saṃbhañjanavasena sabbatthakameva pariyonandhati, evaṃ attabhāvaṃ otthataṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ [M 0.0262] so māluvāya saṃbhañjitvā bhūmiyaṃ pātiyamāno rukkho viya tāya dussīlyasaṅkhātāya taṇhāya saṃbhañjitvā apāyesu pātiyamāno, yathā naṃ anatthakāmo diso icchati, tathā attānaṃ karoti nāmāti attho.

“Utter immorality” means the state of being completely immoral.
